units.la: AN Indignaberis, Proc. Excell. quòd mea hæc Philosophia, de summis, hoc est Reip. curis te hodie vocatum, in ludicram ingenij arenam ducat; Nomenq; tuum, lauris, palmisque, ac triumphis onustum, sibi ad æternum decus, & victoriæ fiduciam inscribat? Hortabar ego, ut nimis grandem compesceret ausum; sed illa gestiens, & novo quodam tripudio exultans, ne minimùm se passa teneri, de schola, de manimanibus, de visu lapsa, in Regia, nempe Valeria Domo, te conuènit, exorauit, suiq; certaminis Præsidem huc felici omine traxit. Iam verò ades; & vtinam sic Aristotelé inuenires tuum, qui nouus Macedo in spem triumphandi tam bene ades. Iam prees; & vtinam sic Platonem haberes tuum, qui Dionysius alter ad virtutis laudem in schola prees. Iam sedes; & vtinam sic Senecam audires tuum, qui Venetus Cæsar pro augendis Philosophiæ coronis hoc loco sedes. Verùm quod nostra tenuitas non facit, hoc à te sperat Gymnastica Pallas, in quo vno mirum est, quot præsidia, quot laudes, quot ferta, quot dignitates, & decora, virtute, nomine, fatisq; tuis praefignata, sese habituram confidat. Si liberi, quidem paucis autem Siluester hoc reuera nomen est, quod syl-uam implet encomiorum. Valerius non aliunde maioris pretij valor, quàm ex hoc titulo venit. Procurator laus videtur eximia, eo murice nitere, quo soli Heroes in tua Rep. fulgent. Bertuccij Filius nil poterat fortuna largiri maius, quàm Patrem habere illum, in quo Venetus Leo subnixus Throno alterum sustinuit Salomonem. Equesg Germaniae, Hispaniaeque, hinc re-cordamur Legationem, qua-nuper ad Margaritam Mariam uxorem functus es. Quid vero in ea, siue à Senatu cum decernitur, siue à te dum suscipitur, vel à nobis cum laudatur, non mirum, non prodigiosum, non superbum occurrit? Videtur ob oculos adhuc versari apparatus, quem Brixiae dabas in conspectum. En tibi currus innumeri senis equis trahuntur. Qui autem currus? rotae, axes, columnae aureis nitent sculpturis; laminae, clauique solido rigent argento; cortinae, ac sellae pretiosa textura rigescunt. Quid etiam equi? nam aurea mandunt fræna, gerunt ephippia vnionibus texta, falleras acupictas demittunt, surriguntur
units.tr: Will you be indignant, Most Excellent Procurator, that this my Philosophy has drawn you, today summoned to the highest cares, that is, the cares of the Republic, into the playful arena of wit, and has inscribed your name, laden with laurels, palms and triumphs, upon itself, for its own everlasting glory and its confidence of victory? I urged it to curb so bold an undertaking. But she, eager and exulting in a new kind of dance of joy, would not let herself be held back in the least. Slipping out of the school, out of the hands of her students and out of sight, she made her way to the palace, namely the Valerian House. She met you, begged you, and with a fortunate omen drew you hither as the President of her contest. Come now. Would that you had Aristotle as your own, for he, like a new Macedonian, is so well present to hopes of triumph. Now stand forth. Would that you had Plato as your own, for he, like another Dionysius, presides in the school for the praise of virtue. Now take your seat. Would that you heard Seneca as your own, for he, as the Venetian Caesar, sits in this place to enlarge the garlands of philosophy. But what our slenderness cannot do, gymnastic Pallas hopes to obtain from you. In this one thing it is remarkable how many protections, how many praises, how many garlands, how many dignities and honours, foreshadowed by your virtue, your name and your destiny, she trusts she will receive. To speak frankly, though briefly, Silvester is indeed a name that fills a whole forest of encomiums. The worth of Valerius derives its greater value from no other source than this title. Procurator seems an outstanding distinction; you shine in that purple by which only heroes shine in your Republic. As Bertuccio's son, fortune could bestow nothing greater than to have had that father, on whom the Venetian Lion, resting on his throne, leaned and supported a second Solomon. And as a knight of Germany and Spain, we recall the embassy which you lately discharged to Margaret Maria, his wife. What in it, whether when it is decreed by the Senate, or when it is undertaken by you, or when it is praised by us, does not strike one as wonderful, prodigious or ostentatious? The equipage that you displayed to view at Brescia still seems to be before our eyes. Behold, countless carriages are drawn for you by six horses each. And what carriages! The wheels, axles and pillars shine with golden carvings; the plates and nails stand stiff with solid silver; the curtains and seats are stiff with precious weaving. And the horses? For they champ golden bridles, wear saddle-cloths woven with pearls, let down embroidered trappings, and hold their necks high,

units.la: [illegible, ~6 letters] collo, despumant ore, quatiunt pedibus terram,sentiunt ipsi ornatum suum, & superbiunt. Quotus vero Aulæ tuæ prorsus Regiæ ordo est? alter Nobilium, qui ad vrbana eruditi officia hærent: Miniftrorum alter, qui fecundis muneribus devouentur: poftremus aurigantium, & pediffequorum, qui minùs digna exequentes, famulatum complent. Hos autem omnes, & serico, & purpura, & auro vestis, vt vel in eo tuaniteat munificentia, quòd ij etiam pretiosè teguntur, à quibus pretia contemni debent. Sed quantum decoris auget circumfusa Equitum phalanx, quæ Venetijs Pa- tauio tauio, Vincentia, Verona, Bergomo, cæterisq; vrbibus, multa, diues, pulchra conuenientia, in eo facit rixam, vt quisque tibi placeat magis; creditq; placere, si ditiori vestiatur amictu; ditiùs vestiri, si pluriuni ferat annorum gazas; & has etiam ferre, si thesauros profundat, vnumquemque te, omnino aureum, omnino gemmeum, omnino pretiosum imitetur. Hac tanta pompa Margaritam Marliam de Mediolanensi Prouincia egressam excipis, tuæ traditam fidei equitatu cingis, & splendidè tutam ad Germaniæ cōfinia ducis. Annon adhuc miraris plausum, qui lætissimo tubarum fragore augetur? iubilum, quod iactis per aerem facibus ingeminatur? famam, quae vbique repetito muralis machinae strepitu euulgatur? frequentiam, quae accurrentibus vndique accolis, per vicos, per castra, per vrbes confusa letitia stipatur? Adeo sane, vt ore suo Imperatrix Margarita confessa sit, se non potuisse Venetae Reip. Maiestatem habere melius conspectam, quam in Valerio, quem gazae omnes, fortuna, honor, triumphi, gentiumq; studia comitantur. Haec omnia hisce oculis videbam ego, & mirabar, cum inter caeteros me quoq; Legationis tuae asseclam, pro eximia, qua fleKteris, humanitate, blandiq; ingenij dulcedine acceptum volueris. Quid vero tantis rependam honoribus? Enimvero si de alieno dederim; hoc fortasse te dignius erit, sed ipsi mihi non satisfaciam. Si de meo; æquum hoc est, sed tuis meritis omnino impar. Facia consultius. Quod tuum est, do libens: hanc nimirum Philosophici cursus opellam, quæ tuis nata sub auspicijs, adeo prosperè visa est adolescere, ut de cunis migrarit statim ad thronum. Accipis? non amplius exigua est. Foues? non amplius indiga est. Tueris? non amplius meticulosa est. Felix erumpit in lucem; &, velim ego, nolimus, se tuam facit. Neque id veneratione
units.tr: [illegible] neck, they froth at the mouth, stamp the ground with their feet, feel their own adornment and grow proud. But how small a part of your truly royal Court is this rank! One part is of the nobles, who are trained for urban duties; another of the ministers, who are devoted to fruitful offices; the last of the charioteers and footmen, who, performing less worthy tasks, fill out the service. Yet all of these are clothed in silk, purple and gold, so that your generosity may shine forth even in this, that those too are richly covered, by whom riches ought to be despised. But how much grace is added by the surrounding Equitum phalanx, which has gathered from Venice, Patauio [Padua], Vicenza, Verona, Bergamo and the other cities, many, rich and handsome, and which creates such rivalry that each wishes to please you more; each believes he pleases if he is clad in a richer cloak, is clothed more richly if he carries the treasures of many years, and carries them if he lavishes his wealth, so that each imitates you, wholly golden, wholly gemmed, wholly precious. With this great pomp you receive Margaritam Marliam [Margaret Marlia], who has come out from the province of Milan, entrusted to your faith; you surround her with a cavalry escort and splendidly lead her, safe, to the borders of Germany. Do you still marvel at the applause, which is increased by the most joyful blare of trumpets? At the jubilation, redoubled by torches thrown through the air? At the fame, spread everywhere by the repeated din of the wall-engines? At the crowd, which, with neighbours rushing in from every side, is pressed through villages, camps and cities in confused gladness? So much so that Imperatrix Margarita [Empress Margaret] herself confessed that she could not have seen the majesty of the Venetae Reip. [Venetian Republic] better displayed than in Valerio [Valerius], whom all treasures, fortune, honour, triumphs and the favour of nations accompany. I saw all these things with my own eyes and wondered, when you were pleased, out of your remarkable and charming kindness, to receive me too, among the others, as an attendant of your embassy. But what shall I repay for such great honours? If I give from what is another's, that will perhaps be more fitting for you, but I shall not satisfy myself. If I give from what is my own, that is fair, but wholly unequal to your merits. Let me act more wisely. What is yours I give gladly: this little work of the philosophical course, which, born under your auspices, has been seen to grow so prosperously that it has passed at once from the cradle to the throne. Do you accept it? It is no longer small. Do you foster it? It is no longer needy. Do you protect it? It is no longer timid. Fortunate, it bursts into the light, and whether I wish it or not, it makes itself yours.

units.la: magis, quàm ambitione vincendi; nam Aquila tua, quæ sibi Germanicam, Hispanicamque associauit, non vnum dabit fulmen, quo dimicet; non exiguam coronam, qua triumphet; non tenues alas, quàrum ope feratur ad gloriā. Deniq; dabit nomen Valerium: quid plura? cedite campum, laurum, triumphum. Victoria meæ Palladis est.
units.tr: not so much from reverence as from a desire to win. For your Eagle, which has joined to itself the German and the Spanish (eagles), will not give a single thunderbolt with which to fight, nor a small crown in which to triumph, nor slender wings by whose help it may be carried up to glory. Finally, it will give the name Valerius. What more need be said? Yield the field, laurel and triumph. The victory belongs to my Pallas.

units.la: AD LECTOREM.
units.tr: TO THE READER.

units.la: PAruulam habes Philosophiam, Bone Lector, sed fortasse non respuendam. Scis enim, illud esse, tam naturæ, quàm artis ingenium, vt quidquid melius est, in exiguis condat. Certè nostra tenuitas nil habet exactius, quod in vno vix lapsi anni decursu elaborauerit. Sed qualecumque hoc sit, vel me reclamante, in publicum exit. Sic prorsus licuit Dilectissimo inter discipulos D. MARCO BEMBO. Hic Adolescens, ingenio, & studio maximus operarum à se conscriptam in vulgus mittit. Prius tamen cum eo pacisceba, vt libelltherefore inscriberet epigraphe: Ad vsum studiosæ Iuuentutis. Inde intelligis, destinari ad Philosophiam nouitios quod non sine rubore in manus iret Sapientum. Sin vero & ad hos casu venerit, nil magis habebit in votis, quàm vt corrigatur. Sic ego morem Apelli geram: Quidquid ceteri arguerint, audiam sub tabula, & meliorem veritatis colorem Philosophiæ reponam.
units.tr: You have here a little Philosophy, kind Reader, but perhaps one not to be scorned. For you know that it is the nature of things, as of art, that whatever is better is stored up in small compass. Surely our slenderness has nothing more finished, which it has laboured over in the course of barely a single year. But whatever sort it is, it goes out to the public even though I protest. In this way it was indeed permitted to our most beloved DOMINUS MARCUS BEMBUS among his pupils. This young man, greatest in talent and zeal, sends into the world the work he has written. Yet first he bargained with me that the little book should be inscribed with the title: For the use of studious youth. From this you may understand that it is intended for beginners in philosophy, lest it come, not without a blush, into the hands of the wise. But if by chance it reaches these too, it will have nothing more in its wishes than to be corrected. Thus I will humour the manner of Apelles: whatever the others argue, I will listen to from behind the picture, and I will put in place a better colour of philosophical truth.

units.la: ICeat iam in ipso Doctrinæ vestibulo frontem componere ad hilaritatem, & subito gaudio mentem afflante, vos hodierna luce hilarius, quàm vnquam salutare, Nobilissimi Auditores. Macte animo pubes optima, & quam in Logicæ sterilitate hucusque pupugit labor, in melioris amœnitatem studij, Philosophia Naturalis excipiat. Hæc videlicet sinum aperit, si aliqua maris procella iactauit; diem accendit, si aliqua nox vmbram affudit; ver pingit lætissimum, si aliqua hyems tristissimâ facie perterruit. Me quoque tædebat, indolem vestram tandiu premi sub morosa Dialecticæ cura (ne dicam quod nonnemo, sub rigida Nouercæ ferula) sed animo tandem absceßit mæror, cùm pia Mater natura gremium ad blanditias factum explicuit. Hoc enim mutero theatrum est, in quo Mundi elementa migrant in scenas, & vel subinde, vel vna simul eductis ad intuitum spectaculis, tædium nobis diuturnæ vitæ leuat, dum recreat. Quindi recreet multus adeo cælestium corporum ignis, ibi vagus in pha-
units.tr: Let me now compose my face for cheerfulness at the very threshold of the doctrine, and let a sudden joy stir the mind. Gentlemen, students, you are today more cheerful than ever, and more fortunate. Take heart, best youth. Natural Philosophy now receives you, after the labour you have endured so far amid the barrenness of Logic, into the pleasantness of a better pursuit. Surely this opens a harbour if some storm of the sea has tossed you; it kindles the day if some night has cast its shadow; it paints a most joyful spring if some winter has frightened you with its gloomy face. I too was distressed that your natural gifts were held down so long under the peevish care of Dialectic (I will not say, as someone has, under the stern rod of a stepmother). But the sorrow has at last been driven from your minds, since kindly Mother Nature has opened her lap, made for caresses. For this is the theatre in which the elements of the world move onto the stage, and, now bringing forward spectacles one after another or all together, they relieve the tedium of a long life while they refresh us. Here, then, let the many fires of the heavenly bodies refresh you: here one wandering as a planet, there one fixed in a star; the Moon gentle, the Sun fierce, Venus golden, Saturn leaden.

units.la: A planeta, illic fixus in astro, in Luna mitis, in Sole acer, aureus in Venere, in Saturno plumbeus? Visum demitte: Quot in aere phaenomena ludunt? sese vapor in nubes adglomerat, in rorem dispergit, in pluuias effundit. Exhalatio nonne vt fax micat? vt capra saltat? vt farua bacchatur? Nil eà validius, cum ventus est; nil eà velocius, cum fulgur est; nil eà horridius, cum fulmen est. Anne roscidam loquar Iridem, quae multicolor in aere pingitur, & oculos vt feriat, in arcum, vel Nuncia pacis, armatur? Globum inspice terraqueum, & stupe. Cur hic statà lege nostra littora linquit mare, ac redeunte in ripas æstu, semet resorbet? Vnde salsedo, quae aquam, si nimia torpeat malacia, tamquam adsperso medicamine, à corruptione tuetur? Quae vis ab imo eructat fluctus, & scopulorum illisos cautibus frangit? Quòdsi placeat rerum in mari latentium series, virtutes, varietates nancisci, poterit quis non vnam ad clepsydram de aquae miraculis perorare. An fatis erit, si ea, quae fert suo gremio Terra, physico intuitu peruestigemus? Illa Protheus est, gaudetque per nouas effectuum vices humanam morari curiositatem. En vt assurgit in montes, vnde flammarum, cinerumque globos non raro emittit, quamquam niue circum affusa rigescant. En vt latam porrigitur in planitiem, vbi vel artis industria, vel ingenio suo enatae stirpes, medicamina pingunt in floribus, & frondes erudiunt ad fructus. En vt syluefcit in nemora,& illic bestias ad securi- tatem recipiendo, alias conuestiæ plumis, vngue armat, rostroque, vt procul auolent, ac rapto viuant: alias in ventrem pronas effingit, pellibus tegit, pede multiplici fulcit: alijs frontem in cornua rumpit, armosque ad ingum abdurat: ne sin- gulas animalium species, tam varias, tam pulchras, tam admirandas recenseam. Quid verò est sub terræ cuniculis, quod Antiquæ Parentis viscera vrget, conceptoque spiritu quatit, lacerat, subruit, vnde lares, vrbes, vastæque regiones repentina ingluuie sorbentur? Vndenam vis auri, argenti, gemmarum, quibus ruinas redimit suas natura, cum hæc omnia de ruderibus, petrarumque scissuris vltro, & sine auatorum solicitudine persæpe mittat, vt non pigeat impensæ ad eam resarciendam, si aliquando se laceraverit. Ea, & innumera prorsus alia educit in scenam. Natura, ne sui fructum perdat, inquit Stoicus de otio sapientis c.32. si tam magna, tam præclara, tam subtiliter dicta, tam nitida, non uno in genere formosa, solitudini ostenderet. Eaque sunt, quibus physici totam debent impendere curam, studium, curiositatem, vt quod in acutis, hoc est plerumque vanitate plenis Logicæ quæstiunculis, tempus contriuerunt, aliquo cum fœnore tandem redimere possint.
units.tr: Turn your eyes away from these. How many phenomena play in the air? Vapour gathers itself into clouds, is scattered into dew, and pours out in rains. Does not an exhalation flash like a torch? Does it not leap like a goat, rage like a frenzied woman? Nothing is more violent than the wind, nothing swifter than lightning, nothing more dreadful than the thunderbolt. Shall I speak of the dewy Iris, who is painted in many colours in the air and, to strike the eyes, is armed as a bow, or as the Messenger of peace? Look upon the terraqueous globe and be amazed. Why does the sea, by a fixed law, leave its shores, and, when the tide returns to the banks, draw itself back again? Whence the saltness which, as if by a sprinkled remedy, protects the water from corruption when a too-great calm makes it stagnant? What force belches up waves from the depths and breaks them, dashed against the rocks? If one wishes to pursue the series, the virtues and varieties of the things hidden in the sea, anyone could deliver a whole lecture on the wonders of water without ever coming to the water-clock. Or will it be enough if we investigate by a physical gaze what the Earth bears in her bosom? She is a Proteus, and she delights in holding human curiosity by new changes of effects. See how she rises into mountains, whence she not infrequently sends out globes of flames and ashes, though they are surrounded by snow and grow stiff with cold. See how she stretches out into a wide plain, where plants grown either by the industry of art or by their own nature paint remedies in their flowers and train their leaves to fruit. See how she grows into woods and there, receiving beasts for safety, arms some with feathers and plumage, with claws and beak, so that they may fly far off and live by plunder; others she shapes prone on their bellies, covers with skins, and supports on many feet; others she breaks the forehead into horns and hardens the shoulders for the yoke. I need not enumerate the individual species of animals, so varied, so beautiful, so admirable. What, indeed, is that beneath the tunnels of the earth which presses on the viscera of the Ancient Parent, shakes them when the breath is conceived, tears and undermines them, and by which household gods, cities and vast regions are swallowed in a sudden gulp? Whence comes the power of gold, silver and gems, with which Nature redeems her ruins, since she so often sends all these from rubble and cracks of rocks of her own accord, without the anxiety of miners, so that one need not grudge the expense of repairing her if she has ever torn herself. These and countless other things she brings onto the stage. Nature, lest she lose the fruit of herself, says the Stoic in his book on the leisure of the wise, chapter 32, if she showed things so great, so splendid, so subtly made, so bright, so beautiful in more than one kind, to solitude. These are the things to which natural philosophers must devote their whole care, study and curiosity, so that they may at last recover with some interest the time they have spent on the subtle little questions of Logic, which are for the most part full of emptiness.

units.la: Verum heu pessima Philosophiæ nostræ conditio! in eam se intrusit commi- nicendi Amor, & Veritatis personam induens, plerique hominum partim fœdiffimè imponit. Siquidem ab eo tempore, quo Ariftotelis libri ex Hispanijs per Europam delati suñt, ingeniosi quidam nimia capti subtilitatis ambitione (vt enim pater filios, ita quà quisque suo marte gignit,plus amat) cæperunt in mentis acumine sibi placere, donec abiectà ipsius Naturæ contemplatione, id solum habuerunt curę, vt sensibilem, ac proinde magis certam perderent Philosophiam. Idcirco poterit quis cum Ariftotele repertre quod refert Strobeus serm.20.de Sap. Huiusmodi pseudophilologos, reiecta Philosophia, similes esse procis Penelopes, qui cum ipsa potiri non possent, ancillis miscebantur. Ex quo nil mirum si fœtus gignuntur indecori vultus, & Reginæ matris, quæ Veritas est, notas non referunt, nam plebeio ex connubio filij quoque non nobiles exoriuntur. Hæ sunt opiniones illæ de priuatione, inceptione, desitione, de formacadauerica, de causa vaga, de possibili, & similibus, quas Metaphysicus phantasia sua confingit, ac in ordinem naturæ violenter intrusas tanto clamore tuetur, vt Iupiter ipse apud Lucianum excusef se, vocem supplicis Timonis non exaudire, præ clamore Philosophorum, qui nugas in terra deblaterant, ac verba mortulium interpellant. Inde fit, vt cum studijs huiusmodi ceperint nonnulli iuuenes dare operam, arbitrentur, se crucibus pene suffigi; nec immerito, nam quid molestius, quam profiteri philosophiam, quæ multu
units.tr: But alas, the worst condition of our Philosophy! Into it has crept the Love of inventing, assuming the person of Truth, and most shamefully deceives most men in part. For from the time when the books of Aristotle were carried through Europe from Spain, certain clever men, captivated by an excessive ambition for subtlety (for as a father loves his sons, so each one loves more what he begets by his own strength), began to take pleasure in the sharpness of their minds, until, neglecting the contemplation of Nature herself, they cared only to lose sensible and therefore more certain Philosophy. Hence one may find with Aristotle what Stobaeus reports in Sermon 20 on Wisdom: Such pseudo-philologists, having rejected Philosophy, are like the suitors of Penelope, who, since they could not win her, consorted with her maids. From this it is no wonder that offspring are born of unseemly face, and do not bear the marks of their queen mother, who is Truth; for from a plebeian marriage the children too are born ignoble. These are those opinions about privation, inception, cessation, the cadaverous form, the vague cause, the possible, and similar things, which the Metaphysician invents from his own fancy, and defends with such great clamour when they are violently thrust into the order of nature, so that Jupiter himself, in Lucian, excuses himself for not hearing the voice of the suppliant Timon, because of the clamour of the Philosophers, who babble trifles on the earth and interrupt the words of the dead. Hence it happens that when some young men have begun to devote themselves to studies of this kind, they think they are being nailed almost to crosses; and not without reason, for what is more troublesome than to profess a philosophy which has much

units.la: Ra habeat spinositatis,& parum fructus? Nö est postea mirandum, si tam facile conqueratur Moralis Philosophus nat. qu. I. 7. c. vltimo. Quis Philosophiam, aut vllum liberale respicit studium, nisi cum ludi intercalantur, cum aliquis pluuius interuenit dies, quem perdere licet? Nequeunt enim adolescentes ea studia tolerare diu, quæ difficilia sunt, præsertim si amænitate nulla condiantur.
units.tr: thorniness and little fruit? It is no wonder, then, that the moral philosopher complains so readily in the last chapter of Book 7 of the Natural Questions: Who looks to Philosophy or to any liberal study, except when school holidays intervene, when some rainy day comes which one may waste? For young men cannot long endure those studies which are difficult, especially if they are seasoned with no pleasantness.

units.la: Proinde vt Discipuli mei sint frequentes in gymnasio, & rerum naturalium disquisitioni libenti animo studeant, in ea cura totus ero, vt meliora seligam, & magis Philosopho digna. Speculationibus non vtar, nisi ad veritatis indagationem. Ea, quæ leuioris momenti erunt, breuissimè absoluam. Quoties aderit materia nobilis, vt in tractatu de motu, de cœlo, de anima, de meteoris, & huiusmodi, non ita sobrie agam. Et quod maxima res est in Philosophia, nulli auctori me ita credam, vt ab eo non sim recessurus, cùm id ratio postulauerit. Quare non ero prorsus Aristoteli addictus, quemadmodum ij, qui eum Sanctè colunt, præsertim quia Philosophus ipse hoc suadet l. 1. Eth. c. 6. vbi ait, Melius videri sua quoque refellere pro salute veritatis; nam cum ambo sint amici, sanctum est veritate præferre. Quò igitur vocabit ratio, experientia, veritas; eò me conferam, debet enim liber esse intellectus, non captiuus. Et sicuti cometes certam non habet viam, inquit Seneca nat. qu. 7. c. 21. Sed quo illum vena pabuli sui fui duxit,illò repit; simili modo mens nostra non sequetur ductum vnius tantùm auctoris, verùm à pluribus ea colliget, quæ sapunt magis, & nutriunt. Ad hoc ipsum hortatur Clem.Alex.l.3.Strom. inquiens, non peculiarem debere sectam eligi; nam quidquid Stoici, Piatonici, Epicurei, Aristotelei dixerunt, hoc totum seletum dicit esse philosophiam. Præcipuè verò duo Fontes erunt, ex quibus deriuabitur Doctrina nostra; & ij quidem vberrimi, Aristoteles nimirum, & Democritus, quorum opiniones afferentur singillatim, examinabuntur, & quod melius fuerit, seligetur. Sic fiet, quemadmodum arbitror, vt Philosophia Nostra placeat ijs, qui nolunt contemni Aristotelem, & ijs etiam, qui hac tempestate Democritum excitant de sepulchris. Iuuat autem hoc loco statim innuere ordinem, quo totum Doctrinæ opus digeri debet. Sit ergo
units.tr: Therefore, so that my pupils may be frequent in the school and may study the inquiry into natural things with a willing mind, I shall be wholly intent on choosing the better things, and those more worthy of a philosopher. I shall not use speculations except for the investigation of truth. Those things which are of lesser importance I shall dispatch very briefly. Whenever a noble subject arises, as in the treatise on motion, on the heavens, on the soul, on meteors and things of that kind, I shall not proceed so soberly. And, which is the greatest thing in Philosophy, I shall not so trust any author that I shall not depart from him when reason requires it. Hence I shall not be wholly bound to Aristotle, as those who worship him reverently are, especially since the Philosopher himself advises this in Book 1 of the Ethics, chapter 6, where he says: It seems better to refute even one's own opinions for the sake of truth; for since both are friends, it is holy to prefer truth. Therefore wherever reason, experience and truth call, there I shall betake myself; for the mind ought to be free, not a captive. And just as a comet has no fixed path, as Seneca says in Natural Questions 7, chapter 21: but wherever the vein of its fuel has led it, there it creeps; in like manner our mind will not follow the guidance of one author only, but will gather from many those things which taste better and nourish more. Clement of Alexandria urges this very thing in Book 3 of the Stromata, saying that no peculiar sect ought to be chosen; for whatever the Stoics, Platonists, Epicureans and Aristotelians have said, this whole selection he says is philosophy. Above all, however, there will be two most abundant Fountains from which our doctrine will be drawn: namely Aristotle and Democritus. Their opinions will be set forth one by one, examined, and what is better will be chosen. So it will come about, as I think, that our Philosophy will please those who do not wish Aristotle to be despised, and also those who in these times are raising Democritus from the tombs. It is now helpful to indicate at this point the order in which the whole work of the doctrine ought to be arranged. Let it be therefore:

units.la: ordinem
units.tr: the order

units.la: Aristoteles nimirum, & Democritus, quorum opiniones afferentur singillatim.
units.tr: Namely Aristotle and Democritus, whose opinions will be set forth one by one.

units.la: PHILOSOPHIÆ NATVRALIS
units.tr: NATURAL PHILOSOPHY

units.la: Oeconomia.
units.tr: Arrangement

units.la: Distribuetur Philosophia nostra in quatuor partes. Prima continebit octo Physicorum libros, hoc ferè ordine. In primo quænam, & quot sint Principia rerum compositiua statuemus. Compositio autem fit per influxus causarum, vnde in secundo libro dicetur de Causis, maximè verò efficiente, quandonam, & quomodo influat; quid requirat, vt operetur, & generet. Sed antequam generatio fiat, solet causa præmittere dispositiones, quæ alterant materiam, & ideo in tertio libro agetur de Alteratione, de qualitatibus, de actione per sympathiam, antipathiam, contagionem, antiperistasim &c. Vbi expleta est actio alterationis, gignitur, & manet naturale compositum; igitur in quarto libro examinabitur Generatio, & quid maneat in genito, quæ partes, quæ materiæ: Vlteriùs quia hoc etiam corrumpitur, disquiremus quomodo fiat naturalis mixti Corruptio. Cùm verò totum compositum, siue partes, in quas resoluitur, sint quantæ, ac extensæ, disputabitur in quinto libro de Quantitate. Quod est quantum, potest localiter moueri, & sic in sexto fiet inquisitio de Motu, eiusque speciebus. Habet verò motus pro termino locum, vnde annectetur statim doctrina de Loco. Deinde que à motu, & loco ascendemus ad Primum Motorem, seu Causam Primam, cuius existentia ex hisce naturalibus rerum effectibus per totum septimum & octauum librum ostenderur. Quæ regula etiamsi non semper omnino Aristotelis ort dinem, congruens tamen Naturæ, atque Doctrinæ ordini est.
units.tr: Our philosophy will be divided into four parts. The first will contain eight books of the Physics, in roughly this order. In the first we shall establish which principles of things are constituent, and how many there are. Composition comes about through the influence of causes, and so the second book will treat of causes, especially of the efficient cause: when and how it acts, and what it requires in order to operate and produce. But before generation takes place, the cause usually sends ahead dispositions that alter the matter. For this reason the third book will treat of alteration, of qualities, and of action through sympathy, antipathy, contagion, antiperistasis, and so on. Once the action of alteration is complete, a natural compound comes into being and remains. Accordingly, the fourth book will examine generation, and what remains in the thing generated, which parts and which matter. Since this too is subject to corruption, we shall further inquire how the corruption of a natural mixed body takes place. Since the whole compound, or the parts into which it is resolved, are quantities and extended, the fifth book will discuss quantity. What is quantified can be moved locally, and so in the sixth book an inquiry will be made into motion and its species. Motion, however, has place as its terminus, and so the doctrine of place will be attached immediately. Then, from motion and place we shall ascend to the First Mover, or First Cause, whose existence will be shown from these natural effects of things throughout the seventh and eighth books. Although this method does not always follow the order of Aristotle entirely, it nevertheless accords with the order of nature and of teaching.

units.la: Secunda Naturalis Philosophiæ pars continebit doctrinam de Mundo, quatuor libris distributam. In primo agemus de Mundo, eiusque productione in vniuersum. In secundo præcipuam illius partem consyderabimus, nempe cœlum. In tertio disputabitur de singulis elementis, igne, aere, aqua, terra; eorumque virtutes, & qualitates ad examen reducemus. In quarto agetur de meteorologicis, quæ intra elementa vbique contingunt.
units.tr: The second part of Natural Philosophy will contain the doctrine of the world, divided into four books. In the first we shall treat of the world and its production in general. In the second we shall consider its chief part, namely the heavens. In the third the individual elements will be discussed: fire, air, water, earth; and we shall examine their powers and qualities. In the fourth we shall treat of meteorological phenomena, which occur everywhere within the elements.

units.la: Tertia pars Naturalis Philosophiæ cōtinebit naturam corporis Animati. Quia vero triplex est Animatorum genus, Vegetatiuum, Sensitiuum, & Rationale, cuique suus liber assignabitur. Primus ergo respiciet Animam Vegetatiuam, & de plantis aget. Secundus verò Sensitiuam, & ibi de brutis. Tertius Rationalem, & eo loco de homine. Hisce autem accedet quartus, in quo de sensibus externis, visu, auditu, gustu, olfactu, tactu; & de internis etiam, eorumque organis modo quodam anatomico differetur. Denique ad animæ discursiuæ potentias, intellectum, memoriam, voluntatem fiet etiam excursus.
units.tr: The third part of Natural Philosophy will contain the nature of the animate body. Since there are three kinds of living things, the vegetative, the sensitive, and the rational, each will be assigned its own book. The first, then, will concern the vegetative soul and treat of plants. The second concerns the sensitive soul and there will deal with brutes. The third concerns the rational soul and there will deal with man. To these will be added a fourth, in which the external senses (sight, hearing, taste, smell, touch) and also the internal senses will be discussed, with their organs, in an anatomical manner. Finally, there will also be a survey of the discursive powers of the soul: understanding, memory, and will.

units.la: Quarta pars Philosophiæ continebit sublimiora scientiam, hoc est Metaphysi-cam, quae licet posita sit extra naturae ordinem, nihilominus habet locum post doctrinam de anima, per cuius contemplationem tota fit. Ea igitur duobus libris distribuetur. In primo excogitabitur ens in communi, & in secundo eiusdem proprietates in particulari. Faueat Deus, & rem aggrediamur.
units.tr: The fourth part of philosophy will contain the more sublime science, that is, Metaphysics, which, although it is placed outside the order of nature, nevertheless has its place after the doctrine of the soul, since the whole of it is reached through contemplation of the soul. It will therefore be divided into two books. In the first, being in general will be considered, and in the second its properties in particular. May God be gracious, and let us take the matter in hand.

units.la: PRIMA PARS PHILOSOPHIÆ NATURALIS.
units.tr: FIRST PART OF NATURAL PHILOSOPHY.

units.la: Octo Physicorum Libros complexa. Quid sit Physica.
units.tr: Comprising the eight books of Physics. What Physics is.

units.la: Graeco nomine Physis, quod Naturam significat, denominatur Physica ea disciplina, quae rerum naturalium contemplationem respicit. Seu quae considerat effectus, qui producuntur; causas, quae producunt; actiones, passiones, & similia, unum ab alio deducendo per discursum.
units.tr: From the Greek word Physis, which means Nature, the discipline that concerns the contemplation of natural things is called Physics. That is, it considers the effects that are produced, the causes that produce them, actions, passions and the like, deducing one from another by reasoning.

units.la: Ex quo tria statim edisci tis. Primum est, quod Physica dici debet Scientia. Probatur auctoritate Aristotelis, qui 6. Metaph. c. 1. dividit scientiam in Physicam, Mathematicam, & Metaphysicam. Secundo etiam ratione, quia Physica est cognitio certa, & evidens rei per causam; ergo scientia dicenda est. Patet antecedens, nam illa cognoscit v. g. mixtum naturale corrumpi, quia componitur ex contrariis: terram esse in infimo loco, quia inter elementa maximè gravis est &c. ergo Physica manet cognitio certa, & evidens rei per causam, & profunde scientia. tia. Neque obstat, quòd in ea sint plures actus incerti, obscuri, opinatiui; hoc enim ex defectu nascitur Physicorum, qui aut nimiùm, aut parùm speculando, naturam faciunt obscuram, vnde Aristotel. 2. Metaph. c. 1. ait, quòd sicuti vespertilionum oculi ad lumen diei se habent, ita & intellectus anima nostra ad ea, quae manifestissima omnium sunt.
units.tr: From this you may at once learn three things. First, that Physics ought to be called a science. This is proved by the authority of Aristotle, who in Metaphysics 6, chapter 1, divides science into Physics, Mathematics and Metaphysics. Second, it is also proved by reason: Physics is certain and evident knowledge of a thing through its cause, and therefore it is to be called a science. The antecedent is plain, for it knows, for example, that a natural mixed body corrupts because it is composed of contraries, and that earth lies in the lowest place because among the elements it is the heaviest, and so on. Therefore Physics remains certain and evident knowledge of a thing through its cause, and is truly a science. Nor is it an obstacle that in it there are several uncertain, obscure and merely opinion-based acts. For this arises from the defect of physicists, who, by speculating either too much or too little, make nature obscure. Hence Aristotle, Metaphysics 2, chapter 1, says that just as the eyes of bats are to the light of day, so is the intellect of our soul to those things which are most manifest of all.

units.la: Secundum est, quòd Physica dici debet in rigore speculatiua. Probatur auctoritate Philosophi 2. ac 3. lib. Metaph. alibique passim. Deinde ratione, quia vt vidimus in Logica, scientia speculatiua dicitur, quae manet in speculatione sui obiecti, neque pro illo efficiendo constituit regulas. Physica verò talis est, non enim dat praecepta, vt fiat ignis, aer, aqua, terra, nec docet ex illis componere mixtum, puta lignum, lapidem &c. sed cogitat solummodo quid sint elementa, quae natura mixtorum, quae causae, ac similia, vnde speculatiua tantum est. Neque dicas: à Physica discimus efficere motum, pluuias, grandines, aurum chymicum &c. ergo illa dirigit ad opus, ideoque vt practica teneri debet. Haec enim opera non fiunt ex intentione Physicae, sed ex applicatione physici, qui contendit per artem imitari naturam. Ea ratio est, nam Physica speculatur v.g. motum coeli, & hunc non docet efficere, nam in se necessarius est, neque fieri potest à nobis. At verò physicus vi-tute ea cognitione, vt consimilem ordinet motum, sicuti Archimedes in chrystalli-na. na sphæra; sed hic motus ex accidenti est, neque consideratur à Physica, verum à Physico. Quare obiectum, quod illa respicit, non considerat, vt faciat: sed vt speculetur.
units.tr: The second is that Physics ought to be called speculative in the strict sense. This is proved by the authority of the Philosopher in Metaphysics books 2 and 3, and passim elsewhere. Then it is proved by reason: as we saw in Logic, a speculative science is one that remains in the contemplation of its object and does not lay down rules for bringing it about. Physics is such a science. It does not give precepts for making fire, air, water or earth, nor does it teach how to compose a mixed body, such as wood or stone, from these. It only considers what the elements are, what the nature of mixed bodies is, what the causes are, and similar things. Hence it is purely speculative. Nor should you say: from Physics we learn to produce motion, rain, hail, chemical gold and so on; therefore it directs toward work and must be held to be practical. For these works are not done from the intention of Physics but from the application of the physicist, who strives by art to imitate nature. The reasoning holds: Physics speculates, for example, on the motion of the heavens, and does not teach how to produce it, for in itself it is necessary and cannot be made by us. But the physicist, by virtue of that knowledge, arranges a similar motion, as Archimedes did in the crystalline sphere. Yet this motion is accidental, and it is considered not by Physics but by the physicist. Therefore Physics does not consider the object it regards so as to make it, but so as to contemplate it.

units.la: Tertium est, quòd Physicæ obiectum dici debet naturale corpus, vt naturale corpus est. Probatur auctoritate Aristotelis vbicumque Physicam vocat scientiam de natura, ex quo sumitur etiam illius denominatio per verbum Physis, vt supra. Deinde probatur etiam ratione, quia illud est obiectum cuiusque scientiæ, per quod illa scientia distinguitur ab omni alia: sed per corpus naturale, vt naturale, Physica distinguitur à quauis alia scientia, ergo. Maior est certa, quemadmodum alibi constat. Probo minorem. Corpus naturale distinguit Physicam à metaphysica, quæ considerat corpus vt ens; à mathematica, quæ respicit illud vt quantum; à medicina, quæ intuetur vt sanabile &c. ergo sola Physica pro sui obiecto habet corpus naturale, vt naturale: in eo enim speculatur naturam; causas nimirum, actiones, proprietates &c. Neque opponas: etiam Astrologia respicit cælum, quod est corpus naturale, igitur non sola Physica pro sui obiecto habet corpus, vt naturale. Respondetur enim, cælum sanè respici ab astrologia, non tamen sub hac ratione quòd naturale sit, verùm sub alia, prout nimirum per astrorum nodos, configurationes, & aspectus aliquid præmostrare-, vel præsagire creditur. Quòd si aliquando Astrologia speculetur in cælo naturam, vt lumen, motum, influxum &c. tunc illa euadit pars Physicæ, quia considerat cælum, quatenus naturale corpus est. Hisce positis circa dignoscendam Physicæ Naturam, sit
units.tr: The third is that the object of Physics ought to be called natural body, as natural body. This is proved by the authority of Aristotle wherever he calls Physics the science of nature, from which its name is also taken through the word physis, as above. It is also proved by reason: the object of any science is that by which the science is distinguished from every other. But Physics is distinguished from every other science by natural body, as natural. The major premise is certain, as is established elsewhere. I prove the minor. Natural body distinguishes Physics from metaphysics, which considers body as being; from mathematics, which regards it as quantity; from medicine, which regards it as curable, and so on. Therefore Physics alone has natural body, as natural, for its object, since in it one speculates on nature, namely its causes, actions, properties and the like. Nor should you object that astrology too regards the heavens, which are a natural body; therefore Physics does not alone have body, as natural, for its object. For the answer is that the heavens are indeed regarded by astrology, but not under the aspect that they are natural; rather under another, namely insofar as through the nodes, configurations and aspects of the stars something is believed to be foreshown or foretold. But if at times astrology speculates on the heavens in respect of their nature, as light, motion, influence and so on, then it becomes a part of Physics, because it considers the heavens insofar as they are a natural body. With these things laid down for recognising the nature of Physics, let us proceed.

units.la: LIBER PRIMUS PHYSICORVM.
units.tr: BOOK ONE OF PHYSICS.

units.la: De rerum naturalium Principijs.
units.tr: On the Principles of Natural Things.

units.la: MOs fuit apud Chaldæos, Ægyptios, & Persas, occultandi arcana scientiarum, signis, figuris, & hyeroglificis, vt à vulgi oculis ea remouerent, quemadmodum ex Pierio, alijsque scriptoribus notum est. Hunc ritum secutus est Moyses, cùm libros legum non cuiq; plebeio, sed solis aperuit sacerdotibus; & Prophetæ omnes id obseruarunt, quoties locuti sunt subobscuris verbis, quorum, sensus non tam facilè capitur. Græci ergo sicuti scientias à Chaldæorum, Ægyptiorumque Magis acceperunt, sic etiam eos imitati sunt obscurè loquendo, & sub velo disciplinas celando.
units.tr: Moses was the custom among the Chaldeans, Egyptians, and Persians to conceal the secrets of the sciences under signs, figures, and hieroglyphs, so that they might keep them from the eyes of the common people, as is known from Pierius and other writers. Moses followed this custom when he entrusted the books of the laws not to every commoner but to the priests alone; and all the prophets observed it whenever they spoke in rather obscure words, whose meaning is not so easily grasped. So the Greeks, just as they received the sciences from the Magi of the Chaldeans and Egyptians, also imitated them by speaking obscurely and hiding their teachings under a veil.

units.la: Hinc tot fuere primo aspectu absurdæ sententiæ de rerum principijs. Nam, vt refert Empir. l. 3. c. 4. Thales Milesius dixit, omnia componi ex aqua, Anaximander ex infinito, Anaximenes, & Leucippus ex atomis, Empedocles ex lite, amicitia, & sphæra, Pythagoras ex numeris, & alij alia, in quorum dictis latent sanè misteria, & sésus occulti, quos quia Hipparcus Pythagoræ discipulus detegere voluit, àschola eiectus est, in eiusq; locum immobilis columna erecta fuit. Perduravit mos ille apud Stoicos, & in Aristotelis etiā gymnasio, unde Philosophus cū libros Acroamaticos euulgassèt (qua de re conquerebatur Alex.Macedo) respondit sic Regi, vt refert Gell.l.20. c.4. scito eos editos, & non editos, intelligibiles enim sunt iis solis, qui nos audierunt.
units.tr: Hence there were so many opinions about the principles of things that seem absurd at first sight. For, as Empiricus reports (Book 3, ch. 4), Thales of Miletus said that all things are composed of water; Anaximander of the infinite; Anaximenes and Leucippus of atoms; Empedocles of strife, friendship, and the sphere; Pythagoras of numbers; and others of other things. Surely hidden mysteries and secret meanings lie in their sayings, and because Hipparchus, a disciple of Pythagoras, wished to disclose them, he was expelled from the school, and in his place an immovable column was set up. That custom persisted among the Stoics and even in the lyceum of Aristotle, whence, when the Philosopher had published his Acroamatic books (a thing over which Alexander of Macedon complained), he answered the King as follows, as Gellius reports (Book 20, ch. 4): "Know that they are both published and not published; for they are intelligible only to those who have heard us."

units.la: Dictas vero iam opiniones acriter impugnat Aristoteles hoc primo Physicorum libro. Deinde subdit sententiam suam circa rerum principia, & ea statuit esse tria, Materiam, Formam, & Priuationem, quae verba quia obscura sunt, ab eo per alia explicantur, sed fortasse non magis clara, vt videbimus. In hanc sententiam Peripatetici fere omnes currunt, nullo facto examine. Quae res nec ipsi Aristoteli placeret, nam & ille obscuriores Praeceptorum suorum doctrinas respuit; vel si aliquas recepit, eaedem prius accuratè perpendit, ac diligenter examinauit.
units.tr: Aristotle, in this first book of the Physics, sharply attacks the opinions just mentioned. Then he adds his own view on the principles of things, and he holds that there are three: Matter, Form, and Privation. Since these words are obscure, he explains them by other terms, which perhaps are no clearer, as we shall see. Nearly all the Peripatetics rush into this opinion without any examination. This would not even have pleased Aristotle himself, for he too rejected the more obscure doctrines of his teachers; or if he accepted any, he first weighed them carefully and examined them diligently.

units.la: Nos ergo, qui de ore Philosophi admonemur, ipsū data opera occultasse doctrinam suam, non caeco more prehendemus quod primò occurrit, sed quae vis, qui sensus, quae significatio subiecta sit hisce vocibus, Materia, Forma, diligentiori quadam cura vestigabimus. Et hoc maximi videtur in philosophia momenti; nam vt inquit Aristoteles 12. Metaph. c.3. Difficile est ex non bene praesuppositis bene dicere. Vnde si principia sint falsa, error etiam transfunditur in ea, quae sequuntur, simili modo quo contingit in plantis, vbi s nor notæ inhærantur ad radices, eædem facilè ascendunt in ramos.
units.tr: We, then, who are warned by the Philosopher's own words that he deliberately concealed his doctrine, will not seize blindly on whatever first presents itself, but with a certain careful diligence we shall investigate what force, what sense, and what meaning underlies these words, Matter and Form. And this seems to be of the greatest importance in philosophy; for, as Aristotle says (Metaphysics 12, ch. 3), "It is difficult to speak well from premises that are not well laid down." Hence, if the principles are false, the error is also carried over into what follows, in the same way that happens with plants, where if harmful matter has taken hold at the roots, it easily rises into the branches.

units.la: Primum ergo Physicorum librum triplici disputatione diuidemus. Prima erit de Materia prima, quæ dicitur primum principium, & disquiret, an illa sit, & quid sit. Secunda verò de Forma, quæ secundum principium est. Postrema de Priuatione, quæ tertium. Quòdsi hæc principia sufficere non videbuntur, addetur Quarta Disputatio, quæ alia, & noua innuere attentabit. Sit ergo.
units.tr: We shall therefore divide the first book of the Physics into a threefold disputation. The first will concern prime Matter, which is called the first principle, and will inquire whether it exists and what it is. The second will concern Form, which is the second principle. The last will concern Privation, which is the third. But if these principles should not seem sufficient, a Fourth Disputation will be added, which will attempt to suggest other and new things. So be it.

units.la: DISPVTATIO PRIMA. De Materia Aristotelea.
units.tr: DISPUTATIO PRIMA. On Aristotle's Matter.

units.la: ETiamsi denegari non possit, aliquam esse materiam in omni corpore naturali, quæ principiû illius intrinsecè constitutiuû sit, nihilominus dubitari potest, an hæc sit illa, quam Aristoteles dicit, ac tenet. Crescit verò dubitatio, quia nō pauci, & sancti, & docti Viri putant, hoc esse merum Aristotelis commentum, & fabulam. Profectò eam irridet S. Basil. in lib. Exam. Cyrill. 1. li. confut. qui nullam dicit esse materiã, nisi elementa, vt etiam docte probat Sebastian. Basso, & Chryf. Magnenus. Parum abest Henricus Regius in suis Physicæ fundamentis c. 1. qui non aliam cognoscit materiam, quàm simplex quoddam corpus completum. Deniq; non ignobiles Philosophi tota iam Gallia, Belgioq; imò & in Italia nonnulli materiam primam, vt explicatur ab Aristotele, damnant. Propterea digna res erit sano Philosopho, inquirere de illa, vtrum sit, priusquam constituatur a nobis principium rerum. Et hoc sanè facimus, ductu Aristotelis, qui 2. Post. c. 1. docet, inquirendum esse de omni re, An sit, Quid sit, Qualis ea sit, Cuius gratia sit. Notetur ergo.
units.tr: Even though it cannot be denied that there is some matter in every natural body, which is an intrinsic constituent principle of that body, one may nonetheless doubt whether this is the matter that Aristotle describes and maintains. The doubt grows because not a few holy, learned, and distinguished men think that this is pure fabrication and fable on Aristotle's part. Indeed St. Basil mocks it in his Hexaemeron, and Cyril in the first book of his Against Julian, who says that there is no matter other than the elements, as Sebastian Basso and Chrysostom Magnenus also learnedly prove. Henricus Regius, in his Foundations of Physics, chapter 1, comes close to the same view, since he recognises no matter other than a simple, complete body. Finally, not undistinguished philosophers throughout France and Belgium, and indeed some in Italy, reject prime matter as Aristotle explains it. For this reason it will be a worthy task for a sound philosopher to inquire about it, whether it exists, before we lay down matter as a principle of things. And this we do indeed, following Aristotle, who in Posterior Analytics 2, chapter 1, teaches that everything must be investigated as to whether it is, what it is, what sort it is, and for what purpose it is. Let this be noted, then.

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA:
units.tr: FIRST DISQUISITION:

units.la: Vtrum detur materia prima Aristotelea.
units.tr: Whether there is a prime matter in the Aristotelian sense.

units.la: PRO intelligentia debet statim explicari, quid ea, & qualis ponatur ab Aristotele, vt inde concludi possit, An sit. Duplici ergo definitione vtitur Philosophus ad exponendam nobis Materiam Prima traditur 7. Metaph. c. 3, his verbis: Dico autem Materiā esse, quæ per se ipsam neq; quid, neque quantum, nec aliud quidpiam dicitur, quibus ens determinatur, est enim de quo singula horum prædicantur. Seu, quod idem est, potentia hæc omnia.
units.tr: To understand the matter, we must first explain what Aristotle means by prime matter and what kind of thing he posits it to be, so that we can then conclude whether it exists. The Philosopher therefore uses two definitions to set out prime matter for us. The first is given in Metaphysics 7, chapter 3, in these words: I say that matter is that which, in itself, is said to be neither a "what," nor a quantity, nor anything else by which being is determined; for it is that of which each of these is predicated. Or, which amounts to the same thing, matter is potentially all of these.

units.la: Sensus autem definitionis eruitur sic: Materia est substantia quædam incompleta, indeterminata, in nullo genere certa, neque ita signatæ rei posita, itaut no sit ignis, non lignum, non terra, non lapis, non aer, non aqua, non lux, non color, non quantitas, non qualitas &c. sed est omnia hæc potentia. Nimirū potest coponere ignem, si habuerit formam ignis: lignum, si genuerit formam ligni: terram, si fuerit cum forma terræ &c. Quare debet sic apprehendi. hændi materia, vt sit quidem substantia, sed illi deest aliquid intrinsecum, aliquid substantiale, aliquid completiuum. Vnde suus etiam Aristoteles eam vocat subiectum informe, deforme, inconcinnum, turpe, quod à forma expectat complementum, pulchritudinem, esse tale, determinatum &c.
units.tr: The sense of this definition is drawn out as follows. Matter is a certain incomplete and indeterminate substance, fixed in no genus, and not placed in any particular thing, so that it is not fire, not wood, not earth, not stone, not air, not water, not light, not colour, not quantity, not quality, and so on; rather it is potentially all of these. Indeed, it can constitute fire if it has the form of fire, wood if it receives the form of wood, earth if it is joined with the form of earth, and so on. Hence matter must be grasped as a substance which lacks something intrinsic, something substantial and something completing. That is why Aristotle himself calls it a formless, shapeless, unordered and base subject, which looks to the form for its completion, its beauty, and for being such and such a determinate thing.

units.la: Ex hac definitione arbitrantur aliqui materiam in se non esse aliquod ens, non habere propriam existentiam, sed existere beneficio formæ; puram esse potentiam, quæ in se non habeat actualitate; nec possit affirmatiuè cognosci aut à Philosophis, aut à Deo, vt ait D. Tho. in li. de princ. rer. nam omnis cognitio fit ad formā rei entitatiuam, & materia neq; forma est, neque in se aliquid subsistens. Deniq; hanc materiam suam Peripatetici tam faciunt exilem, tenuemque, vt penè, imò prorsus redigant ad nihil. Et vtinâ fateantur esse nihil, vt aliquādo rixandi materiam tollant.
units.tr: From this definition some think that matter is not in itself any being, does not have its own existence, but exists by the benefit of form; that it is pure potency, having no actuality in itself; and that it cannot be known affirmatively either by philosophers or by God, as St Thomas says in his book On the Principles of Things, for all knowledge is directed to the entitative form of a thing, whereas matter is neither a form nor something subsisting in itself. Finally, the Peripatetics make this matter of theirs so thin and slight that they all but, indeed utterly, reduce it to nothing. And I wish they would admit it is nothing, so that they might at last end their quarrelling over matter.

units.la: Altera materiæ definitio est positiua, & magis apta rei physicæ. Traditur ab Aristotele 1. Physic. c. 9. sic. Materia est subiectum primum vniuscuiusq; ex quo fit aliquid, cum infit, non secundum accidens, & siquid corrumpitur, in hoc abibit vltimum. Quæ verba nisi sophistice torqueantur, explicare possunt verum, physicumque materiæ conceptum.
units.tr: The second definition of matter is positive and better suited to physics. Aristotle gives it in Physics 1, chapter 9, as follows: Matter is the first subject of each thing, from which something is made, existing in it not accidentally, and into which, when a thing is destroyed, it finally passes. Unless these words are twisted by sophistry, they can explain a true and physical conception of matter.

units.la: Sensus enim eruitur sic. Materia est subiectum, quia recipit, siue vnit ad se formas, qualitates &c. Primum, quia in compositione mixtorum non est alia materia prior. Vniuscuiusque, nam in quouis compo- sito reperitur. Ex quo fit aliquid, eò quòd ex materia fit mixtum. Cum infit, quia cùm sit physica pars, debet esse intrinseca rebus. Non secundum accidens, quandoquidem essentialiter inest composito. Demum fiquid corrumpitur, in hoc abibit vltimum, nempe si mixtum corrumpatur, manent vltimò partes materiæ, vnde componebatur.
units.tr: The sense is drawn out thus. Matter is a subject, because it receives, or unites to itself, forms, qualities and so on. First, because in the composition of mixed bodies there is no other matter prior to it. Of each thing, for it is found in every composite. From which something is made, because the mixed body is made from matter. Existing in it, because, being a physical part, it must be intrinsic to things. Not accidentally, since it is essentially present in the composite. Finally, into which, when a thing is destroyed, it passes, namely, when a mixed body is corrupted, the parts of matter out of which it was composed remain at the last.

units.la: Ex hac definitione deducunt alij Peripatetici ex mente Aristotelis aliquid physicum, & aliquid fictum. Dicunt enim quòd materia est sanè pars physica, realis, entitatiua, & hoc verum est. Porro addunt, quòd illi deest substantiale complementum, & ideo nò potest exi?tere se sola, sed semper indiget forma, per quâ compleatur, adeout sine illa esse nunquâ possit, nisi de absoluta Dei potentia; imò, vt aliqui dicunt, nec per Dei potentiam. Et hoc videtur meo iudicio vanum, atque chymericum. His præmissis, notetur.
units.tr: From this definition other Peripatetics, following the mind of Aristotle, deduce that matter is partly something physical and partly something feigned. For they say that matter is indeed a physical, real and entitative part, and this is true. Further, they add that it lacks a substantial completion, and therefore it cannot exist by itself but always needs a form by which it may be completed, so that it can never be without form, except by the absolute power of God; indeed, as some say, not even by the power of God. In my judgement this is empty and chimerical. With these premises laid down, let the following be noted.

units.la: CONCLVSIO PRIMA.
units.tr: FIRST CONCLUSION.

units.la: Si materia vt in prima definitione accipitur, non est physicum principium in composito naturali.
units.tr: If matter is taken as in the first definition, it is not a physical principle in a natural composite.

units.la: PRobatur primò ex ipso Aristotele, qui 2. de gen. c. 1. ait, nullam esse materiam priorem elementis: nam si daretur, hæc non esset quanta, non calida, non frigida, nec aliquid sensibile, sed potiùs quid n. the-
units.tr: It is proved first from Aristotle himself, who in On Generation 2, chapter 1, says that there is no matter prior to the elements; for if there were, it would be neither quantified, nor hot, nor cold, nor anything sensible, but rather something mathematical, abstract, indeterminate, and so on.

units.la: thematicum ; abstractum indeterminatū, &c. Ergo ex Philosopho repugnat materia, quæ non fit nec quid, nec quale, nec quantum &c. vt in definitione dicebatur. Ac proinde aut Aristoteles contradicit sibi, aut afferendum est, materiam ab eo definitam, esse metaphysicam, & à re sensibili abstractam. Igitur vt sic non est physicum principium in compositio naturali.
units.tr: Therefore, according to the Philosopher, the matter which is neither a what, nor a quality, nor a quantity, and so on, as the definition said, is self-contradictory. Accordingly either Aristotle contradicts himself, or we must affirm that the matter defined by him is metaphysical and abstracted from sensible things. Therefore, as such, it is not a physical principle in natural composition.

units.la: Probatur secundo, & confirmatur prima ratio, quia materia, quam definit Aristoteles per negationem, aut sic definita manet aliquid, aut non: si hoc secundum, ergo nequit esse physicum principium in composito naturali. Si primum, quæritur: hoc aliquid est ne corpus, an spiritus? dici non potest, quòd sit spiritus, alio quin non esset amplius materia: sed neque dicendum est corpus, ergo nullo modo manet principium in composito. Probo minorem ex Aristotele, nam 2. de gen. c. 1. & alibi etiam impugnat eos, qui dicunt, materiam primam esse corpus, alioquin ea foret sensibilis, completa, &c. Deinde probo ratione, quia corpus cognoscitur, tangitur, videtur; materiam verò non modò nullus philosophorum percepit vnquam sensibus; verum nec ipse Deus, vt inquit supra S. Thomas, affirmatiue cognoscit. Ergo hæc materia est conceptus metaphysicus, non principium reale in composito.
units.tr: It is proved secondly, and the first argument is confirmed, because the matter which Aristotle defines by negation either remains something once so defined, or it does not. If the latter, it cannot be a physical principle in a natural composite. If the former, the question arises: is this something a body or a spirit? It cannot be said to be a spirit, for otherwise it would no longer be matter; but neither can it be said to be a body. Therefore in no way does it remain a principle in the composite. I prove the minor from Aristotle, for in On Generation 2, chapter 1, and elsewhere, he also attacks those who say that prime matter is a body, otherwise it would be sensible, complete, and so on. Next I prove it by reason: a body is known, touched, seen; but matter has never been perceived by the senses by any philosopher, nor, as St Thomas says above, is it affirmatively known even by God himself. Therefore this matter is a metaphysical concept, not a real principle in the composite.

units.la: Probatur 3. materia sic definita per negationem, à parte rei nec per Dei potentiā existere potest sè sola; & sine forma, vt mordicus Thomiste volunt, ac defendunt, ergo non est principium physicum, & reale compositi. Probo consequentiam: principium reale substantialis compositi debet esse substantia, vt de se patet (nequit enim componi substantia ex non substantijs) at ista materia talis non esset, ergo. Probo minorem. Hæc materia foret accidens, imò quid imperfectius accidente ipso: accidens enim de absoluta saltem potentia existit se solo, & sine subiecto, quemadmodum in Eucharistia: sed hoc nequit sacere materia prima: ergo hæc materia non est pars compositi substantialis, & sic neque principium physicum substantialiter componens. Manet igitur, vt sit quid metaphysicum, & ratione abstractum.
units.tr: It is proved thirdly: matter so defined by negation, in the reality of things, cannot exist by itself, not even by the power of God, and without form, as the Thomists stubbornly want and defend; therefore it is not a physical and real principle of the composite. I prove the consequence: the real principle of a substantial composite must be a substance, as is plain of itself, for a substance cannot be composed of non-substances. But this matter would not be a substance; therefore... I prove the minor. This matter would be an accident, indeed something more imperfect than accident itself: for an accident, at least by absolute power, exists by itself and without a subject, as in the Eucharist; but prime matter cannot do this. Therefore this matter is not a part of a substantial composite, and so neither is it a physical principle substantially composing. It remains, then, that it is something metaphysical and conceived by reason alone.

units.la: Probatur quarto, nam si materia prima non est quid metaphysicum, & sola ratione conceptum, ergo independenter ab opere intellectus, & à parte rei habet existere suum. Hoc posito, quæro: vel materia hoc suum esse habet à forma, vel à se: si secundum, ergo existit in se, ac propterea est quid certum, signatum, determinatum, quantum (non enim a parte rei datur ens vagum, indeterminatum &c. vnde ob hanc rationem in Logica negatum est vniuersale dari extra intellectum, quia nequit à parte rei esse aliquid sine vltima sui differentia.) Si autem recipit materia suum esse à forma, ergo cum forma in sententia peripateticorum destruatur, & reproducatur, materia etiam toties destruitur, & reproducitur. Hoc autem est contra doctrinam Aristotelea, quæ asserit, materiam esse incorruptibilem, ingenerabilem, æternam. Quod argumentum vrgebitur magis, cùm agemus de forma. Itaq; concludendum est, hanc materiam eo modo, quo explicatur per negationem, non habere suum esse à se, neque ab alio; vnde concipitur solum per intellectum, neque manet physicum principium in composito naturali.
units.tr: It is proved fourthly: for if prime matter is not something metaphysical and merely conceived by reason, then it has its own existence independently of the work of the intellect and in the reality of things. Granting this, I ask: does matter have this existence from form, or from itself? If from itself, then it exists in itself, and so is something certain, signate, determinate and quantified (for in reality there is no vague, indeterminate being; this is why Logic denies that the universal exists outside the intellect, since nothing can exist in reality without its ultimate differentia). If, however, matter receives its existence from form, then, since in the Peripatetic view form is destroyed and reproduced, matter too is destroyed and reproduced as often. But this is contrary to the Aristotelian doctrine, which asserts that matter is incorruptible, ungenerated and eternal. This argument will be pressed harder when we treat of form. Therefore we must conclude that this matter, in the way it is explained by negation, does not have its existence from itself nor from another; hence it is conceived only by the intellect, and does not remain a physical principle in a natural composite.

units.la: CONCLVSIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: SECOND CONCLUSION.

units.la: Si materia secundo etiam modo accipiatur, non est physicum principium in composito naturali.
units.tr: If matter is also taken in the second way, it is not a physical principle in a natural composite.

units.la: PRobatur, quia materia secundo modo accepta dicitur subiectum incompletum, seu substantia incompleta, & per se non subsistens: At in composito naturali non est hæc substantia incompleta, per se non subsistens, ergo materia prima sic explicata dici nequit physicum principium compositi naturalis. Probo minorem. Imprimis quia omne substatiale, vt suo loco videbimus, & in mixto, & extra mixtum per se manet. Secundò quia repugnat dari substantiam, quæ per se completè non subsistat, ergo neque dabitur in naturali composito. Probatur antecedens, nam substantia dicitur à subsistendo, & bene definitur in prædicamentis, Quæ per se subsistit, alioquin nõ differret ab accidente, cuius proprium est subsistere per aliud. Probatur 2. & confirmatur hæc vltima ratio, qūia si aliqua substantia per se non subsisteret, explicari non posset, quinā sit conceptus accidentis, & quinam substantiam, nam vtrumq; inhæreret alteri, penderet ab eo, existeret per illud &c. Secundò: quodlibet accidens posset vocari substantia incompleta. Probatur, nam eodem modo prorsus modo existeret materia in composito, quo existeret accides; ea enim existeret per aliud, & accidens quoque per aliud; ea periret destructa forma, & accidens etiam perit; ea deberet in alio reproduci, & accidens pariter sic reproducitur, &c. Imò accidens multò magis dici deberet substantia, quàm ipsa materia, nam illud in omnium sententia saltem diuinitus existit per se, quemadmodum in Eucharistia. Materia verò in doctrina multorum neque diuinitus manere sola potest.
units.tr: This is proved as follows. Matter taken in the second way is called an incomplete subject, or an incomplete substance, which does not subsist of itself. But in a natural composite there is no such incomplete substance that does not subsist of itself. Therefore prime matter, explained in this way, cannot be called a physical principle of a natural composite. I prove the minor. First, because every substance, as we shall see in its place, remains of itself both in a mixed body and outside a mixed body. Second, because it is impossible that there should be a substance which does not subsist completely of itself; therefore there will not be one in a natural composite either. The antecedent is proved thus: substance is named from subsisting, and it is well defined in the predicaments as "that which subsists of itself." Otherwise it would not differ from an accident, whose property is to subsist through another. The second point is proved, and this last reason is confirmed, because if some substance did not subsist of itself, it could not be explained what the concept of an accident is, or what that of a substance is. For both would inhere in another, depend on it, exist through it, and so on. Third, any accident could be called an incomplete substance. This is proved because matter in a composite would exist in exactly the same way as an accident exists. For it would exist through another, and so would an accident. It would perish when the form is destroyed, and so does an accident. It would have to be reproduced in another thing, and an accident is likewise reproduced in this way, and so on. Indeed an accident ought to be called a substance much more than matter itself is, for in the opinion of all, an accident at least exists of itself by divine power, as in the Eucharist. But according to the doctrine of many, matter cannot remain alone even by divine power.

units.la: Probatur 3. quia cùm dicitur materia substantia incompleta, vel hæc vox incompleta innuit, quòd aliquid substantiale desit materiæ, aut aliquid accidentale, aut nihil. Si primum, ergo materia simpliciter, & absolutè substantia non est. Probatur, nam esse substantiam consistit in indiuisibili, ergo substantia, cui desit aliquid substantiale, iam definit esse substantia. Si secundum, ergo materia non est substantialiter incompleta. Probatur, nam substantia, eò quòd ipsi desit aliquod accides, non ideo caret complemento aliquo substantiali, vt exemplis cuique patet. Si tertium, ergo vox ista, incompleta, nihil dicit
units.tr: It is proved fourth: when matter is called an incomplete substance, the word "incomplete" signifies either that something substantial is lacking to the matter, or something accidental, or nothing. If the first, then matter is not a substance simply and absolutely. This is proved, for the being of a substance consists in indivisibility; therefore a substance which lacks something substantial already ceases to be a substance. If the second, then matter is not substantially incomplete. This is proved, for a substance does not for that reason lack some substantial completion because some accident is lacking to it, as is clear to anyone from examples. If the third, then this word "incomplete" says nothing.

units.la: . dicit, vnde materia subsistet per se tamquam substantia in suo genere completissima, & perfectissima.
units.tr: Says, and so matter subsists of itself as a substance complete and most perfect in its own kind.

units.la: Probatur 4. Nam si Materia prima est incompleta, nec per se subsistens, ergo indiget alio subiecto, à quo sustentetur: sed hoc est contra doctrinam peripateticam, ergo. Maior est certa, quidquid enim per semet non existit, habere debet aliud, in quo existat, sicuti notum est in accidentibus. Minor etiam clarè patet, nam in definitione Materiæ vocatur illa Subiectum primum &c. ergo si & ipsa indiget alio, à quo sustentetur, non est subiectum primum. Hoc autem repugnat doctrinæ Aristotelæ, vt supra.
units.tr: It is proved fifth. For if prime matter is incomplete and does not subsist of itself, then it needs another subject by which it is sustained. But this is contrary to the Peripatetic doctrine. Therefore... The major is certain, for whatever does not exist of itself must have another in which it exists, as is known in the case of accidents. The minor is also clearly evident, for in the definition of matter it is called the first subject, and so on. Therefore if matter too needs another by which it is sustained, it is not the first subject. But this contradicts the doctrine of Aristotle, as above.

units.la: Sed Peripatetici hanc materiam suam acerrima vi tuentur, etiamsi nulla, vt aiunt, indigeat probatione; satis enim ipsa probat se, ostenditque, nec nisi à cæco denegari potest. Quapropter videtur apud eos rem esse dignam risu, & indignatione sapientum, suspicari de illa, cui tanquam basi tota nititur Philosophia. Nihilominus vt cuique satisfaciant, argumentis vtuntur ad eam probandam, & contra nos
units.tr: But the Peripatetics defend this matter of theirs with the utmost vigour, even though, as they say, it needs no proof; for it proves itself and shows itself, and can be denied only by a blind man. Hence among them it appears to be a thing worthy of the laughter and indignation of the wise to suspect that matter on which all of Philosophy rests as its foundation. Nevertheless, in order to satisfy everyone, they use arguments to prove it, and against us they object:

units.la: Obijciunt 1. Si non daretur materia prima, quam cum Aristotele Peripatetici admittunt, res omnes, quæ producuntur, fierent ex nihilo, & sic daretur creatio. Rursus dum corrumpuntur, abirent in nihilum, & sic daretur anihilatio: sed hæc dici non possunt; ergo admitti debet Materia prima, quemadmodum placet Aristoteli, ac Peripateticis. Maior duplicem habet partem. Probatur quoad primam. Dum ex ligno v.g. fit ignis, aut in igne producto manet subiectum, in quo prius erat forma ligni, vel non si primum, ergo datur materia prima, nam hæc illud subiectum est, in quo successiuè omnes formæ recipiuntur. Si secundū, ergo ignis nõ producitur in subiecto, quod prius erat, vnde fit ex nihilo subiecti, & ita creatur. Deinde maior eadem probatur quoad secundam partem. Dum ignis corrumpitur, vel manet materia, in qua contingit illius formæ destructio, vel non si manet, hæc dici debet Materia prima; si non ita, ergo ignis anihilatur, quia nõ sola forma, sed & subiectum ignis destruitur. Hoc autem dicere absurdū est, nõ enim per naturæ vim dari potest creatio, aut anihilatio. Ergo si quid producitur, aut corrumpitur, semper manet subiectum, in quo productio formæ, atque corruptio eiusdem exerceatur. Hoc est materia prima, ergo &c.
units.tr: First: if there were no prime matter, which the Peripatetics admit with Aristotle, all things that are produced would come to be from nothing, and so there would be creation. Again, when things are corrupted, they would pass into nothing, and so there would be annihilation. But these cannot be said. Therefore prime matter must be admitted, as Aristotle and the Peripatetics maintain. The major has a twofold part. The first part is proved thus: when fire is made, for example, from wood, either the subject in which the form of wood previously was remains in the produced fire, or it does not. If the first, then prime matter exists, for that is the subject in which all forms are successively received. If the second, then fire is not produced in a subject which previously existed, and so it comes from nothing of a subject, and thus it is created. Next, the same major is proved with regard to the second part. When fire is corrupted, either matter remains in which the destruction of that form occurs, or it does not. If matter remains, this must be called prime matter. If not, then fire is annihilated, because not only the form but also the subject of the fire is destroyed. But to say this is absurd, for creation or annihilation cannot come about by the power of nature. Therefore, if anything is produced or corrupted, a subject always remains, in which the production of the form and the corruption of it take place. This is prime matter; therefore, and so on.

units.la: Resp. negando vtramque partem Maioris. Ad minorem dico, non posse quidem fieri ex vi naturæ creationem, siue anihilationem. Sed non inde sequitur, dari Materiam primam, vt explicant Aristotelei de mente Philosophi. Quapropter argumentum sanè probat, aliquam esse materiam, ex qua producitur compositum, & in quam vltimò resoluitur; verum hæc non est illud subiectum, siue substatia illa incõpleta, indeterminata, cui deest aliquid intrinsecū, requisitū subsistentialiter &c. Sed est subiectū completū, ac perfectū in genere suo, ex quo fit mixtum, & quo corrupto,separatur, manet,per se subsistit &c. Vnde Aristoteles 3.de cælo c.3.physicè magis, & ad sensum locutus innuit, corruptionem mixti aliud non esse,quàm segregationem elementorum, & sic materia ista, ex qua fit, & in quam soluitur compositum, elementum est,quemadmodum dum patet in igne,dum resoluitur in cineres,halitum, humoré &c. hoc est in materias, quæ per se durant, manentque,præter quas nil datur aliud, ex quo mixtum fiat, vt suo loco dicemus.
units.tr: I reply by denying both parts of the major. As for the minor, I say that creation or annihilation cannot indeed come about by the power of nature. But it does not follow from this that prime matter exists, as the Aristotelians explain it according to the mind of the Philosopher. Therefore the argument certainly proves that there is some matter from which the composite is produced and into which it is finally resolved. But this is not that subject, or that incomplete, indeterminate substance, which lacks something intrinsic required to subsist of itself, and so on. Rather it is a complete and perfect subject in its own kind, from which the mixed body is made, and which, when the body is corrupted, is separated out, remains, subsists of itself, and so on.
