Hence Aristotle, in On the Heavens book 3, chapter 3, speaking more physically and according to the senses, indicates that the corruption of a mixed body is nothing other than the segregation of the elements. And so that matter from which the composite is made, and into which it is dissolved, is an element, just as is evident in fire, when it is resolved into ashes, vapour, moisture, and so on. That is, it is resolved into matters which endure and remain of themselves, beside which there is no other thing from which a mixed body is made, as we shall say in its place.

units.la: Obijciunt Secundo. Quæcumque transmutatio fit de oppositò in oppositum. v. g. transmutatur lignum de non igne in ignem;nix de non crystallo in crystallum; siue de vno contrario ad aliud contrarium, vt cùm res de frigida fit calida; sicca de humida &c.Sed hæc transmutatio fieri debet in aliquo subiecto,in quo nunc adsit vna forma, nunc alia, ergo debet concedi commune aliquod subiectum cuiusque transmutationis receptiuum, & hoc est materia prima, quam Aristoteles tenet. Minor probatur, nam v.g.dum transmutatur lignum in ignem, forma ignis pugnat cum forma ligni, & fit contrariorum luđta. Contraria verò pugnant in aliquo communi subiecto, à quo se inuicem pellunt, ergo transmutatio vnius in aliud fit in subiecto, & sic in materia prima.
units.tr: Second, they object: every change that takes place from one opposite to another, for example, wood is changed from not-fire to fire, snow from not-crystal to crystal, or from one contrary to another contrary, as when a thing is changed from cold to hot, dry from wet, and so on. But this change must take place in some subject, in which now one form is present and now another. Therefore some common subject receptive of each change must be granted, and this is prime matter, which Aristotle holds. The minor is proved thus: for example, when wood is changed into fire, the form of fire fights with the form of wood, and there is a conflict of contraries. But contraries fight in some common subject, from which they drive each other out. Therefore the transformation of one thing into another takes place in a subject, and so in prime matter.

units.la: Respondeo distinguendo minorem. Hæc transmutatio fit in subiecto incopie-
units.tr: I reply by distinguishing the minor. This change takes place in an incomplete,

units.la: tò; to; imperfecto, non subsistente per se, nego; in subiecto (seu melius) à subiecto persecto, & quod suam habet subsistentiam, concedo; ergo fit in materia prima, negatur consequentia. Ad probationem dico, argumentum supponere quod probari debet ab aduersarijs, nimirum dari formam ignis, quae ipsa etiam fit substantia incompleta, & pugnet cum forma ligni pariter incompleta, seseque à communi subiecto, videlicet materia prima expellant. Hoc inquam probari debet, non supponi; & fortasse nunquam probabitur. Quare aduerto duplicem esse transmutationem: alia dicitur accidentalis, quando vnum accidens amittitur, & aliud acquiritur; & haec sane fit in subiecto communi. Ratio est, nam accidentia cum per se non subsistant, aliquo subiecto indigent, in quo pugnent, se alterent, se pellant, quemadmodum in mea manu calor modo expellit frigus; modo frigus calorem. Altera vero transmutatio est substantialis, quando nimirum vna substantia dicitur aliam transmutare, vt cum ignis transmutat lignum: & ista non exercetur in alio subiecto. Fit enim transmutatio per hoc, quòd vna substantia per se subsistens pugnat in aliam, donec eandem soluat, disgreget, diuidatque in elementa, quibus antea mixtum illud componebatur, vt innuit Aristoteles 3. de caelo; non enim datur alia transmutatio, quàm dissolutio partium, quae prius vniebantur; vnde ignis, qui dicitur produci de nouo in ligno, educitur potiùs, & separatur,cùm priùs lateret. Si‑ cut alibi fufiùs dicetur.
units.tr: imperfect subject, not subsisting of itself: I deny this. In a subject (or better, from a perfect subject, which has its own subsistence): I grant this. Therefore it takes place in prime matter: the consequence is denied. As to the proof, I say that the argument presupposes what the opponents ought to prove, namely that there is a form of fire, which is itself also an incomplete substance, and which fights with the form of wood, likewise incomplete, and which drive each other out from a common subject, namely prime matter. This, I say, ought to be proved, not presupposed; and perhaps it will never be proved. Wherefore I observe that there are two kinds of change. One is called accidental, when one accident is lost and another is acquired; and this certainly takes place in a common subject. The reason is that accidents, since they do not subsist of themselves, need some subject in which they contend, alter one another and drive one another out, just as in my hand heat now expels cold, now cold heat. The other change is substantial, when namely one substance is said to change another, as when fire changes wood. This is not carried out in another subject. For the change takes place through this, that one substance which subsists of itself fights against another, until it dissolves it, disintegrates it, and divides it into the elements of which that mixed body was previously composed, as Aristotle indicates in On the Heavens book 3. For there is no other change than the dissolution of the parts which were previously united. Hence fire, which is said to be newly produced in wood, is rather drawn out and separated, since it was hidden before. As will be said more fully elsewhere.

units.la: Obijciunt 3. dum producitur forma compositi naturalis, certè fit in aliquo su‑ biecto: sed hoc esse debet incompletū sub‑ ftantialiter,ergo datur materia prima,quæ nil aliud est. Probatur minor, quia forma substantialis dum producitur, intrinsecè recipitur in subiecto,intrinsecè vnitur, il‑ lud intrinsecè perficit, ergo illi subiecto aliquid intrinsecum deest,quod vltimò recipit à forma; alioquin non conciperetur vnio intrinseca formæ cum materia; neque forma effet perfectiua materiæ, nisi afferret illi complementum aliquod intrinfecum.
units.tr: They object, third: when the form of a natural compound is produced, it certainly comes to be in some subject; but this subject must be substantially incomplete, therefore there is prime matter, which is nothing other than that. The minor is proved, because a substantial form, when it is produced, is received intrinsically into the subject, is intrinsically united to it, and intrinsically perfects it; therefore something intrinsic is lacking to that subject, which it finally receives from the form. Otherwise an intrinsic union of form with matter could not be conceived, nor would the form be perfective of the matter, unless it brought to it some intrinsic completion.

units.la: Respondeo,argumentum supponere materiam Ariftoteleam, non probare il‑ lam.Procedit enim ex falsa imaginatione, qua Peripatetici consueuerunt concipere subiectum aliquod incompletum &c. Ad maiorem igitur nego suppositum, quòd nimirum producatur ea forma fubftan‑ tialis, quam volunt aduersarij, vt loco suo videbimus. Ad minorē, nego absolutè subiectum illud esse incompletum fubftan‑ tialiter,in quo etiam talis forma produce‑ retur. Vnde cùm dicitur forma intrinfe‑ cè recipi,complere,perficere &c. hæc sunt mera verba, & reuera hic vnicus redditur sensus, quòd forma (quid quid postea illa fit) vnitur alteri parti ad faciendum natu‑ rale compositum; sed illa non affert eidem parti substantiale complementum. Patet hoc in anima rationali,quæ vnitur corpo‑ri ri physicè, perfectè, intrinsecè, nec tamen supponit corpus in ratione corporis esse incompletum substantialiter, cui proinde afferat ipsa complementum entitatiuum, substantiale, intrinsecum; sed hoc solum præstat anima, vt vniatur alteri parti completæ, nimirum corpori, cum quo efficit hominem. Vnde patet, hoc subiectum, quod concipiunt incompletum, vocantq; materiam, esse metaphysicum; sicuti animal vt animal, conceptum sine differentijs, metaphysica res est.
units.tr: I answer that the argument presupposes Aristotelian matter and does not prove it. For it proceeds from a false imagination, by which the Peripatetics are accustomed to conceive some subject incomplete and so on. Therefore I deny the major premise, the supposition that the substantial form which our opponents want is produced, as we shall see in its place. As to the minor, I deny absolutely that the subject in which such a form would be produced is substantially incomplete. Hence when it is said that the form is received intrinsically, completes, perfects and so on, these are mere words; and in reality only this sense is given, that the form (whatever it afterwards may be) is united to another part so as to make a natural compound, but it does not bring to that same part any substantial completion. This is plain in the rational soul, which is united to the body physically, perfectly, intrinsically, and yet does not suppose that the body, in its character as body, is substantially incomplete, so that the soul would bring to it an entitative, substantial, intrinsic completion. The soul does only this, that it is united to another part that is already complete, namely the body, with which it makes up the man. Hence it is plain that this subject, which they conceive as incomplete and call matter, is metaphysical; just as animal as animal, conceived without differences, is a metaphysical thing.

units.la: Ex dictis videtur, quòd hæc materia, quam explicant Aristotelei, sit mentale commentum, potiùs quàm reale, physicumque principium in composito naturali. Verùm facta eius hypothesi, & dato, non concesso, quòd ea sit in composito simpliciter naturali, placet hic nonnulla disquirere circa eius naturam cum peripateticis. Ad hoc autè duplex me trahit ratio. Prima est, ne à vobis ignoretur quod scholæ vniuersim docent. Secunda, vt ab ijs, quæ, posita materia prima, cogemur dicere, obscura, difficilia, non consona sensui, pateat magis, quàm ea dubia sit. Rem breui conficiam. Notetur ergo
units.tr: From what has been said it seems that this matter which the Aristotelians explain is a mental fiction rather than a real and physical principle in the natural compound. But, granting the hypothesis and supposing, not conceding, that it is in the simply natural compound, I think it well here to inquire into some points about its nature along with the Peripatetics. Two reasons draw me to this. The first is that you may not be ignorant of what the schools teach generally. The second is that you may see more clearly, rather than doubt, the matters which, once prime matter is posited, we shall be forced to say to be obscure, difficult and not agreeing with common sense. I shall make the matter brief. Let it be noted therefore

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISQUISITION II.

units.la: Vtrum data materia Aristotelea, formam habeat sibi coaevam.
units.tr: Whether, given Aristotelian matter, it has a form coeval with itself.

units.la: PRo intelligentia sciendum est, sententiam fuisse Avicennæ, Porphyrij, aliorumque, dari formam corporeitatis, materiæ coævam, nempe formam, quæ sit substantialis, incorruptibilis, à materia distincta, sed ab ea inseparabilis, cum qua corpus quoddam constituat indeterminatum, quod à formis deinde particularibus accipiat determinationem, & varia composita efficiat. Rem explico exemplo. In homine v.gr. inquiunt isti, præter animam rationalem, datur alia prior forma concreata materiæ, ab eaque indissolubilis, quæ cum ea facit corpus, & illud quidem informe, atque commune, quod tam in mortuo, quàm in homine viuo idem semper manet. Sed hæc forma corporeitatis ab omnibus penè reijcitur, unde fit
units.tr: To understand this, it must be known that the view of Avicenna, Porphyry, and others was that there is a form of corporeity coeval with matter: a form that is substantial and incorruptible, distinct from matter but inseparable from it, and that with matter constitutes a certain indeterminate body, which then receives its determination from particular forms and produces various composites. I will explain the matter by an example. In man, for instance, these thinkers say that, besides the rational soul, there is another, prior form, created together with the matter and indissoluble from it, which with the matter makes the body: an unformed and common body, which remains always the same in a dead man as in a living one. But this form of corporeity is almost universally rejected by everyone, whence it happens that

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Facta hypothesi Materia prima, illa non habet formam corporeitatis distinctam.
units.tr: Given the hypothesis of prime matter, prime matter does not have a distinct form of corporeity.

units.la: PRobatur, quia hæc forma daret esse commune, atque genericum, non verò specificum, & determinatum; sed implicat forma, quæ sic det esse; igitur materia prima ma non habet formam corporeitatis.Major conceditur. Minorē probo. Repugnat forma,quæ sit sub aliquo genere, non verò sub aliqua specie, nam cùm sit à parte rei,eo ipso specifica, talis, ac determinata est;ergo repugnat forma, quæ det esse genericum,& non det esse specificum. Quare diximus in Logica, non dari à parte rei vniuersale, quia esset ens indeterminatum, sine differentijs &c. ergo etiam implicat forma,quæ talis,& cum sua differentia non sit.
units.tr: This is proved because such a form would give being that is common and generic, not specific and determinate; but a form that gives being in this way is impossible. Therefore prime matter does not have a form of corporeity. The major premise is granted. I prove the minor. A form that is under some genus and not under any species is a contradiction, for since it exists in reality, it is by that very fact specific, and of such and such a determinate kind. Therefore it is a contradiction for a form to give generic being and not specific being. This is why we said in the Logic that a universal does not exist in reality, because it would be an indeterminate being, without differences, and so on. Therefore it is also impossible for a form to be such a form and yet not have its own difference.

units.la: Dixi autem notanter in conclusione, non dari hanc formam corporeitatis distinctam. Quia censeo,materiam esse corpoream à se, atque natura sua, vnde superest, quòd ea non à forma distincta rationem corporis habeat. Quare si pro forma corporeitatis intelligat quis rationem corporis,hanc libens admitto in materia. Et ratio conuincit, nam si materia est principium compositi reale, physicum,& materiale, quod saltem per Dei potentiam ab omni forma separatum conseruari potest, hoc profectò corporeum est, non à forma distincta, sed à se. Quæro enim, si materia ex natura sua non inuoluit esse corporis, quem conceptum de illa efformas? quid est? quænam entitas? non mera potentia, non quid incorporeum; ergo corpus, alioquin nullus capiet, quomodo fit subiectum sustinens formam corpoream.
units.tr: I deliberately said in the conclusion that this distinct form of corporeity does not exist. For I hold that matter is corporeal of itself and by its own nature, so it remains that matter does not have the character of body from a form distinct from it. Accordingly, if by a form of corporeity one means the character of body, I gladly admit this in matter. The argument also proves it, for if matter is the real, physical and material principle of the compound, which can be preserved, at least by the power of God, separated from every form, then it is surely corporeal, not from a distinct form but from itself. For I ask: if matter by its nature does not involve being a body, what concept do you form of it? What is it? What kind of entity is it? Not mere potency, not something incorporeal. Therefore it is a body, or else no one could understand how it is a subject sustaining a corporeal form.

units.la: Obijcies 1. subiectum, quod manet in omni transmutatione,corpus est: sed in trafmutatione manet sola materia ; ergo hæc habet formam corporeitatis . Maior patet, nam corrupto v. gr. ligno, manent cineres, halitus, ignis &c. quæ omnia sunt corpus . Minor etiam sequitur ex definitione Aristotelis,nam Siquid corrumpitur, abit vltimo in materiam primam.
units.tr: You will object, first: the subject that remains through every change is a body; but in change only matter remains; therefore matter has the form of corporeity. The major is evident, for when wood, for example, is destroyed, ashes, vapours, fire and so on remain, and all these are bodies. The minor also follows from Aristotle's definition, for if anything is corrupted, it finally resolves into prime matter.

units.la: Respondent meliores Peripatetici concessa Maiori, negando Minorem. Ratio est, nam quod manet post mixti corruptionem non est sola materia, sed sunt elementa, sub quibus latet materia . Manet ignis, terra &c. & sub singulis materia prima est. Hæc tamen responsio videtur esse difficilis: nam si materia iacet sub formis elementorum ; ergo completur ab ijs ; Quo igitur modo in hac ipsa erat priùs etiam forma ligni ? non enim duæ formæ simul esse possunt in materia eàdem. Sed facta hypothesi Materiæ primæ, coguntur sic philosophari. Secundò responderi potest cum distinctione : Materia est corporea per formam distinctam, nego; per se, concedo
units.tr: The better Peripatetics reply by granting the major and denying the minor. Their reason is that what remains after the corruption of a mixed body is not matter alone, but the elements, beneath which matter lies hidden. Fire, earth and so on remain, and under each of them is prime matter. Yet this reply seems difficult, for if matter lies under the forms of the elements, then it is completed by them; how then was the form of the wood in it earlier? For two forms cannot exist at once in the same matter. But, given the hypothesis of prime matter, they are compelled to philosophise in this way. Secondly, one may reply with a distinction: matter is corporeal through a distinct form, I deny; through itself, I grant.

units.la: Obijcies 2. Si materia prima est corpus; vel genericum,& vagum;aut specificum, & determinatum est : neutrum dici potest; ergo . Probatur minor, si enim dicatur primum,ergo à parte rei datur aliquid non signatum, non tale, non determinatum.Si dicatur secundum, contra . Sola foraforma substantialis, quæ aduenit materiæ, dat esse talis corporis, ergo materia non est de se tale corpus. Itaque nec vagum, nec signatum.
units.tr: You will object, second: if prime matter is body, then it is either generic and vague, or specific and determinate. Neither can be said; therefore... The minor is proved thus: if you say the first, then something unmarked, not of such a kind, not determinate, exists in reality. If you say the second, the opposite follows: only the substantial form that comes to matter gives being of such a kind of body; therefore matter is not of itself such a body. So it is neither vague nor marked.

units.la: Resp. aduersarios etiam inuolui eådem difficultate; unde argumentum retorqueri potest, nam omisso nomine corporis, quæro: Materia vel est substantia vaga, & communis, aut in specie terminata: quidquid respondeant, idem illis contingit absurdum, quod nobis opponunt, vt c.p. Directè autem respondeo, materiam esse corpus quoddam simplex, omnino distinctum ab elementis, & rebus compositis; adeo vt non sit ignis, non aer, non aqua, non terra, nec aliquid ex ijs compositum; sed alia substantia materialis, diuersa specie à iam dictis, apta recipere quamcumque formam, vt constituat compositum. Hinc ad argumentum respondeo, materiam non esse vagam, sed in sua specie determinatam; posse tamen rursus determinari à forma, & specificari, non quòd forma tollat materiam de sua specie, constituatque in alia; sed quia forma vt præcipua, & melior compositi pars, cùm vnitur materiæ, denominat illam. Sic dum forma ignis inest materiæ, hanc ipsam denominat ignem, non quòd materia perdiderit suum esse in specie, sed quia forma est pars in composito sensibilior, & principalior. Inde patet responsio ad vltimâ instantiam, forma enim aduenieus materiæ, non dat illi esse cor-
units.tr: I reply that our opponents are entangled in the same difficulty, and so the argument can be turned back on them. Leaving aside the name of body, I ask: matter is either a vague and common substance, or is limited in a species. Whatever they answer, the same absurdity befalls them that they throw at us, as I have said. But I reply directly: matter is a certain simple body, wholly distinct from the elements and from composite things, so that it is not fire, nor air, nor water, nor earth, nor anything compounded of these, but a different material substance, of a species different from those mentioned, fit to receive any form so as to constitute a compound. Hence to the argument I reply that matter is not vague but determinate in its own species; yet it can again be determined and specified by a form. This is not because the form removes matter from its species and constitutes it in another, but because the form, as the principal and better part of the compound, when it is united to matter, names it. Thus, while the form of fire is present in matter, it names this same matter fire, not because the matter has lost its being in species, but because the form is the more sensible and principal part in the compound. From this the answer to the last instance is clear, for a form coming to matter does not give it being of body, neither simply nor as such a kind.

units.la: {y} ... corporis neque simpliciter, neque talis. Cuinam ergo dat esse tale, ac determinatum?compoſito. Nam quia hoc resultat ex duplici entitate materiali, habet ex utraque rationem corporis (duo enim corpora simplicia constituunt aliud tertium compositum) à forma tamen esse corpus tale, quia forma est pars ultima denominans.
units.tr: ...of body, neither simply nor as such a kind. To what, then, does it give such and determinate being? To the compound. For since this results from a twofold material entity, it has the character of body from each of them (for two simple bodies constitute a third, compound body), yet it is a body of this kind through the form, because the form is the last part, which names it.

units.la: DISQVISITIO TERTIA.
units.tr: DISQUISITIO TERTIA.

units.la: Virum data materia Aristotelea, hac exi- stat per existentiam forma.
units.tr: Whether, matter being given in the Aristotelian sense, it exists through the existence of form.

units.la: PRo intelligentia repetite, materiam definiri ab Aristotele non positiue solum, sed etiam negatiue per ea verba 7. Metaph. 3. Dico materiam, qua per se ipsam neque quid, neque quantum &c. Ex quo Thomistæ sibi occasionem faciunt dicendi, materiam carere propria existentia, & per eandem existere, qua existit forma; unde hac sublata, & alia non succedente, materia in nihilum sit abitura. Non placet hæc sententia iis, qui sunt extra scholam D. Thomæ, Scoto præsertim, ac recentioribus. Cum quibus notetur.
units.tr: For the sake of understanding, recall that Aristotle defines matter not only positively but also negatively, in the words of Metaphysics 7, chapter 3: "I say matter is that which of itself is neither a particular thing, nor a quantity, etc." From this the Thomists take an occasion to say that matter lacks an existence of its own, and exists through the same existence by which form exists, so that if form is removed and nothing else takes its place, matter would pass into nothing. This opinion does not please those who stand outside the school of St Thomas, Scotus above all, and the more recent writers. This is to be noted, with whom they disagree.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Falsa hypothesi materia prima, illa non existit per existentiam forma.
units.tr: On the false hypothesis, prime matter does not exist through the existence of the form.

units.la: PRobatur r. quia materia, & forma existentias habent diuersas, ergo illa non existit per existentiam istius. Probo antecedens; nam ea, quæ producuntur per actiones diuersas, existentiam quoque diuersam habent: sed materia, & forma sic producuntur; ergo habent exiftentiam diuersam. Maior patet, nam in fententia Thomiftarum actio productiua est ipsa communicatio existentiæ: igitur vbi diuersa erit actio productiua, existentia etiam diuersa erit. Minor cuique nota est. Materia enim producta fuit per creationem à Deo; & forma per generationem fit à creaturis. Tunc verò cum produxit Deus materiam, illi suam dedit exiftentiam; præcipuè fi verum est quod non nulli dicunt, formas non eodem instanti productas fuisse; quo materia, vt innuunt ea verba Gen. 1. Terra erat inanis, & vacua; propterea nequijt existere beneficio formarum.
units.tr: This is proved first. Matter and form have different existences, so matter does not exist through the existence of the form. I prove the antecedent. Things produced by different actions have different existences, and matter and form are produced by different actions, so they have different existences. The major is clear: in the view of the Thomists, the productive action is itself the communication of existence, so wherever the productive action is different, the existence will also be different. The minor is known to everyone. Matter was produced by God through creation, while form comes to be through generation by creatures. Moreover, when God produced matter, he gave it its own existence. This is especially so if it is true, as some say, that the forms were not produced in the same instant as the matter, as the words of Genesis 1 suggest: The earth was empty and void. Therefore matter could not have existed by the existence of the forms.

units.la: Probatur 2. Materia prima præfupponitur ante formam, & natura saltem est prior illâ; sed pro eo priori habere debet existentiam suam; ergo non existit per existentiam formæ. Maior suadetur, ex eo quòd materia est causa formæ, concurrens vt subiectum ad illius productionem: omnis autem causa præexistit naturà ad suum effectum; ergo materia est naturà prior sua forma. Minor etiam patet, nam si materia pro eo priori non haberet existentiam suam, quomodo foret subiectum concurrens ad sustinendam, & recipiendam in se formam?
units.tr: It is proved secondly. Prime matter is presupposed before the form, and is at least prior to it by nature. But to be prior in this way it must have its own existence. Therefore it does not exist through the existence of the form. The major is supported by the fact that matter is a cause of the form, concurring as the subject in its production. Every cause, however, precedes its effect by nature. Therefore matter is prior by nature to its form. The minor is also clear, for if matter did not have its own existence in that prior state, how could it be the subject concurring to sustain and receive the form within itself?

units.la: Probatur 3. Si materia existeret per existentiam formæ, destrueretur, & reproduceretur scum forma: hoc dici nequit, nam ingenerabilis, & incorruptibilis est, ergo non existit [per existentiam formæ. Probo maiorem. Dum corrumpitur compositum, tota perit forma, & suam amittit existentiam: sed hæc ipsa est existentia materiæ; igitur & materia definit existere, ac proinde corrumpitur. Neque sufficit, si cum Thomistis dicatur, materiam non corrumpi, quia licèt amittat existentiam vnius formæ, statim recipit aliam, vnde numquam pereat. Contra enim est. Destruatur v. gr. forma ignis pro instanti a. tunc non potest existere materia prima, ergo etiam illa destruitur. Probo antecedens. Pro instanti a. tollitur existentia, per quam existeret materia, & non aduenit alia de nouo, per quam existat, ergo pro eodem instanti materia etiam destruitur. tur . Patet antecedens , quia pro instanti . a. quo fit corruptio formæ ignis, potest solùm corrumpi vetus forma , & nequit generari noua , nam corruptio est prior , & generatio posterior ; ergo si pro illo priori corrumpitur forma, & deperdit existentiam , corrumpitur quoque materia , quæ per illam existit . Deinde in instanti . b. sequenti generatur , & existit noua forma ,, ergo generatur etiam , & existit rursus materia_. Eo modo quo si Deus v. gr. tolleret pro instanti. a. existentiam ab Angelo, & redderet ipsi aliam pro instanti. b. Angelus toties destrueretur , & produceretur , quoties periret vna existentia, & succederet alia.
units.tr: It is proved thirdly. If matter existed through the existence of the form, it would be destroyed and reproduced along with the form. This cannot be said, for matter is ungenerated and incorruptible. Therefore it does not exist [through the existence of the form]. I prove the major. When a compound is corrupted, the whole form perishes and loses its existence. But this very existence is the existence of matter. Therefore matter too ceases to exist, and so is corrupted. Nor is it enough, as the Thomists say, to claim that matter is not corrupted, because although it loses the existence of one form, it immediately receives another, and so never perishes. For the contrary follows. Suppose, for example, that the form of fire is destroyed at instant a. Then prime matter cannot exist, and so it too is destroyed. I prove the antecedent. At instant a, the existence by which matter would exist is removed, and no other existence arrives anew by which it might exist. Therefore at that same instant matter is also destroyed. The antecedent is clear, because at instant a, when the corruption of the form of fire takes place, only the old form can be corrupted, and no new one can be generated, for corruption is prior and generation is posterior. Therefore, if at that prior moment the form is corrupted and loses its existence, matter, which exists through it, is corrupted too. Then at the following instant b a new form is generated and exists, and so matter is generated again and exists once more. This is just as if God were to take away an angel's existence at instant a and give it another at instant b: the angel would be destroyed and produced as often as one existence perished and another succeeded.

units.la: Probatur 4. Si materia non haberet propriam existentiam, ergo in composito physico esset vnica tantùm existentia_. V. g. in homine sola reperiretur existentia animæ : sed hoc dici non potest , nam ens completum habere debet existentiam completam , & quemadmodum compositum exurgit ex duplici essentia particulari , hoc modo ex duabus etiam existentijs constare debet .
units.tr: It is proved fourthly. If matter did not have its own existence, then in a physical compound there would be only one existence. For example, in a human being only the existence of the soul would be found. But this cannot be said, for a complete being must have a complete existence. Just as the compound arises from two particular essences, so it must consist of two existences.

units.la: Qbijcies 1. D. Thom. & cum eo Philosophi tenent, materiam primam esse puram potentiam , non ens ; non aliquid &c. ergo illa caret propria existentia .
units.tr: First objection: St. Thomas and, with him, the philosophers hold that prime matter is pure potency, not being, not something, and so on. Therefore it lacks its own existence.

units.la: Respond. cum distinct. Materia est pura potetia Metaphysica, negatur; physica , concediur ; & sic negatur etiâ consequêtia. Duplex igitur est potentia: metaphysica, & consistit in mera possibilitate rei, quae poterit esse, verum de facto non est. Alia physica, & subiectiua, quae dicit quidem esse rei actuale, sed, vt inquiunt, incompletum, adeo vt complementum suum aliunde habere possit. Materia ergo est potentia secundo modo, non primo: est enim subiectum entitatiuum, potens habere a forma perfectionem physicam, non entitatem, quae iam supponitur esse, vt formam recipiat
units.tr: Reply: I distinguish. Matter is pure potency of a metaphysical kind: I deny this. Of a physical kind: I grant it, and so I deny the consequence. There are therefore two kinds of potency. The metaphysical kind consists in the mere possibility of a thing that could be but in fact is not. The other, physical and subjective, indeed signifies something actually existing, but, as they say, incomplete, so that it can have its completion from elsewhere. Matter is therefore potency in the second sense, not the first. It is a subject with being in its own right, able to receive physical perfection from the form, not being, which is already presupposed in order to receive the form.

units.la: Obijcies secundo. Materia propriam habet exi stentiam, & forma pariter habet suam, & sic vtraque manet ens in actu: sed ex duplici ente in actu nequit fieri vnum compositum per se, ac naturale, igitur materia est pura potentia sine actuali existentia. Alioquin forma, quae actus est, reciperetur in alio actu, non in potentia.
units.tr: Second objection: matter has its own existence, and form likewise has its own, and so each remains a being in act. But one per se and natural compound cannot be made from two beings in act. Therefore matter is pure potency without actual existence. Otherwise the form, which is act, would be received in another act and not in potency.

units.la: Respondent distinguendo. Ex duplici ente in actu physico, & completo fieri nequit vnum per se, concedAtur; ex duplici ente, quorum alterum sit in actu metaphysico, seu (quod idem est) incompleto, & alterum in actu physico, negatur: Quocirca debet aduerti, materiam & esse actum, & simul quoque potentiam respectu diuersorum. Dicitur actus in ordine ad meram possibilitatem, quia de facto existit actu, nec mere possibilis est. Deinde quia hoc, quod existit actu, incompletum est, suumque, vt aiunt, complementum habere potest, dicitur esse potentia respectu formae, a qua completur. Dū igitur materiae vnitur forma,non aduenit illi quatenus materia est actus; verum quatenus habet rationem potentiae. Adest exemplum in anima, quae sane actus est respectu corporis, quod actuat; sed ipsa eadem respectu suae intellectionis, a qua perficitur, manet potentia. Sic materia prout actu est,dicitur actus; prout recipit formam,potentia.
units.tr: Reply, distinguishing. One per se cannot be made from two beings in physical and complete act: I grant this. From two beings, one of which is in metaphysical or (which is the same) incomplete act, and the other in physical act: I deny this. Hence it must be noted that matter is both act and, at the same time, potency with respect to different things. It is called act in relation to mere possibility, because it actually exists and is not merely possible. And because what exists actually is incomplete, and can have, as they say, its complement, it is called potency with respect to the form by which it is completed. Therefore, when the form is united to matter, it does not come to matter insofar as matter is act, but insofar as it has the character of potency. An example is the soul, which is certainly act with respect to the body it actuates, yet the same soul remains potency with respect to its own understanding, by which it is perfected. So matter, insofar as it is actual, is called act; insofar as it receives the form, potency.

units.la: Obijcies 3. Datur actus purus,qui omnem excludit potentialitatem, nempe Deus,ergo etiam dari debet pura potentia excludens omnem actualitatem; dato enim vno contrario, debet quoque dari aliud. Sed haec pura potentia est materia prima,ergo &c.
units.tr: Third objection: there is a pure act which excludes all potentiality, namely God. Therefore there must also be a pure potency which excludes all actuality. For once one contrary is given, the other must also be given. But this pure potency is prime matter. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Respondeo negando consequentiam. Ratio est, nam actus purus, & pura potentia opponuntur contradictorie; posito autem vno contradictorio,non est necesse poni & aliud. Quemadmodum ergo ait D. Thom. 1. p. qu. 99. artic. 23. dari summum bonum, nempe Deum, non tamen dari summum malum, ita etiam datur quidem purus actus omnem excludens potentialitatem; sed non est contra pura potentia sine omni actualitate. Ratio est, nam si datur actu haec potentia, ergo habet actum effendi,& sic non excludit omnem actualitatem.
units.tr: I answer by denying the consequence. The reason is that pure act and pure potency are opposed contradictorily, and once one contradictory is posited, it is not necessary to posit the other. Just as St. Thomas says (1 p. q. 99 art. 23) that there is a highest good, namely God, but there is not a highest evil, so there is indeed a pure act excluding all potentiality, but not a pure potency without all actuality. The reason is that if this potency existed in act, it would have the act of being, and so would not exclude all actuality.

units.la: DISQVISITIO QVARTA
units.tr: DISPUTATIO QUARTA

units.la: Vtrum per Dei potentiam possit ma- teria existere sine omni forma substantiali.
units.tr: Whether matter can exist by the power of God without any substantial form.

units.la: PRo intelligentia huiusce rei, videntur satis ea, quæ diximus quæstione superiori. Enimuero si materia propria non caret existentia, sequitur, posse illam sustineri à Deo sine omni forma, per quam, vt vidimus, non existit. Sed ex professo contra illos agendum est, qui ex principijs de materia iactis dicunt, eam neque diuinitus existere posse, omni forma substantiali spoliatam.
units.tr: For understanding this matter, what we said in the previous question seems sufficient. Indeed, if prime matter does not lack existence of its own, it follows that it can be sustained by God without any form, through which, as we have seen, it does not exist. But we must deliberately argue against those who, from the principles laid down concerning matter, say that it cannot exist even by divine power when stripped of every substantial form.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Facta hypothesi materia prima, illa per Dei potentiam existere potest sine omni forma substantiali.
units.tr: Given the hypothesis of prime matter, it can exist through God's power without any substantial form.

units.la: PRobatur primo, quia nulla in hoc apparet contradictio, nam etiamsi materia concipiatur incompleta, & cui deest perfectio intrinseca, nihilominus est subiectum physicum: & reale, quod entitatem suam habet, vnde saltem à Deo sine omni forma conseruari potest existens. Præsertim quia hoc materiæ incomplementum non est physicum, & illi reuera intrinsecum, vt infra dicemus.
units.tr: This is proved first, because no contradiction appears in it. Even if matter is conceived as incomplete and lacking intrinsic perfection, it is nonetheless a physical and real subject, which has its own entity, and so at least it can be preserved by God as existing without any form. This holds especially because this incompleteness of matter is not physical and is not really intrinsic to it, as we shall say below.

units.la: Probatur 2. contra Thomistas ad hominem sic: in eorum sententia dicuntur accidentia existere per existentiam subiecti, non minus ac materia existat per existentiam formæ: sed accidentia per Dei potentiam existunt sine omni subiecto, ergo etiam existere potest materia sine omni forma. Maior est ipsorum, accidens enim dicitur entis ens, quia non existit per se, sed per aliud. Minor est de fide in sacramento Eucharistiæ, vbi sine panis, ac vini substantia, manent accidentia se so-lis.
units.tr: It is proved secondly, against the Thomists, ad hominem, as follows. In their opinion, accidents are said to exist through the existence of their subject, just as matter exists through the existence of its form. But accidents exist through God's power without any subject. Therefore matter too can exist without any form. The major premise is theirs: an accident is called a being of a being, because it does not exist of itself but through another. The minor premise is certain by faith: in the sacrament of the Eucharist, where, without the substance of bread and wine, the accidents remain by themselves alone.

units.la: Probatur tertio pariter ad hominem contra Thomistas. Docent illi 3. p. in Mysterio Incarnationis, quòd anima Christi non habet propriam existentiam, sed existit simul cum materia per existentiam verbi. Hoc posito, arguo sic. Materia Christi non existit in eo per existentiam formæ, scilicet animæ, quia hæc pariter caret existentia sua, ergo materia per Dei potentiam existere potest sine omni forma substantiali. Probo consequentiam. Increata verbi existentia non est forma substantialis, nam forma vt forma, est quid vt aiunt, incompletum, dependens, & imperfectum: sed materia prima Christi existit per Verbum, ergo per Dei potentiam potest materia existere sine omni forma substantiali. Neque dicant, quòd Verbum supplet munus formæ, licet non sit forma. Nam & ego dicam, quòd per Dei potentiam poterit aliud quid supplere hoc idem munus, & sic absq; omni forma existet materia . & quæ hac in re difficultas est ?
units.tr: It is proved thirdly, likewise ad hominem against the Thomists. In the third part of the Summa they teach, in the mystery of the Incarnation, that the soul of Christ does not have its own existence, but exists together with matter through the existence of the Word. Granting this, I argue thus. The matter of Christ does not exist in him through the existence of a form, namely the soul, since the soul likewise lacks its own existence. Therefore matter can exist through God's power without any substantial form. I prove the consequence. The uncreated existence of the Word is not a substantial form, for form as form is, as they say, something incomplete, dependent and imperfect. But the prime matter of Christ exists through the Word. Therefore through God's power matter can exist without any substantial form. Nor should they say that the Word supplies the office of form, although it is not a form. For I too shall say that through God's power something else could supply this same office, and thus matter would exist without any form at all. And what difficulty is there in this?

units.la: Obijcies. i. Si materia existeret sine omni forma , esset in actu , & non esset in actu: sed hoc repugnat,ergo &c. Probatur Maior,quia existeret,ac propterea esset in actu; non haberet formam,vnde non esset in actu,ergo &c.
units.tr: Objection 1. If matter existed without any form, it would be in act and would not be in act; but this is contradictory; therefore etc. The major is proved, because it would exist, and therefore would be in act; it would have no form, whence it would not be in act; therefore etc.

units.la: Respondeo distinguendo maiorem : esset in actu,& non in actu respectu diuersorum, conceditur;respectu eiusdem , negatur . Itaque materia sine forma est in actu entitatiuo, quia proprium habet esse, ac proprium existere. Non est autem in actu completo,& physico , nam in tali casu careret forma, per quam dicunt eam perfici . Similiter distinguendum est ad confirmationem. Ratio autem supra iacta fuit,non enim repugnat,quòd res eadé fit in actu respectu vnius,& nó in actu respectu alterius;Patet hoc in anima,quæ actus est in ordine ad corpus,& non actus in ordine ad intelleictionem,sed potentia .
units.tr: I reply by distinguishing the major: it would be in act and not in act with respect to different things, I grant; with respect to the same thing, I deny. Thus matter without form is in act in an entitative sense, because it has its own being and its own existence. But it is not in complete and physical act, for in that case it would lack the form through which they say it is perfected. The confirmation must be distinguished in the same way. The argument advanced above is not contradictory, for it is not impossible that the same thing should be in act with respect to one thing and not in act with respect to another. This is clear in the soul, which is act in relation to the body, and not act but potency in relation to understanding.

units.la: Obijcies 2. Materia essentialiter exigit esse cum forma, ergo neq; per Dei potentiam potest ab ea separari . Probatur consequentia, Deus enim facere nequit contra essentias rerum, alioquin posset etiam efficere , vt homo esset animal sine ratione,leo sine rugibilitate &c.
units.tr: Objection 2. Matter essentially requires to be with a form; therefore it cannot be separated from it through God's power. The consequence is proved: God cannot act against the essences of things; otherwise he could also bring it about that a man would be an animal without reason, or a lion without the power to roar, and so on.

units.la: Respondeo negando consequentiam . Ratio est,nam etsi Deus à materia separaxet formam , ab ea tamen non tolleret quod essentialiter habet,nimirum exigentiam . Eo modo quo potest sanè Deus lucem foli adimere, quamquam sol non amittat exigentiam ad lucem. Igitur materia non habet formam essentialiter, sed exigentiam ad ipsam; vnde à forma segregari potest; quamuis ab exigentia non possit. Ex quo patet discrimen ad exemplas, nam homo nō solùm habet essentialem sibi exigentiam, vt sit rationalis, verum & rationalitatem. E contra materia essentialem habet exigentiam ad formam, non formam ipsam; ly ergo essentialiter cadit supra exigentiam tantùm.
units.tr: I reply by denying the consequence. The reason is that, even if God were to separate the form from matter, he would not thereby take away from matter what it has essentially, namely its exigency. It is in the way that God can indeed take away light from the sun, although the sun does not lose its exigency for light. Therefore matter does not have the form essentially, but has an exigency for it; whence it can be separated from the form, though not from the exigency. From this the difference from the example is clear, for a man not only has an essential exigency to be rational, but also rationality itself. By contrast, matter has an essential exigency for form, not the form itself; the word "essentially" therefore applies only to the exigency.

units.la: Obijcies 3. Si materia esset absque omni forma, vel maneretquid in specie, determinatum, vel non: si primum, ergo non esset amplius materia, vt c.p. Si secundum, ergo à parte rei daretur substantia communis, indeterminata, vniuersalis &c.
units.tr: Objection 3. If matter were without any form, either it would remain determinate in a species, or it would not. If the first, then it would no longer be matter, as is clear from what precedes. If the second, then in reality there would be a common, indeterminate, universal substance, and so on.

units.la: Resp. quòd materia in eo casu maneret in specie sua, esset enim substantia simplex receptiua formarum, vnde à ceteris per hanc differentiam distingueretur. Neque foret substantia communis, indeterminata, vniuersalis, nisi denominatiue, quatenus, quia incompleta, posset à formis vniuersis per successionem complezi. denominatiuè, quatenus, quia incompleta, posset à formis vniuersis per successionem compleri.
units.tr: Reply: in that case matter would remain in its own species, for it would be a simple substance receptive of forms, and so it would be distinguished from other things by this difference. Nor would it be a common, indeterminate, universal substance, except denominatively, insofar as, being incomplete, it could be completed by successively receiving all forms.

units.la: DISQVISITIO QVINTA.
units.tr: DISPUTATION FIVE.

units.la: Vtrum & naturaliter materia existere possit sine omni forma.
units.tr: Whether matter can naturally exist without any form at all.

units.la: PRo intelligentia hoc diligenter aduertite, solere peripateticos id vtplurimum denegare, quia concipiunt materiam velut subiectum substantialiter incompletum, cui proinde natura semper debeat succurrere, nouam in eo producendo formam, à qua compleatur, actuetur, perficiatur. Nihilominus hoc ita posset explicari, vt non desit materiæ aliquid intrinsecum, atque spectans ad ipsam; sed incompletam dici respectu compositi, eo quòd hæc sola satis non sit ad eum adæquatè constituendum. Simili modo quo anima rationalis dicitur incompleta in ordine ad hominem, quia illi constituendo sola nō sufficit. Sed quidquid sit, retenta etiā communi explicatione, scribatur
units.tr: For the sake of understanding, note carefully that the Peripatetics usually deny this, because they conceive of matter as a substantially incomplete subject, which nature must therefore always come to the aid of by producing a new form in it, by which it is completed, actuated and perfected. Nevertheless, this could be explained in such a way that nothing intrinsic to matter, and belonging to it, is lacking, and that it is called incomplete only with respect to the composite, because matter alone is not enough to constitute the composite adequately. In the same way the rational soul is said to be incomplete in relation to the human being, because it alone does not suffice to constitute him. But whatever the case, even with the common explanation retained, let it be written

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Facta hypothesi materia prima, illa exi- stere potest etiam naturaliter sine om- ni forma substantiali.
units.tr: Given the hypothesis of prime matter, it can exist naturally without any substantial form.

units.la: PRobatur. 1. auctoritate, nam hoc ipsum tenet Marsil. in 3. q. 13. art. 1. Gregor. in 6. dist. 12. q. 2. Bur. 1. phys. q. 1. P. Bonæ Spei. 1. phys. disp. 2. dub. 8. resol. 3. Probatur 2. ratione, quia si materia non posset existere naturaliter sine forma, hoc oritur ex duduplici capite. Vel eo quòd substantialiter est incompleta ; vel quia causæ naturales eam non relinquunt sine forma ; sed hæc duo non impediunt, ergo naturaliter &c.
units.tr: It is proved, first, by authority, for this very thing is held by Marsil. in 3. q. 13. art. 1, Gregor. in 6. dist. 12. q. 2, Bur. 1. phys. q. 1, and P. Bonae Spei, 1. phys. disp. 2. dub. 8. resol. 3. It is proved, second, by reason: if matter could not exist naturally without form, this would arise from one of two causes. Either it is substantially incomplete, or natural causes do not leave it without form. But these two do not prevent it. Therefore it can exist naturally, etc.

units.la: Probari posset minor quoad primam partem, quia hoc materiæ incomplementum non est (si res bene perpendatur) intrinsecū in ipsa, sed in ordine ad compositum, vt supra innuebatur. Materia enim vt materia, est pars compositi physica, est ens reale, propria existentia præditū, non indigens aliena. Sed quod est ens reale, physicum, subsistens per se &c. potest existere naturaliter sine omni alio, per quod non existit, ergo materia naturaliter esse potest sine forma. Probo maiorem. Dicunt Aristotelei, animam quoque rationalem esse partem hominis incompletā, & nihilominus incomplementum hoc non reperitur ipsi animæ intrinsecū, ea enim in ratione substantiæ completissima est; ex quo patet, materiam incompletā esse nō in se, verùm in ordine ad totū, cuius illa tantummodo pars est. Minor etiā patet in anima rationali, nā hæc sine corpore naturaliter manet, quia non existit per existentiam corporis; ergo materia etiā naturaliter manebit sine forma, quia non existit per illam. Sed quia explicatio communis admissa iam est.
units.tr: The minor premise can be proved as to its first part, because this incompleteness of matter is not (if the matter is weighed rightly) intrinsic to it, but is in relation to the composite, as was hinted above. For matter as matter is a physical part of the composite, a real being endowed with its own existence and not needing another's. What is a real, physical being, subsisting through itself, etc., can exist naturally without everything else through which it does not exist. Therefore matter can naturally exist without form. I prove the major premise. The Aristotelians say that the rational soul is also an incomplete part of man, and yet this incompleteness is not found intrinsically in the soul itself, for in the notion of substance it is most complete. From this it is clear that matter is incomplete not in itself but in relation to the whole, of which it is only a part. The minor premise is also clear in the case of the rational soul, for this remains naturally without the body, because it does not exist through the existence of the body. Therefore matter too will remain naturally without form, because it does not exist through it. But since the common explanation has already been admitted, [this need not be pursued further].

units.la: Prob. 2. eadē maior. Cōcessō enim quòd materia sit in se intrisecè incōpleta, si cōtingat (quod cōtingere potest, quèadmodū infra ostendo) vt vnà destructa forma, non adsit causa producens aliam, tunc manebit sine omni forma: ergo naturaliter ac sine miraculo. Probo antecedens: Materia in tali casu non destrueretur, est enim de se naturaliter incorruptibilis; ergo maneret. Non enim conditio materiæ foret eadem, atque accidentium: nā accidentia, deficiente subiecto, corrumpuntur, quia de se naturaliter corruptibilia sunt: E contra quia materia corrumpi nequit, vel sine forma conseruabitur. Alioquin non esset in se quoad entitatem incorruptibilis. Unde sequeretur, quòd nec per Dei potentiam sine nouo miraculo exist̄ere sine forma posset.
units.tr: The second proof has the same major premise. For granting that matter is intrinsically incomplete in itself, if it should happen (as it can happen, as I show below) that when one form is destroyed there is no cause present to produce another, then matter will remain without any form, and so naturally and without a miracle. I prove the antecedent: in such a case matter would not be destroyed, for it is by nature incorruptible in itself; therefore it would remain. For the condition of matter would not be the same as that of accidents. Accidents, when their subject fails, are corrupted, because they are by nature corruptible in themselves. On the contrary, since matter cannot be corrupted, it will be preserved without form. Otherwise it would not be incorruptible in itself as to its entity. Whence it would follow that it could not exist without form even by the power of God without a new miracle.

units.la: Probatur minor quoad secundam partem, quia causæ naturales non semper adsunt materiæ præsentes, vt vna corrupta forma, in ea producant aliam; &si adsunt, non semper vim habent producendi. E.g. si corrumpatur in elambyco rosa, vnde practici eliciunt aquam odorosam; in ea materia, quæ manet post rosæ corruptionem, gignitur de nouo forma, an non? Si hoc secundum, ergo materia naturaliter manet sine vlla forma; si primum, quæro, vt mihi assignes hanc formam, quæ de nouo producitur. Quænam hæc est? aqua odorosa? cineres, qui manent? spiritus, & halitus auolans? Nihil horum dici potest de nouo productum, ergo corrupta vna forma in materia, non adest causa, quæ aliam gignat. Probo minorem. Si cinis, qui terra est, si halitus, aut aqua de nouo producitur, non nisi ab igne, qui latet in elambyco, & rosam dissoluit, hoc fit; sed ignis non producit cineres, & mul-tòtò minùs aquam, cùm potiùs eam absumat,ergo non producitur forma de nouo. Confirmatur,quia terra in communi sententia,frigida, & sicca est, ergo nequit produci ab igne,qui agit per siccitatem_,, atque calorem.Neque dicas, cinerem esse mixtum à pura terra differens, nam hoc ne vix cæco dicendum.Rursus. Aqua frigida,& humida est, ergo non potest produci ab igne calido, & sicco;maximè quia si perseueret actio ignis, aqua dicitur à peripateticis destrui.Sed præter has partes non apparet alia forma, quæ genita fit,ergo si corrupta rosa, manet materia prima, hæc sine vlla substantiali forma de nouo genita, naturaliter perseuerat.
units.tr: The minor premise is proved as to its second part, because natural causes are not always present to matter, so that when one form is corrupted they produce another in it; and if they are present, they do not always have the power to produce. For example, if a rose is corrupted in an alembic, from which practitioners draw fragrant water, is a new form generated in the matter that remains after the rose's corruption, or not? If the second, then matter naturally remains with no form at all. If the first, I ask you to name for me this form which is newly produced. What is it? Fragrant water? The ashes that remain? A vapour or breath that flies off? None of these can be said to be newly produced. Therefore, when one form is corrupted in the matter, there is no cause present that would generate another. I prove the minor premise. If ash, which is earth, or vapour, or water, is newly produced, this happens only from the fire that lies hidden in the alembic and dissolves the rose. But fire does not produce ashes, and much less water, since it rather consumes it. Therefore no form is newly produced. This is confirmed, because earth, in the common opinion, is cold and dry; therefore it cannot be produced by fire, which acts through dryness and heat. Nor should you say that the ash is a mixed body differing from pure earth, for this would be said only by one who is nearly blind. Again, water is cold and moist; therefore it cannot be produced by fire, which is hot and dry, especially since, if the action of the fire persists, water is said by the Peripatetics to be destroyed. But apart from these parts no other form appears that could be generated. Therefore, if the rose is corrupted, prime matter remains, and this, with no substantial form newly generated in it, persists naturally.

units.la: Probatur etiam sic. Demus v.gr. catulum præsocari aquis,& mori. Tunc aiunt peripatetici,corrumpi, atque destrui formam substantialem canis in materia.Hoc supposito, arguo sic.Corrupta forma canis, non succedit in materiam alia de nouo; ergo materia naturaliter manet sine forma substantiali . Probo antecedens, nam quæro, vbinam, & quænam fit hæc forma de nouo genita ? Respondent, esse formam cadauericam in materia resultantem. Contra tamen insto.Forma ista cadauerica neque habet causam, à qua producatur, neque potest, dum moritur canis, produci; ergo materia sine forma naturaliter manet. Probo antecedens quoad primam partem,quia non alia est causa,vnde possit forma produci, nisi aqua; sed aqua vt simplex elementum, nequit producere forsubstantialem compositi,cùm hæc sit perfectior, ergo forma cadauerica non habet causam, à qua producatur. Imò etiamsi aqua de se productiua esset formæ cadauericæ,in tali casu,& similibus producere non posset; vnde probo secundam partem antecedentis hoc medio. Moriatur v.g. in instanti canis : Materia tunc non potest suscipere formam cadauericam de nouo genitam, nisi præparata sit, habeatque dispositiones ad eam formam recquisitas ( & hoc est veluti axioma in doctrina Peripatetica ) sed pro instanti.a.non habet materia canis accidentia, & dispositiones ad formam cadauericam recquisitas, ergo dum moritur canis, non producitur hæc forma cadaueris. Probo minorem. Cane adhuc mortuo, perseuerant aliquo tempore in eo idem color , idemque calor, aliaque accidentia vt priùs ; & hæc non sunt dispositiones formæ cadauericæ ,sed potiùs formæ prioris,ergo tunc adesse nequit in materia forma cadaueris; nulla enim forma introducitur per accidentia sibi contraria. Quid respondebis? an quòd corrupta forma substantiali canis,manent formæ partiales ? ergo falsum est, quòd vna corrupta,producatur alia. Præterea Ergo si corrumpantur & istæ formæ partiales, caro, cutis, os &c. vt possunt corrumpi,tunc saltem,quia vlterius non adeunt aliæ formæ, materia naturaliter manebit sine omni forma.
units.tr: This is also proved thus. Suppose, for example, a puppy is suffocated in water and dies. Then the Peripatetics say that the substantial form of the dog is corrupted and destroyed in the matter. Granting this, I argue thus. When the form of the dog is corrupted, no other form succeeds in the matter anew; therefore matter naturally remains without substantial form. I prove the antecedent, for I ask where and what this newly generated form is. They reply that it is the cadaveric form resulting in the matter. Against this, however, I press the point. This cadaveric form has no cause from which it is produced, nor can it be produced while the dog is dying; therefore matter remains naturally without form. I prove the antecedent as to its first part, because there is no other cause from which the form could be produced except water; but water, as a simple element, cannot produce the substantial form of a compound, since this is more perfect. Therefore the cadaveric form has no cause from which it is produced. Indeed, even if water were productive of the cadaveric form, in such a case and in similar ones it could not produce it. Hence I prove the second part of the antecedent by this means. Suppose the dog dies at this instant. Matter then cannot receive a newly generated cadaveric form unless it has been prepared and has the dispositions required for that form (and this is as it were an axiom in Peripatetic doctrine). But at that instant the dog's matter does not have the accidents and dispositions required for the cadaveric form. Therefore, while the dog is dying, this cadaveric form is not produced. I prove the minor premise. While the dog is still dead, the same colour, the same heat, and other accidents persist for some time in it, as before. These are not the dispositions of the cadaveric form but rather of the former form. Therefore the form of the cadaver cannot then be present in the matter, for no form is introduced through accidents contrary to it. What will you reply? Is it that when the substantial form of the dog is corrupted, partial forms remain? Then it is false that one form, once corrupted, is followed by another. Moreover, if these partial forms, flesh, skin, bone, etc., are also corrupted, as they can be, then at least, since no other forms come after them, matter will remain naturally without any form.

units.la: Obijcies. 1.adest celebre , atque indubitatum axioma , quòd corruptio vnius est generatio alterius, ergo si aliqua forma corrumpitur, eo ipso generatur alia, & sic materia nunquam existere potest naturaliter sine forma. Confirmatur, quia natura non tendit ad corruptionem formæ, vt in ea, tamquam in suo fine quiescat, sed per illam appetit alterius productionem; ergo corruptio vnius est generatio alterius.
units.tr: You will object, first, that there is the famous and undoubted axiom that the corruption of one thing is the generation of another. Therefore, if some form is corrupted, by that very fact another is generated, and so matter can never exist naturally without form. This is confirmed, because nature does not tend toward the corruption of a form as though it rested in that as its end, but through that it seeks the production of another. Therefore the corruption of one is the generation of another.

units.la: Respondetur cum distinctione. Corruptio vnius est generatio alterius formaliter, negatur; consequenter, subdistinguo, si adsit causa sufficiens ad producendum, conceditur; si non adsit, negatur; ergo materia existere nequit sine omni forma, negatur consequentia. Itaq; corruptio formæ, vt corruptio est in suo formali conceptu, dicit solam formæ desitionem, ac proinde non est formaliter productio alterius. Consequenter autem corruptio vnius est generatio alterius, quia post formam in materia corruptam solet generari alia, si tamen (quod est maximè aduertendum) adsit causa, quæ producat. Quòdsi causa producens non adsit, quemadmodum in exemplis vt supra, tunc nulla sequetur formæ generatio, & propterea manebit materia sola. Ad confirmationem dico similiter, natura semper intendere formæ generationem, si tamen causa sit, eaq; potes ad generandum: eo modo quo aiunt physici, naturæ genius esse, vt gignatur quidem homo, sed ex causæ defectu, & debilitate fieri sæpissimè fœminam.
units.tr: I answer with a distinction. The corruption of one is the generation of another formally: denied. Consequently: I subdistinguish. If a sufficient cause is present for producing, granted; if it is not present, denied. Therefore matter cannot exist without any form: I deny the consequence. For the corruption of a form, as corruption in its formal concept, signifies only the ceasing of the form, and therefore is not formally the production of another. But consequently the corruption of one is the generation of another, because after a form is corrupted in the matter another is usually generated, provided, however (and this is most especially to be noted), that a producing cause is present. But if no producing cause is present, as in the examples above, then no generation of form follows, and for that reason the matter will remain alone. As for the confirmation, I say likewise that nature always intends the generation of a form, provided, however, that there is a cause, and that it is able to generate. In the same way the natural philosophers say that it is the nature of the genius that a man be generated, but through a defect and weakness of the cause, a woman is very often produced.

units.la: Obijcies 2. Materia, vt supra dictum est, habet essentialem exigentiam ad formam, ergo naturaliter esse nequit sine omni forma. Probatur consequentia: natura nihil dedit frustra, ergo si materiae ingenuit exigentiam ad formam, in ea quoque semper conseruabit formam; alioquin haec exigentia non reduceretur ad actum, & foret superflua.
units.tr: You will object (2): matter, as said above, has an essential exigency for form, so it cannot naturally exist without some form. The consequence is proved thus: nature gives nothing in vain, so if it has implanted in matter an exigency for form, it will also always preserve that form in matter; otherwise this exigency would never be reduced to act and would be superfluous.

units.la: Resp. cum distinctione. Materia essentialiter habet exigentiam ad formam, itaut ly essentialiter cadat supra exigentiam, concedo: quia reuera siue materia sit cum forma, siue non, semper est natura sua exigitiua, seu apta ad illam: itaut ly essentialiter cadat supra formam, nego: alioquin nec de absoluta potentia Materia existere posset sine illa. Ad probationem dico, naturam non dedisse Materiae hanc exigentiam, seu aptitudinem essentialem, ut semper habeat formam; sed ut semper ad eam recipiendam sit apta: recipiet vero quoties aderit causa, quae formam producat. Simili modo quo natura non dedit lapidi exigentiam, ut semper sit in centro, sed ut sit aptus ad se mouendum eo; & id praestabit quoties non habuerit corpus aliud infra se grauius, in quo casu lapis exiget quidem esse in centro, sed tamen tunc erit naturaliter extra, ut cedat ponderosiori. Sic aeri dedit exigentiam, ut supra aquam emineat; verum si adsit periculum vacui, ut fit in scopulorum cauernis multo aqua depressioribus, & eo aqua deferri non possit, aer tunc naturaliter descendit, manetque secretus a suo toto. Neque per hoc materia erit in statu violento, nam exigentia, quam habet ad formam, non oritur ex anxietate quadam, & appetitu elicito, sed ex aptitudine ad eam recipiendam;imò est aptitudo, & proportio ipsa. Sicut ergo anima rationalis,etiam separata,non est in statu violento, licèt appetat esse cum corpore,quia talis exigentia non est nisi aptitudo naturalis ad illud. Ita&c.
units.tr: I answer with a distinction. Matter essentially has an exigency for form, if the word "essentially" falls on "exigency": I grant it, because whether matter is with form or without it, it is always by its nature exigent, or apt for form. If the word "essentially" falls on "form": I deny it, since otherwise matter could not exist even by God's absolute power without form. To the proof I say that nature did not give matter this essential exigency or aptitude so that it should always have form, but so that it should always be apt to receive it. It will receive form whenever there is a cause present that produces the form. In the same way, nature did not give a stone the exigency always to be at the centre, but made it apt to move itself there; and it does so whenever there is no heavier body beneath it. In that case the stone indeed tends to be at the centre, but it is then naturally outside it, so that it may yield to the heavier body. So too nature gave air the exigency to rise above water; but if there is danger of a vacuum, as happens in the caverns of rocks which lie far below the water, and the water cannot be carried there, the air then naturally sinks and remains separated from its whole. Nor by this will matter be in a violent state, for the exigency it has for form does not arise from some anxiety and elicited appetite, but from its aptitude for receiving form; indeed it is the aptitude itself and proportion. Just as, therefore, the rational soul, even when separated, is not in a violent state, although it desires to be with the body, because such an exigency is nothing but a natural aptitude for it, so too, etc.

units.la: Obijcies 3. Agens naturale dum corrumpit formam in materia,per eadem accidentia, per quæ fit corruptio, disponit materiam pro alia forma: sed materia disposita exigit naturaliter formam; ergo nunquam esse poterit sine illa. Probatur minor exemplis,nam præparato ligno per calorem,& siccitatem, in eo statim gignitur forma ignis; disposito corpore in vtero, confestim creatur à Deo anima informans &c. ergo si vna corrupta forma, disponitur materia, & præparatur ad aliam, ea nunquam erit naturaliter sine forma.
units.tr: You will object (3): a natural agent, while it corrupts a form in matter, by the same accidents through which the corruption takes place, disposes the matter for another form. But matter so disposed naturally demands form; therefore it can never be without one. The minor is proved by examples: when wood has been prepared by heat and dryness, the form of fire is at once generated in it; when the body has been disposed in the womb, the soul that informs it is immediately created by God, etc. Therefore, if once a form is corrupted, matter is disposed and prepared for another, it will never naturally be without form.

units.la: Resp. cum distinctione. Per eadem accidentia, per quæ forma corrumpitur, materia disponitur ad aliam,perfectè semper, & vltimò, nego; initiatiuè,concedo. Similiter ad minorem. Disposita materia, in ea gignitur forma, si disponatur vltimò, transeat; si tantum initiatiuè, negatur. Itaque vt producatur noua forma, debet Materia vltimò, & modo perfectissimo disponi per accidentia omnia tali formæ debita. Aliquando verò naturale agens, quamquam per accidentia contraria corruperit formam, per ea nequit vltimò disponere ad aliam, sed initiatiuè tantùm, eò quòd non sufficiant pro consumata præparatione. Præterea si aqua in carbone accenso producat gradus aliquot frigoris, & humiditatis; hi satis omnino sunt ad formam ignis corrumpendam, nequit enim perseuerare ignis, qui sit frigidus, & humidus: at idem non sufficiunt ad aliam formam de nouo gignendam; ergo hæc non generabitur, & sic materia sine omni forma erit. Probo minorem, quia si aliqua producitur forma, hæc est carbonis; carbo autem calidus, atque siccus est; quomodo ergo produci poterit per frigus, & humiditatem?
units.tr: I answer with a distinction. That matter is disposed for another form, perfectly and ultimately, by the same accidents through which the form is corrupted, I deny; that it is disposed initially, I grant. Likewise for the minor. When matter is disposed, form is generated in it, if it is disposed ultimately; let that pass. If it is only initially disposed, that is denied. Thus, for a new form to be produced, matter must be disposed ultimately and in the most perfect manner, by all the accidents due to that form. Sometimes, indeed, a natural agent, although it has corrupted the form by contrary accidents, cannot by these dispose the matter ultimately for another form, but only initially, because they do not suffice for a complete preparation. Moreover, if water on a burning coal produces some degrees of cold and moisture, these are entirely sufficient to corrupt the form of fire, for fire that is cold and moist cannot persist; but the same degrees are not sufficient to generate another form anew. Therefore this form will not be generated, and so matter will be without any form. I prove the minor: if some form is produced, it is the form of the coal; but the coal is hot and dry, so how can it be produced by cold and moisture?

units.la: Obijcies 4. numquam visa fuit materia prima sine forma; ergo naturaliter esse nequit sine illa. Confirmatur, nam si hoc fieri posset ex vi naturæ, aliquando saltem contigisset: numquam contigit ad sensum; ergo. Confirmatur 2. nam sine forma existeret materia violenter; non igitur naturaliter. Probatur, quia careret suo bono intrinseco &c.
units.tr: You will object (4): prime matter has never been seen without form; therefore it cannot naturally exist without one. It is confirmed: for if this could happen by the force of nature, it would at least have happened at some time; yet it has never happened to the senses; therefore, etc. It is confirmed a second time: for matter without form would exist violently, and so not naturally. This is proved because it would lack its intrinsic good, etc.

units.la: Respondetur, materiam sine forma numquam fuisse visam, quia numquam fuit in rerum natura (sed obliuiscebar me agere Peripateticum) numquam ergo fuit visa, quia cæcam facimus Philosophiam, & quod in omni resolutione intuemur, nimis boni credimus, hoc persona esse, aut formam de nouo inductam, sub qua timida materia, & suæ nuditatis pudibunda semper lateat. Sed reuera non bene arguitur: Numquam fuit visa materia sine forma; ergo sic naturaliter esse nequit; vt exemplis constat. Ad vltimam confirmationem, nego quòd materia sine forma exisseret violenter; adhuc enim esset in se incorruptibilis, vnde natura liter maneret. Naturaliter, inquam, non ex appetentia naturæ, sed ex defectu eiusdem. Simili modo quo vacuum, quod aliquando fit, non contingit naturaliter, perinde quasi appetatur à natura, vt bonum; sed naturaliter, seu ex defectu naturæ, quæ semper non habet vim, vt impediat illud. Similiter materia naturaliter, hoc est ex defectu solo naturæ, ac sine miraculo, potest carere forma, quoties non aderit causa productiua illius. Vnde ad probationem, nego quòd materia careat bono intrinseco; forma enim non est bonum materiæ; sed compositi, gratia cuius est.
units.tr: The answer is that matter without form has never been seen, because it has never been in the nature of things (but I was forgetting to play the Peripatetic). It has never, therefore, been seen, because we make philosophy blind; and what we see in every resolution we too readily believe to be a person, or a form newly introduced, under which timid matter, ashamed of its nakedness, always lies hidden. But in truth the argument is badly constructed: matter has never been seen without form; therefore it cannot naturally be so; as the examples show. To the last confirmation: I deny that matter without form would exist violently, for it would still be incorruptible in itself, whence it would remain naturally. Naturally, I say, not from the appetite of nature, but from its defect. In the same way a vacuum, which sometimes occurs, does not happen naturally as if it were desired by nature as a good, but naturally, that is from a defect of nature, which does not always have the power to prevent it. Similarly, matter can naturally, that is from the defect of nature alone and without a miracle, lack form whenever no productive cause of it is present. Hence, to the proof, I deny that matter lacks an intrinsic good; for form is not the good of matter, but of the compound, for whose sake it exists.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SEXTA.
units.tr: SIXTH DISQUISITION.

units.la: Quonam appetitu appetat Materia Formas.
units.tr: Of What Kind of Appetite Matter Desires Forms.

units.la: PRo intelligentia triplex appetitus distingui debet. Primus est desiderij, hoc est inclinatio ad bonū absens; quod enim abest, desideratur. Secundus complacentiæ, siue gaudij circa bonū præsens, nā gaudemus de bono, quod præsens est. Postremus dicitur appetitus absolutè, præscindendo ab eo, quòd bonū sit absens, aut præsens.
units.tr: To understand this, a threefold appetite must be distinguished. The first is the appetite of desire, that is, an inclination toward a good that is absent, since what is absent is desired. The second is the appetite of complacency or joy in a good that is present, since we rejoice in a good that is present. The last is called appetite absolutely, setting aside whether the good is absent or present.

units.la: Rursus debet sciri quid sit appetitus in communi acceptus. Hic enim est inclinatio quædam,seu propensio, aut aptitudo rei ad habendum bonum, ad quod à natura ordinatur. Duplex est. Primus dicitur naturalis, & innatus, nempe inclinatio ad bonum absque præuia cognitione , quemadmodum lapis appetitum habet ad descensum. Alter elicitus, qui dicitur etiam animalis, & est inclinatio rei ad bonum proprium, sed præuia cognitione, sicuti bos v. gr. fœnum appetit.
units.tr: Again, we must know what appetite means in general. It is a certain inclination or propensity, or the aptitude of a thing to have the good to which it is ordered by nature. It is of two kinds. The first is called natural and innate, namely an inclination toward a good without any prior cognition, as a stone has an appetite for descent. The second is called elicited, which is also called animal, and is the inclination of a thing toward its own good, but with prior cognition, as an ox, for example, desires hay.

units.la: His positis,certum est,materiam non appetere formam appetitu elicito, qui datur operantibus ex cognitione, sed naturali,& innato. Dubium vero manet, sitne appetitus iste complacentiæ, an desiderij. Pro solutione scribatur
units.tr: With these things laid down, it is certain that matter does not desire form with an elicited appetite, which belongs to agents acting from knowledge, but with a natural and innate one. It remains doubtful, however, whether this appetite is one of complacency or of desire. For its solution, let the following be written.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Facta hypothesi materia prima, illa formas appetit,quas habet,per complacentiam; quas non habet,per desiderium.
units.tr: Given the hypothesis of prime matter, it desires by complacency the forms it has, and by desire the forms it does not have.

units.la: PRobatur facilè prima pars, Materia enim complacet sibi, & gaudet in ea forma, pro qua recipienda capacitatem sortita est à natura,vt cum ea naturale compositum constituat. Simili ergo modo quo lapis dū locum occupat, vel in centro,vel centro proximum,dicitur in eo quiescere, atq; sibi cōplacere, ita quoque de materia dicendum est respectu formæ,quā habet.
units.tr: The first part is easily proved. Matter takes pleasure in itself and rejoices in that form for whose reception nature has given it capacity, so that it may constitute a natural compound with it. Just as a stone, while it occupies a place, whether at the centre or near the centre, is said to rest there and take pleasure in itself, so the same must be said of matter with respect to the form it has.

units.la: Probatur etiam secunda pars conclusionis, quia ille appetitus, quem dicimus desiderij, non aliud est (si res bene perpendatur) quàm aptitudo materiæ; seu melius materia ipsa idonea, & apta, vt formas recipiat; sed Materia potest successiuè recipere formas, quas non habet, ergo eas appetit appetitu desiderij. Maior consideranti patet. Minor etiam manet clara, materia enim quamquâ sub vna forma constituta sit, nihilominus aptitudinem habet ad cæteras, nec vni particulari affixa est.
