Ergo cùm hæc potentia, siue aptitudo idem sit, ac appetitus desiderij, materia formas appetit, quas non habet, per desiderium.
units.tr: The second part of the conclusion is also proved, because that appetite which we call desire is nothing else (if the matter is weighed carefully) than the aptitude of matter, or rather matter itself as fit and suited to receive forms. But matter can receive successively forms which it does not have; therefore it desires them with the appetite of desire. The major is plain to anyone who considers it. The minor also remains clear: although matter is constituted under one form, it nevertheless has an aptitude for the others, and it is not fixed to any one particular form. Therefore, since this power or aptitude is the same as the appetite of desire, matter desires by desire the forms it does not have.

units.la: Ex quo manet etiam decisa ea quæstio, an materia formas appetat corruptas. Respoderi enim debet affirmatiuè. Ratio est, quia materia formas appetit omnes, quas recipere succesiuè potest; vnde cùm etiam corruptæ aliqua potentia reproduci possint, hæ quoque à materia expeti dicendæ sunt.
units.tr: From this it also follows that the question is settled whether matter desires corrupted forms. It must be answered affirmatively. The reason is that matter desires all the forms it can successively receive; hence, since even corrupted forms can in some power be reproduced, these too must be said to be desired by matter.

units.la: Obijcies. 1. Materia semper habet aliquam formam, in qua gaudet, sibique complacet; sed ita sufficienter expletur appetitus materiæ, igitur non habet ad alias appetitum desiderij. Probatur minor, quia si materia dum sibi complacet in vna forma, desideraret quoque alias, foret violenter sub illa, nam aliud quid præterea vellet, ergo non habet ad cæteras appetitum desiderij, sed tantùm complacentiæ in ea, qua completur. Cõfirmatur, nam lapis v.g.dummodo locū habeat prope centrum,quiescit in eo,neque alium ęquè vicinum desiderat,ergo à pari materia si vnā retineat formam, alias non appetet per desiderium.
units.tr: Objection 1. Matter always has some form in which it rejoices and takes pleasure; but the appetite of matter is thus sufficiently satisfied; therefore it does not have an appetite of desire toward others. The minor is proved, because if matter, while it takes pleasure in one form, also desired others, it would be under that form against its will, for it would wish for something else besides. Therefore it has no appetite of desire toward the others, but only of complacency in that form by which it is completed. This is confirmed: for a stone, for example, provided it has a place near the centre, rests in it and does not desire another equally near; therefore, by parity, if matter retains one form, it does not desire the others by desire.

units.la: Resp.cum distinctione ad minorē.Sufficienter expletur materia, dū est sub vna forma,ratione complacentiæ,conceditur; ratione aptitudinis ad cæteras, negatur. Ad confirmationem dico, materiam non esse in statu violento, dum sub vna forma expetit alias,nam hoc expetere nō est elicere actum aliquem displicentiæ,siue conatus,vt à præsenti expediat se;verum est capacitas quædam formas alias recipiendi succesiuè,vnam post aliam;& quia hæc aptitudo inest semper materiæ primæ,ideò semper habet appetitum desiderij. Exemplum de lapide fauet nobis, nam etsi prope centrum positus, naturaliter, ac satis quiescat, nihilominus aptus etiam est, vt in alio constituatur,& sic appetitu desidęrij ad alia quoque loca fertur.
units.tr: Reply: I grant the minor with a distinction. That matter is sufficiently satisfied while it is under one form, with respect to complacency, I grant; with respect to its aptitude for the others, I deny. To the confirmation I say that matter is not in a violent state while under one form it desires others, for to desire in this way is not to elicit any act of displeasure or effort to free itself from its present state. It is rather a certain capacity to receive other forms successively, one after another; and because this aptitude is always present in prime matter, it therefore always has the appetite of desire. The example of the stone supports us: although placed near the centre, it rests naturally and fairly, yet it is nevertheless also apt to be placed in another position, and so by the appetite of desire it is carried toward other places as well.

units.la: Obijcies 2. Materia non habet appetitū ad impossibile:sed formę corruptæ sunt aliquid naturaliter impossibile, quia illæ nequeunt amplius reproduci, ergo ma-teria non appetit formas corruptas.
units.tr: Objection 2. Matter does not have an appetite for the impossible; but corrupted forms are something naturally impossible, since they cannot be reproduced any more; therefore matter does not desire corrupted forms.

units.la: Respondetur cum distinctione.Materia non appetit quod est impossibile,si hoc sit impossibile intrinsecè, ac per se,conceditur;si verò extrinsecè,ac per accidens,negatur.Ad minorem.Formæ corruptæ sunt quid impossibile intrinsecè, atq; in se,nego; extrinsecè, ac per accidens,concedo,& & nego consequentiâ. Formæ igitur corruptæ dicuntur impossibiles, non quia repugnent in essentia sua intrinseca, verùm quia causa extrinseca nequit fortasse illas iterum gignere; vndè per accidens est, quòd reproduci à natura non possint. Igitur cùm saltem per Dei potentiâ adhuc in materia reproducibiles maneant, dicendum est quòd appetantur, nam quidquid materia potest recipere, illud etiam desiderat, modo quo supra dictum est.
units.tr: Reply with a distinction. Matter does not desire what is impossible if this is impossible intrinsically and in itself, I grant; if extrinsically and by accident, I deny. To the minor: corrupted forms are something impossible intrinsically and in themselves, I deny; extrinsically and by accident, I grant, and I deny the consequence. Corrupted forms are therefore called impossible not because they are repugnant in their intrinsic essence, but because an extrinsic cause perhaps cannot beget them again; hence it is by accident that they cannot be reproduced by nature. Therefore, since at least by the power of God they remain reproducible in matter, it must be said that they are desired, for whatever matter can receive, it also desires, in the manner stated above.

units.la: DISPVTATIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISPUTATIO SECUNDA.

units.la: De Forma Aristotelea.
units.tr: On the Aristotelian Form.

units.la: SEcundum rei naturalis principium dicitur ab Aristotele Forma substantialis, quæ à causis de novo producitur, & physicè vnita materiæ primæ facit cum illa subsistantiale compositum. Explicant verò hanc formam sic, vt sit quædam substantia, intrinsecè incompleta, non subsistens per se, dependens à materia, & in fieri, & in esse (vna tamen anima rationali excepta) quæ intrinsecè perficiat materiam, & ipsa etiam perficiatur; quæ vltimò constituat compositum in tali esse determinato; vnde ab Aristotele definitur Quod quid erat esse rei; quæ sit radix omnis operatio, n is, virtutis, facultatis &c.
units.tr: According to Aristotle, the principle of a natural thing is called substantial form, which is produced de novo by causes and, being physically united with prime matter, makes with it a substantial composite. Its exponents explain this form as a certain substance, intrinsically incomplete, not subsisting of itself, dependent on matter both in becoming and in being (the rational soul alone excepted), which intrinsically perfects matter and is itself perfected by it, and which ultimately constitutes the composite in such and such a determinate being; hence Aristotle defines it as "that which was the essence of the thing" [Quod quid erat esse rei]; it is the root of every operation, nature, power, faculty, and so on.

units.la: Habet plura hæc explicatio, quæ suspicione ingerunt huius formæ, quemadmodum sunt ea verba, intrinsecè incompleta, per se non subsistens, dependens à materia &c. quæ non tam facilè videntur convenire substantiæ, vt sibi persuasit commu-nis,& Aristotelea opinio. Gliscit verò dubitatio, nam huiusmodi formam negat Galenus cum præcipuis antiquorum, & ex recentioribus Basso, Gassendo, Henricus Regius, aliíque innumeri. Proinde videamus primò, an talis forma in rerum natura sit, nam si patuerit esse, à nobis etiam constituetur principium; si non ita, requirendum erit aliud. Sit ergo
units.tr: This explanation has several features which arouse suspicion about this form, such as the words "intrinsically incomplete, not subsisting of itself, dependent on matter," and so on, which do not seem so easily to belong to a substance, as the common and Aristotelian opinion has persuaded itself. Doubt indeed grows, for Galen denies such a form together with the chief of the ancients, and among the more recent writers Basso, Gassendi, Henricus Regius, and innumerable others. Therefore let us first see whether such a form exists in the nature of things; for if it is shown to exist, we shall also establish it as a principle; if not, another must be sought. Let it be so.

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: DISQUISITION I.

units.la: Vtrum detur forma substantialis Aristotelea.
units.tr: Whether the Aristotelian substantial form exists.

units.la: PRo intelligentia iuuerit hic statim afferre argumenta, quibus probatur hæc forma, & vt aiunt Philosophi, demonstratur. Primum est. In omni re naturali dari debet principium aliquod substantiale, vnde proueniant operationes, accidentia, virtutes propriæ talium rerum; sed hoc principium esse nequit materia prima; ergo forma, & sic datur forma substantialis. Minor probatur, nam de se materia non exigit potiùs hanc figuram, quàm aliam; istud accidens, quàm illud, sed omninò indifferens est. Consequentia patet, nam in composito si adest principium exigitiuum huius qualitatis, virtutis &c. & hoc esse nequit materia, manet quòd sit forma. Confirmatur, quia in composito si pars aliqua deperditur, si qualitas amittitur &c. adest etiam causa quæ reparat amissum, vt patet in aqua calida recuperante suum frigus; in animali restituente se ad pristinum esse, in plantis, quæ formam in trunco, in ramis folia, figuram in fructibus paulatim resarciunt. Ergo datur forma substantialis, quæ agit, reparat, conseruat, &c.
units.tr: To aid understanding, it will be useful to set out at once the arguments by which this form is proved, and, as the philosophers say, demonstrated. The first is this. In every natural thing there must be some substantial principle from which its operations, accidents and proper powers arise. But matter cannot be this principle; therefore it is a form, and so a substantial form exists. The minor premise is proved as follows: matter of itself does not demand this shape rather than another, or this quality rather than that; it is wholly indifferent to them. The consequence is plain, for if in a composite there is a principle that requires this quality, power and so on, and this cannot be matter, it follows that it must be a form. It is confirmed by the fact that in a composite, if some part is lost or some quality is destroyed, there is also a cause that repairs what has been lost. This is evident in warm water recovering its cold, in an animal restoring itself to its former state, and in plants, which gradually make good the form in the trunk, the leaves in the branches, and the shape in the fruits. Therefore a substantial form exists which acts, repairs, preserves and so on.

units.la: Secundum argumentum. Res naturales inter se differunt substantialiter; sed hoc non habent ratione materiæ, igitur ex parte formæ, ac propterea datur forma substantialis. Maior patet, nam lignum substantia est, differens omnino à ferro, & hoc ab auro, & id à lapide &c. Minor etiā constat, quia materia eadem est specie in omnibus, neque illa, quæ manet sub auro, substaliter differt ab ea, quæ reperitur sub ligno. Cum ergo compositum non differat à composito ratione materiæ, differet per formam, quam propterea dari certum est.
units.tr: The second argument. Natural things differ from one another in substance. But they do not have this difference from matter, therefore it comes from the side of form, and so a substantial form exists. The major premise is plain: wood is a substance, wholly different from iron, iron from gold, and gold from stone, and so on. The minor premise is also evident, because matter is the same in species in all things, and the matter that underlies gold does not differ in substance from that which is found under wood. Since therefore one composite does not differ from another in respect of matter, it must differ by its form, which is certainly therefore to be posited.

units.la: Postremum, & efficacius argumentum desumitur ab anima rationali sic. Datur anima rationalis, quæ vera est forma corporis, vt definitur il Concil. Lateranensi sub Leone X. sess. 8. & antea in Vienensi sub Clem. V. ergo dantur & aliæ formæ substantiales. Quod argumentum tanti fit ab Augustino Hipho Peripatetico insigni, vt 1.phys.t.21.dicat, facile negari posse quamcumque formam substantialem, nisi adesset anima rationalis. Verum hæ rationes quantum roboris habeant, videamus; & notetur
units.tr: Last, and more forcible, is the argument drawn from the rational soul, as follows. There is a rational soul, which is the true form of the body, as the Council of Lateran under Leo X defined in session 8, and earlier the Council of Vienne under Clement V. Therefore other substantial forms also exist. Augustinus Niphus, the famous Peripatetic, held this argument in such high esteem that in his commentary on the Physics (t. 21) he says that any substantial form could easily be denied, were it not for the rational soul. But let us see how much strength these arguments have; and let it be noted

units.la: CONCLVSIO PRIMA.
units.tr: CONCLUSION ONE.

units.la: Non satis probatur ex dictis rationibus forma substantialis Aristotelea.
units.tr: The substantial form of the Aristotelians is not sufficiently proved from the arguments given.

units.la: PRobatur, quia prima ratio admittendi hanc formam erat illa. Non sufficit in composito materia prima, debet enim assignari principium, unde oriantur operationes, accidentia, virtutes &c. & hoc erit forma substantialis.Contra. Motiuum ergo admittendi hanc formam est,quia in composito datur materia prima, quae non sufficit ad operationes,accidentia,virtutes &c.Sed haec materia sic imperfecta, indiga,nuda,non datur,vt vidimus, ergo cadit ratio admittendi formam. Contra secundo.Totum id,quod huic formae substantiali tribuitur,oriri potest ab elementis,alijsve substantijs completis,perfectis, per se subsistentibus, quae formaliter in composito manent, vt suo loco dicetur, ergo non satis probatur ex hoc forma ista substantialis,incompleta,imperfecta &c.
units.tr: It is proved as follows: the first reason for admitting this form was this. Prime matter alone does not suffice in a composite, for a principle must be assigned from which operations, accidents, virtues, and so on arise, and this will be the substantial form. To the contrary: the motive for admitting this form is therefore that in a composite there is prime matter, which does not suffice for operations, accidents, virtues, and so on. But this matter, so imperfect, needy and bare, does not exist, as we have seen, so the reason for admitting the form falls. Second objection: everything that is attributed to this substantial form can arise from the elements, or from other complete and perfect substances that subsist through themselves and remain formally in the composite, as will be said in its place. Therefore this substantial form, incomplete and imperfect, is not sufficiently proved from this argument.

units.la: Probatur iterum.Ratio adducta pro secundo argumento erat, quia omne compositum substantiale differt ab alio substantialiter:non ratione materiae, quae utique similis est,ergo ex parte formae, unde probatur dari haec forma substantialis. Contra. Dici potest verisimilius, quod vna substantia siue simplex,siue composita differat substantialiter ab alia,quia in se intrinsecè diuersae naturae, atquae speciei sit.Deus enim,vt suo loco patebit, res ab exordio Mundi creauit non accidentaliter solùm,sed & substantialiter inter se differentes, quæ proinde non egebant differre per formam aliam de nouo productam. Vnde ignis v.gr. non habuit differentiam ab aere ratione formæ, sed immediatè per se, quia factus est substantia in se tota differens ab illo. Itaque lapis non differt ab auro per formam lapidis de nouo genitam in materia; sed quia eius partes constitutiuæ sunt substantiæ diuersæ ab illis, quæ faciunt aurum &c. Ergo ex hac differentia non probatur satis forma substantialis Aristotelea. Confirmatur,nam multi, celebresq; peripatetici docent,cælos non componi ex materia, & forma,cum sint substatiæ simplices; & nihilominus dicunt eos differre substantialiter inter se. Igitur differetia substatialis nō habetur à formis.
units.tr: It is proved again. The reason adduced for the second argument was that every substantial composite differs substantially from another, not by reason of matter (which is surely similar), but on the part of form; whence it is proved that this substantial form exists. Objection: it can be said more probably that one substance, whether simple or composite, differs substantially from another because it is intrinsically of a nature and species diverse in itself. For God, as will appear in its place, created things at the beginning of the world differing not only accidentally but also substantially among themselves, and these therefore did not need to differ through another form newly produced. Hence fire, for example, had no difference from air by reason of form, but immediately through itself, because it was made a substance wholly different from that. Thus stone does not differ from gold through a form of stone newly begotten in matter, but because its constituent parts are substances different from those which make up gold, and so on. Therefore the Aristotelian substantial form is not sufficiently proved from this difference. It is confirmed: many celebrated Peripatetics teach that the heavens are not composed of matter and form, since they are simple substances, and yet they say that the heavens differ substantially from one another. Therefore substantial difference is not had from forms.

units.la: Probatur 3. Postrema ratio afferendi formam substatialem petabatur ex anima rationali, quæ cùm sit vera forma corporis, vt in Lateran: definitum est, cùm actuet materiam, & cum ea vnum per se cõstituat, probat etiam de cæteris formis, quæ pari modo actuant, perficiunt,complentque materiam ad naturalis compositi effectionem. Contra. Nulla est paritas inter animam rationalem,& formas cæteras materiales, ergo ex illa nō bene arguitur ad istas. Probo antecedens. Anima rationalis creatur à Deo, non dependet à materia,spiritualis est, completa, persecta, subsistens per se, à corpore separabilis &c. E contra Materiales formæ didicantur produci à causis, quæ vtplurimum neque sunt, neque vim habent gignendi, vt supra. Deinde producuntur in materia, & dependenter ab illa, itaut sint quidem substantiæ, sed per se non subsistētes, incompletæ substantialiter, imperfectæ, non separabiles à materia &c. quæ omnia videntur non esse de conceptu rei substantialis. Quapropter si ex anima rationali probatur aliqua forma, hæc non erit illa, quam dicunt peripatetici; sed alia intrinsecè completa, per se subsistēs, independens. Imò si per separationē à corpore arguitur anima rationalis, è contra per inseparationem argui potest, non dari formas, quæ sint materiales.
units.tr: It is proved thirdly. The last reason for asserting a substantial form was drawn from the rational soul which, since it is the true form of the body (as was defined at the Lateran Council), actuates matter and constitutes one per se with it. It is thought to prove the same of the other forms, which in like manner actuate, perfect and complete matter for the production of a natural composite. Objection: there is no parity between the rational soul and the other material forms, and therefore it is not validly argued from the former to the latter. I prove the antecedent. The rational soul is created by God, does not depend on matter, is spiritual, complete, perfect, subsisting per se, separable from the body, and so on. On the contrary, material forms are known to be produced by causes which for the most part neither are nor have the power of begetting, as above. Then they are produced in matter and dependently on it, so that they are indeed substances, but not self-subsisting, substantially incomplete, imperfect, and not separable from matter, and so on. All of these seem not to belong to the concept of a substantial thing. Wherefore, if some form is proved from the rational soul, it will not be the form that the Peripatetics speak of, but another, intrinsically complete, self-subsisting and independent. Indeed, if the rational soul is argued for from its separation from the body, conversely it can be argued from its inseparability that material forms do not exist.

units.la: CONCLVSIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: SECOND CONCLUSION.

units.la: Probabile videtur, non dari materialem formam Aristoteleam.
units.tr: It seems probable that there is no material form in the Aristotelian sense.

units.la: PRobari potest conclusio ijsdem argumentis, quæ fiunt contra materiam primam, ex eo quòd repugnat substantia intrinsecè incompleta, non subsistens, quæ sic dependeat à materia, vt esse absque illa non possit &c. Sed præcipuè hac duplici ratione conclusionem probo, quia vt plurimum non adest causa talis formæ productiua, & quia si produceretur, fieret ex nihilo. Vnde crearetur. Itaque:
units.tr: This conclusion can be proved by the same arguments that are brought against prime matter, namely that a substance which is intrinsically incomplete and not subsistent, and which so depends on matter that it cannot exist without it, is impossible. But I prove the conclusion chiefly on two grounds: first, because for the most part no productive cause of such a form is present; and second, because if it were produced, it would come from nothing, and so would be created. Therefore:

units.la: Probatur 1. conclusio. Sæpissimè non potest assignari causa, quæ producat in materia huiusmodi formam substantialè, ergo. Probatur antecedens de forma cadauerica supr. disp. 1. disq. 5. Deinde probatur quoad formas viuentium. E. gr. cum pluuia modefacit æstiuum puluerem, sub ipsis intuentium oculis oriuntur ranæ, organizatæ, accidentibus instructæ. Boum viscera si exponantur soli, videntur exoriri apes, quarum structura mira est, ingeniique prodigiosum. Poma si putrescant, fiunt vermes; cum fouentur in sinu bombicum femina, bombices alij nascuntur. Ex ocymo contuso scorpij, ex madido stramine bubones, ex lacte lumbrici &c. quæ non solum historiæ Plinij, Cardani, Neirembergij, aliorumque dabunt, sed experientia ipsa ostendit. Quæro igitur, dū pluit, quænam causa producit ranam? seu formam substantialem ranæ de novo? An pluuia? sed quod est inanime nequit producere animatum; nec res imperfecta quod perfectius est. Complexio accidentium: calor, frigus, humiditas, siccitas? verum accidentia non possunt attingere substantiam. Quænam ergo causa? Similiter dum rusticolæ in sinu recondunt bombicum femina, quodnam illud est, quod substantialem bombicis formam in natura gignit? cum fiunt apes de viscere bouino, à quonam agente producuntur? à sole per vim caloris? at sol cum anima careat, quomodo illa in viuente generat? Rursus nonne sol eodem quoque modo calefacit lutum, aquam &c. deberet ergo ex his etiam omnibus educere apes. Quid ais? non educere, quia sola boum viscera dispositiones hahabent ad apum genituram? sed quænam causa ponit in ijs disposiciones cõsimiles? oritur enim circa istas eadem quæ de forma, difficultas. Vnum esse videtur, quod tota respondet Philosophia Peripatetica; horũ causas effectuum esse cælũ, astra, ranã, apemq; vagã, Deũ ipsum, &c. Hoc vero est contra Philosophum, qui non semel arguit Anaxagorã, Quòd tanquam machina vtitur intellectu (nempe Deo) ad mundi generationem; & cum dubitat, propter quam causam res est, tunc eum trahit.
units.tr: The first conclusion is proved as follows. Very often no cause can be named that produces a substantial form of this kind in matter; therefore... The antecedent is proved for the cadaver's form above, in disputation 1, question 5. Next it is proved for the forms of living things. For example, when rain has moistened summer dust, frogs arise before the very eyes of onlookers, organized and furnished with their organs. If the entrails of oxen are exposed to the sun, bees seem to arise from them, whose structure is wonderful and whose skill is prodigious. If apples rot, worms come from them; when the seeds of silkworms are kept warm in a bosom, other silkworms are born. From crushed basil come scorpions, from damp straw come bubones, from milk come earthworms, and so on. These examples are given not only by the histories of Pliny, Cardan, Nieremberg and others, but experience itself shows them. I ask therefore: while it is raining, what cause produces the frog? Or what cause produces the substantial form of the frog anew? Is it the rain? But what is inanimate cannot produce what is animate, nor can an imperfect thing produce what is more perfect. Is it the combination of accidents: heat, cold, moisture, dryness? But accidents cannot reach the substance. What cause then is there? Similarly, when countrymen shut silkworm seeds in their bosoms, what is it that generates the substantial form of the silkworm in nature? When bees arise from the ox's entrails, by what agent are they produced? By the sun through the force of its heat? But since the sun lacks a soul, how does it generate in a living thing? Again, does not the sun in the same way warm mud, water and so on? It ought therefore to bring forth bees from all of these as well. What do you say? That it does not bring them forth because only the entrails of oxen have dispositions for the generation of bees? But what cause places similar dispositions in them? For the same difficulty arises about these as about the form. There seems to be one answer that the whole Peripatetic philosophy gives: that the causes of these effects are the heavens, the stars, the frog, the wandering bee, God himself, and so on. But this is against the Philosopher, who more than once charges Anaxagoras with using intellect (that is, God) as a machine for the generation of the world, and when he is at a loss to say why a thing is, then dragging it in: That he uses intellect as a machine for the generation of the world; and when he is at a loss to say for what cause a thing is, then he drags it in.

units.la: Probatur 2.conclusio. Si de nouo fieret substãtialis hæc forma in natura, produceretur ex nihilo, & crearetur: hoc repugnat, ergo talis forma de nouo non gignitur. Maior probatur sic. Dum agens naturale producit formã in materia, vel hæc forma erat priùs in illa secundùm se tota, vel secundũ sui parte, vel secundũ nihil: Primũ, aut secundũ dici non potest, ergo tertiũ; & sic datur creatio, quæ nõ aliud est, quã pro ductio rei ex nihilo. Probo, quòd forma producta nõ erat priùs in materia secũdũ se tota, alioquin in materia latitaret infinitæ formæ, cũ omnes dicatur posse fieri ex eadem. Imò si præcederent formæ in illa, ergo simul esset forma, & priuatio, nã v.g. in ligno esset aurũ, licèt in ligno verè aurum non sit. Deniq; vel istæ formæ præcedentes in materia essent productæ, vel nõ: si productæ, igitur ex nihilo, nã priùs nihil erant, & ita creatæ: si sũt inproductæ, neque ergo esse producibiles, aut corruptibiles, quod est cõtra Peripateticam, vndæ reijcitur hęc opinio à D.Th. 1.p.q.45.ar.3. à Scoto etiam in 2.dist.18.q.vnica. Secūdū formæ non præexistunt in materia secūdū aliquā suī partem, aut secundū inchoationes, vt dicunt, nā si forma latitat in materia secundū aliquid, ergo secundū aliud non latitat; hoc igitur aliud, seu hæc alia pars nihil est; vnde cū fit, ex nihilo producitur, & ita creatur. Præterea si antequam producatur forma, lateret in materia secundū suī partē, non generaretur tota : rursus foret diuisibilis, quod absurdum est; forma enim vt forma nō habet extensionē, quare si latet secundū partē, tota latet, &c. Itaque concludendū, formas antequam generentur, non latitare in materia, nec secundū totū, nec secundū aliquid. Ergo priusquam generantur, nihil sunt. Ergo fiunt ex nihilo. Ergo creantur. Exemplum afferri potest de anima rationali, quæ cum prius non sit in materia, & ex nihilo sui fiat à Deo per creationem producitur.
units.tr: The second conclusion is proved as follows. If this substantial form were newly generated in nature, it would be produced from nothing and created. This is impossible; therefore such a form is not generated anew. The major premise is proved thus. When a natural agent produces a form in matter, either this form existed beforehand in that matter wholly in itself, or in part, or in no way. The first cannot be said, therefore the third; and so there is creation, which is nothing other than the production of a thing from nothing. I prove that the produced form did not exist beforehand in matter wholly in itself: otherwise infinitely many forms would lie hidden in matter, since all are said to be able to come from the same matter. Indeed, if these forms existed in it beforehand, a form and its privation would exist together; for example, gold would be in the wood, although gold is not truly in the wood. Finally, either these preceding forms in matter were produced or they were not. If produced, then they came from nothing, for before this they were nothing, and so they were created; if they are unproduced, then they are neither producible nor corruptible, which is contrary to the Peripatetic doctrine. For this reason this opinion is rejected by St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 45, art. 3, and also by Scotus, in 2 dist. 18, q. unica. Secondly, the forms do not preexist in matter in some part of themselves, or according to beginnings, as they say; for if a form lies hidden in matter according to something, then according to something else it does not lie hidden. This something else, or this other part, is therefore nothing; hence when it comes to be, it is produced from nothing, and so it is created. Moreover, if before the form is produced it lay hidden in matter in part of itself, it would not be generated whole; again it would be divisible, which is absurd. For a form, as form, has no extension; so if it lies hidden in part, it lies hidden wholly, and so on. Therefore we must conclude that forms, before they are generated, do not lie hidden in matter, neither wholly nor in any part. Therefore before they are generated they are nothing. Therefore they come to be from nothing. Therefore they are created. An example can be taken from the rational soul, which, since it did not previously exist in matter, and comes to be from nothing of itself, is produced by God through creation.

units.la: Respondent Aristotelei multiplici modo. Imprimis dicunt aliqui, materiales formas non creari, quia si fiunt ex nihilo sui, non tamen fiunt ex nihilo subiecti, continētur enim in potentia naturali materiæ, à qua educuntur per vim causæ naturalis. E contrà vero anima rationalis creatur, eò quòd non continetur in potentia materiæ, neque potest ab ipsa educi, sed potius aduenit materiæ, quàm ex illa educatur. Ita philosophi vniuersim.
units.tr: The Aristotelians answer in several ways. First, some say that material forms are not created, because although they come to be from nothing of themselves, they do not come to be from nothing of the subject. For they are contained in the natural potency of matter, from which they are drawn out by the power of a natural cause. On the contrary, the rational soul is created, because it is not contained in the potency of matter, nor can it be drawn out of matter, but rather it comes to matter rather than being drawn out of it. So the philosophers generally hold.

units.la: Cōtra tamē est. Rogo enim, quid significant hæc verba, Forma fit ex nihilo sui, non ex nihilo subiecti?est ne sensus, quòd aliquid formæ præexistat in subiecto, an nihil? si primum, incidimus in argumenta supra facta de inexistentia formarum; si secundum, ergo forma creatur, nam priusquam fiat, non solùm in se nihil est, sed neque in subiecto. Contra secundo, quia hæc alia verba, Forma continetur in potentia materia, non impediunt creationem, ergo si producitur, creatur. Probo antecedens. Nam & anima rationalis dici potest contenta: in potentia materiæ, quæ tamen per creationem fit; ergo & omnis alia forma creabitur. Explico: Quid est dicere, Forma continetur in potentia materia, seu educitur de materia? certè hoc solum, quòd Materia potentiam habet ad formam, seu quòd materia potest suscipere formam (neq; alium sensum reddere possunt phrases peripateticorum) sed tam bene materia potentiam habet ad animam rationalem, sicut ad aliam formam; imò magis, nā ab ipsa potest melius perfici; ergo si anima rationalis creatur, quamuis dici possit esse in potentia materiæ, queuis etiam alia forma creabitur, nā siue dicatur esse in potētia, siue ab illa educi, hoc seper manet verū, nihil priùs fuisse talis formæ.
units.tr: Yet the reply is this. I ask what these words mean: "A form comes to be from nothing of itself, not from nothing of the subject." Is the sense that something of the form preexists in the subject, or nothing? If the first, we fall into the arguments already made against the inexistence of forms; if the second, then the form is created, for before it comes to be it is not only nothing in itself but also nothing in the subject. Again, secondly, those other words, "the form is contained in the potency of matter," do not prevent creation; therefore if it is produced, it is created. I prove the antecedent. For the rational soul too can be said to be contained in the potency of matter, and yet it comes to be through creation; therefore every other form too will be created. I explain: what does it mean to say, "The form is contained in the potency of matter, or is drawn out of matter"? Surely only this, that matter has a potency for the form, or that matter can receive the form (and the phrases of the Peripatetics can yield no other sense). But matter has just as much potency for the rational soul as for any other form; indeed more, for it can be perfected better by it. Therefore if the rational soul is created, although it may be said to be in the potency of matter, any other form will be created too; for whether it is said to be in potency or to be drawn out of matter, this always remains true: that nothing of such a form existed before.

units.la: Respondent alij, non creari materiales formas; quia dependêt à materia, cōcurrēte, causante, præbēte influxū, & sustinente illas, quæ omnia significatur per illud verbū, educi. Verum anima rationalis quia nō dependet, neq; ad eius productionē concurrit materia, vt causa sustentans,& influens,bene creatur.Quod autè concurrat materia per influxum,vt causa,patet; quia formæ separari à materia non possunt fine illarum destructione, igitur ab ea continuum habent influxum, & dependentiam,& hæc ratio est,cur non creentur.
units.tr: Others answer that material forms are not created, because they depend on matter, which concurs, causes, gives influence and sustains them; all of which is signified by the word "drawn out." But the rational soul, because it does not depend on matter, nor does matter concur in its production as a sustaining and influencing cause, is rightly created. That matter concurs by influence, as a cause, is clear; for forms cannot be separated from matter without their destruction, therefore they have a continual influence and dependence upon it, and this is the reason why they are not created.

units.la: Contra tamen.Nam hæc verba. Materia influit, sustinet &c. alterum ex his debent significare, vel quòd cum agente concurrit effectiuè ad productionem formæ;vel quòd est subiectum,patiens,& recipiens forma.Si primum(quòd tamen dici nequit,vt c.p.)adhuc sequitur, formam creari;nam reuera(quidquid concurrat ad eius productionem ) priùs nihil erat.Si fecundù,non euitatur creatio, quia materia suis organis disposita, est fubiectū animæ rationalis,ad eamq; concurrit fe fubijciendo,recipiendo,patiendo. Hoc tamen non obstante,anima rationalis creatur, quia fit ex nihilo fui,ergo &c. Contra.z. quia hæc dependentia, quam dicunt habere formā à materia,non tollit creationem.Probatur. Creet Deus aliquod corpus: hoc sanè vbicumq; fit, pendet semper à loco, fiue intrinfeco,seu extrinseco,& nihilominus cū hæc dependentia verè creatur corpus, ergo etiam forma,vtcumq;dependeat à materia,fi fit ex nihilo fui , creatur. Præterea qualitates,& accidentia spiritualia pendét aliquo modo ab anima, quatenus ista est fubiectū illorum,nō enim existere possunt fe solis,& tamen hoc etiam dato,illa reuera creatur à Deo.Ergo etiamsi forma dica-tur
units.tr: On the contrary: these words, "matter influences, sustains," etc., must signify one of two things: either that matter concurs effectively with the agent in producing the form, or that it is the subject, the patient, and the receiver of the form. If the first (which, as I have shown, cannot be said), it still follows that the form is created; for in truth, whatever concurs to its production, before this it was nothing. If the second, creation is not avoided, because matter, disposed by its organs, is the subject of the rational soul, and it submits itself to the soul, receives it and undergoes it. Nevertheless the rational soul is created, because it comes to be from nothing of itself; therefore etc. Again, secondly: this dependence which they say a form has on matter does not remove creation. This is proved. Let God create some body: wherever it comes to be, it always depends on place, whether intrinsic or extrinsic; and nevertheless, with this dependence, the body is truly created; therefore the form too, however it may depend on matter, if it comes to be from nothing of itself, is created. Moreover, qualities and spiritual accidents depend in some way on the soul, in so far as it is their subject, for they cannot exist by themselves; and yet, even granting this, they are truly created by God. Therefore even if the form is said

units.la: Respondent alij, formas non creari, quia non fiunt per se, neq; producuntur; sed composita fiunt per se primò ex præiacente materia; formæ verò confiunt, seu coproducuntur, vnde nō possunt dici creari, sed coproduci ad compositi productionem, & vt habet D. Thomas 1. p. q. 45. art. 8. fieri per accidens. Ex qua explicatione colligitur, quòd si formę per se fierēt primario in materia, & non compositum, deberet actio illa esse creatio, quæ iam talis nō est, quia per eā generatur cōpositū.
units.tr: Others reply that forms are not created, because they are not made per se, nor produced; rather, composites are made per se, first, out of the pre-existing matter, while forms are made together, or co-produced, and so cannot be said to be created but co-produced with the production of the composite; and, as St Thomas holds (1. p. q. 45, art. 8), they come to be per accidens. From this explanation it follows that if forms were made per se, primarily in matter, and not the composite, that action would have to be creation; but that action is no longer creation, because through it the composite is generated.

units.la: Contra tamen. Nam actio illa, quæ facit compositum, immediatè, per se primò, & principaliùs attingit formam; ergo forma non comproducitur ad compositū, sed potiùs compositum cōproducitur ad formam. Probatur, quia priùs aliquo modo intelligi debet fieri forma, vt actualis terminus generationis, quàm vniri materiæ ad constituendum compositum, ergo forma producitur per se primò, & ex illa comproducitur compositum. Hinc ratio, quæ dicit, formā non creari, quia fit consequenter ad cōpositum, nulla est. Contra 2. Anima etiā rationalis inquit Scot. in 2. dist. 17. q. 1. & in 4. dist. 43. q. 2. non producitur actione propria, scilicet per se, verùm coproducitur ad productionem cōpositi: Per hoc tamen, ait, non tollitur, quin anima ipsa creetur. Ergo etiamsi cęterę formæ consequenter fiant ad compositum, seu eadem actione, qua ipsum, dici debent creari, quia hoc, etiam dato, fiunt ex nihilo.
units.tr: To the contrary, however: that action which makes the composite acts immediately, per se, first and more principally upon the form; therefore the form is not co-produced with the composite, but rather the composite is co-produced with the form. This is proved because the form must in some way be understood to come to be before it is united to matter to constitute the composite, as the actual term of generation; therefore the form is produced per se, first, and the composite is co-produced from it. Hence the argument which says that forms are not created, because they come to be consequently upon the composite, is worthless. Against the second point: Scotus (in 2. dist. 17, q. 1, and in 4. dist. 43, q. 2) says that the rational soul too is not produced by its own action, that is, per se, but is co-produced with the production of the composite; yet, he says, this does not prevent the soul itself from being created. Therefore, even if the other forms come to be consequently upon the composite, or by the same action by which it comes to be, they must be said to be created, because even on this supposition they come to be out of nothing.

units.la: Respondent vltimò, formam substantiaslem non creari, quia producitur de nouo dependenter à subiecto, & hanc rationem esse ab omnibus admittendam. Alioquin vnusquisq; nostrum, imò animantes omnes, & res etiam inanimes, quotiescumq; suas obeunt actiones, crearent. Cur ergo cum homo intelligit, non dicitur creare actum intellectionis? cur animal cum se mouet, non creat motum? cur planta cū nutritur, lapis cùm descendit, ignis cùm calefacit, non exercent actiones, què sint creatiuæ? an fortasse intellectio, motus, nutritio, calefactio, &c. non sunt actiones, quæ fiant ex nihilo sui? Respondebitur id, quod verum est; nimirū, quia hæc omnia fiunt dependenter à subiecto. Hoc ipsum de forma substantiali dicendum est, nimirum non creari, eò quòd ǎ subiecto dependet.
units.tr: They reply last that a substantial form is not created, because it is produced anew dependently upon a subject, and that this reason must be admitted by all. Otherwise every one of us, indeed all living things, and even inanimate things, would create whenever they perform their actions. Why, then, when a man understands, is he not said to create an act of understanding? Why, when an animal moves itself, does it not create motion? Why, when a plant is nourished, a stone when it falls, or fire when it heats, do they not exercise actions that are creative? Or perhaps understanding, motion, nutrition, heating, and so on, are not actions which come to be out of nothing of their own? The answer will be what is true, namely, that all these things come to be dependently upon a subject. The same must be said of a substantial form, namely that it is not created, because it depends upon a subject.

units.la: Contra tamen est, nam aduersarij adducunt pro ratione, quod probare debent, committuntque circulum: quoties enim rogantur, cur forma substantialis non creetur, dicunt, quia dependet à materia. Cùm rursus inquiruntur, cur hæc substantia dependeat ab alia, respondet, quia si non dependeret, crearetur. Hic autem difficultas hæret, quomodo forma, quæ substantia est, in suo esse completa, persecta, nihili ab intrinseco indiga, tamen dici debeat incompleta, dependensque à materia. imò si materia ipsa valde imperfectior, quàm forma, & incompleta pleta, non dicitur dependere ab alia, cuius forma, nobilior substantia, pendebit? Fateor ergo, dici satis probabiliter, accidentia non creari, quia fiunt cum dependentia (non enim ratio melior occurrit) sed hoc non militat pro forma, quæ cum sit substantia, ideoque subsistens per se, non apparet, quomodo ab alia essentialiter pendere valeat. Si ergo non pendet, quotiescumque fit de novo, creatur. Hoc non conceditur, ergo forma non fit.
units.tr: To the contrary, however, is this: the opponents adduce as a reason what they ought to prove, and so they commit a circular argument. For whenever they are asked why a substantial form is not created, they say, because it depends upon matter. When again they are asked why this substance depends upon another, they answer, because if it did not depend it would be created. Here, however, the difficulty sticks: how can a form, which is a substance, complete and perfect in its own being, needing nothing intrinsic, nevertheless be said to be incomplete and dependent upon matter? Indeed, if matter itself, far more imperfect than the form, and incomplete, is not said to depend upon another, upon what will a form, the nobler substance, depend? I admit, therefore, that it can be said with considerable probability that accidents are not created, because they come to be with dependence (for no better reason occurs to me); but this does not hold for the form, which, since it is a substance and therefore subsists per se, does not appear how it could depend essentially upon another. If, therefore, it does not depend, then whenever it comes to be anew, it is created. This is not granted; therefore the form does not come to be.

units.la: Verùm quia nonnulla sunt, quæ in Schola Peripatetica sciri non possunt, nisi facta earum hypothesi, præstat supponere, formas de novo substantialiter generari, ut ea non ignoremus, quæ consequenter agitari solent. Sit ergo
units.tr: But because there are some things which cannot be known in the Peripatetic School unless their hypothesis is granted, it is better to suppose that forms are generated anew substantially, so that we may not be ignorant of those matters which are customarily discussed in consequence. Let it be so, therefore:

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISQUISITIO SECUNDA.

units.la: Virum data forma substantiali Aristote- lea, hæc possit cum aliis esse simul in materia.
units.tr: Whether, with a substantial form given in the Aristotelian manner, another form can exist at the same time in the matter.

units.la: PRo intelligentia præmittendum est, huiusmodi quæstionem fieri solere tam in statu naturæ, quàm per vim supernaturalem. Quæri enim potest, an plures formæ simul esse possint naturaliter in materia. Secundò si naturaliter hoc nequeat, an saltem fieri possit ex Dei virtute. Rursus loqui possumus aut de formis totalibus, aut de partialibus. Modò igitur inquirimus, an plures totales in una, eademque materia simul esse naturaliter possint. V.gr. vtrum in materia ligni possit naturaliter simul reperiri etiam forma ignis. Pro qua re decidenda, notetur
units.tr: Before we begin, it must be said that this question is usually raised both in the state of nature and through supernatural power. For one may ask whether several forms can naturally exist together in one matter; and, secondly, if this cannot happen naturally, whether it can at least come about by the power of God. Again, we may speak either of total forms or of partial ones. Now, then, we inquire whether several total forms can naturally exist together in one and the same matter; for example, whether the form of fire can also be found naturally together with the matter of wood. To settle this matter, let the following be noted.

units.la: CONCLVSIO PRIMA.
units.tr: FIRST CONCLUSION.

units.la: Plures formæ totales nequeunt simul esse in una, eademque materia naturaliter.
units.tr: Several total forms cannot naturally be together in one and the same matter.

units.la: PRobatur facile, quia forma, vt aiunt Aristotelei, est actus, qui physicè actuat, satiat, complet materiam, adeout naturalis potentia illius perficiatur intrinsecè, atque omnino expleatur à forma. Ergo si adsit in materia v.gr. forma ligni, factum est satis naturæ, neque aliam admittit.
units.tr: This is easily proved, because form, as the Aristotelians say, is an act which physically actuates, satisfies and completes matter, so that the natural potency of matter is intrinsically perfected and wholly filled up by the form. Therefore if the form of wood, for example, is present in the matter, nature has been sufficiently provided for, and it admits no other.

units.la: Probatur 2. Nam quemadmodum corruptio vnius est generatio alterius; ita è contra generatio vnius est alterius corruptio. Ergo si gignitur noua forma in materia, opus est aliam corrumpi, & sic duæ simul esse non possunt. Confirmatur, quia vt noua inducatur forma in materiam, præmitti debent accidentia propria illius; hæc autem sunt destructiua præcedentis formæ; igitur forma præcedens non manebit simul cum noua. Sic v.g. ignis non inducit similem sibi formam, nisi præmittat calorem, & siccitatem, quæ alterent, corrumpantque formam ligni. Quare cùm hoc fieri semper à natura videamus, concludendum est, multiplicé formā esse naturaliter non posse in materia simul.
units.tr: Proof 2. For just as the corruption of one thing is the generation of another, so conversely the generation of one thing is the corruption of another. Therefore if a new form is generated in matter, another must be corrupted, and so two cannot be together. It is confirmed: in order for a new form to be induced into matter, its proper accidents must first be introduced, and these are destructive of the preceding form; therefore the preceding form will not remain together with the new one. Thus, for example, fire does not induce a form like itself unless it first brings heat and dryness, which alter and corrupt the form of wood. Since we always see this done by nature, it must be concluded that several forms cannot naturally be in matter at the same time.

units.la: Obijcies 1.In vno, eodemque composit[…] to manent simul quatuor elementa; sed hæc habent suas formas, ergo naturaliter plures formæ sunt simul. Maior patet in resolutione mixti, quam sæpe videmus in terram,aquam,aerem, & ignem fieri. Minor etiam est certa, nam elementa cum_ transmutari possint, componi debent ex forma,quæ sola corrumpitur, amittiturque.
units.tr: You will object: 1. In one and the same composite, the four elements remain together; but these have their own forms; therefore several forms are naturally together. The major is evident in the resolution of a mixed body, which we often see turned into earth, water, air and fire. The minor is also certain, for since the elements can be transmuted, they must be composed of a form which alone is corrupted and lost.

units.la: Respondeo negando minorem. Elementa enim sunt corpora quædam simplicia, non composita ex materia, & forma. Vnde cum reperiatur in composito simul, non adsunt in eo plures formæ. Ad probationem itaque, nego elementa substantialiter corrumpi, ac transmutari, quod suo loco ad sensum patebit.
units.tr: I answer by denying the minor. For the elements are certain simple bodies, not composed of matter and form. Hence, since they are found together in the composite, there are not several forms in it. As for the proof, I deny that the elements are substantially corrupted and transmuted, which will be clear in its place.

units.la: Obijcies 2. Corpus humanum plures habet formas in eadem materia: sed hoc naturaliter fit,ergo &c. Probatur maior, nam v.gr.si accipiatur os,in huius materia est forma offis, & forma etiam animæ rationalis. Maior citra dubium versatur, nam forma offis naturaliter gignitur in_ materia; & anima pariter ab auctore Naturæ,qui se naturali accômodat exigentiæ rerum.
units.tr: Objection 2. The human body has several forms in the same matter; but this happens naturally; therefore etc. The major is proved: for example, if one takes a bone, in its matter there is the form of bone and also the form of the rational soul. The major is beyond doubt, for the form of bone is naturally generated in matter, and the soul likewise by the Author of Nature, who accommodates himself to the natural requirements of things.

units.la: Respondeo distinguendo maiorem. Habet plures formas in eadem materia totales,& non subordinatas,nego;partiales,& subordinatas, concedo, & nego consequentiam. Ratio est,nam duplex distingui debet formarum genus,aliæ sunt per se totales,& non subordinatæ alteri à natura quæquemadmodum v.gr.forma lapidis, auri &c. quæ constituunt lapidem,aurumque, nec ad aliud ordinatæ sunt. Quædam verò formæ dicuntur partiales, quæ subordinantur superiori, & sunt veluti ad ipsam dispositiones. Ita forma oculi, forma ossis,forma carnis &c.sunt partiales,quia partim constituunt humanum corpus: & sunt subordinatæ,quia fiunt à natura velut organa, & dispositiones ad animam. Forma ergo partialis bene, vt aiunt, potest simul esse cum totali; Non verò totalis cum alia quoque totali, vt alibi susius.
units.tr: I answer by distinguishing the major. It has several forms in the same matter which are total and not subordinate: I deny. Partial and subordinate: I concede, and I deny the consequence. The reason is that a twofold kind of form must be distinguished. Some are in themselves total and not subordinate by nature to anything else, such as the form of stone, of gold, etc., which constitute stone and gold and are not ordered to anything else. Other forms are called partial, which are subordinate to a superior and are, as it were, dispositions towards it. So the form of the eye, the form of bone, the form of flesh, etc., are partial, because they partly constitute the human body; and they are subordinate, because they are made by nature as organs and dispositions for the soul. A partial form, therefore, can well, as they say, be together with a total one; but a total form cannot be together with another total form, as I have explained more fully elsewhere.

units.la: Addis: forma ossis complet materiæ capacitatem, vnde animâ etiam sublatâ, materia cum ea sola manet, quemadmodum patet in cane mortuo. Resp. quòd forma ossis nec adhuc dici potest forma totalis, quamuis enim satiet materiam in sua speciejillam tamen non satis naturaliter incapacem alterius: quod requiritur ad conceptum formæ totalis.
units.tr: You add: the form of bone completes the capacity of the matter, so that even with the soul removed, the matter remains with it alone, as is evident in a dead dog. Reply: the form of bone cannot yet be called a total form. For although it satisfies the matter in its own species, it is not so naturally incapable of another form, and this is required for the concept of a total form.

units.la: D CON-
units.tr: D CON-

units.la: CONCLVSIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: CONCLUSION TWO.

units.la: Plures formæ totales bene possunt per Deū potentiam in una, eademque materia esse si- mul.
units.tr: Several total forms can, by the power of God, be together in one and the same matter.

units.la: PRobatur,nam tota ratio,cur hoc naturaliter fieri non possit, hæc esse dicitur,quia generatio vnius est corruptio alterius,& dum noua producitur forma, expellitur vetus,quæ aderat prior:Sed potest Deus impedire hanc formæ veteris expulsionem,ergo in tali casu erunt plures formæ totales in eadem materia simul. Maior tenetur ab omnibus.Minor probatur;nam Deus impedire potest secundarium effectum cuiuscumq; causæ:sed expulsio formæ veteris est effectus secundarius formæ nouæ, igitur à Deo impediri potest. Consequentia currit;nam si Deus cùm introducitur forma ignis, impediat, ne à materia expellatur forma ligni, tunc aderit hæc forma duplex in eodem subiecto simul.
units.tr: It is proved thus: the whole reason why this cannot happen naturally is said to be this, that the generation of one thing is the corruption of another, and while a new form is produced, the old form which was present before is expelled. But God can prevent this expulsion of the old form; therefore in such a case there will be several total forms together in the same matter. The major is held by all. The minor is proved: for God can prevent the secondary effect of any cause whatever; but the expulsion of the old form is a secondary effect of the new form; therefore it can be prevented by God. The consequence holds: for if, when the form of fire is introduced, God prevents the form of wood from being expelled from the matter, then this double form will be present in the same subject at once.

units.la: Pro qua re magis capienda, hoc aduertite, quòd causa formalis duplicem habet effectum formalem. Alter dicitur primarius;alter verò secundarius. Ille non est, nisi forma ipsa in materia. Iste autem aliud quid ab ea consequens. V.g.calor in ferro habet effectum primarium, nempe constituere calidum, & hic non aliud est, quàm caloris forma in subiecto. Deinde scsecundarium, videlicet expellere frigus, & id consequitur ad primum. Itaque Deus non potest sane primum effectu impedire, nam posito calore in subiecto, repugnat quòd non sit calor in eo, & non resultet quid calidum. Potest nihilominus impedire secundarium, scilicet expulsionem frigoris, in quo casu adesset in ferro calor, frigusque simul. Hoc ipsum à pari de formis, nam v. gr. introducta forma ignis in lignum, neq; Deus efficere potest, quin hoc sit ignis; bene tamen impedire potest, ne destruatur forma præcedens ligni; & sic duplex aderit forma, ignis, & ligni.
units.tr: To grasp this matter more easily, take note that a formal cause has a twofold formal effect. The one is called primary, the other secondary. The first is nothing but the form itself in the matter; the second is something else, following from it. For example, heat in iron has a primary effect, namely to make the iron hot, and this is nothing other than the form of heat in the subject. Then it has a secondary effect, namely to drive out cold, and this follows from the first. Thus God cannot indeed prevent the primary effect: once heat is posited in the subject, it is contradictory that there should not be heat in it, and that something hot should not result. Nevertheless he can prevent the secondary effect, namely the expulsion of cold; in that case there would be heat and cold together in the iron. The same holds by parity for forms: for instance, when the form of fire is introduced into wood, God cannot bring it about that this is not fire; yet he can prevent the previous form of wood from being destroyed, and so there will be a double form, of fire and of wood.

units.la: Obijcies 1. si plures formæ diuinitus sorent in vna materia; v. gr. si adesser simul forma ferri, & auri, compositum esset chimæricum, ergo nec diuinitus potest hoc fieri. Antecedens patet, nam res eadē foret aurum simul, & ferrum, eo modo quo si duæ naturæ hirci, atq; cerui simul forent, idē esset hircus, & ceruus, quod implicat.
units.tr: You will object, first: if several forms were brought about by God in one matter, for example if the form of iron and the form of gold were present together, the compound would be chimerical; therefore not even by God's power can this happen. The antecedent is plain: the same thing would be gold and iron at once, in the way that if two natures, of a he-goat and a stag, were together, the same thing would be a goat and a stag, which implies a contradiction.

units.la: Resp. negando antecedens. Et ratio est, nam forma ferri, & auri essent profectò simul penetratæ, non tamen identificatæ, quamuis enim in vna materia reperirentur, nihilominus inter se distinctæ manerent, quia vna non esset alia, quàquā intimè præsens illi. Ad probationē dico, quòd res eadem, seu materia esset ferrum, & aurum respectu diuersorum, nam quatenus habet formam auri, aurum est; quatenus ferri, ferrum est. Non tamen aurum prout aurum esset ferrū, quia requiritur ad hoc non sola vnius formæ cum alia penetra-tio, tio, sed praeterea identificatio. Exemplum de natura hirci, & cerui simul, non facit ad rem, neque probat chimæram, ly enim simul dicit vnionem, non identificationem, vnde hircus adhuc esset hircus; ceruus adhuc ceruus, &c. Quòdsi natura vnius non vniretur tantùm; sed cum alia etiam identificaretur, in eo quidem casu chimæra foret.
units.tr: I answer by denying the antecedent. The reason is this: the form of iron and the form of gold would indeed be penetrated together, but not identified; for although they would be found in one matter, they would nevertheless remain distinct from each other, since one would not be the other, however intimately present to it. As for the proof, I say that the same thing, or the matter, would be iron and gold with respect to different things: insofar as it has the form of gold, it is gold; insofar as it has the form of iron, it is iron. But gold would not be iron as gold, because for this there is required not merely the penetration of one form with another, but also identification. The example of the nature of a he-goat and a stag together does not bear on the matter, nor does it prove a chimera; for the word "together" signifies union, not identification, whence the he-goat would still be a he-goat and the stag still a stag, and so on. But if the nature of one were not merely united, but also identified with another, then in that case there would indeed be a chimera.

units.la: Vrges. Compositū, quod aurum est, nullo modo potest esse ferrum: sed posita duplici forma, idem prorsus compositum efset aurum, & ferrum, ergo sequeretur quid chimæricum. Patet maior, aurum enim, vt aurum, est natura talis, contradistincta omnino à natura ferri. Minor quoque probatur, nam si forma, auri & ferri simul inessent in vna materia, vtraque componeret in suo genere, vnde prima efficeret aurum; secunda ferrum, ergo idem compositum effet aurum, & ferrum.
units.tr: You press: the compound which is gold can in no way be iron; but if a double form were posited, the very same compound would be both gold and iron; therefore something chimerical would follow. The major is plain, for gold, as gold, is a nature wholly distinct from the nature of iron. The minor is also proved: for if the forms of gold and of iron were together in one matter, each would compose in its own kind, so that the first would make gold and the second iron; therefore the same compound would be gold and iron.

units.la: Respondeo, concessa maiori, negando minorem. Ratio est, nam posita duplici forma in materia, non fieret vnum tantummodo compositum; sed omninò duplex; & propterea non esset res eadem aurum, & ferrum, quamuis adessent simul & aurum, & ferrum. Ad probationem dico, quòd forma auri cum materia componeret sanè aurum, & hoc est vnum compositum. Rursus forma ferri cum eadem materia constitueret ferrum, sed hoc est aliud compositum; vnde non sequitur, idem fore aurum, et ferrum. Ratio assignatur, nam distinctio compositi sumitur à forma, quæ pars præcipua & constitutiua est. Duplex autem adesset forma, ergo duplex compositum.
units.tr: I answer: granting the major, I deny the minor. The reason is this: once a double form is posited in the matter, there would not be only one compound, but altogether two; and therefore the thing would not be gold and iron at once, although gold and iron were present together. As for the proof, I say that the form of gold, together with the matter, would indeed compose gold, and this is one compound. Again, the form of iron with the same matter would constitute iron, but this is another compound; whence it does not follow that the same thing would be gold and iron. The reason is assigned: for the distinction of a compound is taken from its form, which is the principal and constitutive part. Now there would be a double form, therefore a double compound.

units.la: Vrges iterum. Materia esset vna; sed cōstitueretur simul in esse auri, & ferri, ergo res eadem esset aurum, & ferum. Patet minor, nam vna, eademque materia perficeretur a forma auri, & sic maneret aurum; & eadem quoque a forma ferri, & ita esset ferrum. Vnde ferrum esset aurum, & è contra.
units.tr: You press again: the matter would be one; but it would be constituted at once in the being of gold and of iron; therefore the same thing would be gold and iron. The minor is plain: the one and the same matter would be perfected by the form of gold and so remain gold, and likewise by the form of iron and so be iron. Whence iron would be gold, and conversely.

units.la: Respondeo cum distinctione ad minorem: constitueretur simul in esse auri, & ferri per vnicam formam, nego; per duplicem, concedo. Ergo res eadem esset aurū, & ferrum respectu diuersorum, conceditur, respectu eiusdem, negatur. Itaq; dico, materia fore in eo casu aurū, sed quatenus alligata formæ auri, & ferrum, sed quatenus vnita formæ ferri. Ex quo tamen non sequitur illa consequentia: Ergo aurum effet ferrum, & è contra. Ratio est, nam aurum dicit duo, nempe materiā, & formā auri; quoniam verò hæc auri forma semper distinguetur à forma ferri, ob id aurum nunquam erit ferrum; sed bene auri materia per formam ferri erit ferrum.
units.tr: I answer, with a distinction, to the minor: that it would be constituted at once in the being of gold and of iron through a single form, I deny; through a double form, I grant. Therefore the same thing would be gold and iron with respect to different things, which I grant; with respect to the same thing, I deny. So I say that in that case the matter would be gold, insofar as it is joined to the form of gold, and iron, insofar as it is united to the form of iron. From this, however, the following inference does not follow: therefore gold would be iron, and conversely. The reason is that "gold" signifies two things, namely the matter and the form of gold; and since this form of gold will always be distinguished from the form of iron, gold will never be iron; but the matter of gold, through the form of iron, will indeed be iron.

units.la: Objicies secundo. Si duæ formæ totales possent simul inesse in vna materia, ergo posset quis esse simul homo, & cadauer: sed hoc repugnat, alioquin esset homo, & non homo; viuens, & non viuens, ergo absurda conclusio.
units.tr: You will object secondly: if two total forms could be together in one matter, then someone could be at once a man and a corpse; but this is repugnant, otherwise he would be a man and not a man, living and not living; therefore the conclusion is absurd.

units.la: Respondeo imprimis negando sequellam. Ratio est, nam cadaver non constituitur per formam cadaueris positiuam; sed per meram animæ priuationem, & sic quia nequit simul esse priuatio cum forma, neque potest quis esse simul homo, & cadauer. Secundo, facta hypothesi, quòd cadauer fiat per formam positiuam, quam vocant cadauericam, dico posse aliquem simul esse hominem, & cadauer; quia Deus quæ positiua sunt, potest relinquere simul. Ad Minorem dico, non sequi hæc duo contradictoria: esset homo, & non homo; viueret, & non viuēret. Ratio est, nam etsi ratione formæ cadauericæ non esset homo, respectu tamen alterius, nempe animæ, talis esset.
units.tr: I answer, first, by denying the consequence. The reason is that a corpse is not constituted by a positive form of corpse, but by the mere privation of the soul; and so, since privation cannot be together with form, neither can someone be at once a man and a corpse. Second, granting the hypothesis that a corpse comes about through a positive form, which they call the cadaveric form, I say that someone can be at once a man and a corpse, because God can leave together things which are positive. As for the minor, I say that these two contradictories do not follow: he would be a man and not a man; he would live and not live. The reason is that, although by reason of the cadaveric form he would not be a man, nevertheless with respect to the other, namely the soul, he would be such.

units.la: Simili modo quo si adesset simul in eodem subiecto calor, & frigus, male diceretur: est calidum, & non calidum, quamuis enim ex parte frigoris non calescat; aliunde tamen respectu caloris tale omnino est.
units.tr: In the same way, if heat and cold were together in the same subject, one would wrongly say: it is hot and not hot; for although it is not heated on the side of the cold, nevertheless with respect to the heat it is altogether such.

units.la: DISPVTATIO TERTIA.
units.tr: DISPUTATIO TERTIA.

units.la: De Priuatione Aristotelea.
units.tr: On the Aristotelian Privation.

units.la: TErtium rei naturalis principium dicitur à Philosopho Priuatio. Quoties enim compositum naturale fit, non solùm adest materia, vt subiectum, & forma, quæ in eo recipitur; sed quia materia transit à priuatione formæ ad formam, propterea in conceptu generationis tria sunt; Materia, quæ transit; Forma, ad quam transfit; Priuatio, à qua transit. Quæ dicuntur principia corporis naturalis in fieri. Duo autem sunt in Facto esse, Materia, & Forma, nam postquam compositum factum est, hæc duo tantummodo manent.
units.tr: The third principle of a natural thing is called by the Philosopher Privation. For whenever a natural composite comes to be, there is present not only matter, as subject, and the form which is received in it; but because matter passes from the privation of a form to the form, therefore in the concept of generation there are three things: matter, which passes; form, to which it passes; and privation, from which it passes. These are called the principles of a natural body in becoming. There are, however, two that remain in the finished state, matter and form, for once the composite has been made, only these two remain.

units.la: Priuatio autem est ipsum non esse rei, sed in subiecto apto ad illam. V.g. cæcitas in oculo dicitur priuatio visus, nam etsi oculus non videat, nihilominus aptitudinem habet ad visum. E contra si non esse rei fit in subiecto non apto ad ipsam, vocatur negatio. E.g. carentia visionis in lapide, negatio est, quia lapis non solùm non videt; sed neque aptus est ad videndum. Vnde patet quomodo priuatio differat à negatione, scilicet penes aptitudinem subiecti, quam dicit priuatio, non verò negatio.
units.tr: Privation, moreover, is the non-being of a thing itself, but in a subject apt for it. For example, blindness in the eye is called privation of sight, for although the eye does not see, it nevertheless has an aptitude for sight. On the contrary, if the non-being of a thing is found in a subject not apt for it, it is called negation. E.g., the lack of sight in a stone is a negation, because a stone not only does not see, but is not even apt for seeing. Hence it is clear how privation differs from negation, namely in respect of the aptitude of the subject, which privation implies and negation does not.

units.la: Duplex est priuatio, Proxima, & Remota. Proxima est carentia formæ in subiecto proximè apto ad eam habendam. V.g. materia ligni si iam fit cum calore, ac siccitate, quæ disponunt ad ignem, habet priuationem formæ ignis proximam. Remota verò est carentia formæ in subiecto, quod non habet aptitudinem proximam, vt formam suscipiat. V.g. lignum absque calore, ac siccitate manet cum priuatione remota formæ ignis.
units.tr: Privation is twofold, proximate and remote. Proximate is the lack of a form in a subject that is immediately apt to have it. For example, the matter of wood, when it already has heat and dryness, which dispose it toward fire, has the proximate privation of the form of fire. Remote, however, is the lack of a form in a subject that does not have a proximate aptitude to receive the form. For example, wood without heat and dryness remains under the remote privation of the form of fire.

units.la: Duo verò quæri possunt à nobis in materia de Priuatione. An hæc habeat aliquod esse à parte rei, ratione cuius dici valeat principium. Secundò, Quandonam dici debeat exercere munus principij. Quod attinet ad primum, fit.
units.tr: Two questions, however, can be raised by us concerning privation in matter. First, whether it has some being in the thing itself, by reason of which it may be rightly called a principle. Second, when it ought to be said to exercise the office of a principle. As regards the first, it is so.

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: DISQUISITIO PRIMA.

units.la: Vtrum Priuatio habeat aliquod esse à parte rei.
units.tr: Whether privation has some being on the part of the thing.

units.la: PRo intelligentia sciendum est id, quod aiunt frequentes Peripatetici, esse rei distingui & in esse rei positiuum, & in esse rei priuatiuum, seu negatiuum. Esse rei positiuum aliquid est, realemque dicit entitatem, vt cuique patet. Sed etiam esse rei priuatiuum, aut negatiuum aliquid est; nam reuera in lapide v.g. datur non esse auri, non esse ferri, non esse ligni, vnde vera est hæc propositio: lapis non est aurum, non ferrum, non lignum &c. Quare priuatio hæc formarum habet aliquod esse à parte rei. Sed contra & sit.
units.tr: For clarification, it must be understood that, as the frequent Peripatetics say, the being of a thing is distinguished into positive being and privative, or negative, being. Positive being is something real and signifies a real entity, as is plain to everyone. But privative or negative being is also something; for in a stone, for example, there is a not-being of gold, a not-being of iron, a not-being of wood, whence this proposition is true: the stone is not gold, not iron, not wood, etc. Therefore this privation of forms has some being on the part of the thing. But on the contrary, let it be considered.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Priuatio, vt priuatio non habet esse à partei rei.
units.tr: A privation, as a privation, does not have being from the side of the thing.

units.la: PRobatur, quia priuatio est merum non esse formæ: sed merum non esse rei nullum habet esse, igitur nec priuatio. Maior de se patet. Minor probatur sic. Non esse rei si habet aliquod esse, aut hoc esse, quod habet, positiuum est, aut negatiuum. Si primum, ergo non esse habet positiuum esse, quod repugnat. Si secundum, ergo non esse reuera nullum habet esse, quia esse negatiuum nihil est.
units.tr: This is proved because a privation is the mere non-being of a form; but the mere non-being of a thing has no being, and therefore neither does a privation. The major is evident of itself. The minor is proved thus. If the non-being of a thing has some being, then either the being it has is positive or it is negative. If the first, then non-being has positive being, which is contradictory. If the second, then non-being in truth has no being, because negative being is nothing.

units.la: Probatur 2. Si negatio, & priuatio haberent aliquod esse verum in se, ac independenter ab intellectu, hoc esset improductum, independens à Deo, æternum, infinitum actu, & alia sequerentur absurda. Ergo &c. Sequella probatur quoad primum, quia Mundus ab æterno habuit negationem sui, ergo si negatio est aliquid, hoc fuit ab æterno, improductum, & independens; nam omnia, quæ sunt ab æterno, talia sunt. Probatur etiam quoad secundum, quia de facto dantur iam negationes infinitorum hominum, orbium, siderum; ergo si negatio aliquid est, actu datur infinitas in genere negationum &c.
units.tr: Proof 2. If negation and privation had some true being in themselves, and independently of the intellect, this being would be unproduced, independent of God, eternal, and actually infinite, and other absurd consequences would follow. Therefore etc. The consequence is proved as to the first point: the world has had the negation of itself from eternity; therefore, if negation is something, it has been from eternity, unproduced and independent, for all things that exist from eternity are such. It is also proved as to the second point: in fact there already exist the negations of infinitely many men, worlds and stars; therefore, if negation is something, there actually exists an infinity in the genus of negations, etc.

units.la: Obijcies 1. veræ sunt hæ propositiones. In ligno datur priuatio formæ ignis: in auro adest priuatio formæ lapidis &c. ergo priuatio habet aliquod esse à parte rei. Confirmatur, quia ex duobus oppositis alterum semper esse debet à parte rei : sed priuatio est oppositum formæ ; igitur si non adest in ligno forma ignis , adest in eodem illius priuatio .
units.tr: You will object, first, that these propositions are true: "In wood there is a privation of the form of fire"; "in gold there is present a privation of the form of stone," etc. Therefore privation has some being from the side of the thing. It is confirmed, because of two opposites one must always have being from the side of the thing; but privation is the opposite of form; therefore, if the form of fire is not present in the wood, the privation of it is present in the same wood.

units.la: Resp. negando consequentiam . Ratio est, nam vt illæ propositiones verę sint, requiritur solummodo ipsum non esse formæ , vnde licet priuatio attingatur in recto, dicendo v.g. datur priuatio formæ, tamen ex intentione sana significandi redditur hic sensus . Forma non est in subiecto . Ad confirmationem dico, priuationem, & formam opponi quidem , sed priuatiuè, non contrariè, sicuti ergo tenebræ, quæ priuatiuè opponuntur luci , non habent esse à parte rei, sic omnino quæuis alia priuatio .
units.tr: I answer by denying the consequence. The reason is that for those propositions to be true, only the non-being of the form itself is required; hence, although privation is taken directly in the words, when one says, for example, "there is a privation of the form," nevertheless, by a sound intention of signifying, this sense is conveyed: "the form is not in the subject." As to the confirmation, I say that privation and form are indeed opposed, but privatively, not contrarily; just as therefore darkness, which is privatively opposed to light, does not have being from the side of the thing, so entirely does any other privation.

units.la: Obijcies 2. Bona est diuisio entis in positiuum, & priuatiuum, ergo non primum tantummodo, sed etiam hoc secundum est verum ens , habetque à parte rei aliquod esse .
units.tr: You will object, second, that the division of being into positive and privative is a good one; therefore not only the first but also this second is a true being, and has some being from the side of the thing.

units.la: Resp. cum distinctione. Bona est diuisio entis in priuatiuum, quoad entitatem rei, nego; quoad veritatem propositionis, concedo : igitur priuatio est ens, habetque à parte rei aliquod esse, negatur. Explicat id S. Thomas. 1. p. 48. art. 2. ad 2. Ens , inquit, dupliciter dicitur , uno modo secundum quod significat entitatem rei; & hoc modo priuatio non est ens; alio modo secundum quod significat veritatem propositionis, & sic cæcitatem dicimus esse in oculo &c. Non igitur dicimus , cæcitatem esse vere in oculo, quia hæc aliquid fit, sed quia vera est propositio negans in oculo visionē.
units.tr: I answer with a distinction. That the division of being into privative is a good one, as regards the entity of the thing, I deny; as regards the truth of the proposition, I concede. Therefore privation is a being and has some being from the side of the thing, this is denied. St. Thomas explains this, 1 p. q. 48 art. 2 ad 2: "Being," he says, "is said in two ways: in one way according as it signifies the entity of a thing, and in this way privation is not a being; in another way according as it signifies the truth of a proposition, and thus we say that blindness is in the eye," etc. Therefore we do not say that blindness is truly in the eye because it is something, but because the proposition denying vision in the eye is true.

units.la: Ergo priuatio cūm nihil sit, quomodo bene dicetur principium corporis in fieri? Vnde patet hoc quoque principium, quod assignant Aristotelei, esse suspectum.
