Præcipuè quia potest concipi compositum in fieri non includendo priuationem. Si enim Deus creet materiam, & in eodem instanti producat in ea, & dependenter ab ea formam, sanè fit compositum per veram generationem, & nihilominus forma non transit à priuatione sui, quia nunquam talis priuatio fuit in materia. Quidquid tamen sit, supponamus priuationem esse aliquid, & esse principiū, quæritur in hac hypothesi, quonā tempore munus principij exerceat. Sit ergo.
units.tr: Therefore, since privation is nothing, how can it rightly be called a principle of the body in becoming? Hence it is clear that this principle, which the Aristotelians assign, is also open to suspicion. Especially because a compound can be conceived as coming into being without including privation. For if God creates matter, and in the same instant produces in it, and dependently on it, a form, then surely the compound comes to be through true generation, and nevertheless the form does not pass out of a privation of itself, because such a privation never existed in the matter. Whatever be the case, let us suppose that privation is something and is a principle; the question in this hypothesis is at what time it exercises the office of a principle. Let it be so.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.

units.la: Quandonam Priuatio exerceat munus principij.
units.tr: When Privation Exercises the Function of a Principle.

units.la: PRo intelligentia debetis aduertere quod supra inhuimus, compositum in duplici statu assumi posse, nimirum in fieri, & in esse facto. Nunc eum primo expendimus modo, videlicet quatenus fit, in quo casu tria dicit principia, Materiam, Formam, Priuationem. Imprimis enim generatio exercetur in subiecto, & sic adest materia. Deinde habet suum terminum, & hæc est forma. Rursus quod gignitur, debet prius non fuisse, transfit enim à non efse sui,& hoc non esse Priuatio est,quæ dicitur principium reale generationis, non quia in se aliquid reale sit, verùm quia forma debet realiter non esse, vt possit generari. Oritur autem controuersia inter scholasticos, an priuatio exerceat munus principij ad generationem eo tempore,quo est; an eo potiùs, quo non est. Res mihi videtur parui momenti, quidquid alij rixantes contendant. Notetur ergo.
units.tr: For understanding, you must notice what we pointed out above: a composite can be taken in two states, namely in becoming (in fieri) and in completed being (in esse facto). Now we examine it first in the way it is becoming, and in that case there are three principles: matter, form, and privation. First, generation takes place in a subject, and so matter is present. Next, it has its terminus, and this is form. Further, what is generated must previously not have been, for it passes from the non-being of itself; and this non-being is privation, which is called the real principle of generation, not because it is anything real in itself, but because the form must really not be, in order that it may be generated. Now a controversy arises among the scholastics, whether privation exercises the function of a principle for generation at the time when it is, or rather at the time when it is not. The matter seems to me of little moment, whatever others may argue with their quarrels. Let it be noted, then.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Priuatio exercet munus principij ad generationem compositi eo pri- mo instanti, quo non est.
units.tr: Privation exercises the function of a principle for the generation of a composite at the first instant in which it is not.

units.la: PRobatur. r. nam eo primo instanti, quo non est priuatio formæ, generatur forma in materia, & fit compositum, ergo priuatio exercet munus principij eo primo instanti, quo non est. Probo antecedens. Detur instans, a: in quo lignum suscipiat formam ignis, quæro: vel pro instanti, a: est adhuc priuatio formæ ignis, vel non: si primum, ergo manet simul forma, & priuatio, quod repugnat, alioquin possent quoque simul esse tenebræ, ac lux, cæcitas, visus &c. Si secundum, igitur eo instanti, quo suscipitur forma in materia, illius priuatio non est; ergo priuatio exercet munus principij ad generationem compositi quando primo non est.
units.tr: It is proved. First, because at the first instant in which the privation of the form is not, the form is generated in the matter and the composite comes to be; therefore privation exercises the function of a principle at the first instant in which it is not. I prove the antecedent. Let there be an instant, a, at which the wood receives the form of fire. I ask: either at instant a the privation of the form of fire is still there, or it is not. If the first, then form and privation remain together, which is contradictory; otherwise darkness and light, blindness and sight, etc., could also be together. If the second, then at the instant in which the form is received into the matter, its privation is not; therefore privation exercises the function of a principle for the generation of the composite when it first is not.

units.la: Probatur 2.conclusio. Non potest priuatio exercere munus principij, nisi quando materia transit à priuatione ad formam; sed eo instanti priuatio non est, ergo dici debet principium eo primo instanti quo non est. Maior patet, quia priuatio est principium compositi dum fit, non in facto esse, ac propterea exercet munus principij quando materia transit. Minor probatur, materia enim dum transit à priuatione, tunc primò priuatio non est, ergo dici debet principium eo primo instanti, quo non est. Confirmatur, nam si priuatio esset principium quando est, modò fieret in hoc ligno generatio formæ ignis, quia in eo adest iam talis formæ priuatio. Neque dicas, non adesse vltimò hanc priuationem: licèt enim hoc instans a. foret vltimum priuationis, adeout in sequenti debeat intelligi forma produci: Attamen pro toto instanti. a. compositum non fit; ergo priuatio durans pro instanti. a. esse nequit principium compositi vt infieri.
units.tr: The second conclusion is proved. Privation cannot exercise the function of a principle except when matter passes from privation to form; but at that instant privation is not; therefore it ought to be called the principle at the first instant in which it is not. The major is plain, because privation is the principle of the composite while it is becoming, not in completed being, and therefore it exercises the function of a principle when the matter passes over. The minor is proved: for matter, while it passes from privation, at that very time privation first is not; therefore it ought to be called the principle at the first instant in which it is not. It is confirmed: for if privation were a principle when it is, then now in this wood the generation of the form of fire would be taking place, since in it such a privation of the form already is. Nor may you say that this privation does not last to the very last: for although instant a would be the last instant of the privation, so that in the following instant the form ought to be understood as produced, nevertheless the composite does not come to be for the whole instant a; therefore privation, lasting for the instant a, cannot be the principle of the composite as in becoming.

units.la: Obijcies. 1. non potest verificari propositio de secundo adiacente, nisi verificetur de primo. V.g. dici nequit, Petrus est doctus, Leo est rugiens, nisi priùs dicatur: Petrus est, Leo est. Ergo priuatio si non est, dici non potest esse principium generationis.
units.tr: You will object: first, a proposition about a second adjacent cannot be verified unless it is verified of the first. For example, it cannot be said, "Peter is learned," or "The lion is roaring," unless it is first said, "Peter is," "The lion is." Therefore, if privation is not, it cannot be said to be the principle of generation.

units.la: Respondeo cum distinctione. Verificari nequit propositio de secundo adiacente, nisi verificetur de primo, in entibus positiuis conceditur; in negatiuis negatur.
units.tr: I answer with a distinction. A proposition about a second adjacent cannot be verified unless it is verified of the first: this is granted in positive entities; it is denied in negative ones.

units.la: Et ratio disparitatis affertur, quia hæc propositio v.g. Petrus est doctus, prædicat doctrinam, quæ accidens est positiuū, de Petro; unde requirit etiam quòd sit subiectum, cui physicè inhæreat; si enim Petrus non sit, quomodo in eo doctrina erit? Verum si loquamur de prædicato negatiuo, sicut reuera hoc in se nil positiuum est; sic non requirit subiectum, quod actu sit. Propterea cùm priuatio sit principium negatiuum, non positiuum, de illa prædicari potest hic terminus principium quando primò non est.
units.tr: And the reason for the difference is given: this proposition, for example, "Peter is learned," predicates doctrine, which is a positive accident, of Peter; hence it also requires that there be a subject in which it physically inheres; for if Peter were not, how would learning be in him? But if we speak of a negative predicate, since this in itself is nothing positive, it does not require a subject that actually is. Therefore, since privation is a negative, not a positive, principle, the term "principle" can be predicated of it when it first is not.

units.la: Obijcies 1. quod non est, nequit vllo modo esse principium, ergo &c. Probatur antecedens, nam esse radix est omnium. Confirmatur, quia materia si non esset, neque dici posset principium: ergo à simili priuatio quandiu non est, assumi vt principium non debet.
units.tr: You will object: what is not can in no way be a principle; therefore, etc. The antecedent is proved, for being is the root of all things. It is confirmed: because matter, if it were not, could not even be called a principle; therefore, by parity, privation, as long as it is not, ought not to be taken as a principle.

units.la: Resp. cum distinctione. Quod non est, dici nequit principium à quo, & negatiuum, nego; principium quod, & positiuum, concedo. Ad confirmationem patet: disparitas inter materiam, & priuationé; illa enim est principium quod, & positiuum; hæc verò à quo, & negatiuum, vnde non requirit esse, vt vocetur principium. Explicari potest exemplo, nam tenebræ quia sunt quid priuatiuum, eo primo instanti quo non sunt, dicuntur esse principium diei, quia dies tunc fit.
units.tr: I answer with a distinction. What is not cannot be called a principle "from which" (a quo) and negative: I deny it; a principle "which" (quod) and positive: I grant it. The confirmation is answered: there is a difference between matter and privation; for the former is a principle "which" and positive, whereas the latter is "from which" and negative, and hence it does not require being in order to be called a principle. It can be explained by an example: darkness, because it is something privative, is said at the first instant in which it is not to be the principle of day, because day then comes to be.

units.la: Obijcies 3. Principia, & principiatum relatiua esse debent simul, ergo principia sunt simul cum principiato. Quare cum priuatio sit principium, ea simul esse debet cum suo principiato, quod est compositum in fieri: ergo male dicitur esse principium, quando primo non est.
units.tr: You will object: principles and the principled must be relative things, and relatives must be together; therefore principles are together with what is principled. Therefore, since privation is a principle, it ought to be together with its principled thing, which is the composite in becoming; therefore it is wrongly said to be a principle when it first is not.

units.la: Respondeo distinguendo minorem. Relatiua permanentia esse debent simul, concedo; succesiua, nego; ergo principia sunt simul cum principiato, si permanentia sint, concedo; si vero succesiua, nego. Priuatio autem non est principium, quod maneat, sed succesiuum, & a quo; ideo non exigit esse, dum fit eius principiatum. Adest instantia in numeris; nam prius dicit relationem ad suum posterius; & nihilominus haec duo relatiua nec unquam sunt, nec esse possunt simul, quia succes-siua.
units.tr: I answer by distinguishing the minor. Permanent relatives must be together: I grant it; successive relatives: I deny it. Therefore principles are together with what is principled, if they are permanent: I grant it; but if they are successive: I deny it. Privation, however, is not a principle that remains, but a successive one, and a principle "from which"; therefore it does not require to be while its principled thing comes to be. There is an instance in numbers: for the prior relates to its posterior, and nevertheless these two relatives neither ever are, nor can be, together, because they are successive.

units.la: DISPVTATIO VLTIMA.
units.tr: LAST DISPUTATION.

units.la: De aliis rerum naturalium principiis.
units.tr: On the other principles of natural things.

units.la: Etulimus principia, quae ponunt Aristotelei ad corporis naturalis generationem. Vtrum physica, & vera, ex iis, quae dicta sunt, vnusquisque colligere potest. Ego quidem non ita facile adducor, vt ea credam. Quod enim aiunt de Materia vidimus dubium esse, imo contra physicae substantiae naturam. Quod pariter de Forma, nequit illud suaderi, tot de nouo substantias generari, maxime inopinato, absque praevia dispositione, ac sine influ-
units.tr: We have set out the principles which Aristotle posits for the generation of a natural body. Whether they are physical and true, each person can gather for himself from what has been said. I, for my part, am not so easily brought to believe them. For what they say about matter we have seen to be doubtful, indeed contrary to the nature of a physical substance. Likewise regarding form, it cannot be persuaded that so many substances are newly generated, especially so unexpectedly, without prior disposition and without the influx of causes.

units.la: XII xu causarum. Quòd etiam de Priuatione,constat quàm inutile fit, præsertim quia hæc trahit in quæstiones plerumque vanas, & quæ nil habent, nisi clamorem, fortasse iurgia, certè laborem. Adeovt si non meliora philosophemur, similes videamur ijs, qui cancros rodunt,Luna silente captos; nam vt inueniant nihil, dentes in sola putaminum corrosione fatigant. Ob id nostri non immemor instituti,fert animus alia quædam innuere principia rerum, quæ physica magis, & rationi, atque sensui accommoda sint. Non enim dicere ausim euidentia, & certa, cùm in physicis plerumque accidat nobis, quemadmodum Inexercitati in prælio faciunt; etenim (ait Arist.1.Metaph.cap.4.) illic circumeuntes, egregias plerumque plagas infligunt, sed non ex scientia. Ita nobis etiamsi contingerit egregiè aliquando collimare ad scopum, idcasu fiet; non scitè, ac semper. Sed vtcumque oriatur, & quandocumque me- lior de rebus intelligentia iuuat rem attenta- re.
units.tr: As for privation, it is clear how useless it is, especially because it draws us into questions that are mostly vain, which yield nothing but noise, perhaps quarrels, and certainly labour. So, unless we philosophize better, we seem like those who gnaw at crabs caught during a silent moon; for, in order to find nothing, they wear out their teeth on nothing but the corroded shells. Therefore, not forgetful of our plan, I am inclined to point out certain other principles of things, which are more physical and better suited to reason and to sense. For I would not dare to call them evident and certain, since in physical matters it often happens to us as the inexperienced do in battle; for (Aristotle says, Metaph. 1, ch. 4) running about there, they often inflict excellent blows, but not from knowledge. So, if we should happen at some time to aim well at the mark, it will be by chance, not skilfully and always. But however it arises, and whenever a better understanding of things helps, let us attempt the matter with care.

units.la: Notio Principiorum.
units.tr: The Notion of Principles.

units.la: ARistoteles 1.Phyf.t.43. definit principia rerum naturalium intrinseca, Quæ neque fiunt ex alijs, neque ex alterutris,sed ex his omnia. Sensus est, principia, quæ componunt naturale mixtum, ipsa non componi ex alijs; nam & hæc alia rursus componi deberent, vnde fieret processus ad infinitum.Nec ex alterutris, videlicet vnum principium non causat intrinsecè aliud, sed supponit omnino in ratione principij completum. Ex quo licet suspicari, an forma substantialis, quæ, vt explicant Ariftotelei, fit ex materia concurrente,ab eaque intrinsecè completur,fit principium. Ex his ergo fiunt omnia;seu principia talia sunt in fe, vt ex ijs non compositis cætera omnia componantur.
units.tr: Aristotle, Phys. 1, t. 43, defines the intrinsic principles of natural things as those which are not made from other things, nor from one another, but from which all things are made. The sense is that the principles which compose a natural mixed body are not themselves composed of others; for these others would in turn have to be composed, and there would be an infinite regress. Nor from one another: that is, one principle does not intrinsically cause another, but presupposes something complete in the notion of a principle. From this one may suspect whether substantial form, which the Aristotelians explain as arising from concurrent matter and being intrinsically completed by it, is a principle. Therefore all things are made from these; or such principles are in themselves such that all other things are composed from those which are not themselves composite.

units.la: Habita notione principiorum, hic statim quæreндum est, quid sint ea principia, quæ physicè naturalia mixta componunt.Deinde quænam sint, seu cuiufnam generis. Postea quot sint. His enim cognitis, non erit valdè arduum explicare naturæ arcana,quorum solutio ab exacta principiorum cognitione tota pendere videtur. Itaque notetur
units.tr: Having grasped the notion of principles, we must at once ask here what those principles are which physically compose natural mixed bodies; then, of what kind they are, or to what genus they belong; and afterwards, how many there are. For once these are known, it will not be very difficult to explain the secrets of nature, the solution of which seems to depend entirely on an exact knowledge of the principles. Let it therefore be noted

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: DISQUISITION I.

units.la: Quid sint rerum naturalium principia.
units.tr: What the principles of natural things are.

units.la: PRo intelligentia hoc maximè velim teneatis, quod ab initio innuebamus, nimirum Veteres philosophos in eam sententiam abijsse omnes, vt dixerint, rerum naturalium principia esse corpora quædā substantialiter completa, quæ inuicem vnita non se intrinsecè actuarent per modum actus, & potentiæ, sed actu compositum constituerent; nec sibi esse completum, existentiamque communicarent, sed soli composito darent esse, ac subsistere, quo deinde corrupto, ipsa non perirent, sed ab inuicem soluta diiungerentur. Itaque vt refert Empir. l. 3. c. 4. Pherecides terram dixit omnium esse principium, Thales aquam, Anaxinienes aerem &c. Alij verò vt Xenophanes terram, & aquam, Oenopides Chius ignem, & aerē, Aristoteles ignem, aerem, aquam, terram, Democritus, & Epicurus atomos. Quæ opiniones quamquam dissideant in principiorum differentijs, in hoc tamen conueniunt omnes, quòd ea sint substantiæ completæ, perfectæ, per se subsistētes, alio non indigentes &c. quemadmodum omissa etiam auctoritate, ratio, & experientia suadet. quare sit
units.tr: For understanding, I would above all have you hold to what we indicated at the beginning: namely, that all the ancient philosophers came to the opinion that the principles of natural things are certain bodies, each substantially complete, which, when united, do not actuate one another intrinsically by way of act and potency, but form a composite by their actual union. Nor does each complete the other or communicate existence to it; rather, they give being and subsistence to the composite alone, and when that is corrupted, they themselves do not perish but are separated and divided from one another. Thus, as Empiricus reports (book 3, chapter 4), Pherecydes said that earth was the principle of all things, Thales water, Anaximenes air, and so on. Others, such as Xenophanes, held earth and water; Oenopides of Chios held fire and air; Aristotle held fire, air, water and earth; and Democritus and Epicurus held atoms. Although these opinions differ over the distinctions among the principles, all agree on this point: that they are complete, perfect substances, subsisting through themselves and needing nothing else. This is what reason and experience also persuade us of, even when authority is set aside. Therefore, let it be

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Rerum naturalium principia sunt cor- pora sensibilia, & omnino completa.
units.tr: The principles of natural things are sensible bodies, and wholly complete.

units.la: PRobatur i. experientia sic. Patet ipsis oculis, quòd mixtum naturale in corpora sensibilia, & omnino completa resoluitur: sed ex ijs tantùm, vt principijs componebatur, ergo rerum principia sunt corpora sensibilia, & omnino completa. Maior est clara in quacumq; mixti resolutione, si enim v. g. corrumpatur lignum aut combustione, aut putrefactione (qui duo modi resoluendi assignantur à Philosopho lib.4. Meteor.) manet cinis, vel terra, manet humor, aut aqua, & manet ignis. Ita etiam si animalium cadauera fiant, videntur superesse caro, pellis, ossa, nervi, &c. Iterum si hæc omnia putrescant, siue igne adurantur, cernimus ossa paulatim abire in pulueres, carnes quoq; in cineres, in humorem, in vaporem, & in ignem solui. Similiter hoc intuemur in sublimationibus, nam quoties in clambyco resoluuntur ligna, folia, flores; altera pars aquea exprimitur, & guttatim in phialas cadit: altera cinerea subsidit, altera spiritosa, quæ ignea est, foras auolat; cuius rei testis est odoratus. Præterea si vnaquæq; harum partium quæ manent, adhuc resoluantur ex arte, in cineribus fit separatio eorum, qui sunt crafcrassiores, fœculentioresq; ab alijs, qui magis homogenei, subtiles, & impermixti sunt. Sic etiam aqua si vlterius depuretur, alia pars manet spissior, turbidior; alia verò magis clara, pura, diaphana. Demum siue prima, siue secunda, siue postrema solutio fiat, hoc semper oculis patet, quidquid manet corrupto mixto, esse corpus completum, perfectum, per se subsistens, &c. Minor verò propositi argumenti probatur ex eo celebri axiomate. Vnumquodq; componitur ex iis,in qua resoluitur. Siue: vltimum in resolutione, primum est in compositione: sed mixtum resoluitur in corpora omnino completa, ergo ex ijs tantùm componitur. Confirmatur, quia præter hæc non adest in composito ea forma substantialis incompleta, vt dicunt; ergo. Probo antecedens. Hæc substantia si adest in composito, vel eo corrupto, ipsa quoque corrumpitur, vel non. Si non corrumpitur, ergo debet videri, quemadmodum videtur cinis, aqua, &c. Si corrumpitur, ergo noua generatur, nam vt aiunt, generatio vnius est corruptio alterius: hoc autem non fit, enim soluto composito, nihil de nouo genitum intuemur. Ergo concludendum est, principia rerum naturalium componentia, esse tantùm corpora omninò sensibilia, & completa.
units.tr: It is proved first by experience, thus. It is plain to the eyes that a natural mixed body is resolved into sensible and wholly complete bodies, and it was compounded out of these alone as its principles. Therefore the principles of things are sensible and wholly complete bodies. The major premise is clear from any resolution of a mixed body. If, for example, wood is corrupted either by burning or by putrefaction (the two modes of resolution which the Philosopher assigns in the fourth book of the Meteorology), there remains ash or earth, there remains moisture or water, and there remains fire. So too, when the carcasses of animals decay, there seem to remain flesh, skin, bones, sinews, and so on. Again, if all these putrefy or are consumed by fire, we see the bones gradually turn into powder, and the flesh too dissolve into ashes, moisture, vapour and fire. We observe the same in sublimations: whenever wood, leaves or flowers are resolved in an alembic, one watery part is pressed out and falls drop by drop into the flasks, another, ashy part settles, and another, spirituous part, which is fiery, flies off; of this fact the sense of smell is witness. Moreover, if each of the remaining parts is further resolved by art, the ashes separate into those which are cruder and more feculent and those which are more homogeneous, subtle and unmixed. So too, if water is purified further, one part remains thicker and cloudier, while another is clearer, purer and transparent. Finally, whether the first, second or last solution is made, it is always plain to the eyes that whatever remains when the mixed body is corrupted is a complete, perfect, self-subsisting body, and so on. The minor premise of our argument is proved from that famous axiom: Each thing is composed of those things into which it is resolved; or, the last in resolution is first in composition. But a mixed body is resolved into wholly complete bodies; therefore it is composed of these alone. This is confirmed because, besides these, there is not present in the composite that incomplete substantial form, as they call it. I prove the antecedent. If this substance is present in the composite, then when the composite is corrupted it is either corrupted too or it is not. If it is not corrupted, it ought to be seen, just as the ash and water are seen. If it is corrupted, then a new one is generated, for, as they say, the generation of one thing is the corruption of another; but this does not happen, for once the composite is dissolved we see nothing newly generated. Therefore it must be concluded that the principles of natural things which compose them are only wholly sensible and complete bodies.

units.la: Probatur 2. ratione sic. Partes istæ, quæ manent, corrupto mixto, non potuerunt de nouo produci, ergo priùs erant in illo: sed sunt partes completæ substantialiter,ergo mixtum componebatur ex corporibus omnino completis. Probo antecedens hac experientia: comburitur lignum, & manet cinis, aqua, vapor, exhalatio, &c. Quæro, cur ignis, qui comburit, adeo varias gignit substantias, cùm ille sit vnus, & semper idem? quomodo per calorem terra generatur, quæ naturaliter quærit frigus? quomodo aqua, humida, & frigida, producitur à contrario, calido, & sicco? Quare substantiam vapidam, subtilem, feruidamque foras educit, quæ super iniecta manu sentitur? Quid respondes? an quòd lignum dispositiones habet varias ad cinerem, ad aquam, ad exhalationem, quibus dum ignis accommodat se, tam diuersa producit? Contra: lignum easdem vbiq; habet dispositiones, vbique homogeneum est, vbiq; simile, vbiq; paris temperamenti, nā vbicunq; forma ligni est, eadem quærit accidentia, sine quibus haud quaquam induci potu isset. Ergo ignis non producit hæc multa, hæc varia, hæc tam diuersa ratione dispositionum, quia hæ diuersæ sint. Rursus: idem ignis cum eadem vi, & etiā maiori, si agat in aquâ, & cineres, nihil ex ijs producit, cùm tamen aqua, & cinis habeant quoq; dispositiones ad aliquid; ergo neque primò substantias de nouo produxit. Similiter contingit in putrefactione, &c. Addi possent experientiæ Chymicorum, qui mixta in corpora omnino completa separant, rursusque comcomponunt, sed hæc fusius cùm de Generatione. Confirmatur, quia Homo est naturale compositum: sed partes habet omnino completas, animam, & corpus; ergo similiter de quouis alio composito. Minor patet, nam in interitu corpus, & anima separantur, subsistunt, per se durant. Neq; dicant, corpus fieri completum, quia per formam cadauericam tale constituitur. Vidimus enim, hanc pessimè olere da forma cadauerica philosophiam. Igitur concludendum est, principia rerum naturalium componentia, esse corpora omninò sensibilia, & completa.
units.tr: It is proved secondly by reason, thus. Those parts which remain when a mixed body is corrupted could not have been newly produced; therefore they were already in it. But they are substantially complete parts; therefore the mixed body was composed of wholly complete bodies. I prove the antecedent by this experience: wood is burned, and there remains ash, water, vapour, exhalation, and so on. I ask: why does the fire which burns generate such various substances, since it is one and always the same? How is earth generated by heat, when earth naturally seeks cold? How is water, which is moist and cold, produced from the contrary, hot and dry? Why does it drive out a vapid, subtle and boiling substance, which is felt when the hand is held over it? What is your answer? Is it that the wood has various dispositions towards ash, towards water, towards exhalation, and the fire adapts itself to these, producing such diverse things? On the contrary: the wood has the same dispositions everywhere; it is everywhere homogeneous, everywhere alike, everywhere of equal temperament, for wherever the form of wood is, it seeks the same accidents, without which it could by no means have been induced. Therefore the fire does not produce these many, varied and so diverse things because of diverse dispositions, since these dispositions are not diverse. Again: the same fire, with the same force, and even with greater force, if it acts on water and ashes, produces nothing from them, although water and ash also have dispositions towards something. Therefore it did not originally produce the substances anew. The same happens in putrefaction, and so on. The experiments of the chemists could be added, who separate mixed bodies into wholly complete bodies and then recompose them, but these will be discussed more fully when we treat of generation. This is confirmed because man is a natural composite, yet he has wholly complete parts, soul and body; and similarly with any other composite. The minor premise is plain, for at death body and soul are separated, subsist and endure of themselves. Nor let them say that the body becomes complete because it is constituted as such through the cadaveric form. For we have seen that this philosophy of the cadaveric form smells very bad. Therefore it must be concluded that the principles of natural things which compose them are wholly sensible and complete bodies.

units.la: Probatur 3. authoritate. Imprimis omnium veterum Philosophorum, qui non alia cognouerunt principia rerum, quâ quæ physica, realia, & completa sunt. Vnde Albertus Magn. de gen. tract. 1. c. 12. peculiariter Democritum laudans inquit. Democritus autem propriis, & physicis sermonibus videtur facere persuasionem in eo, quod ponit physica ex physicis componi. Quare cùm Democritus constituat principia rerum esse atomos, quæ substantiæ sunt omnino completæ, videtur hæc esse locutio physica, non abstracta, & metaphysica, vt cùm aiunt Peripatetici de materia, & forma incompletis, non subsistentibus, &c. Secundo Aristoteles 3. de Cæl. c. 3. impugnat Anaxagoram, qui dixerat, omnia in elementis contineri secundùm particulas minimas, & ait, quòdsi caro, sanguis, ossa, &c. essent v. g. in igne, segregarentur ex illo; at non videmus ea segregari ex igne; igitur in eo non sunt. Ergo (addam ego) per Aristotelem arguuntur ea fuisse in corpore, quae segregantur ex illo. Sed nos intuemur segregari composita in substantias omnino completas, ergo principia mixtorum completa sunt. Tertio. Idem Philosophus l. 5. Metaph. t. 4. habet. Elementa corporum dicuntur, in quae ultima resoluuntur corpora, ipsa vero non amplius resoluuntur in alia corpora specie differentia. Ex his duo colligo. Primum est, cognosci quaenam sint rerum elementa, seu principia ex resolutione. Igitur soluto composito, manent haec principia, & ita completa sunt, secus non manerent. Secundum est, deveniri tandem ad ultima principia, quae resolui non possunt in alia, neque corrumpi, ergo falsò dicitur, quòd corrupto cóposito, noua semper adsit forma, quae generetur; alioquin id, quod manet, semper esset resolubile in nouas formarum species, quia semper alia, & alia forma, quae corruptibilis esset, reperiretur. Legatur Philosophus, praesertim in lib. de Caelo, de Gen. de Meteoris, vbi res physicas physicè magis tractauit, indeq; patebit, nonaliam fuisse Aristotelis mentem, de principijs compositi naturalis, quàm quòd sint corpora physicè in se completa.
units.tr: It is proved thirdly by authority. First, by that of all the ancient philosophers, who recognised no principles of things other than those which are physical, real and complete. Hence Albertus Magnus, On Generation, tract. 1, ch. 12, praising Democritus in particular, says: Democritus, however, seems to persuade by proper and physical language, in that he holds that physical things are composed of physical things. Therefore, since Democritus holds that the principles of things are atoms, which are wholly complete substances, this seems to be physical language, not abstract and metaphysical, as when the Peripatetics speak of matter and form as incomplete and not subsisting, and so on. Second, Aristotle, On the Heavens, book 3, ch. 3, attacks Anaxagoras, who had said that all things are contained in the elements in minimal particles. Aristotle says that if flesh, blood, bones and so on were, say, in fire, they would be separated out of it; but we do not see them separated out of fire; therefore they are not in it. Therefore (I add) Aristotle argues that those things which are separated out of a body were in it. But we see composites separated into wholly complete substances; therefore the principles of mixed bodies are complete. Third, the same Philosopher, Metaphysics, book 5, text 4, says: The elements of bodies are said to be those into which bodies are ultimately resolved, which themselves are no longer resolved into other bodies differing in species. From these words I draw two conclusions. The first is that the elements, or principles, of things are known from resolution. Therefore, when the composite is dissolved, these principles remain, and so they are complete; otherwise they would not remain. The second is that we arrive at last at ultimate principles, which cannot be resolved into others, nor corrupted. Therefore it is false to say that when a composite is corrupted a new form is always present and is generated; otherwise what remains would always be resolvable into new species of forms, because always another and another corruptible form would be found. Let the Philosopher be read, especially the books On the Heavens, On Generation and On Meteorology, where he treated physical things more physically; from these it will be plain that Aristotle's mind concerning the principles of a natural composite was none other than that they are bodies which are physically complete in themselves.

units.la: Obijcies primò. ex mixti resolutione malè arguuntur principia rerum, quidquid enim eo corrupto manet, de nouo genitū est. Quare licèt aqua, terra, ignis, hahalitus, &c. in quæ abit compositum, completæ substantiæ sint, hæc tamen nullo modo preerant, ergo.
units.tr: You will object first: principles of things are wrongly inferred from the resolution of a mixed body, for whatever remains when it is corrupted is newly generated. Therefore, although water, earth, fire, vapour (halitus) and so on, into which the composite passes, are complete substances, yet these did not in any way pre-exist.

units.la: Respônsum est iam argumento in secunda probatione conclusionis nostræ, vbi patet, hæc tam varia, in quæ mixtum soluitur, nullo modo ab agente corruptiuo fuisse genita, & sic præfuisse necessum est. Recole dicta.
units.tr: This has already been answered by the argument in the second proof of our conclusion, where it is plain that these many varied things into which the mixed body is resolved were in no way generated by the corrupting agent, and so must necessarily have pre-existed. Recall what was said there.

units.la: Obijcies secūdo. Si mixtū fieret per corpora completa, non differret ab artificiali, non enim partes vnirentur in eo per modum actus, & potentiæ, nam vna non actuaret, perficeretque intrinsecè aliam, vtpotequæ completa iam esset. Hoc autem dici nequit, ergo.
units.tr: You will object secondly: if a mixed body came about through complete bodies, it would not differ from an artificial one, for the parts would not be united in it by way of act and potency, since one would not actuate and intrinsically perfect the other, being already complete. But this cannot be said; therefore the conclusion stands.

units.la: Respondendum erit alibi huic argumento, nam opportunius afferetur in materia de generatione. Idcirco satis erit si negetur antecedens, eo quòd mixtum naturale, quia partes habet meliori, strictiori, perfectiori vinculo nexas, ideo ab artificiali differt. Gratis autem dicitur, in mixto naturali partes vniri per modum actus, & potentiæ; vt videbimus.
units.tr: This argument must be answered elsewhere, for it will be raised more appropriately in the topic of generation. Here it will be enough to deny the antecedent: a natural mixed body differs from an artificial one because its parts are bound together by a better, closer and more perfect bond. It is also gratuitous to say that in a natural mixed body the parts are united by way of act and potency, as we shall see.

units.la: Obijcies tertio. Si compositum fieret ex ijs corporibus, quæ facta solutione manent, nihil periret, dum compositum perit, quidquid enim prius inerat, illud totum perseuerat. Sed hoc dici non potest, nam videmus lignum, ignem, animalia destrui, ergo.
units.tr: You will object, third: if a compound were made of those bodies which remain after dissolution, nothing would perish when the compound perishes, for whatever was in it before still persists in its entirety. But this cannot be said, for we see that wood, fire and animals are destroyed. Therefore...

units.la: Respondeo cum distinctione. Nihil perit simplex, & substantiale, concedo; nihil mixtum, & accidentale, nego. Perit ergo, & definit esse mixtum, soluto. gno, amplius hoc mixtum, seu lignum non est; sed partes, & substantiæ, quæ constabant lignum, ipse non pereunt substantialiter. Sic soluta domo, perit hoc totum, sed non sic lapides, cæmenta, trabes &c. Fit ergo talis corruptio ex ablatione vnionis, & ex partitum deiunctione. Confirmatur ex corruptione, siue destructione hominis, quæ vera, & substantialis corruptio est. In ea tamen nulla substantia perit, neque definit esse anima enim perseuerat immortalis, & separata manet; corpus etiam durat, nec nisi per lentam resolutionem in partes alias item completas resoluitur. Sed hæc alibi fusius.
units.tr: I answer with a distinction. Nothing simple and substantial perishes: I grant this. Nothing mixed and accidental perishes: I deny this. So the mixed thing does perish and ceases to be a mixed thing when it is dissolved: once the wood is dissolved, this mixed thing, or the wood, is no longer there. But the parts and substances which made up the wood do not perish substantially. So when a house is taken apart, this whole perishes, but its stones, mortar, beams and so on do not. Such corruption therefore comes about through the removal of the union and the separation of the parts. This is confirmed by the corruption or destruction of a human being, which is a true and substantial corruption. Yet in this no substance perishes, nor does the soul cease to be: the soul remains immortal and continues separate, and the body too endures, being dissolved only slowly into other parts that are again complete. But these matters are treated more fully elsewhere.

units.la: Obijcies 4. Si principia mixti naturalis forent ista completa, quæ in resolutione videmus, compositum non esset vnum. Præterea: istæ materiæ completæ non actuarentur intrinsecè à forma totali compositi; quæ omnia sunt absurda. Sequela probatur, quia compositum esset ignis, aqua, terra, &c. ergo non foret vnum. Deinde quoad secundum patet, quia hæ substantiæ, quæ manent in resolutione, completæ sunt, ergo non complentur ab alio: sed in mixto adest forma mixti, quæ vere actuat; ergo est id, quod actuat; & non est quod actuatur &c.
units.tr: You will object, fourth: if the principles of a natural mixed body were those complete things which we see in dissolution, the compound would not be one. Moreover, those complete materials would not be actuated intrinsically by the total form of the compound; all of which is absurd. The consequence is proved, because the compound would be fire, water, earth and so on, and therefore would not be one. Next, as for the second point, it is plain, because those substances which remain in dissolution are complete, and therefore are not completed by another. But in a mixed body there is the form of the mixed body, which truly actuates; therefore it is that which actuates, and it is not that which is actuated, and so on.

units.la: Respond. negando sequelas. Ad probationem dico, quòd mixtum licet conster ex pluribus, vt constare debet, reuera tamen unum est: Partes enim non sunt illæ, quæ tunc seorsim denominantur; sed totum, quod ex iis resultat, hoc denominatur, ut patet in composito humano, quod non dicitur vel corpus, vel anima, sed homo, licet in eo, & corpus, & anima sit, &c. Dico ad secundum, quod argumentum supponit formam Aristotelica, quæ actuat materiam incompletam; & quia vidimus hanc non dari, cadit vis argumenti. Sed alibi hac de re diceimus.
units.tr: I answer by denying the consequences. As to the proof, I say that although the mixed body is made up of several things, as it must be, it is nevertheless truly one. For the parts are not those things which are then named separately; rather, the whole which results from them is what is named, as is clear in the human compound, which is called neither body nor soul but man, although both body and soul are in him. As to the second point, I say that the argument presupposes the Aristotelian form, which actuates incomplete matter; and since we have seen that there is no such form, the force of the argument falls. But we have spoken of this matter elsewhere.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: Second Disquisition.

units.la: Quænam sint rerum primordia?
units.tr: What are the first beginnings of things?

units.la: PRO intelligentia rei, quæ totius Physicæ summus cardo est, supponi debet, quod SS. PP. multi, & grauissimi docent, ab exordio Mundi fuisse à Deo creata rerum omnium semina, & per elementa, ignem, aerem, aquam, terram, undequaque dispersa, ut sequentium generationum principia forent. Quapropter 2. Gen. dicitur: Deus die septimo cessasse ab omni opere, quod creauit, ut faceret; siue ut est in Hebreo, ad faciendum: Sicut
units.tr: To understand the matter, which is the chief hinge of all physics, it must first be granted that many weighty Fathers teach that from the beginning of the world God created the seeds of all things and scattered them everywhere through the elements of fire, air, water and earth, so that they might be the principles of all later generations. For this reason Genesis 2 says that God ceased on the seventh day from all the work that he had created in order to make, or, as it is in Hebrew, for making: As

units.la: Sicut ergo solers, prouidusq; Typographhus omnes ab initio characteres efformat, ex quorum deinde varia combinatione, tam varia, tam diuersa, tam contraria componit, non absimili modo Maximus omnium Opifex, rerum cunctarum seminarium cödidit à primordijs mundi, substantias nimirum tenuissimas, ab inuicem specie differentes, intrinsecè completas, & substantialiter varias, quæ diuersimodè per naturæ vinculum nexæ vnaquæque mixtorum genera efformarent.
units.tr: Just as a skilful and provident printer first forms all the letters and then, by combining them in many ways, composes things so varied, so diverse and so contrary, the greatest of all Makers, in a manner not unlike this, laid up from the beginning of the world the seminal stores of all things. These were, namely, very fine substances, differing in kind from one another, complete in themselves and substantially various, which, joined together by the bond of nature in different ways, would form each of the kinds of mixed bodies.

units.la: Quòd autem hæc rerum semina lateat in elementis mundi, non obscura est D. Aug. sent. 3. de Trin. c. 7. vbi docens quomodo Magi, & Dæmones in Aegypto non creauerint, sed produxerint serpentes applicando actiua passiuis, hoc est corpora corporibus addendo, inquit: Omnium, quæ corporaliter, visibiliterque nascuntur, occulta quædam semina in istis corporeis Mundi huius elementis latent. Itaque si Dæmones, ait Sanctus, effecere serpentes, non ideo fas est dicere creatores; & addit rationem: Quia semina rerum istarum nobis occultiora nouerunt, & ea per contemperationes elementorum latenter spargunt, atq; ita gignendarum rerum, & accelerandorum incrementorum præbent occasiones. Quòd etiâ hæ substatiæ tenuissimæ sint, atq; insensibiles idé Sanctus ibi dé cóteftatur, dú ait, Surculum semen esse; hoc verò semen si grandiusculum sit, aliô etiâ femine cótexi, quod etsi oculo videre nequeamus, ratione tamen conijcere possumus. Præterea quòd hæc femina easint, quæ ab initio Mundi extitere vt rerum omnium primordia, innuitur ab eodem c.9. Ista quippe originaliter, & primordialiter in quadam textura elementorum cunctaiam creata sunt, sed acceptis opportunitatibus prodeunt;nam sicuti. Matres grauida sunt fœtibus,sic ipse mundus grauidus est causis nascentium, quæ in illo non creantur, nisi ab illa summa essentia &c. Accedit etiam auctoritas aliorum PP. & maximè Nisseni, Basilij, Clem. Alex. quorum sententiæ alibi asserentur. Hinc ortum duxit quod ait Velleius apud Cic. de nat. Deor. Eum, qui mundi statuit initium, primis vt dicitur labris gustasse Philosophiam. Deus enim locando in seminibus initia rerum, vnde tot effectus, varij, mirabilesque oriuntur, omnem philosophiæ naturalis rationem in vno exordio conclusit.
units.tr: That these seeds of things lie hidden in the elements of the world is clear from St. Augustine, De Trinitate, book 3, ch. 7, where, teaching how the Magi and demons in Egypt did not create but produced serpents by applying active to passive, that is, by adding bodies to bodies, he says: Certain hidden seeds of all things that are born bodily and visibly lie concealed in these corporeal elements of this world. So if demons, says the Saint, produced serpents, it is not right to call them creators. He adds the reason: Because they know the seeds of these things better than we do, and they scatter them secretly through the mixing of the elements, and so provide occasions for things to be generated and for growth to be hastened. That these substances are also very fine and insensible the same Saint testifies there, when he says: A twig is a seed; and if the seed is somewhat larger, it is covered by another seed, which we cannot see with the eye, though we can conjecture it by reason. Moreover, the same author shows in ch. 9 that these seeds are those which existed from the beginning of the world as the first principles of all things: For these were created originally and primordially, all of them together, in a certain texture of the elements, but they come forth when opportunities are received; for just as mothers are pregnant with offspring, so the world itself is pregnant with the causes of things born, which are not created in it except by that highest essence, etc. The authority of other Fathers adds weight, especially Gregory of Nyssa, Basil and Clement of Alexandria, whose opinions will be asserted elsewhere. Hence came the saying of Velleius in Cicero, De natura deorum: He who established the beginning of the world, as they say, tasted philosophy with the first lips. For God, by placing the beginnings of things in seeds, from which so many varied and wonderful effects arise, has comprised the whole account of natural philosophy in one beginning.

units.la: Ob id fortasse Dei Prouidentia vernũ tempus ad Mundi creationem elegit, ne adhuc tenella femina sol æstiuus adureret, aut nimius rigor frigoris enecaret, sed in vna veris clementia, tamquam de lacte vberis nutrirentur vigerent, crescerent, prolificarent. Inde Virg. 2. Georg.
units.tr: For this reason, perhaps, God's Providence chose spring for the creation of the world, so that the summer sun might not scorch the still tender seeds, nor excessive cold kill them, but that in the one gentle season of spring they might be nourished as from a full breast, and grow, thrive and multiply. Hence Virgil, Georgics 2:

units.la: Ver illud erat, ver magnus agebat Orbis, & hibernis parcebant flatibus Euri.
units.tr: That was spring; spring was the great season of the world, and the east wind spared the wintry blasts.

units.la: Seruata sunt igitur femina, & quemadmodum ex elementis ad rerum generationes educuntur, sic in mixtorum corruptionibus dispersa manent in elementis. Nam pars, quae subtilior, viuidior, & spiritosior est, auolat in aerem, vt rursus descendat, fitque circulatio naturae, de qua loquitur passim Philosophus. 1. Meteor. Pars alia crassior in aqua sistit, ac terra, qua de re legi potest Columella, Varro, Virgilius; possunt conferri peritiores agricolae; potest cognosci quod habet Lucret. Carus l. 1.
units.tr: The seeds are therefore preserved, and just as they are drawn out of the elements for the generation of things, so in the corruption of mixed bodies they remain scattered in the elements. For the part that is subtler, livelier and more spirituous flies off into the air, so that it may come down again, and so there is a circulation of nature, of which the Philosopher speaks throughout, Meteorology book 1. The grosser part settles in water and earth. On this matter Columella, Varro and Virgil may be read; more skilled farmers may be consulted; and one may learn what Lucretius has in book 1 of his poem.

units.la: Esse videlicet in terris primordia rerum,
units.tr: That, namely, there are in the earth the first beginnings of things,

units.la: Quae nos fecundas vertentes vomere glebas,
units.tr: Which, when we turn the fruitful clods with the plough,

units.la: Terraque solum subigentes, cimus ad ortus.
units.tr: And, working the soil of the earth, we bring to the light of birth.

units.la: Hinc est, quod tellus debet vomere findi, annuisque arationibus versari, vt semina, quae nimis latent, foras egerantur. Hinc iuuant irrigationes, maxime si fiant pluuialibus aquis, nam istae ab aere spiritus ferunt seminales, qui continuo trahuntur a sole, aut prae ingenita leuitate ascendunt, vnde S. Thomas in lib. de Gener. ait pariculas igneas, quae hospitantur in aere, deferri per pluuias in terram; qua etiam de causa dum aestiuo tempore pluit, grandinatque, sulphureum sentimus odorem. Hinc explicatur, quomodo herbae, stipites, aliaque mixta formaliter calida generentur sub aquis marium, lacuumque. Hinc patet, cur arua si diu nimis colantur, denique sterilescant, nam ex continua prolificatione iacturam seminum faciunt. Quocirca illud Ouidij, & philosophicum, & poeticum extat, fructibus assiduis lassa senescit humus. Hinc scimus philosophi quod ignorat vulgus, cur è domorum…, turriumque parietibus arbusta, flores, plantæ innascantur; quare in statuarum capitibus, & vestium plicis egerminent herbæ, calami, arundines &c. seminula… enim aut in cæmentis illuc asportantur; aut per vapores, ventos, pulueres toto aere feruntur; dumque illa parietum rimis, & statuarum crispis hærent, immanentq; incipiunt calere sole, madere pluuiâ, & augeri, quousq; tandem accepta vi, & energia, in sobolem progrediuntur. Hinc est, inquit Aug. 3. de Trin. c. 8. quòd animalia quædam in terra, siue in aqua nullis coeuntibus parentibus orta sint. Quia nimirum femina pro illorum genitura iam à Deo creata, debito, & exquisito modo coaluerunt. Et certè apes, addit Sanctus, filiorum femina non coeundo concipiunt, sed tamquam sparsa per terras colligunt: inuisibilium enim seminum creator, ipse creator est omnium rerum &c.
units.tr: Hence the earth must be cut with the ploughshare and turned over by yearly ploughings, so that the seeds that lie too deeply hidden may be drawn out. Hence irrigation helps, especially when it is done with rainwater, for these bring seminal spirits from the air, which are continually drawn up by the sun or rise through their innate lightness. Whence St. Thomas, in his book On Generation, says that fiery particles which dwell in the air are carried down to the earth by the rains. For this same reason, when it rains and hails in summer, we perceive a sulphurous smell. Hence it is explained how herbs, stalks and other mixed bodies that are formally hot are generated under the waters of seas and lakes. Hence it is clear why fields, if cultivated too long, finally become barren, for through continual fruitfulness they lose their store of seeds. Hence there is that saying of Ovid, both philosophical and poetical: the earth, worn out by constant crops, grows old. Hence we philosophers know what the common people do not: why shrubs, flowers and plants sprout from the walls of houses and towers, and why herbs, reeds, canes and the like sprout from the heads of statues and the folds of garments. The little seeds are either carried there in mortar, or are borne through the whole air by vapours, winds and dust. While they cling to the cracks of walls and the crevices of statues, and begin to dwell there and grow warm in the sun, become wet with rain and increase, they at last, having received strength and energy, advance into offspring. Hence, says Augustine, De Trinitate 3, ch. 8, certain animals have arisen in earth or in water with no parents coupling. For in that case the seeds, already created by God for the generation of those animals, have come together in the due and exact manner. And indeed bees, adds the Saint, conceive their offspring without coupling, but gather the seeds scattered as it were over the earth: for the creator of invisible seeds is himself the creator of all things, etc.

units.la: Ex quibus alijsq; dubitare non licet, adesse in elementis mundi femina rerum, quæ prout commodo recipiuntur loco, ita se vniunt, augent, corroborant ad generationes. Et quia ea, quæ gignuntur, substantialiter differentia sunt, proinde tenendum est, hæc etiam femina substantias esse inter se differentes, adeout quibusque mixtorum speciebus primigenia sua corpora specie diuersa respondeant. Idcirco placet nobis
units.tr: From these and other considerations it is not permitted to doubt that in the elements of the world there are seeds of things, which, as they are received in a suitable place, so unite, grow and strengthen for generation. And since the things that are generated are substantially different, it must therefore be held that these seeds too are substances differing among themselves, so that to each species of mixed bodies there correspond its original bodies of a different species. For this reason it pleases us

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Prima rerum principia videntur esse atomi, siue corpora minima, iuxta varias mixtorum species inter se differentia, vt alia sint pro metallicis, alia pro vegetantibus, alia pro sensitiuis.
units.tr: The first principles of things seem to be atoms, or minimal bodies, which differ from one another according to the various kinds of mixed bodies, so that some are for metals, others for plants, and others for animals with senses.

units.la: PRima pars conclusionis probata iam est in solutione mixtorum, & alibi fusius confirmabitur. Secunda etiam probatur, quia corpora mixta differunt substantialiter inter se, igitur & principia. Confirmatur, nam si lignum, aurum, ferrum, imò & centum genera rerum soluantur in minima, siue hoc per artem, seu per naturam fiat, numquam particulæ vnius adinuenientur partes virtute, pondere, figurà cum aliis, ergo ab accidentium diuersitate colligendum est, ibi etiam adesse corpora inter se substantialiter differentia. Confirmatur secundò experientia Chymicorum, quos veluti naturæ Antistites Physica tota consulere debet. Experiuntur enim, quòd si Mercurius, argentum, & huiusmodi soluantur, quantumuis terant, coquant, expurgent, vnam semper, eamdemque seruant naturam; vnde post solutionem, rursus in molem suam redigi possunt &c.
units.tr: The first part of the conclusion has already been proved in the discussion of mixed bodies, and it will be confirmed more fully elsewhere. The second part is also proved, because mixed bodies differ from one another in substance, and therefore so do their principles. It is confirmed thus: if wood, gold, iron, and indeed a hundred kinds of things are dissolved into their smallest parts, whether this happens by art or by nature, the particles of one kind will never be found to match the others in power, weight, and shape. Therefore from the diversity of accidents we must conclude that bodies differing in substance are present there too. It is confirmed a second time by the experience of the chemists, whom, as it were, the high priests of nature, all of physics ought to consult. For they find that if mercury, silver, and such things are dissolved, however much they are ground, heated, and purified, they always keep one and the same nature; so that after dissolution they can be brought back again into their former mass, and so on.

units.la: Probatur 2. Nam si corpora primigenia non differrent, vbique substantialiter non differrent, vbique eadem res nascerentur. Hoc locorum eædem res non fit,ergo. Maior patet consideranti; reperirentur enim vbiq; locorum femina eadem, eiusdemq; speciei, vnde substantiae mixtae nascerentur eaedem, neq; differrent plusquam numero, mole, figura, & accidentibus, quod quamfit procul ab experientia,nemo non videt. Quis enim dicat minima crystalli v. g. eiusdem esse substantiae cum puluisculis auri? atomos adamantinas eiusdem naturae cum ijs, quae conflant succinum, paleam, &c? Vnde Lucret. Carus lib. 1. habet, quod
units.tr: It is proved secondly. For if the primary bodies did not differ, they would not differ in substance anywhere, and the same things would be born everywhere. But the same things are not born in every place; therefore, etc. The major premise is evident to anyone who considers it: for the same seeds, of the same kind, would be found everywhere, and so the same mixed substances would be born, and would differ only in number, mass, shape, and accidents. That this is far from experience, no one fails to see. For who would say that the smallest particles of crystal, for instance, are of the same substance as the grains of gold dust? Or that the adamantine atoms are of the same nature as those that make up amber, straw, and so on? Hence Lucretius, in book 1 of De rerum natura, says:

units.la: Hac re nequeunt ex omnibus omnia gigni,
units.tr: From these things nothing can be born from everything,

units.la: Nam certis in rebus inest secreta facultas.
units.tr: For in certain things there lies a hidden power.

units.la: Nimirum in diuersis rerum substantijs diuersa quoq; virtus ad operandum. Et paulò post rogat Lucretius, quare ver expectetur à rosa, vt floreat; à vitib. autumnus, vt racemos impleant,
units.tr: Clearly, in different substances of things there is also a different power for acting. And a little later Lucretius asks why spring is awaited from the rose so that it may bloom, and autumn from the vines so that they may fill their clusters:

units.la: Si non certa suo quia tempore semina rerum
units.tr: If the seeds of things, each at its own certain time,

units.la: Cum confluxerunt, patefit quodcumq; creatur?
units.tr: Did not come together, how would anything that is created be revealed?

units.la: Non enim omnia semina sufficiunt ad omnem generationem, sed expectanda sunt propria cuiusq; rei principia, vt ad sua loca,& suo tempore nouis rebus gignendis inseruiat. Hinc est quod certis floribus certae quaedam terrae, certae aquae, certi venti prosunt, alij nocent, in ijs in deferuntur semina congrua, non in istis. Inde oritur, cur non vbique aurum, non vbiq; argentum, non vbiq; segetes, vuae, sacçafaccarum, cassiæ, crocus, &c. innascantur. Quia enim eædem substantiæ seminales vbiq; non sunt, ideo non omnis fert omnia tellus.
units.tr: For not all seeds suffice for every generation; rather, the proper principles of each thing must be awaited, so that they may serve, in their own places and at their own time, for the begetting of new things. Hence it is that certain lands, certain waters, and certain winds help certain flowers, while others harm them; the suitable seeds are carried to these places and not to those. From this arises the reason why gold does not grow everywhere, nor silver everywhere, nor crops, grapes, sugar canes, cassia, saffron, and so on. For since the same seminal substances are not everywhere, therefore not every land bears everything.

units.la: Quæ autem fert, progeneratq; ob hanc vnicè causam formas habent substantialiter differentes, quia ex primigenijs corporibus inter se pariter differentibus enascuntur; vnde mixta inquit. Aug. 3.de Trin. c. 8. Incrementa debita magnitudinis, distinctionesq; formarum ab originalibus (nempe ab atomis primigenijs) tamquam à regulis sumunt.
units.tr: Those things, however, which the earth bears and produces have forms that differ in substance, for this one reason alone: they arise from primary bodies that likewise differ from one another; hence the mixed bodies. Augustine, De Trinitate 3, ch. 8, says: They take the due increments of size, and the distinctions of forms, from the original elements (namely, the primary atoms), as from rules.

units.la: Probatur 3. vltima pars conclusionis. Quemadmodum enim in communi sententia Peripatetica metallorum formæ discrimen habent substantiale à vegetantibus: & hæ pariter à formis differunt sensitiuorum, ita prorsus atomi primigeniæ aliæ sunt pro metallicis, aliæ pro vegetantibus, alię pro sensitiuis. Confirmatur, quia si principia metallicorum eadem sunt cum ijs, quæ faciunt vegetantia, & sensitiua, igitur metalla vegetabuntur, & sentient. Secundò res metallicæ nutrire possent vegetantes, ac sensitiuas, quod falsum est. Hinc obseruant peritiores Medici, aurum, quod vocant potabile, nō assumi ad nutrimentum, sed vt prauis causis, quæ agerent in perniciem ægroti, alia præparetur materia, in quam agendo, vim suum retundant. Ex quib. omnib. clarum fit, prima rerum principia esse minima corpora, siue atomos, iuxta varia mixtorum genera inter se substantialiter differentes. Hinc Aug.l.3.de Gen.ad lit.c 14.ait quòd in corporibus animalium putrescentibus, inest vis quaedam naturalis, quasi praeseminata materia, & quodammodo initiata primordia futurorum animalium, qua de corruptionibus taliū corporū pro suo quaq; genere, ac differentijs erant exortura.
units.tr: It is proved thirdly, which is the last part of the conclusion. For just as, in the common Peripatetic opinion, the forms of metals differ in substance from those of plants, and these likewise differ from the forms of animals with senses, so in the same way the primary atoms are some for metals, some for plants, and some for animals with senses. It is confirmed: if the principles of metals were the same as those which make plants and animals, then metals would grow and would feel. Secondly, metallic things could nourish plants and animals, which is false. Hence the more skilled physicians observe that gold, which they call potable, is not taken as nourishment, but so that, against harmful causes which would act to the destruction of the sick person, another matter is prepared, upon which they may act and so blunt their force. From all these things it is clear that the first principles of things are minimal bodies, or atoms, which differ in substance according to the various kinds of mixed bodies. Hence Augustine, De Genesi ad litteram 3, ch. 14, says that in the putrefying bodies of animals there is a certain natural power, as it were a matter sown beforehand, and in some way the first beginnings of the animals to come, which from the corruptions of such bodies were to arise, each according to its own kind and differences.

units.la: Obijcies 1. Mixta componuntur ex ijs, in quæ resoluuntur: sed resolutio non fit in atomos, ergo. Probatur minor, si enim soluatur mixtum, id quod manet, ignis est, aqua, terra, &c. ergo non sunt atomi.
units.tr: You will object first: mixed bodies are composed of those things into which they are resolved; but the resolution is not into atoms; therefore, etc. The minor premise is proved: if a mixed body is dissolved, what remains is fire, water, earth, and so on; therefore these are not atoms.

units.la: Resp. distinguendo minorem. Prima, & secunda solutio non fit in atomos, trasfeat; vltima, negatur. Ad probationem dico, lignum primò resolui in aquam, ignem, &c. sed hæc etiam ex atomis conflata sunt.
units.tr: I reply by distinguishing the minor premise: the first and second dissolutions are not into atoms, granted; the last, denied. As for the proof, I say that wood is first resolved into water, fire, and so on; but these too are made up of atoms.

units.la: Obijces 2. Mixta omnia resoluuntur in ignem, terra, aquam, vapore, ergo principia rerum omnium eadem sunt, neq; differunt in mixtis pro diuersitate specierum.
units.tr: You will object second: all mixed bodies are resolved into fire, earth, water, and vapour; therefore the principles of all things are the same, and they do not differ in mixed bodies according to the diversity of species.

units.la: Resp. negari posse antecedens. Non .n. omnia, sed aliqua tantummodo mixta resoluuntur in prædicta, vnde crystallus, adamas, aurum, & similia nunquam videntur in aquam solui. Resp. 2. etiam data prædicta resolutione, terram illam non esse vnius tantùm speciei, nec aquam vnius, vt obseruant chymici, vnde non omnes aquæ ad maculorum abstersiones valent, nec ad opera omnia cineres omnes, vt experiuntur vitriarij Murianenses, qui solos adhibent Hispanicos, &c.
units.tr: I reply that the antecedent can be denied. For not all, but only some mixed bodies, are resolved into the things named; hence crystal, adamant, gold, and similar things are never seen to dissolve into water. Second reply: even granting that resolution, that earth is not of only one kind, nor that water is of only one kind, as the chemists observe; hence not all waters are effective for cleansing stains, nor all ashes for all works, as the glassmakers of Murano, who use only Spanish ashes, find by experience.

units.la: Obijcies 3. In mixtorum corruptionibus non videntur istæ atomi, quæ dicuntur componere, nam quidquid manet, corporeum est, ac facilè diuisibile, igitur atomi difflandæ sunt.
units.tr: You will object third: in the corruptions of mixed bodies those atoms which are said to compose them do not appear; for whatever remains is corporeal and easily divisible; therefore atoms must be dispersed.

units.la: Resp. non bene argui: Non videntur, ergò non sunt, quia nec peripateticus materiam videt primam, quam tamen admittit. 2. resp. quòd si non videntur, saltem odorantur, tanguntur, gustantur. 3. si nullo etiam sensu in se cognoscantur, ab effectu tamen cognosci possunt. V. g. quia capilli sensim in aëre spisso madescunt, vestesq; guttularum adhæsione sudant, arguimus, paulatim accreuisse atomos aqueas. Ita cum labra puteorum, vbi demittunt funes, videantur disecta in canaliculos; templorum limina præ assiduo pedum affrictu diminuta; vomeres continuo ex vsu consumpti, cognoscimus corpora minima, & atomos, etiamsi non sentiantur, semper diuelli, & migrare aliò. Hoc enim in causa est, inquit Carus l. 2. quòd Annulus in digito subtertenuatur habendo, Stillicidi casus lapidem cavat, vncus aratri Ferreus occultè decrescit vomer in aruis.
units.tr: I reply that the argument is badly made. They are not seen, therefore they do not exist; for neither does the Peripatetic see prime matter, which he nevertheless admits. Second reply: even if they are not seen, at least they are smelled, touched, and tasted. Third reply: even if they are known by no sense in themselves, they can still be known from their effects. For example, because hairs gradually become damp in thick air, and garments sweat from the adhesion of droplets, we conclude that watery atoms have gradually accumulated. So too, when the rims of wells, where ropes are let down, are seen to be worn into little grooves; when the thresholds of temples are diminished by the constant rubbing of feet; when ploughshares are continually consumed by use, we recognise that minimal bodies and atoms, even though they are not felt, are always being torn away and migrating elsewhere. For this is the cause, says Lucretius in book 2, that a ring on the finger grows thinner from wearing it, that the falling of drops hollows out a stone, and that the iron hook of the plough, the ploughshare, secretly wears away in the fields.

units.la: Imò siquis credendum sensui magis, quàm rationi putet, quæritq; oculis, ait Nissenus, indiuidua, ac cæca illa corpuscula contueri, is poterit aerè talibus particulis refertum aspicere, quando radij solis per fenestram excepti, cam aeris partem clariorem reddiderint. Hic enim infinita corpusculorum in aere volitantium multitudo, quae in reliquo aeris spatio oculis cerni non potest, radiorum beneficio perspicitur. Hucusque Nissen. orat. 1. exam. Sed res videtur otij plena longiùs profesequi diuulsiones atomorum, quae à corporibus fiunt, cùm ex hac sola causa meteora omnia consentur, propagentur odores, eueniant contagiones &c. quae suo loco explicabimus. Hoc vnum sat erit, quod inter cæteros aphorismos habet Sanctorius in sua Statica Medica. Pespiratio ait, qua salubriter aufert e corpore multum, idque inutile pondus, non est quae cum sudore fit, sed ille halitus inuisibilis, qualis hyeme uno die naturali ad quinquaginta vncias, & vltra exhalare potest. Vnde nisi per cibum reficiantur deperditi spiritus, contingit lassitudo, & aliquando interitus. Hæc autem omnia fiunt, etiamsi fortasse nullo sensu percipiantur Vsqueadeo, repetit sæpe Lucretius Corporibus cæcis natura agit res.
units.tr: Indeed, if anyone thinks that the senses are to be trusted more than reason, and seeks with his eyes to behold those indivisible and blind little bodies, he will be able to see the air full of such particles, when rays of the sun, admitted through a window, have made that part of the air brighter. For here the infinite multitude of little bodies flying about in the air, which cannot be seen by the eyes in the rest of the space of the air, is made visible by the help of the rays. So far Gregory of Nyssa, Oratio 1, Exameron. But the matter seems too leisurely to pursue at length the dispersions of atoms which come from bodies, since all meteors are attributed to this cause alone, odours are spread, contagions occur, and so on, which we shall explain in their proper place. One thing alone will be enough, which Sanctorius includes among his other aphorisms in his Medical Statics: "Perspiration, by which the body is healthily relieved of much, and that useless weight, is not what happens with sweat, but that invisible vapour which in winter can be exhaled to fifty ounces and more in one natural day. Hence, unless the lost spirits are restored by food, weariness comes on, and sometimes death." Yet all these things happen even if perhaps they are perceived by no sense. So often Lucretius repeats it: Nature acts through bodies that are blind.

units.la: DISQISITIO TERTIA.
units.tr: Third Disquisition.

units.la: Quot sint rerum principia naturalium.
units.tr: How many principles of natural things there are.

units.la: PRo intelligentia præmitti debet, non quæri à nobis hoc loco de rerum principijs, quæ mixta componunt in species. Siquidem innumeræ sunt rerum species, quæ à Deo conditæ fuerunt initiò, & quorum naturæ variæ, diuersæ, magis, minusve mixtæ nobis omnino ignotæ manent. Quapropter cùm singulæ sub intuitu non cadant, velle de omnibus quærere singillatim, res foret nimij laboris. Itaque disquisitio nostra tendit ad principia rerum in communi acceptarum, eo prorsus modo, quo etiam Aristotelei non descendendo ad peculiaria, de principijs in cõmuni disquiunt. Ij verò tria constituunt; mox duo, prout res in diuersò accipitur statu; nā si res actu fiat, Materia, forma, & privatio principia sunt; si facta sit, Materia & forma.
units.tr: It should first be understood that the question here is not about the principles of those things which combine to form the species of mixed bodies. For the species of things are innumerable, having been created by God at the beginning, and their natures, varied, diverse, more or less mixed, remain wholly unknown to us. Since individual species do not fall under our sight, to inquire into all of them one by one would be a task of excessive labour. Our inquiry therefore aims at the principles of things taken in general, in exactly the way that the Aristotelians too, without descending to particulars, dispute about principles in general. They indeed posit three, and then two, according as the thing is taken in a different state. For if the thing is made actually, matter, form and privation are its principles; if it has been made, matter and form.

units.la: Nobis igitur difficile non erit, statuere de numero principiorum, si mixta in quotuplicem soluantur partem, videamus. Docet autem experientia in omni solutione duo esse, quæ si maneant vnita simul, compositum quoque manet; si separentur, compositio amplius non est. Dicei ergo poterunt rerum principia in facto, esse duo; alteri quorum, vtpote crassiori, liceat dare denominatione materiæ; alteri tanquam subtiliori, & magis actiuo denominationem formæ. Rursus quia res in fieri, seu componi transit à nō n esse compositi ad esse, addi etiam poterit aliud principium, videlicet priuatio, siue negatio. Et sic erit nobis
units.tr: We therefore will not find it difficult to settle the number of principles, if we see into how many parts mixed bodies are resolved. Experience teaches that in every dissolution there are two things which, if they remain joined together, the compound also remains, and if they are separated, the composition no longer exists. It can therefore be said that the principles of a thing in its completed state are two: one of them, as being cruder, may be given the name of matter; the other, as being subtler and more active, the name of form. Again, because a thing in the process of becoming, or being composed, passes from not being composed to being, another principle may also be added, namely privation, or negation. And thus we shall have

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Principia rerum in facto esse duo sunt; substantia crassa, & corpulentior, quæ materia dici potest. Alia subtilior, & magis actiua, quæ forma. In fieri vero addi potest etiam priuatio.
units.tr: The principles of things in their completed state are two: a crude and grosser substance, which can be called matter; and another, subtler and more active, which is form. In the process of becoming, however, privation can also be added.

units.la: PRobatur prima pars cōclusionis, quia in omnium resolutione mixtorum cernimus quādam subsidere massam, quæ de se iners est, rudis, immota, & quò magis ad primigeniam sui naturam per nouas, nouasq; resolutiones redigitur, eò magis virtutum expers, & ad operationes inepta manet. Vnde si quid sensitiuum in corpus eterogeneum soluatur, & hoc etiā in partes alias; tandē superērit moles quædam crassa, materialis, & stupida, quæ nec motum, neque operationem dabit vllam. Est autem hæc materia in se talis, vt possit etiam assumi ad alia mixta in eodem genere conflanda, si tamen noua illi aduenerit pars, quæ actiua, efficax, & principium sit noui compositi, de qua infra dicetur. Hinc est, quòd si animalia putrescant in arvis, ibi lætiores euen-iunt segetes, attrahuntur. n. illius massæ particulæ à vi plastica seminum, & sensim claelaboratæ, digestæ, alijsq; additæ componunt calamū, aristam, triticum. Denuo si paleam quoq; sepelias, vt coloni periti faciunt, substantia eadem per alia semina, & radices attracta nouis rerum generationibus inseruiet, foliumq; pomumque, aut quid huiusmodi conflabit. Denique si hæc etiam sumantur à pecudibus in cibū, ea ipsa materia, prout varijs addetur diuersisq; substantiis in animali, carne, ossa, pellem, &c. efficiet. Vnde Carus in 2.
units.tr: The first part of the conclusion is proved as follows. In the resolution of all mixed bodies we see a certain mass settling out which is inert in itself, raw, immobile; and the more it is reduced by new and new resolutions to its primeval nature, the more it remains devoid of powers and unfit for operations. Hence, if anything sensitive is dissolved into a heterogeneous body, and this again into other parts, there will at last remain a certain gross, material and stupid mass, which will give no motion or operation whatever. This matter, however, is of such a nature that it can be taken up again to make other mixed bodies of the same kind, provided that a new part comes to it which is active, efficacious, and the principle of the new compound, of which more below. Hence it is that if animals putrefy in the fields, the crops there turn out more joyful, for those particles of that mass are drawn in by the plastic power of the seeds, and gradually elaborated, digested and joined with other things, and they compose stalk, ear and wheat. Again, if you bury even the straw, as skilled farmers do, the same substance, drawn in through other seeds and roots, will serve new generations of things, and will form leaf, apple, or something of the kind. Finally, if these things too are taken by beasts as food, that same matter, as it is added in the animal to various and diverse substances, will produce flesh, bones, skin, and so on. Hence Lucretius in book 2:

units.la: Vertūt se fluuij, frodes, & pabula lætaIn pecudes, vertunt pecudes in corporanostra naturam.
units.tr: The rivers turn themselves, and fruits and joyful pastures, into beasts; the beasts turn into our bodies.

units.la: comittitur .n. quidam in natura circulus, dū quod flos, frons, fructus est, in cibū sumitur, & pars crassior fit substantia animalis, donec eo quoq; corrupto, partes eædē crassiores ad segetū generationes iterū redeant. Idcirco quia pars ista corpulentior, & crassa indifferens est, accurritq; ad varias mixtorū species, dici poterit Materia rerū, nō illa sane metaphysica, in se incōpleta, quā dicitant Aristotelei, sed realis, physica, sensibilis, tägibilis.
units.tr: For a certain circle is kept up in nature: what is flower, leaf and fruit is taken as food and becomes the grosser substance of an animal, until that too, being corrupted, the same grosser parts return again to the generation of crops. Therefore, because this grosser and coarser part is indifferent and flows to the various species of mixed things, it may be called the matter of things; not indeed that metaphysical matter, incomplete in itself, of which the Aristotelians speak, but real, physical, sensible and tangible matter.

units.la: Probatur etiā secūda pars conclusionis. Patet .n. in solutionibus cōpositorū fieri assiduā, cōtinuāqux substātiæ insensibilis transpirationem, qua euaporante, partes cæteræ languent, motumque deperdunt, energiam, virtutem. Inde videbitis per cōbustionem exhalare fumum, ac tenuem substantiā, quæ secū defert acores, dulcores, odores: quapropter accessus ad ignem aliquando bonus, aliquando malus
units.tr: The second part of the conclusion is also proved.
