For it is plain that in the dissolution of compounds there occurs a constant and continual transpiration of an insensible substance, and when this evaporates, the other parts languish and lose their motion, energy and virtue. Hence you will see that in combustion smoke and a thin substance exhale, which carries away with it sharpnesses, sweetnesses and odours; therefore the approach to the fire is sometimes good, sometimes bad

units.la: prout varia est corporum, quæ foras mittuntur, euaporatio. Ita quoque in putrefactione mixta corrumpuntur ex tenuissimæ substantiæ abscessu, per quem oritur, vt res putrescendo paulatim fiat passa, ostendat rimas, deperdat pondus, quousque toto sublato humido cinerescat. Ex quo pender varia, & curiosa problematum explicatio. Cur nimirum viride lignum ponderet magis; pomum nuper ex arbore carptum fit solidius, ac durius; mox euadat in mollius, corrugetur, & comprimi possit. Quæ omnia suo loco in disquisitionem trahentur.
units.tr: according as the evaporation of the bodies that are sent forth is of one kind or another. So too in putrefaction mixed bodies are corrupted by the departure of the most subtle substance, through which it arises; so that the thing, by rotting, gradually becomes passive, shows cracks, loses weight, until, with all moisture removed, it turns to ash. From this depends a varied and curious explanation of problems: why, namely, green wood weighs more; why a fruit newly plucked from the tree becomes more solid and hard, then soon turns softer, shrivels, and can be compressed. All these things will be drawn into discussion in their proper place.

units.la: Est autem in se talis hæc substantia tenuis, & vapida, vt sit melior compositi pars, eum distinguat à cæteris, & omni virtute ad agendum informet. Hoc patet primò in sensitiuis, quorum formæ sunt substantiæ quædam viuidæ, actiuæ, igneæ, quæ vnum ab alio specie distinguunt. 2. patet in vegentantibus, quæ per animam vegetatiuam inter se differunt, hæc enim non est aliud, quâ substantia immaterialior, subtilior, & facilius vaporo sa. 3. patet in metallicis, inquibus periti duplicem partem distinguunt, alteram crassiorem, alteram subtilem magis, ac puram, vnde in quauis metallorum decoctione separatur semper aliquid fæcis, & scoriæ; sed quod purius est, manet. Demum partet vniuersaliter, quòd caro, si pars humida, & vaporosa vltimò extrahatur, non manet amplius caro; neque os manet in natura ossis; nec simile quid in esse suo
units.tr: Now this thin and vaporous substance is in itself such that it is the better part of the compound, which distinguishes it from the others and gives it form for every power of acting. This is shown first in sensitive things, whose forms are certain living, active, fiery substances, which distinguish one species from another. Second, it is shown in vegetables, which differ among themselves by the vegetative soul; for this is nothing other than a substance more immaterial, subtler, and more easily vaporised. Third, it is shown in metals, in which skilled workers distinguish a double part, one grosser, the other subtler and purer; hence in any boiling of metals something of dross and scum is always separated, but what is purer remains. Lastly, it is plainly true in general that when the moist and vaporous part is finally drawn out of flesh, the flesh no longer remains; nor does bone remain in the nature of bone; nor does anything similar keep its being

units.la: perseuerat, quoties ab intimo, & in insi- gni copia substantiæ euaporant. Imò cum his pereunt simul odores, virtutes, facultatesque ad operandum. Ex quo discimus, cur chymici, & spagirici, stipitum, herbarum, ac metallorum fæces repudient, quia nimirum educta per sublimationem subtiliori, ac meliori substantiâ, virtus omnis abit cum illa. Ergo pars ea substantialis, quæ subtilior, & magis actiua est, dici potest forma substantialis mixtorum, non ea tamen, quam volunt Aristotelei, non completam, non per se subsistentem &c. sed completa, physica, subsistens, realis.
units.tr: whenever substance evaporates from within and in considerable quantity. Indeed, together with these, odours, virtues and faculties for operating perish at the same time. From this we learn why chemists and spagyrists reject the dregs of wood, herbs and metals: because, namely, when the subtler and better substance has been drawn off by sublimation, all virtue departs with it. Therefore that substantial part which is subtler and more active may be called the substantial form of mixed bodies; not, however, that form which the Aristotelians want, incomplete, not subsisting through itself, and so on, but a complete, physical, subsisting and real form.

units.la: Probatur denique tertia pars conclusionis, quia compositum eo ipso quod fiat, concipitur transfire de non esse ad esse compositum, ergo in tali conceptu adest negatio, vt principium à quo: seu dum partes in compositione simul vniuntur, fit quidam transitus à priuatione vnionis ad ipsam, & sic priuatio ingredi potest conceptum compositi naturalis in fieri. Quare illius principia tria erunt, Materia, Forma, & Priuatio.
units.tr: Lastly, the third part of the conclusion is proved, because a compound, by the very fact that it comes to be, is conceived to pass from not being to being a compound. Therefore in such a concept there is present a negation as the principle from which; that is, while the parts are joined together in composition, a certain transition is made from the privation of union to union itself, and so privation can enter into the concept of a natural compound in becoming. Hence its principles will be three: matter, form, and privation.

units.la: Quæ omnia sicut iis, qui Aristoteleismo præoccupati non sunt, videri possunt magis ad sensum, & physicè dicta, sic fortasse probabilia magis, & verosimilia. Nec ausim dicere vera, quandoquidem in re physica, sphynges multæ, rarus œdipus, & nullius forsitan est. Vnde hic appositè repetas quod Manilius de Mundo l.1. habet Semper erit genus in pugna, dubiumque manebit quod latet. āderit enim nonnemo, qui hæc minùs approbet, imò refellat, impugnet, ac meliora, & magis veritati congrua ferat. Quod tamen quia nobis hucusque non accidit, Philosophia nostra hisce nixa principiis ad cæteros Physicorum libros ita procedet, vt iisdem, cùm opus erit, accommodè ỹsura sit.
units.tr: All these things, as they may be seen by those who are not preoccupied with Aristotelianism, and as they are stated more by sense and physically, so perhaps they are more probable and more likely. I would not venture to call them true, since in physical matters there are many sphinxes, a rare Oedipus, and perhaps none at all. Hence here you may fittingly repeat what Manilius says in the first book of his Astronomica: "There will always be a field for battle, and what lies hidden will remain in doubt." For there will certainly be someone who will approve these things less, indeed refute and attack them, and bring forward better things more in accord with truth. Since, however, this has not happened to us so far, our Philosophy, resting on these principles, will proceed through the other books of Physics in such a way that it will be suitably used for the same whenever there is need.

units.la: Primi Libri Finis.
units.tr: End of the First Book.

units.la: LIBER SECUNDVS PHYSICORVM
units.tr: BOOK TWO OF NATURAL THINGS

units.la: De rerum naturalium causis.
units.tr: On the causes of natural things.

units.la: VIdimus hucusque principia,quibus vnaquæque res naturalis intrinsecè conflatur, & in esse suo perfectissimo constituitur. Iam verò explicandum foret, quomodo hæc principia conueniant simul, vnianturque ad compositi effectionem. Sed quia id non fit, nisi ex prævio causarum influxu, propterea nobis aderit in hoc libro Tractatus de causis. Quid nimirum sit Causa, quotuplex, quid in se requirat, vt operetur, quid expectet ab alio,& huiusmodi. Quæ vtplurimum tam Aristoteli, quàm cæteris philosophis communia cùm sint, ideo sine multo dissidio à nobis pertractabuntur.
units.tr: We have seen so far the principles by which each natural thing is intrinsically put together and constituted in its most perfect being. Now it remains to explain how these principles come together and are united to bring about the composite. But since this does not happen except through a prior influx of causes, there will be in this book a treatise on causes. Namely: what a cause is, how many kinds there are, what it requires in itself in order to act, what it expects from another, and such things. Since these are for the most part common both to Aristotle and to the other philosophers, they will be treated by us without much dispute.

units.la: Diuidetur autem hoc opus quadruplici disputatione. Prima erit de causis in communi. Secunda fiet de causa Efficiente particulari. Tertia de Finali. Quarta de causa Prima, nempe Deo, cuius influxu omnis causa secunda tam eget, vt sine illo nequeat prorsus operari. Et quia Deum contemplatur Philosophia, tamquam naturæ Auctorem, fiet inde occasio nonnulla explicandi circa naturam, provt ab arte contradistincta est. Notetur itaque
units.tr: This work will be divided into four disputations. The first will concern causes in general. The second will deal with the particular efficient cause. The third with the final cause. The fourth with the first cause, namely God, on whose influx every secondary cause so depends that without him it cannot act at all. And since philosophy contemplates God as the Author of nature, there will thereby arise some occasion for explaining, in connection with nature, how it is distinguished from art. Let it therefore be noted that

units.la: DISPVTATIO PRIMA.
units.tr: DISPUTATIO PRIMA.

units.la: De causis in communi.
units.tr: On causes in general.

units.la: VErsatur in hoc vno tota Philosophia, vt rerum causas vestiget, ac teneat. Quod mens nostra cùm primum assequitur, maximè sibi adblanditur, & in sua rerum scientia gaudens, admirationem dedíscit, quæ oritur ab ignorantia, & stupidum hominem quodammodo facit. Adeo sanè vt mirari debeat nemo, si Archimedes inuentà rei abditæ causà, tamquam ex attonito exiliens, non semel, sed iterum gestiens illud reperi dictitarit. Vsqueadeo causarum notio esse cordi Philosopho debet. Ad hanc vt pergamus, fiat nobis.
units.tr: The whole of philosophy is concerned with this one thing: to track down and grasp the causes of things. When our mind first attains this, it takes great delight in itself, and, rejoicing in its knowledge of things, it puts aside the wonder that arises from ignorance, which makes a man in a way dazed. So much so that no one should be surprised if Archimedes, having discovered the hidden cause of a thing, leapt up as if thunderstruck and, not once but again and again, exulting, kept crying out "I have found it!" [reperi]. So dear to the philosopher ought the notion of cause to be. Let us proceed to this, and let it be done.

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: First Disquisition.

units.la: Quid sit causa, & quotuplex.
units.tr: What a cause is, and how many kinds there are.

units.la: PRo intelligentia rei, quæ plena difficultatis est, aduertite, duplici ex capite laborare philosophos, vt causæ in communi acceptæ definitionem adducant. Primò quia in Diuinis Pater Æternus vere influit, ac dat esse Verbo, & nihilominus in sensu Catholico dici non potest causa Verbi. Secundò quia inter causas aliæ cùm sint extrinsecæ, aliæ verò intrinsecæ, non tam facilè adinuenitur conceptus, qui omnibus vnà, & simul acceptis congruere valeat. Vnde Aristoteles data fortasse operà talem omisit definitionem. A recentioribus autem diuersimodè causa definitur. Seligamus meliorem, & sit
units.tr: To understand the matter, which is full of difficulty, note that philosophers labour under a twofold problem in trying to give a definition of cause in the general sense. First, because in divine matters the Eternal Father truly flows into the Word and gives it being, and yet in the Catholic sense he cannot be called the cause of the Word. Second, because some causes are extrinsic and others intrinsic, and it is not so easy to find a single concept that can fit all of them taken together at once. Hence Aristotle perhaps omitted such a definition on purpose. Later writers, however, define cause in various ways. Let us choose the better one, and let it be

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Causa in communi accepta bene definitur Principium, à quo influente per se aliquid pendet.
units.tr: A cause, taken in general, is well defined as a principle from which something depends per se, by its influence.

units.la: PRobatur explicando singulas in allata definitione particulas. Primò dicitur principium loco generis, quia omnis causa principium est, non è contra, vnde P. Æternus etsi causa Verbi non sit, nihilominus principium illius manet. Secundò dò à quo influente, vt excludantur causæ remotæ, quę reuera causæ non sunt,quia non influunt actu, quemadmodum est Adam respectu nostrum, 3. per se ad remotionem causæ per accidens, & conditionum,quæ in rigore dici causæ non debent: Inde Musicus ædificans nō est caufa ædificij vt musicus; & approximatio ad ignem non est vera causa caloris, nam sine illa potest ignis ex Dei saltem potentia facere calidum. Postremò dicitur causa id, à quo pendet aliquid, nam siue actu efficiat, siue moueat,siue componat, hoc quod efficitur, quod mouetur, quod componitur, actu pendet. Quapropter ob hanc particulam, excluditur Pater Æternus à conditione causæ respectu Filij, quia Filius in rigore dependentiam ab eo non habet, recipit enim ex vi generationis essentiam, quæ cùm sit eadem in Patre, dependere non potest, maximè quia dependentia qua talis infert imperfectionem.
units.tr: This is proved by explaining the individual particles of the definition just given. First, the word principle is put in the place of the genus, because every cause is a principle, but not conversely; hence the Eternal Father, although he is not the cause of the Word, nevertheless remains its principle. Second, I add from which, by its influence, so that remote causes are excluded, which are not truly causes, because they do not influence actually, as Adam is with respect to us. Third, per se is added to exclude accidental cause and conditions, which ought not strictly to be called causes. Thus a musician building a house is not the cause of the house as a musician; and bringing something near the fire is not the true cause of heat, for without that, fire could, by the power of God alone at least, make a thing warm. Lastly, the cause is said to be that from which something depends, for whether it effects, or moves, or composes, that which is effected, moved, or composed depends actually. For this reason, by this particle, the Eternal Father is excluded from the condition of cause with respect to the Son, because the Son strictly speaking does not have a dependence on him; for he receives his essence from the very generation, and since this is the same in the Father, it cannot depend, especially because dependence as such implies imperfection.

units.la: Quòd verò attinet ad causæ diuisionem,ea dicitur esse quadruplex. Efficiens, Finalis, Materialis, Formalis. Deprehenditur autem numerus causarum sic. Res,quæ fiunt,ab aliquo sanè producuntur, ergo datur causa producens, aut efficiens. Hæc verò non agit, nisi ob aliquem finem, igitur adest etiam causa finalis. Verùm nequit res aliqua produci, nisi fiat ex præiacente subiecto; vnde habetur causa subiectiua, & materialis.Hęc demum est subiectū alicuius formæ,quapropter datur etiam causa formalis.Porrò ex his duæ intrinsecæ sunt, materia, & forma; duæ aliæ manent extrinsecæ, finalis, & efficiens. At
units.tr: As to the division of cause, it is said to be fourfold: efficient, final, material, formal. The number of causes is discovered thus. Things that are made are certainly produced by someone, so there is a producing or efficient cause. But this does not act except for some end, so there is also a final cause. Yet no thing can be produced unless it is made from a pre-existing subject; hence there is a subjective and material cause. This subject, finally, is the subject of some form, so there is also a formal cause. Moreover, of these, two are intrinsic, matter and form; two others remain extrinsic, the final and the efficient. But

units.la: Obijcies 1 contra causæ definitionē sic. Allata definitio non conuenit causæ finali, ergo mala. Probatur antecedens. Causa finalis non influit in effectum vere, ac realiter: non enim finis, quo agens mouetur ad agendum, imprimit motum: quis enim dicat pomi dulcoré v. g. trahere physicè, ac mouere puerum, vt illud amet? Est ergo finis pura cōditio,qua posita, voluntas per se mouetur, ergo causa finalis vera causa non est.
units.tr: You will object 1 against the definition of cause thus: the stated definition does not apply to the final cause, therefore it is bad. The antecedent is proved: the final cause does not truly and really influence the effect; for the end by which the agent is moved to act does not impart motion. Who would say that the sweetness of an apple, for example, physically draws and moves a boy so that he loves it? The end is therefore a mere condition, which, being posited, the will is moved of itself; therefore the final cause is not a true cause.

units.la: Resp. negando antecedens. Ad probationem distinguo:causa finalis non influit efficienter,concedo; non influit finaliter, nego,alioquin si primo influeret modo, non esset amplius finalis, sed efficiens. Ergo finis est pura conditio, negatur, vt suo loco dicemus,cùm de causa finali.
units.tr: I answer by denying the antecedent. As to the proof, I distinguish: the final cause does not influence efficiently, I grant; it does not influence finally, I deny; for if it influenced in the first way, it would no longer be final but efficient. Therefore the end is a mere condition: this is denied, as we shall say in its place, when we treat of the final cause.

units.la: Obijcies 2. Pater Æternus non est causa Filij,& nihilominus hic pendet à Patre, igitur malè dicitur causa id, à quo aliquid pendet; vel sic. Filius Æternus pendet à Patre, igitur iste est causa Filij;quod si dicatur,absurdum erit. Probatur vtrumque antecedens, nam reuera Filius procedit, atq; accipit esse à Patre, nec sine illo esse potest, ergo pendet.
units.tr: You will object 2. The Eternal Father is not the cause of the Son, and yet the Son depends on the Father; therefore it is badly said that a cause is that from which something depends. Or thus: the Eternal Son depends on the Father; therefore the Father is the cause of the Son; and if this is said, it will be absurd. Both antecedents are proved, for in truth the Son proceeds from the Father and receives being from him, nor can he be without him; therefore he depends.

units.la: Resp.negando antecedens, non enim sufficit ad rigorosam dependentiam,quòd filius nequeat esse absq; Patre, alioquin Pater etiā penderet à Filio, quia nec illo absq; isto esse potest. Adsunt ad hoc exempla, nam neq; materia in communi sententia sine forma esse potest, quamuis à forma dependentiam non habeat; neque corpus absq; loco, etsi à loco non dependeat. Quòdsi repetas, Filium pendere à Patre, quia suum esse ab illo habet, dico non esse hoc rigorosè dependere, non enim recipit essentiam ab eo distinctam, sed eandem.
units.tr: I answer by denying the antecedent. For it is not enough for strict dependence that the Son cannot exist without the Father; otherwise the Father would also depend on the Son, since he too cannot exist without him. There are examples of this: for in the common opinion matter cannot exist without form, although it does not have dependence upon form; nor does a body exist without place, although it does not depend on place. But if you repeat that the Son depends on the Father because he has his being from him, I say that this is not strictly to depend, for he does not receive an essence distinct from the Father's, but the same essence.

units.la: Obijcies 3. etiam ab actione pendet efsectus, at verò actio non dicitur causa, ergo id, à quo pendet aliquid, non semper causa est; mala igitur definitio.
units.tr: You will object 3. Also, an effect depends on an action, yet an action is not called a cause; therefore that from which something depends is not always a cause; the definition is bad.

units.la: Resp. cum distinctione. Ab actione pendet effectus vt ab eo quo, concedo; vt ab eo quod, nego. Requiritur ergo ad rationem causæ, vt sit in recto id, quod influit; non id quo, siue instrumentum, aut influxus: actio autem est influxus, non id, quod influit, ergo, &c.
units.tr: I answer with a distinction. An effect depends on an action as on that by which (a quo), I grant; as on that which (ab eo quod), I deny. For the notion of cause, therefore, it is required that what influences be the thing in the direct sense, and not that by which, that is, the instrument or the influx; but action is the influx, not that which influences; therefore, etc.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: SECOND DISQUISITION.

units.la: An, & quomodo causa prior sit suo effectu.
units.tr: Whether and how a cause is prior to its effect.

units.la: PRo intelligētia repetite, quòd sicut in summulis docui, vnum esse potest prius alio tripliciter, nimirum tempore, natura, origine. Tempore, cùm res aliam in duratione præcedit: sic hodierna dies prior est crastina. Natura, quando res non tempore, sed independentia præcedit: v. g. sol est prior luce, quia non pendet ab eo, sed è contra. Origine, cum res influit in aliam, sed non efficit dependentem: ita Pater Æternus prior est origine Filio, quia illum generat, sed in rigore Filius à Patre non pendet; unde licet unus absque alio esse, aut cógipi nequeat, non ideo tamen inter eos dependentia_ ulla rigorosa est, nam hæc videtur secum trahere imperfectionem. Hisce positis, notetur.
units.tr: For clarity, recall what I taught in the Summulae: one thing can be prior to another in three ways, namely in time, in nature, and in origin. Something is prior in time when it precedes another in duration, as today is prior to tomorrow. Something is prior in nature when it precedes without being earlier in time, but by independence: for example, the sun is prior to its light, because the light depends on the sun and not the reverse. Something is prior in origin when it flows into another but does not make that other dependent: thus the Eternal Father is prior to the Son in origin, because he begets him, yet strictly speaking the Son does not depend on the Father. So although the one cannot be without the other, or be conceived without the other, there is no strict dependence between them, since such dependence seems to carry imperfection with it. With these things laid down, let the following be noted.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Omnis causa, ut causa, prior est saltem natura effectu suo.
units.tr: Every cause, as cause, is prior at least in nature to its effect.

units.la: PRobatur facilè, quia causa dat esse totum effectui, ergo est naturà prior effectu. Consequentia currit, nam effectus eò quòd à causa suum esse accipiat, pendet ab illa, & è contra causa non pendet ab effectu, quia non recipit esse ab eo, igitur causa prior est naturà effectu. Confirmatur, nam sublata causa, & nulla succedente in eius locum, non ponitur effectus; & ex aduerso effectu ablato, nō tollitur causa, vt in sole clarum fit, ergo causa semper habet effectum à se dependentem, & sic naturà prior est.
units.tr: This is easily proved, because a cause gives the whole of its being to the effect, and so is prior in nature to the effect. The inference holds: the effect, since it receives its being from the cause, depends on it, whereas the cause does not depend on the effect, since it does not receive its being from it. Therefore the cause is prior in nature to the effect. It is confirmed thus: when the cause is removed, and nothing succeeds in its place, the effect is not posited; but when the effect is removed, the cause is not taken away, as is clear in the case of the sun. Therefore the cause always has an effect that depends on it, and so it is prior in nature.

units.la: Quæri poterit, an causa prior etiam sit naturà causalitate sua. Pro intelligentia, nota quòd omnis causa dicit actum primum, & secundum. Actus primus non aliud est, quàm virtus causæ potentis agere, quemadmodum actus primus v. g. ignis dicit virtute ignis aptam natam produeere calorem. Porro actus iste primus duplex est, Proximus, & Remotus. Actus primus proximus dicitur virtus, cui omnia requisita insunt ad operandum, sed adhuc non operatur. Actus primus remotus est virtus causae de se potentis agere, sed carens requisitis, vt agat: sic v. g. in igne Babylonico respectu trium puerorum fuit actus primus remotus, nam reuera ignis vim habebat ex se comburendi, verum non poterat vrere actu, ob influxus Diuini absentiam. Vt enim causa constituatur in actu primo proximo, requiritur Dei concursus, & remotio impedimenti ab agente inauferibilis, quare surdus a natiuitate non diceretur in actu primo proximo ad me audiendum, quia inesset illi surditas ab ipso inauferibilis. Actus autem secundus causae dicit causam in actu secundo agente; seu causam quatenus producit, influitq; in essectum. Hisce positis adest.
units.tr: It may be asked whether a cause is also prior in nature by its causality. For clarity, note that every cause involves a first act and a second act. The first act is nothing other than the power of a cause that is able to act, just as the first act of fire is, by the power of fire, its fitness and nature to produce heat. This first act is twofold: proximate and remote. A proximate first act is a power in which everything required for acting is present, but which does not yet act. A remote first act is the power of a cause that is able to act of itself but lacks the requisites for acting. Thus, for example, in the Babylonian furnace with respect to the three boys, the fire was a remote first act: in truth the fire had in itself the power of burning, but it could not burn in act, because the divine influx was absent. For a cause to be established in proximate first act, both the concurrence of God and the removal of an impediment that cannot be removed by the agent are required. Hence a man deaf from birth would not be said to be in proximate first act for hearing me, because the deafness is in him and cannot be removed by him. The second act of a cause, however, is the cause acting in second act, that is, the cause as it produces and flows into the effect. With these points established, there follows:

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Causa in actu primo est prior natura, causalitate sua. Non ita in actu secundo.
units.tr: A cause in first act is prior in nature by its causality. Not so in second act.

units.la: PRobatur prima pars conclusionis, quia causa in actu primo non debet concipi constituta per suam causalitatem, sed tantummodo per aptitudinem vt ipsa eliciat; ergo est prior causalitate, nec pendet ab illa. E contra verò causalitas dependentiam habet à causa, nec esse, aut concipi sine illa potest, ergo causalitas est posterior natura.
units.tr: The first part of the conclusion is proved because a cause in first act is not to be conceived as established by its causality, but only by its aptitude to bring forth its effect; therefore it is prior to causality and does not depend on it. On the other hand, causality has its dependence from the cause, and it can neither be nor be conceived without it; therefore causality is posterior in nature.

units.la: Probatur etiam secunda pars, quia causa in actu secundo non est causa tantùm, sed complexum ex causa, & causalitate, igitur hoc totum non est posterius natura causalitate, secus enim causalitas foret posterior se ipsa, & penderet à se, quod tamen fieri nequit.
units.tr: The second part is also proved, because a cause in second act is not the cause alone, but a compound of cause and causality. Therefore this whole is not posterior in nature to causality; otherwise causality would be posterior to itself and would depend on itself, which cannot happen.

units.la: Quæri vltimò potest ad quæstionis complementum, an causalitas ipsa prior sit natura effectu suo. Pro intelligentia debet adverti, quòd causalitas, quotiescumq; reperitur inter causam, & efsectum, est actio, influxus, aut id, quo causa operatur. Id autem quo, antecedenter intelligitur ad effectum, & ratio est, nam actio dirigitur ad illum, vt ad terminum; non ita effectus ad actionem. Quamobrem etiamsi actio, siue causalitas necessariò sit alicuius rei causalitas, vndè sine termino esse nequit, nihilominus quia hæc ordinatur ad rem, ad effectum, ad aliud, prior aliquo modo esse debet, quàm res. Fiat ergo.
units.tr: Lastly, to complete the question, it can be asked whether causality itself is prior in nature to its effect. For clarity it must be noted that wherever causality is found between cause and effect, it is an action, an influx, or that by which the cause operates. Now that by which is understood as antecedent to the effect, and the reason is that the action is directed towards the effect as its term, whereas the effect is not directed towards the action. Wherefore, even though an action or causality must necessarily be the causality of something, and so cannot be without a term, nevertheless, because it is ordered to the thing, to the effect, to something else, it must in some way be prior to the thing. So let it be.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Causalitas prior est naturâ suo effectu.
units.tr: Causality is prior by nature to its effect.

units.la: PRobatur facilè, nam causa ideo est prior naturâ suo effectu, quia hic accipit esse, atq; pendet ab illa; sed etiam effectus accipit esse aliquo modo, & pendet à causalitate, igitur & causalitas erit natura prior suo effectu. Minor patet, nam causalitas ordinatur; & est actio ipsa, qua producitur effectus, ergo hic habet esse, atq; pendet ab illa, &c.
units.tr: Proof is easy. A cause is prior by nature to its effect because the effect receives its being from the cause and depends on it. But the effect also receives its being in some way and depends on causality, so causality too will be prior by nature to its effect. The minor premise is clear: causality is ordered to something, and it is the very action by which the effect is produced. Therefore the effect has its being from it and depends on it, and so on.

units.la: Opponis. Imò causalitas pendet ab effectu, ergo non est prior illo naturâ. Probatur antecedens. Causalitas absque effectu esse non potest, ergo pendet ab illo. Consequentia currit, nam illud tantùm priùs est alio naturâ, quod se solo esse potest, ac sine illo: huiusmodi non est causalitas, ergo.
units.tr: You object: on the contrary, causality depends on the effect, so it is not prior to it by nature. The antecedent is proved: causality cannot exist without an effect, so it depends on the effect. The consequence holds, because only that which can exist alone, without the other, is prior by nature to it. Causality is not of this kind. Therefore...

units.la: Resp. distinguendo: causalitas pendet ab effectu à posteriori, concedo; à priori, nego; ergo non est prior naturâ, negatur consequentia. Ad probationem, nego illud tantùm esse priùs alio naturâ, quod esse potest sine illo. Adest exemplum in materia prima, quæ dicitur esse non posse nec sine quantitate, nec sine forma, tametsi naturâ prior sit illâ: in corpore locato, quod absq; loco esse nequit, cùm nihilominus naturâ sit priùs loco, &c.
units.tr: I reply by distinguishing. Causality depends on the effect a posteriori: I concede. A priori: I deny. So it is not prior by nature: I deny the consequence. As to the proof, I deny that only that which can exist without another is prior by nature to it. There is an example in prime matter, which is said to be unable to exist either without quantity or without form, and yet it is prior by nature to them. Likewise a located body cannot exist without place, and yet it is prior by nature to place, and so on.

units.la: Itaq. aliud est pendere à posteriori; aliud à priori ; causalitas dependentiâ habet ab effectu à posteriori, quia si est causalitas ergo alicuius rei est, unde si res, aut essectus iste posterior non sit, neq; causalitas, erit. Effectus autem pendet à causalitate à priori, nam per eam fit, producitur, habet esse, illa ergo est prior natura.
units.tr: So depending a posteriori is one thing, and depending a priori is another. Causality has a dependence on the effect a posteriori, because if there is causality, it is the causality of something; hence if that thing, or this posterior effect, is not, neither will causality be. But the effect depends on causality a priori, for through causality it is made and produced, and it has its being. Therefore causality is prior by nature.

units.la: Patet etiam ex dictis, causam non esse in actu secundo constitutam ex entitate sua tantum; potest enim causa esse in se, atq; concipi, quamuis actu non operetur. Fit ergo agens, aut operans in actu secundo per aliquid superadditum, scilicet per causalitatem, influxum, actionem. Quaeritur modo, Quid sit causalitas ista, influxus, & actio.
units.tr: It is also clear from what has been said that a cause is not constituted in second act from its entity alone. For a cause can be in itself and can be conceived even though it does not actually operate. Therefore it becomes an agent or operator in second act through something superadded, namely through causality, influx, or action. The question now is what this causality, influx, and action is.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Causalitas, aut influxus causæ in effectum, est modus quidam à causa distinctus, & ab effectu.
units.tr: Causality, or the influx of a cause into its effect, is a certain mode distinct from both the cause and the effect.

units.la: PRobatur, quia omnes fere causæ naturales ita producunt suos effectus, ut ijdem esse possint absq; illarum causalitate, ac influxu, ergo causalitas in essectum, est modus quidam à causa distinctus, & ab effectu. Probo consequentiam. Potest esse causa, & effectus licet hic à tali causa non pendeat; ergo pendere, seu effici à tali causa, est aliud quid praeter causam, & effectum. V. g. potest existere sol; potest existere hodierna lux, etsi sol non influat in hanc lucem, puta si
units.tr: Proof: almost all natural causes so produce their effects that the same effects could exist without the causality and influx of those causes. Therefore the causality of a cause into its effect is a certain mode distinct from the cause and from the effect. I prove the consequence. A cause and an effect can exist although the effect does not depend on such a cause. Therefore to depend on such a cause, or to be effected by it, is something other than the cause and the effect. For example, the sun can exist, and today's light can exist, even if the sun does not flow into this light. Suppose God, by withholding concurrence from the sun, produced this light by himself alone.

units.la: Deus denegando soli concursum, producere se solo hanc lucem, ergo lucem hanc pendere, producì, habere influxum à sole, est quid aliud præter lucem, & solem; non nisi actio, seu modus causandi, ergo solis causalitas in lucem est modus à sole distinctus, & à luce.
units.tr: Therefore for this light to depend on the sun, to be produced by it, and to have influx from it, is something other than the light and the sun. It is nothing but action, or the mode of causing. So the sun's causality towards the light is a mode distinct from both the sun and the light.

units.la: Opponis. Etiam ipsa causalitas effici debet à causa sua, ergo per modum alium à causa, & causalitate distinctum. Probatur consequentia; nam effectus omnis producitur à causa per modum superadditum, sed etiam causalitas est effectus; ergo & ipsa per modum superadditum fieri debet, quo posito abimus in infinitum. Vel si causalitas immediatè à causa manat sine vllo superaddito, consimiliter de quouis effectu dicendum.
units.tr: You object: causality itself must be effected by its cause, and so through a mode other than the cause and causality, distinct from both. The consequence is proved thus: every effect is produced by its cause through a superadded mode, but causality is also an effect, so it too must be produced through a superadded mode. And once that is posited, we proceed to infinity. Or if causality flows immediately from the cause without any superadded thing, the same must be said of any effect.

units.la: Resp. negando consequentiam. Disparitas est, quia causalitas est ratio ipsa formalis causandi, & dependendi, essentialiter per se talis, vnde non potest fieri per quid aliud. Eo modo quo albedo v. g. quia est ratio formalis constitutiva albi, non efficitur alba ipsa per aliam. Ad confirmationem dico, effectum produci per modum à causa distinctum, si veniat ab ipsa vt id quod; non si dimanet vt id quo.
units.tr: I reply by denying the consequence. There is a disparity. Causality is the very formal reason of causing and of depending, essentially and per se such, and so it cannot come about through anything else. It is like whiteness: because whiteness is the formal constitutive reason of the white thing, the white thing is not made white through another. To the confirmation I say that an effect is produced through a mode distinct from the cause if it comes from the cause as that which is produced; it is not so if it flows from the cause as that by which it is produced.

units.la: DISQVISITIO TERTIA.
units.tr: DISQVISITIO TERTIA.

units.la: Virum causa requirat existentiam ad ope- randum.
units.tr: Whether a cause requires existence in order to act.

units.la: PRo intelligentia sciendum est, contendere Thomistas, causā posse agere, siue influere ad effectum eo primo instanti, quo non est, seu quod sequitur ad illius corruptionem. v.g. ignem, qui extinguitur in instanti. a. posse cōburere in instanti. b. Quoniam vero 4. enumerantur causae, concedunt intrinsecas non posse agere, aut componere, nisi quandiu actu sunt. E contra in hoc omnes conueniunt, quod Finalis agat, moueatque ad sui consecutionem, quando etiam non est. Recidit ergo difficultas in causam efficientem, an scilicet operari valeat in instanti, quo ipsa non exstitit. Pro solutione sit
units.tr: For understanding this, it must be noted that the Thomists maintain that a cause can act, or flow into its effect, at the very first instant when it does not yet exist, or that which follows upon its corruption; for example, a fire which is extinguished in an instant can burn in that instant (a). Since, however, four causes are enumerated, they concede that intrinsic causes cannot act or compose anything except for as long as they actually exist (b). On the contrary, all agree on this, that the final cause acts and moves towards its own attainment even when it does not exist. The difficulty therefore comes down to the efficient cause, namely whether it can operate in the instant in which it does not exist. For the solution, let the following be laid down:

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Causa debet esse in eo instanti, quo agit, nec satis est, si fuerit imme- diate antecedenti.
units.tr: A cause must be in that instant in which it acts; it is not enough that it be immediately antecedent.

units.la: PRobatur, nam in instanti, quo causa non est, neque adest virtus productiua causae, nec potentia vt agat, alioquin adesset ipsa causa, quae non aliud censeri debet, quam talis potentia, & virtus ad operandum. Ergo pro illo instanti egeagere nequit. Probo consequentiam. Repugnant hæc duo, actu operari, & nō posse operari: sed eo instanti, quo causa non est, operari non potest, ergo tunc temporis non operatur. Patet minor, quia nemo dat, quod non habet; causa pro illo instanti non habet esse, quo igitur modo esse alteri dabit?
units.tr: This is proved, for in the instant in which the cause is not, neither is the productive power of the cause present, nor is there a power to act; otherwise the cause itself would be present, which ought to be regarded as nothing other than such a power and capacity for acting. Therefore for that instant it cannot act. I prove the consequence: two things are incompatible, to act actually and not to be able to act; but in that instant in which the cause is not, it cannot act, therefore at that time it does not act. The minor is evident, because no one gives what he does not have; the cause for that instant does not have being, so how will it give being to another?

units.la: Probatur 2. nam si causa valet producere aliquid, cum primò non est, ergo poterit etiam pro aliis instantibus. Consequentia patet, quia nil magis causæ in hoc instanti est, quàm in reliquis, æquè enim non existit in uno, ac in aliis; in aliis autem per Thomistas agere nequit, ergo nec in primo aget.
units.tr: It is proved secondly: for if a cause is able to produce something when it does not yet exist, it will be able also for other instants. The consequence is clear, because the cause is in no way more present in this instant than in the rest; for it does not exist in one just as it does not exist in the others. But according to the Thomists it cannot act in the others, therefore neither will it act in the first.

units.la: Probatur 3. ex ipsis Thomistarum principijs. Docent enim ad actionem requiri præsentiam agentis; quo posito, arguo sic. Agens, quod non est, neq; præsens adesse potest. 2. actio requirit potentiam agentis, ergo multò magis ipsum esse agentis. 3. ideo requiritur agentis præsentia, quia si absit agens, perinde est, ac si non esset, ergo si revera non sit, revera non aget.
units.tr: It is proved thirdly from the very principles of the Thomists. For they teach that action requires the presence of the agent; this being granted, I argue thus. An agent that is not cannot be present. Second, action requires the power of the agent, therefore much more the very being of the agent. Third, the presence of the agent is required because if the agent is absent, it is just as if it were not; therefore if in reality it is not, in reality it will not act.

units.la: Obijcies 1. causa moralis operatur quando non est, igitur hoc ipsum poterit causa physica. Patet antecedens, nam operatio bona præterita potest hodie movere principem, ut præmium conferat.
units.tr: You will object first: a moral cause acts when it is not, therefore a physical cause also will be able to do so. The antecedent is clear, for a good action performed in the past can today move a prince to bestow a reward.

units.la: Resp. negando conseq. disparitas est, quia causa moralis non elicit operationem, non se mouet, non influit actu, sed satis est si proponatur ab intellectu vt luntati, vt hæc deinde moueat se ipsam vnde licet non sit, operari suo modo potest. Non ita causa physica, vt c. p.
units.tr: I reply by denying the consequence: there is a disparity, because a moral cause does not elicit the operation, does not move itself, does not flow in actually; it is enough that it be proposed by the intellect to the will, and the will then moves itself; hence, although the cause does not exist, it can act in its own way. It is not so with a physical cause, as I have said.

units.la: Obijcies 2. causa remota operatur, etiamsi non existat, v. gr. auus quamquam defunctus, causa est nepotis, ergo, &c.
units.tr: You will object second: a remote cause acts even when it does not exist; for example, a grandfather, although dead, is the cause of his grandson, therefore, etc.

units.la: Resp. auum, esse causam nepotis non agentem, & quæ influat, sed attributiuè, quatenus nimirum cùm sit causa causæ, ipsi etiam attribuitur postremus effectus.
units.tr: I reply that a grandfather is the cause of his grandson not by acting and flowing into him, but attributively, namely in that, since he is the cause of the cause, the final effect is also attributed to him.

units.la: Obijcies 3. iaciat quis lapidem in hoc instanti, mox pereat statim: lapis mouebitur per multa instantia, quæ sequentur; sed mouens erit ille, qui non est, ergo.
units.tr: You will object third: suppose someone throws a stone in this instant and then immediately dies; the stone will be moved through many instants that follow; but the mover will be one who no longer exists, therefore...

units.la: Resp. negando minorem. Ratio est, quia lapis mouetur ad sequens tempus non à motore, qui eum iecit; sed ab impetu impresso, quem in eo reliquit.
units.tr: I reply by denying the minor. The reason is that the stone is moved in the following time not by the mover who threw it, but by the impetus impressed on it, which he has left in it.

units.la: DISQVISITIO QVARTA.
units.tr: Fourth Disquisition.

units.la: Vtrum, & quomodo causa referatur ad effectus.
units.tr: Whether a cause is related to its effects, and how.

units.la: PRO intelligentia supponendum est, quod vniuersim aiunt philosophi, causam, prout causa est, respicere suum essectum, qui respectus dicitur vulgo relatio. Repetite autem è summulis quid sit relatio, definitur enim ab Aristotele, cuius totum esse est se habere ad aliud, nimirum talis entitas inter aliqua duo, vt ipsa tota sit ad aliud, & per eam vnam vna extremitas referatur ad aliam.
units.tr: For understanding, we must first note what philosophers commonly say in general: a cause, as a cause, looks toward its effect, and this looking-toward is commonly called relation. Recall from the summulae what relation is. Aristotle defines it as that whose whole being is to be related to another. It is, namely, an entity between two things such that it is wholly directed toward the other, and through it one extreme is referred to the other.

units.la: Diuiditur in duplicem. Alia vocatur prædicamentalis, alia transcendentalis. Illa est, per quam duo extrema referuntur accidentaliter, ita nimirum, vt possint etiam non referri; sic Petrus Pater accidentaliter, seu prædicamentaliter ad filium refertur, quia sine relatione Patris adhuc poterat esse Paulus. Relatio transcendentalis, aut essentialis ea est, per quam vna res ita refertur ad aliam, vt sine illa nec esse, nec intelligi possit; hoc modo creatura omnis transcendentaliter ad Creatorem refertur, & hæc relatio non aliud est, quàm essentialis creaturæ dependentia, vt alibi dicetur.
units.tr: Relation is divided into two kinds. One is called predicamental, the other transcendental. The predicamental kind is that by which two extremes are related accidentally, so that they can also be unrelated. Thus Peter is related to a son as father accidentally, or predicamentally, since Paul could still exist without Peter's being a father. Transcendental or essential relation is that by which one thing is so related to another that neither can be nor be understood without it. In this way every creature is transcendentally related to its Creator, and this relation is nothing other than the essential dependence of the creature, as will be said elsewhere.

units.la: Quærimus ergo hic, an & quomodo causa relationem habeat cum effectu. Effectus autem alij sunt possibiles, alij existentes. Primi dicunt meram ad esse possibilitatem, seu non repugnantiam, vt sint. Secundi superaddunt existentiæ actum. Hoc posito scribatur. (?)
units.tr: We therefore ask here whether and how a cause has a relation to its effect. Effects are of two kinds: some are possible, others existing. The former signify only the possibility of being, or the absence of repugnance to their being. The latter add the act of existing. With this laid down, let the following be written. (?)

units.la: CONCLVSIO PRIMA.
units.tr: FIRST CONCLUSION.

units.la: Causa in actu primo nullam habet relationem, aut connexionem, realem, quacunque, sit, cum effectibus in sepossibilibus.
units.tr: A cause in the first act has no real relation or connection of any kind with effects that are merely possible.

units.la: PRobatur vnico, sed non inualido argumento. Ad hoc vt vnu referatur ad aliud, habeatq; reale cu eo connexionem, debet hoc aliud esse quid reale in se, atq; distinctu ab illo: sed effectus merè possibilis nō est quid reale in se ipso, & à causa distin&ct; ergo causa nō refertur, seu non habet connexione relationis realē cu effectu, qui sit merè possibilis. Maior euidēs est, quia relatio dicit esse ad aliud, hoc ergo aliud esse debet in se quid reale, non .n. relatio datur ad nihil. Secūdo quia relatio est quaedā connexio duorum, ergo si vnū tantūmodo sit, nulla poterit excogitari relatio. Minor verò probatur, nā essectus merè possibilis, quā talis est, nullā in se habet realitatē, esse nullū intrinsecum, quod à causa distiuctu sit. Quæro .n. aut mundi possibilitas, quæ ab æterno erat, fuit aliquid in se, reale, ac distinctu à Deo, vel non: si primū ergo ab æterno extitit aliquid præter Deū, & hoc nullus dicet. Si secundū, ergo possibilitas rei, quā talis, non est in se quid reale, atque; à causa distinctum. Rursus, hæc possibilitas mundi si fuit aliquid ab æterno, aut
units.tr: This is proved by a single argument, but not a weak one. For one thing to be related to another and to have a real connection with it, the other must itself be something real in its own right and distinct from the first. But a merely possible effect is not something real in itself and distinct from its cause; therefore the cause is not related to, or does not have a real connection of relation with, an effect that is merely possible. The major premise is evident, because a relation is a relation to something else, so that something else must be real in itself; a relation cannot be directed to nothing. Second, a relation is a connection between two things, so if only one exists, no relation can be conceived. The minor premise is proved as follows. A merely possible effect, as such, has no reality in itself and no intrinsic being distinct from its cause. For I ask whether the possibility of the world, which existed from eternity, was something real in itself and distinct from God, or not. If the first, then something existed from eternity besides God, and no one will say this. If the second, then the possibility of a thing, as such, is not something real in itself and distinct from its cause.

units.la: hoc aliquid, produxit extra se Deus, aut non primum repugnat fidei, quæ docet, nil fuisse à Deo productum ab æterno, præter Verbum; si Deus non produxit hoc aliquid, ergo nihil erat: secus enim fuisset à se, atq; independens à Deo, quod absurdum est. Postremò consequentia currit, quia si effectus vt mere possibilis, non est in se quid reale, à causa distinctu, ergo causa non habet veram, realemq; relationé ad ipsum. Confirmatur ex D. Th. in 1. q. 18. art. 4. vbi explicans quomodo quæ facta sunt, in ipso, scilicet Deo, vita erant, inquit. Res prout in Deo, sunt essentia Diuina: & quia essentia Diuina est vita, ideo, &c. Ergo res antequam sint, sunt ipsa Dei essentia; ergo causa non habet relationem ad effectus mere possibiles.
units.tr: Again, if this possibility of the world was something from eternity, either God produced this something outside himself or he did not. The first contradicts the faith, which teaches that nothing was produced by God from eternity except the Word. If God did not produce this something, then it was nothing; otherwise it would have been from itself and independent of God, which is absurd. Finally, the inference holds, because if an effect, as merely possible, is not something real in itself distinct from its cause, then the cause does not have a true and real relation to it. This is confirmed from St. Thomas, in 1, q. 18, art. 4, where, explaining how the things that were made were life in him, that is, in God, he says: Things, as they are in God, are the Divine essence; and because the Divine essence is life, therefore, etc. Therefore things, before they exist, are the very essence of God; therefore the cause does not have a relation to merely possible effects.

units.la: Obijcies 1. effectus possibilis est vere, ac realiter in se possibilis, ergo ad ipsum causa vere dicit relationem. Probatur consequentia, nam causa refertur vere ad id, quod producere potest; sed effectus possibilis talis est, ergo ad effectum possibilem vere habet relationem.
units.tr: You will object first: a possible effect is truly and really possible in itself; therefore the cause truly bears a relation to it. The inference is proved as follows: a cause is truly related to that which it can produce; but a possible effect is such a thing; therefore the cause truly has a relation to a possible effect.

units.la: Resp distinguendo antecedens. Essectus possibilis est vere, ac realiter in se possibilis per intrinsecam ipsi entitatem, nego; per extrinsecam virtutem causæ concedo; ergo causa dicit ad ipsum relationem, distinguo; intentionalem, concedo; realem, & physicam, nego, & explico. Non dicitur effectus possibilis, quia in se possibilitas hæc aliquid sit entitatiuum, à causa distinctum. &c. secus enim redirét absurda vt supra.Sed vocatur possibilis ob id tantùm, quòd reperitur causa potens illũ producere;vndè possibilitas est mera denominatio extrinseca. Ad probationem quoq; distinguo, causa refertur ad id, quod producere potest,intétionaliter, concedo: realiter, nego. Aduerte igitur,duplicé esse relatione. Altera dicitur physica, seu realis, & est physicus quidā ordo, resultans inter duo extrema realia, qui verè nō datur inter causā, & effectū purè possibilè, quomodo n. causa connexione, ordinéq; dicit realè ad id, quod ad huc non est, sed esse tantū potest? Secūda relatio est intentionalis, aut rationis, & ista dicitur ille ordo mentalis,quo nos cocepto effectu possibili,tanquam re aliqua, ordinamus causam ad ipsum, licèt in se nil entitatiuum, & reale sit.
units.tr: I answer by distinguishing the antecedent. A possible effect is truly and really possible in itself through its own intrinsic entity: I deny; through the extrinsic power of the cause: I concede. Therefore the cause refers to it: distinguish. Intentionally: I concede. Really and physically: I deny, and I explain. An effect is not called possible because this possibility is something entitative in itself, distinct from the cause, etc.; otherwise the absurdities mentioned above would follow. Rather it is called possible only because a cause is found that is able to produce it, so that possibility is a mere extrinsic denomination. As for the proof, I distinguish: the cause is referred to what it can produce, intentionally: I concede; really: I deny. Note therefore that there are two kinds of relation. The first is called physical or real, and is a certain physical order arising between two real extremes. This truly does not hold between a cause and a merely possible effect, for how can a cause really be related by connection and order to what is not yet, but can only be? The second relation is intentional, or of reason, and this is the mental order by which we, having conceived a possible effect as if it were some thing, order the cause to it, although in itself it is nothing entitative or real.

units.la: Obijcies 2. illud habet verá cū alio relatione, quod sine illo esse non potest, sed causa esse non potest sine effectibus in se possibilibus, ergo ad hos verá dicit relatione. Probatur minor, qnia reddito essectu impossibili,tollitur etiam illius causa, v.g. si foret impossibilis hic mundus, bene arguereturjergo nō adest causa productiua mundi, secus nō esset impossibilis. Ideo .n. effectus dicitur possibilis,quia datur causa potens ad illius productionē, & è cōtra,impossibilis, quia nulla reperitur causa, quæ producere possit. Ergo causa, vt causa nequit esse absq; effectībus in se possibilibus, & sic dicit veram ad eos relationem.
units.tr: (2) You will object: that has a true relation to another which cannot exist without it. But a cause cannot exist without merely possible effects; therefore it has a true relation to them. The minor is proved: when an effect is made impossible, its cause is also removed. For example, if this world were impossible, one would rightly argue that there is no productive cause of the world, since otherwise it would not be impossible. For an effect is called possible because a cause is given that can produce it, and conversely impossible because no cause can be found that can produce it. Therefore the cause, as cause, cannot exist without effects that are possible in themselves, and so it has a true relation to them.

units.la: Resp. d. maiore. Illud habet cum alio relatione, quod sine illo esse nequit, si hec verè duo sint, ac realiter distincta, c. si nō ita, n. Ad minorem: sed causa esse nequit sine effectibus in se possibilibus, d. adeout hi sint res aliqua distincta, n. res aliqua identificata, c. ergo dicit verā ad eos relatione, negatur. Et explico. Effectus merè possibilis nō est, quemadmodū supra, entitasaliqua in se intrinseca, & à causa verè distincta, sed à parte rei nil præterea dicit, quā causæ virtute potentis producere, vnde reddito effectu aliquo impossibili, causa etiam talis foret, non quia tolleretur aliquid extra causam, sed quia in ea desineret esse virtus illa intrinseca, & formalis, quę tali effectui correspondet. Quare impossibilitato effectu, nō redditur impossibilis causa, quia desinat esse aliquid ab ea distinctū, sed potius aliquid cum ea identificatū, nēpe virtus productiua. Simili modo ablata in homine rationalitate, aufertur & animalitas, non tāquam res distincta, quæ cū illa connexionem habeat, sed tāquā res identificata. Ex quo patet, in causa non esse relationem ad effectus merè possibiles, cum hi non sint aliquid à causa ipsa distinctum, &c.
units.tr: I distinguish the major. That has a relation to another which cannot exist without it, if these two are truly two and really distinct: I concede; if not, I deny. To the minor: a cause cannot exist without effects possible in themselves. Distinguish: insofar as these are some distinct thing, I deny; insofar as they are some identified thing, I concede. Therefore it has a true relation to them: I deny. And I explain. A merely possible effect is not, as above, some intrinsic entity truly distinct from the cause; in the reality of things it says nothing beyond the power of the cause to produce it. Hence, if some effect were made impossible, the cause would also become such, not because something outside the cause would be removed, but because in the cause that intrinsic and formal power which corresponds to such an effect would cease to be. So when an effect is made impossible, the cause is not made impossible because something distinct from it ceases to exist, but rather because something identified with it, namely productive power, does. In a similar way, when rationality is removed from a man, animality is removed too, not as a distinct thing that has a connection with it, but as a thing identified with it. From this it is clear that there is no relation in the cause to merely possible effects, since these are not something distinct from the cause itself, etc.

units.la: Obijcies 3. cū Thomistis. Dātur ab æterna nōn esse sētiæ rerū à causa distinctæ, seu prædicata rerū essentialia, homo, n. in essentia sua fuit sēper animal rationale, atq; ita de cæteris, ergo res possibilis est quid à causa distinctū. Rursus cū Scotistis. Creaturæ possibiles cognoscuntur à Deo in se ipsis, &ra& ratione huius cognitionis acquirunt quoddam esse diminutum, ergo. Denique cum recentioribus. Datur non repugnatia rerum, vi cuius Leo v.g. est possibilis ab æterno; & repugnantia etiam, ob quam chimæra impossibilis est, ergo possibilitas, & impossibilitas est aliquid ex parte rei extra causam.
units.tr: (3) You will object with the Thomists: there are from eternity essences of things distinct from the cause, that is, the essential predicates of things. Man, for example, was always in his essence a rational animal, and so with the others; therefore a possible thing is something distinct from the cause. Again, with the Scotists: possible creatures are known by God in themselves, and by reason of this knowledge they acquire a certain diminished being; therefore. Finally, with the more recent writers: there is a non-repugnance of things, by virtue of which Leo, for example, is possible from eternity; and there is also a repugnance, on account of which a chimera is impossible. Therefore possibility and impossibility are something on the part of the thing, outside the cause.

units.la: Resp. ad omnia distinguendo. Ab æterno dantur essentiæ rerum; creaturæ possibiles cognoscuntur; Adest non repugnatia effectus, &c. vt aliquid à causa, siue à Deo distinctum, n. vt quid cum virtute causæ identificatū, concedo; ergo essentiæ, creaturæ possibiles, non repugnantiæ, &c. sūt aliquid in se intrinsecū, negatur. Vel. n. hoc aliquid esset à Deo productum, vel non: primū est contra fidē; secundum dici nequit, sic enim ab æterno daretur aliquid productum, & non à causa prima, dependens, & non ab illa dependens. Dicitur ergo essentiæ ab æterno fuisse, quia semper fuit causa productiua rerum cum suis prædicatis essentialibus. Item cognoscuntur à Deo res possibiles, quia cognoscit virtute suam illas potentem producere. Similiter dicitur dari non repugnantia rerum, quia datur causa productiua earundem. Quare à primo ad vltimum res merè possibilis ab entitate causæ intrinseca distincta non est.
units.tr: I answer all of these by distinguishing. From eternity there are essences of things; possible creatures are known; there is a non-repugnance of the effect, etc. As something distinct from the cause, or from God: I deny. As something identified with the cause's power: I concede. Therefore essences, possible creatures, non-repugnances, etc., are something intrinsic in themselves: I deny. For either this something was produced by God, or it was not. The first is against the faith; the second cannot be said, for in that case something would have existed from eternity that was produced by no first cause, and was dependent and not dependent on it. So it is said that essences existed from eternity because there always was a productive cause of things together with their essential predicates. Likewise possible things are said to be known by God because he knows that he is able to produce them by his power. Similarly, there is said to be a non-repugnance of things because there is a productive cause of them. Wherefore, from first to last, a merely possible thing is not distinct from the intrinsic entity of the cause.

units.la: CON-
units.tr: CON-

units.la: CONCLVSIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: SECOND CONCLUSION.

units.la: Imò causa neque ad effectus existentes vi- detur habere veram, realemque rela- tionem, quæ sit modus à cau- salitate distinctus.
units.tr: Indeed, a cause does not seem to have a true and real relation to its existing effects that is a mode distinct from causality.

units.la: PRobatur, quia peracta causalitate, seu præterito influxu causæ in effectum, non videtur manere, nisi causa, & essectus, ergo illa non habet relationem, quæ sit modus à causalitate distinctus, ad effectum. Probatur antecedens, eò quòd si daretur hic modus inter causam, & effectú à causalitate distinctus, omnino superfluus, & ad nihil inseruiens foret, ergo. Probo sequelam. Hic modus non constitueret causam in esse causæ, nam potiùs resultat post eam constitutam: Nec essectam, qui omni sublato modo, in suo esse manet. Multò minùs requiritur, vt referat causam, satis enim ista refertur per actionem, influxum, causalitatem, quæ praterita, nulla est necessitas, vt referatur, ergo superfluus est.
units.tr: It is proved because, once causality is complete, that is, once the causal influence has passed from cause into effect, nothing seems to remain except the cause and the effect. Therefore the cause has no relation to the effect that is a mode distinct from causality. The antecedent is proved as follows. If there were such a mode between cause and effect, distinct from causality, it would be wholly superfluous and serve no purpose. I prove the consequence. This mode would not constitute the cause in its being as a cause, since it would rather result after the cause is already constituted. Nor would it constitute the effect, which remains in its being even with every mode removed. Still less is it needed to relate the cause, for the cause is sufficiently related through the action, influence and causality, which are past, and there is no necessity for any further relating. Therefore the mode is superfluous.

units.la: Opponis. Pater etiam transfacta causalitate, siue actu generandi, est physicè, atq; realiter alicuius Filij Pater, sed talis est gratia relationis, quæ paternitas dicitur, ergo causa refertur ad effectum ob relationem à causalitate distinctam. Confirmatur, quia in Diuinis datur vera, & realis relatio Paternitatis, qua Pater ad Filium; & Filiationis, qua Filius ad Patrem rerefertur, ergo & in humanis dabuntur hæ relationes.
units.tr: You object: a father, even after the generating act or causality has passed, is physically and really the father of some son. But such a relation, which is called paternity, is of this kind. Therefore the cause is related to its effect by a relation distinct from causality. It is confirmed: in the divine nature there is a true and real relation of paternity by which the Father is related to the Son, and of filiation by which the Son is related to the Father. Therefore these relations will also exist in human affairs.

units.la: Resp. distinguendo: Pater etiā transsacta generatione &c. est physicè Pater per physicam denominationem, concedo; per modū à parte rei enascētem, nego. Ad minorem similiter d. talis est gratia relationis à causalitate distinctæ, n. non distinctæ, concedo. Pater ergo quia functus est aliquādo actione generantis, habet fundamentum; vt semper, & quouis tempore valeat accipere physicam, realemque denominationem Patris, vnde non talis est, quia inter ipsum, & Filium resultet modus quidam relationis, alioquin defuncto filio non posset amplius dici pater. Sed vocatur talis, ratione causalitatis, quam exercuit. Ad confirmationem resp. in Diuinis dari Paternitatem, & filiationem, quæ sunt relationes entitatiuæ, ac reales, quia numquā cessat actio generandi, semper enim Pater Æternus generat Filium. Quare confirmatur potius conclusio nostra. Sicut enim Pater ille habet semper ad Filium relationem, quia semper habet actum generandi; sic Pater humanus non habebit physicam, realemque relationem ad filium, nisi quandiu perdurat generatio, & causalitas: hæc non semper manet, ergo illà transactà, nulla superest vera, & realis relatio. Imò quandiu est, à causalitate non distinguitur.
units.tr: I answer by distinguishing. The father, even after the generation is past, is physically a father by a physical denomination: I grant this; by a mode arising from the thing itself: I deny this. To the minor premise, likewise, I distinguish: such is the grace of a relation distinct from causality: I deny it; not distinct from causality: I grant it. So the father, because at some time he performed the action of begetting, has the foundation on which he can at any time and always receive the physical and real denomination of father. It is not therefore the case that some mode of relation results between him and the son; otherwise, once the son has died, he could no longer be called father. Rather he is called father by reason of the causality he exercised. To the confirmation I reply that in the divine nature there is paternity and filiation, which are real and entitative relations, because the act of generating never ceases; the eternal Father always generates the Son. Therefore our conclusion is rather confirmed by this. For just as that Father always has a relation to the Son because he always has the act of generating, so a human father will not have a physical and real relation to the son except as long as the generation and causality endure. These do not always remain. Therefore, once they are past, no true and real relation survives. Indeed, for as long as the causality lasts, it is not distinguished from it.

units.la: DISPVTATIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: Second Disputation.

units.la: De causa Efficiente.
units.tr: On the efficient cause.

units.la: VIdimus nonnulla, quæ attinent ad cau- sas vniuersim acceptas. Nunc singulæ in quæstionem adducendæ sunt. Primò autem ab Efficiente ordiamur, quæ ceteris virtute, ac dignitate præstare videtur.
units.tr: We have seen some things that pertain to causes taken in general. Now each kind must be brought into question. But first let us begin with the efficient cause, which seems to surpass the others in power and dignity.

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: First Inquiry.

units.la: Quid sit, & quotuplex causa efficiens.
units.tr: What an efficient cause is, and how many kinds there are.

units.la: PRo intelligentia seligamus definitionem, quam ab Aristotele pluribus doctrinæ suæ locis traditam colligunt Peripatetici. Causa efficiens est principium primum, à quo incipit motus, & quies.
units.tr: To understand it, let us choose the definition which the Peripatetics gather from Aristotle, given in several places of his teaching: The efficient cause is the first principle from which motion and rest begin.

units.la: Dicitur principium, in quo conuenit cū alijs causis. Primum, vt distinguatur à materiali, & Formali, imò etiam à Finali, quæ licèt ordine intentionis prima sit, in executione manet postrema. A quo incipit motus, nam ab ea fit, atq; pendet effectus extrinsecus; intrinsecus enim dicitur pendere à causa, vt ex qua, ex illa enim fit, seu componitur. Et quies, nam per causam efficientem habetur, vt effectus in se maneat, seu constituatur, ac veluti quiescat.
units.tr: It is called a principle, which it shares with the other causes. It is first, so that it is distinguished from the material and formal cause, and indeed also from the final cause, which, although it is first in the order of intention, remains last in execution. It is that from which motion begins, for the effect is made by it and depends on it from outside; for a thing is said to depend intrinsically on a cause as that from which it is, since it is made or composed from it. And rest, because through the efficient cause the effect is had so that it remains in itself, or is established, and as it were comes to rest.

units.la: Quod attinet ad causæ diuisionem, ea solet assignari multiplex. Primò enim est causa Prima, nempe Deus, & Secunda, seu agens creatum. Secundò proxima, quæ immediatè producit effectum, vt pater filium,& Remota,quæ non effectum, sed causam effectus gignit,& sic auus dicitur causa nepotis. Tertiò vniuoca, quæ producit effectum sibi similem, vt ignis ignem; & Æquiuoca,quæ dissimilem,seu speciei diuersæ dat effectum,vt vinum respectu caloris. Quartò causa Per se, quæ ad effectum ex natura sua ordinatur, vt ars musicalis ad cantum;& Per accidens, quæ non ordinatur,vt Musicus ædificans. Quintò Physica, quæ actu influit in essectum,& Moralis, cui physicè non influéti à prudentib.tamen tribui solet effectus, vt admonitio,cohortatio. Sextò Totalis,à qua totus pendet effectus,vt eleuans pondus ; & Partialis , quæ sola non sufficit, quemadmodum plures trahentes nauim ; Huic similis est Adæquata gignens totum effectum , vt Deus hominem ; & Inadæquata,producens partem , vt vir Virum . Septimò Principalis,quæ debitum sibi ponit effectum, vt ignis calorem ; & Instrumentalis,quæ inseruit alteri,vt virtus organica,quæ non sibi , sed animæ venturæ organizat corpus.Octauò Libera,quæ positis omnibus requisitis, potest non operari ; & necessaria , quæ necessariò agit, quemadmodum sol necessario lucet.Quæ sunt præcipuæ causarum diuisiones.
units.tr: As to the division of cause, it is usually given as manifold. First, there is the first cause, namely God, and the second cause, or created agent. Second, the proximate cause, which immediately produces the effect, as a father produces a son, and the remote cause, which does not beget the effect but the cause of the effect, and so a grandfather is said to be the cause of a grandson. Third, the univocal cause, which produces an effect like itself, as fire produces fire, and the equivocal cause, which gives an effect unlike itself, or of a different species, as wine with respect to heat. Fourth, the cause per se, which is ordered by its nature to the effect, as the musical art is to song, and the cause per accidens, which is not so ordered, as a musician who builds. Fifth, the physical cause, which actually flows into the effect, and the moral cause, which does not flow in physically but is usually credited with the effect, as admonition or exhortation is. Sixth, the total cause, on which the whole effect depends, as one who lifts a weight, and the partial cause, which alone does not suffice, as several men pulling a ship. Similar to this is the adequate cause, which produces the whole effect, as God produces a man, and the inadequate cause, which produces a part, as a man produces a man. Seventh, the principal cause, which posits the effect as owed to itself, as fire produces heat, and the instrumental cause, which serves another, as an organic power which organizes the body not for itself but for the soul that is to come. Eighth, the free cause, which, when all requisites are present, can refrain from acting, and the necessary cause, which acts of necessity, as the sun shines necessarily. These are the principal divisions of causes.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISQUISITIO SECUNDA.

units.la: Quid causa efficiens operari valeat.
units.tr: What an efficient cause is able to effect.

units.la: PRo intelligentia, res videtur citra dubitationem, quòd cuiq; causæ creatæ inest virtus ad producendum. Quæ opinio reijcitur auctoritatibus, & ratione. Accedit etiam ratio, primò enim constat, causam liberam elicere actus, aut bonos, aut malos, alioquin nec meritũ haberet, neq; demeritũ. 2 si Deus tantũ ageret, ipse dici deberet causa peccati. 3 actus vitales fiunt ab anima per quendam potentiæ conatum, quem nos experimur, vnde virtus multam post operam lassari solet.
units.tr: To begin with, the matter seems beyond dispute: every created cause has within it a power to produce something. This opinion is rejected both on the authority of writers and by reason. Reason also confirms it. First, it is evident that a free cause elicits actions, whether good or evil; otherwise it would have neither merit nor demerit. Second, if God alone acted, he himself would have to be called the cause of sin. Third, vital acts are performed by the soul through a certain effort of its power, which we experience ourselves; hence the power is often wearied after much labour.

units.la: Difficultas ergo ad hoc reduci videtur, quid causa efficiens producere valeat. Pro qua re duplex causarum genus distingui debet. Aliæ siquidem accidentia sunt, aliæ substantiæ. Quid singulæ possint, per sequentes conclusiones explicabo
units.tr: The difficulty therefore seems to come down to this: what is an efficient cause able to produce? To resolve this, a twofold kind of cause must be distinguished. For some causes are accidents, others are substances. What each of them can do I shall explain through the following conclusions.

units.la: CONCLVSIO PRIMA.
units.tr: CONCLUSIO PRIMA.

units.la: Substantia vim habet immediatè producTiuam accidentium.
units.tr: Substance has the power to produce accidents immediately.

units.la: PRobatur, quia intellectus immediatè producit actus intellectionum; potentia motiua immediatè motum; volitiua immediatè volitiones &c. sed hæc omnia sunt accidentia, quæ à substantia proveniunt, ergo. Minor quoad primam partem clara est. Quoad secundam probatur, nam potentiæ, vt voluntas, intellectus &c. non distinguuntur à substantijs, quapropter idem est dicere; intellectus operatur, & anima operatur, ergo actus isti accidentales immediatè à substantia nascuntur. Addunt aliqui hanc, & huiusmodi experientias. Aqua calida, remoto contrario, se se paulatim ad pristinum redigit, reproducendo sibi suum frigus; hoc autem frigus nequit à calore, qui aquæ inexistit, produci; ergo immediatè ab aqua, & sic probant inesse vim substantiæ, vt immediatè accidentia producat. Sed hæc instantia non videtur sufficere, dici enim potest, quòd aqua non gignat reuera nouum frigus, verùm expellendo à se corpora calida, quæ ab igne recepit, aliquando maneat qualis primò fuit, quamuis enim ex admixtione substantiæ calidæ intra poros non sentiretur frigus ante, non idcirco illud abfuit vmquam, vt nos alibi explicabimus, cùm de alteratione fiet sermo.
units.tr: It is proved because the intellect immediately produces acts of understanding; the motive power immediately produces motion; the volitive power immediately produces volitions, and so on. But all these are accidents which proceed from substance; therefore... The minor premise is clear as to its first part. As to the second part it is proved thus: the powers, such as the will, the intellect and so on, are not distinguished from the substances, so that to say "the intellect operates" is the same as to say "the soul operates"; therefore those accidental acts arise immediately from the substance. Some add this and similar experiences: warm water, when the contrary is removed, gradually returns to its former state, reproducing its own cold; but this cold cannot be produced by the heat which is in the water; therefore it is produced immediately by the water, and in this way they prove that substance has a power to produce accidents immediately. But this instance does not seem sufficient, for it can be said that the water does not truly generate a new cold, but by expelling from itself the warm bodies which it received from the fire, it at length remains as it was at first; for although, owing to the mixture of warm substance within its pores, the cold was not felt before, it was not therefore ever absent, as we shall explain elsewhere, when there is discussion of alteration.

units.la: CONCLVSIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: SECOND CONCLUSION.

units.la: Accidens videtur habere vim producendi aliud accidens.
units.tr: An accident seems to have the power of producing another accident.

units.la: PRobatur ab aliquibus hac instantia. Sit aqua calida, & manu tangatur: quàdiu id fiet, producetur in manu calor: sed hic non efficitur ab aqua, ergo à calore inexistēte; vnde accidens vim habet ad aliud. Probatur minor. Aqua enim vt aqua solius frigoris productiua est, non caloris; ergo calor producitur à calore, non ab aqua. Respondēri tamen facilè potest, calorē, qui sentitur in manu, aut produci à particulis igneis, quæ aquà totà permixtæ manent; seu meliùs, non esse hunc de nouo genitum, sed ignem ipsum, qui latet in aqua, manui adhærere, ipsamque reddere calidam.
units.tr: This is argued by some on the following instance. Let the water be warm and let it be touched by the hand. As long as this lasts, heat is produced in the hand, but this is not caused by the water, so it is caused by the heat that is present, and therefore an accident has power over another accident. The minor premise is proved thus: water, as water, is productive only of cold, not of heat; therefore the heat is produced by heat, not by the water. It can easily be answered, however, that the heat felt in the hand is produced either by igneous particles, which remain mixed throughout the water, or, better, that it is not newly generated at all, but that the fire itself, which lies hidden in the water, adheres to the hand and makes it warm.
