units.la: Probatur ergo efficacius conclusio, nā accidentia tam materialia, quàm spiritualia videntur esse productiua accidentium. Sic albedo, nigredo, coloresque omnes gignunt speciem sui, aut quasdam imagines tenuissimas, vt ijs ad ocularem potentiam emissis fiat visio, quæ certè sine re aliqua ex obiectis refusa elici nequit. Vnde quamuis concipi satis non possit, quomodo albedo v.g. ita sit in continua productione suæ imaginis, vt illam per singula instantia physicè gignat, in aerem imprimat, longissimè transmittat &c. nihilominus denegari nequit effectus.
units.tr: The conclusion is therefore proved more effectively, for both material and spiritual accidents seem to be productive of accidents. Thus whiteness, blackness and all colours generate a likeness of themselves, or certain very thin images, so that vision comes about when these are sent out to the power of sight; for certainly vision cannot be elicited unless something is reflected back from the objects. Hence, although it cannot sufficiently be conceived how whiteness, for example, is in such continual production of its image that it physically generates it at each instant, impresses it on the air, and transmits it over very great distances, nevertheless the effect cannot be denied.

units.la: Prænisi fortasse recurramus ad lumen, quod ab obiectis diuersimodè reflexum illa repræsentet loco speciérum; de qua re mihi verisimiliori fortasse dicetur aliquid cùm de luce. Præterea quæcunque intellectio, & volitio, quæ sunt accidentia spiritualia, producunt speciem sui, hæc enim relicta in organis est sola causa, cur præterita recordemur. Ergo &c.
units.tr: Unless perhaps we have recourse to light, which, reflected in various ways from objects, represents them in place of species; something more plausible may perhaps be said about this matter when we treat of light. Moreover, whatever intellection and volition, which are spiritual accidents, produce a species of themselves; for this is the only cause, left in the organs, why we recall past things. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Probatur vltimò efficacissimè in sacramento Eucharistiæ. Si enim hostia consecretur, quæcunque illa sit, panis, vinumve, sola manét accidentia panis, aut vini, & substantia nulla. Quo posito, arguo sic. Accidentia vini producunt odorem, frigus &c. ergo accidens vim habere videtur productiuam accidentis. Neque dicas odorem per odorosa corpora de speciebus vini effundi, nam sub ijs nullum corpus, excepto Christi Domini, est. Imò nec addas, odorem sentiri, quia species ipsæ transeunt, migrantque hinc inde afficiendo sensum odoratus, nam accidens non migrat se solo, ergo quod sentitur, producitur. Nisi adesset nouum Dei miraculum, transferentis aliò species, quòd gratis asseritur.
units.tr: It is proved most conclusively of all in the sacrament of the Eucharist. For if the host is consecrated, whatever it may be, bread or wine, only the accidents of bread or wine remain, and no substance. Given this, I argue thus. The accidents of wine produce odour, cold, etc.; therefore an accident seems to have a productive power over an accident. Nor may you say that the odour is poured out from odorous bodies in the species of wine, for under those species there is no body, except the body of Christ the Lord. Nor may you add that the odour is perceived because the species themselves pass over and migrate hither and thither, affecting the sense of smell; for an accident does not migrate by itself, so what is perceived is produced. Unless there were a new miracle of God transferring the species elsewhere, which is asserted without reason.

units.la: CONCLVSIO TERTIA.
units.tr: THIRD CONCLUSION.

units.la: Accidens nullam habet vim producendi substantiam.
units.tr: An accident has no power to produce a substance.

units.la: PRobatur à recentioribus cum Scoto in 1. dist. 37. q. 1. & in 4. dist. 12. q. 3. contra Thomistas, qui putant, substantiam non esse immediatè productiuam substantiæ, sed producere medio instrumento, scilicet accidente, cui communicat efficaciam, & vim, vt physicè, ac realiter aliam substantiam cum se producat, adeòt si non adsit accidens intermedium, quod actu physicè influat per virtutem à causa receptam, substantia producere nequeat substantiam. Sed contra.
units.tr: This is proved by the more recent writers, with Scotus (on 1 Sent. dist. 37, q. 1, and on 4 Sent. dist. 12, q. 3), against the Thomists. The Thomists hold that substance is not immediately productive of substance, but produces through an instrument, namely an accident, to which it communicates efficacy and power, so that it may, physically and really, produce another substance. Thus, if no intermediate accident were present that actually flows in physically through the power received from the cause, substance could not produce substance. But against this:

units.la: Probatur 1. conclusio, quia nemo dat, quod non habet: sed accidens nec formaliter, nec virtualiter habet, seu continet substantiam, ergo illam effectiuè dare non potest. Minor probatur: Imprimis enim accidens non est substantia entitatiuè, ac formaliter; secundo non habet vim eam attingendi, est enim res ignobilior, imperfectior, omnimodè inferior, causa verò vt causa concurrere debet per æqualem virtutem ad effectum. Neque dicant hoc verum esse de causa principali, non instrumentali. Contra enim, &
units.tr: The first conclusion is proved, because no one gives what he does not have. But an accident neither formally nor virtually has or contains substance, so it cannot give substance effectively. The minor is proved as follows. First, an accident is not a substance either entitatively or formally. Second, it has no power to reach substance, since it is a more ignoble, more imperfect and altogether inferior thing; but a cause, as a cause, ought to concur to the effect with equal power. Nor may they say this holds of a principal cause and not of an instrumental one. For against this, and

units.la: Probatur 2. conclusio. Per Thomistas causa principalis habere debet parem cum effectu virtutem: sed plerumq; causa principalis productiua substantiæ foret
units.tr: The second conclusion is proved. According to the Thomists, a principal cause ought to have power equal to its effect. But for the most part the principal cause productive of substance would be

units.la: accidens, ergo si effectiuè produceret substantiam, deberet esse virtutis æqualis cum illa. Probo minorem. Causa principalis ea est, à qua totus, & immediatè pendet effectus: tale plerumq; foret accidens, ergo esset causa principalis. Minor patet exemplis. Detur ferrum candens, & admoueatur paleæ, certè palea succenditur, in eaq; vt aiunt, producitur substantia ignis. Quæro causam illius productiuam. Non aliam assignas, nisi calorem in ferro existentem; ergo calor est causa principalis ad substantiam. Similiter quando ex putri nascuntur vermes, ranæ, apes, ac talia, dicuntur à Thomistis accidentia, quæ ibi reperiuntur, effectiuè concurrere ad eos effectus. Peto, adestne alia causa, præter accidentia? si adest, vel præsens, vel absens est: præsens nulla videtur; absens non sufficit, nam per Thomistas perinde se habet, ac si non esset, ergo accidentia influunt sola, & vt causa principalis. Neq; respondeas accidentia esse instrumenta ranæ vt sic, ranæ vagæ, aut astrorum. Imprimis enim rana vaga nec adest, nec viuit, nec in rerum natura determinatum habet esse, ideoq; nec influere determinatè potest. Astra vero vniuersales habét influxus, non peculiares: imò cùm ea sint experria vitæ, nequeunt effectiuè producere viuens, alioquin falsum esset quod inquiunt, causam principalem influere in effectum per virtutem ipsi æqualem. Itaq; si concurrit accidens, concurrit se solo, & vt causa præPrincipalis ad substantiæ productionem. Sed hoc non admittitur à Thomistis, ergo nullo modo effectiuè concurrit, sed solum dispositiuè.
units.tr: an accident. Therefore, if it produced substance effectively, it would have to be of equal power with that substance. I prove the minor. A principal cause is that on which the whole effect depends, and immediately so. For the most part an accident would be such a thing, so it would be the principal cause. The minor is clear from examples. Let a glowing iron be given and brought near to straw; the straw certainly catches fire, and in it, as they say, the substance of fire is produced. I ask what productive cause there is. You can assign no other than the heat existing in the iron; therefore heat is the principal cause of the substance. Similarly, when worms, frogs, bees and such things arise from putrefaction, the Thomists say that the accidents found there concur effectively to those effects. I ask: is there any other cause besides the accidents? If there is, it is either present or absent. Present, it seems to be none; absent, it does not suffice, for by the Thomists' own account it stands as if it were not there. Therefore the accidents flow in alone, and as the principal cause. Nor may you reply that the accidents are instruments of the frog as such, of wandering frogs, or of the stars. In the first place, a wandering frog is neither present, nor alive, nor has determinate being in the nature of things, and so it cannot flow in determinately. The stars have universal influences, not particular ones; indeed, since they are the reasons of life, they cannot effectively produce a living thing, or else what they say would be false, namely that a principal cause flows into its effect through power equal to it. So if the accident concurs, it concurs by itself and as the principal cause of the production of substance. But this is not admitted by the Thomists. Therefore it concurs in no way effectively, but only dispositively.

units.la: Probatur 2. à Scotistis, quia illud est principium immediatè agendi, quod maiorem habet proportionem, essentiaeque similitudinem cum effectu; sed forma substantialis est huiusmodi, & non accidens; ergo illa immediatè agit, non istud. Maior de se patet. Minor probatur, nam proculdubio maior est proportio, ac similitudo substantiæ cum substantia, quàm accidentis cum eadem; ergo illa immediatè producit; non accidens, quod vt instrumentum, vim solummodo habet disponendi.
units.tr: It is proved secondly by the Scotists, because that is the principle of immediate action which has the greater proportion and likeness of essence to the effect. But substantial form is of this kind, and not the accident. Therefore the former acts immediately, not the latter. The major is evident in itself. The minor is proved, for without doubt the proportion and likeness of substance to substance is greater than that of accident to the same. Therefore the former produces immediately, not the accident, which, as an instrument, has only the power of disposing.

units.la: Probatur 3. quia si accidentia vim habent producendi substantiam, ergo idem accidens ab eadem causa profluens eandem semper substantiam efficiet: sed hoc patet falsum, ergo. Maior clara est, nam existente causa eadem, eodemque instrumento, effectus etiam esse debet idem. Probatur minor, quia calor solis v.g. in terræ visceribus quàm varia, diuersa, & contraria producit? Quæro ergo, cur idem calor in quibusdam materijs progignit formas crystalli, ferri, adamantis naturaliter frigidas, in alijs verò, ignis, herbarum, & mineralium actu formaliter calidas? cur in hoc subiecto formam viuentis; non sic in alio? cur in isto potiùs ranæ substantiam, in illo scorpionis &c. Dicis, quia in tali materia calor inuenit dispositiones, & accidentia, quæ quæ debentur potius formæ crystalli, quā ignis, &c. Contra. Vel etiam hæ dispositiones effectiuè producunt crystallum aut non:si secundum,ergo nec illum producet solaris calor, qui minùs tali formæ debetur. Si primum, vel hę dispositiones sunt causæ instrumentales, aut principales. Non secundum,quia dicis accidentia esse merè instrumenta,quæ ab alia causa virtutem accipiunt effectiuè producendi. Assignetur ergo hęc alia causa primaria, beneficio cuius accidentia producunt vermes in marmorum fibris, adamantes in niue, in limo cocleas, argentum in minera; &c. Ergo aut accidens causa est præcipua, & sola productiua substantiæ; aut cùm alia nequeat assignari, minimè vim habent productiuam substantiæ. Sed
units.tr: It is proved thirdly, because if accidents have power to produce substance, then the same accident, flowing from the same cause, would always produce the same substance. But this is plainly false; therefore. The major is clear, for when the cause is the same, and the instrument the same, the effect must also be the same. The minor is proved: how many different, diverse and contrary things does the heat of the sun, for instance, produce in the bowels of the earth? I ask, therefore, why the same heat in some materials gives rise to the forms of crystal, iron and diamond, which are naturally cold, but in others to fire, plants and minerals, which are actually and formally hot? Why in this subject the form of a living thing, and not in another? Why in this one rather the substance of a frog, and in that one of a scorpion, and so on? You say that in such matter the heat finds dispositions and accidents which are due rather to the form of crystal than to fire, and so on. But against this: either these dispositions effectively produce the crystal or they do not. If not, then the solar heat, which is due less to such a form, will not produce it either. If they do, then either these dispositions are instrumental causes or principal causes. Not the second, because you say accidents are merely instruments, which receive from another cause the power of producing effectively. Let this other primary cause then be assigned, by whose benefit the accidents produce worms in the fibres of marble, diamonds in snow, snails in mud, silver in the ore, and so on. Therefore either the accident is the chief and sole productive cause of substance, or, since no other can be assigned, it has in no way the power of producing substance. But

units.la: Obijcies 1. Fundamentum doctrinæ Thomisticæ, quod proponunt Complutenses discalceati disp. 10. q. 4. sic. In agente naturali distinguitur esse, & operari, ergo etiam distingui realiter debet potentia ad esse, & potentia ad operari. Sed potentia ad esse non aliud est, quàm substantia causæ; igitur potentia ad operari erit quid aliud à substantia distinctum, nempe facultas accidentalis, & principiū agendi. Et sic substantia nō immediatè ipsa operatur, sed media virtute, potētia, facultate, ac principio agendi. Ex quo inferūt auctores Deū tantùmodo habere substantiā immediatè operatiuā, quia in ipso nō distinguitur esse, & operari cau fas autem fecundas agere semper medijs accidentibus, adeout hæc sint immediatè operatiua.
units.tr: You will object, first: the foundation of the Thomist doctrine, which the Discalced Complutensians set out (disp. 10, q. 4), is as follows. In a natural agent, being and operating are distinguished; therefore the power for being and the power for operating must also be really distinguished. But the power for being is nothing other than the substance of the cause. Therefore the power for operating will be something distinct from the substance, namely an accidental faculty and principle of acting. And so the substance does not operate immediately itself, but by means of a middle power, faculty and principle of acting. From this the authors infer that God alone has a substance immediately operative, because in him being and operating are not distinguished; but secondary causes always act through intermediate accidents, so that these are immediately operative.

units.la: Resp. imprimis admisso antecedente negando primam consequentiam. Ratio est, nam esse causæ distinguitur sanè ab operari vt patet; sed non ideo potentia ad esse distingui debet à potentia operandi, potentia enim ad esse nihil reuera est in se reale, quod possit distingui, sed meram dicit possibilitatem, vt supra. Quomodo ergo realiter distinguetur à potentia operandi; si ea realiter in se nihil est? Ad minorem nego, quòd potentia ad esse sit ipsa substantia rei, hæc enim potiùs est actus ipse realis, & physicus essendi, vt c. p. Ad consequentiam pariter nego, quòd potentia ad operari distinguatur à substantia; hæc enim est ipsum principium immediatè operatiuum, actiuum, effectiuum; vnde substantia immediatè operatur. Quare non differt Deus a creatura in modo agendi per hoc, quòd sit substantia immediatè operatiua; sed quia Deus est ipsa sua operatio, &c.
units.tr: I reply, first, by granting the antecedent and denying the first consequence. The reason is that the being of a cause is certainly distinct from its operating, as is clear. But it does not follow that the power for being must be distinguished from the power for operating. For the power for being is in truth nothing real in itself that could be distinguished; it signifies merely possibility, as above. How then would it be really distinguished from the power for operating, if in itself it is really nothing? To the minor I deny that the power for being is the substance of the thing itself; for this is rather the actual and physical act of being, as stated in the chapter above. To the consequence likewise I deny that the power for operating is distinguished from the substance; for this is itself the immediately operative, active and effective principle. Hence the substance operates immediately. Therefore God does not differ from creatures in the manner of acting by being a substance immediately operative, but because God is his own operation, and so on.

units.la: Resp. 2. retorquendo argumentum sic. Distinguitur in omni causa esse ab operari, ergò etiam potentia ad esse, & potentia ad operandum; sed in accidente potentia ad esse est ipsa entitas accidentis, ergo potentia ad operandum erit quid aliud ab ea distinctum; & sic accidens non operabitur immediatè, sed mediante hoc alio, de quo rursus fiet argumentum, & sic in infinitum. Quemadmodum ergo tenentur concedere Thomistæ, quòd accidens, in quo distinguitur esse ab operari, tamè ipsum agat immediatè; sic multò magis de subsistantia videtur asserendum, vt p.c.
units.tr: I reply, second, by turning the argument back thus. In every cause, being is distinguished from operating; therefore the power for being and the power for operating are also distinguished. But in an accident the power for being is the very entity of the accident. Therefore the power for operating will be something distinct from it; and so the accident will not operate immediately, but through this other thing, about which the argument will again be made, and so on to infinity. Just as the Thomists are therefore bound to concede that an accident, in which being is distinguished from operating, nevertheless acts immediately itself, so much more should it be asserted of substance, as above.

units.la: Objicies 2. Dum è silice ignis excutitur, causa productiua huiusce subsistantiæ non est alius ignis; at verò motus, & calor. 2. si super candela, quò flamma non pertingat, suspendatur carta, in ea gignitur de nouo ignis: non à flamma, quæ non ascendit eò vsque, igitur à calore. 3. si phiala, quæ aquæ sit plenà, exponatur soli, & calescat, ponè se accendit paleam, fomitemque; sed ibi non adest nisi calor producens, ergo accidens vim habet ad subsistantiam.
units.tr: You will object, second: when fire is struck out of flint, the productive cause of this substance is not another fire, but motion and heat. Second, if paper is hung above a candle, to which the flame does not reach, fire is generated afresh in it; not from the flame, which does not rise so far, therefore from the heat. Third, if a flask full of water is exposed to the sun and warms, it sets fire at once to straw and tinder; but there is nothing there except the producing heat. Therefore the accident has power over substance.

units.la: Resp. ad hæc, & similia causam ignis productiuam (si tamen de nouo producitur) esse subsistantiam, non accidens. Quapropter ignis in carta suspensa producitur à vapore subsistentiali, qui supra flammam ascendit, ignisq; formaliter est, quemadmodum suo loco videbimus. Ita etiam post phialam gignitur subsistantia flammæ à solaribus radijs, qui subsistantialiter ignei sunt, facta enim ex obiecto corpore coitione conualescunt magis, cōburuntq; vt alibi ostendetur. Vltimò ignis, qui de petra excuti solet, non producitur, sed retegitur, elicitur, deducitur, cùm prius lateret: quod etiam videbimus.
units.tr: In reply to these and similar arguments: the productive cause of fire (if it is indeed produced anew) is a substance, not an accident. Accordingly, the fire in the suspended paper is produced by a substantial vapour that rises above the flame, and it is formally fire, as we shall see in its place. Likewise, after the flask, the substance of the flame is produced by the rays of the sun, which are substantially fiery. For when the rays meet the object body they gather strength and burn more, as will be shown elsewhere. Lastly, the fire that is usually struck from a stone is not produced but uncovered, drawn out, and brought forth, since it lay hidden before. This too we shall see.

units.la: Obijciet 3. Si accidentia effectiuè non producerent subsistantiâ, raræ admodum fierent subsistantiarum productiones: Hoc est contra experientiam, ergo. Probatur sesequela, nam substantiæ viuentes dum progignuntur, non habent causam sibi præsentem, à qua fiant v. g. dum rana in puluere madido exoritur, dum in viscere nascitur apis, dum in plantæ cortice vermis, dum in indusio præmortuæ cicadæ cicada &c. vbi est substantialis causa? vbi agens principale ? vbi rana producens? vbi apis alia præsens, &c? Ergo cùm dicantur progigni de nouo hæ substantiæ, nullaque præterea fit causa_, quàm humiditas, & siccitas; calor frigusque in materia, dicendum est, quòd accidentia physicè, realiter, effectiuè, ad substantiarum productiones concurrant.
units.tr: The third objection runs: if accidents did not produce substances effectively, the production of substances would be very rare. This is contrary to experience, therefore the premise holds. The consequence is proved as follows. Living substances, while they are being generated, do not have a present cause by which they are made. For example, when a frog arises in damp dust, when a bee is born in the flesh of an animal, when a worm arises in the bark of a plant, when a cicada arises in the shell of a dead cicada, and so on: where is the substantial cause? Where is the principal agent? Where is the frog that produces it? Where is another bee present to produce the bee? Therefore, since these substances are said to be generated anew, and no cause other than moisture and dryness, heat and cold in the matter is present, it must be said that accidents concur physically, really and effectively in the production of substances.

units.la: Respondét Scotistæ meliores,in huiusmodi casibus id, quod principalius agit, esse Deum, qui vt causa prima tenetur supplere defectum secundæ, quoties ista non adest. Quemadmodum ergo in vtero matris bene digestà, vltimeq; disposita fœtus fabricà, præstò est Dei concursus in creatione animæ; ita dum alia materia vltimò præparatur, & exigit formam;Deus in ea talem formam producit; neq; accidentia vim habent maiorem,quàm disponendi ad ipsam.
units.tr: The better Scotists reply that in cases of this kind the principal agent is God, who as first cause is bound to supply the defect of the secondary cause whenever the latter is absent. Just as, in the womb of a mother, when the foetus has been well digested and is at last fashioned in its final disposition, God's concurrence is at hand in the creation of the soul, so when other matter is finally prepared and calls for a form, God produces such a form in it. Nor do accidents have any greater power than that of disposing the matter for the form.

units.la: Hęc tamen respondsio non omnino placet, quamuis enim in aliquo casu, quiper accidens obtingat, recursus iste ad causam primam admitti possit; non tamen licet in infinita propemodum serie substantiarum, quæ producuntur, consugere in Cælum; secus natura defecisset in necessarijs. Instantia de anima rationali non suffragatur, ea enim a solo Deo creatur, quia ille non posuit causam, cum qua simul crearet; substantijs vero materialibus constituit suas causas, & cum ijs decreuit praebere concursum; vnde si causa secunda non agat, neque Deus in tali casu se solo aget.
units.tr: Yet this reply does not wholly satisfy. For although in some case, where something comes about through an accident, recourse to the first cause may be admitted, still it is not permitted, in an almost infinite series of substances that are produced, to flee to heaven. Otherwise nature would have failed in what is necessary. The instance of the rational soul does not support them, for that is created by God alone, because he did not establish a cause with which he would create it at the same time. But for material substances he has set up their causes, and has decreed to lend his concurrence along with them. Hence, if a secondary cause does not act, neither will God act alone in such a case.

units.la: Praeterea non videtur valida ratio Scotistarum, qua dicunt produci formas a Deo, quia materia disposita exigit illas; vnde si non induceretur, fieret materiae violentia. Quomodo enim in moribus, & aquis frigidissimis potuit materia disponi ad formas herbarum, & mineralium, quae calidissimae sunt? Quomodo in sententia peripatetica eo potuit penetrare calor, & siccitas, ibiq; diutius immorari ad materiae dispositionem? Quomodo si malleo tundas lapidem, adeo vt in frusta disiliat, eo solo, & primo ictu materia sic praeparatur, disponitur, & redditur exigitiua formae ignis, adeo vt Deus teneatur producere tot scintillas? Quomodo vnus ictus in lapidis materiam induxit calorem, & siccitatem vt octo, quae sint satis ad formam lapidis corrumpendam, & Deum quodammodo trahendum, vt nouam substantiam ignis cudat? &c.
units.tr: Moreover, the Scotists' argument seems not to be sound, by which they say that forms are produced by God because the prepared matter demands them, so that if they were not brought in, violence would be done to the matter. For how could the matter have been disposed to the forms of herbs and minerals in cold mountains and waters, when these forms are most hot? How, on the Peripatetic view, could heat and dryness have penetrated there and remained there longer to dispose the matter? How, if you strike a stone with a hammer so hard that it splits into pieces, is the matter so prepared, disposed, and made apt to receive the form of fire by that one blow alone and at its first stroke, that God is bound to produce so many sparks? How has one blow introduced into the matter of the stone heat and dryness as much as eight, which would suffice to corrupt the form of the stone and to draw God, as it were, to forge a new substance of fire? And so on.

units.la: Exinde videmus, vtraq; sententia, Thomisticam, & Scoticam suis premi difficultatibus, ijsq; maximis. Primo enim accidens producere nequit substantiam. Secundo si accidens causa non est, ergo solus Deus. Hoc vero si dicas, parum philosophice loqueris, maxime quia non adsunt plerumq;in materia dispositiones, quæ hunc citissimum Dei accursum exposcant, &c. Quid ergo ? Philosophia tam rationis indiga ? & ad vnum effectū sic obstupescens ? Inde se ipsa, velimus, nolimus, venit
units.tr: From this we see that both opinions, the Thomist and the Scotist, are pressed by their own difficulties, and very great ones. For first, an accident cannot produce a substance. Second, if an accident is not the cause, then God alone is. But if you say this, you speak little philosophically, chiefly because in matter there are often no dispositions that demand this most swift concurrence of God, and so on. What then? Is philosophy so lacking in reason, and so dumbfounded at a single effect? From this, whether we wish it or not, it itself comes forth.

units.la: CONCLVSIO QVARTA.
units.tr: FOURTH CONCLUSION.

units.la: Ex prædicta sententia, Thomistica, & Scotica probabile manet, nullam produci formam substantialem actu formaliter de nouo.
units.tr: From the aforesaid opinion, Thomistic and Scotist alike, it remains probable that no substantial form is actually and formally produced anew.

units.la: PRobatur, quia nulla potest assignari causa huiusce formæ substantialis, ergo manet probabile, non produci. Antecedens iam patet, nam talis causa vel vniuersalis est, vel particularis: non primum, alioquin natura defecisset in necessarijs non determinando peculiaribus effectibus causas etiam peculiares : non secundum, causa enim particularis, aut accidés est, aut substantia ; non accidens, vtpote omnino insufficiens; neq; substantia, quia hæc assignatur plerumque vaga, & absens: quod autem abest, agere nequit in materiam distantem. Ergo nulla causa potest assignari, quæ formæ sit productiua, & sic verofimile videtur, eam substantialiter non produci. Sed
units.tr: This is proved because no cause can be assigned for such a substantial form, and so it remains probable that it is not produced. The antecedent is now plain. For such a cause is either universal or particular. Not the first, for otherwise nature would have failed in the necessary matters by not assigning peculiar causes to peculiar effects. Not the second, for a particular cause is either an accident or a substance. Not an accident, since it is wholly insufficient; nor a substance, because the substance usually assigned is vague and absent, and what is absent cannot act upon matter at a distance. Therefore no cause can be assigned that is productive of the form, and so it seems likely that it is not produced substantially. But

units.la: Opponis. Etiamsi lateat causa productiuu substantiæ, non est hæc ratio suffisufficiens, vt denegetur effectus, ergo mala conclusio. Probatur antecedens, quia productio substantiæ de nouo, vel ipsis nota cæcis est; nam quis non videat fieri de nouo substantialiter ignem? lignum? flores? aurum? ferrum? animantes? & innumera, quæ priùs in natura non erant? Confirmatur, nam dato, quòd aliquando causa principalis non fit suis effectibus præsens; vt plurimum tamen non indistans est; ergo tunc producet. Sic homo generat hominem; Leo leonem; arbor fructus, vt supra ex Genesi dictum est. Confirmatur 2. nam sublata productione substantiæ, tollitur etiam actiuitas causæ atq; operatio.
units.tr: you object: even if the cause productive of a substance is hidden, this is not a sufficient reason for denying the effect; therefore the conclusion is false. The antecedent is proved because the production of a substance anew is known even to the blind. For who does not see that fire, wood, flowers, gold, iron, living creatures, and countless other things that did not previously exist in nature, are made anew in substance? It is confirmed: suppose that sometimes the principal cause is not present to its effects; for the most part, however, it is not at a distance, and so it will then produce. Thus a man begets a man, a lion a lion, a tree its fruit, as was said above from Genesis. It is confirmed secondly: if the production of substance is removed, the activity of the cause and its operation are removed too.

units.la: Resp. distinguendo antecedens. Non est sufficiens ratio; si effectus, qui videntur, non possint alio modo explicari, concedo; si alia ratione magis physica explicentur, nego. Ad probationem dico, ignem non fieri de nouo substantialiter, sed à subiecto educi, & retegi, vt supra diximus, & ex professo alibi dicetur. Ligna verò, flores, ferrum, & similia ex præiacentium vnione partium exoriuntur, nec nisi vnio de nouo producitur.
units.tr: I reply by distinguishing the antecedent. It is not a sufficient reason if the effects that appear cannot be explained in another way: I grant that. If they can be explained by a more physical reason, I deny it. To the proof I say that fire is not made anew in substance, but is drawn out of and uncovered from its subject, as we said above and shall say at length elsewhere. But wood, flowers, iron and similar things arise from the union of pre-existing parts, and nothing new is produced except the union.

units.la: Exemplum adest in auro, quod aliquando arte chymica excussum, nonnisi per substantias variè permixtas, concoctas, elaboratas extitit. Animantes etiam fiunt ex materijs, quæ vi seminali mouetur, trahuntur, concinnantur. Quarè ad confirmationem resp causas vtplurimum adesse quidem præsentes effectibus, veverum eas agere dumtaxat mouendo, & vniendo, non substantiam de nouo generando, vt lib. tertio. Qua in re afferri poterit ad robur conclusionis id, quod eam oppugnare videbatur. Homo enim physicè, realiterq; generat hominem. Sed rogo, quamnam de nouo producit illE substantiam? non animam, quæ creatur à Deo; non materiam, quæ ingenerabilis est, ergo nullam. Quid ergo facit? vnit solummodo, seu in materia dispositiones relinquit ad vnionem. A simili ergo quæuis alia generatio ex præexistētium vnione partium fiet. Postremò resp. causæ virtutem, & efficaciam in hoc satis exerceri, vt accidentia producat; mox vt corpora motu excitet, à se mittat, aliò insinuet, prouocet, misceat, impellat, vulneret, &c. Vnde patet, non tolli causarum operationes.
units.tr: An example is at hand in gold, which, when at times it has been extracted by chemical art, has existed only through substances variously mixed, concocted and worked up. Living creatures too come to be from materials that are moved, drawn together and fashioned by a seminal power. Hence, to the confirmation I reply that causes are indeed for the most part present to their effects, but they act only by moving and uniting, not by generating substance anew, as in book three. In this matter, that which seemed to oppose the conclusion can be brought forward to strengthen it. For a man physically and really begets a man. But I ask, what substance does he produce anew? Not the soul, which is created by God; not the matter, which is ungenerable. Therefore none. What, then, does he do? He merely unites, or leaves dispositions in the matter for the union. By analogy, then, every other generation will come about from the union of pre-existing parts. Lastly, I reply that the power and efficacy of a cause is sufficiently exercised in this, that it produces accidents, as soon as it stirs bodies by motion, sends them out from itself, insinuates them elsewhere, provokes, mixes, impels, wounds, and so on. Hence it is plain that the operations of causes are not taken away.

units.la: DISQVISITIO TERTIA.
units.tr: DISQVISITIO TERTIA.

units.la: Quasnam conditiones requirat causa efficiens, vt operetur.
units.tr: What conditions a efficient cause requires in order to operate.

units.la: PRO intelligentia sciendum, quòd etsi duæ conditiones præcipuæ videantur necessario requiri, vt causa efficiens agat; Existentia, & Præsentia nonnulli tamen in aduersum opinanti sunt; nam Thomistæ putant, causam operari posse quando etiam non est: Scotistæ verò dati actionem in distans. Illos iam impugnauimus. Contra hos manet discutiendum: An, & qualis causæ præsentia esse debeat ad operandum.
units.tr: To understand this, it must be known that although two principal conditions seem necessarily to be required for an efficient cause to act, namely existence and presence, some have held the contrary opinion: for the Thomists think that a cause can act when it does not even exist, while the Scotists grant action at a distance. We have already refuted those. Against these we must still discuss whether, and of what kind, the presence of the cause must be for it to act.

units.la: Proponi etiam solet hæc disquisitio hisce terminis, An ad actionem requiratur contactus. Pro qua re opus est scire, duplicem esse contactum, nempe mathematicum, & physicum. Primus dicitur cùm duo corpora suas habent simul extremitates, aut (quod idem est) immediatè vicinas. Ita v. gr. duo digiti se mathematicè tangunt, cùm proximi sunt. Contactus physicus est cùm duo corpora non solùm extrema simul habent, sed præterea inter se admittunt actionem, repassionemq; vt v.gr. cùm ignis applicatur ligno,in quod agit, & à quo repatitur.
units.tr: This question is also customarily put in these terms: Whether contact is required for action. For this it is necessary to know that contact is twofold, namely mathematical and physical. The first is said to occur when two bodies have their extremities together, or (which is the same thing) immediately adjacent. Thus, for example, two fingers touch mathematically when they are close together. Physical contact is when two bodies not only have their extremities together but also mutually admit action and reaction, as when fire is applied to wood, on which it acts and by which it is acted upon.

units.la: Præterea notandum est, contactum physicum adhuc esse duplicem, immediatum videlicet, ac mediatum Contactus immediatus est quando inter agens, & passum non mediat corpus, in quod causa priùs agat. Sic flamma, quæ undique ambit lignum, immediatum habet contactum. Contactus verò mediatus est quando inter agens, & passum corpus aliud iacet contiguum vtrique. Sic ignis tangit mediatè manum, quia inter manum, ignemque medius est aer, primo calefactus.
units.tr: Furthermore, it must be noted that physical contact is again twofold, namely immediate and mediate. Immediate contact is when no body intervenes between the agent and the patient, on which the cause would first act. Thus a flame that surrounds wood on every side has immediate contact. Mediate contact, however, is when another body lies contiguous to both the agent and the patient. Thus fire touches the hand mediately, because between the hand and the fire there is air, first heated.

units.la: Postremò adhuc notandū, intelligi posse duplici modo, quòd causa operetur in distās; primò exclusiuè; secundo inclusiuè. Agere in passum distans exclusiuè idē est, ac producere formā in subiecto remoto nil producēdo in spatio intermedio. Agere in passum distans inclusiuē significat producere, formam in subiecto remoto, simul tamen producendo aliquid in spatio intermedio. Hisce prænotatis explicatur sententia nostra per sequentes conclusiones.
units.tr: Lastly, it must further be noted that a cause's operating at a distance can be understood in two ways: first exclusively, second inclusively. To act on a patient at a distance exclusively is the same as producing a form in a remote subject while producing nothing in the intervening space. To act on a patient at a distance inclusively means producing a form in a remote subject while at the same time producing something in the intervening space. With these things premised, our opinion is explained through the following conclusions.

units.la: CONCLVSIO PRIMA.
units.tr: FIRST CONCLUSION.

units.la: Naturale agens nequit agere indi- stans exclusiuē, seu nihil agen- do per medium.
units.tr: A natural agent cannot act at a distance without acting through the intervening medium.

units.la: PRobatur conclusio autoritate Arist. Nā 7. phys.c.2. probat mouens debere simul esse cum mobili, vt hoc moueri possit. Similiter 1.de gen. & 2. de an.t.14. ait, quòd si contingeret vacuum, nō modò perspicuē non videretur obiectum distans, verùm nullo modo. Item 1.Meteor: inquit, oportere mundum inferiore supernis lationibus contiguum esse, vt inde omnis eius virtus regatur, & gubernetur.
units.tr: The conclusion is proved by the authority of Aristotle. In Physics 7, ch. 2, he shows that the mover must be together with the moved if the moved is to be moved at all. Similarly, in De generatione 1 and De anima 2, text 14, he says that if there were a vacuum, a distant object would not be seen clearly, indeed not at all. Also in Meteorology 1 he says that the world below must be contiguous with the upper revolutions, so that all its power is ruled and governed from above.

units.la: Probatur 2. experientia, qua perspicuum fit, naturale agens non esse præditum ea virtute, vt non agendo in medio valeat agere in distans. Ita sol non illustrat cubiculum, si obiecta fenestra non illuminet prius medium. Sic magnes non trahit ferrum, si manus, aut quid simile interponatur, quod actionem impediat per medium. Luna quoq; non tam offendit rheumaticos, quamdiu bene clauso clanso cubiculo aer medius excluditur. Ignis pariter non calefacit, si obex inter illum, passumque iaceat. Ex quibus, cæteris sq; fieri potest inductio, nullum agens naturale operari posse in distans, nisi prius aliquid per medium agat. Sed vrgent etiam experientiæ in contrarium, & illæ maximæ quidem. Propterea
units.tr: It is proved by a second experience, which makes clear that a natural agent is not endowed with the power to act at a distance without first acting in the medium. Thus the sun does not light a room unless the window first illuminates the air between. The magnet does not draw iron if a hand or something similar is placed between them, which blocks the action through the medium. The moon too does not much affect those who suffer from catarrh as long as the room is well closed and the air in between is shut out. Likewise fire does not warm if a barrier lies between it and the thing warmed. From these and other examples induction can be made: no natural agent can operate at a distance unless it first acts through the medium. But experiences to the contrary also press hard, and very great ones. Therefore...

units.la: Obiicies 1. succinum, adamas, &c. corpora trahunt etiam distantia nihil agêdo per medium, ergo datur actio in distans exclusiuè, sed absque actione in medio. Antecedens pater experientia, videmus enim trahi stipulas ab adamante, paleasque à succino, etiamsi nil agant in aere medio. Et Probatur, nam inter paleam, & succinum, vno palmo verbi gratia distantia, si adsit acus leuissima, seu quid simile, hoc non trahitur quanquam vicinius, ergo succinum non agit in medio agendo in distans.
units.tr: Objection 1: amber, adamant and other bodies attract even distant objects while doing nothing through the medium. Therefore there is action at a distance by itself, without action in the medium. The antecedent is proved by experience: we see straws drawn by adamant and chaff drawn by amber, even though they do nothing in the air between. It is also proved thus: between the chaff and the amber, say a palm's breadth apart, if a very light needle or something similar is present, it is not drawn, although it is nearer. Therefore amber does not act in the medium while acting at a distance.

units.la: Resp. negâdo antecedens quoad secundâ partem, attractio enim paleæ fieri potest ab adamante, & succino duplici modo; aut per emissionem corpusculorum, quæ aptam sortita figurâ sese paleæ, stipuleq; poris insinuét, ac circûpulsando eas cogât ad se (vnde notatione dignum est quòd succinum, adamasq; indigent affrictu aliquo, vt melius trahant, quia sic abstergitur crassus aer, & superficies eo motu incalescens corpora facilius emittit; vel quia succinum (& sic de omni substantia electrica) qualitatem gignit certi cuiusdâ corporis attractiuam. Vnde nullo modo do sequitur actio in distans, nam aut corpuscula transeunt per medium; aut quaelitas toto medio producitur. Experimentum de acu, folio, &c. quae inter succinum, paleamq; interiecta non attrahuntur, nullatenus probant nō exerceri actionē in medio. Siquidē ista nō attrahuntur, vel quia corpuscula nō inueniūt in ijs aptas meatuū, pororumq; texturas, vt infinuent se, quare dū impingunt, alio statim resiliunt; vel quia si producitur qualitas, haec nō cuiusq; corporis attractiua est, &c.
units.tr: Reply: I deny the antecedent as to its second part. The chaff can be attracted by adamant and amber in two ways: either by the emission of small corpuscles, which, having a suitable shape, insinuate themselves into the pores of the chaff and straw and, by pushing round them, force them towards themselves (and it is worth noting that amber and adamant need some rubbing to draw better, because this wipes away the thick air, and the surface, heated by the motion, emits bodies more easily); or because amber (and so with every electrical substance) produces a certain quality which attracts a certain kind of body. So in no way does action at a distance follow, for either the corpuscles pass through the medium, or the quality is spread through the whole medium. The experiment with the needle, leaf and so on, which are not attracted when placed between amber and chaff, in no way proves that no action is exercised in the medium. For these things are not attracted either because the corpuscles do not find in them suitable passages or pore-textures by which to insinuate themselves, so that when they strike they immediately rebound elsewhere; or because, if a quality is produced, it is not attractive to every body, and so on.

units.la: Obijcies 2. Basiliscus, & Catobleba, vt est apud Plinium l. 8. cap. 21. solo intuitu obuios interimunt. Secundò Mulieres meftruatæ solo visu maculas inducūt speculis. 3. Testudines procul distantes intuitu solo fouent ova, & pullos excludunt. 4. si duæ sint citharæ ab inuicem semotæ, vniusque fides pulsetur, alterius etiam fides vniffona confestim vibratur. Similiter organorū fistulæ chordas ad parem toni mensuram intensas à longinquo mouent, quod se vidisse refert Kirch. de arte Magn. li. 3. p. 8. 5. si in domicilijs cōcameratis ad quatuor angulos exquisitè ductis vox in vno angulo submisse profertur, in altero etiam oppositō exauditur, & non in medio. Ergo haec omnia probāt, fieri actionē in distans, & non per medium.
units.tr: Objection 2: the basilisk and the catoblepas, as Pliny reports in book 8, ch. 21, kill those they meet by sight alone. Second, menstruating women stain mirrors merely by looking at them. Third, tortoises at a distance hatch eggs and bring forth chicks by sight alone. Fourth, if there are two lyres set apart, and the string of one is plucked, the string of the other tuned in unison immediately vibrates. Similarly the pipes of organs set strings tuned to the same pitch in motion from afar, which Kircher says in De arte magnetica, book 3, p. 8, he saw for himself. Fifth, if in a vaulted room with four corners exactly placed a voice is uttered softly in one corner, it is heard in the opposite corner too, and not in the middle. Therefore all these prove that action takes place at a distance and not through the medium.

units.la: Resp. neg. consequentiam, quidquid enim ex praedictis contingat, per aliquāactionem in medio exercitam fit. Vnde Basiliscus, & Catobleba solo visu necant, siue nocent saltem, eò quòd spiritus nonoxios, & maligne affectus ab oculis mittunt. In caluaria enim duo foramina sunt, alterum oculi centro directè opposițum, per quod neruus opticus procedit: alterum ad latus, vbi protenditur neruus motiuus. Ex hoc igitur postremo, vnde lacrymæ de cerebro manant, per exteriores oculi partes inter palpebras, & albam tunicam stillando, spiritus etiam efferuntur, & quia pro animalis temperie noxij sunt, ideò quo perueniunt, plagas, aut necem infligunt. Exinde oritur spcculorum infectio à menstruosis,& & explicatur etiam, cur obtigerit quibusdam noctu visisse, vt de Augusto, Tiberio,alt̃sq; ferunt; spiritus enim ignei prout ex hirquis turmatim, & allisi egrediuntur, oculare potentiam illustrant, dū versatur ob ipsam, non minus ac fulgetrū è nube discussum. Quod inquiunt de testudinibus, consimili ratione solui potest; seu dici, nil agere testudines in oua, sed excubare tantum; hæc verò ab intrinseca virtute mouere se, vt omnia semina faciunt,quemadmodū constat in cæpis,quę licet non implantentur, egerminant.
units.tr: Reply: I deny the consequence. Whatever happens from the things mentioned comes about through some action exercised in the medium. Hence the basilisk and the catoblepas kill, or at least harm, by sight alone, because they send out from their eyes harmful spirits and malignly disposed effluvia. For in the skull there are two openings: one directly opposite the centre of the eye, through which the optic nerve passes; the other at the side, where the motor nerve extends. Through this latter, from which tears flow out of the brain and drip through the outer parts of the eye between the eyelids and the white tunic, spirits too are sent forth; and because they are harmful according to the temperament of the animal, they inflict wounds or death wherever they reach. From this arises the staining of mirrors by menstruating women. It also explains why some people are said to have seen at night, as is reported of Augustus, Tiberius and others: fiery spirits, issuing in herds from goats and struck, illuminate the power of sight while it is directed at them, no less than lightning discharged from a cloud. What they say about tortoises can be solved by a similar reasoning: either it can be said that tortoises do nothing to the eggs but merely sit upon them, while the eggs move themselves by an intrinsic power, as all seeds do, as is evident in onions, which sprout even when not planted.

units.la: Ref.2. citharæ distantis,& intactę sc ıū fieri hoc modo.Ex impulsu chordę,qui fit in altera cithara, mouetur proximus aer : hic motū eumdē pari vibratione imprimit vicino:mox in aliū agitatio eadē exundat, quoufq; tandē in alterius citharæ chordā inciderit. Hæc si paris fuerit quantitatis, & qualitatis,eandem percipit vibratione aeris, ab eaque vt sibi congruā moueri se finit,
units.tr: Reply to the second, the lyres set apart and the untouched string, is that this happens in the following way. From the impulse of the string in one lyre, the nearby air is moved. This imprints the same motion, by an equal vibration, on the neighbouring air; soon the same agitation spreads on to another part, until at last it strikes the string of the other lyre. If that string is of equal size and quality, it perceives the vibration of the air and allows itself to be moved by it, as congruent with itself,

units.la: finit, finis vnde fit sonus. Quare notant periti, quòdsi crispationes illæ aut vibratiunculæ aeris, vento, siue alia causa interrumpantur, numquam dabitur alter sonus. Ex qua doctrina explicari etiam potest, cur musica tam varios animi conciet affectus, prout enim aer motus, & subsultans aurium tympanum licit, musculosque internos varia numerorum lege vibrat, sic diuersimodè spiritus intimi agitantur, & passio fit diuersa. Hinc lenis, mitisque cantus mulcet animam, & soporè conciliat: è contra frequens, cõcitus, acer, depressionibus, elationibusq; intercisus animú effert, vrget, ferocemq; ad arma, & impetus facit, quemadmodū lyrifte Timotheo, expertus est Alexander. Hinc videtur sonare fabulá id, quod Io: Bapt. Porta ex Pythagora, Theophrasto, aliisque deducere studet, nempe citharam lupinis fidibus instructam, incitatamque oues reddere attonitas, & propemodum semianimes. Pellibus etiam elephanti, aut camelli si tympana fiant, exterreri equos &c. Patet enim horū effectuū causa esse aeré, prout varia numerorū lege vibratur, & ad organū auditus propellitur.
units.tr: and so the sound arises. Hence skilled people note that if those crispations or little vibrations of the air are interrupted by the wind or some other cause, no sound will ever arise. From this doctrine it can also be explained why music arouses such varied emotions in the mind. For as the air is moved and makes the drum of the ear leap, and the inner muscles vibrate according to a varied law of numbers, so the inner spirits are agitated in different ways, and the passion becomes different. Hence a gentle, mild song soothes the soul and brings on sleep; on the contrary, a frequent, excited, sharp song, broken by falls and rises, lifts up the spirit, urges it on, and makes it fierce for arms and attacks, as Alexander experienced with the lyre-player Timotheus. Hence what Giovanni Battista della Porta seeks to derive from Pythagoras, Theophrastus and others seems to be a fable: that a lyre fitted with wolf-gut strings, when struck, makes sheep astonished and almost half dead. Likewise, if drums are made of elephant or camel hide, horses are terrified, and so on. For the cause of these effects is clearly the air, as it is vibrated according to a varied law of numbers and driven to the organ of hearing.

units.la: Resp. ad tertium, in cubiculo concameraro vocem loquentis ab vno angulo exaudiri etiam in opposito, eò quòd aer inangustia duorum parietum elisus, quouique similem inuenit fabricæ dispositione, similis etiam sibi, & inuariatus procedit. Hæc igitur disposition cùm in angulo quoque opposito sit, aer, quia ad superficiem camerę circum ascenderat, statim ac in-eafeasdem, similesque angustias offendit, rursus primam subit vibrationem (si fortasse illam abruperit) unde talis adest in opposito, qualis fuerat in primo angulo, & sic vox eadem auditur. Illi vero, qui morantur in medio, non audiunt, quia non fit ad ipsos eadem elisi, & conformati aeris latio. Ex quo dissemus, non dari actionem in distans, non enim vox fertur ex diametro ad opposita, sed ab vno latere in aliud circulariter.
units.tr: Reply to the third: in a vaulted room, a voice spoken in one corner is heard also in the opposite corner, because the air, struck within the narrowness of the two walls and finding a similar arrangement of structure, proceeds in the same way and unchanged. Since this arrangement is also present in the opposite corner, the air, having risen to the surface of the room all around, as soon as it meets the same kind of narrowness again undergoes the first vibration (if perhaps it had broken it off), so that in the opposite corner there is such a vibration as there was in the first corner, and so the same voice is heard. But those who stay in the middle do not hear it, because the reflection and shaping of the struck air does not reach them in the same way. From this we conclude that there is no action at a distance; for the voice is not carried along a diameter to the opposite points, but circularly, from one side to the other.

units.la: Obijcies 3. Ignis, qui lebeti subijcitur, minus fundum calefacit, quàm partem summam, vt experitur quicumque remoto igne, statim subijcit manum. Similiter qui nuper occidit hominem, si adsit praesens, facit sanguinem occisi de vulneribus ebullientem, quamvis eum non tägat. Rufus cù vittæ, seu pannus vulnerati sanguine intinctus, puluere sympathico aspergitur, curaturque. hic vulneribus icti etiam absentis medetur. Pari modo phalagiu quos momorderit, eos cogit quantuis distantes artubus totis tremere, atque interdum agere choreas. Vi etiā fteganographiæ, seu horologij sympathici duo fædere inito sibi manifestant occultos animi sensus, vt Strada l.2.prol.6.poeticæ nitidè, ac eleganter suo more describit. Parétes vi sola imaginatiuæ diuersas notas, & maculas imprimunt fœtibus. Demùm polare fidus magnetem ad se vertit; magnesque ipse ferrum prodigiosè rapit. Quæ omnia, & similia concincunt actionem in distans peragi, & non in medio.
units.tr: Objection 3. A fire placed under a cauldron warms the bottom less than the top, as anyone can test by removing the fire and at once putting a hand underneath. Likewise, if a man who has just killed another is present, the blood of the slain boils up from the wounds, even though he does not touch them. A cloth or rag soaked in the wounded man's blood is sprinkled with a sympathetic powder and the wound is cured; here the injured person is healed even when absent. In the same way, the phalangium (spider) that has bitten someone makes him tremble all over, however far his limbs are from the bite, and sometimes makes him dance. By sympathetic force too, two persons who have made a pact reveal their hidden thoughts to each other through a steganographic or sympathetic clock, as Strada describes neatly and elegantly in his own manner (Prolusio 6). Mothers by imagination alone imprint various marks and spots on their offspring. Lastly, the polar star turns the magnet toward itself, and the magnet itself wonderfully snatches iron. All these things, and similar ones, seem to show that action takes place at a distance and not through a medium.

units.la: Resp. id non sequi. Nam quod attinet ad lebetis, ibi minor sentitur calor ex duplici causa, quia nimirum ignis parū sub fundo moratur,diutiùs verò ad latera, dū ascendit 2. quia dū ignis particulæ nituntur sursū, humiditas aquæ ab ijsdē vt potè à cōtrario recedit magis; & sic ad fundū, vbi minus reperit ignis, descēdens, eū reddit minùs calidū. Ad instantiā de sanguinis obullitione (si vera est)dici potest, quòd cū præsentis homicidæ agitati sint vehementer spiritus,egredianturq;de naribus,ore,porisq; hi fortasse in occisi vulnera ingressi, alios excitāt spiritus, qui ad fouendā partē læsam accurrerāt, vnde sāguinis motio, & ebullitio fit. Nisi mauis dicere,sanguinē suapte naturā,& ex inter na motione aliquando feruere in bullas. Quod autē ferūt de puluere sympathico, qui medendo vittis, vulnera distantiū curat, valdè suspectū est, si .n. curatur vulnus ob sympathiam sanguinis in vitta,cur etiā non peius euadit ob sympathiam sanguinis, qui putrescit,cadit dependitur,cōculcatur ? Deinde obseruant, non sanari vulnus, nisi continuò purgetur, ac mundum feruetur,ex qua mūditie potest oriri sanitas, cū partes, quæ à natura in remediū sufficiuntur, non ità facilè causā habeant putrescendi. Quidquid tamen sit, effectus non ad omnē distantiā contingit; quapropter dici posset, effluuia puluisculorum si aliquando feruntur de vittis ad vulnera, ibi etiam remedia conferre; non ita verò, si eò non impingant.
units.tr: Reply: that does not follow. As for the cauldron, the lesser heat felt there has a twofold cause. First, the fire lingers only briefly under the bottom but longer at the sides as it rises. Second, while the particles of fire strive upward, the moisture of the water withdraws from them as from its opposite; so the heat, descending to the bottom where the fire is weaker, makes it less warm. As for the instance of the blood boiling up (if it is true), it may be said that, since the presence of the murderer agitates his spirits violently and they go out through nose, mouth and pores, these spirits perhaps enter the wounds of the slain and stir up other spirits, which rush to foster the injured part; whence the movement and boiling of the blood follows. Unless you prefer to say that blood, by its own nature and internal motion, sometimes seethes into bubbles. As for what they report about the sympathetic powder, which cures wounds at a distance by being applied to the cloth, it is very suspect. For if the wound is cured through sympathy with the blood in the cloth, why does it not grow worse through sympathy with blood that rots, falls, is dispersed and trampled? Next, they observe that a wound is not healed unless it is continually cleansed and kept clean, and from this cleanliness health can arise, since the parts that nature supplies for the remedy do not easily have cause to rot. Whatever the case, the effect does not reach every distance. It could therefore be said that the effluvia of the powder, when carried from the cloths to the wounds, there too confer a remedy; but not if they do not strike there.

units.la: Resp. 2. phalangiū non agere in distās, neq; .n. ab eo mouentur qui eius morsu vulnerati vel tremere, vel saltare videntur. Itaq; res ita contingit. Phalangiū suo morsu virus quoddā relinquit in poris, fibrisq; fauciorū: Hoc autem serpit sensim, corripitq; arterias, musculos, & omne corporis mēbrū, præsertim æstiuo tépore, quo calor sese insinuando, humores omnes agitat, magisq; ad intima trudit. Ex hoc nascitur titillatio quedā persimilis illi, qua interdū leuissimo digitulorū tactu, celeriq; in superficie pellis decursu excitamur ad motū, saltū, gesticulatione, & risū. Inde patet, cur tarantulati frequentissimis exerciti saltibus, aliquando tandē à morbo exsoluantur, quia videlicet, concepto calore per motū, laxatur pori, extruditurq; ope sudoris venenum. Patet etiā, cur tarantulatos nō quicūq; soni, sed certi quidā cogant saltare, nēpe quia diuersi diuers sā pororū textura habent, vnde nō omnis moti aeris agitatio vnūquemq; mouet, subit, vellicat, sed certa certos. Denū patet, cur icti à phalangio rideant in dolore ipso, nā spiritus conciti diaphragma impellunt, hoc verò arterias mouet, maxillarumq; membranas, vnde fit risus, qui Sardonicus dicitur, quemadmodum experimur & nos, quandiu stupidum aliquod membrū sese in priftinū restituit per sanguinis, & spirituum ad sua loca recessum.
units.tr: Reply 2: the spider does not act at a distance, for those wounded by it are not moved by it, though they seem to tremble or leap. The thing happens thus. The spider leaves by its bite a certain poison in the pores and fibres of the wounded. This creeps slowly, seizes the arteries, muscles and every member of the body, especially in summer, when the heat insinuates itself, stirs all the humours and drives them further inward. From this arises a tickling very like that by which we are sometimes stirred to movement, leaping, gesturing and laughter by the lightest touch of the fingertips and a quick run across the surface of the skin. Hence it is clear why the tarantula-stung, exercising themselves in very frequent leaps, are at last freed from the disease: the heat generated by movement loosens the pores, and the poison is expelled by sweat. It is also clear why not every sound but certain sounds compel the tarantulati to dance: different pores have different textures, so not every agitation of the moved air stirs, enters or tickles every person, but certain sounds certain persons. Lastly, it is clear why those struck by the phalangium laugh even in the pain itself. The stirred spirits press upon the diaphragm, and this moves the arteries and the membranes of the jaws, whence the laughter arises that is called sardonic, as we too experience whenever some numbed limb recovers its former state through the return of blood and spirits to their places.

units.la: Resp. 3. Id, quod aiunt de Stenographia, seu horologijs quæ symphatica sūt, fabulosū censeri. Et suadetur ex ijs, quæ didicuntur, nempe huiusmodi horologia fieri non magnete solùm, sed etiam unguento sympathico, quod vtriusque amici sanguine plasmatur, & quidem sanguine non ab omni corporis membro, sed à certis elicito, ad hoc vt ij ad omnem locorum distantiam se inuicem alloqui possint. Hanc sanè rem beneficio magnetis, certo tamen interuallo, fieri posse tribus modis ostendit Kircherus l. 2. artis Magneticæ p. 5. c. 3. quem videre licet per otiû. Sed non sequitur inde actio vlla in distans, vt inquiunt.
units.tr: Reply 3: what they say about the steganography, or sympathetic clocks, is to be regarded as fable. This is suggested by what is taught about them: such clocks are made not by a magnet alone but by a sympathetic ointment, moulded from the blood of both friends, and indeed from blood drawn not from every member of the body but from certain ones, so that they can speak to one another across any distance. Kircher, in book 2 of his Magnetic Art, part 5, chapter 3, shows that this can be done in three ways by means of a magnet, though at a fixed interval; one may consult him at leisure. But no action at a distance follows from this, as they claim.

units.la: Resp. 4. imaginationis effectum esse mirabilem, quomodo illa tantâ polleat vi, vt maculas, notas, figuras, colores imprimat fetibus. Huc referri possunt septem illæ Augusti maculæ, quæ toto pectore dispersæ ordinem, numerumque siderum, in cælesti vrsa lucentium imitabantur. Huc etiam signatus gladius in dextero Scanderbegi bracchio, vt Potan. l. 2. belli Neap. Crux aurea in dorso Friderici Electoris Saxoniæ, vt Bucholc. in Cronol. Leo, gladius, & corona in corpore Iacobi Magnæ Britaniæ Regis, vt Camer. hor. subcif. Huc pariter quod refert Heliodor. de Persina Æthiopissa, quæ imaginem pueri albi contuita, filiam genuit albæ facie. Sicuti è contra, imperante Carolo, alia mulier iconem S. Io. Baptistæ sæpius videndo, hirsutum peperit filium. Huc denique redigenda est vitiata membrorum, & maximè oris deformitas, dum intuemur aliquando carneum ficum, cerasam, cucurbitulam naribus pendulam; vuuarum granula implantata cilijs, sfrusta carnis tostæ innata genis, rubras vini maculas in palpebris &c. Quorum effectuum ardua prorsus,& inuentu difficillimæ causa est. Solet autem hæc à doctioribus ferri. Dum potentia quæcumque operatur, in conatu quodam,& violentia est, vnde spiritus excitat, qui ad omnem vitæ functionem instrumenta sunt, eosque innumera pene copia varie miscet, subigit, conformat: Hinc phantasia quia in fœminis excitatur vehemens, attenta,& fixa, trahit secum vapores terreos, melancholicos, viscidos, quibus præcipuè scatent prægnantes,& hi iuxta rerum imagines, quæ acriùs apprehenduntur, agitantur, mouentur, imò texturis quibusdam infensilibus configurantur. Mox verò ad fœtus conformationem delati, cum impressa rei conceptæ imaguncula, siue specie, adhærescentes paulatim augentur, adeout crescente fœtu notam explicent magis,& sensibilem faciant, quemadmodum in leui characterè, qui paruulus inciditur arbori,& mox ere. scit in magnum, explicari potest.
units.tr: Reply 4: the effect of imagination is remarkable, how it has such power as to imprint spots, marks, figures and colours on offspring. To this may be referred those seven spots of Augustus, which, scattered over his whole chest, imitated the order and number of the stars shining in the celestial Bear. To this also belong a sword marked on the right arm of Scanderbeg (Pontanus, book 2 of the Neapolitan War); a golden cross on the back of Frederick, Elector of Saxony (Buchholtz, in his Chronology); a lion, a sword and a crown on the body of James, King of Great Britain (Camerarius, Horae subcisivae). Likewise what Heliodorus reports of Persina the Ethiopian woman, who, having gazed on the image of a white boy, bore a daughter of white face; and conversely, under Charles, another woman, who had often looked at an icon of St John the Baptist, bore a hairy son. Finally, to this must be referred the deformity of the limbs, and especially of the mouth, when we sometimes look at a fleshy fig, a cherry, a little gourd hanging from the nostrils; grape-seeds planted in the eyelashes, scraps of roasted flesh born on the cheeks, red wine-stains on the eyelids, and so on. The cause of these effects is very obscure and extremely hard to discover. The more learned usually put it thus. Whenever any power operates, it does so in a certain effort and violence, whence it stirs up the spirits, which are the instruments of every vital function, and mixes, subdues and shapes them in an almost countless variety. Hence the imagination, since in women it is excited vehemently, intent and fixed, draws with it earthy, melancholic, viscous vapours, of which pregnant women especially are full; and these, according to the images of things apprehended more keenly, are agitated, moved and even configured into certain textures. Then, carried to the formation of the foetus, with the little image or species of the conceived thing impressed upon them and adhering, they gradually grow, so that as the foetus grows they unfold the mark more and make it more perceptible; just as a slight character cut in a young tree is soon seen to grow into a large one.

units.la: Resp.4.Magnetis quoque naturam esse prodigiosam adeout D. Aug. l.21. de Ciu. c.4. edixerit.Magnetem lapidem nouimus mirabilem ferri raptorem, quod cum primum vidi vehementer inhorrui. Et sanè cui stupor non fiat penè lapideus, cùm lapis natura contumax, ad actiones tamè ferè vitales reddatur mitis. Quid enim ait Plin.l.36.c.16. lapidis rigore peius? ecce sen-
units.tr: Reply 4 (again): the nature of the magnet is also prodigious, as St Augustine declared in City of God, book 21, chapter 4: We know the magnet stone, a wonderful snatcher of iron, at the sight of which when I first saw it I shuddered greatly. And indeed, who would not be almost stunned into stone, since a stone, stubborn by nature, is rendered gentle toward nearly vital actions? For what does Pliny say, book 36, chapter 16? Worse than the hardness of a stone? Behold, it has sen-

units.la: Note: The printed signature mark and the small mark near "crescente" were not transcribed. sensus, manusque tribuit illi natura. Quid ferri duritia pugnacius? sed cedit, & patitur mores. Huius vero attractionis causam in magnete, inquit Claud.
units.tr: sense, and nature gives it hands. What is more combative than the hardness of iron? Yet it yields and submits to character. As to the cause of this attraction in the magnet, Claudian says:

units.la: Siquid deprehendere verum Mens valeat, expediat.
units.tr: Whether the mind is able to grasp anything true, let us set forth.

units.la: Ea siquidem à pluribus attentatur, à nullo fortasse adhuc scitur. Plato in Timaeo, vt est apud Gallenum; Epicurus, qui recetes quidam sequuntur, & primò Henricus Regius c.7. putauerunt id fieri simili modo, quo nos raptum paleae à succino factu supra exposuimus, videlicet per circumpulsione, quatenus corpora minima, quae à magnete insensibili traspiratione difluunt, aere intermedium abigunt, eiusq; motu ferrum ad magnete compellunt, siue rapiunt.
units.tr: Many have attempted this, but perhaps no one has yet known it. Plato in the Timaeus, as Galen reports it; Epicurus, whom certain modern writers follow; and above all Henricus Regius (ch. 7) thought that it happens in the same way as we explained above concerning the attraction of straw by amber, namely by a kind of circular pushing: the smallest bodies, which flow out from the magnet through an imperceptible perspiration, drive away the intervening air, and by their motion compel the iron to the magnet, or seize it.

units.la: Quòdsi putes arduum concipere, quomodo magnes apprimè compactus, contumax, durus tam facilè, tà longè, tam abundè substantias mittat à se tenuissimas, dicito ab eo produci qualitatem ferri attractiuam. Cur autem ferri tantum? quia nimirum, vt inquit Kircher.l.1. art. Magn. p.2.prop.3. Magnes, & ferrum genuini terrae filij sunt, fiunt enim ex illa magis naturali, magis pura, magis homogenea, & simili; vnde cùm similia naturae vi aggregentur similibus, vnum attrahit aliud, ab eoque attrahitur.
units.tr: But if you think it hard to conceive how a magnet, so dense, stubborn and hard, can so easily, so far and so abundantly send out from itself substances so very fine, you may say that the attractive quality of iron is produced by it. But why only iron? Because, as Kircher says (book 1, art. Magnes, p. 2, prop. 3), the magnet and iron are genuine children of the earth. For they are made from that matter which is more natural, purer, more homogeneous and alike; hence, since like things are gathered to like by the power of nature, one attracts the other and is attracted by it.

units.la: Respondet vltimò idem auctor loco citato, Magnetem vergere semper ad polu, siue ad polare sub vrsae cauda fidus, non quia reuera, eò tendat immediatè Magnes vi aliqua occulta eius astri motus; verum quia se ad borealem terræ partē conuertit, vnde cūm hæc protendatur ad Vrsæ polum, videtur & Magnes ad eundem ferri.Sed cur etiam terræ partem austrinā non appetit magnes? an quia versus eam non adsunt mōtes, vbi nascitur, & ad quos naturali propensione sese conuertat? sed hoc repugnat experientijs eorum, qui orbem obnauigarunt.Cur ergo? Ait Kircherus, terræ polos magnetica vi detineri, & veluti defigi iuxta Mundi polos, & hoc à Deo, cui sunt cardines terræ, constitutum esse, ne inferior hęc machina ventorū impetu, marium æstu, planetarum decursu à fixa sui sede commoueretur. Deinde Magnetis Minerę in quauis terræ plaga sint, reperiuntur omnes ab Austro in septentrionem inclinantes, propendentes, excurrentesque, perinde ac firmo, solidoque huiusmodi nexu transfuersum ácto laterales terræ partes, quæ nimiùm fortasse ob solis æstum super Zona torrida hiscerent, colligarentur. Quare Magnete hoc primæuo naturaliter ad Boream vergente, alia pars quæcumque Magnetis non ab alio rapta, sed vi naturali ad eundem vergit locum, in quo meliùs à natura conseruatur. Quidquid sit, non conuincitur actio exclusiuè in distans, vt ex dictis patet.
units.tr: The same author answers finally, in the passage cited, that the magnet always tends toward the pole, or toward the pole star beneath the tail of the Bear. This is not because the magnet is directly carried there by some occult power of that star's motion, but because it turns itself toward the northern part of the earth; and since this part extends to the pole of the Bear, the magnet also seems to be carried toward the same point. But why does the magnet not also seek the southern part of the earth? Is it because there are no mountains there where it is born, and toward which it turns by natural propensity? But this contradicts the experience of those who have sailed around the globe. Why then? Kircher says that the poles of the earth are held by magnetic force and, as it were, fixed beside the poles of the world, and that this was ordained by God, to whom the hinges of the earth belong, so that this lower machine would not be moved from its fixed seat by the onslaught of winds, the surge of the seas, or the course of the planets. Next, since deposits of magnetic ore are found in every region of the earth, all of them inclining, hanging and running from south to north, the lateral parts of the earth are bound together, as if by such a firm and solid bond driven across; otherwise they might gape open, perhaps too much, because of the sun's heat above the torrid zone. Hence, since this primal magnet naturally tends toward the north, any other part of a magnet, not drawn by another but by its own natural force, tends toward the same place, where it is better preserved by nature. Whatever the case, action at a distance is not proved to be exclusively so, as is clear from what has been said.

units.la: CONCLVSIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: SECOND CONCLUSION.

units.la: Naturale agens intra spheram suæ actiuitatis agit immediatè in partes etiam distantes.
units.tr: A natural agent acts immediately, even on parts at a distance, within the sphere of its activity.

units.la: PRobatur conclusio experientijs. Dum solis radius ingreditur per fenestram in cubiculum, partes in recta linea magis illuminantur, quàm quæ à lateribus iacent, quamquam istæ magis propinquæ sint soli; ergo sol immediatè agit in partes recta linea distantes. Probo consequentiam. Hoc maius lumen in partibus recta linea distantibus non producitur à radio ingrediente fenestram, hic n. cùm sit vicinior aeri laterali, ageret etiam æquo modo, imò magis ad latera; ergo maior ea lux producitur immediatè à sole distante, non à radio in medio, & prope fenestram existente.
units.tr: Proved by experience. When a ray of the sun enters a room through a window, the parts lying in a straight line from it are more illuminated than those lying at the sides, although the latter are nearer the sun. Therefore the sun acts immediately on parts distant in a straight line. I prove the consequence. This greater light in the parts distant in a straight line is not produced by the ray entering the window, for that ray, being nearer the air at the sides, would act equally there, or even more so toward the sides. Therefore that greater light is produced immediately by the distant sun, not by the ray in the middle, which exists near the window.

units.la: Probatur 2. Sit aliquis ad ostium clibani accensi, & vehementissimum sentiat calorem: deinde claudatur ex improuiso fornax, aut obex aliquis interponatur, cessabit illico tantus calor, ergo hic immediatè oriebatur à solo igne. Probatur consequentia; nam si produceretur ab aere in medio calefacto, non tam citò, ac repentè calor vehemens remitteretur. Ergo ignis, & in vicinas, & in partes etiam distantes immediatæ operatur.
units.tr: It is proved secondly. Let someone stand at the mouth of a lit oven and feel very strong heat. Then if the furnace is suddenly shut, or some barrier is placed in the way, that great heat will cease at once. Therefore it arose immediately from the fire itself. The consequence is proved: for if it were produced by the air in between being heated, the intense heat would not be withdrawn so quickly and suddenly. Therefore fire acts immediately both on neighbouring parts and on parts even at a distance.

units.la: Probatur 3. ratione. Quando agens calefacit immediatè passum, aut calefit prima,& indiuisibilis tantùm superficies: aut pars diuisibilis: si secundum, ergo agens immediatè operatur, & in medio, & in distans: si primum, ergo agens tam vehementissimæ, quàm exiguæ virtutis æquè ageret, nam vtrumq; actione sua immediata in vnicam tantummodo superficiem operaretur, quod falsum est.
units.tr: It is proved thirdly, by reason. When an agent heats a patient immediately, either only the first and indivisible surface is heated, or a divisible part is. If the second, then the agent acts immediately both through the medium and at a distance. If the first, then an agent of very great power and one of small power would act equally, since both would operate by their immediate action on a single surface only. This is false.

units.la: Opponis. Hoc si verum esset, naturale agens operaretur in distans,& nō per medium,& sic daretur actio exclusiuè in distans; ergo.Probatur sequela : ignis verbi gratia produceret calorem in vltima parte huius aulæ remissum, & non produceret eundem in proxima vbi calor est intensus, ergo. Confirmatur, quia ignis non est præsens cuique parti huius aulæ, igitur nequit agere immediatè in omnes.
units.tr: You object: If this were true, a natural agent would act at a distance and not through a medium, and so there would be action exclusively at a distance. Therefore... The consequence is proved: fire, for example, would produce heat in the farthest part of this hall, weakened, and would not produce the same in the nearby part where the heat is intense. Therefore... It is confirmed: because fire is not present to every part of this hall, it cannot act immediately on all.

units.la: R.esp.negando sequelam. Ad probationem dico, non sequi actionem exclusiuè in dictans,nam ignis tam in medium agit, quàm in partem remotam, licèt non pari modo,sed iuxta maiorem, minoremque passi distantiam. Ad confirmationem distinguo: ignis non est præsens cuique parti aulæ mathematicè, concedo; physicè, subdistinguo; non est præsens physicè præsentia suppositi,concedo; præsentia virtutis, nego. Quamuis enim ignis non applicetur quoad suppositum, nempe secundum se ipsum omnibus aulæ partibus,attamen ratione virtutis,& efficaciæ, quam habet, dicitur iis præsens physicè, quia tanta sphæra, seu tantum interualli spaspatium respectu validi agentis, vt quid vnum est. Sic v. g. si sit causa tantæ actiuitatis, vt valeat agere in decem palmos interposïti aeris, hi decem palmi vnica sphæra sunt, in quam totam virtus illa causæ simul agere potest; vnde causa dū agit, dicitur esse immediatè omnibus præsens, non præsentia suppositi, sed virtutis, per quam simul pertingit ad omnes.
units.tr: I answer by denying the consequence. To the proof I say that it does not follow that action is exclusively at a distance, for fire acts both on the medium and on the remote part, though not in the same way, but according to the greater or lesser distance of the patient. To the confirmation I distinguish: fire is not present to every part of the hall mathematically, I grant; physically, I subdistinguish: it is not physically present by the presence of its substance, I grant; by the presence of its power, I deny.
