For although fire is not applied with respect to its substance to all parts of the hall, nevertheless by reason of the power and efficacy it has, it is said to be physically present to them, because so great a sphere, or so great an interval of space relative to a powerful agent, is as one thing. Thus, for example, if a cause is of such activity that it can act through ten palms of interposed air, those ten palms are one sphere, into which that power of the cause can act all at once in its entirety. Hence the cause, while acting, is said to be immediately present to all, not by presence of substance but by presence of power, through which it reaches all at once.

units.la: CONCLVSIO TERTIA.
units.tr: THIRD CONCLUSION.

units.la: Si naturale agens accipiatur vt in partes diuisum, tunc vna eius pars agit in distans, & non in medium.
units.tr: If a natural agent is taken as divided into parts, then one of its parts acts at a distance and not through a medium.

units.la: PRobatur hac experientia. Sit ignis bipalmaris, & applicetur ligno, non solummodo aget in lignum palmus ignis, qui est illi contiguus, verum & palmus remotior: sed remotior non agit in medium, ergo. Maior probatur, quia ignis profunditate bipalmaris maiorem producit calorem, quàm palmaris tantum, vt experientia conuincit. Minor etiam patet ratione, palmus enim ignis remotior omnino similis est palmo viciniori: sed simile non agit in simile; ignis ergo remotior non agit in medium. Quæro quid operaretur? an magis calefaceret primum ignem? non, quia ignis est calidus in summo.
units.tr: This is proved by experience. Let there be a fire two palms deep, and apply it to wood. Not only will the palm of fire that is contiguous to the wood act on it, but also the more remote palm. Yet the more remote palm does not act on the medium. Therefore... The major premise is proved, because a fire two palms deep produces greater heat than one palm alone, as experience shows. The minor is also evident by reason: the more remote palm of fire is wholly similar to the nearer palm, but like does not act on like. Therefore the more remote fire does not act on the medium. I ask, what would it act upon? Would it heat the first fire more? No, because fire is already at its highest heat.

units.la: Probatur 2. Detur tabula, & insuper constituatur globus ex æcome maximus: hic sanè tabulam non tangit secundum se totum, sed in puncto, siue in exigua sui parte, cùm tamen partes omnes dicti globi grauitent in tabulam, eamq; fortasse infringant. Hoc posito, arguo sic. Partes globi, quæ à tabula distant, non agunt in alias immediatè subiectas, & nihilominus agunt in tabulam, quæ distans est, ergo. Probo antecedens. Vnaquæq; pars globi accepta in pari quantitate parem habet grauitatem cum alia, ergo cùm simile non agat in simile, vna non grauitat in aliam. Secundò, corpus coniunctum corpori non imprimit in illud vim, aut impulsum, vt experientia docet, non enim caput grauitat in collum, neq; istud in pectus, neque hoc in fæmora, &c. Ergo primæ globi partes cùm faciant vim in tabulam, & non in medias, agent in distans. Reuera tamen quia partes in globo non agunt singillatim, vt plures causæ, sed vt vna ex pluribus integrata, idcirco non datur actio rigorosè in distans ex natura rei, sed concipitur, facta ex diuisione per intellectum.
units.tr: It is proved secondly. Let there be a board, and let a very large globe of ebony be placed on it. This globe certainly does not touch the board with its whole surface, but only at a point, or in a small part of itself, although all the parts of that globe press down on the board and perhaps break it. Given this, I argue thus. The parts of the globe that are distant from the board do not act immediately on the parts immediately beneath them, and yet they act on the board, which is distant. Therefore... I prove the antecedent. Each part of the globe, taken in equal quantity, has the same weight as another, and therefore, since like does not act on like, one part does not weigh upon another. Secondly, a body joined to a body does not impress force or impulse upon it, as experience teaches: the head does not weigh on the neck, nor the neck on the chest, nor the chest on the thighs, and so on. Therefore the outer parts of the globe, since they exert force on the board and not on the parts in the middle, will act at a distance. Truly, however, because the parts in the globe do not act singly, like several causes, but as one thing made up of many, action is not strictly at a distance by the nature of the thing. It is conceived as such only by the intellect, through division.

units.la: DISQVISITIO QVARTA.
units.tr: DISQVISITIO QVARTA.

units.la: Vtrum positis conditionibus ad agendum, causa possit causare se ipsam.
units.tr: Whether, with the conditions for acting posited, a cause can cause itself.

units.la: PRo intelligentia suppono, sensum quæstionis non esse, an res primò vale at se ipsam producere, deberet enim supponi existens antequam esset. Quæritur ergo, an res iam existens possit secundò producere se ipsam. V. g. ignis a. qui actu est, poteritne iterum generare seipsum?
units.tr: To begin with, I assume that the question is not whether a thing can first produce itself, for that would require it to be already existing before it exists. The question, then, is whether a thing that already exists can produce itself a second time. For example, can fire a, which is actually burning, generate itself again?

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Non implicat, quòd causa causet secundò se ipsam.
units.tr: It is not contradictory that a cause should cause itself a second time.

units.la: PRobatur 1. quia Christus de facto replicat semet ipsum in hostia, seu (quod inquiunt alij) reproducit: ergo similiter quæuis alia causa per Dei virtutem valebit reproducere, aut secundò causare se. Consequentia patet, non enim exigitur maior virtus in hoc, ut Deus eleuet creaturam, & simul cum ea concurrat ad se rursus producendam; ac requiratur, dum Christus replicat, seu reproducit se ipsum: ergo. Confirmatur, nam Deus potest se solo producere iterum, & quoties voluerit Petrũ; igitur potest etiã wti eodem ad sui productionem. Quod enim se solo facit, cum alio etiam facere potest, si non adsit manifesta implicantia. Hinc
units.tr: It is proved first, because Christ in fact replicates himself in the host, or (as others put it) reproduces himself. Therefore any other cause, by the power of God, will likewise be able to reproduce itself, or to cause itself a second time. The consequence is plain: no greater power is needed for God to raise up a creature and at the same time concur with it in producing it again than is needed when Christ replicates or reproduces himself. It is confirmed: God can produce himself again by himself alone, and as often as he wills, for Peter; therefore he can also use the same concurrence for his own production. For what one does alone, one can also do with another, unless a manifest contradiction is present.

units.la: Probatur conclusio 2. quia eatenus causa nequit producere se primò, quia sic influeret priusquam esset: sed influendo secundò, non contingeret sic, ergo. Probo minorem, quia causa vt producat secundò se ipsam, debet supponi iam primò existens, constituta in se, omnino perfecta, & potens ad agendum; ergo tunc posset agere producendo se iterum. Confirmatur, quia causa vniuoca gerit virtutem producendi effectum sibi omnino in entitate consimilem, & æquè perfectum; ergo non repugnat, quòd etiam efficiat se ipsam.
units.tr: The second conclusion is proved as follows. Up to this point a cause cannot produce itself primarily, because it would then exert influence before it existed. But if it exerts influence a second time, this does not happen; therefore. I prove the minor: in order to produce itself a second time, a cause must already be supposed to exist first, established in itself, wholly perfect and able to act. Therefore, at that point, it could act by producing itself again. It is confirmed: a univocal cause has the power to produce an effect wholly similar to itself in being and equally perfect; therefore it is not repugnant that it should also effect itself.

units.la: Obijcitur. Causa efficiens debet influere in aliud: sed posita conclusione, id non fieret, ergo. Maior est certa, nam causa extrinseca, & effectus, aliud, & aliud sunt. Minor autem constat, quia si res produceret se, causa, & effectus manerent vna, & eadem entitas. Consequentia currit.
units.tr: It is objected: an efficient cause must influence something else. But if the conclusion is granted, this would not happen; therefore. The major is certain, for an extrinsic cause and its effect are different, one from the other. The minor is plain, because if a thing produced itself, cause and effect would remain one and the same entity. The consequence holds.

units.la: Resp. 1. quòd causa efficiens debet influere in aliud, quoties applicatur alteri subiecto, in quo terminum à se distinctum producit. Verùm si causa, vt in suppositione, assumatur à Deo, & applicetur circa se ipsam, tunc cessat commune axioma, quòd influat in aliud. Quare si cur actio, qua Christus in hostia replicatur siue reproducit se, non terminat in aliud, ita &c. Secundò respondeo, quòd causa sa, vt secundò producta dici potest aliud quid à re producente distinctum, licèt .n. causa, & effectus entitatiuè accepti omnino sint idem, tamen causa in ratione producti, & producentis diuersum habet conceptum, vnde causa vt producens, est vnum quid, vt verò producta, est aliud quid.
units.tr: Reply 1: an efficient cause must influence something else whenever it is applied to another subject, in which it produces a term distinct from itself. But if the cause, as in the supposition, is taken up by God and applied to itself, then the common axiom, that it influences something else, ceases to hold. Hence, if the action by which Christ is replicated in the host, or reproduces himself, does not terminate in something else, the same holds here. Reply 2: a cause, when it is produced a second time, can be called something distinct from the thing producing it. Although cause and effect, taken as entities, are wholly the same, the cause has a different concept as product and as producer. Hence the cause as producing is one thing, and as produced it is another.

units.la: Obijcitur 2. Si causa produceret se ipsam, effectus non penderet à causa: sed hoc repugnat, ergo. Maior probatur, quia affectus productus esset ipsissima entitas causæ talis omninò, qualis est: sed vt causa non pendet, secus idem penderet à se ipso, ergo.
units.tr: It is objected secondly: if a cause produced itself, the effect would not depend on the cause; but this is repugnant; therefore. The major is proved because the produced effect would be the very entity of the cause, altogether such as it is. But as cause it does not depend; otherwise the same thing would depend on itself; therefore.

units.la: Resp. negando maiorem. Ad probationem dico, quòd causa in tali statu penderet à se ipsa, verùm sub diuerso conceptu: nam vt producens, foret independens: & vt producta penderet: Exemplum adest in replicatione, siue reproductione corporis Christi.
units.tr: I reply by denying the major. To the proof I say that the cause in such a state would depend on itself, but under a different concept. For as producing it would be independent, and as produced it would depend. An example is present in the replication, or reproduction, of the body of Christ.

units.la: DISQVISITIO QVINTA.
units.tr: FIFTH DISQUISITION.

units.la: Vtrum duæ causæ possint causare se ipsas.
units.tr: Whether two causes can cause each other.

units.la: PRo intelligentia suppono, fieri posse quæstionem de causis tam in eodem, quàm in diuerso genere. v. g. de duplici efficiente; seu de altera efficiente, altera finali; vna materiali, alia formali, &c. Qua in re philosophi vniuersim tenent, neq; per naturæ, neq; per Dei potentiam causas in eodem genere posse inuicem fe causare v. g. ignem .a. qui est causa ignis .b. non posse ab eodem .b. produci. Attamen frequens opinio est apud Thomistas, quòd causæ diuersi generis mutuò causare fe possint etiam naturaliter. Sic, aiunt, materia in genere causæ materialis dat esse formæ; forma verò, vt causa formalis causat materiam.
units.tr: To begin, I assume that the question can be raised about causes both within the same genus and across different genera, for example about two efficient causes, or about an efficient and a final cause, or a material and a formal cause, and so on. On this point the philosophers generally hold that, neither by the nature of things nor by the power of God, can causes of the same genus cause each other. For example, fire a, which is the cause of fire b, cannot be produced by b. Nevertheless, it is a common opinion among the Thomists that causes of different genera can cause each other mutually, even naturally. Thus, they say, matter, as a material cause, gives being to form, and form, as a formal cause, causes matter.

units.la: Secundò notandum, posse quæri dupliciter, an duæ res valeant fe mutuò caufare. Primo quoad idem esse physicum: fecundo quoad esse diuersum. V.g. Potest ne materia dare physicam entitatem formæ, atq; ab ea physicè recipere suam? Rursus, Potest ne causa efficiens dare physicum esse causæ finali, & causari ab eodem fine in genere causæ intentionalis? Circa fecundum affirmant omnes. Vnde quoad esse diuersum res eadem prior est, ac poste. rior, v. g. medicina in genere physico præcedit sanitatem: sanitas in esse cognito, fiue intentionali antecedit medicinam.
units.tr: Secondly, it should be noted that the question can be asked in two ways: whether two things can cause each other mutually, first with respect to the same physical being, and second with respect to a different being. For example, can matter give physical entity to form and receive its own from it physically? Again, can an efficient cause give physical being to a final cause and be caused by that same end within the genus of intentional cause? All agree on the second. Hence, with respect to a different being, one and the same thing is both prior and posterior: for example, medicine precedes health in physical being, while health precedes medicine in cognitive or intentional being.

units.la: Quod attinet ad primum, fit.
units.tr: As to the first, the answer is as follows.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Implicat, quòd Causæ physicæ, siue in eo- dem, siue in diuerso genere sint, in- uicem se se causent quoad esse idem.
units.tr: It implies that physical causes, whether of the same or of different kinds, mutually cause each other with respect to the same being.

units.la: PRobatur, quia causa, quæ physicè producit effectum, non potest ab eodem physicè produci, ergo duæ causæ nequeunt se inuicem causare, quoad esse idem. Probo antecedens: Causa, quæ physicè dat effectum, prior est saltem naturâ causalitate sua; ergò etiam effectu suo, ergo nequit produci ab effectu. Probo consequentiam. Causa iam producta esset, existeret; haberet actualitatem suam; secus non daret illam effectui, ergo ab effectu produci nequit. V. g. sit ignis .a. qui producere debeat ignem b. vt producat, necessariò debet prius esse; nam operari est secundus actus, qui dependet, sequiturq; ad esse: quomodo ergo ignis .a. prior causalitate sua, & effectu, recipiet suum esse physicum ab igne b?
units.tr: It is proved because a cause that physically produces an effect cannot be physically produced by that same effect; therefore two causes cannot cause each other with respect to the same being. I prove the antecedent: a cause that physically gives an effect is prior, at least by nature, in its causality, and therefore also prior to its effect; so it cannot be produced by the effect. I prove the consequence: a cause already produced would exist and would have its actuality; otherwise it would not give that actuality to the effect; therefore it cannot be produced by the effect. For example, let there be fire a, which ought to produce fire b. In order to produce, it must necessarily exist beforehand, for to operate is a second act, which depends on being and follows it. How, then, will fire a, prior to its effect and to its causality, receive its physical being from fire b?

units.la: Probatur 2: Si causa produceretur ab effectu suo, nullo modo siue naturâ, siue ratione prior esset influxu, & causalitate sua: hoc repugnat, ergo. Probo maiorem. Causa reciperet esse physicum post causalitatem suam, ergo nullo modo esset prior illa. Patet antecedens: Acciperet esse physicum ab effectu suo, qui ab actione causatiua pendet, eàq; posterior est, ergo haberet esse physicum post causalitatem. V. g. sit materia b. à qua præbente influxum educatur forma c. Dicis quòd forma, quæ accipit esse à materia dat etiam esse materiē. Contra ergo materia quoad esse physicum non est prior forma causante: igitur nec prior intelligi potest causalitate, per quam producitur forma: sed forma producitur ex causalitate materiæ; igitur materia, nec esse, nec intelligi potest causalitate sua prior.
units.tr: It is proved secondly: if a cause were produced by its effect, it would in no way be prior, either by nature or by reason, to its influx and its causality. This is repugnant; therefore the thesis holds. I prove the major: the cause would receive physical being after its causality, and therefore would in no way be prior to it. The antecedent is plain: it would receive its physical being from its effect, which depends on the causal action and is posterior to it, so it would have physical being after its causality. For example, let matter b, supplying influx, be that from which form c is drawn. You say that the form, which receives its being from matter, also gives being to the matter. On the contrary: matter is not prior to the causing form as regards physical being; therefore neither can it be understood to be prior to it in the causality through which the form is produced. But the form is produced by the causality of matter; therefore matter can be neither prior in its being nor prior in its causality.

units.la: Probatur 3. Debeant se duæ causæ inuicem causare in instanti .a. Quæro, vel sunt in eodem instanti, vel non: si primum, ergo nequeunt se amplius causare, quia iam sunt: si secundum, ergo multò minus causabunt, quia non habent esse, ad quod sequitur operari. Neq; dicas: pro instanti .a. sunt, quia se causant. Contra .n. vrgeo: vel pro instanti .a. causant illud esse, per quod sunt, vel non: si primum, ergo prius intelliguntur agere quàm sint: si secundum, ergo sunt priusquam causent; vnde non se inuicem causant.
units.tr: It is proved thirdly. Let two causes cause each other in instant a. I ask: are they in the same instant, or not? If the first, then they can no longer cause each other, since they already are. If the second, then they will cause even less, since they do not yet have the being to which operating follows. Nor say that they are at instant a because they cause each other. For I press the point: either at instant a they cause that being through which they are, or they do not. If the first, then they are understood to act before they are; if the second, then they are before they cause. Whence they do not cause each other.

units.la: Obijcies 2. Materia dat esse physicum formæ, atq; ab ea recipit suum, ergo duæ causæ diuersi generis possunt se inuicem causare quoad esse idem. Probatur antecedens, quia materia est subiectum, à quo educitur forma, ergo vt causa materialis dat esse formæ: deinde forma dat ipsi materiæ suum existere; materia enim non existit à se; igitur & forma causat materiam.
units.tr: You will object secondly: matter gives physical being to form and receives its own from it; therefore two causes of different kinds can cause each other with respect to the same being. The antecedent is proved thus: matter is the subject from which form is drawn, so as material cause it gives being to the form; and then the form gives to matter its existence, for matter does not exist of itself. Therefore the form also causes the matter.

units.la: H 4. Resp. n. secundam partem antecedentis, vidimus enim materiam, vt subiectum primum, existere à fe, neq; dependere in esse physico à forma, vnde nequit esse tanquam effectus eiusdem.
units.tr: I deny the second part of the antecedent. For we have seen that matter, as the first subject, exists of itself and does not depend on form for its physical being; hence it cannot be an effect of the same form.

units.la: Obijcies 2. Introductio nouæ formæ in materiam, causat expulsionem veteris; & expulsio veteris causat quoq; introductionem nouæ; igitur duæ causæ causant fe inuicem. Antecedens patet, quia forma ingrediens pellit priorem, & prioris expulsio est causa, cur noua ingrediatur.
units.tr: You will object again: the introduction of a new form into matter causes the expulsion of the old; and the expulsion of the old also causes the introduction of the new; therefore two causes cause each other. The antecedent is plain: the entering form drives out the prior one, and the expulsion of the prior one is the reason why the new one enters.

units.la: Resp. n. secundam partem antecedentis. Ratio est, nam expulsio veteris formæ non causat nouæ introductionem; sed supponit, consequiturq; ad illam, vt effectus formalis secundarius illius. Et quomodo expulsio, quæ quid negatiuum est, causabit physicam formæ introductionem? Itaq; ad summum expulsio veteris est conditio ad nouam, non causa.
units.tr: I deny the second part of the antecedent. The reason is this: the expulsion of the old form does not cause the introduction of the new one; rather, it presupposes it and follows upon it, as its secondary formal effect. And how could expulsion, which is something negative, cause the physical introduction of a form? Therefore, at most, the expulsion of the old form is a condition for the new one, not a cause.

units.la: Obijcies 3. Sint duo baculi adinuicem innixi; vnus regit alium, & regitur ab illo, ergo datur mutua causalitas. Probatur, nam vbicatio baculi a. causat vbicationem baculi b. rursus vbicatio baculi b. causat vbicationem baculi a. ergo quod causat, causatur.
units.tr: You will object thirdly: let there be two sticks leaning against each other; one supports the other and is supported by it; therefore there is mutual causality. It is proved: the placing of stick a causes the placing of stick b; again, the placing of stick b causes the placing of stick a; therefore what causes is also caused.

units.la: Resp. n. consequentiam. Ad probationem n. quod vbicatio vnius causet vbicationem alterius, & ab eadem causetur. Baculus enim a. ipse causat vbicationem in baculo b. atq; hic pariter vbicationem aliam in baculo a. quare vbicatio ipsa non causat, sed tantùm causatur, est solùm effectus, non causa efficiens. Dato igitur pro vno, eodemq; instanti duplici baculo, vnusquisq; dum innititur alteri, causat vbicationem in illo, sed ipse non causatur, & sic non adest mutua causalitas. Dici secundò potest, quòd vbicationes non causent se, sed vnaquæque à suo baculo causata inuicem sibi resistant, ne baculi cadant. Vnde non erunt causæ sui effectiuæ, sed resistitiuæ.
units.tr: I deny the consequence. As for the proof: the placing of the one causes the placing of the other, and is caused by the same. For stick a itself causes a placing in stick b, and stick b in turn causes another placing in stick a; so the placing itself does not cause but is only caused; it is merely an effect, not an efficient cause. Granting, therefore, two sticks at one and the same instant, each one, while it leans on the other, causes a placing in that other, but is not itself caused, and so there is no mutual causality. It can be said secondly that the placings do not cause each other; rather, each placing, caused by its own stick, resists the other, lest the sticks fall. Whence they will be not efficient but resistive causes of their effects.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SEXTA.
units.tr: SIXTH DISQUISITION.

units.la: Vtrum duæ causæ causare possint eundem effectum.
units.tr: Whether two causes can produce the same effect.

units.la: PRo intelligentia notetur, causas dici alias partiales, & alias totales. Primæ sunt, quarum nulla vim habet sufficientè producendi se sola effectum, simul tamen cum alia producit. V.gr. Si quatuor sint, qui nauim simul trahant, quilibet eorum dicitur causa partialis, quia concurrit cū alio, neque trahere nauim se solo potest. Inde causa totalis ea dicitur, quæ sola, sine alterius auxilio satis est ad effectus productionem. V.g. ignis.a.qui fit applicitus ligno, est causa totalis ad comburendum, eò quòd se solo absque ope alterius efficit combustionem.
units.tr: For clarity, it should be noted that causes are called partial in some cases and total in others. Partial causes are those none of which has the power to produce the effect by itself, but which produce it together with another. For example, if there are four men pulling a ship together, each of them is called a partial cause, because he concurs with another and cannot pull the ship alone. A total cause, on the other hand, is one that by itself, without another's help, is sufficient to produce the effect. For example, fire (a), when applied to wood, is a total cause of burning, because it brings about the combustion by itself, without the help of another.

units.la: Secundò notetur, quòd tam causa totalis, quàm partialis assumi possunt vel in actu primo, vel in actu secundo. Totalis in actu primo est illa, quæ virtutem habet adæquatam effectui, siue postea in actu secundo totaliter concurrat, siue non; quo pacto vir corpore validus, qui se solo trahere nauim poterit, dicitur causa totalis in actu primo ad nauis tractionem. Partialis in actu primo ea est, quæ habet virtutem se sola insufficientem ad effectus productionem, unde necessariò indiget alia concausa. E contra causa totalis in actu secundo illa dicitur, quæ vim exerit suam, & actu sufficienter se sola totum præstat effectum: talis est homo robustus, qui solus totam nauim trahat, neq; ad hoc alienum habeat auxilium. Partialis in actu secundo est, quæ actu non præstat sufficienté effectui concursú, sed alterius causæ opem admittit, siue postea in actu primo habeat vim adæquatam, siue non.
units.tr: Secondly, it should be noted that both total and partial causes may be taken either in first act or in second act. A total cause in first act is one whose power is adequate to the effect, whether or not it afterwards wholly concurs in second act. Thus a man strong of body, who could pull a ship by himself, is called a total cause in first act of the pulling of the ship. A partial cause in first act is one whose power is insufficient by itself to produce the effect, so that it necessarily needs another concause. By contrast, a total cause in second act is one that exerts its power and by its action alone accomplishes the whole effect; such is a robust man who pulls the whole ship alone, with no outside help. A partial cause in second act is one that, in act, does not supply sufficient concurrence to the effect but admits the help of another cause, whether or not it afterwards has adequate power in first act.

units.la: His positis, quæritur an idem numero effectus produci possit à duplici causa totali, seu quæ totaliter, & adæquatè per duplicem actionem concurrat: v.g. si duo ignes æquè applicentur eidem ligno, sanè quilibet eorum in actu primo est idoneus ad producendum totum effectum: quæritur, an etiam sic appliciti eandem ignis formam indiuisibilem vnusquisq; actione sua totali actu realiter producat, an non; sed influant vt causæ partiales tantùm.
units.tr: With this laid down, the question is whether one and the same effect, numerically speaking, can be produced by a double total cause, that is, by causes that concur wholly and adequately through a double action. For example, if two fires are applied equally to the same wood, then surely each of them, in first act, is fit to produce the whole effect. The question is whether each of them, so applied, really and actually produces by its own total action the same indivisible form of fire, or whether they flow in only as partial causes.

units.la: Nominales, quorum sententiæ nuper alij adhærere, tenent posse duplicem causam iam totalem eiusdem generis, & ordinis totaliter concurrere ad eundem numero effectum; & id quod naturaliter. Ex adverso defendunt Scotus, & non pauci Thomistae hoc etiam diuinitus repugnare. Aliqui Recentiores media incedentes via putant, repugnantiam adesse in natura: sed per Dei virtutem posse fieri effectum. Quae sententia etsi plausibilis, non tamen satis placet. Nam etiamsi nunquam contingat produci effectum a duplici totali, quia fieri deberet penetratio causarum, vt eidem passo applicarentur; Attamen si Deus plures penetret causas totales, applicetq; vni, & eidem subiecto, arbitror eas ad producendum exhibituras totalem concursum etiam naturaliter. Quare sit..
units.tr: The Nominalists, whose opinions some others have lately adopted, hold that two causes, each already total and of the same kind and order, can concur totally to one numerically identical effect, and that this happens naturally. On the other side, Scotus and not a few Thomists defend the view that this is repugnant even to divine power. Some more recent writers take a middle way: they think there is a repugnance in nature, but that the effect can be produced by the power of God. Although this opinion is plausible, it does not altogether satisfy me. For even if an effect is never produced by two total causes, because their penetration would have to occur so that both are applied to the same patient, nevertheless, if God were to make several total causes penetrate and apply them to one and the same subject, I think they would exhibit total concurrence even naturally in producing the effect. Wherefore let it be...

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Non modo possunt de absoluta Dei potentia duae causae totales eundem effectum producere: sed hoc naturaliter etiam non repugnat..
units.tr: Not only can two total causes produce the same effect by the absolute power of God, but this is not even naturally repugnant.

units.la: PRobatur prima pars conclusionis argumento communi, quia hoc non implicat; si enim duplex causa totalis penetretur, eidemq; materiae sit applicita, Deus tunc efficere poterit, ne vlla concursum diminuat suum, siue attemperet, seu partialem reddat; in quo casu omnes causae totis viribus, & per actiones tales concurreret ad producendum essectum. V.g.si penetretur ignis.a.& ignis.b. simulque applicentur materiæ. c. dicunt in communi sententia, quòd naturaliter ignis vterque remitteret de sua vi,& con. curreret per duplicem actionem partialē, vnius totalis integratiuam. Sed tamen ex voluntate Dei vnicuique relinqui posset sua vis,& actio totalis,in quo casu illi duo ignes totaliter concurrerent ad eundem effectum. Vnde concludunt,per Dei potentiam fieri posse, vt plures causæ totales in vnum influant effectum. Ex his ergo
units.tr: The first part of the conclusion is proved by a common argument: it does not imply a contradiction. For if two total causes were made to penetrate and were applied to the same matter, God could then ensure that neither diminishes its concurrence, tempers it, or makes it partial. In that case all the causes would concur with their full strength, and by such actions would produce the effect. For example, if fire (a) and fire (b) penetrate each other and are applied simultaneously to matter (c), the common opinion says that naturally each fire would remit something of its power and concur by a double partial action, which together make up one total action. But by the will of God each could keep its power and its total action, in which case those two fires would totally concur to the same effect. Hence they conclude that by the power of God it can happen that several total causes flow into one effect. From these things, therefore,

units.la: Probo secundam conclusionis partem. Sint duo ignes eidem subiecto æquè applicati: vnusquisque causa est ad agendū necessariò determinata; vnusquisque habet omnia requisita ex parte actus primi, vt viribus totis agat; vnusquisque causa est naturalis, & applicantur cum tota ea virtute, quam haberent, si etiam separati ab inuicem applicarentur; sed in eo casu ignis. a. totum produceret essectum, & ignis. b. totum quoque suum, ergo & simul appliciti concurrent hi duo ignes totaliter ad effectum. Probo consequentiam.Si hoc non facerent, maxime quia vel vnus maneret otiosus, vel vterque partialiter tantùm influeret: neutrum dici posset; ergo agerent omnes totaliter. Probo minorem quoad primum. Causa necessaria determinata ad agendum cum omnibus prærequisitis ex parte actus primi, necessariò agit, ergo alter ignis in eo casu non maneret otiosus. Probo etiam quoad secundum sic. Ex eo quòd ignis. a. eidem subiecto applicetur simul cum igne. b. non deperdit vim suam intrinsecam, qua etiam seorsim ab illo ageret. Quid enim ex consortio ignis. b. deperdit ignis. a ? quid illi advenit, cur ligetur eius actiuitas ? Quare suum robur debet imminuere ? fortasse ob venerationem illius ? perinde ac sciat, debere totaliter influere si solus influat; partialiter verò si maneat cum alio, vt ipsi etiam relinquat commodum influendi ? Ergo cùm ignis. a. nihil deperdat intrinsecum ex applicatione ignis. b. cùmque sit causa, naturaliter ad actionem determinata, totaliter etiam influet in efsectum.
units.tr: I prove the second part of the conclusion. Let two fires be equally applied to the same subject. Each is a cause necessarily determined to act; each has all the requisites on the side of first act, so that it acts with its whole strength; each is a natural cause; and they are applied with the full power each would have if they were applied separately from one another. But in that case fire (a) would produce the whole effect, and fire (b) would also produce its whole effect. Therefore, when applied together, these two fires will concur totally to the effect. I prove the consequence: if they did not do this, it would be chiefly because either one would remain idle, or each would flow in only partially. Neither can be said; therefore both would act totally. I prove the minor as to the first point: a cause necessarily determined to act, with all the prerequisites on the side of first act, necessarily acts; therefore in that case the other fire would not remain idle. I prove the second point as follows. The fact that fire (a) is applied to the same subject together with fire (b) does not deprive it of its intrinsic power, by which it would act even if separated from it. For what does fire (a) lose from the company of fire (b)? What happens to it that its activity should be bound? Why should it diminish its strength? Perhaps out of reverence for fire (b)? As though it knew that it must flow in totally if alone, but only partially if it remains with another, so that it would leave the other the advantage of flowing in? Therefore, since fire (a) loses nothing intrinsic from the application of fire (b), and since it is a cause naturally determined to act, it will also flow into the effect totally.

units.la: Probatur 2. si ignis b. adueniens non finit ignem. a. totaliter agere, vel id facit per se, vel per actionem suam, vel per subiectum: nil ex his dici potest, ergo non impedit, quò minus totaliter agat. Probo minorem quoad primam partem. Ignis. b. adueniens non habet oppositionem cum igne.a. in entitate, imò cùm sint eiusdem speciei, fouent se potius, & iuuant, vt patet. 2. non opponuntur quoad actionem, alioquin nec partialiter agerent. Rursus, quia si v.gr. duae animae penetrarentur, vnaquaeque pari modo, ac priùs exerceret se in agendo. 3. non opponuntur quoad subiectum, quia hoc patiuè tantùm se habet, recipitque actionem, siue ab vna, siue à multiplici causa, prout illi fuerit applicita. Ergo duo ignes æquè applicati nullo modo impediuntur, ne totaliter agant.
units.tr: It is proved a second way. If fire (b), when it arrives, does not prevent fire (a) from acting totally, it must either do so through itself, or through its action, or through the subject. None of these can be said; therefore it does not hinder fire (a) from acting totally. I prove the minor as to the first part: fire (b), arriving, has no opposition to fire (a) in its entity; indeed, since they are of the same species, they rather foster and help each other, as is evident. Second, they are not opposed in action, otherwise they could not even act partially. Again, if, for example, two souls were made to penetrate one another, each would exercise its action in the same way as before. Third, they are not opposed in the subject, because the subject is merely passive and receives action, whether from one cause or from many, according as it has been applied to them. Therefore two fires equally applied are in no way prevented from acting totally.

units.la: Respondét aduersarij, non acturos ita per duplicem actionem totalem, quia vna forent superflua, quod est repugnans naturæ. Contra: etiamsi foret superflua, quid magis contra naturam videtur: admittere superfluum ex accidenti, an causas necessariò determinatas ad agendum non operari? Dicunt rursus, non acturas duplici actione totali, quia secus produceretur duplex forma, & non vna. Contra: ponunt ipsi materiam vnius tantùm formæ naturaliter capacem, ergo si causæ naturaliter agunt, vnam tantummodo producent. Rursus: replicetur lignum .a, & apponantur ipsi duo ignes, alter Venetijs, alter Muriani. Quæro, producét vnicam, an duplicem formam? Dicunt aduersarij vnicam, quia vnica est materia. Hanc & ego do responsionem: Repetunt non acturos ita naturaliter, quia vt eidem subiecto applicentur, penetrari debent; penetratio verò supernaturalis est. Contra: etiamsi penetratio per vim fiat supernaturalem, actio tamen, quæ sequitur à causis, naturaliter omnino exercetur, alioquin deberet fieri nouum miraculum. Ita si Deus homine penetraret cum homine, illoque sic relinqueret, absq; nouo miraculo ij naturaliter sua munera obirent.
units.tr: The opponents reply that the causes would not act thus by a double total action, because one of them would be superfluous, which is repugnant to nature. Against this: even if one were superfluous, what seems more contrary to nature: to admit something superfluous by accident, or that causes necessarily determined to act should not operate? They say again that they would not act by a double total action, because otherwise a double form would be produced and not one. Against this: they themselves posit that the matter is naturally capable of only one form; therefore, if causes act naturally, they will produce only one. Again: let there be the same wood (a), and let two fires be applied to it, one at Venice and one at Murano. I ask: will it produce a single form or a double form? The opponents say a single one, because the matter is single. I too give this answer. They repeat that the causes would not act thus naturally, because in order to be applied to the same subject they must penetrate, and penetration is supernatural. Against this: even if penetration is brought about by a supernatural force, the action that follows from the causes is nonetheless exercised wholly naturally; otherwise a new miracle would have to occur. So, if God were to make one man penetrate another man and left him so, without any new miracle they would naturally discharge their functions.

units.la: Objicies 1. Si effectus idem à duplici causa totali produceretur, dependeret ab illa, & non dependeret: hoc implicat; ergo neq; diminutus, neq; naturaliter à duplici totali producti potest. Probatur sequela. Detur ignis a. & ignis b. qui totaliter producant ignem c. Hic dependeret ab igne a. vt supponimus; non dependeret, quia etiam remoto igne a. totus maneret ignis c. ergo dependeret, & non dependeret.
units.tr: You will object: if the same effect were produced by two complete causes, it would both depend on them and not depend on them; this is contradictory; therefore it cannot be produced naturally by two complete causes, neither diminished nor whole. The consequence is proved thus. Let there be fire a and fire b, which together completely produce fire c. This would depend on fire a, as we suppose; yet it would not depend on it, because even with fire a removed, the whole fire c would remain. Therefore it both depends and does not depend.

units.la: Resp. negando sequelam: Ratio est, nā ignis c. dependeret ab vtroque; fieret enim ab ea duplici causa ex intrinseco influente; non tamen dependeret essentialiter, quia subláto altero, adhuc totus effectus maneret. Eo modo quo lux ista non ne dependet à sole, à quo fit? nihilominus, etiam sublato sole, perseueraret, influente Deo vice solis; vnde non sequitur: ergo non dependet à sole, dependet .n. sed non essentialiter.
units.tr: I answer by denying the consequence. The reason is that fire c depends on both, for it is produced by that twofold cause flowing into it from within; yet it does not depend essentially, because when one is removed the whole effect still remains. In the same way, does this light not depend on the sun, by which it is produced? Nevertheless, even with the sun removed, it would continue, God flowing in in the sun's place. Hence it does not follow, "therefore it does not depend on the sun": it does depend, but not essentially.

units.la: Obijciēs 2. causa naturaliter operari nequit circa effectum ab alia producẜum; sed hoc sequeretur data conclusione; igitur, &c. Probatur minor; quia ignis a. produceret effectum, qui ab igne b. iam esset productus, ergo ageret circa effectum ab alia causa productum.
units.tr: You will object secondly: a cause cannot naturally act upon an effect already produced by another cause; but this would follow from the conclusion given; therefore, etc. The minor is proved: fire a would produce an effect which was already produced by fire b; therefore it would act upon an effect already produced by another cause.

units.la: Respond. n. minorem. Et ratio est, nam ignis à. & b. producerent effectum eundem simul, vnde nullus eorum ageret circa rem iam producẜam; alioquin contra suppositionem aliquis agisset priùs alio, & se solo non appli-
units.tr: I deny the minor. The reason is that fire a and fire b would produce the same effect simultaneously, so that neither of them would act upon a thing already produced; otherwise, contrary to the supposition, one would act before the other and would not be applied by itself alone,

units.la: cation. applicitus cum altero.
units.tr: but would be applied together with the other.

units.la: Obijcies. Duæ causæ cognoscitiuæ, quoties concurrunt ad eundem effectum præstant influxum partialiter, ergo etiam duæ causæ naturales non cognoscitiuæ. Probatur antecedens. Adsint v. g. 4. homines, qui singuli trahere nauim totaliter possint; sed eam tamen vnitim, & simul trahant: in tali casu experitur vnusquisque, se minùs laborare: igitur nullus concurrit viribus totis, vt potest, sed partialiter.
units.tr: You will object: two cognitive causes, whenever they concur to the same effect, exert their influence partially; therefore two natural non-cognitive causes do so too. The antecedent is proved thus. Suppose there are, say, four men, each of whom could draw a ship entirely by himself; yet if they draw it together and at the same time, in such a case each one experiences that he labours less; therefore none concurs with his whole strength, as he is able, but only partially.

units.la: Resp. dato etiam antecedenti, negando consequentiam. Disparitas est, quia si duæ causæ apprehensiuæ applicentur ad agendum simul, vnaquæq; cognoscit præsens auxilium, & inde minùs de suo impendit: verùm quia causa naturalis non cognoscitiua nil imaginatur de præstita ope, idcirco vi tota, nisiq; suo integro facit. Secundò antecedens negari poterit, si vniuersaliter accipiatur. Nam etiam duæ causæ cognoscitiuæ, nisi de industria vim suam remittere velint, agere totaliter possunt in eundem numero effectum. V. g. si duo vectrum tollant de scamno simul hunc leuissimum calamum, non ne ambo pari modo agetis, ac si vnusquisque singillatim ageret?
units.tr: I answer: granting the antecedent, I deny the consequence. The disparity is that if two apprehensive causes are applied to act together, each one perceives the help present, and therefore contributes less of its own; but because a non-cognitive natural cause imagines nothing of the help rendered, it therefore acts with its whole force and without holding back. Secondly, the antecedent can be denied if it is taken universally. For even two cognitive causes, unless they deliberately wish to remit their force, can act entirely upon one and the same effect in number. For example, if two men lift this very light reed from a bench together, do not both of you act in the same way as if each acted singly?

units.la: Obijcies vltimo. Causa partialis dicitur illa, quæ admittit consortium alterius ad effectum; ergo causa totalis erit illa, quæ tale consortium excludit. Confirmatur, quia causa partialis idco ideo precisè admittit cōsortium alterius quia caret virtute adæquatè influendi; sed totalis non caret virtute adæquatè influédi, ergo hæc necessariò excludet cōsortiū.
units.tr: Finally you will object: a partial cause is that which admits the partnership of another in producing the effect; therefore a total cause will be that which excludes such partnership. It is confirmed, because a partial cause admits the partnership of another precisely because it lacks the power to flow in adequately; but a total cause does not lack the power to flow in adequately; therefore this one will necessarily exclude partnership.

units.la: Respond. causæ partialis conceptum non esse in hoc, vt habeat consortium alterius; verùm vt partialiter influat.
units.tr: I answer that the concept of a partial cause does not consist in this, that it has the partnership of another, but in this, that it influences partially.

units.la: Quamuis autem hoc dato sequatur necessitas in effectu habendi alterius influxum, tamen in eo causæ partialis conceptus formaliter non consistit. Similiter essentia causæ totalis non est in hoc, vt aliam excludat ab effectu, sed vt actionem totalem præstet. Ad confirmationem distinguo: ideo præcisè causa partialis admittit consortium, &c. consortiū ad actionem, concedo: consortium ad effectum, nego. Causa igitur non est partialis, eò quòd aliam admittat in ordine ad effectum, si .n. duæ simul adæquatè ad eundem concurrerent, adhuc illæ totales forent: sed vocatur partialis, quando ad actionē suā illa, quæ de se insufficiens est, aliam habet concausam. Deinde concessa minori, distinguo consequens: Ergo causa totalis excludit consortium alterius ab actione sua, concedo; ab effectu, in quem influit, nego. Itaque causa totalis ea dicitur, quæ totalem, & adæquatam exerit actionem, adeout non expectet auxilium ab alia, vt fit actio totalis. Quòd autem simul cum ea influat alia etiā causa, hoc nō probat, nō esse totale, dūmodo .n. totaliter agat, si & cētū alię simul ageret, illa semper totalis erit.
units.tr: Although, granted this, it follows by necessity that the effect has the influence of another, nevertheless the formal concept of a partial cause does not consist in that. Similarly, the essence of a total cause does not lie in this, that it excludes another from the effect, but in its exerting a total action. As to the confirmation, I distinguish: "therefore a partial cause admits partnership, etc." — partnership in the action, I grant; partnership in the effect, I deny. A cause is therefore not partial because it admits another in relation to the effect; for if two were to concur adequately to the same effect, both would still be total. Rather, it is called partial when, for its action, it has another concause, since it is in itself insufficient. Then, the minor being granted, I distinguish the consequence: "therefore a total cause excludes the partnership of another from its action" — I grant; "from the effect into which it flows" — I deny. Thus a total cause is that which exerts a total and adequate action, so that it does not await help from another in order to act totally. Moreover, that another cause also flows in together with it does not prove that it is not total; provided that it acts totally, even if the others act at the same time, it will always be total.

units.la: Quæres, vtrum causa efficiens determinata sit ad certum numerum, & tot indiuiduationes effectuum in sua specie; an verò producere possit quemcumque intra speciem eandem? Resp. non esse determinatam. Ratio est, quia effectus, qui per actionem distinctam producuntur à causis (nam quæstio de his est) possunt ijdem ab aliis produci. V.g. lux, quæ à sole producitur, & à Deo simul, potest produci à solo Deo. Ergo ad talem effectus indiuiduationem sol essentialiter determinatus non est, adeout ab alia causa hic dependere nequeat.
units.tr: You will ask whether an efficient cause is determined to a certain number, and to so many individuations of effects in its species, or whether it can rather produce any one whatever within the same species. I answer that it is not determined. The reason is that effects which are produced by causes through distinct action (for the question concerns these) can be produced by others as well. For example, the light which is produced by the sun and by God at once can be produced by God alone. Therefore the sun is not essentially determined to such an individuation of the effect that the effect cannot depend on another cause here.

units.la: Esset hic agendum de ijs etiā causis, quę intrinsecæ sunt; Materia videlicet, ac forma; sed hæc opportuniùs cùm de composito. Quæres tamen quomodo Materia, quæ dicitur efficere formam, causet eandem? Resp. causare materialiter, hoc est recipiendo, seu patiendo. Quare causalitas materiæ in formam non est, vt aliqui dicunt, vnio; sed passio. Probatur, quia forma vniri potest materiæ; licet non causetur ab illa, vt patet in anima rationali, ergo causalitas Materiæ in formam non est vnio. Secundo actus vitales causantur materialiter à suis potentijs, & non vniuntur illis, ergo &c.
units.tr: Here one would have to treat also of the intrinsic causes, namely matter and form; but these are more suitably discussed with the composite. Yet you will ask how matter, which is said to produce form, causes it. I answer that it causes materially, that is, by receiving or by being passive. Hence the causality of matter with respect to form is not, as some say, a union, but a passion. This is proved, because form can be united to matter, although it is not caused by it, as is clear in the rational soul; therefore the causality of matter with respect to form is not union. Secondly, vital acts are caused materially by their powers, and are not united to them; therefore, etc.

units.la: DISPVTATIO TERTIA.
units.tr: THIRD DISPUTATION.

units.la: De causa Finali.
units.tr: On the Final Cause.

units.la: QVæuis causa in natura agit propter finem, ad quem auctor suus eam Diuino consilio destinauit. Quare damnatur in hoc Democriti opinio, censentis naturam non operari ad finem, sed omnia ex causali atomorum concursu procreari. Si hoc est, irridat Seneca Democritum l. 4. de benefic. 19. Te quoq; atomi, & ipsemica tua forte, ac temere conglobauerunt. Quamuis autem responderet Democritus, non casu aliquo se factum esse, quia natura ex visu operandi comparauit habitum ad ea peragenda, quæ semel casu peregit; in hoc tamen quidquid ille respondeat, inepte inquit Lactantius delirauit. Nihil enim certius, quam res in natura tam varias, ita fuisse ab initio, sicuti nunc, ad certum finem sapientissima lege productas. Vnde Aristoteles 1. de par. anim. c. 5. In natura operibus constans illud præcipuè, ut nihil temere ac fortuna committatur, sed alicuius gratia, &c. Præsertim verò si de natura intellectuali sermo fit. Proinde nobis de causa finali disputatio erit, quæ ut ordine suo tractetur, fiat.
units.tr: Every cause in nature acts for the sake of an end, to which its author has directed it by divine counsel. Hence the opinion of Democritus is condemned, who held that nature does not work toward an end, but that everything is produced by the chance concourse of atoms. If that is so, Seneca mocks Democritus in De beneficiis book 4, ch. 19: "You too, atoms, and your very chance, have gathered yourselves together rashly." Although Democritus might reply that it was not by any chance that he was made, because nature, from the habit of acting, acquired a capacity for performing those things which it had once done by chance, Lactantius says that, whatever he replies, he raves foolishly in this matter. For nothing is more certain than that the things in nature, so varied, were from the beginning, just as they now are, produced for a definite end by a most wise law. Hence Aristotle, in De partibus animalium book 1, ch. 5: "In the works of nature this above all is constant: nothing is done rashly or by chance, but for the sake of something, and so on." This is especially so when we speak of intellectual nature. Therefore our disputation will be about the final cause, and let it be treated in its proper order.

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: DISQUISITIO PRIMA.

units.la: Quid fit finis, & quotuplex.
units.tr: What an end is, and how many kinds there are.

units.la: RECIPITVR ab omnibus hæc definitio finis, quam tradit Ariftoteles in 2. phyf. c. 3. Finis est id, cuius gratia cætera sunt. Res de fe patet. Diuisio autem abit in multiplicem. Primò enim Diuiditur in finem Cuius,& finem cui. Finis cui præexiftit ipsi amori, ac desiderio, & est illud ens, cui bonum exoptatur. Finis verò cuius dicitur illud ipsum bonum, cuius acquirendi gratia operamur. Sunt hi duo fines ab inuicem inseparabiles, non enim possumus bene velle cuiquam, nisi aliquod ei bonum exoptemus; nec optamus bonum aliquod, nisi eum alicui desideremus. Porro si amor tendat in finem cui, vocatur beneuolentia: si dirigatur in finem cuius gratia, dicitur concupiscentia.
units.tr: This definition of end, which Aristotle gives in Physics 2, chapter 3, is accepted by everyone: An end is that for the sake of which the other things are. The matter is clear in itself. The division, however, branches out into many parts. First, it divides into the end for whom (cui) and the end of which (cuius). The end for whom is the being which exists before love and desire, the being for which good is wished. The end of which is that good itself, the acquisition of which we work for. These two ends cannot be separated from one another: we cannot truly wish well to anyone unless we wish some good for him, nor do we wish any good unless we desire it for someone. Further, if love tends to the end for whom, it is called benevolence; if it is directed to the end for the sake of which, it is called concupiscence.

units.la: Diuiditur 2. finis in formale,& Obiectiuum. Finis obiectiuus, qui etiam dicitur finis qui, est illud obiectum, quod exoptamus. Formalis, qui vocatur etiam finis quo, est ipsa possessio, vel vnio cum bono amato. V. g. Finis noster supernaturalis obiectiuus est Deus: Formalis autem ipsa possessio Dei, seu clara ipsius visio, vt putat D. Thomas; vel amor eiusdem, vt Scotus. Porrò hi duo fines vnu constituunt finem totalem, & sic finis noster supernaturalis totalis est Deus, vt clarè visus.
units.tr: Second, the end is divided into the formal and the objective. The objective end, which is also called the end by which (finis qui), is the object we desire. The formal end, also called the end in which (finis quo), is the possession itself, or the union with the good that is loved. For example, our supernatural end objectively is God; formally, it is the possession of God, or his clear vision, as St. Thomas thinks, or the love of him, as Scotus thinks. These two together make up the whole end, and so our whole supernatural end is God, as clearly seen.

units.la: Diuiditur 3. in finem qui fit, & in finem Qui obtinetur. Finis qui fit, est ille, qui non supponitur existere, sed per actionem agentis constituitur in esse: v.g. sanitas respectu ægroti. Finis qui obtinetur, est ille, qui iam existit, sed tamen nondum possidetur, atq; adeo per actionem operantis non ponitur eius de nouo existentia, sed possessio tantum. Sic numi sunt finis auari, quia licèt existant, eorum tamen possessio in auaro non est.
units.tr: Third, the end is divided into the end that is brought about and the end that is obtained. The end that is brought about is that which is not presupposed to exist, but is set into being by the action of the agent: for example, health with respect to a sick person. The end that is obtained is that which already exists, but is not yet possessed; so through the action of the one working, its existence is not newly posited, only its possession. Thus money is the end of the miser, because although it exists, it is not in the miser's possession.

units.la: Diuiditur 4. in Vltimatum, & non vltimatum, cui etiam similis est, proximus, & remotus. Ille dicitur, in quo vltimo sistit agens, & quæ non ordinat aliò, vt Beatitudo respectu nostri. Secundus est, in quo non quiescit agens, verùm dirigit eundem ad consecutionem alterius. V. g. virtutum acquisitio est finis hominum, sed non vltimatus, quandoquidem ijs vtimur ad beatitudinem. Aliæ supersunt finis diuisiones, at hæ præcipuæ sufficiant.
units.tr: Fourth, the end is divided into the ultimate and the non-ultimate, to which is similar the division into proximate and remote. That is called ultimate in which the agent rests at last and which it does not order to anything else, as blessedness is with respect to us. The second is that in which the agent does not rest, but directs itself to the attainment of something else. For example, the acquisition of virtues is the end of men, but not an ultimate one, since we use them for blessedness. There are other divisions of the end, but these principal ones are sufficient.

units.la: Porrò aduertite ad finis consecutione interuenire plures actus, quorum aliqui spectant ad ordinem intentionis; aliqui ad ordinem executionis. Qui attinent ad intentionem ij sunt, per quos proponitur finis, verùm non producitur, nec acquiritur. V. g. cognoscitur finis, amatur, determinatur, excogitantur media, examinantur, eliguntur. Actus verò, qui spectant ad ordinem executionis, hi sunt; executio mediorum, consecutio finis, delectatio in eodem, &c.
units.tr: Furthermore, observe that several acts intervene in the attainment of an end, some of which belong to the order of intention, others to the order of execution. Those that belong to intention are those by which the end is set before us, but not produced or acquired. For example, the end is known, loved, determined; the means are devised, examined, and chosen. The acts that belong to the order of execution are these: the carrying out of the means, the attainment of the end, delight in it, and so on.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISQUISITIO SECUNDA.

units.la: Quomodo finis causet.
units.tr: How the end causes.

units.la: PRo intelligentia praemitto, quaestionē hanc in multiplici sensu posse intelligi. Primò, quomodo finis causet, nimirum an vt bonus tantùm, an etiam sub ratione mali. Secundo, moueatne bonitas finis prout est intrinseca subiecto, an quatenus cognita. Tertio, an cognitio bonitatis finis sit pura conditio, an virtus verè motiua. Quoad primum notetur
units.tr: By way of preface, I point out that this question can be understood in several senses. First, how the end causes, namely whether it causes only as good, or also under the aspect of evil. Second, whether the goodness of the end moves according as it is intrinsic to the subject, or insofar as it is known. Third, whether the knowledge of the goodness of the end is a mere condition, or a truly motive power. As to the first, let it be noted

units.la: CONCLVSIO PRIMA.
units.tr: FIRST CONCLUSION.

units.la: Finis non causat, seu non mouet vo- luntatem, nisi vt bonus.
units.tr: The end moves the will only as good; it does not cause or move the will except as good.

units.la: PRobatur, quia bonum vt bonum, est formale obiectum voluntatis, quemadmodum verum vt verum, est obiectum intellectus, ergo cùm nulla potentia ferri possit extra suum obiectum, voluntas ferri non poterit, nisi ad bonum. Confirmatur, eò quòd nullus agit ratione praecisa mali, sed aliqua semper ductus ratione boni, siue postea hoc physicum sit, aut morale, seu bonum verum, aut putatum.
units.tr: This is proved because the good, as good, is the formal object of the will, just as the true, as true, is the object of the intellect. Since no power can be carried beyond its object, the will cannot be carried except toward the good. It is confirmed because no one acts from the bare consideration of evil, but is always led by some consideration of good, whether that good is physical or moral, real or merely supposed.

units.la: Opponis. Aliquando tendunt homines in malum, & operantur gratia illius, fiunt enim, occidunt &c. Vlteriùs, optat quis aliquando mori, non esse, damnari, & similia, prout illum desperatio adegerit. rit. Sed hæc omnia sunt mala, nec vllam habent rationem boni, ergo finis non mouet semper vt bonus. Probatur minor, nam esse fundamentum est cuiusque boni, ergo qui desiderat non esse, non mouetur ab vlla ratione boni.
units.tr: You object: sometimes people tend toward evil and act for its sake, as when they kill, steal, and so on. Further, someone sometimes wishes to die, not to exist, or to be damned, and similar things, when despair has driven him to it. But all these things are evil and have no aspect of good, so the end does not always move as good. The minor is proved thus: existence is the foundation of every good, so whoever desires not to exist is moved by no aspect of good.

units.la: Resp. ad primum d. furari, occidere, ac similia sunt malum materialiter, c. formaliter, n. Fur ergo non amat furtum quatenus actio illa est mala; sed quatenus latina est alicuius commodi, ratione cuius formalitatis bona est furanti. Ad secundum pariter dico, quòd non esse materialiter, ac simpliciter est quid malum; sed formaliter bonum, quia proponi potest sub aliqua ratione boni. Ad confirmationem resp. quòd principium totius boni est profectò ipsum esse, verùm quia hoc summis malis circumscribi potest, in tali casu ipsum non esse putatur quid melius, aut minus malum, & quia minus malum habet rationem apparentis boni; qui cupit non esse, mouetur à bono; bono inquam non physico, & positiuo, sed negatiuo, & apparenti; quod satis est ad mouen-dum.
units.tr: I answer to the first point: to steal, to kill, and similar acts are evil materially but not formally. The thief, then, does not love theft insofar as that action is evil, but insofar as it brings some advantage, and by reason of this formality it is good for the thief. To the second I likewise say that not to exist is materially and simply something evil, but formally good, because it can be presented under some aspect of good. To the confirmation I answer that the principle of all good is indeed existence itself. But since existence can be cut off by extreme evils, in such a case non-existence itself is thought to be something better, or a lesser evil. And because the lesser evil has the aspect of an apparent good, one who desires not to exist is moved by a good: I mean not a physical and positive good, but a negative and apparent one. This is enough to move him.

units.la: CONCLVSIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: SECOND CONCLUSION.

units.la: Bonitas finis non mouet voluntatem, prout est intrinseca in obiecto, sed quatenus in intellectu, seu in esse intentionali, & cognitio est.
units.tr: The goodness of the end does not move the will as it is intrinsic in the object, but as it is in the intellect, that is, in intentional being, and is a cognition.

units.la: PRobatur, quia fi bonitas moueret prout est solùm intrinseca in obiecto, sequeretur voluntatem non moueri quoties illa in obiecto non effet: sed hoc est falsum, ergo. Probo minorem. Potest quis rem optare impossibilem, & pro illa operari, v. g. si quis ex ignorantia oret Deum, vt se conuertat in Angelum, quæ res chimærica est,neq; in se bonitatem habet. Rursus potest quis amare v. g. pomum ob eius dulcedinem, quamuis reuera in se tunc amarorem habeat: Sed in hisce casibus non est bonitas in obiecto intrinseca, & nihilominus mouet, ergo.
units.tr: This is proved because, if goodness moved the will only as it is intrinsic to the object, it would follow that the will is not moved whenever that goodness was not in the object. But this is false, therefore the conclusion holds. I prove the minor. Someone may desire an impossible thing and act for it, for example if out of ignorance he prays to God that he may be turned into an angel. That is a chimera, and has no goodness in itself. Again, someone may love an apple, for example, because of its sweetness, although in reality it may then have bitterness. But in these cases the goodness is not intrinsic in the object, and yet it moves. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Probatur etiam secunda pars conclusionis, quia si bonitas non mouet voluntatem quatenus in obiecto manens, ergo quatenus in intellectu. Hinc est quòd in ordine ad motum nihil interest, idem esse bonum, aut apparens bonum. Vnde Arist. in Ethic. Amat, inquit, vnusquisq; non quod bonum est,sed quod appareret: apparentia autem in intellectu est. Ergo.
units.tr: The second part of the conclusion is also proved: if goodness does not move the will as it remains in the object, then it moves it as it is in the intellect. Hence, as regards motion, it makes no difference whether a thing is good or only apparently good. Whence Aristotle in the Ethics says: "Each person loves not what is good, but what appears" [to be good]. But appearance is in the intellect. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Opponis. Bonitas in esse cognito, seu quatenus in intellectu, non est nisi cognitio circa rei bonitatem : sed cognitio vt cognitio non mouet, ergo bonitas non mouet voluntatem, prout in esse cognito est. Minor probatur, nam cognitio est pura conditio, qua posita, bonitas in re formaliter exiſtens mouet, ergo cognitio de se vt cognitio, non mouet; igitur nec bonitas prout cognita.
units.tr: You object: goodness in known being, or as it is in the intellect, is nothing but knowledge of the goodness of the thing. But knowledge, as knowledge, does not move. Therefore goodness does not move the will insofar as it is in known being. The minor is proved: knowledge is a mere condition, and once it is posited, the goodness existing formally in the thing moves. Therefore knowledge, of itself as knowledge, does not move; and so neither does goodness as known.

units.la: Resp. d. minorem. Cognitio vt formaliter cognitio, & sub hac præcisa ratione non mouet, c. cognitio, vt expressio rei non mouet, n. Ad probationem nego, quòd cognitio sit pura conditio, vt infra patebit. Quare cùm infertur, ergo bonitas intrinseca in re mouet, d. mouet quatenus realiter intrinseca, n. quatenus putata intrinseca, & vt sic apprehensa, c. Aduerte igitur, in cognitione duplicem distingui posse formalitatem: prima est actus ipse cognitionis, prout vitalis est: Secunda formalis rei expressio, siue actus idem vt exprimens, & sub hac formalitate cognitio mouet. Vnde non est bonitas realiter inexiſtens rei, quæ moueat; sed bonitas, vt putata in re, vt concepta in re vt apprehensa, quasi foret in re.
units.tr: I answer: I distinguish the minor. Knowledge, as formally knowledge and under this bare aspect, does not move: I concede. Knowledge as the expression of a thing does not move: I deny. As to the proof, I deny that knowledge is a mere condition, as will be made clear below. Therefore, when it is inferred that goodness intrinsic in the thing moves, I distinguish: it moves insofar as it is really intrinsic: I deny; insofar as it is supposed to be intrinsic and is so apprehended: I concede. Note, then, that two formalities can be distinguished in cognition. The first is the act of cognition itself, as it is vital. The second is the formal expression of the thing, or the same act as expressing; and it is under this formality that cognition moves. Hence it is not a goodness really inhering in the thing that moves, but the goodness as supposed in the thing, as conceived in the thing and apprehended, as if it were in the thing itself.

units.la: (*) I CON-
units.tr: (*) I CON-

units.la: CONCLVSIO TERTIA.
units.tr: Third Conclusion

units.la: Cognitio quatenus expressiua non est pura conditio, sed virtus forma- liter, & immediatè mo- tiua finis.
units.tr: Knowledge, insofar as it is expressive, is not a mere condition but formally and immediately a moving force toward the end.

units.la: PRobatur, quia pura conditio non influit in effectum ; sed ea supposita, requiritur causa, quæ agat, moueatq; vt patet v. gr. in approximatione ad ignem; sed cognitio, vt expressiua,talis non est, ergo dici nequit pura conditio . Probo minorem . Posita cognitione sola expressiua, & ablata quacumq; bonitate finis in se, sequitur amor: è contra,posita quauis bonitate in subiecto, & sublata cognitione, non sequitur amor; ergo cognitio, vt expressiua non est pura conditio . Probo antecedens, vt supra . Detur pomum amarum, & proponatur alicui vt dulce; ille mouebitur ad amandum : sed ibi non est dulcor in re, qui moueat; ergo sola cognitio expressiua dulcoris; ergo posita cognitione tantùm, & quauis alia sublata causa, sequitur amor ; unde cognitio exprimens pura conditio non est. Quæro enim, vt præcisa cognitione sic exprimente,assignetur causa mouens: non dulcor in re,quia non est: ergo dulcor in esse cognito:sed hic non distinguitur à cognitione, vt exprimens est;igitur . Probo minorem . Dulcor vt cognitus non est nisi cognitio expressiua dulcoris, adeò vt res exexpressa formaliter intrinseca sit cognitioni, quemadmodum alibi fusè patebit.
units.tr: This is proved as follows. A mere condition does not flow into the effect. Given such a condition, a cause is still required that acts and moves, as is clear, for example, in the case of approaching a fire. But knowledge, as expressive, is not such a cause, so it cannot be called a mere condition. I prove the minor. Suppose expressive knowledge alone is posited and every goodness of the end in itself is removed: love follows. Conversely, suppose some goodness is present in the subject but knowledge is removed: love does not follow. Therefore knowledge, as expressive, is not a mere condition. I prove the antecedent as above. Let a bitter apple be given and presented to someone as sweet. He will be moved to love it, yet there is no sweetness in the thing to move him. Therefore the expressive knowledge of sweetness alone is the cause. So when that knowledge is posited and every other cause is removed, love follows, and knowledge that expresses is not a mere condition. For I ask: with that expressing knowledge considered precisely by itself, what moving cause can be assigned? It is not the sweetness in the thing, because there is none. So it must be the sweetness as it is known. But this is not distinct from the knowledge insofar as it expresses; therefore the conclusion stands. I prove the minor. Sweetness as known is nothing other than the expressive knowledge of sweetness, so that the thing expressed is formally intrinsic to the knowledge, as will be shown at length elsewhere.

units.la: Opponis. Illa est ratio motiua finis, propter quam, & cuius gratia, operatur agens, & qua obtenta quiescit: sed agens non operatur gratia cognitionis, neque in ea quiescit; ergo cognitio non est virtus motiua finis, unde manebit pura conditio. Maior est certa. Minor probatur, quia nemo impendit laborem, vt habeat cognitionem de beatitudine tantùm, sed vt ipsam consequatur beatitudinem; nemo vt cognoscat diuitias, verùm vt eorum possessor euadat.
units.tr: You object: that is the moving reason of the end, for the sake of which and by whose favour the agent acts, and in which, once obtained, it rests. But an agent does not act for the sake of knowledge, nor does it rest in knowledge. Therefore knowledge is not a moving power of the end, and so it will remain a mere condition. The major is certain. The minor is proved: no one undertakes labour to have knowledge of blessedness only, but to attain blessedness itself; no one seeks to know riches, but to become their possessor.

units.la: Resp. d. maiorem. Illa est ratio motiua finis, propter quam operatur agens, motiua vt quod, materialiter, ac terminatiuè, c. motiua vt quo, & formaliter, nego. Sed agens non operatur ob cognitionem, d. tanquam ob id, quod intendit, c. ob id, quo mouetur, n. Igitur cognitio non est virtus motiua finis, vt quod, materialiter, ac terminatiuè, c. vt quo, & formaliter, n. Explico. Dum cognitio exprimit obiectum aliquod vt bonum, certè voluntas mouetur ad amorem boni, quod sit in re, physicum, & reale, neq; cupit bonum intellectum, quatenus intellectum, seu cognitionem de illo, sed bonum entitatiuum in se subsistens; & hoc quia est id, quod amatur, dicitur mouere vt quod, materialiter, ac terminatiuè, nam ad ipsum vltimò terminat amor. Cognitio verò talis boni espressiua, licèt ipsa non sit id, quod amatur, est nihilominus
units.tr: I reply: I distinguish the major. That is the moving reason of the end for which the agent acts, moving as the what (materially and terminatively), I concede; moving as the by-which (formally), I deny. The agent does not act for the sake of knowledge: I distinguish. For the sake of what it intends, I concede; for the sake of that by which it is moved, I deny. Therefore knowledge is not a moving power of the end as the what (materially and terminatively), I concede; as the by-which (formally), I deny. To explain: when knowledge represents some object as good, the will is certainly moved to love that good, which is physical and real and exists in the thing. It does not desire the good as understood, insofar as it is understood, or the knowledge of it, but the good subsisting in itself as a real entity. Because this is what is loved, it is said to move as the what, materially and terminatively, for love finally terminates on it. But the knowledge of such a good, as expressive, although it is not itself what is loved, is nevertheless

units.la: Note: the rest of the page is blank apart from the catchword. minus id, quo voluntas formaliter mouetur, seu formalis ratio mouendi, nam ea posita, sequitur formaliter motio, siue postea bonum à parte rei fit, siue non.
units.tr: nevertheless the thing by which the will is formally moved, that is, the formal reason of moving. For when this is posited, formal motion follows, whether or not the good afterwards becomes actual in reality. [Note: the rest of the page is blank apart from the catchword.]

units.la: Exemplum. Videt quis parietem album: quid mouet visionem actu, & formaliter? certè species impressa, illa enim est id, quo visio fit: paries verò mouetne? distinguo: mouet, seu potius dicitur mouere, vt quod materialiter, ac terminatiuè, quia res est, ad quam vltimò terminat visio, non quæ formaliter moueat. Aliud exemplum. Aduolarunt auiculæ ad Xeusidis vuas: quid immediatè mouit illas? certè vuæ, vt expresse: at expetebantne vuas expressas? nequaquam, sed veras, realesque. Igitur vuæ vt pictæ fuerunt id, quo motæ sunt auiculæ; vuæ autem verè dici possunt id quod. Sic à pari bonum expressum à cognitione mouet vt quo formaliter; bonum verò reale dici potest mouere, vt quod. Vnde cognitio vt exprimens, non est pura conditio, ea enim tantùm posita, siue postea bonum sit à parte rei, siue non, sequitur motio, quem admodum vuæ pictæ satis fuere ad mouendum, etsi nullæ tunc adfuerint reales. Quamobrem si fiant huiusmodi argumenta. Illud mouet, quod appetitur, quod amatur, quod vltimò exquiritur, &c. distinguite, vt quod, materialiter, ac terminatiuè; c. Vt quo, & formaliter, n.
units.tr: An example. Someone sees a white wall. What moves the vision actually and formally? Certainly the impressed species, for that is that by which the seeing happens. But does the wall move it? I distinguish: the wall moves, or rather is said to move, as the what, materially and terminatively, because it is the thing at which the vision finally terminates; it is not what formally moves. Another example. Little birds flew to the grapes of Zeuxis. What immediately moved them? Certainly the grapes, as painted. But did they desire painted grapes? By no means; they desired true and real ones. So the grapes as painted were that by which the birds were moved, whereas the grapes themselves can truly be called that which is moved toward. Likewise, the good expressed by knowledge moves formally, as the by-which, while the real good can be said to move as the what. Hence knowledge, insofar as it expresses, is not a mere condition. When it alone is posited, motion follows whether or not the good is afterwards real in the thing, just as painted grapes were enough to move the birds even though no real grapes were present. Therefore, if arguments of this kind are put: "That moves which is desired, which is loved, which is ultimately sought," etc., distinguish: as the what, materially and terminatively, I concede; as the by-which, formally, I deny.

units.la: DISQVISITIO TERTIA.
units.tr: DISQUISITIO TERTIA.

units.la: De nonnullis, quae sunt circa finem.
units.tr: Concerning some matters that relate to the end.

units.la: PRO maiore intelligentia causae finalis quaeri primò potest, quinam sit illius effectus. Dico breuiter, esse actus omnes, qui ad ordinem spectant intentionis, & executionis. Ratio est, quia omnes hi actus non temerè, casuue fiunt, sed ex ordine ad finem, à quo metaphoricè dicuntur causari, nam idcirco fiunt, quia finis propositus ratio est, cur hi actus effectiue à potentijs producantur.
units.tr: For a greater understanding of the final cause, one may first ask what its effect is. I answer briefly: it is all those acts which belong to the order of intention and execution. The reason is that all these acts do not happen by chance or accident, but from an order toward the end, by which they are said metaphorically to be caused; for they occur for this reason, that the proposed end is the ground on account of which these acts are effectively produced by the powers.

units.la: Potest quaeri 2. quibusnam conueniat agere propter finem. Resp. conuenire solis agentibus intellectu praeditis, Deo, angelis, & hominibus proprie, ac rigorosè. Minùs proprie, nimirum ex quadam propensione naturae ad suum bonum inclinante agunt etiam bruta, quem admodum elephanti, apes, formicae, ac similia, quae ob finem aliquem solerti se industria gerunt. Dixi minùs proprie, non enim operantur ex consilio vnum alteri medium subordinando.
units.tr: Second, one may ask to whom it belongs to act for the sake of an end. I answer: it belongs only to agents endowed with intellect, namely God, the angels, and men, properly and strictly speaking. Less properly, by a certain natural inclination tending toward its own good, brute animals also act, as elephants, bees, ants, and similar creatures, which conduct themselves with clever industry for some end. I say "less properly," for they do not act from deliberation, subordinating one means to another.

units.la: Potest quaeri 3. Vtrum agentia non cognoscitiua, & purè naturalia operentur ex fine. Resp. non agere propter finem ex se, non enim cognoscitiua sunt, verùm prout substant directioni, & ordinationi Primae Causae, seu quatenus à prima Causa in fines proprios aguntur.
