Vnde in natura videmus euenire quod melius est. Ex quo nata sunt illa. Opus naturae, opus intelligentiae: Natura nihil agit frustra: Natura prouidens est, sagax, & c. Quae cum naturae per se sumptae conuenire nequeant, conueniunt illi, qua tenus Diuinae subest directioni. Quod optime indicat S. Thomas exemplo sagittarij sagittam dirigentis ad scopum; tendit enim illa in finem, nonquia sibi eum praefixerit, sed quod a Sagittario illuc destinatur.
units.tr: Third, one may ask whether non-cognitive agents, which are purely natural, act for the sake of an end. I answer that they do not act for an end of themselves, for they are not cognitive; but insofar as they are subject to the direction and ordering of the First Cause, or as they are driven by the First Cause to their proper ends. Hence we see in nature that what is better comes about. From this arose such sayings as: "The work of nature is the work of intelligence"; "Nature does nothing in vain"; "Nature is provident, shrewd," and so on. Since these cannot belong to nature considered in itself, they belong to it insofar as it is subject to Divine direction. St. Thomas indicates this very well by the example of an archer directing an arrow at its mark; for the arrow tends toward the end not because it has set that end for itself, but because it is aimed there by the archer.

units.la: Potest quaeri 4. cur si agentia naturalia operantur ob finem, oriantur multoties monstra, quae sunt praeter naturae intentionem, & finem? Respond. causas prout ad eas attinet, agere semper vno,eodemq;modo,sed ob aliquod impedimentum non posse quandoq; consequi finem, vt etiam de agentibus intellectu praeditis dicendum est. Exinde autem probatur potius, naturam agere ob finem; quia si quoties contingunt monstra,haec praeter naturae intentionem sunt; Ergo natura in agendo habet finem, ad quem tendit.
units.tr: Fourth, one may ask: if natural agents act for the sake of an end, why do monsters often arise, which are beside the intention and end of nature? I answer that, as far as their causes are concerned, they always act in one and the same way, but on account of some hindrance they cannot sometimes attain the end; as must also be said of agents endowed with intellect. Moreover, it is rather proved from this that nature acts for an end; for if monsters arise whenever they occur, they are beside the intention of nature. Therefore nature, in acting, has an end toward which it tends.

units.la: APPENDIX PRIMA.
units.tr: APPENDIX PRIMA.

units.la: De Idea, & Instrumento.
units.tr: On the Idea and the Instrument.

units.la: AGentia, quae ob finem agunt, dicuntur operari ex Idea operis faciendi, quem sibi solet quisque in mente prius conformare, quam in externa materia operetur. Et quia in agendo eam solemus, tanquam exemplar intueri, propterea consueuit idea reduci ad rationem causæ. Causa vero ad operandum instrumentis vtitur suis; & ideo hic breuiter de idea, & instrumento nonnulla subijcio.
units.tr: Agents that act for an end are said to work from the idea of the work to be made, which each person usually first forms in his mind before he works on external matter. And because in acting we usually look to it as a model, the idea is commonly reduced to the category of cause. The efficient cause, however, uses its own instruments in working; so here I add briefly a few things about the idea and the instrument.

units.la: Primo igitur definitur idea, fiue causa exemplaris à Diu. Thoma q. 3. de verit. art. 1. sic. Exemplar est forma, quam imitatur effectus ex intentione agentis, determinantis sibi finem. Quæ definitio sumpta est ex Aug. 20. de Ciuit. cap. 15.
units.tr: First, then, the idea, or exemplary cause, is defined by Divus Thomas, De veritate, q. 3, art. 1, thus: An exemplar is the form which an effect imitates, from the intention of the agent determining its end for itself. This definition is taken from Augustine, City of God, book 20, chapter 15.

units.la: Dicitur forma, quia est imago, ad cuius conformitatem producitur aliquid. 2. quam effectus imitatur, quia prout illa concipitur, sic etiam res elaboratur. 3. ex intentione agentis, nam si casu effectus aliquis conformaretur imagini alicui, hęc dici non posset illius idea; v. g. si quis casu templum extruat simile huic Salutis; hoc nostrum non est idea illius. 4. determinantis sibi finem, vt excludantur agentia non intellectualia, vnde licet forma ignis producentis habeat similitudinem cum igne producto, dici nequit idea, cùm ignis non agat ex fine à se præconcepto & intento. Contra vero architectus v.g. operatur ex idea, quia primò statuit domum estruendam; posteà vel in mente, vel in externa materia idolum, siue imaginem rei faciendæ ponit, operaturq; ad illius exemplar.
units.tr: It is called a form because it is an image, to whose conformity something is produced. (2) The effect imitates it, because as the image is conceived, so the thing is also worked out. (3) It is from the intention of the agent: for if by chance some effect were shaped to some image, this could not be called its idea; for example, if someone by chance builds a temple like this one of Salus, our temple is not its idea. (4) It determines its end for itself, so that non-intellectual agents are excluded. Hence, although the form of the fire that produces it has a likeness to the fire produced, it cannot be called an idea, since fire does not act from an end preconceived and intended by itself. On the contrary, the architect, for example, works from an idea, because he first decides that a house is to be built; afterwards he sets up, either in his mind or in external material, a model or image of the thing to be made, and works to its pattern.

units.la: Quapropter idea duplex est, Interna, &Ex& externa. Prima dicitur illa imago rei faciendæ, quam sibi artifex mente prius fabricat,mox agendo imitatur.Externa est figmentum aliquod extrinsecum sensibili materia conflatum, vt apud artifices intuemur. Circa primam oritur difficultas,quid sit idea mentalis; & in quo consistat.
units.tr: Hence the idea is twofold: internal and external. The first is called the image of the thing to be made, which the craftsman first fashions in his mind and then imitates in working. The external is some figure put together from sensible matter, such as we see among craftsmen. Concerning the first, a difficulty arises: what a mental idea is, and in what it consists.

units.la: Communis explicatio est, quòd mentalis idea sit illud esse obiectiuum rei, siue idolum, quod in ipso actu cognoscendi fit.Vnde à S.Clem. Alex.vocatur Mens Diuina 4.Strom.Regio idearum, quia sibi omnia proponit Deus,& prædicata cuiusque rei essentialia in sua mente habet, priusquam fiant.Et hę sunt ideæ,à quibus volebat Plato, Deum exemplaria sumere in creaturarum productione, Siquidem non parentes, aiebat, fœtum veluti manibus elaborant,sed mens adest Diuina,quæ prout illius rei habet ideam,sic materiam conformat.Sic tritico dum culmum facit, aristas,grana &c.applicat Deus ideam illi debitam. Exinde Seneca ep.66. exemplaria,inquit,rerum omnium Deus intra se habet, numerosque vniuersorum, quæ agenda sunt, & modos mente complexus est.Plenus hic figuris est, quas Plato ideas appellauit, immortales, immutabiles, infatigabiles. At verò hæ figuræ, simulaera hæc, & ideæ sunt ne aliquid à cognitione Diuina distinctum? nequaquam; sed ipsa formalis cognitio repræsentans in se res omnes, eo prorsus modo, & ordine, quo fieri debent, quare id ipsum dequauis idea puto dicendum, quòd à formali cognitione non distinguatur.
units.tr: The common explanation is that the mental idea is the objective being of the thing, or the likeness, which comes to be in the very act of knowing. Hence Clement of Alexandria, Stromata book 4, calls it the Divine Mind, the region of ideas, because God sets before himself all things and has the essential attributes of each thing in his mind before they come to be. And these are the ideas by which Plato wished God to take his exemplars in producing creatures. For, he said, parents do not fashion the offspring with their hands like a thing being shaped, but the Divine Mind is present, and as it has the idea of that thing, so it conforms the matter. Thus when God makes the stalk of the wheat, he applies the ears, grains, etc., to it, the idea due to it. Hence Seneca, letter 66: God, he says, has within himself the exemplars of all things, and has grasped in his mind the numbers of all things that are to be done and their modes. He is full of these figures, which Plato called ideas, immortal, immutable, untiring. But are these figures, likenesses, and ideas something distinct from the Divine knowledge? By no means; rather they are that very formal knowledge, representing all things in the exact manner and order in which they ought to come to be. Therefore I think it must be said of the idea that it is not distinct from formal knowledge.

units.la: Quod attinet ad instrumentum, quo causa indiget ad operandum, eius formalis ratio, & conceptus consistit in hoc, ut illud sit, quo vtitur causa operans, & cui effectus improportionatus est, alioquin si proportionem cum eo haberet, iam esset causa principalis, non instrumentalis. Quod autem inquiunt Thomistæ, instrumentum accipere à causa principali virtutem, qua eleuatur ad effectiue producendum, vidimus iam falsò dici, quia instrumentum quà tale, nec formaliter, nec virtualiter continet effectum causæ principalis. Repetite dicta supra de causa efficiente.
units.tr: As for the instrument, which a cause needs in order to work, its formal character and concept consists in this: that it is that which the operating cause uses, and to which the effect is disproportionate. Otherwise, if it had a proportion to the effect, it would already be a principal cause, not an instrumental one. As for what the Thomists say, that the instrument receives from the principal cause a power by which it is raised to produce the effect, we have already seen that this is wrongly said, because the instrument as such contains the effect of the principal cause neither formally nor virtually. Repeat what was said above about the efficient cause.

units.la: APPENDIX SECVNDA.
units.tr: Second Appendix.

units.la: De Casu, Fortuna, & Fato.
units.tr: On Chance, Fortune, and Fate.

units.la: ETiamsi natura vbique rerum, & locorum operetur ex fine, aut per se, aut per alium intento, nihilominus quædam nomina vindicantur à superstitiosis hominibus, quæ præfixum agendi scopum videntur à causis adimere, quotiescumque naturales effectus dicuntur contingere casu quodam, fortunâ, & fato. Hæc itaque nomina videamus quoniam sensu à Philosophis accipi debeant.
units.tr: Although nature everywhere, in all things and places, acts for an end, either of itself or through something else directed to that end, superstitious people nevertheless claim certain names that seem to strip causes of their fixed aim whenever natural effects are said to happen by some chance, by fortune, or by fate. Let us therefore see in what sense philosophers ought to understand these names.

units.la: Primò igitur Fortuna colebatur apud Ethnicos vt Dea cæca, vaga, inconstans, incerta, humanorum actuum temeraria præses, cui Adriatico in littore Fanum dicauerant Romani, totius orbi religione splendidissimum, à quo & hodie oppidum Italiæ vocatur Fanum in Piceno. De hac Plin. lib. 2. c. 7. Toto, inquit, mundo, & locis omnibus, omnibusq; horis, omnium vocibus Fortuna sola invocatur, vna nominatur, vna accusatur, &c.
units.tr: First, the heathen worshipped Fortune as a blind, wandering, inconstant, uncertain goddess, the rash ruler of human affairs, to whom the Romans dedicated a shrine on the Adriatic shore, the most splendid in the reverence of the whole world. From it a town of Italy, Fanum in Picenum, is still called Fanum today. On this see Pliny, book 2, ch. 7: "Throughout the whole world," he says, "in all places and at all hours, Fortune alone is invoked by the voices of all, alone is named, alone is accused," etc.

units.la: Sed alio sensu viri Docti Fortunam accipiunt. Aliqui enim effectum, qui dicitur inopinatò contingere, vocant fortunam, vt Lactantius l. 3. c. 28. Fortuna est accidentium rerum subitus, atq; inopinatus euentus. Alij nomine Fortunæ intelligunt ipsum diuersarum causarum concursum absq; mutuo consilio factum. V. g. si aliquo terram fodiente, inueniatur thesaurus, circumstantia loci, occultatio thesauri, & effossio dicuntur Fortuna, quia sunt causæ non ex præuio consilio ad hoc ordinatæ.
units.tr: But learned men understand Fortune in another sense. Some call Fortune the effect that is said to happen unexpectedly, as Lactantius does, book 3, ch. 28: Fortune is the sudden and unexpected outcome of accidental things. Others understand by the name of Fortune the very concurrence of different causes, made without mutual counsel. For example, if a treasure is found while someone is digging the ground, the circumstance of the place, the hiding of the treasure, and the digging are called Fortune, because they are causes not ordained to this result by any prior plan.

units.la: Verùm Aristoteles, alijq; Philosophi diuerso adhuc sensu Fortunam sumunt, ab ijs enim sic definitur: Causa per accidens effectuum, qui raro contingunt in agentibus ex intentione. V. g. in allato exemplo; Fossor, quiest causa per accidens inuentionis thesauri, (nam ille sibi præfixerat effossionem tantum) dicitur Fortuna, & inuentio auri fortuita, quia talis inuentio, cum hac effossione, cum hoc loco, cæterisq; circumstantijs necessariò connexa sit, vnde vt sic non est fortuita, nihilominus vocatur talis in ordine ad causam, quæ fossionem eligit. Ex hoc patet sensus dicti Aristotelici 2. Magn. Mor. c. 9. quòd nimirum, Vbi multum est fortuna ibi mens perexigua sit. Ad quæ congruenter in metaphysicis repetit Fortunam esse inimicam artis, & imperitiæ comitem. Quoties enim quis operatur, sed finem ex illo actu futurum nec videt, nec media pro illius consecutione adhibenda tenet, agit vt ignorans, & parum consultus: vnde si per accidens finem obtineat: dicitur ex casu, non ex consilio egisse. Patet igitur cur ibi sit parum iudicij, vbi fortunæ multum, & quare Fortuna curam dicatur habere stultorum:
units.tr: But Aristotle and other philosophers take Fortune in a still different sense, for they define it thus: A cause by accident of effects which rarely happen from agents acting with intention. For example, in the case given: the digger, who is only the accidental cause of the discovery of the treasure (for he had set before himself only the digging), is called Fortune, and the discovery of the gold is called fortuitous. Such a discovery, taken with this digging, this place, and the other circumstances, is necessarily connected, so as such it is not fortuitous; yet it is nevertheless called so in relation to the cause that chose the digging. From this is clear the sense of the Aristotelian saying in the Magna Moralia, book 2, ch. 9, namely that where there is much fortune, there the mind is very small. Agreeing with this, in the Metaphysics he repeats that Fortune is the enemy of art and the companion of inexperience. For whenever someone acts without seeing that the end will follow from that act, and without holding the means to be used for attaining it, he acts as one ignorant and ill-advised. Hence, if he obtains the end by accident, he is said to have acted by chance, not by counsel. It is therefore clear why there is little judgment where there is much fortune, and why Fortune is said to take care of fools.

units.la: Casus autem idipsum est, ac Fortuna: sed cum hac extrinseca differentia, quòd in agentibus intelle&tiuis dicitur Fortuna, in iis, quæ rationem non habent, casus. Vnde res infensatæ, siue irrationales non vocantur fortunatæ. Porrò neq; casus, neque Fortuna locum habet in Deo, qui omnia sapientissimo præuidet consilio, infinita sapientia facit, immensa prouidentia moderatur.
units.tr: Chance (casus) is the same thing as Fortune, but with this extrinsic difference: among intelligent agents it is called Fortune, and among those that lack reason, chance. Hence unreasoning, irrational things are not called fortunate. Moreover, neither chance nor Fortune has any place in God, who foresees all things with most wise counsel, makes them with infinite wisdom, and governs them with immense providence.

units.la: Deniq; Fatum acceptum est ab aliquibus pro necessitate quadam agendi omnino inuincibili, quæ à Deo, siue stellis immissa cogat homines, & inexplicabili tanquam catenâ vinctos trahat ad agendum, adeout illius violentiæ resistere non possint. Quæ stulta opinio inter dogmata Stoicorum, & gentium superstitiones acceptissima, nunc à Religione Christiana tamquam carnifex humanæ libertatis procul exulauit.Neque immeritò, experimur enim liberè nos vti arbitrio nostro, proponere finem vtvr libuerit, media expedire ad ipsum,consequi, omittere, contrarium eligere, quæ omnia nostri iuris non essent, si nos fatû,siue fatalis necessitas cogeret, ac miserè traheret captiuos .
units.tr: Finally, Fate has been taken by some to mean a certain wholly invincible necessity of acting, which, sent by God or by the stars, compels men and drags them along, bound as if by an inexplicable chain, so that they cannot resist its violence. This foolish opinion, most acceptable among the doctrines of the Stoics and the superstitions of the nations, has now been driven far away by the Christian religion as the executioner of human liberty. And not undeservedly. For we experience that we freely use our own will: we propose whatever end we wish, prepare the means to it, attain it, omit it, or choose the contrary. None of this would be within our right if fate, or a fatal necessity, forced us and dragged us about as captives.

units.la: Alio igitur,& sano sensu Doctores Catholici Fatum admittunt,quod S.Thomas 4.doctissimis titulis explicat, 1.p.q.116. vt per otium videri potest . Neque desunt alij, qui eum circumscribant. Exponitur enim à Minutio Felice sic: Quid enim aliud est Fatum, quàm id, quod de vnoquoque nostrum fatus est Deus? dicitur enim fatum à fando, perinde ac illud fit decretum,& effatum Dei. Quare à Lipsio etiam definitur;Sanctio,& veluti vox Diuina mentis: Adhuc tamen communiùs recipitur definitio Fati, quæ traditur à Boetio l.4. de Consol. prosa 6. Fatum est dispositio immobilis inhærens reb.mobilibus , per quam Diuina prouidentia suis quaqua nestit ordinibus.
units.tr: In another, sound sense, the Catholic teachers admit Fate, which St Thomas explains with most learned arguments, 1 p., q. 116, as can be seen at leisure. Nor are there lacking others who define it. Minucius Felix explains it thus: For what else is Fate than that which God has spoken concerning each of us? For Fate is named from speaking, just as it is the decree and utterance of God. Wherefore Lipsius also defines it: A sanction, and as it were the divine voice of the mind. Yet the definition of Fate that is more commonly accepted is the one given by Boethius, book 4 of the Consolation, prose 6: Fate is an immovable disposition inhering in movable things, through which divine providence arranges its own in their several orders.

units.la: Primo itaque vocatur dispositio, idest ordinatio causarum. 2. immobilis, quia certò,& infallibiliter influit ad effectum . 3.Inhærens reb.mobilibus,quia ordinatio illa causarum causas secundas relinquit mobiles, hoc est liberas.4. Per quæ Diuina Prouidentia &c.quia per eam Deus sinnes obtinet suos in rerum creatarum gubernatione. Non ergo Deus
units.tr: First, then, it is called a disposition, that is, an ordering of causes. Second, it is immovable, because it flows into its effect certainly and infallibly. Third, it inheres in movable things, because that ordering of causes leaves secondary causes movable, that is, free. Fourth, it is the means through which divine providence etc., because through it God secures his ends in the governing of created things. Therefore God does not

units.la: Fata quoq;& vitas hominum suspendit ab astris. vt habet Manil. in 3. sed ipse Deus fatum nostrum est, qui ad humanas operationes debitam ordinat seriem causarum. Quomodo autem infallibilis hæc dispositio, quam Diuina Prouidentia nobis accommodat, humanam seruet libertatem, nobisque,siue bonum, siue malum sit quod facimus, relinquat,in sequenti disputatione subiicitur.
units.tr: Manilius, book 3, has: He also suspends the fates and lives of men from the stars. But God himself is our fate, who arranges the due sequence of causes for human actions. How this infallible disposition, which divine providence adapts to us, preserves human liberty and leaves it to us whether what we do is good or evil, is discussed in the following disputation.

units.la: DISPVTATIO QVARTA.
units.tr: Disputation Four.

units.la: De Causa prima, siue Deo.
units.tr: On the First Cause, or God.

units.la: SVppono hic dari causam Primam, cuius existentia 8. Phys. demonstrabitur. Suppono etiam, Causam Primam, siue Deum produxisse Mundum, eiusq; partes, vt constabit ex Genesi. Denique suppono, Deum immediatè influere ad conseruandas creaturas omnes, itaut sine illius concursu implicet, aliquam perseuerare in esse suo. Colligitur id ex scripturis: ad Rom. 11. ex ipso, & per ipsum sunt omnia. Ad Hebr. 1.3. Portans omnia verbo virtutis suæ. Actor. 17.28 Non longè est ab vnoquoque nostrum, in ipso enim viuimus, mouemur, & sumus. Accedit communis omnium PP. consensus. à quo recedere piaculum omnino est. Ratio verò desumitur ex perfectissimo, & essentiali Primæ Causæ dominio in creaturas omnes, de quibus pro libito potest quocumque instanti disponere, illas etiam destruendo, quæ dedestructio per id solum fieret, quòd creaturis deesset concursus à Deo praestitus in conseruando. His positis, fiat.
units.tr: I assume here that there is a First Cause, whose existence will be demonstrated in the eighth book of the Physics. I also assume that the First Cause, or God, produced the world and its parts, as is clear from Genesis. Finally, I assume that God immediately influences all creatures to conserve them, so that without his concurrence it is impossible for any of them to persist in its being. This is gathered from Scripture: Rom. 11: from him, and through him, are all things. Heb. 1.3: upholding all things by the word of his power. Actor. 17.28: For in him we live, and move, and have our being; he is not far from each one of us. To this is added the common agreement of all the Fathers, from which it is utterly sacrilegious to depart. The reason is drawn from the most perfect and essential dominion of the First Cause over all creatures, over whom it can dispose at its pleasure at any moment, even destroying them; and this destruction would come about solely because the creatures lacked the concurrence that God gives in conserving them. With these things laid down, let us proceed.

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.

units.la: An Deus ad actiones causa creata immediatè concurrat.
units.tr: Whether God immediately concurs with created causes in their actions.

units.la: PRo intelligentia iuuat praescire quid opinetur Durandus in 2. sent. dist. 1. q. 5. nimirum naturales causas ab initio mundi habuisse à Deo vim, & facultatem agendi, vt effectus producerent sibi congruentes, ad quos proinde sine Primae causae concursu influerent solae, neque Deus in earum actionibus actu immisceret se. Hanc Durandi opinionem excitare conatus est P. Lodouicus à Dola Capuccinus, & nuperrimè, vt ego vidi, Hallemandetus Paulinus 4. parte suae Philosoph. disput. 4. vbi ex traditta doctrina de non praestito Dei concursu ad actiones creaturarum, explicat facilè, quomodò istae liberae maneant in agendo; & quomodo non sit Deus causa peccati. Quia, inquit, non influit ipse ad Actionem, sed relinquit creaturas, in manibus consilij sui, vt solae operentur.
units.tr: To understand the question, it helps first to know what Durandus holds in his commentary on the Sentences, dist. 1, q. 5: namely, that from the beginning of the world natural causes received from God the power and faculty of acting, so as to produce effects suited to them; that these effects therefore follow from the causes alone, without the concurrence of the First Cause, and that God does not actually intermingle himself in their actions. Father Lodovicus a Dola, the Capuchin, tried to revive this opinion of Durandus, and most recently, as I have seen, Hallemandetus Paulinus in the fourth part of his Philosophical Disputations, disputation 4. There, from the doctrine that God does not concur in the actions of creatures, he explains easily how these remain free in acting, and how God is not the cause of sin. For, he says, God does not flow into the action itself, but leaves creatures in the hands of their own counsel, to work alone.

units.la: Prorsus ex diametro huic sententiae opponitur Auctor Philosoph. Mosaicae, qui supponit, nullum adesse in natura effectum, in quem causae secundae praestent influxum; sed Spiritum Diuinitatis tatis quibusq; rebus intimum, & iuxta illud Genesis 1. Aquis incubantem, omnia in omnibus agere, singula mouere, animare, adeout creaturæ tantummodo sint organa quædam, per quę, & in quibus Dei virtus pro beneplacito suo, Spirituum, Angelo-rum, que ministerijs operetur ad extra. Cui rei videntur occinuisse veterum Philosophorum dicta, quòd Mens Diuina per vniuersum orbem diffusa rerum omnium architecta sola sit, atq; motrix. Unde Virg. in 6.
units.tr: Directly opposed to this opinion is the author of the Mosaic Philosophy, who supposes that there is no effect in nature into which second causes exert any influence. Rather, the Spirit of the Deity is inward to all things and to each thing, and, according to that word of Genesis 1, brooding over the waters, acts in all things and moves and animates each one. Creatures are merely certain instruments, through which and in which the power of God works outwardly at his good pleasure, through the ministries of spirits and angels. To this idea the sayings of the ancient philosophers seem to have harmonised, that the Divine Mind diffused through the whole universe is alone the architect and mover of all things. Hence Virgil, in book 6:

units.la: Spiritus intus alit, totamq: diffusa per artus
units.tr: The spirit within nourishes it, and the mind, poured through all its limbs,

units.la: Mens agitat molem, & magno se corpore miscet.
units.tr: stirs the whole mass and mingles with the great body.

units.la: Dicebant enim, Deum esse animam mundi, quæ rebus naturalibus vteretur ad operandum, sicuti anima corporis membris, potentijsq; sensitiuis. At verò media sententia magis pia, magis Primę, secundisq; causis congrua, magis Christiană Philosophiă digna est. Unde fiat.
units.tr: For they said that God is the soul of the world, which uses natural things for acting, just as the soul uses the members of the body and the sensitive powers. But the middle opinion is more pious, more agreeable to both the First and the secondary causes, and more worthy of Christian philosophy. Hence the following conclusion.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Deus actu influit in actiones, quibus creatura omnes agunt.
units.tr: God acts concurrently in the actions by which every creature acts.

units.la: Probatur prima pars conclusionis auctoritate S.S. P.P. ac Theologorum, qui tam graues, tam docti, tam pij, ac multi sunt, vt vnius concilij vim habere videantur. Eorum aliqui videri possint apud Conimbr. lib. 2. phyf. cap. 7. q. 12. artic. 2. Et vos interim eruditionis gratia memoriæ consignabitis pulcherrima Diu. Auguft. verba ex lib. 5. de Genesi cap. 20. Monet Deus occulta potentia, eoq; motu illa versat, dum Angeli infa perficiunt, dum circumeunt sidera, dum alternant venti, dum abyssus aquarum lapsibus agitatur, dum vireta pullulant, suaque femina euoluunt, dum animalia gignuntur, dum iniqui iustos exercere permittuntur: explicat facula, qua illis cùm primum condita sunt implicita indiderat: qua tamen in suos cursus non explicarentur, fi ea ille, qui condidit, prouido motu administrare cessaret.
units.tr: The first part of the conclusion is proved by the authority of the Holy Scriptures, the Fathers and the theologians, who are so weighty, so learned and so pious, and so numerous, that they seem to carry the force of a whole council. Some of them may be seen in the Conimbricenses, On the Physics, book 2, chapter 7, question 12, article 2. And for the sake of learning, you will also commit to memory the most beautiful words of St. Augustine, from On Genesis, book 5, chapter 20: God moves and governs things by a hidden power, while the angels accomplish what they do, while the stars go round, while the winds alternate, while the depths of the waters are stirred by their falls, while the green things sprout and unfold their seeds, while animals are born, while the wicked are permitted to test the righteous. He unfolds the seeds which, when they were first created, he had implanted in them enfolded; yet they would not unfold into their courses if he who created them ceased to govern them by his providential motion.

units.la: Probatur fecundo ratione, qtia res omnis, & actio creata est ens participatum, ac fluens à primo ente; dependet à Deo maxima, & summà dependentia, qua maior alia excogitari non potest. Ergo causa Prima influit actu ad actiones creaturarum. Probo confeq. Si Deus actu non influeret ad actiones creaturarum, actio exercita penderet magis à creatura, quàm à Deo, quod abfurdiffimum est. Patet sequela, nam effectus pendet magis ab eo, à quo accipit esse, quàm à quo conferuatur; sed actio haberet esse à creatura tantùm, & à Deo conferuatione, ergo penderet magis à creatura, quàm à Deo. Confirmatur, quia conseruatio est continuata rei productio, ergo fi Deus creaturarum actiones conferuat, eas etiam producit.
units.tr: The second proof is by reason. Every created thing and every action is a participated being, flowing from the first being, and depends on God with the greatest and utmost dependence, than which no greater can be imagined. Therefore the First Cause acts concurrently with the actions of creatures. I prove the consequence. If God did not act concurrently with the actions of creatures, the action performed would depend more on the creature than on God, which is most absurd. The sequence is clear: an effect depends more on that from which it receives its being than on that by which it is preserved; but the action would have its being from the creature alone, and its preservation from God; therefore it would depend more on the creature than on God. This is confirmed, because preservation is a continued production of the thing; therefore if God preserves the actions of creatures, he also produces them.

units.la: Probatur 3. Si Deus concursum subtrahat suum, nulla prorsus fit actio creaturæ, igitur si fiat, actu effectiuè Deus concurrit ad illam. Antecedens patet in igne Babylonico, qui dempto Diuino influxu, nil peregit. Consequentia probatur. Deus non concurrit conseruando actionem tantummodò, ergò effectiuè influendo. Probo antecedens,quia si tantum concurreret conseruando, subtracta conseruatione, adhuc fieret actio, etiamsi postea instantaneè periret, quia non_ adesset causa conseruans: fieret inquā eò quòd reperiretur creatura se sola, & sine alterius concursu agens;periret autè,quia profluens actio non haberet causam, à qua conseruaretur; sed tamen actio fieret. Hoc autem absurdum est, quia_ si Deus non concurrat, non solùm_ non conseruatur actio, sed nullo modo fit, ergo vt fiat, Deus actu effectiuè concurret ad illam.
units.tr: It is proved thirdly: if God withdraws his concurrence, no action of the creature occurs at all; therefore, if it occurs, God concurs effectively with it as its cause. The antecedent is clear in the case of the Babylonian fire, which, when the divine influence was removed, accomplished nothing. The consequence is proved thus: God does not concur merely by preserving the action, but by effectively influencing it. I prove the antecedent: if he concurred only by preserving, then, once the preservation were withdrawn, the action would still occur, even if it then perished at once, because no preserving cause would be present. It would occur, I say, because the creature would be found acting alone and without any other's concurrence; but it would perish, because the flowing action would have no cause by which it was preserved. Yet the action would occur. This is absurd, because if God does not concur, the action is not merely not preserved but in no way occurs. Therefore, in order that it occur, God must act concurrently and effectively with it.

units.la: Probatur etiam Secunda pars conclusionis, quòd nimirum etiam creaturæ, actu, & effectiuè agant, secus enim non peccaret homo, sed ipse_ Deus in homine; non mereretur creatura, sed in ea Creator; non trahueretur à Magnete ferrum, sed à Deo in magnete. Imò quodcumque agens nullum haberet limitem in agendo,eò quia in illo virtus infinita operaretur, & sic Venetijs, nec ab igne Vesuuij, nec ab Apuliæ phalangijs tuti essemus.
units.tr: The second part of the conclusion is also proved, namely that creatures too act actually and effectively. Otherwise man would not sin, but God himself would sin in man; the creature would not merit, but the Creator would merit in it; iron would not be drawn by the magnet, but God would draw it in the magnet. Indeed, any agent would have no limit in acting, because an infinite power would be operating in it; and thus we would not be safe at Venice, neither from the fire of Vesuvius nor from the phalanxes of Apulia.

units.la: Obijcies 1. pro sententia Durandi. Si Deus actu influeret ad actiones creaturarum, esset causa peccati; hoc non est dicendum; ergo. Probatur sequela à simili. Creaturæ ideo præcisè imputatur peccatum, quia concurrit ad hanc actionem v. g. furti, homicidij, odij, &c. sed etiam Deus influeret in eadem omnino, ergo & Deus foret causa peccati. Confirmatur quia malitia peccati aut consistit in aliquo positiuo, aut in mera priuatione, vt aliqui dicunt, rectitudinis debitiæ: quidquid sit, sequitur Deum esse causam peccati, ergo. Probatur minor. Si enim peccati malitia est quid positiuū in actu, Deus facit hoc totum positiuum: Si quid priuatiuum, hoc necessariò, & infallibiliter sequitur ad positionem actus, itaut neq; à Deo impediri possit; dato enim actu odij, est impossibile quòd non sequatur priuatio rectitudinis debitæ; igitur qui elicit actum odij, est causa physica huiusce priuationis, atq; adeo peccati.
units.tr: Objection 1, in favour of the opinion of Durandus: if God acted concurrently with the actions of creatures, he would be the cause of sin; this must not be said; therefore. The sequence is proved by a like case. Sin is imputed to the creature precisely because it concurs in this action, for example theft, homicide, hatred, etc.; but God would also concur in exactly the same actions; therefore God too would be the cause of sin. This is confirmed: the malice of sin either consists in something positive, or in a mere privation, as some say, of the due rectitude. Whichever it is, it follows that God is the cause of sin. The minor is proved: if the malice of sin is something positive in the act, God produces this whole positive element; if it is something privative, this necessarily and infallibly follows from the positing of the act, so that it cannot even be prevented by God; for given an act of hatred, it is impossible that the privation of the due rectitude should not follow. Therefore he who elicits an act of hatred is the physical cause of this privation, and so of sin.

units.la: Resp. imprimis cum Becano, & alijs, Deum non esse causam peccati, si pro tali causa intelligatur peccator, siue ille, qui peccat. Deus enim cùm non sit legi subiectus, etiamsi ad actum concurrat malum, peccare tamen non dicitur. Eo modo quo nec habitus acquisitus peccat, licèt ad actus malos concurrat, quia enim subiectus legi non est, ideo neq; tenetur illi, neque parere debet.
units.tr: I reply first, with Becanus and others, that God is not the cause of sin, if by such a cause is understood the sinner, or he who sins. For God, since he is not subject to the law, does not sin even if he concurs with an evil act. He is not said to sin in the way that an acquired habit does not sin, although it concurs with evil acts; for since it is not subject to the law, it is therefore not bound by it, nor ought it to obey.

units.la: Resp. 2. Deum non esse causam, siuè auctorem peccati, quia non concurrit ad actum ex intentione, ut sequatur malitia (quidquid postea illa fit, sive positiuum, sive negatiuum) Deus .n. quantum ex se præbet concursum voluntati creatæ ad omnia indifferenter, & ita præbet, ut semper tamen intendat bonū. Sed quia voluntas praua Diuino concursu abusa se se flectit ad malum, eò etiam quoad actū positiuū descendit Deus, non tamen desiderans, & intendens malum. Vnde inquit Psalmista quòd malitiam Deus odiit. D. Iac. Deum esse malorum intentatorem, &c.
units.tr: Reply 2: God is not the cause or author of sin, because he does not concur with the act with the intention that malice should follow (whatever it afterwards becomes, whether positive or negative). For God, so far as he is concerned, offers his concurrence to the created will indifferently for all things, and so offers it that he always nevertheless intends the good. But because the wicked will, abusing the divine concurrence, bends itself towards evil, God also descends, in respect of the positive act, to that extent, yet not desiring or intending evil. Hence the Psalmist says that God hates wickedness. St. James: that God is a tempter of evil, etc.

units.la: Ex quib. concluditur, Deum non esse causam peccati. Explicari potest à simili de natura particulari, quæ non dicitur causa monstri, licet ad illud concurrat, eò quòd ex se non intendit monstrum. Sic Potentia progressiua non vocatur causa claudicationis, quauis enim ad talem influat motum, de se aliud videlicet rectù intendit. Accipe verba expressa D.Th.1. p.q.49. art. 2. Sicut quidquid est motus in claudicatione causatur à virtute motiua: sed quod est obliquitatis in ea, non est ex virtute motiua, sed ex curuitate cruris; ita in actione mala quidquid est defectus non causatur à Deo, sed à causa secunda deficiente, &c. Resp.3. Deum non esse causam peccati, etiamsi ad actionem concurrat materialem, quia ex officio tenetur præstare concursum creaturæ, ad hoc vt ipsa liberè se determinat ad agendum. Creatura verò est causa peccati, eò quòd non solùm non tenetur sic facere, sed neque debet, nam talis operatio illi prorsus inhibita est.
units.tr: From these things it is concluded that God is not the cause of sin. It can be explained by a likeness from natural particulars, which is not called the cause of a monster, although it concurs with it, because in itself it does not intend the monster. Thus a progressive power is not called the cause of limping, for although it influences such a motion, it in itself intends something else, namely what is right. Take the express words of St. Thomas, Summa 1, part, question 49, article 2: Just as whatever there is of motion in limping is caused by the motive power, but what there is of crookedness in it is not from the motive power but from the curvature of the leg; so in an evil action whatever there is of defect is not caused by God, but by the deficient secondary cause, etc. Reply 3: God is not the cause of sin even if he concurs with the action materially, because he is bound by his office to supply the concurrence to the creature, so that it may determine itself freely to act. But the creature is the cause of sin, because it not only is not bound to act in this way, but ought not to, for such an operation is utterly forbidden to it.

units.la: Obijcies 2. pro secunda sententia. Creaturę si effectiuè concurrerent ad res efficiendas, haberent virtutem infinitam: hoc dici nequit, ergo. Probatur sequela, nam extrahere aliquid ex nihilo arguit virtutem infinitam; unde creatio, quæ rem producit ex nihilo, est opus Dei, non creaturæ: sed si creatura effectiuè produceret aliquid, hoc extraheretur ex nihilo, priùs enim erat nihil; ergo. Confirmatur ex D. Thoma quæst. 3. de malo, art. 2. in corpore, unde; aliqui deducunt necessitatem Diuini cöcursus ad actiones creaturarũ, quia hæ eũ sint virtutis finitæ, nũquã produceret aliquid se solis. Quod etiã acutè prosequitur P. Palauicinus, iam S.R.E. Card. Eminentissimus l. 1. assertionum Theol.
units.tr: Objection 2, in favour of the second opinion: if creatures concurred effectively in producing things, they would have an infinite power; this cannot be said; therefore. The sequence is proved, for to draw something out of nothing argues an infinite power; hence creation, which produces a thing out of nothing, is the work of God, not of the creature; but if the creature effectively produced something, this would be drawn out of nothing, for previously it was nothing; therefore. This is confirmed from St. Thomas, Question 3, On Evil, article 2, in the body, where some deduce the necessity of divine concurrence for the actions of creatures, because these, being of finite power, could never produce anything by themselves alone. Father Palavicino, now the most eminent Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, pursues this acutely in book 1 of his Theological Assertions.

units.la: Respondent communiter negando sequelam, & ad probationem concedunt, quòd producere aliquid ex nihilo sui, & subiecti virtutem arguit infinitam, nonita producere aliquid ex nihilo sui tantùm. Sed hæc responsio non videtur sufficere, vt vidimus l. 1. disp. 2. Quare dici posset, creaturas reuera influere cum Deo ad actiones omnes, & accidentia, quæ cùm produci debeant dependenter à subiecto, non requirunt in causa virtutem infinitam. E contra non influere cum Deo ad producendam substantiam de nouo, quia fortasse nulla iam producatur de nouo, sed à solo Deo fuerint omnes ab initio mundi productæ: vnde omnis actio, quæ modò exercetur, fit vnitiua fubftantiafum non productiua. Sed quidquid fit, manet inconcussum, quod cum creaturis Deus præbet influxum ad actiones earum, & ita quidem, vt Dei, & Creaturæ vnica fit actio indiuisibilis, non enim potest concipi aliquid fluens à creatura, quod essentialiter non pendeat à Deo, summa, & maxima dependentia, & sic quod ab ipso non fiat.
units.tr: They commonly answer by denying the consequence, and concede in reply to the proof that to produce something out of nothing of one's own and of one's subject argues an infinite power, but not to produce something out of nothing of one's own alone. But this reply does not seem sufficient, as we saw in book 1, disputation 2. Hence it could be said that creatures really influence together with God in all actions and accidents, which, since they ought to be produced dependently on a subject, do not require an infinite power in the cause. On the contrary, they do not influence together with God in producing substance anew, because perhaps no substance is now produced anew, but all were produced from the beginning of the world by God alone; whence every action that is now exercised is unitive of substance, not productive. But whatever the case, it remains unshaken that God, together with creatures, supplies influence for their actions, and in such a way that the action of God and of the creature is one indivisible action; for nothing can be conceived as flowing from the creature which does not essentially depend on God with the highest and greatest dependence, and so which is not also made by him.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.

units.la: Vtrum causa Prima subordi- nentur secunda in poten- tia obedientiali.
units.tr: Whether the first cause is subordinated to secondary causes in obediential power.

units.la: PRO intelligentia præmitto quid sit potentia obedientialis. Illa nimirum capacitas quædam est, ratione cuius potest res aliqua in se aliquid recipere, vel operari, non quidem ex naturali sua propensione, sed vt subordinata superiori, cui debet obedire, nec resistere potest. Vg. lapis habet potentiam obedientialem ascendendi, nam ex se quidem petit descensum, nihilominus quia non potest resistere fortiori agenti, est etiam capax motus sursum.
units.tr: Before going further, I set out what obediential power is. It is a certain capacity by virtue of which a thing can receive or do something in itself, not from its natural inclination but because it is subordinate to a superior, to which it must submit and cannot resist. E.g. a stone has the obediential power of rising, for by its own nature it tends downward, yet because it cannot resist a stronger agent, it is also capable of being moved upward.

units.la: Proinde creaturæ non solùm subordinantur Deo per hoc, quòd sine ipso nihil possunt facere, sed etiam quia ipso iubente sæpissimè plura efficiunt contra, & supra suæ naturæ inclinationem, & ideo potentia hæc vocatur obedientialis.
units.tr: Accordingly, creatures are subordinated to God not only because they can do nothing without him, but also because, when he commands, they very often produce many effects contrary to and beyond the inclination of their nature. For this reason the power is called obediential.

units.la: Hinc Sap. 15. vbi referuntur mirabilia quædam facta in creaturis,additur. Creatura n. tibi Factori suo deseruiens ardescit in tormentum aduersus iniustos, & lenior fit ad benefaciendum pro his, qui in te confidunt. Accedit D. Aug. l. 9. de Gen. ad lit. c. 17. vbi asserit, supra cursum, & virtutem naturæ Deum habere potestatē agendi multa de rebus, vt scilicet steriles in senectute pariat; lignum aridum sine terra, & aqua repente floreat, & & fructum gignat. Demum est insignis auctoriras D. Thomæ q. 6. de pot. art. 2. ad 2. vbi hec habet: Vnde nihil prohibet, quin natura creata sit in potentia ad aliqua facienda per D. potentiam, qua inferior potentia facere non potest, & ista vocatur potentia obedientialis; secundum quam qualibet creatura obedit Creatori.
units.tr: Hence Sap. 15, where certain wonders wrought in creatures are recounted, adds: For the creature, serving you its Maker, grows fierce as a torment against the unjust, and becomes gentler to do good for those who trust in you. Augustine also agrees, De Gen. ad lit. 9, c. 17, where he asserts that God, above the course and power of nature, has the power of doing many things with things, namely to make the barren bear in old age; a dry stick without earth and water to flower suddenly and bear fruit. Finally, there is the notable authority of Thomas, q. 6 de pot. art. 2 ad 2, where he holds: Hence nothing prevents a created nature from being in potency to certain things to be done by divine power, which an inferior power cannot do; and this is called obediential power, according to which every creature obeys its Creator.

units.la: Quemadmodum vero potentia naturalis duplex est; Actiua ad agendum, & Passiua ad recipiendum; sic pariter potentia obedientialis omnino duplex: Actiua, qua res eleuatur ad agendum aliquid supra suas vires, quemadmodum intellectus Beati physice producit visionem beatificam; voluntas amorem; & potentiæ vitales in viatoribus producunt actus fidei, spei, & charitatis christianæ, qui sunt entitatiuè supernaturales. Passiua potentia est, qua res eleuatur ad recipiendum aliquid in se; quod omnino excedit naturalem ipsius facultatem. Sic anima recipit gratiam, & habitus quoscumq; supernaturales infusos.
units.tr: Just as natural power is twofold, active for acting and passive for receiving, so obediential power is likewise wholly twofold: active, by which a thing is raised to do something beyond its own powers, as the intellect of the blessed physically produces the beatific vision, and the will produces love; and the vital powers in wayfarers produce the acts of Christian faith, hope and charity, which are supernatural in their being. Passive power is that by which a thing is raised to receive something in itself that wholly exceeds its natural faculty. Thus the soul receives grace and all supernatural habits infused into it.

units.la: Posita doctrina, quæritur, an in omni creatura detur hæc obedientialis potentia præsertim actiua in ordine ad quoslibet effectus, qui specialiter non repugnant. V.g. in igne potentia producendi aquam; in aqua potentia efficiendi gratiam, in musca potentia gignendi Angelum, &c. Pro solutione sit.
units.tr: With this doctrine laid down, the question is whether this obediential power is found in every creature, especially active power in relation to any effects whatever that are not specifically contradictory. E.g. in fire, the power of producing water; in water, the power of effecting grace; in a fly, the power of begetting an angel, etc. For the solution, let the following be said.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLVSIO.

units.la: Datur in omni creatura obedientialis potentia tum passiua, tum actiua pro quauis forma, & operatione licet indebita, & naturaliter improportionata: dummodo non adsit specialis implicantia.
units.tr: In every creature there is obediential power, both passive and active, for any form and operation, although unowed and naturally disproportionate, provided no special contradiction is present.

units.la: POstrema verba in conclusione ponuntur ad excludendos effectus, qui à creatura neque per Dei elevationem fieri possunt. V.g. nihil potest elevari à Deo, vt primo se ipsum producat; deberet .n. existere antequam esset. Nihil potest elevari, vt albedinem constituat albam, quia talis de se formaliter, & essentialiter est.
units.tr: The final words of the conclusion are added to exclude effects which a creature cannot produce even by God's elevation. E.g. nothing can be elevated by God so as to produce itself first; for it would have to exist before it existed. Nothing can be elevated so as to make whiteness white, because it is what it is formally and essentially.

units.la: Probatur ergo quoad effectus, qui non dicunt in se repugnantiam. Primò auctoritate D. Aug. D. Thomæ aliorumq; P. P. Secundo ratione, quia si Deus potest se solo producere angelum, cur non poterit cum musca simul? Tertiò quia sic magis elucet Diuina virtus, dum omni creaturâ etiam vilissimâ vti potest ad mirabiles effectus. Vnde sicuti cederet in laudem pictoris, dum quouis baculo arrepto delineare posset formam quamque pulcherrimam, etsi abiectum, ineptumq; instrumentum foret; sic, &c.
units.tr: It is therefore proved for effects which do not imply contradiction in themselves. First, by the authority of Augustine, Thomas and the other Fathers. Second, by reason: if God can produce an angel by himself alone, why could he not do so together with a fly? Third, because the divine power shines forth more clearly when it can use every creature, even the most worthless, for wonderful effects. Hence, just as it would redound to the praise of a painter if, seizing any stick, he could draw the most beautiful form, even though the instrument were base and unfit, so, etc.

units.la: Probatur 2. Si enim non datur in omni creatura obedientialis potentia pro quolibet effectu, maximè quia creatura improportionem habet ad illos: at hæc ratio nulla est, ergo. Probo minorem, quia nec anima proportionem habet vllam, neque aptitudinem naturalem, vt recipiat gratiam, & habitus, qui sunt Supernaturales; attamen per potentiam obedientialem eos recipit. Quare in exemplo de potentia obedientiali passiua, retorqueri possunt argumenta omnia, quæ faciunt aduersarij contra potentiam actiuam.
units.tr: It is proved secondly. For if obediential power for any effect is not given in every creature, it is chiefly because the creature has no proportion to those effects; but this reason is null; therefore. I prove the minor: the soul has no proportion at all, nor any natural aptitude, to receive grace and habits, which are supernatural; yet through obediential power it receives them. Therefore, in the example of passive obediential power, all the arguments which the opponents bring against active power can be turned back.

units.la: Obijcies 1. Si quævis creatura elevari posset ad quodlibet, illa esset infinitæ virtutis: hoc repugnat: ergo. Sequela patet, nam valeret ad producendos infinitos efsectus etiam specie diuersos.
units.tr: You will object first: if any creature could be elevated to anything whatever, it would be of infinite power; this is impossible; therefore. The consequence is clear, for it would be able to produce infinite effects, even of diverse species.

units.la: Respond. n. maiorem, quia creatura maneret semper instrumentum, & esset causa remota, incompleta, quæ nunquam dici potest infinitæ virtutis, per hoc quòd infinitos effectus etiam specie differentes producat. Patet enim quòd intellectus etsi virtutis limitatæ, ad infinitas tamen intellectiones potest à speciebus determinari. Multò magis ergo ad effectus etiam specie infinitos valebit creatura, si elevetur.
units.tr: I reply by denying the major, for the creature would always remain an instrument and would be a remote, incomplete cause, which can never be called of infinite power merely because it produces infinite effects, even of differing species. For it is clear that the intellect, though of limited power, can be determined by species to infinite acts of understanding. Much more, then, will a creature, if elevated, be able to produce effects that are infinite even in species.

units.la: Obijcies 2. Aqua v. g. quantumuis eleuata nunquam potest gratiæ proportionari; ergo ad eam producendam eleuari nequit. Probatur antecedens. Eleuatio non immutat ab intrinseco entitatem aquæ, vnde si ante non erat proportionata, nec postea erit. Antecedens notum est;eleuatio enim non ponit aliquid intrinsecum rei, sed merè se adiungit extrinsecè.
units.tr: You will object secondly: water, for example, however elevated, can never be made proportionate to grace; therefore it cannot be elevated to produce it. The antecedent is proved: elevation does not change the entity of water intrinsically, so if it was not proportionate before, it will not be afterwards. The antecedent is known, for elevation does not posit anything intrinsic to the thing, but merely adjoins itself extrinsically.

units.la: Resp. n. antecedés,reddítur enim aqua proportionata gratiæ per extrinsecam eleuationem;sicut intellectus ad visionem; potentia naturalis ad actus fidei,spei, &c. Ad probationé c. quòd eleuatio non immutat ab intrinseco rem, sed neq; hoc requiritur,sufficit.n. si adsit extrinseca eleuatio, vt aqua cōplete valeat producere gratiā. Itá neq;influxus Dei cū causis naturalibus affert ijs aliquid intrinsecum, etsi eas faciat cōpletè potentes ad efficiendum. Ratio autem est, quia esse aliquid potens duo dicit, vnum intrinsecú, nēpe causæ ipsius entitaté; aliud extrinsecú,videlicet eleuationé, siue aliā concausam.
units.tr: I deny the antecedent, for water is rendered proportionate to grace through extrinsic elevation, just as the intellect is to vision, and natural power to acts of faith, hope, etc. As to the proof, I grant that elevation does not change the thing intrinsically; but this is not required, for it suffices that extrinsic elevation be present for water to be fully capable of producing grace. Thus God's influence with natural causes does not bring anything intrinsic to them, even though it makes them fully able to effect. The reason is that to be able to do something signifies two things: one intrinsic, namely the entity of the cause itself; the other extrinsic, namely elevation, or another concause.

units.la: Obijcies 3. ex Conincko. Ex hac sententia sequitur, posse brutū eleuari ad intelligendum; oculum ad audiendū ; auré ad videndū, &c. quamuis .n. hæc nó sint subiecta naturaliter ad hoc apta., supernaturaliter tamen reddi talia possunt.Hoc autem dici nequit, ergo.
units.tr: You will object thirdly, from Coninck: on this view it follows that a brute beast could be elevated to understand, the eye to hear, the ear to see, etc. For although these are not naturally fitted for this, they can be made such supernaturally. But this cannot be said; therefore.

units.la: Resp. n.sequelā.Et ratio est,quia dátur nonnullæ actiones,quę pendent essétialiter à tali subiecto,&organo,adeout si hoc desit,nec actiones illæ produci per vllam potentiam queant. Sic visio ita fit per organum oculare, vt vbi hoc non fuerit, ea elici nequeat: sic auditio, &c. Verùm aliæ sunt actiones, quæ à causis non pendent essentialiter, neque de se necessario exigunt hanc potius, quàm aliam. Ita calor sic producitur ab igne, vt idem numero produci potuerit à sole, à silice percusso, &c. Ad eos igitur effectus,qui vt fiant, neq; hoc subiectum, neque hoc organum essentialiter exigùt, omnis causa eleuari potest. Vnde patet ad argumentum disparitas. &c.
units.tr: I deny the consequence. The reason is that there are some actions which depend essentially on such a subject and organ, so that if this is absent, those actions cannot be produced by any power. Thus sight is effected through the organ of the eye in such a way that, where this is lacking, it cannot be elicited; likewise hearing, etc. But there are other actions which do not depend essentially on their causes, nor of their nature necessarily require this rather than that. Thus heat is produced by fire in such a way that the same heat, numerically one, could have been produced by the sun, by struck flint, etc. Therefore, for those effects which, in order to come about, do not essentially require this subject or this organ, any cause can be elevated. Hence the disparity in the argument is clear, etc.

units.la: Obijcies 4. Nulla est proportio v. g. inter muscam, & Angelum, ergo illa nequit eleuari ad hunc producendum. Antecedens per inductionem patet consideranti.
units.tr: You will object fourthly: there is no proportion, for example, between a fly and an angel; therefore the fly cannot be elevated to produce one. The antecedent is clear by induction to anyone who considers it.

units.la: Respond. d. nulla est proportio remota, siue vt aiunt inchoata,n. proxima, & completa, c.Quocirca etiamsi musca non proportionetur Angelo quoad omnia praedicata,spiritualis,intellectiui &c.nihilominus adest proportio aliqua remota, & inchoata, Musca enim est ens, est substantia, est viuens, &c. vnde si habeat eleuationem, vt sic in sensu composito fit proximè,atque completè proportiona-ra.
units.tr: I reply: there is no proximate proportion, but there is a remote, or, as they say, inchoate proportion; not proximate and complete. Therefore, even if the fly is not proportionate to the angel in respect of all predicates, spiritual, intellective, etc., nevertheless some remote and inchoate proportion is present. For a fly is a being, is a substance, is living, etc. Hence, if it has elevation, it becomes proximately and completely proportionate in the composite sense.

units.la: DISQVISITIO TERTIA.
units.tr: DISQUISITIO TERTIA.

units.la: Vtrum creatura eleuari etiam possit ad creandum.
units.tr: Whether a creature can also be raised up to create.

units.la: PRo intelligentia praemoneo, quid sit creatio. Aduertite, duplicem agendi modum solere attribui Deo. Alter dicitur ad intra, & est ille inexplicabilis processionum. Alter vocatur ad extra, ille nimirum quo Deus producit creaturas. De primo Theologi: de secundo hic breuiter.
units.tr: Before proceeding to the matter, I first explain what creation is. Note that God is usually ascribed a twofold mode of acting. The first is called ad intra, and it is that inexplicable procession of the divine persons. The second is called ad extra, namely that by which God produces creatures. The theologians treat of the first; here I shall deal briefly with the second.

units.la: Propria igitur Dei actio ad extra est creatio, seu productio rei ex nihilo subiecti (vt aiunt) seu ex nullo praesuppposito subiecto; & id nulli creaturae naturaliter conuenire potest, nam ea semper cum dependentia a subiecto agit.
units.tr: The proper action of God ad extra, therefore, is creation, or the production of a thing out of nothing of a subject (as they say), or out of no presupposed subject. This can naturally belong to no creature, for a creature always acts with dependence on a subject.

units.la: Distinguitur autem creatio a causa agente scilicet Deo, fuit enim ab aeterno Deus absq; creatione vlla. Distinguitur etiam a termino, licet nu res, quae creatur essentialiter, qualis est actio ipsa creatiua, non distinguatur a creatione sui; tamen alij effectus, qui essentialiter non creantur, fiunt per actionem distinctam, vt de angelis, de animalibus, &c. probabile manet.
units.tr: Creation is distinguished from its efficient cause, namely God, for God existed from eternity without any creation. It is also distinguished from its term: although the thing that is created essentially, such as the creative action itself, is not distinguished from its own creation, nevertheless other effects, which are not created essentially, come about through a distinct action, as is probably the case with the angels, with animals, and so on.

units.la: Recipitur actio creatiua in termino creato, non tanquam in subiecto, aliquin terminus intelligi deberet existens, priusquam produceretur; sed tanquam in re terminante; vnde sic explicatur Quòd non inhæreat, sed tantùm adhæreat rei creatæ, seu terminet ad illam, sicuti de vnione in ordine ad animam dicunt.
units.tr: The creative action is received in the created term, not as in a subject (otherwise the term would have to be understood as existing before it was produced), but as in a terminating thing. Hence it is explained that it does not inhere in the created thing but merely adheres to it, or terminates at it, just as they say of the union in relation to the soul.

units.la: Quæres hic quid possit à Deo creari? Resp. substantias omnes, & accidentia realia, vt patet in Sacramento Eucharistiæ, vbi quantitas, albedo, frigus, calor, &c. conseruantur sine subiecto, & sic primo creari possunt. Accidentia verò modalia puto non posse creari. V. g. curuitas, sessio, &c. fieri non possunt sine virga curua, sine corpore sedente, &c. Ratio est, quia modi essentialiter pendêt à subiecto; ergo produci nequeunt, nisi eidem affixi, ergo non creantur.
units.tr: Here you will ask what can be created by God. I answer: all substances and real accidents, as is clear in the sacrament of the Eucharist, where quantity, whiteness, cold, heat and so on are preserved without a subject; and so these can be created first of all. But I think modal accidents cannot be created: for example, curvedness, sitting and the like cannot come about without a curved rod or a sitting body. The reason is that modes essentially depend on a subject; therefore they cannot be produced unless they are affixed to that subject, and so they are not created.

units.la: Quæres 2. an creatura per Dei potentiam eleuari ad creandum possit? Pro solutione sit.
units.tr: You will ask, second, whether a creature can be raised by the power of God to create. For the solution, let it be said as follows.

units.la: CONCLUSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Creatura vt instrumentum Dei eleuari potest ad creandum.
units.tr: A creature, as an instrument of God, can be raised up to create.

units.la: PRobatur facilè conclusio, quia in hac re nulla videtur esse repugnantia, ergo potest. Antecedens patebit ex argumentorum solutionibus, quæ ad exercendum ingenia vrgeri solent.
units.tr: The conclusion is easily proved, because in this matter there seems to be no contradiction; therefore it is possible. The antecedent will be clear from the solutions of the arguments that are usually urged to exercise the wits.

units.la: APPENDIX
units.tr: APPENDIX

units.la: De Natura, & Arte.
units.tr: On Nature and Art.

units.la: TRia sunt, quæ in hoc ordine rerum vim habent operatiuam, Deus, Natura, & Ars, quæ sicuti diuersa inter se manét, sic diuersis omnino modis agunt. Deus enim facit rem ex nihilo sui, & subiecti, quia non indiget præiacente materia, & sic dicitur creare. Natura gignit formam ex nihilo sui, sed præsupponit materiam,& dicitur producere. Ars verò & materiam, & formam præiacentem habet, in eamque figuram tantummodò, seu varias partium dispositiones inducit, & sic dicitur facere, aut fingere.
units.tr: There are three things that have operative power over things: God, Nature, and Art. Although they remain distinct from one another, they act in entirely different ways. God makes a thing out of nothing, both of his own substance and without any underlying subject, because he needs no pre-existing matter; and so he is said to create. Nature begets a form out of nothing of its own, but it presupposes matter, and so it is said to produce. Art, however, has both matter and a pre-existing form, and it only brings a figure, or various arrangements of parts, into that matter; and so it is said to make or to fashion.

units.la: Verùm hæc doctrina, quæ dudum communis fuit, nön omnibus hoc tépore arridet. Nā si natura producit formā ex nihilo sui, nempe substantiā de nouo, quæ priùs non erat, quomodo nō creat? Dicis, quia operatur in materia. Sed hoc nil videtur afferre nisi verba, si res bene pédatur. Imprimis enim ea materia nihil de suo dat, unde cum dicitur: materia sustinet formam, influit in illam, &c. hoc tantùm sonat quòd materia recipit formam, & vnitur cum illa; vnio autem non tollit creationem, vt patet in anima rationali vnita corpori. Deinde quantumuis præiaceat materia, in ea nil præiacer substantiæ, quę de nouo producitur, ergo ista creatur. Vnde vt virtus Dei magis eluceat in operando, quæcumq; productio substantiæ de nouo à natura tollenda, soliqúe Deo concedenda esse videtur.
units.tr: Yet this doctrine, which was long common, does not please everyone at present. For if nature produces a form out of nothing of its own, namely a substance anew which previously did not exist, why does it not create? You say that it works on matter. But this seems to add nothing except words, if the matter is weighed carefully. First, that matter contributes nothing of its own; so when it is said that matter sustains the form, flows into it, and so on, this means only that matter receives the form and is united with it. Yet union does not remove creation, as is plain in the rational soul united to the body. Next, however much matter may pre-exist, nothing of the substance that is produced anew pre-exists in it; therefore that substance is created. Hence, so that the power of God may shine more clearly in his working, it seems that every production of substance anew must be taken away from nature and granted to God alone.

units.la: Porro hanc opinionem conantur defendere Democritei argumentis, quæ potissimum ex arte sumuntur. Nam si ars, inquiunt, efficit opera naturæ, non producendo substantias de nouo; sed eas, quę iam sunt diuersimodè vniendo, subigendo, compingendo, cur hoc ipsum de natura dici non poterit? Maximè quia productio substantiæ de nouo difficilis est, neq; vtplurimum causam habet. Proinde in re, quæ non leuis momenti est, operæ pretium duxi paululum immorari, nam si hoc de arte constiterit, non exiguum puto accessurum Philosophiæ lumen, quo naturales effectus intro magis rimetur.
units.tr: Moreover, the Democritean adherents try to defend this opinion with arguments drawn chiefly from art. For if art, they say, produces the works of nature not by producing substances anew, but by joining, shaping, and compacting those that already exist in various ways, why could this same thing not be said of nature? Especially since the production of a substance anew is difficult and for the most part has no cause. Therefore, since this is a matter of no small weight, I thought it worth the effort to linger on it a little; for if this is settled concerning art, I think no small light will be added to philosophy, by which it may penetrate more deeply into natural effects.

units.la: Consultò igitur huic secundo libro appendicem attexo de natura, & arte, vt cum patuerit in quibus conueniant, in quibus differant, earum quoque modus operandi, & quod vtraque valeat efficere, magis deprehendatur. Sit ergo.
units.tr: Accordingly, I have deliberately appended to this second book an appendix on nature and art, so that once it has become clear in what respects they agree and in what they differ, their modes of operating, and what each is able to effect, may be better understood. So be it.

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: FIRST DISPUTATION.

units.la: Quid sit natura, & an diffe- rat ab arte.
units.tr: What nature is, and whether it differs from art.

units.la: PRO intelligentia varios præmitto significandi modos, quibus accipi solet Natura. Imprimis enim assumitur pro Deo, quem barbarè vocant Natura naturante. 2. pro quouis principio creato, seu creatura, quæ item barbarè vocatur Natura naturata 3. pro essentia rerum, & sic dicimus, per definitionem explicari naturam rei, 4. pro collectione causarum omnium secundarum, in quo sensu dicitur miraculum superare vires naturæ. 5. pro collectione causarum omnium comprehendendo & Deum, prout est causa naturalis; & ita dicimus, naturam nil frustra moliri. 6. pro temperamento, propensione, indole: quo pacto dicitur quis habere hanc, illamq; naturam. Similiter hoc nomen Naturale diuersimodè assumi potest vt alibi dicetur.
units.tr: To prepare the reader's understanding, I first set out the various senses in which the word Nature is commonly taken. First, it is taken for God, whom the scholastics barbarously call natura naturans. Second, for any created principle or creature, which is likewise barbarously called natura naturata. Third, for the essence of things, and so we say that the nature of a thing is explained by its definition. Fourth, for the totality of all secondary causes; in this sense we say that a miracle surpasses the powers of nature. Fifth, for the totality of all causes, including God insofar as he is a natural cause; and so we say that nature does nothing in vain. Sixth, for temperament, inclination, or disposition; in this way we say that someone has this or that nature. Similarly, the adjective naturale can be used in several ways, as will be said elsewhere.

units.la: His præmissis accipi solet à philosophis natura pro quauis causa secunda, in quo sensu definitur ab Aristotele 2. phys. t. 3. sic: Natura est principium, & causa movendi, & quiescendi in eo, in quo est, primò, ac per se, & non secundum accidens.
units.tr: With these things set out, philosophers commonly take nature for any secondary cause, and in this sense Aristotle defines it in Physics 2, text 3, as follows: Nature is the principle and cause of motion and of rest in that in which it is, primarily and in itself, and not according to accident.

units.la: Dicitur principium loco generis. Deinde causa, non enim est quodcumque principium, sed causa vere influens. 3. mouendi, & quiescendi, seu motus, & quietis (per motum verò intelligitur omnis mutatio, seu alteratio; per quietem duratio in forma, quæ per alterationem acquiritur) 4. in eo, in quo est, quia natura debet esse principium intrinsecum rei, vbi fit motus, aut alteratio, & quies. 5. dicitur primum, eò quòd non dependet ab alio principio, sed ipsa suarum operationum prima radix manet. 6. per se, vt excludantur danitur causæ per accidens, qua de causa medicina in medico fe fanâte nõ est natura, nam quòd medicâ exerceat ille, qui fa. nitatē acquirit, per accidenseft; poterat .n. conualescere, quâuis medicus non fuisset.
units.tr: The word "principle" is put in the place of the genus. Next comes "cause", for not every principle is a cause, but one that truly influences the thing. "Of motion and of rest" (by motion is meant every change or alteration; by rest, the persistence in a form that has been acquired by alteration). "In that in which it is": because nature must be the intrinsic principle of the thing in which the motion, alteration, or rest occurs. "Primarily": because it does not depend on another principle, but remains the first root of its own operations. "In itself", so as to exclude accidental causes. For this reason, the healing of a physician who is himself made well is not nature; for the fact that the one who regains his health practises medicine is accidental, since he could have recovered even if he had not been a physician.

units.la: Hinc sequitur, materiam esse naturam, illa .n. est principium cuiusque actionis, aut motus passiuè saltem. 2. forma etiam natura est, & quidem nobiliòr, cũ fit radix actiua operandi. Compositum quoque natura, constat enim ex partibus, quæ singulæ natura sunt. 3. & cælum dici debet natura, nam fiue à fe, fiue ab intelligentia moueatur, intrinsecum habet principium fui motus exigitiuè saltem, neq; obstat, quòd cælum non quiescit, natura enim est principium fe mouēdi, & quiefcendi, non vnitim, verùm disiunctim, scilicet principiū motus, cū hic adest; principium quietis, cū hæc aderit. 4. Anima rationalis rigorosè natura est, vt pote forma corporis, & radix agendi. E contra forma, quæ assistens dicitur, puta intelligentia respectu cæli, fiue dæmõ respectu obsessi non est natura, manet enim principium extrinsecum, non intrinsecum, quia non habet physicam ad corpus vnionem.
units.tr: From this it follows, first, that matter is nature, for matter is the principle of every action or motion, at least passively. Second, form is also nature, and indeed a nobler one, since it is the active root of operating. The composite too is nature, for it consists of parts, each of which is a nature. Third, the heavens ought to be called nature, for whether they are moved by themselves or by an intelligence, they have within themselves a principle of their motion, at least in potency; nor does it count against this that the heavens do not come to rest, for nature is the principle of moving and of resting, not in a single respect but disjunctively: the principle of motion when motion is present, the principle of rest when rest will be present. Fourth, the rational soul is strictly speaking nature, as being the form of the body and the root of acting. On the other hand, a form that is said to be assisting, such as an intelligence with respect to the heavens, or a demon with respect to a possessed person, is not nature, for it remains an extrinsic principle, not an intrinsic one, since it has no physical union with the body.

units.la: Quod facit pro fecundo quæstionis puncto, Natura, & Ars partim cõueniunt; partim differunt. Conueniunt primò in hoc, quòd vtraq; operatur ad finem. 2. quòd agit successiuè. 3. quòd supponit aliquid rei faciendæ; natura materia, vt aiùt: ars cõpositū. 4. quòd certos in operâdo terminos habet. Dicitur autè differre, primò quia natura veros habet effectus, & ars fere omnes fictos. 2. quia natura, vt agat nō supponit artē: ars verò natură. 3. quia natura est circa intrinseca, & ars vt plurimum in externa superficie occupatur. 4. quia effectus naturæ alium quoque producit sibi similem, vt canis canem; leo leonem; artis autem non ita. Demum quia natura perfectiori modo partes vnit coponendo; non sic ars.
units.tr: As for the second point of the question: nature and art partly agree and partly differ. They agree, first, in that both operate for an end; second, that both act successively; third, that both presuppose something from which the thing is to be made (nature, matter, as they say; art, a compound); fourth, that both have fixed limits in their operating. They are said to differ, first, because nature has true effects, while art has almost all of them feigned; second, because nature does not presuppose art in order to act, whereas art presupposes nature; third, because nature is concerned with what is intrinsic, while art is occupied for the most part with the external surface; fourth, because the effect of nature produces another like itself, as a dog produces a dog, a lion a lion, but this is not so with the products of art. Finally, because nature unites the parts by composing them in a more perfect way; art does not do so.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISQUISITION II.

units.la: Quid sit ars, & an opera naturæ facere possit.
units.tr: What art is, and whether it can perform the works of nature.

units.la: PRo intelligentia primi quæsiti repetite à Logicis verba Philosophi 6. Eth. c. 4. vbi artem sic definit. Ars est habitus cum recta ratione factiuus. Nimirū habitualis quædācognitio, quæ dictat modū operis faciendi per hoc, quòd regulas tradit, ac præcepta, quibus dū vtimur, consultò, prudenter, ac scitè aliquid facimus.
units.tr: To understand the first question, let us take again from the Logicians the words of the Philosopher, Ethics 6, ch. 4, where he defines art thus: Art is a productive habit joined with right reason. That is, it is a habitual knowledge which dictates the manner of making a work, by laying down rules and precepts, by following which, we make something deliberately, prudently and skilfully.

units.la: Artes colunt Medici, Alchimistæ, Magi, Mechanici, Mathematici, qui omnes aut perficiendo, aut domando naturam, essectus omninò prodigiosos præstitere, adeo vt in manu peritorum Ars merito dicta fuerit Simia Naturæ. Qua de re consulite Martinum Del Rio, & Kircherum. Sanè Archimedes, in vna ficti orbis machina tā scitè r exercuit mathesim, vt exiterit error Epicureorū, quos refert Cic. 2. de nat. Deor. Archimedē plus valuisse in imitandis sphæra conuersionibus, quā natumirabiles effectus. Vnde sicuti cederet in laudem pictoris, dum quouis baculo arrepto delineare posset formam quamque pulcherrimam, etsi abiectum, ineptumq; instrumentum foret; sic, &c.
units.tr: Medical men, alchemists, magicians, mechanics and mathematicians cultivate art, and all of them, by either perfecting or taming nature, have produced wholly prodigious effects, so that in the hands of the skilled art has rightly been called the ape of Nature. On this matter consult Martin Del Rio and Kircher. Indeed Archimedes, in a single machine imitating the sphere, exercised mathematics so skilfully that the error of the Epicureans, which Cicero reports in De natura deorum 2, was refuted: Archimedes was more able in imitating the revolutions of a sphere than nature was, [in producing such wonderful effects]. Hence, just as it would redound to a painter's praise if he could sketch the most beautiful form with any stick whatever he picked up, even though it were a mean and unfit instrument; so, etc.

units.la: Probatur 2. Si enim non datur in omni creatura obedientialis potentia pro quolibet effectu, maximè quia creatura improportionem habet ad illos: at hęc ratio nulla est, ergo. Probo minorem, quia nec anima proportionem habet vllam, neque aptitudinem naturalem, vt recipiat gratiam, & habitus, qui sunt Supernaturales; attamen per potentiam obedientialé eos recipit. Quare in exemplo de potentia obedientiali passiua, retorqueri possunt argumenta omnia, quæ faciunt aduersarij contra potentiam actiuam.
units.tr: It is proved secondly: if there is not in every creature an obediential power for every effect, chiefly because the creature has no proportion to those effects; but this reason is no reason at all; therefore. I prove the minor: because the soul has no proportion whatever, nor any natural aptitude, to receive grace and habits, which are supernatural; yet it receives them through an obediential power. Wherefore, in the example of passive obediential power, all the arguments which our opponents bring against active power can be turned back.

units.la: Obijcies 1. Si quæuis creatura eleuari posset ad quodlibet, illa esset infinitę virtutis: hoc repugnat: ergo. Sequela patet, nam valeret ad producendos infinitos efsectus etiam specie diuersos.
