units.tr: You will object first: if any creature could be raised to anything whatever, it would be of infinite power; this is repugnant; therefore. The consequence is plain, for it would be able to produce infinite effects, even of different species.

units.la: Respond. n. maiorem, quia creatura maneret semper instrumentum, & esset causa remota, incompleta, queque nunquam dici potest infinitæ virtutis, per hoc quòd infinitos effectus etiam specie differentes producat. Patet enim quòd intellectus etsi virtutis limitatæ, ad infinitas tamen intellectiones potest à speciebus determinari. Multò magis ergo ad effectus etiam specie infinitos valebit creatura, si eleuetur.
units.tr: I deny the major, because the creature would always remain an instrument, and would be a remote and incomplete cause, which can never be called of infinite power merely because it produces infinite effects, even of different species. For it is plain that the intellect, though of limited power, can be determined by species to infinite intellections. Much more, then, will a creature, if raised up, be able to produce even infinite effects of different species.

units.la: Obijcies 2. Aqua v. g. quantumuis eleuaeleuata nunquam potest gratiæ proportionari; ergo ad eam producendam eleuari nequit. Probatur antecedens. Eleuatio non immutat ab intrinseco entitatem aquæ, vnde si ante non erat proportionata, nec postea erit. Antecedens notum est; eleuatio enim non ponit aliquid intrinsecum rei, sed merè se adiungit extrinsecè.
units.tr: Second objection: water, for example, however much it is raised, can never be made proportionate to grace; therefore it cannot be raised to produce it. The antecedent is proved: elevation does not change the intrinsic entity of water, so if it was not proportionate before, it will not be afterwards. The antecedent is well known, for elevation does not posit anything intrinsic to the thing, but merely attaches itself from outside.

units.la: Resp. n. antecedés, reddítur enim aqua proportionata gratiæ per extrinsecam eleuationem; sicut intellectus ad visionem; potentia naturalis ad actus fidei, spei, &c. Ad probationé c. quòd eleuatio non immutat ab intrinseco rem, sed neq; hoc requiritur, sufficit.n. si adsit extrinseca eleuatio, vt aqua cōpletè valeat producere gratiā. Itā neq; influxus Dei cū causis naturalibus affert ijs aliquid intrinsecum, etsi eas faciat cōpletè potentes ad efficiē dum. Ratio autem est, quia esse aliquid potens duo dicit, vnum intrinsecū, nēpe causæ ipsius entitate; aliud extrinsecū, videlicet eleuationē, siue aliā concaufam.
units.tr: I deny the antecedent: for water is rendered proportionate to grace through an extrinsic elevation, just as the intellect is to vision, and natural power to acts of faith, hope, etc. To the proof of the consequent: elevation does not change the thing intrinsically, but neither is this required; it is enough that extrinsic elevation be present for water to be fully able to produce grace. Thus neither does God's influx, together with natural causes, bring anything intrinsic to them, even though it makes them fully powerful to effect. The reason is that to be something powerful signifies two things: one intrinsic, namely the very entity of the cause; the other extrinsic, namely elevation, or another concause.

units.la: Obijcies 3. ex Conincko. Ex hac sententia sequitur, posse brutū eleuari ad intelligendum; oculum ad audiendū; auré ad videndū, &c. quamuis .n. hæc nō sint subiecta naturaliter ad hoc apta, supernaturaliter tamen reddi talia possunt. Hoc autem dici nequit, ergo.
units.tr: Third objection, from Coninck. From this opinion it follows that a brute animal could be raised to understand, the eye to hear, the ear to see, etc. For although these are not subjects naturally apt for this, they can be made such supernaturally. But this cannot be said; therefore.

units.la: Resp. n.sequelā. Et ratio est, quia dātur nonnullæ actiones, quę pendent essētialiter à tali subiecto, &organo, adeout si hoc desit, nec actiones illæ produci per vllam poapud Conimbr. lib. 2. phyf. cap. 7. q. 12. artic. 2. Et vos interim eruditionis gratia memoriæ consignabitis pulcherrima Diu. Auguft. verba ex lib. 5. de Genesi cap. 20. Monet Deus occulta potentia, eoq; motu illa versat, dum Angeli iussa perficiunt, dum circumeunt sidera, dum alternant venti, dum abyssus aquarum lapsibus agitatur, dum vireta pullulant, suaque femina euoluunt, dum animalia gignuntur, dum iniqui iustos exercere permittuntur: explicat fæcula, qua illis cum primum condita sunt implicita indiderat: qua tamen in suos cursus non explicarentur, fi ea ille, qui condidit, prouido motu administrare cessaret.
units.tr: I deny the consequence. The reason is that there are some actions which depend essentially on such a subject and organ, so that if this is lacking, those actions cannot be produced by any power whatever [...]; see the Conimbricenses, Physics book 2, ch. 7, question 12, article 2. And meanwhile, for the sake of learning, you will commit to memory the most beautiful words of Saint Augustine, from book 5 On Genesis, ch. 20: God moves by a hidden power, and by that motion governs those things, while the angels carry out his commands, while they go round the stars, while the winds alternate, while the abyss of waters is stirred by its falls, while greenery sprouts and the females unfold their own offspring, while animals are generated, while the wicked are permitted to trouble the just: he unfolds the seeds which he had implanted implicitly when they were first created; which yet would not be unfolded into their courses if he who created them ceased to govern them by his providential motion.

units.la: Probatur secundo ratione, qula res omnis, & actio creata est ens participatum, ac fluens à primo ente; dependet à Deo maximà, & summmà dependentià, qua maior alia excogitari non potest. Ergo causa Prima influit actu ad actiones creaturarum. Probo consequentiam. Si Deus actu non influeret ad actiones creaturarum, actio exercita penderet magis à creatura, quàm à Deo, quod absurdissimum est. Patet sequela, nam effectus pendet magis ab eo, à quo accipit esse, quàm à quo conseruatur; sed actio haberet esse à creatura tantum, & à Deo conseruatione, ergo penderet magis à creatura, quàm à Deo. Confirmatur, quia conseruatio est continuata rei productio, ergo si Deus creaturarum actiones conseruat seruat, eas etiam producit.
units.tr: It is proved secondly by reason: because every thing and every created action is a participated being, flowing from the first being; it depends on God with the greatest and highest dependence, than which no greater can be imagined. Therefore the First Cause actually influences the actions of creatures. I prove the consequence. If God did not actually influence the actions of creatures, an action performed would depend more on the creature than on God, which is most absurd. The sequence is plain, for an effect depends more on that from which it receives its being than on that by which it is conserved; but the action would have its being from the creature alone, and its conservation from God; therefore it would depend more on the creature than on God. It is confirmed: because conservation is a continued production of the thing; therefore if God conserves the actions of creatures, he also produces them.

units.la: Probatur 3. Si Deus concursum subtrahat suum, nulla prorsus fit actio creaturæ, igitur si fiat, actu effectiuè Deus concurrit ad illam. Antecedens patet in igne Babylonico, qui dempto Diuino influxu, nil peregit. Consequentia probatur. Deus non concurrit conseruando actionem tantummodò, ergò effectiuè influendo. Probo antecedens,quia si tantùm concurreret conseruando, subtracta conseruatione, adhuc fieret actio, etiamsi postea instantaneè periret, quia non adesset causa conseruans: fieret inquā eò quòd reperiretur creatura se sola, & sine alterius concursu agens;periret autē,quia profluens actio non haberet causam, à qua conseruaretur; sed tamen actio fieret. Hoc autem absurdum est, quia si Deus non concurrat, non solùm non conseruatur actio, sed nullo modo fit, ergo vt fiat, Deus actu effectiuè concurret ad illam.
units.tr: It is proved thirdly: if God withdraws his concurrence, no action of a creature is made at all; therefore if it is made, God actually concurs in it effectively. The antecedent is plain in the case of the Babylonian fire, which, with divine influx removed, accomplished nothing. The consequence is proved: God does not concur merely by conserving the action; therefore he concurs by effectively influencing it. I prove the antecedent: for if he concurred only by conserving, then with conservation withdrawn the action would still be made, even if it then instantly perished, because no conserving cause would be present. It would be made, I say, because the creature would be found acting alone and without another's concurrence; it would perish, however, because the flowing action would have no cause by which it is conserved; yet the action would still be made. But this is absurd, because if God did not concur, the action would not merely fail to be conserved, but would in no way be made at all. Therefore, in order that it be made, God actually concurs in it effectively.

units.la: Probatur etiam Secunda pars conclusionis, quòd nimirum etiam creaturæ, actu, & effectiuè agant, secus enim non peccaret homo, sed ipse Deus in homine; non mereretur creatura, sed in ea Creator; non traheretur à Magnete ferrum, sed à Deo in magnete. Imò quodcumque agens nullum haberet limitem in agendo,eò quia in illo virtus infinita operaretur, & sic Venetijs, nec ab igne Vesuuij, nec ab Apuliæ phalangijs tuti essemus.
units.tr: The second part of the conclusion is also proved, namely that creatures too act actually and effectively. Otherwise man would not sin, but God himself in man; the creature would not merit, but the Creator in it; iron would not be drawn by the magnet, but God in the magnet. Indeed, any agent whatever would have no limit in acting, since infinite virtue would operate in it; and thus we would not be safe at Venice, nor from the fire of Vesuvius, nor from the phalanxes of Apulia.

units.la: Obijcies 1. pro sententia Durandi. Si Deus actu influeret ad actiones creaturarum, esset causa peccati ; hoc non est dicendum ; ergo . Probatur sequela à simili. Creaturæ ideo præcisè imputatur peccatum, quia concurrit ad hanc actionem v. g. furti, homicidij, odij , &c. sed etiam Deus influeret in eădem omnino, ergo & Deus foret causa peccati . Confirmatur quia malitia peccati aut consistit in aliquo positiuo , aut in mera priuatione, vt aliqui dicunt, rectitudinis debitiæ: quidquid sit, sequitur Deum esse causam peccati, ergò . Probatur minor . Si enim peccati malitia est quid positiuū in actu , Deus facit hoc totum positiuum : Si quid priuatiuum, hoc necessariò , & infallibiliter sequitur ad positionem actus, itaut neq; à Deo impediri possit ; dato enim actu odij, est impossibile quòd non sequatur priuatio rectitudinis debitæ ; igitur qui elicit actum odij,est causa physica huiusce priuationis,atq; adeo peccati.
units.tr: First objection, in favour of Durand's opinion: if God actually influenced the actions of creatures, he would be the cause of sin; this is not to be said; therefore. The consequence is proved by a parallel. Sin is imputed to the creature precisely because it concurs in this action, for example of theft, homicide, hatred, etc.; but God would influence exactly the same thing; therefore God too would be the cause of sin. It is confirmed: the malice of sin consists either in something positive, or in mere privation, as some say, of due rectitude. Whichever it is, it follows that God is the cause of sin. The minor is proved: if the malice of sin is something positive in the act, God produces all of this positive element; if it is something privative, this necessarily and infallibly follows the positing of the act, so that it cannot be prevented even by God. For given an act of hatred, it is impossible that the privation of due rectitude does not follow; therefore he who elicits an act of hatred is the physical cause of this privation, and so of sin.

units.la: Resp. imprimis cum Becano , & alijs, Deum non esse causam peccati, si pro tali causa intelligatur peccator , siue ille, qui peccat. Deus enim cùm non sit legi subiectus, etiamsi ad actum concurrat malum,peccare tamen non dicitur.Eo modo quo nec habitus acquisitus peccat,licet ad actus malos concurrat , quia enim subiectus legi non est,ideo neq; tenetur illi,neque parere debet.
units.tr: I reply first, with Becanus and others, that God is not the cause of sin, if by such a cause is meant the sinner, or the one who sins. For God, since he is not subject to the law, does not sin even if he concurs in a wicked act. In the same way, an acquired habit does not sin, although it concurs in evil acts, because it is not subject to the law and so is neither bound by it nor obliged to obey it.

units.la: Resp. 2. Deum non esse causam, siue auctorem peccati, quia non concurrit ad actum ex intentione, ut sequatur malitia (quidquid postea illa sit, siue positiuum, siue negatiuum) Deus n. quantum ex se præbet concursum voluntati creatæ ad omnia indifferenté, & ita præbet, ut semper tamen intendat bonum. Sed quia voluntas prava Diuino concursu abusa se se flectit ad malum, eò etiam quoad actū positiuū descendit Deus, non tamen desiderans, & intendens malum. Unde inquit Psalmista quòd malitiam Deus odit. D.Iac. Deum esse malorum intentatorem, &c.
units.tr: Second, God is not the cause or author of sin, because he does not concur in the act with the intention that wickedness should follow (whatever that wickedness is afterwards, whether positive or negative). For God gives to the created will, as far as lies in himself, a concurrence that is indifferent to all things, and he gives it in such a way that he always intends what is good. But because the depraved will, abusing the divine concurrence, bends itself towards evil, God descends to the positive side of the act as well, yet without desiring or intending evil. Hence the Psalmist says that God hates wickedness, and St James says that God is no tempter of evils.

units.la: Ex quib. concluditur, Deum non esse causam peccati. Explicari potest à simili de natura particulari, quæ non dicitur causa monstri, licet ad illud concurrat, eò quòd ex se non intendit monstrum. Sic Potentia progressiua non vocatur causa claudicationis, quauis enim ad talem influat motum, de se aliud videlicet recti intendit. Accipe verba expressa D.Th.1. p.q.49. art. 2. Sicut quidquid est motus in claudicatione causatur à virtute motiua: sed quod est obliquitatis in ea, non est ex virtute motiua, sed ex curuitate cruris; ita in actione mala quidquid est defectus non causatur à Deo, sed à causa secunda deficiente, &c. Resp.3. Deum non esse causam peccati, etiamsi ad actionem concurrat materialem, quia ex officio tenetur præstare concursum creaturæ, ad hoc ut ipsa liberè se determinet ad agendum. Creatura verò est causa peccati, eò quòd non solùm non tenetur sic facere, sed neque debet, nam talis operatio illi prorsus interdicta est. Obij-
units.tr: From these points it follows that God is not the cause of sin. This can be explained by an analogy from particular nature: a particular nature is not called the cause of a monster, although it concurs in producing it, because it does not of itself intend a monster. Likewise the power of locomotion is not called the cause of limping, for although it contributes to such a motion, it intends something else of itself, namely what is straight. Take the express words of St Thomas, Summa I, q. 49, art. 2: Just as whatever is motion in limping is caused by the motive power, but what is crookedness in it is not from the motive power but from the bending of the leg; so in a wicked action, whatever is defect is not caused by God but by the deficient secondary cause, and so on. Third reply: God is not the cause of sin, even if he concurs in the material act, because by his office he is bound to supply concurrence to the creature so that it may determine itself freely to act. But the creature is the cause of sin, because it is not only not bound to act in this way, but ought not to, for such an operation is absolutely forbidden to it. Object-

units.la: Obijcies 2. pro fecunda sententia. Creaturę si effectiuè concurrerent ad res efficiendas, haberent virtutem infinitam: hoc dici nequit, ergo. Probatur sequela, nam extrahere aliquid ex nihilo arguit virtutem infinitam; vnde creatio, quæ rem producit ex nihilo, est opus Dei, non creaturæ: sed si creatura effectiuè produceret aliquid, hoc extraheretur ex nihilo, priùs enim erat nihil; ergo. Confirmatur ex D. Thoma quæst. 3. de malo, art. 2. in corpore, vnde; aliqui deducunt necessitatem Diuini cöcursus ad actiones creaturarũ, quia hæ eũ sint virtutis finitæ, nūquā producerēt aliquid se solis. Quod etiā acutè prosequitur P. Palauicinus, iam S.R.E. Card. Eminentissimus l. 1. assertionum Theol.
units.tr: Second objection, in favour of the second opinion. If creatures concurred effectively in producing things, they would have infinite power; this cannot be said; therefore neither can the first. The consequence is proved: to draw something out of nothing argues infinite power; hence creation, which produces a thing out of nothing, is the work of God and not of a creature; but if a creature produced something effectively, this would be drawn out of nothing, for previously it was nothing; therefore. It is confirmed from St Thomas, Quaestio 3, De malo, art. 2, in the body of the article, where he says: some infer the necessity of divine concurrence for the actions of creatures because, since these have finite power, they would never produce anything by themselves. Father Pallavicino, now the most eminent Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, pursues this subtly as well, in book 1 of his Assertions of Theology.

units.la: Respondent communiter negando sequelam, & ad probationem concedunt, quòd producere aliquid ex nihilo sui, & subiecti virtutem arguit infinitam, nonita producere aliquid ex nihilo sui tantùm. Sed hæc responsio non videtur sufficere, vt vidimus l. 1. disp. 2. Quare dici posset, creaturas reuera influere cum Deo ad actiones omnes, & accidentia, quæ cùm produci debeant dependenter à subiecto, non requirunt in causa virtutem infinitam. E contra non influere cum Deo ad producendam substantiam de nouo, quia fortasse nulla iam producatur de nouo, sed à solo Deo fuerint omnes ab initio mundi productæ: vnde omnis actio, quæ modò exercetur, fit vnitiua substantiasum non producłiua. Sed quidquid sit, manet inconcussum, quòd cum creaturis Deus præbet influxum ad actiones earum, & ita quidem, vt Dei, & Creaturæ vnica sit actio indiuisibilis, non enim potest concipi aliquid fluens à creatura, quod essentialiter non pendeat à Deo, summa, & maxima dependentia, & sic quod ab ipso non fiat.
units.tr: Commonly they respond by denying the consequence, and they concede the proof: that to produce something out of nothing of its own and of its subject argues infinite power, but not to produce something out of nothing of its own alone. But this reply does not seem sufficient, as we saw in book 1, disputation 2. Hence it could be said that creatures do indeed flow in together with God into all actions and accidents, which, since they must be produced dependently on a subject, do not require infinite power in the cause. On the other hand, they do not flow in together with God to produce substance anew, because perhaps no substance is now being produced anew, but all were produced from the beginning of the world by God alone; so that every action which is now exercised makes a substance to be united, not to be produced. But whatever the case, this stands unshaken: God, together with creatures, supplies influence for their actions, and in such a way that the action of God and of the creature is one indivisible action; for nothing can be conceived as flowing from a creature which does not essentially depend on God with the highest and greatest dependence, and so which is not also done by him.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISPUTATION II.

units.la: Vtrum causa Prima subordi- nentur secunda in poten- tia obedientiali.
units.tr: Whether the First Cause is subordinated to second causes in obediential power.

units.la: PRO intelligentia præmitto quid sit potentia obedientialis. Illa nimirum capacitas quædam est, ratione cuius potest res aliqua in se aliquid recipere, vel operari, non quidem ex naturali sua propensione, sed vt subordinata superiori, cui debet obedire, nec resistere potest. V. g. lapis habet potentiam obedientialem ascendendi, nam ex se quidem petit descensum, nihilominus quia non potest resistere fortiori agenti, est etiam capax motus sursum.
units.tr: By way of preface, I first state what obediential power is. It is a certain capacity by virtue of which a thing can receive or do something in itself, not indeed from its natural inclination, but as subordinate to a superior, which it must obey and cannot resist. For example, a stone has the obediential power to rise, for by its own nature it tends downward, yet because it cannot resist a stronger agent, it is also capable of being moved upward.

units.la: Proinde creaturæ non solùm subordinantur Deo per hoc, quòd sine ipso nihil possunt facere, sed etiam quia ipso iubente sæpissimè plura efficiunt contra, & supra suæ naturæ inclinationem, & ideo potentia hæc vocatur obedientialis.
units.tr: Accordingly, creatures are subordinated to God not only in that they can do nothing without him, but also because, at his command, they very often produce many effects against and beyond the inclination of their nature, and for this reason this power is called obediential.

units.la: Hinc Sap. 15. vbi referuntur mirabilia quædam facta in creaturis, additur. Creatura.n.tibi Factori suo deseruiens ardescit in tormentum aduersus iniustos, & lenior fit ad benefaciendum pro his, qui in te confidunt. Accedit D. Aug. l. 9. de Gen. ad lit. c. 17, vbi asserit, supra cursum, & virtutem naturæ Deum habere potestatem agendi multa de rebus, vt scilicet steriles in sene facta pariat; lignum aridum sine terra, & aqua repente floreat, & fructum gignat. Demum est insignis auctoritas D. Thomæ q. 6. de pot. art. 2. ad 2. vbi hæc habet: Unde nihil prohibet, quin natura creata sit in potentia ad aliqua facienda per D. potentiam, qua inferior potentia facere non potest, & ista vocatur potentia obedientialis, secundum quam quaelibet creatura obedit Creatori.
units.tr: Hence Wisdom 15, where certain wonders wrought in creatures are recounted, adds: For the creature, serving you its Maker, grows fierce as a torment against the unjust, and becomes milder to do good for those who trust in you. St. Augustine also agrees, in book 9 of the Literal Commentary on Genesis, chapter 17, where he asserts that God, beyond the course and power of nature, has the power of doing many things with things, namely to make barren women bear children in old age; a dry stick, without earth and water, suddenly flowers and bears fruit. Finally, there is the notable authority of St. Thomas, Quaestio 6 On Power, article 2, reply to objection 2, where he has these words: Hence nothing prevents a created nature from being in potency to certain things to be done through the divine power, which a lower power cannot do; and this is called obediential potency, according to which every creature obeys the Creator.

units.la: Quemadmodum verò potentia naturalis duplex est; Actiua ad agendum, & Passiua ad recipiendum; sic pariter potentia obedientialis omnino duplex: Actiua, qua res eleuatur ad agendum aliquid supra suas vires, quemadmodum intellectus Beati physicè producit visionem beatificam; voluntas amorem; & potentiæ vitales in viatoribus producunt actus fidei, spei, & charitatis christianæ, qui sunt entitatiuè supernaturales. Passiua potentia est, qua res eleuatur ad recipiendum aliquid in se; quod omnino excedit naturalem ipsius facultatem. Sic anima recipit gratiam, & habitus quoscumq; supernaturales infusos. Posita doctrina, quæritur, an in omni creatura detur hæc obedientialis potentia præsertim actiua in ordine ad quoslibet effectus, qui specialiter non repugnant. V.g. in igne potentia producendi aquam; in aqua potentia efficiendi gratiam, in musca potentia gignendi Angelum, &c. Pro solutione fit.
units.tr: Just as natural power is twofold, active for acting and passive for receiving, so obediential power is likewise wholly twofold: active, by which a thing is raised to do something beyond its own powers, as the intellect of the blessed physically produces the beatific vision, and the will produces love, and the vital powers in wayfarers produce acts of Christian faith, hope and charity, which are supernatural in their being. Passive power is that by which a thing is raised to receive something in itself which wholly exceeds its natural faculty. Thus the soul receives grace and any supernatural habits infused. With this doctrine established, the question arises whether this obediential power exists in every creature, especially active power in relation to any effects whatever which do not specifically contradict it. For example: in fire, the power of producing water; in water, the power of effecting grace; in a fly, the power of begetting an angel, and so on. The answer follows.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Datur in omni creatura obedientialis potentia tum passiua, tum actiua pro quauis forma, & operatione licet indebita, & naturaliter improportionata: dummodo non adsit specialis implicantia.
units.tr: In every creature there is obediential power, both passive and active, for any form and operation whatever, even if undue and naturally disproportionate, provided no special contradiction stands in the way.

units.la: POstrema verba in conclusione ponuntur ad excludendos effectus, qui à creatura neque per Dei elevationem fieri possunt. V.g. nihil potest eleuari à Deo, vt primo se ipsum producat; deberet .n. existere antequam effet. Nihil potest eleuari, vt albedinem constituat albam, quia talis de se formaliter, & essentialiter est.
units.tr: The final words of the conclusion are added to exclude effects which a creature cannot produce even by God's elevation. For example, nothing can be raised by God so as to produce itself first; for it would have to exist before it existed. Nothing can be raised so as to make whiteness white, because whiteness is such in itself, formally and essentially.

units.la: Probatur ergo quoad effectus, qui non dicunt in se repugnantiam. Primò auctoritate D. Aug. D. Thomæ aliorumq; P. P. Secundo ratione, quia si Deus poteft se solo producere angelum, cur non poterit cum musca simul? Tertiò quia sic magis elucet Diuina virtus, dum omni creatura etiam vilissima vti potest ad miraeleuata nunquam potest gratiæ proportionari; ergo ad eam producendam eleuari nequit. Probatur antecedens. Eleuatio non immutat ab intrinseco entitatem aquæ, vnde si ante non erat proportionata, nec postea erit. Antecedens notum est;eleuatio enim non ponit aliquid intrinsecum rei, sed merè se adiungit extrinsecè.
units.tr: It is therefore proved with respect to effects which do not involve contradiction in themselves. First, by the authority of St. Augustine, St. Thomas and the other Fathers. Second, by reason: for if God can produce an angel by himself alone, why could he not do so together with a fly? Third, because the divine power shines more clearly when even the most worthless creature can be used for miracles. The argument may be put thus: a thing which is by nature disproportionate to grace can never be made proportionate to it; therefore it cannot be raised to produce grace. The antecedent is proved as follows: elevation does not change the being of water from within; so if it was not proportionate before, it will not be afterwards. The antecedent is known, since elevation does not add anything intrinsic to a thing, but joins itself to it merely from outside.

units.la: Resp. n. antecedés,reddítur enim aqua proportionata gratiæ per extrinsecam eleuationem;sicut intelleƈtus ad visionem; potentia naturalis ad actus fidei,spei, &c. Ad probationē c. quòd eleuatio non immutat ab intrinseco rem, sed neq; hoc requiritur,sufficit.n. si adsit extrinseca eleuatio, vt aqua cōpletè valeat producere gratiā. Itā neq;influxus Dei cū causis naturalibus affert ijs aliquid intrinsecum, etsi eas faciat cōpletè potentes ad efficiendum. Ratio autem est, quia esse aliquid potens duo dicit, vnum intrinsecū, nēpe causæ ipsius entitatē; aliud extrinsecū,videlicet eleuationē, siue aliā concausam.
units.tr: I reply by denying the antecedent: water is in fact made proportionate to grace through extrinsic elevation, just as the intellect is made proportionate to vision, and natural power to acts of faith, hope, and so on. To the proof, I grant that elevation does not change the thing from within; but this is not required either, for it is enough that extrinsic elevation be present, so that water may be fully able to produce grace. Likewise, the influx of God together with natural causes brings nothing intrinsic to them, even though it makes them fully capable of effecting. The reason is that to be able to do something says two things: one intrinsic, namely the being of the cause itself; the other extrinsic, namely elevation, or another concause.

units.la: Obijcies 3. ex Conincko. Ex hac sententia sequitur, posse brutū eleuari ad intelligendum; oculum ad audiendū; auré ad videndū, &c. quamuis .n. hæc nó sint subieƈta naturaliter ad hoc apta, supernaturaliter tamen reddi talia possunt.Hoc autem dici nequit, ergo.
units.tr: You will object, third, following Coninck: from this opinion it follows that a brute animal could be raised to understand, the eye to hear, the ear to see, and so on. For although these are not naturally fitted to such things, they can nevertheless be made such supernaturally. But this cannot be said; therefore...

units.la: Resp. n.sequelā.Et ratio est,quia dătur nonnullæ actiones,quę pendent essētialiter à tali subieƈto,&organo,adeout si hoc desit,nec actiones illæ produci per vllam potentiam queant. Sic visio ita fit per organum oculare, vt vbi hoc non fuerit, ea elici nequeat: sic auditio, &c. Verùm aliæ sunt actiones, quæ à causis non pendent essentialiter, neque de se necessariò exigunt hanc potius, quàm aliam. Ita calor sic producitur ab igne, vt idem numero produci potuerit à sole, à silice percusso, &c. Ad eos igitur effectus,qui vt fiant, neq; hoc subiectum, neque hoc organum essentialiter exigunt, omnis causa eleuari potest. Vnde patet ad argumentum disparitas. &c.
units.tr: I reply by denying the consequence. The reason is that there are some actions which depend essentially on such a subject and organ, so that if this is lacking, those actions cannot be produced by any power whatever. Thus sight takes place through the eye, so that where this is not present it cannot be elicited; likewise hearing, and so on. But there are other actions which do not depend essentially on their causes, nor of necessity require this rather than that in themselves. Thus heat is produced by fire in such a way that the same numerically could have been produced by the sun, or by flint struck, and so on. Therefore, for those effects which, in order to come about, require neither this subject nor this organ essentially, any cause can be elevated. Hence the disparity in the argument is clear.

units.la: Obijcies 4. Nulla est proportio v. g. inter muscam, & Angelum, ergo illa nequit eleuari ad hunc producendum. Antecedens per inductionem patet consideranti.
units.tr: You will object, fourth: there is no proportion, for example, between a fly and an angel; therefore the fly cannot be elevated to produce one. The antecedent is evident to anyone who considers it by induction.

units.la: Respond. d. nulla est proportio remota, siue vt aiunt inchoata, n. proxima, & completa, c. Quocirca etiamsi musca non proportionetur Angelo quoad omnia predicata, spiritualis, intellectiui &c. nihilominus adest proportio aliqua remota, & inchoata, Musca enim est ens, est substantia, est viuens, &c. vnde si habeat eleuationem, vt sic in sensu composito fit proximè, atque completè proportiona-ra.
units.tr: I reply: I deny that there is no proportion; there is a remote proportion, or, as they say, inchoate, but not a proximate and complete one. Accordingly, even if the fly is not proportioned to the angel in all predicates, as spiritual, intellective, and so on, nevertheless some remote and inchoate proportion is present. For a fly is a being, is a substance, is living, and so on; hence if it has elevation, then in the composite sense it becomes proximately and completely proportioned.

units.la: DISQVISITIO TERTIA.
units.tr: DISQVISITIO TERTIA.

units.la: Vtrum creatura eleuari etiam possit ad creandum.
units.tr: Whether a creature can also be raised to create.

units.la: PRo intelligentia præmoneo, quid sit creatio. Aduertite, duplicem agendi modum solere attribui Deo. Alter dicitur ad intra, & est ille inexplicabilis processionum. Alter vocatur ad extra, ille nimirum quo Deus producit creaturas. De primo Theologi: de secundo hic breuiter.
units.tr: To begin with, I explain what creation is. Note that a twofold mode of acting is usually attributed to God. The first is called ad intra, and it is that inexplicable mode of the processions. The second is called ad extra, namely that by which God produces creatures. The theologians treat the first; here I speak briefly of the second.

units.la: Propria igitur Dei actio ad extra est creatio, seu productio rei ex nihilo subiecti (vt aiunt) seu ex nullo præsuppoposito subiecto; & id nulli creaturæ naturaliter conuenire potest, nam ea semper cum dependentia à subiecto agit.
units.tr: Creation, therefore, is God's proper action ad extra: the production of a thing out of nothing of a subject (as they say), or out of no presupposed subject. This can belong to no creature by nature, for a creature always acts with dependence on a subject.

units.la: Distinguitur autem creatio à causa agente scilicet Deo, fuit enim ab æterno Deus absq; creatione vlla. Distinguitur etiam à termino, licèt n. res, quæ creatur essentialiter, qualis est actio ipsa creatiua, non distinguatur à creatione sui; tamen alij effectus, qui essentialiter non creantur, fiunt per actionem distinctam, vt de angelis, de animalibus, &c. probabile manet.
units.tr: Creation is distinguished from its agent cause, namely God, for God existed from eternity without any creation. It is also distinguished from its term. Although the thing that is created essentially, such as the creative action itself, is not distinguished from its own creation, other effects, which are not created essentially, come about through a distinct action, as with angels, with animals, and so on. This remains probable.

units.la: Recipitur actio creatiua in termino creato, non tanquam in subiecto, alioquin terminus intelligi deberet existens, priusquam produceretur; sed tanquam in re terminante; vnde sic explicatur
units.tr: The creative action is received in the created term, not as in a subject; otherwise the term would have to be understood as already existing before it was produced. Rather, it is received as in a thing that terminates the action, whence it is explained thus.

units.la: APPENDIX
units.tr: APPENDIX

units.la: De Natura, & Arte.
units.tr: On Nature and Art.

units.la: TRia sunt, quæ in hoc ordine terrum vim habent operatiuam, Deus, Natura, & Ars, quæ sicuti diuersa inter se manét, sic diuersis omnino modis agunt. Deus enim facit rem ex nihilo sui, & subiecti, quia non indiget præiacente materia, & sic dicitur creare. Natura gignit formam ex nihilo sui, sed præsupponit materiam, & dicitur producere. Ars verò & materiam, & formam præiacentem habet, in eamque figuram tantummodò, seu varias partium dispositiones inducit, & sic dicitur facere, aut fingere.
units.tr: There are three things which in this order have operative power: God, Nature, and Art. Though they remain distinct from one another, they act in entirely different ways. For God makes a thing out of nothing, both of itself and of its subject, since he has no need of a pre-existing matter; and thus he is said to create. Nature begets a form out of nothing of its own, but presupposes matter, and is said to produce. Art, however, has both matter and a pre-existing form, and merely induces a shape or various arrangements of parts; and thus it is said to make, or to fashion.

units.la: Verùm hæc doctrina, quæ dudum communis fuit, non omnibus hoc tépore arridet. Nā si natura producit formā ex nihilo sui, nempe substantiā de nouo, quæ priùs non erat, quomodo nō creat? Dicis, quia operatur in materia. Sed hoc nil videtur afferre nisi verba, si res bene pédatur. Imprimis enim ea materia nihil de suo dat, vnde cum dicitur: materia sustinet formam, influit in illam, &c. hoc tantùm sonat quòd materia recipit formam, & vnitur cum illa; vnio autem non tollit creationem, vt patet in anima rationali vnita corpori. Deinde quantumuis præiaceat materia, in ea nil præiacet substantiæ, quę de nouo producitur, ergo ista creatur. Vnde vt virtus Dei magis eluceat in operando, quæcumq; productio substantiæ de nouo à natura tollenda, folique Deo concedenda esse videtur.
units.tr: Yet this doctrine, which was long common, does not please everyone in our time. For if nature produces a form out of nothing of its own, namely a substance anew, which did not exist before, why does it not create? You say that it works upon matter. But this seems to add nothing except words, if the matter is weighed properly. In the first place, that matter gives nothing of its own; so when it is said that matter sustains the form, flows into it, and so on, this means only that matter receives the form and is united with it; but union does not abolish creation, as is plain in the rational soul united to the body. Next, however much matter may lie beneath, nothing that lies beneath is of the substance which is produced anew; therefore that substance is created. Hence, so that the power of God may shine more clearly in working, every production of a substance anew seems to be taken away from nature and granted to God alone.

units.la: Porro hanc opinionem conantur defendere Democritei argumentis, quæ potissimum ex arte sumuntur. Nam si ars, inquiunt, efficit opera naturæ, non producendo substantias de nouo; sed eas, quæ iam sunt diuersimodè vniendo, subigendo, compingendo, cur hoc ipsum de natura dici non poterit? Maximè quia productio substantiæ de nouo difficilis est, neq; vt plurimum causam habet. Proinde in re, quæ non leuis momenti est, operæ pretium duxi paululum immorari, nam si hoc de arte constiterit, non exiguum puto accessurum Philosophiæ lumen, quo naturales effectus intro magis timetur.
units.tr: Moreover, the Democriteans try to defend this opinion with arguments drawn chiefly from art. For if art, they say, effects the works of nature, not by producing substances anew, but by joining, shaping, and compacting those which already exist in various ways, why can the same not be said of nature? Especially since the production of a substance anew is difficult, and for the most part has no cause. Therefore, in a matter which is of no slight importance, I thought it worth while to linger a little; for if this is established concerning art, I think no small light will be added to philosophy, by which natural effects are better understood within.

units.la: Consultò igitur huic secundo libro appendicem attexo de natura, & arte, vt cum patuerit in quibus conueniant, in quibus differant, earum quoque modus operandi, & quod vtraque valeat efficere, magis deprehendatur. Sit ergo.
units.tr: Accordingly, I deliberately append to this second book an appendix on nature and art, so that, once it has become clear in what they agree and in what they differ, the manner of their operation, and what each is able to bring about, may be better grasped. So be it.

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.

units.la: Quid sit natura, & an diffe- rat ab arte.
units.tr: What nature is, and whether it differs from art.

units.la: PRO intelligentia varios præmitto significandi modos, quibus accipi solet Natura. Imprimis enim assumitur pro Deo, quem barbarè vocant Natura naturante. 2. pro quouis principio creato, seu creatura, quæ item barbarè vocatur Natura naturata 3. pro essentia rerum, & sic dicimus, per definitionem explicari naturam rei, 4. pro collectione causarum omnium secundarum, in quo sensu dicitur miraculum superare vires naturæ. 5. pro collectione causarum omnium comprehendendo & Deum, prout est causa naturalis; & ita dicimus, naturam nil frustra moliri. 6. pro temperamento, propensione, indole: quo pacto dicitur quis habere hanc, illamq; naturam. Similiter hoc nomen Naturale diuersimodè assumi potest vt alibi dicetur.
units.tr: To prepare for understanding, I first set out the various senses in which the word Nature is customarily taken. First, it is taken for God, whom they barbarously call nature naturing. Second, for any created principle or creature, which is likewise barbarously called nature natured. Third, for the essence of things, and so we say that the nature of a thing is explained by its definition. Fourth, for the collection of all secondary causes, in which sense a miracle is said to surpass the powers of nature. Fifth, for the collection of all causes, including God insofar as he is a natural cause, and so we say that nature undertakes nothing in vain. Sixth, for temperament, inclination, or disposition, in which sense someone is said to have this or that nature. Similarly, the adjective natural can be used in several ways, as will be said elsewhere.

units.la: His præmissis accipi solet à philosophis natura pro quauis causa secunda, in quo sensu definitur ab Aristotele 2. phys. t. 3. sic: Natura est principium, & causa mouendi, & quiescendi in eo, in quo est primò, ac per se, & non secundum accidens.
units.tr: With these things set out, philosophers customarily take nature for any secondary cause. In this sense Aristotle defines it in the second book of the Physics, text 3, thus: Nature is the principle and cause of motion and of rest in that in which it is primarily and of itself, and not according to accident.

units.la: Dicitur principium loco generis. Deinde causa, non enim est quodcumque principium, sed causa vere influens. 3. mouendi, & quiescendi, seu motus, & quietis (per motum verò intelligitur omnis mutatio, seu alteratio; per quietem duratio in forma, quæ per alterationem acquiritur) 4. in eo, in quo est, quia natura debet esse principium intrinsecum rei, vbi fit motus, aut alteratio, & quies. 5. dicitur primum, eò quòd non dependet ab alio principio, sed ipsa suarum operationum prima radix manet. 6. per se, vt exclu quia natura veros habet effectus, & ars ferè omnes fictos. 2. quia natura, vt agat nō supponit arte: ars verò natura. 3. quia natura est circa intrinseca, & ars vt plurimum in externa superficie occupatur. 4. quia effectus naturæ alium quoque producit sibi similem, vt canis canem; leo leonem; artis autem non ita. Demum quia natura perfectiori modo partes vnit coponendo; non sic ars.
units.tr: It is called a principle in place of genus. Next, a cause: for it is not any principle whatever, but a cause that truly influences. (3) Of motion and rest, or of change and of stillness; by motion is meant every change or alteration, and by rest the persistence in a form that has been acquired through alteration. (4) In that in which it is: because nature must be the intrinsic principle of the thing, where the motion or alteration and the rest take place. (5) It is called first, because it does not depend on another principle, but remains the first root of its own operations. (6) Of itself, so as to exclude what is accidental: nature has true effects, and art almost all of them feigned. Again, (2) because nature, in order to act, does not presuppose art, whereas art presupposes nature. (3) Because nature is concerned with what is intrinsic, while art for the most part occupies itself with the external surface. (4) Because the effect of nature also produces another like itself, as a dog produces a dog and a lion a lion; but this is not so with art. Finally, because nature unites the parts by composing them in a more perfect manner, which art does not do.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: Disquisition II.

units.la: Quid sit ars, & an opera naturæ facere possit.
units.tr: What art is, and whether art can produce the works of nature.

units.la: PRo intelligentia primi quæsiti repetite à Logicis verba Philosophi 6. Eth. c. 4. vbi artem sic definit. Ars est habitus cum recta ratione factiuus. Nimirum habitualis quædam cognitio, quæ dictat modum operis faciendi per hoc, quòd regulas tradit, ac præcepta, quibus dū vtimur, consultò, prudenter, ac scitè aliquid facimus.
units.tr: To understand the first question, let us take up again the words of the Philosopher, cited by the logicians from the Sixth Book of the Ethics, chapter 4, where he defines art thus: Art is a productive habit joined with right reason. Clearly it is a kind of habitual knowledge which dictates the manner of making a work, since it hands down rules and precepts by which, when we use them, we make something deliberately, prudently and skilfully.

units.la: Artes colunt Medici, Alchimistæ, Magi, Mechanici, Mathematici, qui omnes aut perficiendo, aut domando naturam, essectus omninò prodigiosos præstitere, adeo vt in manu peritorum Ars merito dicta fuerit Simia Natura. Qua de re consulite Martinum Del Rio, & Kircherum. Sanè Archimedes in vna ficti orbis machina tā sciēter exercuit mathesim, vt exciterit error Epicureorū, quos refert Cic. 2. de nat. Deor. Archimedē plus valuisse in imitandis sphera conuersionibus, quā natunaturam in efficiendis. Ita Dædalü vetustas mirata est quando pinnis tergo adaptatis volantem se præbuit. Architas etiam ligneas columbas latente machina sursū impulit. Salmoneus pariter, nubem,fülgur,tonitru, ignemq; fulmineum conslauit, edidit, accendit. Vnde fabula de Ioue apud Claud. extat.
units.tr: Physicians, alchemists, magicians, mechanics and mathematicians practise art, and all of them, by perfecting or taming nature, have produced wholly prodigious effects, so that in the hands of skilled people art has rightly been called the ape of nature. On this matter consult Martin Del Rio and Kircher. Indeed Archimedes, in a single machine imitating the heavens, so skilfully exercised mathematics that he provoked the error of the Epicureans, whom Cicero cites in the second book of On the Nature of the Gods: Archimedes was more able to imitate the rotations of the sphere than nature was in producing them. So antiquity marvelled at Daedalus when, with wings fastened to his back, he showed himself flying. Archytas also sent wooden doves aloft by a hidden mechanism. Likewise Salmoneus fashioned, produced and kindled a cloud, a lightning flash, thunder and fiery bolts. Hence the fable about Jupiter that is found in Claudian.

units.la: Quid falso infantem tonitru Salmo- nea miror? Æmula natura parua reperta manus.
units.tr: Why do I wonder that Salmoneus falsely imitated thunder? Nature, rivalled, was found in a small hand.

units.la: Et vtinam vigeret adhuc imitandæ naturæ cupido; aut siquæ viget, magis etiam per fomenta excitaretur. Equidem tunc postliminio rediret naturalis Philosophia, quæ dudū ad spatia imaginaria exulauit.
units.tr: I wish that the desire to imitate nature still flourished, or, if it does flourish, that it were stirred up even more by encouragement. Indeed natural philosophy would then return from exile, for it has long since been banished to imaginary spaces.

units.la: Sed vt accedamus ad secundam quæstionis partem, Valeatne ars naturæ opera efficere, Distinguamus oportet diuersa genera rerum. Aliæ siquidem animatæ sunt, aliæ inanimes. Quædam inter animatas habent sensum; quædā vegetāt solū. Pariter ex ijs, quæ sentiunt, aliæ persectæ sunt, puta homo, leo; aliæ minūs perfectæ; vt vermis, rana, serpens, &c.
units.tr: But to come to the second part of the question, whether art can produce the works of nature, we must distinguish the different kinds of things. Some things are animate, others inanimate. Among the animate, some have sense, while others only grow. Again, among those that have sense, some are more perfect, such as man and the lion, and others less perfect, such as the worm, the frog, the serpent, and so on.

units.la: Dico igitur primo. Ars nequit efficere opera naturæ, quæ sint animalia persecta. Ratio est, nam illa fiunt per semina variè digesta, subacta, calore debito concocta; & ad hoc non quicumq; sufficit locus, aut vas, & minera, sed quædam certa in visceribus animalium, vbi loculamenta reperiuntur accommoda, congrua, proportionata; extra quę non videtur posse coire, animari, crescere fœtus. Ita leo in vno leenæ vtero gignitur; catulus in gremio catellæ, &c.
units.tr: I say, therefore, first: art cannot produce the works of nature that are perfect animals. The reason is that these come into being through seeds variously arranged, worked upon, and brought to maturity by the due heat; and for this no place, vessel or matrix will suffice, but only certain fixed parts in the bodies of animals, where suitable, fitting and proportioned receptacles are found; outside these the offspring does not seem able to unite, to come alive, or to grow. So the lion is generated in the womb of the lioness, and the whelp in the lap of the bitch, and so on.

units.la: Dico 2. Ars potest efficere opera naturæ, quæ sint animalia imperfecta, sed mediatè solùm, & vt aiunt applicando actiua passiuis. Assertio explicatur sic. Per artem vniri possunt naturalia corpora, & semina rerum; eademque ita per calorem, humiditatem, qualitatesq; cæteras (quod est, vt aiunt, applicare actiua passiuis) modificare; vt deinde natura ijs immediatè det, figuram, motum, energiam, animam. Ita si ocymum conteratur, & inter laterculos exponatur subdio, nascuntur scorpiones. Puluis cum aggeritur; & aquæ guttulis madet, generantur pulices. Lixiuium si terræ, ac simo commisceatur, educuntur scarabei, & hoc prorsus modo in Ægypto Magi serpentes conflarunt; qua de re in l.1. Hisce autem in casibus vnit quidem ars corpora; varieq; permiscet; sed natura perficit, conformat, & animat. Hinc August. 3. de Trin. c. 9. ait, forinsecus quidem posse adhiberi causas, quæ tametsi non sunt naturales, tamen secundum naturam adhibentur, vt ea, quæ secreto natura sinu abdita continentur, erumpant, &c.
units.tr: I say, second: art can produce the works of nature that are imperfect animals, but only mediately, and, as they say, by applying active things to passive things. The assertion is explained thus. By art, natural bodies and the seeds of things can be united, and these same things can be modified by heat, moisture and other qualities (which is, as they say, applying active to passive), so that afterwards nature gives them immediately figure, motion, energy and life. Thus if basil is crushed and left out in the open air between bricks, scorpions are born. When dust is heaped up and moistened with drops of water, fleas are generated. If lye is mixed with earth and dung, beetles are brought forth; and in precisely this way the magicians in Egypt produced serpents, as is said in the first book. In these cases, however, art indeed unites the bodies and mixes them in various ways, but nature completes, shapes and animates them. Hence Augustine, in the third book On the Trinity, chapter 9, says that causes may be applied from outside, which, although they are not natural, are nonetheless applied according to nature, so that those things which are hidden in the secret bosom of nature may burst forth, and so on.

units.la: Dico 3. Ars potest efficere opera naturæ, quæ sint animata vegetantia, sed mediatè, scilicet applicando actiua passiuis, vt supra. Videmus enim quòd vt enascantur arbusta quædam, flores, & herbæ, adsportant periti has, illasue terras: hanc, & illam aquam; admouent ignem, calidamq; ad radices effundunt, maximè cũ præcoqua poma, floresque ad mensarum, nariumq; luxuriem desiderantur, in quo casu ars naturam cogit, hyemique ver, & autumnos ineftat. Hucspectat id, quod habet Iacobus Gafarellus in curiositatibus inauditis. Medicus quidam Polonus gratum spectaculum hospitibus vt exhiberet, phialam, in cuius fundo rosci cineres erat, suspensam in aere sustinens, facem suppositit. Vix calor se se per vitrum insinuauerat, cum ecce tibi moueri pulueres, agitari, diuersimodè commisceri, donec modò vicinius, modò remotius applicito igne, corpuscula cæperunt coire, aptiusq; connecti, adeo tandem, vt in rosam coaluerint; Mox autem remota facc, in cineres, quemadmodum priùs, tota machina dissiluerit. Cuius rei testes appellat non paucos, & graues. Certè Gafarellus, & Quercetanus Galliarum Regis Consiliarius, & Medicus eam à se visam refert in defens. contra Anonimum c. 20.
units.tr: I say, third: art can produce the works of nature that are animate and vegetative, but mediately, that is, by applying active things to passive things, as above. For we see that to make certain trees, flowers and herbs spring up, skilled people bring in this or that earth, this or that water, apply fire, and pour warm water on the roots, especially when early fruits and flowers are wanted for the luxury of tables and noses; in such a case art forces nature, and introduces spring and autumn into winter. To this belongs what Jacob Gaffarel has in his Unheard-of Curiosities. A certain Polish physician, wishing to show his guests a pleasing spectacle, hung a flask, in whose bottom was the ash of a rose, suspended in the air, and set a torch beneath it. Scarcely had the heat penetrated through the glass, when behold, the powders began to move, to stir, and to mix in various ways, until, as the fire was applied now nearer, now further away, the particles began to come together and to join more fittingly, so that at last they coalesced into a rose; then, the torch being removed, the whole structure fell apart again into ash, just as before. He calls upon not a few serious witnesses to this thing. Certainly Gaffarel, and Quercetanus, Counsellor and Physician to the King of France, report that they saw it, in their defence against the Anonymous, chapter 20.

units.la: Dico 4. Ars verè, ac realiter potest efficere immediatè opera naturæ, quę animata, sensu, & partibus organicis carent. Constat .n.experientia fieri per artem tonitrua, fulgura, & fulmina, si quis probè noverit aerem in angustias cogere, mox laxare, igneosq; spiritus, & exhalationes per antiperistasim coercere. Prosecto ex aqua sursum dispersa, & lumine ponè adiecto fiunt iridès omnino pares ijs, quæ videntur in nubibus, licèt breuiùs uiús durent. Conflantur grandines ope salnitri; excitantur pluuiæ, ros, & alia meteora solo artis ingenio educuntur.Lapides etiam, & metalla conficit ars vniedo corpora, connectendo, & sæpius coquendo, vt experiuntur alchymistæ periores, nam cum videant in mixtorum solutionibus quænam sint primigenia corpora, & materiæ, quibus conflabantur, eadem rursus colligunt, lentaque patientia ita vniunt, vt denique in mixta non minus perfecta redigantur. Quapropter.
units.tr: I say, fourth: art truly and really can produce immediately the works of nature that are animate, lacking sense and organic parts. It is established by experience that thunder, lightning and thunderbolts are produced by art, if someone knows well how to press the air into narrow spaces, then loosen it, and to restrain the fiery spirits and exhalations by antiperistasis. Indeed, when water is sprayed upward and light is placed behind it, rainbows are produced entirely like those seen in the clouds, although they last for a shorter time. Hailstones are formed with the help of saltpetre; rains, dew and other meteors are brought forth by the sole ingenuity of art. Art also makes stones and metals by uniting bodies, by joining them and by frequent heating, as the more skilled alchemists find: for when they see from the dissolution of mixed bodies what the primary bodies and materials were from which they were compounded, they gather the same again and, with patient perseverance, unite them so that at last they are reduced into mixed bodies no less perfect. Wherefore:

units.la: Dico vltimò. Ars verum aurum efficere potest. Ratio potissima videtur esse,quia iam in natura miscibilia omnia, siue corpora sunt, quibus aurum costat, vnde fatis erit ea colligere, debitoque modo, proportione, ac temperie coaptare, quod fit præsertim per caloris ministerium. Inde aiunt Chymici se quidem tenere materias omnes ad auri confectionem requisitas, nempe Mercurium, sulphur, salnitrum, aliasque corrodentes, corroborantes: difficultatem vero in eo totam esse, vt vniant æquè, ac temperie iustà, quæ res vtplurimum labores chymicorum vanos fecit. Nihilominus adsunt experientiæ, quæ si fides habeatur historijs, docent aurum fuisse aliquando confectum. Legatur Albertus Magnus libro tertio de Miner. c. 9. Itè Andreas Libavius in defensione chymiæ transmutatoriæ contra Guiberrum
units.tr: I say finally: art can make true gold. The chief reason seems to be that all the miscible things of which gold consists already exist in nature, so that it will be enough to gather them and fit them together in the due manner, proportion and temperature, which is done especially by the service of heat. Hence the chemists say that they indeed hold all the materials required for making gold, namely mercury, sulphur, saltpetre, and other corroding and strengthening agents; but that the whole difficulty lies in uniting them equally and in the just temperature, a matter which for the most part has made the labours of the chemists vain. Nevertheless there are experiences which, if histories are believed, show that gold was at some time made. Let Albertus Magnus be read, book three On Minerals, chapter 9. Likewise Andreas Libavius in his defence of transmutational chemistry against Guibert.

units.la: Rulandus quoque in progymnasma­tis chymicis, aliqué. Nominatim verò dicuntur fuisse veri auri effectores Teophrastus Paracelsus, Eduardus Helleus Anglus, Picus Mirandulanus, qui plusquam viginti modos auri conflandi tenuit, cui proinde Romæ fuit epitaphium subscriptum; Auri ex plumbo collectori. Certè in ædibus Magni Ducis Etruriæ clauus visitur altera parte ferreus, altera verò aureus, &c.
units.tr: Rulandus too, in his chemical gymnasmata, and others. By name, Theophrastus Paracelsus, Edward Kelley the Englishman, and Pico della Mirandola are said to have been true makers of gold; the last, who held more than twenty ways of making gold, therefore had this epitaph written under him at Rome: Collector of gold from lead. Certainly in the palace of the Grand Duke of Etruria a nail is seen, iron on one side and gold on the other, etc.

units.la: Neq; obstat, quòd aurum ex chymia factum adulterinum sit, minùs ponderosum, & sophisticum. Id enim sæpissimè quidem oritur ob ignorantiam proportionis in applicandis miscibilibus; verùm si casu, aut consultò materiæ probè atteperentur, quemadmodum alia metalla fiunt, non secus & aurum fiet. Quæ tamen res quia difficilis est, ideo non cuiq; chymicorum credere oportet; nam vt beneSennertus, aurum quo carent, conficiant sibi priùs chymici, postea si lubet, alios doceant artificium.
units.tr: Nor does it stand in the way that gold made by chemistry is adulterate, less heavy and counterfeit. For this most often arises from ignorance of the proportion in applying miscible things; but if the materials were properly weighed, whether by chance or deliberately, gold would be made just as other metals are made. Since, however, this matter is difficult, one ought not therefore to believe every chemist; for, as Sennert well says, let the chemists first make for themselves the gold they lack, and afterwards, if they like, teach others the art.

units.la: Neq; obstat 2. quòd chymia cum toto suo igne senserit excommunicationis fulmen à Ioanne XII. euibratum in extrauagantij quæ incipit, Spondet. Dico enim huiusce artis exercitium Pontificia lege prohiberi, non quia nequeat componi aurum, sed ne quisq; pro impetu credarse chymicum natum, & dum conatur efficere aurum, certa prodigat pro incertis, ploretq; inopiam suam ad camini fumum; & Mercurium, quem figere ten-rat. tat, ad opes tamen surripiendas latrones callidissimum auolare sentiat. E contra vero Diocletianus etiam, vt refert Suidas, omnes de chymica libros conquiri iussit, cremariq; in Ægypto, ne i populi, ex auri fabrica ditati, pecuniaq; freti, rebellarent imposterum, vt notat Sennertus.
units.tr: Nor does it stand in the way, secondly, that chemistry, with all its fire, has felt the thunderbolt of excommunication hurled by John XII in the extravagant decretal that begins Spondet. For I say that the practice of this art is forbidden by papal law, not because gold cannot be composed, but so that no one, rashly trusting that he is born a chemist, may squander certain things for uncertain ones, and, while he tries to make gold, lament his poverty over the smoke of the furnace; and may perceive that the mercury which he tried to fix has flown away, the most cunning thief for stealing his wealth. On the contrary, Diocletian too, as Suidas reports, ordered all books on chemistry to be sought out and burned in Egypt, lest the people, enriched by the manufacture of gold and relying on their money, should rebel in future, as Sennert notes.

units.la: Neque obstat 3. Quòd natura pro auro gignendo constituerit mineras in terræ visceribus, & solem vt causam illius effectuam; vnde arguunt nonnulli nec extra eum locum, nec nisi a sole posse aurum produci. Resp. enim solis calorem non habere maiorem vim, quàm habeat ignis, qui eiusdem speciei est. Mineræ autem locus non requiritur necessariò, cùm quicumque alius, vbi sint miscibilia, & apta qualitatum temperies artificiosè inducta, sufficere possit. Hoc pariter modo natura pluuijs, grandinibus, cæterisque meteoris locum statuit, cùm tamen hæc omnia extra illum ex arte fiant.
units.tr: Nor does the third objection stand in the way: that nature has set up mines in the bowels of the earth for the generation of gold, and the sun as the efficient cause of it; whence some argue that gold can be produced neither outside that place nor except by the sun. I reply that the heat of the sun has no greater power than that of fire, which is of the same kind. Nor is a mine's location strictly required, since any other place where the miscible things are present and a suitable temperament of qualities is artificially induced can suffice. In the same way, nature has assigned a place to rains, hail and the other meteors, although all of these are also produced outside that place by art.

units.la: Ex dictis ergo colligite: quàm verisimilis ea reddatur opinio, quòd natura non ex aliqua substantialis formæ productione suos edat effectus; verùm per solas præexistentium corporum vniones, commixtionesq; consilio totius naturæ factas. Indidit enim ab initio Deus appetitum, & vim corporibus, vt simile moueretur ad simile, fugeret à dissimili; se se incitarent, impellerent, alterarent, nunc manent. rent componendo, nunc agitarentur corrumpendo, &c. Experimentum desumitur ab arte, quæ si aliqua naturæ opera solo corporum motu efficere potest, argumento est, naturam quoque eon simili ratione in omnibus operari.
units.tr: From what has been said, therefore, draw this conclusion: how probable it is that the opinion is correct which holds that nature does not produce its effects through any production of a substantial form, but only through the unions and mixtures of pre-existing bodies, brought about by the design of the whole of nature. For God imparted to bodies from the beginning an appetite and power, so that like is moved toward like and flees from unlike; they stir, impel and alter one another, now remaining together while they compose, now being agitated while they corrupt, and so on. The proof is drawn from art: if art can bring about some works of nature by motion of bodies alone, this is evidence that nature also operates in all things by a similar method.

units.la: LIBER TERTIVS PHYSICORVM
units.tr: LIBER TERTIVS PHYSICORVM

units.la: De motu Alterationis.
units.tr: On the Motion of Alteration.

units.la: X ijs, quæ præcedenti libro dicta sunt, patet satis dari causas, per quarum actiones tota natura mouetur, & viuit. Motus autem omnis definitur hic à Philosopho, Actus entis in potentia, prout in potentia, quam definitionem vt probè capiatis, expendite v.g. calefactione, in ea siquidè occurrunt duo, calor nimirū, qui acquiritur, & insuper acquisitio ipsa, seu fluxus ad calorem. Vterque dicitur actus, alter tamen perfectus, nempe calor, quia est forma constituens calidum; alter imperfectus, videlicet calefactio, quia hæc non perficit, neq; actuat vltimò, sed est veluti via, & ductio ad perfectionem. Hoc posito, definitio enodatur sic. Motus est Actus, eò quòd rem actuat, licèt non omninò perficiat; Entis nempe subiecti, pam hoc recipiendo in se talem actum mouetur; In potentia, eo quia subiectum esse debet capax ad id, quod recipit; Quatenus in potentia, vnde intelligitur subiectum non actuari, & vltimò expleri per motum, se relinqui adhuc in potentia, vt ab alio perficiatur.
units.tr: From what has been said in the preceding book, it is sufficiently plain that there exist causes through whose actions the whole of nature is moved and lives. Now the Philosopher defines all motion here as the act of a being in potency, insofar as it is in potency. So that you may grasp this definition properly, consider for example heating: in it two things occur, namely the heat which is acquired, and in addition the acquisition itself, or the flow toward heat. Both are called acts, but the one is complete, namely the heat, because it is the form constituting the hot thing; the other is incomplete, namely the heating, because this does not complete or finally actuate, but is as it were the way and the leading toward perfection. This being laid down, the definition is explained thus. Motion is an act, in that it actuates the thing, although it does not wholly complete it; of a being, namely of a subject, which, by receiving this act into itself, is moved; in potency, because the subject must be capable of that which it receives; insofar as it is in potency, whence it is understood that the subject is not yet actuated and finally filled up by the motion, but is left still in potency, to be perfected by another.

units.la: Communis autem opinio tenet fieri motum ad quadruplicem terminum, scilicet ad substantiam, & dicitur generatio; ad quantitatem, & vocatur augmentatio; ad qualitatem, & est alteratio; ad locū, & emergit localis latio; unde patet, motum a solo termino ad quem specificari. Hæ igitur sunt quatuor species motus in communi, & latè accepti, de quibus fortasse non sine aliquo fructu disputabimus.
units.tr: The common opinion, however, holds that motion is made to four termini: to substance, and this is called generation; to quantity, and it is called augmentation; to quality, and it is alteration; to place, and it gives rise to local motion. Whence it is plain that motion is specified by the terminus to which alone it tends. These, then, are the four species of motion in the general and broad sense, concerning which we shall perhaps dispute not without some profit.

units.la: Verùm vt seruetur œconomiæ ordo, quo totam physicam initiò digessimus, hoc tertio libro Motum alterationis tantummodò prosequemur; nec immeritò, si enim causæ naturales, vt suos gignant efsectus, materiam (quæcumque sit) priùs disponunt, medijsq; accidentibus alterât, hæc operatio, quæ naturæ ordine antecedit generationem, poscit etiam esse prior doctrinâ. Contingit autem omnis alteratio per qualitates, quæ in subiectis aut de nouo producuntur, aut per effluuia mittuntur; aut per oppositionem luctantur, & idcirco ad materiam de qualitatibus trahendus est sermo, qui primo de illarum productione disquiret. Postea de modo afficiendi subiectum. Tertio de mutua contrarietate, qua invicè se oppugnāt. Quarto de motu locali per effluuia iuxta veteres atomistas, vnde fiet occasio, nonnulla etiam deducendi circa operationes per sympathiam, antipathiam, contagionem, antiperistasim, & huiusmodi, quæ omnia concludent librum quatuor disputationibus.
units.tr: But in order that the order of the economy by which we first arranged the whole of physics may be preserved, in this third book we shall pursue only the motion of alteration; and not undeservedly. For if natural causes, in order to produce their effects, first dispose the matter (whatever it may be) and alter it by intermediate accidents, this operation, which precedes generation in the order of nature, ought also to precede doctrine. Now every alteration comes about through qualities, which either are newly produced in subjects or are sent forth by emanations, or struggle through opposition; and therefore the discussion must be carried to the matter of qualities, which first inquires into their production. Afterwards, into the manner of affecting the subject. Third, into their mutual contrariety, by which they oppose one another. Fourth, into local motion through emanations according to the ancient atomists, whence an occasion will arise also of deducing some matters concerning operations through sympathy, antipathy, contagion, antiperistasis, and the like, all of which will conclude the book in four disputations.

units.la: DISPVTATIO PRIMA.
units.tr: DISPUTATIO PRIMA.

units.la: De productione qualitatum.
units.tr: On the production of qualities.

units.la: OMitto quæstionem, an sit qualitas, cum satis pateat ex Sacramento Eucharistiæ dari qualitates reales, & figuras, quæ à substantia panis, & vini distinctæ sunt. Similiter non quæro quid ea sit, eius enim definitio dudum innotuit ex Logicis, nimirum esse id quo subiectum fit quale, nec melior afferri solet, aut potest. Maior difficultas vrget de illius productione, circa quam.
units.tr: I omit the question whether there is such a thing as quality, since it is sufficiently clear from the sacrament of the Eucharist that there are real qualities and figures which are distinct from the substance of bread and wine. Likewise I do not ask what quality is, for its definition has long been known from the logicians, namely that it is that by which a subject is made such-and-such, nor is a better one usually offered, or indeed possible. The greater difficulty presses concerning its production, about which

units.la: Docet communis opinio Aristoteleorum, in agente naturali esse vim gignendi qualitatem in se, atque in externo sub-iecto. In se quidem veluti proprietatem sibi naturaliter debitam, vnde si aliquâ do illam amiserit, virtute innata restaurat: in subiecto etiam externo, ad quod virtus agentium se se extendit. Supposita ergo sententia de qualitatum productione, quam tamen vbiq; non ita puto euidentem, aliqua circa ipsam oriuntur dubia statim explicanda. Sit igitur.
units.tr: The common opinion of the Aristotelians teaches that in a natural agent there is a power of generating quality both in itself and in an external subject. In itself, indeed, as a property naturally due to it, so that if it has lost this at any time, it restores it by its innate power; and in an external subject also, to which the power of agents extends. Supposing, then, the doctrine of the production of qualities, which, however, I do not think is evident everywhere, some doubts arise concerning it which must be explained at once. Let it be so.

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: FIRST DISPUTATION.

units.la: An, & quaratione qualitas diffundatur ab agente per sphaeram.
units.tr: Whether and in what way a quality is diffused by an agent through a sphere.

units.la: PRo intelligentia sciendum est, recipi vt vulgatam in philosophia sententiam, quòd naturale agens dum qualitate producit, eandem circumcirca, & quaquauersum emittit, adeout ipsum sit veluti centrum sphærę proferens æquè lineas agendi versus omnes interualli partes, & propterea tota illa intermedij spatij area, in qua operatur, consueuit vocari sphæra actiuitatis. Patet hoc experientia maximè in lumine, quod videmus per circuitum, & ex quacumq; differentia loci ex æquo diffundi. Non est autem hæc sphæra infinita, sed intra certos limites iuxtà robur agentis coarctata, constat enim in igne non extendi actionem æquè ad omnem spatij partem, siquidem calefit magis quæ propior, & minùs quæ remotior est.
units.tr: To understand the question, it must be known that the following opinion is accepted in philosophy as commonly held: when a natural agent produces a quality, it sends the same quality out all around and in every direction, so that it is like the centre of a sphere, extending its lines of action equally toward every part of the surrounding interval. For this reason the whole area of that intervening space in which it acts is customarily called the sphere of activity. Experience shows this most clearly in light, which we see all around us and which spreads equally from any position. This sphere, however, is not infinite. It is confined within certain limits according to the strength of the agent. For it is clear that the action of fire does not extend equally to every part of the space: what is nearer is heated more, and what is farther away less.

units.la: Oritur hinc dubitatio circa secundum quæstionis punctum, qua scilicet ratione qualitas per sphæram suam diffundatur. An nè vniformiter difformiter, adeout in omni excogitabili parte proportionali viciniori producatur maior; & in omni subsequente proportionali remotiori minor? An verò potiùs fit extensio qualitatis ad sphæræ aream areám per hoc quòd in aliqua parte certa, determinata, & signata gignatur qualitas omnino æqualis, itaut v. g. si assumatur in ligno pars mensuræ digitalis, in ea tota pares omnino gradus qualitatis reperiantur, non plures in primo, & pauciores in altero extremo? Vt soluatur quæstio, notetur.
units.tr: From this arises a doubt about the second point of the question, namely in what way a quality is diffused through its sphere. Is it uniform and yet non-uniform, so that in every conceivable proportional part nearer the agent a greater degree is produced, and in every following proportional part farther away a lesser one? Or rather, does the quality extend over the area of the sphere in this way: that in some certain, determined and marked part a quality entirely equal is generated, so that, for example, if a part of the measure of a finger's breadth is taken in a piece of wood, the same degrees of quality are found throughout that whole part, and not more at one end and fewer at the other? To resolve the question, let the following be noted.

units.la: CONCLVSIO:
units.tr: CONCLUSION:

units.la: Qualitas diffunditur ab agente in subiectum, adeout uniformis difformitas per partes fiat aliquotas, & determinatas, non proportionales.
units.tr: A quality is diffused from the agent into the subject so that the non-uniformity becomes uniform across certain determinate parts, not proportional ones.

units.la: EXplicatur conclusio. Dum ignis v.g. calefacit lignum, producit simul certos gradus caloris in parte ligni determinata, puta 4. in primo digito, & hic digitus in omni sua parte calidus æqualiter est, adeout si diuidatur in duplicem semidigitum, licèt semidigitus primus vicinior sit igni, alter autem remotior, attamen vtraque pares habeat caloris gradus. Verùm in alijs digitis determinatè sequentibus productio fit semper minor, & minor quousque; in vltimo sphærę spatio qualitas tota euanescat.
units.tr: The conclusion is explained as follows. When fire, for example, heats a piece of wood, it simultaneously produces certain degrees of heat in a determined part of the wood, say four degrees in the first finger's breadth. This finger is equally hot in every part, so that if it is divided into two half-fingers, the first half, which is nearer the fire, and the other, which is farther away, both have the same degree of heat. But in the following fingers, taken in order, the production is always smaller, and smaller again, until in the last space of the sphere the whole quality vanishes.

units.la: Probatur primò, quia in omni generatione viuétis forma introducitur in parte materiæ determinata, ergo hæc materia fuit simul tota dispositá per æquales gradus qualitatis. Probo cõsequentiã, quia si tota non fuit, simul ex æquo dispositá, ergo prima pars tantùm habuit sufficientê dispositionem, non ita secunda. Hoc autem dici nequit, secus enim oritur absurdum, quòd scilicet prima pars materiæ vltimò dispósita sit, nec tamen recipiat formam, eo quòd non æquè dispósita fuerit secunda, requisita omnino ad illius receptionem. Dici autem nequit adesse in materia particulam vltimò pro forma dispositam, quæ careat forma.
units.tr: It is proved first, because in every generation of a living thing the form is introduced into a determined part of matter; therefore this matter was at the same time disposed throughout to equal degrees of the quality. I prove the consequence: if the whole was not disposed equally at the same time, then the first part had only sufficient disposition and the second did not. But this cannot be said, for otherwise there follows the absurdity that the first part of the matter is finally disposed and yet does not receive the form, because the second part, which is wholly required for its reception, was not disposed equally. Nor can it be said that a small particle of matter is finally disposed for the form and yet lacks the form.

units.la: Probatur 2. experientijs, nam si granò sulphurei pulueris aptetur ignis, illico totum exardet, ergo calor, & siccitas in omnes grani partes æque inducuntur, alioquin si quæ distant, minùs, & minùs dispósita forent, non accenderentur simul cum prioribus. Item dum palea, seu fomes corripitur flammá, in instanti côburitur pars aliqua certa, signata, determinata, ergo ipsa eadem parem vbique recepit dispositionem vt octo, sinè qua tota comburi non potuisset. Consimiliter dum ventus impellit cimbam, pari impetus recipitur simul vbique; illa enim tota, & simul mouetur. Ergo, &c. Sed.
units.tr: It is proved secondly by experience. For if fire is applied to a grain of sulphurous powder, the whole of it at once bursts into flame; therefore heat and dryness are induced equally in all parts of the grain. Otherwise, if some parts were farther away and therefore less and less disposed, they would not catch fire together with the others. Likewise, when a piece of straw or tinder is seized by flame, a certain determined part is burned in an instant; therefore that same part received an equal disposition everywhere, without which the whole could not have been burned. Similarly, when the wind drives a boat, an equal force is received everywhere at once, for the whole boat is moved together and at the same time. Therefore, and so on. But:

units.la: Obijcies 1. Si agens posset ex æquo agere in partem vicinam, & remotam, haberet sphæram actiuitatis infinitam, quod est absurdum. Probatur sequela, non enim alia de causa limitatam habet sphæram, nisi quòd eius actio in progressu ad spatium distans attenuatur, & vltimò deficit: sed in nostro casu non deficeret, ergo. Resp. n. sequelam. Ad probationem dico, actionem agentis debilitari quidem in progressu, verum per partes certas, & aliquotas, non proportionales.
