Ita manus limitatæ virtutis est, quia potest imprimere vim vni trabi determinatæ, non maiori; lucerna item vim habet circumscriptam, quia primùm aeris palmum æquè totum illuminat, secundum remissius, &c.
units.tr: You will object first: if an agent could act equally on a near part and a remote part, it would have an infinite sphere of activity, which is absurd. The sequence is proved as follows: the sphere is limited for no other reason than that its action weakens as it progresses toward the distant space and finally fails; but in our case it would not fail; therefore, and so on. I deny the sequence. As to the proof, I say that the action of the agent does indeed weaken as it progresses, but in certain determined and proportional parts, not in proportional ones. Thus a hand has limited power, because it can impress force on one determined beam, not a larger one. Likewise a lamp has a circumscribed force, because it lights the first palm of air equally throughout, and the next more faintly, and so on.

units.la: Obijcies 2. Sit agens approximatum parti aliquotæ, ac determinatæ: in ista reperiuntur adhuc aliæ particulæ vicinióres, & remotiores, ergo non inducet in omnes parem qualitatem. Probatur consequentia, nam agens naturale agit efficacius in proximum, & minùs validè in remotum, vt experientia docet.
units.tr: You will object secondly: suppose the agent is brought near to a certain determined part; within that part there are still other particles nearer and farther away; therefore it will not induce an equal quality in all of them. The consequence is proved as follows: a natural agent acts more effectively on what is near and less strongly on what is remote, as experience teaches.

units.la: Resp. n. consequentiam. Ad probationem distinguo, naturale agens minùs efficaciter agit in partem remotam, si remota sit loco, & virtute, concedo; si tantum loco, siue suppositò, nego. Aduertite igitur, quod supra diximus lib. 2. posse agens fieri subiecto proximum duplici modo; nimirum loco, & suppositò, cùm illud proximè tangit; secundo virtute, quando scilicet distat quidem præsentia, sed vim habet in se, qua in illud etsi distans agere potest. Hoc modo sol toti aeri dicitur esse præsens virtute, quia vires habet, vt eum simul totum illuminet. Pars ergo aliquota licèt in se alias habeat particulas ab agente distantes, quia tamen ad has (vtpote quæ sunt intra sphæram actiuitatis virtute sua pertingit agens, non censentur ab eo formaliter esse distantes, ergo in illas omnes æquo modo aget.
units.tr: I deny the consequence. As to the proof, I distinguish: a natural agent acts less effectively on a remote part if the part is remote in place and in power, I grant; if it is remote only in place or in supposit, I deny. Note therefore what we said above in book 2, that an agent can be near its subject in two ways: first in place and in supposit, when it touches it directly; second in power, when it is indeed distant in presence but has in itself a power by which it can act even on what is distant. In this way the sun is said to be present to the whole air by its power, because it has the strength to illuminate the whole of it at once. Therefore a determined part, although in itself it has other particles distant from the agent, is not regarded as formally distant from the agent, since the agent reaches them by its power, as they lie within its sphere of activity. Hence it acts equally on all of them.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISQUISITIO SECUNDA.

units.la: An qualitas ab agente succesiuè producatur.
units.tr: Whether a quality is produced successively by the agent.

units.la: PRo intelligentia est aduertendum, qualitatem successiuè produci, nil esse aliud, nisi priùs fieri vnum illius gradum, deinde alium; & quidem in eadem subiecti parte, si qualitas producatur intensiuè; in diuersa verò, si extensiuè, differt enim intensio ab extensione per hoc, quòd illa plures dicit gradus qualitatis in vna, eademque parte materiæ; ista plures in pluribus.
units.tr: For the sake of understanding, it should be noted that a quality being produced successively is nothing other than one degree of it first coming to be and then another; and indeed in the same part of the subject if the quality is produced intensively, but in a different part if it is produced extensively. For intension differs from extension in this: that the former signifies several degrees of a quality in one and the same part of matter, the latter several degrees in several parts.

units.la: Rursus aduerto, qualitates in duplici ordine constitui, aliæ siquidem habent contrarium; aliæ carent. Circa secundas opinio communis docet, in instanti, & sine vlla successione produci, vt est v.g. lux & species missæ ab obiectis; alias verò qualitates, calorem, frigus, &c. fieri successiuè, quia cum debeant oppugnare contrarium, nequeunt simul, & in instanti afficere subiectum: sed per gradus, vnû post alium introducuntur. Hisce positis, notetur.
units.tr: Again I observe that qualities are constituted in a twofold order: some have a contrary, others lack one. Concerning the second kind, the common opinion teaches that they are produced in an instant and without any succession, as for instance light and the species sent forth from objects; but the other qualities, heat, cold, and so on, come to be successively, because, since they must oppose their contrary, they cannot affect the subject at once and in an instant, but are introduced one after another, by degrees. With these things laid down, let it be noted.

units.la: CONCLVSIO PRIMA.
units.tr: FIRST CONCLUSION.

units.la: Qualitates etiam carentes contrario cum aliqua successione in sua Sphæra producuntur.
units.tr: Qualities that lack a contrary are nonetheless produced with some succession within their own sphere.

units.la: PRobatur experientia satis clara de luce, in nubibus enim ,quæ fiunt æstiuo tempore tà nostro vertice distantibus milliaria circiter decem clarissimè obseruamus, fulgetri lucem non expandi simul, & instantaneè per omnes aeris partes ergo illuminatio fit successiuè. Antecedens patet, nam oculus optimè distinguit principium illuminationis ante finem illius, videtq; lucis originem, ex qua sensim expansus fulgor ad cæteras nubium partes illabitur. Verùm si splendor ille totus in instanti, ac simul propagaretur,non posset oculus rìtè distinguere priucipium à fine, tunc etenim forent simul hæc duo. Simili modo quo cùm ingredimur cubiculum iam ante plenum luce, non est qui discernat quæ pars' loci priùs illustretur, & quę posterius. nam respectu videntis totum cubiculi spatium irradiatur simul. Ergo si oculus in data experientia distinguit illuminationis principium à fine, lux cum aliqua successione producitur.
units.tr: This is proved by an experience clear enough concerning light. For in clouds that form in summer, about ten miles distant from our zenith, we observe very clearly that the lightning's light is not spread through all parts of the air at once and instantaneously. Therefore illumination occurs successively. The antecedent is plain, for the eye distinguishes very well the beginning of the illumination from its end, and sees the source of the light, from which the flash, spreading gradually, flows into the other parts of the clouds. But if that whole splendour were propagated all at once and at the same time, the eye could not properly distinguish the beginning from the end, since these two would then be simultaneous. It is like when we enter a room already full of light: no one can discern which part of the place is illuminated first and which afterwards, for to someone looking, the whole space of the room is irradiated at once. Therefore, if in a given experience the eye distinguishes the beginning of the illumination from its end, light is produced with some succession.

units.la: Probatur 2. experientia de sono, quàuis .n. sonoræ species nô habeant contrariû,in ea sphæra, per quam diffunduntur euincendum, attamen cum successione se se propagant. Sic bombardæ sonitum audit prius qui prope manet, posteriùs autem qui procul. Et nos dum aliquem à longe intuemur, secuti, aut malleo ventem, cernimus passim fieri secundum ictum, priusquam sonitum primi audiamus, ergo sonora qualitas cum successione producitur.
units.tr: It is proved by a second experience, that of sound. Although sonorous species have no contrary within the sphere through which they are diffused, they nonetheless propagate themselves with succession. Thus a man hears the report of a bombard sooner if he is near, and later if he is far away. And when we look at someone from a distance hammering, we see the second blow happen before we hear the sound of the first. Therefore the sonorous quality is produced with succession.

units.la: Opponis: lux non habet contrarium, ergo per totam sphæram sine resistentia diffunditur, & sic in instanti. Confirmatur experientia solis, qui ab horizonte per totum aerem simul irradiat, luceque sua primam, & vltimam sphæræ partem vna peruadit. Similiter flamma bombardæ illo instanti, quo exardet, lucem emittit ad oculos distantium. Id ipsum contingit in aliis, quæ carent contrario, ergo.
units.tr: You object: light has no contrary, therefore it is diffused through the whole sphere without resistance, and so instantaneously. This is confirmed by the experience of the sun, which shines from the horizon through the whole air at once, and by its light pervades the first and last part of the sphere together. Similarly, the flame of a bombard, at the very moment it flares up, sends its light to the eyes of those at a distance. The same happens in other things that lack a contrary. Therefore...

units.la: Respond. concesso antecedenti, cum distinctione ad consequens; diffunditur lumen sine resistentia contrarij per medium, c. sine resistentia formali agentis, n. Duplicem ergo resistentiam potest habere causa, dum agit: primam ab aliquo contrario, quod fit in medio, & impediat actionem, quomodo frigus in ligno resistit calori; secundam resistentiam potest agens habere à se, quia virtutis est exiguæ, limitatę, ac finitæ, unde non valet actionem suam omni perfectiori modo extendere in sphæram, & ita sibi quodammodo resistit. Lux ergo caret quidem contrario, & resistentia in medio; non tamen resistentia in causa: Quæ distinctio debet probè teneri ad solutiones argumentorum. Adest autem instantia in graui cadentę per vacuum, quod successiuè moueretur, licèt carens contrario, &c. Experientiæ igitur ab aduersarijs adductæ ostendunt sanè illuminationem esse pernicissimam, non tamen matematicè instantaneam. Videte Galileum dialog. 1. q. mechan. vbi nostram conclusionem ingeniosè indicat.
units.tr: I reply: I grant the antecedent, but make a distinction regarding the consequent. Light is diffused through the medium without resistance from a contrary, but not without resistance from the agent; that is, without formal resistance of the agent. A cause may have a twofold resistance while it acts. The first is from some contrary which is present in the medium and hinders the action, as cold in wood resists heat. The second resistance an agent may have from itself, because its power is small, limited and finite, so that it cannot extend its action into the sphere in the most perfect manner, and thus in some measure resists itself. Light therefore indeed lacks a contrary and resistance in the medium, but not resistance in the cause. This distinction must be carefully kept in mind for solving the arguments. There is also an instance in a heavy body falling through a vacuum, which moves successively even though it lacks a contrary. The experiences adduced by our opponents therefore show indeed that illumination is very swift, but not mathematically instantaneous. See Galileo, Dialogue 1, on the mechanical question, where he ingeniously points to our conclusion.

units.la: CONCLVSIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: CONCLUSION TWO.

units.la: Qualitates, quæ habent contrarium, succes-siuè quidem producuntur, non tamen quoad omnes partes intensionis, aut extensionis.
units.tr: Qualities that have a contrary are indeed produced successively, but not as regards all parts of their intensity or extension.

units.la: EXplicatur conclusio. Si causa producat in subiecto qualitatem, ineoq; contrarium inueniat, non gignit eâ simul, neque totam in instanti ad omnes partes extendit, verùm procedit successiuè. Sed tamen hæc successio non ita rigorosè fit, vt primo instanti temporis vnum tantummodo gradum producat; secundo alium; quinimo duos, vel tres, aut quatuor gradus contingit aliquando simul produci, & ad plures materiæ partes propagari.
units.tr: The conclusion is explained as follows. If a cause produces a quality in a subject and finds a contrary there, it does not generate the quality at once, nor extend the whole of it to all parts in an instant, but proceeds successively. Yet this succession does not take place so strictly that in the first instant of time it produces only one degree, in the second another, and so on. Indeed it sometimes happens that two, three or four degrees are produced at once and spread to several parts of the matter.

units.la: Probatur quoad primum, quia si v. g. ponatur ignis in aula, in priori suæ positionis momento, nec totum alterat spacium, nec totâ facit caloris intensionem; ergo tam intensiuè, quàm extensiuè qualitas habens contrarium cum successione producitur. Antecedens patet, nam post horam calescit magis ea pars aeris vicina, quæ ante calescebat minùs, ergo in illa noui gradus caloris cum successione gignuntur. Ita etiam partes alię spatij distantes de nouo fiunt calidæ, igitur calor etiam quoad extensionem successiuè producitur. Et ratio est, nam contraria qualitas in passo resistit agenti, moraturq; illius actionem.
units.tr: As to the first point, this is proved as follows. If, for example, a fire is placed in a hall, then in the first moment of its placement it neither alters the whole space nor produces the whole intensity of heat. Therefore a quality that has a contrary is produced successively, both in intensity and in extension. The antecedent is evident: after an hour, the part of the air nearest the fire, which had been heated less before, is heated more, so new degrees of heat are generated successively in that part. Likewise, other parts of the space at a distance become warm anew. Therefore heat is also produced successively as to extension. The reason is that the contrary quality in the patient resists the agent and delays its action.

units.la: Probatur etiam quoad secundum. Siquis enim se ad fornacem repentè fistat, illico, & ab initio sensibilem percipit calorem, ergo aliqua eius intensio fuit simul producta, non enim vnicum indiuisibile qualitatis ita sentiretur, & afficeret subiectum. Simili modo applicet quis alteram, alteramq; manum æquè frigidam duplici agenti non æquè calido; vno, eodemque momento, quo manus applicita debiliori sentit minus caloris; altera sentit maius; ergo agens, quod robustius est, producit simul in mamu plures gradus caloris, et sic alteratio non fit successiua quoad omnes partes intensionis, itaut vnus gradus post alium semper gignatur.
units.tr: The second point is also proved. For if someone suddenly stands before a furnace, he at once and from the beginning perceives a sensible heat. Therefore some intensity of it was produced at once, for a single indivisible degree of the quality would not be felt in this way or affect the subject so. In a similar way, if someone applies one hand and then another, equally cold, to a double agent that is not equally hot, then at one and the same moment the hand applied to the weaker agent feels less heat, and the other feels more. Therefore the stronger agent produces several degrees of heat at once in the hand, and so the alteration is not successive as to all parts of its intensity, so that one degree is always generated after another.

units.la: Opponis. Alteratio est motus, vt hic Philosophus docet: sed motus fit successiuus quoad omnes partes, ergo.
units.tr: You object: alteration is motion, as this Philosopher teaches; but motion is successive as to all parts; therefore alteration is too.

units.la: Rursus. Vnaquæque pars in subiecto quantumuis minima est imbuta qualitate contraria, ergo vnaquæq; resistit, prima nimirum, deinde secunda ; mox tertia, &c. unde non finit quod agens introducat nisi gradum post gradum; ergo alteratio fit successiue quoad omnes gradus , neque plures gignuntur simul.
units.tr: Again: every part of the subject, however minute, is imbued with the contrary quality; therefore each part resists, first one, then a second, soon a third, and so on. Hence the agent can introduce only degree after degree. Therefore alteration is successive as to all degrees, and several are not generated at once.

units.la: Respond. quoad primum distinguendo minorem . Motus est successiuus quoad omnes partes physicas, & notabiles,c. mathematicas, n. Alteratio igitur, seu productio qualitatis certe motus est, non quia semper vnus tantum… gradus fiat post alium , sed ex eo etiam quod vna collectio sensibilis graduum gignatur post aliam . Respond. ad secundum , quod pars vnaquaeq; subiecti est quidem imbuta qualitate contraria, verum non resistunt singulae distributiue, vna scilicet, mox alia, &c. sed plures vnitim, & simul; quapropter agės quod plures inuenit gradus per modum vnius resistentes , plures etiam simul debellat,pluresque alterius qualitatis vno tempore introducit, nec est necesse, vt vnus tantum post alium in rigore ma. thematico producatur.
units.tr: I answer to the first, by distinguishing the minor premise: motion is successive as to all physical and notable parts, but not as to mathematical parts. Alteration, or the production of a quality, is certainly motion, not because one degree is always made after another, but also because one sensible collection of degrees is generated after another. To the second: each part of the subject is indeed imbued with the contrary quality, but the individual parts do not resist distributively, one first, then another, and so on, but several together and at once. Therefore an agent that finds several degrees resisting as one also overcomes several at once, and introduces several degrees of the other quality in one time. Nor is it necessary that, in strict mathematical terms, only one degree be produced after another.

units.la: CONCLVSIO TERTIA.
units.tr: THIRD CONCLUSION.

units.la: Qualitas intensiua, & extensiua, ita suc- cessiuè, atq: continuè producitur, vt nullis morulis interrumpatur, nisi validum obstet con- trarium.
units.tr: A quality, whether intensive or extensive, is produced successively and continuously, so that it is interrupted by no pauses, unless a strong contrary opposes it.

units.la: EXplicatur conclusio. Ignis v.g.dum aliquem caloris gradum producit in instanti .a. non quiescit pro sequente instanti .b. vt quodāmodo vim resumat ad rursus agendum in tertio instanti c. sed quouis assignabili temporis momento in exercitio est, non quiescit, non otiatur, quidquid putent alij dicentes, alterationē non esse rigorosè continuam.
units.tr: The conclusion is explained. For example, fire, while it produces some degree of heat at one instant, a, does not rest at the following instant, b, so that it regains its strength to act again at a third instant, c. Rather, at any assignable moment of time it is at work; it does not rest or lie idle, whatever others may say who claim that alteration is not strictly continuous.

units.la: Probatur facilè, nam causa naturalis ad agendum determinata, & non impedita, semper, & necessariò agit, vnde ignis inducto primo caloris gradu, non potest manere otiosus, verum vlterius pro sequente instanti operatur, ergo alteratio nullis morulis interrumpi videtur. Confirmatur, quia hucusq; sol v. g. omni momento vim habuit naturalem illuminandi, calefaciendi, &c. ergo alterationes ab eo inductæ nullà interruptæ sunt morà, & sic de cæteris.
units.tr: This is easily proved, for a natural cause that is determined to act and is not impeded always and necessarily acts. Hence, once fire has induced the first degree of heat, it cannot remain idle, but works further at the following instant. Therefore alteration seems to be interrupted by no pauses. It is confirmed by the fact that until now the sun, for example, has at every moment had its natural power of illuminating, warming, and so on. Therefore the alterations induced by it have been interrupted by no delay, and so with other things.

units.la: Dixi autem notanter, nisi validum obstet contrarium, quia tunc fortasse cum Arriaga defendi potest, qualitatem non fieri continuam, sed interrumpi. Sic v.g. ignis, qui apponitur, vt calefaciat lapidem, si multum frigoris in eo reperiat, non videtur posse continuò, & sine interruptione inducere gradus caloris. Et ratio est, nam licet ipsum agens continuò, & semper agat, modò pugnando qualitatem contrariam, & modò suam inducendo, passum tamen successiuè per aliqua instantia resistit, ergo tunc non suscipit calorem, sed suscipiet; quapropter alteratio rumpitur. Et id contingit defectu agentis, nam hoc (vt dicebam) continuò agit, vel vrgendo frigus, vel inducendo calorem; sed ratione subiecti per qualitatem contrariam subinde resistentis.
units.tr: I added the qualification "unless a strong contrary opposes it" deliberately, for then perhaps it can be defended, with Arriaga, that the quality is not made continuous but is interrupted. Thus, for example, fire that is applied to warm a stone, if it finds much cold in it, does not seem able to induce degrees of heat continuously and without interruption. The reason is this: although the agent itself acts continuously and always, now by fighting the contrary quality and now by inducing its own, the patient nonetheless resists successively for some instants; therefore at that time it does not receive heat but will receive it, and so the alteration is broken off. This happens through a defect in the agent, for the agent (as I was saying) acts continuously, either by overcoming the cold or by inducing heat; but on account of the subject, it is from time to time resisted by the contrary quality.

units.la: Opponis, causa naturalis determinata est ad operandum; quouis momento vim habet; nunquam otiatur, &c. ergo inducit continuò qualitatem, quæ proinde non interrumpitur.
units.tr: You object: a natural cause is determined to act; at every moment it has power; it is never idle, and so on. Therefore it induces the quality continuously, and the quality is consequently not interrupted.

units.la: Resp. concesso antecedenti, negando consequentiam. Ratio est iam allata, quia etsi agens continuò agat, non tamen semper inducit in passum qualitatis gradum; habet enim aliam actionem, quam exercet, nempe cum suo contrario valido, & resistenti luctam; quæ res quotiescumq; fit, eo momento abrumpitur inductio qualitatis, vt c. p. Ex qua doctrina conciliantur duæ sententiæ, illorum, qui dicunt alterationē interrumpi; & eorum, qui afferunt, agens nunquam cessare agendo.
units.tr: I reply: I grant the antecedent and deny the consequence. The reason has already been given: although the agent acts continuously, it does not always induce a degree of the quality in the patient; for it has another action which it exercises, namely its struggle with its strong contrary. Whenever this occurs, the induction of the quality is broken off at that moment, as is the case, for example, above. By this doctrine the two opinions are reconciled: that of those who say that alteration is interrupted, and that of those who affirm that the agent never ceases to act.

units.la: DISQVISITIO TERTIA.
units.tr: Third Disputation.

units.la: An gradus qualitatis producta sint homogenei.
units.tr: Whether the degrees of a produced quality are homogeneous.

units.la: PRO intelligentia quæstionis aduertite, gradus eos dici homogeneos, qui sunt omnino similes, & æqualem habent perfectionem inter se, adeout alter alterum non excedat. Ex aduerso siqui fierent dissimiles, & persectione inæquales, dicerentur eterogenei. Quæritur ergo: dum agens intendit qualitatem addendo primo gradui v. gr. caloris, frigorisve alios, hi gradus omnes itane habent se, vt sint similes ? æquales ? æquè perfecti ? an potiùs è contra, vt putat Suarez, Hurtadus, & alij, secundus perfectior est primo, tertius maior secundo ? &c. Pro solutione, sit.
units.tr: For the understanding of the question, note that those degrees are called homogeneous which are wholly similar and have equal perfection among themselves, so that one does not exceed the other. On the contrary, if they were dissimilar and unequal in perfection, they would be called heterogeneous. The question therefore is this: when an agent intensifies a quality by adding to the first degree, for example of heat or cold, further degrees, do all these degrees stand in such a relation that they are similar, equal, and equally perfect? Or rather, on the contrary, as Suarez, Hurtado, and others think, is the second degree more perfect than the first, and the third greater than the second, and so on? For the solution, let it be as follows.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Gradus qualitatis intensa homogenei sunt, unde qualitas intensa non differt a remissa, nisi per hoc quod illa plures, hac pauciores habet gradus.
units.tr: The degrees of an intense quality are homogeneous; hence an intense quality differs from a remiss one only in that the former has more degrees and the latter fewer.

units.la: PRobatur 1. quia si duo gradus omnino similes producantur in eadem subiecti parte, constituunt maiorem intensionem, ergo intensio qualitatis fit per gradus omnino similes. Probo antecedens : duo gradus caloris in una subiecti parte constituti eam reddunt magis calidam, quàm si unicus tantùm adesset, quemadmodum patet de se; igitur calor fit maior, & crescit ex gradibus inter se paribus.
units.tr: It is proved first: if two wholly similar degrees are produced in the same part of a subject, they constitute a greater intensity; therefore the intensity of a quality arises from wholly similar degrees. I prove the antecedent: two degrees of heat established in one part of a subject make it hotter than if only one were present, as is evident in itself. Therefore heat becomes greater and grows from degrees that are equal to one another.

units.la: Probatur 2. hac experientia. Producat ignis primum caloris gradum in manu ; deinde interponatur obstaculum ; certè in hoc producetur ille prorsus calor, qui fuisset productus in manu, si obstaculum non aduenisset. Hoc posito, inquiro : vel iste gradus est similis gradui, qui & in manu exiftit, vel non: si primum, vera est conclusio: si secundum, contra : causa producens eadem est dum agit in obstaculum, ac dum agebat in manum, ergo, & in illud æqualem producet calorem. Non itaque gradum, qui fit maior, perfectior, intensior, &c.
units.tr: It is proved second by this experiment. Let a fire produce a first degree of heat in the hand; then let an obstacle be interposed. Certainly in this case there will be produced exactly that heat which would have been produced in the hand had the obstacle not come between. Granting this, I ask: is this degree similar to the degree which exists in the hand, or not? If the first, the conclusion is true; if the second, it is against the conclusion. The producing cause is the same whether it acts on the obstacle or on the hand; therefore it will produce an equal heat in the obstacle too. Therefore it does not produce a degree that becomes greater, more perfect, more intense, and so on.

units.la: Probatur 3. quia vel gradus octauus, qui per aduersarios dicitur perfectissimus omnium, sine alijs totam facit qualitatis intensionem, aut eam componit cum aliis imperfectioribus: primum dici nequit, secus .n. gradus imperfecti priores omnino forent superflui. Si octauus cum cæteris imperfectioribus intendit qualitatem, ergo poterit eam componere cum æquè perfectis. Vnde.
units.tr: It is proved third. Either the eighth degree, which our opponents call the most perfect of all, by itself makes up the whole intensity of the quality, or it combines with the other, more imperfect degrees to make it up. The first cannot be said, for otherwise the earlier, imperfect degrees would be wholly superfluous. If the eighth, together with the other more imperfect degrees, intensifies the quality, then it will be able to combine with degrees equally perfect. Hence...

units.la: Probatur 4. experientijs, nam si duo soni, qui singuli sint vnius gradus a duplici corpore sonoro fiant, maior sentitur sonus, & ad aures intenditur. Item si duo luminaria, quae singillatim duos producerent gradus lucis, applicentur simul, fiet lux intensa, vt 4. & nisi velimus data opera cæcutire, maior oculis apparet. Neq; video cur ob acutulas ingenij speculationes temnant aduersarij experientias.
units.tr: It is proved fourth by experience. If two sounds, each of one degree, are produced by a double sounding body, a greater sound is perceived and is intensified to the ears. Likewise, if two lights, which singly would produce two degrees of light, are brought together, an intense light results; and unless we wish to make ourselves blind on purpose, it appears greater to the eyes. Nor do I see why our opponents, on account of their over-subtle speculations of wit, scorn experience.

units.la: Obijcies 1. qualitas intensa vt 8. est perfectior, quam extensa vt 8. ergo gradus intensionis haudquaquam sunt simules. Probatur antecedens, nam qualitas intensa producit effectum perfectiorem, disponitq; vltimò ad formam substantiam, quod non facit extensa.
units.tr: First objection: an intense quality, such as the eighth, is more perfect than an extensive quality, such as the eighth; therefore the degrees of intensity are by no means similar. The antecedent is proved: an intense quality produces a more perfect effect and ultimately disposes the matter towards the substantial form, which an extensive quality does not do.

units.la: Resp. distinguendo antecedens. Qualitas intensa perfectior est essentialiter, n. modaliter, c. & nego consequentiam. Ratio est, quia tam intensa, quàm extensa partes habet omnino similes, & solum differunt circa modum afficiendi subiectum, illa enim habet octo gradus in vnica parte subiecti; hæc autem octo, sed in octo partibus. Quemadmodum ergo si decem homines penetrati existerent in vnico loco, non essent perfectiores decè alijs, qui decem spatia vnus post alium occuparent, sic etiam, &c. Ad probationem dico, qualitatem intensam dare maiorem effectum, quia gradus habet simul, virtus autem vnita fortior est, & separata remissior, vt exemplis constat.
units.tr: I reply by distinguishing the antecedent: the intense quality is more perfect not essentially but modally. I deny the consequence. The reason is that both the intense and the extensive quality have wholly similar parts, and they differ only in the manner of affecting the subject. For the one has eight degrees in a single part of the subject, the other eight in eight parts. Just as, if ten men were interpenetrated in a single place, they would be no more perfect than ten others who occupied ten spaces one after another, so too, and so on. As to the proof, I say that an intense quality gives a greater effect because it has its degrees together; for united power is stronger and separated power weaker, as examples make plain.

units.la: Obijcies 2. Qualitas intensa potest aliquid producere, quod nequit remissa, ergo illa partes habet perfectiores. Antecedens patet, nam intensa vt octo disponit vltimò materiam, & præparat ad formam; non sic intensa v. gr. vt quatuor.
units.tr: Second objection: an intense quality can produce something which a remiss quality cannot; therefore it has more perfect parts. The antecedent is clear: an intense quality of eight ultimately disposes matter and prepares it for the form; an intense quality of, say, four does not do so.

units.la: Respond. n. consequentiam, non enim intensa qualitas habet gradus perfectiores, verùm plures; vndè persectius agit, sicut validius operantur decem homines, quàm octo, licèt singuli sint æquales.
units.tr: I deny the consequence. For an intense quality does not have more perfect degrees but more of them. Hence it acts more perfectly, just as ten men work more effectively than eight, although each is equal.

units.la: Obijcies 3. Si gradus intensionis omnino sunt similes, ergò qualitas augeri poterit in infinitum, nam agens quocumque gradu producto, valet producere alium similem primo, non enim ad hoc requiritur maior virtus.
units.tr: Third objection: if the degrees of intensity are wholly similar, then a quality can be increased to infinity; for once any degree has been produced, the agent is able to produce another similar to the first, since no greater power is required for this.

units.la: Respond. n. antecedens. Ratio est, nam etsi gradus parem habeant persectionem, causa operans limitatur, & post multam actionem lassatur. Item quia forma substantialis producenda exigit certam, ac determinatam qualitatem. Tertio quia omne subiectum est capax tot graduum qualitatis, non plurium, &c. Cum igitur causa operans limitatæ sit virtutis, atque se accommodet exigentijs formæ, subiectique, sistet aliquando, nec vlterius procedet.
units.tr: I deny the antecedent. The reason is that, although the degrees have equal perfection, the operating cause is limited and grows weary after much action. Also, because a substantial form to be produced requires a certain and determinate quality. Third, because every subject is capable of only so many degrees of quality, and not more, and so on. Since, therefore, the operating cause is of limited power and adapts itself to the demands of the form and of the subject, it will at some point stop and proceed no further.

units.la: DISPVTATIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISPUTATIO SECUNDA.

units.la: De qualitatibus in ordine ad subiectum.
units.tr: On qualities in relation to their subject.

units.la: QValitates hucusq; consideravimus, prout ipsæ ab agente naturali producuntur. Manet iam, vt easdem expendamus in ordine ad subiectum, in quo receptæ alterationem faciunt. Qua in re vt clarius procedatur, adest.
units.tr: Hitherto we have considered qualities insofar as they are produced by a natural agent. It remains now that we weigh them in relation to the subject in which, once received, they bring about alteration. In this matter, so that we may proceed more clearly, there is

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: DISPUTATION I.

units.la: Quodnam sit subiectum qualitatis.
units.tr: Which is the subject of quality.

units.la: PRo intelligentia moneo, posse nos loqui de subiecto quod, seu denominationis, & de subiecto immediato, vel receptionis. Circa primum, res est acceptissima, qualitatem habere pro subiecto denominationis totum compositum, quia hoc solum denominatur esse tale per ipsam. Sic non dicitur: materia lapidis est frigida; sed lapis est frigidus: forma hominis est docta, sed homo est doctus, &c. Sin autem fiat sermo de subiecto, quod immediatè, ac proximè qualitatem recipit, difficultas est, quæ trahi etiam solet ad quantitatem. Facta ergo hypothesi, quantitatem tatem esse accidens à materia distinctum (quod absolutè adhuc non assero) primò circa istam notetur.
units.tr: For the sake of understanding, I note that we can speak of the subject that, or of denomination, and of the immediate subject, or of reception. As to the first, the matter is quite uncontroversial: the quality is taken to have as its subject of denomination the whole composite, since only this is called such by means of it. Thus we do not say "the matter of the stone is cold" but "the stone is cold"; "the form of the man is learned," but "the man is learned," and so on. But if the discussion concerns the subject which receives the quality immediately and most nearly, there is a difficulty, which is also usually drawn into the question of quantity. Therefore, supposing it granted that quantity is an accident distinct from matter (which I do not yet assert absolutely), this should first be noted about it.

units.la: CONCLVSIO PRIMA.
units.tr: FIRST CONCLUSION.

units.la: Subiectum quantitatis est sola materia.
units.tr: The sole subject of quantity is matter.

units.la: PRobatur, quia in homine quantitas non recipitur in forma, quæ vtpote spiritualis, atque indiuisibilis extendi nequit; sed in materia tantùm: igitur & in alijs compositis hoc ipsum accidere verisimillimum est. Probo consequentiam, eo quòd materia hominis eadem est specie, virtute, ac potentia cum alijs omnibus, ergo si existit in homine, vt adæquatum subiectum quantitatis, vbique talis existet.
units.tr: It is proved because in man quantity is not received in the form, which, being spiritual and indivisible, cannot be extended; but only in the matter. Therefore it is most likely that the same holds also in other composites. I prove the consequence: because the matter of man is the same in species, power, and potency as in all others; therefore, if it exists in man as the adequate subject of quantity, it will exist in the same way everywhere.

units.la: Opponis. Cæteræ formæ, præter animam rationalem sunt extensæ, quantæ, habent partes extra partes, ergo in ijs etiam recipitur quantitas, non in sola materia. Probatur consequentia: Extensio est effectus formalis quantitatis, ergo vbicumque fuerit extensio, ibi & quantitas aderit: sed formæ compositorum sunt extensæ, igitur in se recipiunt quantitatem, ac proinde non sola materia pro subiecto adæquato illius habenda est.
units.tr: You object: the other forms, apart from the rational soul, are extended, quantified, and have parts outside parts; therefore quantity is received in them too, and not in matter alone. The consequence is proved thus: extension is the formal effect of quantity; therefore wherever there is extension, quantity is there also. But the forms of composites are extended; therefore they receive quantity in themselves, and so matter alone should not be held to be the adequate subject of quantity.

units.la: Respond. concesso primo antecedenti. negando consequentiam. Ad probationem dico, quòd extensio quidem est efsectus formalis quantitatis; verum potest haberi etiam de consequenti, nam duplici modo aliquid extenditur, vel quia in se reuera quantitatem recipiat, & sic extenditur materia; vel quia ipsum recipiatur in subiecto extenso, & ita extenditur forma. Ratio est, nam cum extensio cosistat in continuatione partium, itaut prima vniatur secundæ; ista tertiæ, &c. per hoc præcisè quòd forma recipiatur in materia quanta, sequeq; illi adapter, vnionem inter partes acquirit, ac extendit se; cùm quidquid recipitur, ad modum recipientis recipiatur. Forma ergo quanta est, non recipiendo in se subiectiuè quantitatem, sed quia recipitur ipsa in requanta, cui se accommodat. Vnde cùm dicunt aduersarij: omnis extensio est effectus quantitatis, distinguo, vel receptæ, vel subiectæ, c. receptæ solum, n.
units.tr: I reply: I grant the first antecedent, and deny the consequence. To the proof I say that extension is indeed the formal effect of quantity, but it can also be taken from the consequent. For a thing is extended in two ways: either because it really receives quantity in itself, and so matter is extended; or because it is received in an extended subject, and so the form is extended. The reason is this: since extension consists in the continuation of parts, so that the first is joined to the second, that to the third, and so on, the form, merely by being received in quantified matter and adapting itself to it, acquires a union between its parts and extends itself; for whatever is received is received according to the mode of the recipient. The quantified form is therefore quantified not by receiving quantity in itself as its subject, but because it is itself received in a quantified thing to which it accommodates itself. Hence, when the opponents say: every extension is an effect of quantity, I distinguish: of quantity as received, or as subject; I grant it of quantity as received only, I deny it of quantity as subject.

units.la: CONCLVSIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: SECOND CONCLUSION.

units.la: Catera etiam accidentia insola materia, non in quantitate recipiuntur.
units.tr: The other accidents also are received not in quantity but in matter alone.

units.la: PRobatur facilè, nam in eo tanquam in subiecto recipiuntur accidentia, quod ab ijs disponitur, alteratur, & præparatur ad formam: sed sola materia præparatur ab accidentibus ad formam, non quantitas, ergo accidentia in sola materia, non in quantitate recipiuntur. Maior est t certa, nam dispositio, quam accidentia inducunt, est ipsa eorundem receptio. Tinor etiam patet, non enim preparatur quantitas, quæ accidens est, ad recipiendam formam, quæ substantia est, sed materia, ergo accidentia in sola materia recipiuntur.
units.tr: It is easily proved. For accidents are received in that which, as their subject, is disposed, altered, and prepared by them for the form. But matter alone is prepared by accidents for the form, not quantity; therefore accidents are received in matter alone, not in quantity. The major is certain, for the disposition which accidents induce is itself their reception. The minor is also plain: quantity, which is an accident, is not prepared to receive the form, which is a substance, but matter is; therefore accidents are received in matter alone.

units.la: Opponis fundamentum contrariæ fententiæ. In hostia consecrata non manet materia, & nihilominus adest subiectum accidentium, nempe quantitas, ergo accidentia in ea recipiuntur, vt in subiecto. Antecedens probatur, quia calor, humiditas, albedo, &c. quæ sunt in hostia, sustinentur à quantitate ne cadant, ergo.
units.tr: You object the foundation of the opposing opinion: in the consecrated host the matter does not remain, and yet the subject of the accidents is present, namely quantity; therefore the accidents are received in it as in a subject. The antecedent is proved because heat, moisture, whiteness, and so on, which are in the host, are sustained by quantity so that they do not fall; therefore...

units.la: Refpond. quærendo ab aduersarijs: & ipsa quantitas quodnam subiectum habet? à quo sustinetur ne cadat? Refpondent, à Deo per miraculum. Id ipsum dico ego de reliquis: miraculose contineri, ac seruari, quemadmodum fi adefset sua materia, in qua prius recepta erat. Quæ difficultas in hoc? Ad summum ergo accidentia sunt in quantitate adhæfiuè, non inhæsiuè, vt in subiecto.
units.tr: I reply by asking the opponents: what subject does quantity itself have, by which it is sustained lest it fall? They answer: by God through a miracle. I say the same of the rest: they are contained and preserved miraculously, just as if their own matter were present, in which they had previously been received. What difficulty is there in this? At most, therefore, the accidents are in quantity adhesively, not inherently as in a subject.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.

units.la: Quomodo qualitas in subiecto intendatur.
units.tr: How a quality is intensified in its subject.

units.la: PRo intelligentia repetite quod præcedenti disputatione innuebamus, qualitatem extendi, & intendi. Extenditur, quoties habet multos gradus ad multas partes. etiam subiecti partes vnum post alium continuos. Intenditur vero cum omnes hi gradus penetrati simul in vnica materiae parte sunt, in quo casu sensibilior fit qualitas, & robustior. Aduertendum vero hanc intensionem conuenire qualitati, quae suscipit magis, & minus, non ita caeteris accidentibus. Primo enim quantitas non intenditur, etsi enim partes haberet penetratas, non ideo tamen fieret sensibilior, nec magis daret esse quantum. Vbi non intenditur, quomodo enim potest res magis, aut minus vbicari? Relatio non intenditur, nam referri consistit prorsus in indiuisibile. Addo: nec materia est capax intensionis, quia caret subiecto priori se, in quo intenditur; Nec forma substantialis, vt inquit S. Thom. q. de virt.
units.tr: To understand this, recall what we hinted at in the preceding disputation: that a quality is extended and intensified. It is extended whenever it has many degrees across many parts, that is, across successive continuous parts of the subject. It is intensified when all these degrees are penetrated together in a single part of matter, and in that case the quality becomes more perceptible and more robust. But note that this intensification belongs to a quality that admits of more and less, and not to the other accidents. First, quantity is not intensified: even if it had penetrated parts, it would not for that reason become more perceptible, nor would it give more quantitative being. Where there is no intensification, how can a thing be more or less located? Relation is not intensified, for to be related consists entirely in the indivisible. I add: nor is matter capable of intensification, because it lacks a prior subject in which it could be intensified; nor is a substantial form, as St. Thomas says in the quaestio on virtues.

units.la: Difficultas ergo est circa qualitates, quae suscipiunt magis, minusue, vt sunt primae quatuor, & habitus omnes; in qua disquiritur modus, quo talis accretio, siue intensio fit. Nos itaque praecipuas auctorum sententias huc referemus, vt ijsdem reiectis, conclusio tandem nostra suadeatur.
units.tr: The difficulty therefore concerns the qualities that admit of more or less, such as the four primary qualities and all habits; and here the question is the manner in which such augmentation or intensification takes place. Accordingly, we shall set out the chief opinions of the authors here, so that, once these have been rejected, our own conclusion may finally be established.

units.la: Durandus, alij q; docuerunt, fieri per hoc intensionem, quod tota prior qualitas deperditur, & succedat alia persectior. E, g. quoties calor intenditur, non est primus calor, qui perficiatur, quinimo totus ille definit, aliusq; maior subsistit in eadem parte subiecti. Ratio Durandi est, quia perit semper terminus a quo. to, dum terminus aduenit, ad quem; sed i intensione terminus ad quem est maior qualitas, ergo perit minor.
units.tr: Durandus and others have taught that intensification occurs in this way: the whole prior quality is destroyed, and a more perfect one takes its place. For example, whenever heat is intensified, it is not the first heat that is perfected; rather, that whole heat ceases and a greater heat comes to exist in the same part of the subject. Durandus's reason is that the terminus a quo always perishes while the terminus ad quem arrives; but in intensification the terminus ad quem is the greater quality, therefore the lesser perishes.

units.la: Contra, quia si fieret hoc modo intensio, ergo etiam remissio ita continueret, vt maior qualitas destrueretur, & alia minor de nouo produceretur. Sed hoc dici nequit, ergo &c. Probo minorem sic. Dum glacies v. g. infrigidat calidam, & ex Durando totus ille calor intensus destruitur, quæ causa est, à qua remissior calor producatur? an fortasse glacies? Hoc ego non deglutiam. Resp. ergo ad rationem Durandi, terminum à quo destrui, cum ille non ingreditur vt pars integratiua maioristermini; at minor qualitas nequit perire, quia ex ea, & alio addito integrari debet maior. Exemplü adest in augmétatione, per quā res par ua fit magna, nonnisi quia primæ quantitati actu manenti alia noua superaddatur.
units.tr: Against this: if intensification happened in this way, then remission would also happen in the same way, so that the greater quality is destroyed and a lesser one is newly produced. But this cannot be said; therefore etc. I prove the minor thus. When ice, for example, cools warm water, and according to Durandus that whole intense heat is destroyed, what is the cause by which a milder heat is produced? Perhaps the ice? I will not swallow this. So I answer Durandus's reasoning: the terminus a quo is destroyed, since it does not enter as an integral part of the greater terminus; but the lesser quality cannot perish, because the greater must be made up from it together with something added to it. An example is found in augmentation, by which a small thing becomes large, and only because a new quantity is added to the first quantity, which remains actually in place.

units.la: Dixerunt alij, qualitatem intendi per maiorem expulsionē contrarij. Sed contra quia nonnullæ sunt qualitates, omni contrario carentes, quæ tamen intedüntur, vt lux. Aliæ possunt esse intensæ, ac remissæ absq; vlla præsentia cōtrarij, vt habitus intellectus, & volūtatis. Aliæ fiunt maiores, & nullū de facto habere possunt cōtrariū, vt fides, charitas, nā hæ dū augētur ne vix indiuisibile odij, aut infidelitatis cōpatiūtur. 2. quia intelligi potest materia fine vllo frigore paulatim fieri calidior, in quo casu intedetur qualitas absq; cōtrario: ergo intensio per illius expulsionē non fit.
units.tr: Others have said that a quality is intensified by the greater expulsion of its contrary. But against this: there are some qualities that lack every contrary and yet are intensified, such as light. Others can be intense and remiss without any presence of a contrary, such as the habits of the intellect and will. Others become greater and in fact can have no contrary at all, such as faith and charity; for when these are increased they scarcely tolerate even an indivisible trace of hatred or unbelief. Second, it can be understood that matter, without any cold, gradually becomes warmer; in that case the quality is intensified without a contrary; therefore intensification does not occur by the expulsion of a contrary.

units.la: Denique cum Thomistis putant alij, qualitatis intensionem consistere in nescio quo modo maioris radicationis in subiecto, unde qualitas eadem specie inuariata maior erit, siue intensa, quando magis radicabitur; minor autem, vel remissa, quando minus habebit radicem in subiecto. In quo autem consistat maior haec radicatio explicant diuersimodè Thomistæ. Aliqui dicūt in hoc sitam esse, quòd qualitas, deperdita primâ existentia, nouam acquirat perfectionem. Alij quòd producatur perfectior vnio, cuius vi magis inhæret subiecto. Alij quòd resultet modus quidam ab ipsa vnione distinctus, ob quem radicatur magis, & suscipitur qualitas, etiamsi hæc inuariata semper existat.
units.tr: Finally, with the Thomists, others think that the intensification of a quality consists in some unknown manner of greater rooting in the subject, whence the same quality, unchanged in species, will be greater, or intense, when it is rooted more firmly, and lesser, or remiss, when it has less root in the subject. The Thomists explain in various ways what this greater rooting consists in. Some say that it lies in this, that the quality, having lost its first existence, acquires a new perfection. Others, that a more perfect union is produced, by whose power it adheres more closely to the subject. Others, that a certain mode distinct from the union itself results, on account of which the quality is more firmly rooted and received, even though the quality itself always remains unchanged.

units.la: Contra tamen, & imprimis nequit augeri, siue intendi qualitas per maiorem in subiecto radicationem. Probatur, nam qualitas intensa potest saltem diuinitus deiungi à subiecto, & in eo casu manere adhuc intensa, vt patet in hostia consecrata, vbi sine materia calor est, frigusue aliquando intensum; ergo intensio non consistit formaliter in hoc, quòd in subiecto qualitas radicetur. Contra 2.non .n. fit hæc intensio, quia manente qualitate semper eadem, acquiratur existentia persectior. Probo, nam existentia, vt videbitur in Metaph. non distinguitur ab entitate rei, ergo amissa prima existentia qualitatis, tota etiam ipsa qualitas deperditur, & sic nec intensa, nec remissa prorsus manet. ianet. Contra 3. nam qualitas non vietur fieri sensibilior per maiorem vnionem. Probo,quia non potest vniri magis, magisq; subiecto, forma enim statim ac n subiecto est, vnitur illi, maiori modo quo potest, nam hoc vniri quid est aliud, nisi tradere se ipsam totam? Deinde,qualitas v. g. vt vnum quomodo aget vt duo, vt tria, vt octo per hoc quòd magis vniatur, si vnio non agit? Contra 4. nam qualitas non videtur augeri eò quia producatur maior modus radicandi. Probo: Ignis v. g. producto primo gradu caloris, non producit in secundo instanti modum quo illum radicet, sed calorem de nouo, vt patet si manus post primam actionem interponatur. Vlteriùs quia, modus iste radicandi non est calor, ergò nequit efficere magis calidum. Tum quia dum qualitas intenditur, subiectum participat magis effectum formalem qualitatis, ergo ipsam qualitatem. Demum quia vi huiusmodi radicationis non mutatur intrinsecè prior qualitas, ergò de se formaliter non immutat, neq; alterat subiectū; Et multò minus hoc faciet modus, qui formaliter calor non est. Qualitas ergò per hunc modum superadditum intendi nequit. Hisce reiectis notetur.
units.tr: Against these, and first of all: a quality cannot be increased or intensified by greater rooting in the subject. This is proved, for an intensified quality can at least be separated from its subject by divine power, and in that case it would remain intensified; as is seen in the consecrated host, where there is heat without matter, or sometimes an intense cold. Therefore intensification does not formally consist in the quality being rooted in the subject. Against the second: this intensification does not occur because, while the quality remains always the same, a more perfect existence is acquired. I prove it: for existence, as will be seen in the Metaphysics, is not distinguished from the entity of a thing; therefore, once the first existence of the quality is lost, the whole quality itself is lost, and so it remains neither intensified nor remitted. Against the third: a quality is not seen to become more perceptible through a greater union, for it cannot be united more, and more closely, to the subject. For a form, as soon as it is in a subject, is united to it in the greatest manner it can be; for what is it to be united, if not to give oneself wholly? Moreover, how does a quality, for example, act as one thing in the way it acts as two, as three, as eight, through being more united, if the union does not act? Against the fourth: a quality does not seem to be increased by the production of a greater mode of rooting. I prove it: fire, for example, having produced the first degree of heat, does not in the second instant produce a mode by which it roots that heat, but produces heat anew, as is evident if a hand is interposed after the first action. Further, because this mode of rooting is not heat, and so it cannot make a thing warmer. Again, because when a quality is intensified, the subject participates more in the formal effect of the quality, and therefore in the quality itself. Lastly, because by the power of such rooting the prior quality is not changed intrinsically; therefore it does not of itself formally change or alter the subject; and much less will a mode do so, which is not formally heat. Therefore a quality cannot be intensified by this superadded mode. With these points rejected, let the following be noted.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSIO.

units.la: Qualitas intenditur ex additione plu- rium graduum in eadem parte subiecti existentium.
units.tr: A quality is increased by the addition of several degrees existing in the same part of the subject.

units.la: PRobarur 1. Quia hoc videtur satis conforme hominum existimationi, & vel ipso sensu comprobatur, manus enim iam calida cum igni admouetur, & calescit magis, certe nouum sentit calorem, qui sic producitur, ac si tunc primo calefieret. Hic vero nouus calor non destruit praecedentem, eo quod homogenus illi est, atque similis, igitur cum eodem vnitur: sed tunc in subiecto resultat maior calor, ergo qualitas intenditur per additionem gradus ad gradum.
units.tr: It is proved first: this seems quite in agreement with men's opinion, and is confirmed by sense itself. For when a hand that is already warm is brought near a fire, it becomes warmer; it certainly feels a new heat, produced as if it were then first being warmed. Yet this new heat does not destroy the earlier one, because it is homogeneous with it and similar to it, so it unites with it. But then a greater heat results in the subject. Therefore a quality is intensified by the addition of degree to degree.

units.la: Probatur 2. à simili, nam quantitas fit maior, aut minor, eo quod ipsi addantur partes, vel detrahantur. Ergo etiam qualitas maior erit, ac intensa, cum gradus addetur gradui; minor, & remissa, cum adimetur.
units.tr: It is proved second, by analogy: a quantity becomes greater or smaller because parts are added to it or taken away. Therefore a quality will also be greater and intense when degree is added to degree, and less and remitted when it is taken away.

units.la: Probatur 3. quia iustus per bona opera in gratia, & ex gratia facta meretur augmentum habitualis gratiae sanctificantis; nequit autem augeri gratia sanctificans, nisi per additam gratiam; quae sola facit Deo gratum; ergo habitus intenditur ex additione partis ad partem.
units.tr: It is proved third: the righteous man, through good works done in grace and from grace, merits an increase of habitual sanctifying grace. But sanctifying grace cannot be increased except by added grace, which alone makes a man pleasing to God. Therefore a habit is intensified by the addition of part to part.

units.la: Probatur 4. auctoritate, Caietanus enim nim & Diu. Thomas nomine radicaonis videntur intelligere nouam quatis additionem. Probatur, quia priius illam vocat eductionem de poteni subiecti, & Secundus secunda sec. iæst. 24. artic. 4. ad 3. habet. Proiam vocem ignorauerunt, qui dicunt aritatem (quod hic de charitate, inllige de omni qualitate) cum intenitur, non augeri secundum suam esentiam,vel secundum radicationem. Er-o videntur esse idem essentia, & racatio. Vtcumque tamen sit de menaliorum, sententia nostra verisimior apparet. Sed
units.tr: It is proved fourth by authority. For Cajetan and St. Thomas seem to understand by the name radication a new addition of quality. This is proved because the former calls it an eduction from the power of the subject, and the latter, in II-II q. 24 art. 4 ad 3, has: those who say that charity, when it is intensified, does not grow according to its essence or according to radication have ignored the proper word (which here, concerning charity, must be understood of every quality). Therefore essence and radication seem to be the same thing. However that may be about the opinions of these men, our view appears more probable.

units.la: Obijcies 1. Si qualitas constaret ex adibus, vtique forent solo numero dincti: sed hoc esse nequit; ergo. Protur minor, accidentia enim solo nuero distincta, esse non possunt in eom subiecto.
units.tr: You will object first: if a quality consisted of additions, they would certainly be distinct only in number; but this cannot be; therefore. The minor is proved, for accidents distinct only in number cannot exist in the same subject.

units.la: Resp. n. minorem, & dico accidentia, m partialia sunt, vnamque integrant alitatem, bene manere posse in vnate subiecti. Preterea, si per aduersarios identia, quæ specie distinguuntur, tamanent (pars .n. v. gr. lactis vna,eanq; indiuisibilis dulcorem habet, ac aline) cur si numero tantum distingui-, simul esse nequibunt? Argumentum nimis, aut nihil probat.
units.tr: I deny the minor, and I say that accidents which are partial, and which together make up one quality, can well remain in one subject. Moreover, if by your own account accidents that differ in species remain together (for example, one part of milk has a sweetness that is indivisible, and another part likewise), why could they not be together if they differ only in number? The argument proves too much, or nothing.

units.la: Obijcies Secundo. Si qualitas autur per graduum additiones, foens, & aggregatum per accidens. im. Qualitas est actus purus, ergo nullam habere potest compositionem.
units.tr: You will object second: if a quality is made by additions of degrees, it is a thing made up and an aggregate by accident. But a quality is pure act, so it can have no composition.

units.la: Resp. ad primum n. antecedens, vniūtur enim partes illæ per indiuisibiles,physicasq; vniones, quemadmodum qualitas extensa, & quantitas ipsa, quæ tamen non sunt aggregata per accidens. Ad secundum quoq; dico, qualitatem esse purum actum respectu subiecti, quod actuat, non verò purum actum integraliter, seu respectu suarum partium, quæ habent potentiam, vt inter se vnionem recipiant. Resp. vltimò, dato etiam, quòd gradus non vniantur in ratione actus, & potentiæ inter se; tamen qualitas adhuc intenditur, quia omnes in vno subiecto recipiuntur, & dant maiorem effectū. Neque dicas tunc futurum ens per accidens, Distinguo enim; per accidens nēpe non ex intentione naturæ, nego; per accidens, nimirum ex aggregatu accidentium, concedo.
units.tr: I answer to the first, denying the antecedent: those parts are united by indivisible, physical unions, just as an extended quality and quantity itself are, and yet these are not aggregates by accident. To the second also I say that a quality is pure act with respect to the subject which it actuates, but it is not pure act wholly, or with respect to its own parts, which have the potency to receive union among themselves. Lastly I answer: even granting that the degrees are not united among themselves as act and potency, a quality is still intensified, because all are received in one subject and give a greater effect. Nor should you say that it would then be a being by accident. I distinguish: by accident, that is, not from the intention of nature, I deny; by accident, that is, from an aggregate of accidents, I concede.

units.la: Obijcies 3. intensio non est perfectio essentialis qualitati, sed accidentalis, ergò est modus ab ea distinctus. Præterea: essentiæ rerum sunt indiuisibiles, ergò qualitas consistit in indiuisibili, & sic non habet partes.
units.tr: You will object third: intensity is not an essential perfection of a quality but an accidental one; therefore it is a mode distinct from it. Moreover: the essences of things are indivisible; therefore a quality consists in an indivisible and so has no parts.

units.la: Respond ad primum negando consequentiam, nam etsi qualitati non sit essentialis intensio, potest enim illa concipi, & esse absq; intensione, idcirco non bene infertur: ergo est modus. Habeo exemplum. Quantitati, vt quantitas est, non manet essentialis v. g. pars .a. & tamen pars .a. non est modus. Ad secundum quoq; resp. essentias rerum esse indiuisibiles metaphysicè, non physicè. Ita homo, qui metaphysicè diuidi nequit in alias animalium species, physicè tamen in corpus, & animam diuiditur. Similiter ergo qualitas metaphysicè talis est, vt diuidi non possit in aliam, sed physicè in suas partes, quibus conflatur, diuidi potest.
units.tr: I answer to the first by denying the consequence. For although intensity is not essential to a quality, the quality can be conceived and can exist without intensity, so it is not rightly inferred: therefore it is a mode. I give an example. Part A is not essential to quantity as quantity, and yet part A is not a mode. To the second also I answer that the essences of things are indivisible metaphysically, not physically. Thus man, who cannot be divided metaphysically into other species of animals, is nevertheless divided physically into body and soul. Similarly, then, a quality is metaphysically such that it cannot be divided into another quality, but physically it can be divided into the parts of which it is composed.

units.la: Obijcies 4. Causa efficiens aliquando producit maiorem effectum, aliquando minorem, ob variam solummodo subiecti dispositionem, ergò etiam causa formalis eadem inuariata manens ob diuersitatem alicuius modi superadditi, magis, & magis afficiet subiectum; vnde intensio per modum superadditum fieri potest.
units.tr: You will object fourth: an efficient cause sometimes produces a greater effect and sometimes a lesser, solely because of the varying disposition of the subject; therefore also a formal cause, remaining unchanged, may by the diversity of some superadded mode affect the subject more and more; whence intensity can come about through a superadded mode.

units.la: Respond. negando consequentiam. Disparitas est, quia causa formalis non distinguitur ab effectu formali, ac proinde tribuere nequit maiorem effectum, nisi & ipsa maior formaliter fit. Causa verò efficiens manet effectui extrinseca, & distincta, vnde potest cum eadem essentia variare influxum, & actionem, iuxta variam subiecti capacitatem. Qualitas ergò cùm sit causa formalis, nequit efsectum alterare, si formaliter ipsa non alteretur.
units.tr: I answer by denying the consequence. There is a disparity: a formal cause is not distinct from its formal effect, and so it cannot bestow a greater effect unless it itself becomes greater formally. But an efficient cause remains extrinsic and distinct from its effect, whence it can vary its influx and action with the same essence, according to the varying capacity of the subject. Therefore a quality, since it is a formal cause, cannot alter its effect if it is not itself formally altered.

units.la: Obijcies 5. si qualitas intenditur per additionem gradus ad gradum in eadem parte subiecti, ergò hi gradus penetrantur simul: sed hoc dicere absurditas est, ergo, &c. Probatur minor, quia gradus quiquicumque siue caloris, aut frigoris, sunt materiales ; entia vero materiae sed nequeunt penetrare, nam hoc speciebus tantum debetur.
units.tr: You will object fifth: if a quality is intensified by the addition of degree to degree in the same part of the subject, then these degrees interpenetrate at the same time; but to say this is absurd; therefore, etc. The minor is proved: whatever degrees of heat or cold there are, they are material; but material beings cannot interpenetrate, for this belongs only to species.

units.la: Respond. esse quidem conceptu ficillimum quomodo accidentia materialia in vna, eademq; indiuisibili parte subiecti maneant simul, & idcò semper vsa est probabilior, magis physica veterum sententia, qui excantt qualitatis intensionem per gradum substantiae additum gradui, in parte materiae indiuisibili, sed sibili, vt in vltima disputatione dicitur. Verum quia fumus in communi doctrina, Respond. gradus qualitatum esse materiales quidem, ita tamen minutos, vt valeant penetrari simul. Et hoc tenentur fateri omnes peripatetici, qui concedunt eamdem subiecti partem habere plura similia accidentia, vt in pomo dulcorem, humiditatem, colorem, &c. Quemadmodum ergo multa haec specie diuersa penetrata manent, similiter manebunt, si numero tantum distincta sint.
units.tr: I answer that it is indeed most difficult to conceive how material accidents can remain together in one and the same indivisible part of the subject; and therefore the more probable and more physical opinion of the ancients has always been preferred, who explain the intensification of a quality by substance added to degree, in an indivisible part of matter, yet subtle, as is said in the last disputation. But since we stand with common doctrine, I reply that the degrees of qualities are indeed material, yet so minute that they can be penetrated together. And all Peripatetics are bound to admit this, who concede that the same part of the subject has several similar accidents, as in an apple sweetness, moisture, colour, and so on. Just as these, though specifically different, remain interpenetrated, so they will remain if they are distinct only in number.

units.la: DISPVTATIO TERTIA.
units.tr: DISPUTATIO TERTIA.

units.la: De qualitatibus inter se comparatis.
units.tr: On qualities compared with one another.

units.la: QValitates, vt dixi, aliæ carent contrario, vt lux, & species intentionales; quædam contrarium habent, quemadmodum primæ 4. habitus, colores, &c. Oritur inde, vt si quando in vno, eodemq; subiecto sint, mutuò pugnent, agant, reagant, expellant se. Modò igitur comparandæ sunt ad inuicem, & primò disquirendum, qua ratione actio ista, & reactio, resistentia, & pulsio qualitatum. Vndè sit.
units.tr: Some qualities, as I have said, lack a contrary, such as light and intentional species; others have a contrary, as the first four habits, colours, and so on. Hence it follows that, when they are in one and the same subject, they fight each other, act upon and react against each other, and drive each other out. Therefore they must now be compared with one another, and first we must inquire by what manner this action and reaction, this resistance and pushing of qualities, takes place. Whence does it arise?

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: FIRST DISQUISITION.

units.la: Quomodo qualitates in subiecto reagant.
units.tr: How qualities react in a subject.

units.la: PRO Intelligentia meminisse debetis commune philosophorum axioma; quod agens agendo repatitur, hoc est, qualitates contrariæ quotiescunq; pugnât, vna imminuit aliam, & vicissim ab ea imminuitur. Ratio autem est, nam qualitas aggressa non solùm resistit passiuè se opponendo, sed etiam actiuè conando aliquid, agendo, vulnusque infligendo. Porrò actio differt à reactione iuxta modum operandi, nam actio validior simpliciter actio denomina-
units.tr: To understand this, you must remember the common axiom of the philosophers, that the agent is repelled by its own acting. That is, whenever contrary qualities clash, one diminishes the other, and in turn is diminished by it. The reason is this: a quality that attacks does not only resist passively by opposing itself, but also actively strives, acts, and inflicts harm. Moreover, action differs from reaction according to the mode of operating: the stronger action is simply called action, while the weaker action is usually called reaction.

units.la: denominatur, actio verò imbecillior, dici solet reactio. Similiter passio dicitur quæ maior est, repassio quæ minor. V.gr. si ferrum candens calefacit aquam vt 4. & hæc frigefacit ferrum vt duo ; calefactio vt veniens à ferro dicitur actio, vt recepta in aqua, passio ; frigefactio verò profluens ab aqua vocatur reactio, & recepta in ferro repassio.
units.tr: Similarly, the stronger is called passion, the weaker repassion. For example, if hot iron heats water to 4, and the water in turn cools the iron to 2: the heating, as it comes from the iron, is called action, and as it is received in the water, passion; but the cooling, as it flows from the water, is called reaction, and as it is received in the iron, repassion.

units.la: Aduerto præterea, nonnullos axioma illud ita limitasse, vt dixerint reactionem non fieri ad eandem omnino partem, & contrarietatem, sed potiùs ad aliam; hoc est illa pars agentis frigidi, quæ patitur ab agente calido, non est ea, quæ reagit, sed altera pars, quæ non patitur, illa reagit : quòdsi pars repassa etiam agat, non aget eàdem_ contrarietate, sed omnino diuersâ; v.g. si patitur calorem, non reaget producendo frigus, verùm potiùs humiditatem. Sic Burleus, & Ricardus Suiset, cognomento Calculator, qui à Cardano lib. 16. de subtil. inter ingenia_ subtilissima, quæ ab orbe condito exiterint, enumeratur. Pro solutione scribatur.
units.tr: I note, moreover, that some have qualified that axiom so as to say that the reaction does not occur in the same part and with the same contrariety, but rather in a different part. That is, the part of the cold agent which suffers from the hot agent is not the part that reacts; rather, another part, which does not suffer, reacts. And if the part that has been re-suffered also acts, it will not act with the same contrariety but with a wholly different one: for example, if it suffers heat, it will not react by producing cold, but rather moisture. So Burley, and Richard Suiseth, surnamed Calculator, who is listed by Cardano in book 16 of De subtilitate among the most subtle minds that have appeared since the world began. For the solution, let the following be written.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Datur actio, & reactio quoad eandem subiecti partem, adeout pars illa, qua agit, eadem repatiatur ab alia.
units.tr: There is action and reaction with respect to the same part of a subject, so that the part which acts is itself undergoing being acted upon by another.

units.la: PRobatur 1. ratione, quia mixtio vbi fit, exigit habere qualitates in gradu remisso, & per mutuam pugnam refracto: sed in quacumq; subiecti parte datur mixtio; ergo in ea sunt qualitates in gradu remisso, & refracto. Proinde quæcumq; subiecti pars non agit solùm, sed patitur, ergo datur actio, & reactio quoad eamdem subiecti partem.
units.tr: This is proved first by reason: where mixture occurs, it requires that the qualities be present in a remitted degree and broken by mutual conflict. But mixture occurs in every part of a subject; therefore in every such part there are qualities in a remitted and broken degree. Hence every part of the subject not only acts but is also acted upon; therefore there is action and reaction with respect to the same part of the subject.

units.la: Probatur 2. experientia, quia si pars frigidæ misceatur cum calida, hæc producit calorem in frigida, & ista gignit frigus in calida, ex quo tertium quid resultat, nempe aqua tepida. Ergo pars illa subiecti, quæ producit calorem in alio, suscipit in se frigus, & patitur ab illo. Itaque actio, & reatio fit ad eādem subiecti partem. Difficultas tota est penes modum explicandi.
units.tr: It is proved second by experience: if a part of something cold is mixed with something hot, the hot produces heat in the cold, and the cold produces cold in the hot, from which a third thing results, namely lukewarm water. Therefore that part of the subject which produces heat in another also takes cold into itself and is acted upon by it. Thus action and reaction occur in the same part of the subject. The whole difficulty lies in the manner of explaining it.

units.la: Quare dico. Si duo agentia inuicem applicentur, vt agant, supponi debent in ijs aliqui gradus qualitatis intensæ. Ponamus itaquè in altero adesse gradus caloris vt 8. in altero frigoris vt 8. quo dato, res ita explicari potest. Gradus caloris in agente calido agunt in parte frigidam, ibiq; debellant primum gradumfrigoris, ita tamen vt aliquis etiam gradus caloris infirmetur, ac debilitetur ob resistentiam, aliqualemq; reactionem contrarij. Mox vero cum subsequentes gradus frigoris inueniant in agente calido vim refractam, robur exerunt suum, & ibi frigus producunt, sed non impune, patiuntur enim & ipsi, vnde rursus faciunt locum primo agenti, vt nouum gradum suæ qualitatis producat. Ex quo intelligitur, quamdam fieri mixtionem in gradibus, quia calidum recipit frigus, debile tamen, ratione contrarij; & frigidum suscipit calorem pariter debilem. Datur ergo actio, & reactio quoad eandem subiecti partem.
units.tr: Wherefore I say: if two agents are applied to one another so that they act, some degrees of intense quality must be supposed in them. Let us suppose, then, that in one there is a degree of heat, say 8, and in the other a degree of cold, say 8. Granted this, the matter can be explained as follows. The degrees of heat in the hot agent act upon the cold part and there overcome the first degree of cold; yet some degree of heat is also weakened and debilitated by the resistance and a certain slight reaction of the contrary. But soon, when the following degrees of cold find in the hot agent a broken force, they exert their strength and produce cold there, yet not without cost, for they too are acted upon, whence in turn they yield place to the first agent, so that it produces a new degree of its quality. From this it is understood that a certain mixture takes place in the degrees: the hot receives cold, weak however on account of the contrary, and the cold likewise receives heat, equally weak. Therefore there is action and reaction with respect to the same part of the subject.

units.la: Obijcies 1. ex Burleo. Aut ea, quæ agunt inuicem, sunt æqualis virtutis, aut inæqualis. Primum si dicatur, ergo neutrum aget, omnis enim actio prouenit ab excessu, & agentis victoria supra vires patii. Si secundum, ergo tantummodo aget illud, quod maioris est roboris, & ita nulla fiet reactio.
units.tr: You will object first, from Burleus: either the things that act upon one another are of equal power or of unequal power. If the first is said, then neither will act, for every action arises from excess, and the agent's victory comes from exceeding the strength of the patient. If the second, then only that which is of greater strength will act, and so no reaction will occur.

units.la: Respond. ea, quæ inuicem agunt, semper esse inæqualis virtutis, non ideo tamen deneganda est reactio debiliori. Et ratio afferri potest, quia magis actiuum est minus resistituum, vt in communi sententia. Qualitas ergo actiuitate, ac virtute minor agit in maiorem, quia reperit illam in resistentia minorem. Explicari hoc potest exemplo. Acus v. gr. quò subtilior est, eò magis acuta penetrat, seseque in solidum corpus insinuat; verùm ex ipsamet sua-subtilitate habet etiam, vt sit minùs refiftitiua, poffitq; à solido frangi, &c.
units.tr: I reply: things that act upon one another are always of unequal power, yet a reaction must not therefore be denied to the weaker. And a reason can be given, because what is more active is less resistant, as in the common opinion. Therefore a quality that is less in activity and power acts upon the greater, because it finds that greater in less resistance. This can be explained by an example. A needle, for instance, the finer it is, the more sharply it penetrates and insinuates itself into a solid body; yet from this very fineness it also has that it is less resistant and can be broken by a solid body, and so on.

units.la: Obijcies 2. cum Ricardo. Si daretur actio, & reactio quoad partem subiecti eandem, res eadem moueretur simul duplici motu contrario, hoc est haberet duo contraria, effet calidum, & frigidum, quod repugnat. Explicatur sequela. Sit calidum, & frigidum sic applicita, vt inter vtrumq; mediet aer: certè actio tam calidi, quàm frigidi transsire debet per medium, ergò pars eadem aeris frigescet per actionem frigidi, & simul calefiet per actionem calidi.
units.tr: You will object secondly, with Richard: if action and reaction were given with respect to the same part of the subject, the same thing would be moved at once by a double contrary motion, that is, it would have two contraries, it would be both hot and cold, which is absurd. The consequence is explained thus. Let there be something hot and something cold placed so that air lies between them: certainly the action of both the hot and the cold must pass through the middle; therefore the same part of the air will be cooled by the action of the cold and at the same time warmed by the action of the hot.

units.la: Respond. concedendo sequelam. Nec absurdum est, quòd pars eadem aeris moueatur duplici contrario, habeatque simul calorem, & frigus, in gradu tamen remisso. Quæ res contingeret quidem in casu dato, nam quæuis actio transeundo per medium, haberet obuiam sibi contrariam, à qua infirmaretur, quemadmodum in aqua tepida explicatum est supra.
units.tr: I reply by granting the consequence. Nor is it absurd that the same part of the air should be moved by a double contrary and have heat and cold at once, though in a remitted degree.
