This would indeed happen in the given case, for any action passing through the medium would meet a contrary action opposing it, by which it would be weakened, just as has been explained above in the case of lukewarm water.

units.la: Obijcies 3. ex Aristotele, qui t. 89. ait, posse interdum contingere, vt ex duplici corpore contrario secundum qualitates, alterum sit passiuum tantummodo, alterū verò parū passiuum, aut nihil, in quo casu passū non reageret. Ex quo infertPhilosophus nō omnia esse ad mixtionem apta.
units.tr: You will object thirdly from Aristotle, who in text 89 says that it can sometimes happen that of two bodies contrary in qualities, one is merely passive, the other slightly passive or not at all, in which case the patient would not react. From this the Philosopher infers that not all things are apt for mixture.

units.la: Resp. Philosophi mentem esse, quòd alialiquando passum vires habet sic paucas, & infirmas, vt reagat quidem, sed omnino insensibiliter. Hoc vero non est sufficiens ad mixtionem, quæ in omni parte subiecti sensibilem exigit alterationem, vt suo loco dicetur.
units.tr: I reply that the mind of the Philosopher is that the patient sometimes has so few and weak powers that it does react, but altogether imperceptibly. Yet this is not sufficient for mixture, which in every part of the subject requires a perceptible alteration, as will be said in its place.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISQUISITIO SECUNDA.

units.la: Quomodo qualitates à subiecto se pellant.
units.tr: How qualities are driven out of a subject.

units.la: PRo intelligentia tenete quod nouissimè dictum est, agentia contraria inuicem agere, atq; reagere quoad partem subiecti eandem. Ex qua re sequitur continuò per mutuam pugnam qualitates pelli à subiectis. Quæritur modò, fiatne talis expulsio quoad omnes gradus contrarios, an tantummodo aliquos. V.g. dum quod erat calidum vt & incipit frigefieri à contrario, amittitne gradus omnes caloris, an retinendo aliqualem calorem frigus quoque aliquale in se admittit.
units.tr: To understand this, keep in mind what was said most recently: contrary agents act upon and react against each other with respect to the same part of the subject. From this it follows at once that, through their mutual conflict, qualities are driven out of their subjects. The question now is whether such expulsion happens with respect to all contrary degrees, or only some. For example, when something that was hot begins to become cold through the contrary, does it lose all degrees of heat, or, by retaining some degree of heat, does it also admit some degree of cold into itself?

units.la: Durandus, aliique docuere, nunquam in eodem subiecto esse simul calorem, & frigus; neq; cum res sit minus calida, seu frigida putant aliquid contrariæ qualitatis admisceri, sed potius induci medias alias qualitates, quarum natura inter vtrüque contrarium iacens, de nulla tamen participet, sed quid tertium sit; Contra, & notetur.
units.tr: Durandus and others have taught that heat and cold never exist together in the same subject; and when a thing is less hot or less cold, they do not think that a contrary quality is mixed into it, but rather that other intermediate qualities are induced, whose nature, lying between the two contraries, participates in neither of them but is something third. Against this, note the following.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Qualitates contraria ita se pellunt à subiecto, vt in eo tamen simul esse possint in gradu re- misso, non vero in- tenso.
units.tr: Contrary qualities so drive each other out of a subject that they can nevertheless be together in it when remitted, but not when intensified.

units.la: PRobatur prima pars conclusionis, quia in mixto debent esse aliquo modo elementa, si non formaliter, saltem quoad accidentia, & qualitates contrarias, vt concedunt omnes; ergo qualitates istæ contrariæ manent simul in mixto: non in gradu intenso, quemadmodum probo infra, ergo in gradu remisso.
units.tr: The first part of the conclusion is proved as follows. In a mixed body the elements must be present in some way, if not formally then at least as to their accidents and contrary qualities, as everyone concedes. Therefore these contrary qualities remain together in the mixed body. They do not remain in an intense degree, as I prove below, so they remain in a remitted degree.

units.la: Probatur 2. nam aqua tepida virtutem habet calefaciendi, ac refrigerandi, ergo ipsi calor, & frigus inexistunt simul. Probo antecedens, nam corpus frigidum si mergatur in tepida, calefit; è contra si corpus calidum, frigescit, ergo tepida vim habet calefaciendi, & refrigerandi.
units.tr: It is proved secondly, because lukewarm water has the power both to warm and to cool. So heat and cold inhere in it together. I prove the antecedent: a cold body, if it is plunged into lukewarm water, becomes warm; conversely, a warm body becomes cold. Therefore lukewarm water has the power of warming and of cooling.

units.la: Probatur 3. experientia, eoquòd animal sentit frigus in se, vt aliquis vestrum in manu, qui hæc scribitis hyeme, igitur qui sic percipit, in eadem parte habet calorem. Probo consequentiam: qui sentit, viuit; qui viuit, habet calorem, vita enim est calor in humido; ergo animal ea parte, qua sentit frigus, habet quoque calorem.
units.tr: It is proved thirdly by experience. An animal feels cold in itself, as one of you who are writing this in winter feels it in your hand. Therefore whoever perceives cold in this way has heat in the same part. I prove the consequence: whoever feels is alive; whoever is alive has heat, for life is heat in moisture. Therefore the animal, in the part where it feels cold, also has heat.

units.la: Probatur etiam secunda pars conclusionis, quia satis constat, duo agentia con-
units.tr: The second part of the conclusion is also proved, because it is quite clear that

units.la: traria cum inter fe mutuò agunt , remittere nonnihil de vi suà , & qualitate ; vnde quod erat calidum vt oão, nequit manere tale , si patiatur à frigido, frigus enim adueniens labefaćtat calorem; & calor frigus ob aćtionem, & reaćtionem, vt supra vidimus.
units.tr: when two contrary agents act upon each other, each remits somewhat of its force and quality. Hence what was hot in act cannot remain so if it is acted upon by the cold, since the cold arriving weakens the heat, and the heat weakens the cold, through action and reaction, as we saw above.

units.la: Opponis cum Durando. Qualitates contrariæ pugnant ad inuicem ratione … suæ naturæ, non ratione intensionis ; ergo siue in gradu remisso , siue in … intenso nunquam poterunt esse simul, quia semper contrariæ sunt.
units.tr: You object with Durandus: contrary qualities fight one another by reason of their nature, not by reason of intensity. Therefore whether in a remitted or in an intense degree they can never be together, because they are always contrary.

units.la: Respond. qualitates contrarias pugnare inuicem ratione suæ naturæ , sed tamen in ordine ad subiećtum, omnis enim physica oppositio in subiecto fit. Quoniam verò in gradu remisso dum pugnant ; neutra vires habet sufficientes destruendi aliam, quæ resistit, nisi successu temporis ; hinc est, quòd interim dum fit aćtio , & resistentia … reaćtio , & pugna , qualitates remissæ adsint in subiećto simul.
units.tr: I answer: contrary qualities fight one another by reason of their nature, but nevertheless in relation to the subject, for every physical opposition takes place in a subject. But since, while they are in a remitted degree and fighting, neither has sufficient strength to destroy the other which resists, except with the passage of time, it follows that meanwhile, while action and resistance, reaction and conflict are taking place, the remitted qualities are present together in the subject.

units.la: Quòdsi aliqua tandem … prævaleat, sanè totam oppositam expellet ; sed tamen ante mansit cum illa.
units.tr: But if at last one prevails, it will certainly expel the whole of the opposed quality; yet it remained together with it before.

units.la: DISQVISITIO TERTIA.
units.tr: Disquisition Three.

units.la: An similis qualitas agat in similem.
units.tr: Whether a similar quality acts on a similar one.

units.la: PRO intelligentia quæstionis aduerto, non tantùm contrarias qualitates posse inter se conferri, sed etiam similes, vt si calorem calori, frigus frigori comparemus. Circa quod est commune axioma desumptum à Philosopho, Simile non agere in simile. Hoc est si adsit agens calidum vt 4. non aget in possum quoque calidum vt 4. seu non intendet, nec augebit in eo calorem vt 5. inueniendo enim gradus æquè validos, actionem suspendet suam. Ita patet quòdsi duæ aquæ pariter calidæ, aut frigidæ approximentur, neutra euadit calidior, aut frigidior, &c. Porro dictum illud non de quacumque similitudine procedit, sed tantùm de similibus in intensione, significando, quòd quæ pares habent gradus qualitatis eiusdem in intensione, inter se non agunt.
units.tr: To understand the question, I note that not only contrary qualities can be compared with one another, but also similar ones, as when we compare heat with heat or cold with cold. On this there is a common axiom taken from the Philosopher: Like does not act on like. That is, if a hot agent of degree 4 is present, it will not act on a hot patient also of degree 4, nor will it intensify the heat in it to degree 5. For on finding degrees equally strong, it suspends its action. Thus it is plain that if two waters equally warm, or equally cold, are brought near each other, neither becomes warmer or colder, and so on. Moreover, this saying does not hold for every kind of likeness, but only for things alike in intensity, meaning that those which have equal degrees of the same quality in intensity do not act on one another.

units.la: Nobis etiam placet axioma vnde fiat.
units.tr: We also approve of the axiom, and of how it comes about.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Simile non potest agere in simile.
units.tr: Like cannot act on like.

units.la: PRobatur satis experientijs cuique obvijs. Ratione autem sic. Omne {ɔ}agens natura sua operatur ex ea intentione, ut sibi assimilet passum; neque solummodo causa vniuoca substantialis intendit producere formam in subiecto sibi similem; sed agens etiam accidentale{ɔ} Quoties ergo passum adinuenitur iam simile, cessat finis agentis, unde ab illo non amplius actio dimanat.
units.tr: This is sufficiently proved by experiences that are open to everyone. The reason is this: every agent by its nature acts with the aim of making the patient like itself. Not only does the substantial univocal cause intend to produce a form in the subject similar to itself, but an accidental agent does so too. Whenever the patient is found already to be alike, the agent's aim ceases, and so the action no longer flows from it.

units.la: Praeterea etiam ratio esse potest, quia omne agens, ut incipiat agere, debet excedere passum virtute; actio enim est impetus, & conatus quidam superioris in inferius, cum oporteat, inquit Aristot. 4. Meteor. c 1. id quod motum affert, vincere. Itaq; si nullum sit inferius debilius, sed utrobiq; par actiuitas, efficacia, virtus, nulla sequetur actio; & ita simile nunquam in simile aget.
units.tr: There may also be another reason. Every agent, if it is to begin acting, must surpass the patient in power. For action is an impulse and a certain striving of the superior against the inferior, since it is necessary, as Aristotle says in Meteor. 4, c. 1, that the thing which causes motion should overcome. Therefore, if there is no inferior that is weaker, but the activity, efficacy and power are equal on both sides, no action will follow, and so like will never act on like.

units.la: Opponis. Adsit fax luminosa, ut 4. in hoc gymnasio: haec tantum lumen producet in aere, quantum habet in se. Applicetur deinde noua fax luminosa etiam ut 4. constat, lumen crescere in aere; igitur corpus luminosum ut 4. aget in aliud luminosum ut 4. ergo simile in simile.
units.tr: You object: let there be a luminous torch, as in this lecture hall, four of them. It will produce in the air only as much light as it has in itself. Then let a new luminous torch be brought near, and, as is established among the four, the light increases in the air. Therefore a luminous body, as among the four, acts on another luminous body, as among the four; so like acts on like.

units.la: Respond. agens luminosum non producere in aere sibi vicino tantum lucis, quantum habet in se, imò semper minus, & minus. Etenim sphæra, quæ dicitur actiuitatis fingi debet adinstar trianguli, pro cuius basi constitutum agens qualitatem semper minorem, & minorem post se diffundat. Quare fax adueniens augebit sanè lucem in aere, quam reperit minùs intensam, sed facem ipsam non reddet vnquam lucidiorem, vt patet, si oculos in eam solerter figas.
units.tr: I reply: a luminous agent does not produce in the air near it as much light as it has in itself, but always less and less. For the sphere of activity, which is said to be fashioned like a triangle, must be imagined such that the agent, placed at its base, diffuses a quality that is always smaller and smaller as it moves away. So the approaching torch will indeed increase the light in the air, which it finds less intense, but it will never make the torch itself brighter, as is plain if you fix your eyes on it carefully.

units.la: Vrges, hæc responsio non videtur sufficiens, nam etiamsi fax non intendat lumen facis, attamen si prima lucida vt 4. producat in aere lucem v. g. vt vnum, & secunda quoque vt vnum, hæ saltem duæ luces intendunt se mutuò; ergo simile agit in simile. Probatur antecedens. Lux, quam producit fax a. & lux, quam producit fax b. sunt ambæ vt vnum: sed positæ simul in eadem parte aeris illam reddunt magis lucidam; ergo lux prima intendit aliam; ergo similis qualitas agit similem.
units.tr: You press: this answer does not seem sufficient. For even if the torch does not intensify the light of the torch, nevertheless, if the first luminous body, say as one, produces light in the air, and the second likewise as one, these two lights at least intensify one another. Therefore like acts on like. The antecedent is proved thus: the light which torch a produces and the light which torch b produces are both as one; but when placed together in the same part of the air, they make it brighter. Therefore the first light intensifies the other, and so a similar quality acts on a similar one.

units.la: Respond. negando, quòd luces prædictæ intenderent se. Ratio est, quia positæ simul in eodem aere, hunc sanè magis illuminarent, nam tunc temporis ex vnione lucis nouæ fieret maior qualitas, ac proinde maior etiam effectus; verùm lux a. nunquam intenderet lucem b. illam reddendo maiorem, seu magis lucem. Alteratio igitur per aduenientem lucem, non in alia priori luce, sed in aere tantùm foret.
units.tr: I deny that the aforementioned lights intensify one another. The reason is that, placed together in the same air, they would indeed illuminate it more, for at that moment the union of the light would produce a greater quality, and consequently a greater effect too. But light a would never intensify light b by making it greater, or more luminous. Therefore the alteration caused by the arriving light would take place not in the other light already there, but only in the air.

units.la: DISQVISITIO QVARTA.
units.tr: DISQUISITION IV.

units.la: An idem agat in se ipsum.
units.tr: Whether the same thing acts upon itself.

units.la: PRO intelligentia quæstionis duplicem causam distinguo. Alia est vniuoca, & dicitur illa, quæ producit efsectum sibi similem, seu quæ formaliter habet in se qualitatem, quam debet effectui communicare, vt ignis igné; homo hominem, &c. Alia æquiuoca, & illa est, quæ dat effectum à se prorsus dissimilem. Sic anima producit in se motum: aqua calida generat in se frigus, & ideo respectu horum effectuum causæ dicuntur æquiuocæ.
units.tr: For the understanding of the question I distinguish two kinds of cause. One is univocal, and it is that which produces an effect like itself, that is, which formally possesses in itself the quality it must communicate to its effect, as fire produces fire, man produces man, and so on. The other is equivocal, and it is that which gives rise to an effect wholly unlike itself. Thus the soul produces motion in itself, and warm water generates cold in itself, and so with respect to these effects the causes are called equivocal.

units.la: Procedit autem disquisitio non circa illas quæ vt constât exemplis, agunt in se. Verùm circa vniuocas, vtrum valeant agere in se ipsas augendo, siue intendendo qualitatem suam. V, g. calidum vt 4. po. testne in se calorem intendere, vt quinque? Placet nobis.
units.tr: The inquiry, however, does not concern those causes which, as the examples show, act upon themselves. It concerns univocal causes, and whether they are able to act upon themselves by increasing or intensifying their own quality. For example, can what is warm at four degrees intensify its heat in itself up to five? This is what we shall examine.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Idem agere nequit in se ipsum.
units.tr: A thing cannot act upon itself.

units.la: PRobatur 1. auctoritate Aristotelis, qui probat, simile non agere in simile, quia hoc modo sequeretur, idem posse agere in se. Igitur ex Philosopho vera manet conclusio.
units.tr: It is proved first by the authority of Aristotle, who proves that like does not act on like, since in this way it would follow that the same thing could act on itself. Therefore the conclusion stands true on the authority of the Philosopher.

units.la: Probatur 2. ratione, quia omne agens vniuocum ideo agit, ut sibi assimilet passum: sed nequit assimilare se ipsum sibi; ergo non aget in se. Maior patet inductione. Ignis v. gr. operatur, ut faciat ignem; calor ut gignat calorem &c. Minorem nullus negabit. Consequentia currit, & probatur, nam omnis actio in passum incipere debet à causa validiori; nihil autem est se ipso validius; ergo agens non aget in se.
units.tr: It is proved second by reason. Every univocal agent acts in order to make the patient like itself, but it cannot make itself like itself; therefore it will not act on itself. The major is plain by induction: fire, for example, acts so as to produce fire, and heat so as to beget heat, and so on. No one will deny the minor. The consequence holds, and it is proved thus: every action upon a patient ought to begin from a cause that is stronger, but nothing is stronger than itself; therefore an agent does not act on itself.

units.la: Obijcies 1. calidum v.g. ut 4. potest gignere in subiecto externo alios gradus caloris à se distinctos, ergo & in se producet eosdem. Probatur consequentia, non.n. requiritur maior virtus, ut quintum, sextum, caeterosque generet in se, quàm in alio, nam vbicunq; sint gradus, omninò sunt pares, homogenei, & similes.
units.tr: You will object first: heat, for instance, can in an external subject produce other degrees of heat distinct from itself, therefore it will also produce the same degrees in itself. The consequence is proved thus: a greater power is not required for it to generate a fifth, a sixth and the rest in itself than in another, for wherever the degrees are, they are altogether equal, homogeneous and similar.

units.la: Resp. n. consequentiam. Ratio est, quia omnis causa operatur ad assimilandum sibi passum, vt supra; vnde poterit agere in subiectum externum, non ita in se. Ad probationem dico, non sequitur actio-nem. nem respectu subiecti, eò quòd istud nequeat assimilari.
units.tr: I deny the consequence. The reason is that every cause acts so as to make the patient like itself, as above; hence it can act upon an external subject but not in the same way upon itself. To the proof I say that it does not follow that there is action with respect to the subject, because that subject cannot be made like it.

units.la: Obijcies 2. Aqua in puteo hyemali tempore calescit: sed huiusmodi calor produci nequit ab aere circumobstante frigidissimo; ergo aqua ipsa operatur in se. Consimiliter pepones, qui ad breue tempus exponuntur æstiuo soli, dicuntur frigefieri: sed hoc ab externo calore solis non oritur, ergo substantia peponis immediatè agit in se. Item in madida, frigidaq; nube fit ignis; in fundo maris, ac fluminum limus tepescit &c. ergo cum hi effectus à causa extrinseca non oriantur, ab ipso met agente nascuntur: sed agens ipsum recipit eosdem in se, igitur &c.
units.tr: You will object second: water in a well calls itself warm in winter, but such heat cannot be produced by the extremely cold air surrounding it; therefore the water itself acts on itself. Similarly, melons that are put out for a short time in the summer sun are said to become cold; but this does not arise from the external heat of the sun, therefore the substance of the melon acts immediately on itself. Likewise fire is produced in a damp, cold cloud; and mud at the bottom of the sea and of rivers grows tepid, and so on. Therefore, since these effects do not arise from an external cause, they are born from the agent itself; but the agent receives the same effects in itself; therefore, and so on.

units.la: Respondent in communi sententia qualitates huiusmodi, frigus, calorem &c. non produci de nouo ab agentibus, verùm sentiri tantùm de nouo beneficio antiperistasis, aut per contrarij circumobsistentiam, quod idem est. Antiperistasis verò in allatis experietijs explicatur sic. Dum aer hyemali tempore frigidissimus circumobsidet aquam, cogit corpuscula calida, quæ à terra per effluuium continuò vaporant, recedere à se (contraria in se mutuò pellunt) hæc verò ab ambiente pulsa intra terræ meatus redeunt, ibi se colligunt, fouent, corpusq; illud, in quo manent, reddunt etiam calidius. Quapropter non generatur de nouo calor, sed tantùm, quia magis collectus est, sentitur. Sic de cæteris, quæ humescunt, infrigidantur &c. Vnde non sequitur, idem agere in se, verùm tantummodo quæ dispersa erant, colligi magis, & ideo venire ad sensum.
units.tr: The common opinion answers that qualities of this kind, cold, heat and so on, are not newly produced by the agents, but are only perceived anew through the benefit of antiperistasis, or through the surrounding of a contrary, which is the same thing. In the experiments adduced, antiperistasis is explained thus. While the air, extremely cold in winter, surrounds the water, it forces the warm corpuscles, which are continually vaporised from the earth through effluvia, to withdraw from it (contraries thrust each other apart), and these, driven back by the surrounding air, return within the pores of the earth, there gather together and are cherished, and make that body in which they remain even warmer. Therefore heat is not generated anew, but is only perceived because it has been gathered more closely. So it is with other things that become moist, grow cold, and so on. Hence it does not follow that the same thing acts on itself, but only that what was dispersed is gathered more, and so comes to be sensed.

units.la: Hæc explicatio, quam faciunt passim Aristotelei, mire concinit veterum philosophiæ, qui omnes alterationes per effluuia corporum frigidorum, calidorum &c. exponebant. Vnde siquando corpus aliquod calescit, frigefit, exsiccatur, humescit, non ex noua qualitatum productione, sed per motus atomorum varios, aut, per effluuia tenuissimæ substantiæ huc illuc, & circum emissa id explicabant. Quæ res acuta minùs, & ideo minùs morosa, magis etiam physica mihi semper visa est. Inde non inconsultò hanc postremam attexo disputationem, in qua veterum placita de alteratione prosecuturus, aliqualem nostræ physicæ lucem polliceor.
units.tr: This explanation, which the Aristotelians everywhere give, agrees remarkably well with the philosophy of the ancients, who all explained alterations through effluvia of cold bodies, warm bodies, and so on. Hence, whenever some body grows warm, cold, dry or moist, they explained it not by a new production of qualities but by the various motions of atoms, or by very fine effluvia of substance sent hither and thither and around. This approach has always seemed to me subtle rather than tiresome, and more physical. Hence I not unadvisedly append this last disputation, in which, intending to pursue the opinions of the ancients concerning alteration, I promise some light for our own physics.

units.la: DISPVTATIO QVARTA.
units.tr: DISPUTATION FOUR.

units.la: De alteratione iuxta principia veterum.
units.tr: On alteration according to the principles of the ancients.

units.la: VEteres philosophi, præsertim Democritus, Leucippus, Epicurus, Lucretius, & alij mutationes omnes in natura fieri per hoc dicebant, quòd atomi primigeniæ motu locali diuersimodè actæ, vniantur simul, deuniantur; subeant, hæreant, abscedant, auolent; se misceant, se repellant &c. Inde generatio substantialis contingit ex eorum sententia, quia minimæ substantiæ miscentur, & corruptio è contra, quia quæ priùs erant mixta, separantur. Consimiliter Alteratio in sola vnione, aut separatione atomorum ab ijs constituta est. Porro dicebant generationem, & corruptionem à simplici alteratione adhuc differre; nam generatio substantialis vocari debet quoties atomi tantâ copià, taliq; ordine vniuntur, vt sint principium certarum in natura operationum, & nomen acquirant substantiale, ac certum. E contra si tam enormiter illa minima separentur, vt nomen non retineant amplius, nec maneant principium agendi vt priùs, dicitur corruptio substantialis. Alteratio autem fit quotiescunq; aut acquiritur, aut deperditur aliquid substantiæ, sed non in tanta copia, neque ita sensibiliter, vt mixtum soluatur, & desinat vocari tale. V.gr. si rosa in elambyco per sublimatoriam, in cinerem, aquam, halitumq; tota soluatur, hæc est substantialis corruptio, eò quòd illa, etsi partes non destruantur, non tamen vt priùs manet, nec talis deinde vocari potest. Ex aduerso, si dictæ partes mole, ordine, ac figura, qua priùs, iterum colligerentur, esset generatio substantialis. Verùm si rosa non tota soluatur, sed aliqua transmittendo corpuscula, deperdat colorem, aut odorem, si tabescat, si fiat exsucca &c. tunc dicitur alterari, quia retinendo quod maius est, nomenque suum, paulisper immutatur. De generatione sequenti libro agemus. Hic alterationem aggredimus tali ordine, vt primò inquiramus, an reuera transmittantur à corporibus atomi. 2. an in alia corpora suscipiantur. 3. an istæ sint, quæ ibi alterationem efficiant. Ex quibus deinde sequentur explicationes actionum,quæ dicuntur contagiosæ, antiperisticæ, sympaticæ, antipaticæ, &c.
units.tr: The ancient philosophers, especially Democritus, Leucippus, Epicurus, Lucretius and others, said that all changes in nature come about in this way: the primordial atoms, moved by local motion in various ways, join together and come apart; they approach, cling, depart and fly off; they mix with one another and repel one another, and so on. Hence, in their view, substantial generation occurs when the smallest particles mix, and corruption, on the contrary, when those that were previously mixed are separated. Likewise, alteration was constituted by the union or separation of atoms alone. Moreover, they said that generation and corruption still differ from simple alteration. For substantial generation ought to be called whenever atoms unite in such quantity and in such order that they become the principle of certain operations in nature and acquire a substantial and definite name. On the other hand, if those minute particles are separated so violently that they no longer retain the name and no longer remain the principle of acting as before, it is called substantial corruption. Alteration, however, occurs whenever something is acquired or lost from a substance, but not in such quantity, nor so noticeably, that the compound is dissolved and ceases to be called what it was. For example, if a rose in an alembic is wholly dissolved by sublimation into ash, water and vapour, this is substantial corruption, because even though the parts are not destroyed, the rose no longer remains as it was and can no longer be called a rose. Conversely, if those parts were gathered together again with the same bulk, order and figure as before, there would be substantial generation. But if the rose is not wholly dissolved, yet by giving off some small particles it loses its colour or its scent, or it wilts, or it becomes dry and so on, then it is said to be altered, because it still retains what is greater and its name, though it is changed for a little. We shall treat of generation in the following book. Here we approach alteration in such an order that we first inquire: (1) whether atoms are really transmitted from bodies; (2) whether they are received into other bodies; (3) whether these are the ones that bring about alteration there. From these questions there will follow then the explanations of actions that are called contagious, antiperistatic, sympathetic, antipathetic, and so on.

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: DISQUISITION I.

units.la: An transmittantur à corporibus atomi.
units.tr: Whether atoms are transmitted from bodies.

units.la: PROintelligentia est adnotandum; corpora naturalia, & maximè quæ mixta sunt, innumeris constare partiBculis eterogeneis, quæ singulæ proprijs imbutæ qualitatibus in vna compositi fabrica manent. Hoc docemur experientia, quoties naturale mixtum, siue per artem, siue naturæ ingenio dissoluitur. Enimverò chymia per ignem separat metalla, & repetitis coctionibus aliquam semper adinuenit fæcem, scoriamq; diuersi generis, & virtutis. Ita spagyrica disgregat stipites, herbas, flores, deprehenditq; in singulis humorem, terram, halitum,odore,sapore,alijsq; accidentibus varium.Similiter si lapides, & gemmæ ipsæ terantur,manent puluisculi tam diuersi, vt alij sint asperi, & quidam læues; non pauci calidi,& multi frigidi; corrodentes isti, suaues illi, & huiusmodi.
units.tr: To begin with, it should be noted that natural bodies, and especially mixed bodies, consist of countless heterogeneous particles, each of which, imbued with its own qualities, remains within the structure of the compound. Experience teaches us this whenever a natural mixed body is dissolved, whether by art or by the workings of nature. Chemistry, for instance, separates metals by fire, and after repeated firings it always finds some dregs and slag of different kinds and powers. So too the spagyrist breaks down logs, herbs and flowers, and in each he finds moisture, earth and vapour, varying in smell, taste and other accidents. Likewise, if stones and gems themselves are ground down, there remain powders so varied that some are rough and some smooth, not a few hot and many cold, some corrosive and others gentle, and so on.

units.la: Oritur inde, vt naturalia mixta clandestinam quodammodo sentiant pugnam, & in ipsis caca quadam vulnera, inquit Lucretius, continuò infligantur. Nam minimæ substantiæ, siue atomi accidentibus referte contrariis opponuntur, agunt, reagunt, luctantur, donec se se ab inuicem expediant, ac soluant. Ex quo intelligis, cur aliqua corpora, etiamsi ab externa læsione remoueris, attamen patiantur, & aliquando tandem intereant, quia videlicet hostis militat intus, dum conatus quidam, & rixa fit à contrarijs inuicem se lancinantibus. Idcirco non omni no iuuat si aromata pyxidibus vitreis concludantur, nam paulatim sibi faciunt cariem, se rodunt, ac terunt. Neque pomum, aut florem diu tuebere illæsum, quamuis ab externo contrario serues, eo quòd in se suæ necis radicem habet. Sic omnino vniones alterantur ab intrinseco, cuadunt fuscæ, callum obducunt. Ebur antiquum dehiscit, per venulas fit rubrum, & fragilius. Calami auium se comaculant, conterunt, vermes generant &c. vnde patere cuique potest, in omni mixto suæ adesse principium alterationis, quæ in sola contrariorum pugna, & insensibili motu sita esse videtur.
units.tr: From this it comes about that natural mixed bodies feel, as it were, a hidden war, and that certain blind wounds, as Lucretius puts it, are continually inflicted within them. For the smallest substances, or atoms, laden with opposing accidents, face one another, act and react, struggle, until they disentangle and release themselves from each other. From this you can understand why some bodies, even when you have kept them free from external injury, nevertheless suffer and at last sometimes perish: namely because the enemy wages war within, while a kind of strife and quarrel arises from contraries tearing at one another. Hence it is of no use to shut aromatics up in glass boxes, for gradually they cause their own decay, gnawing and wearing themselves away. Nor can you keep a fruit or a flower long unharmed, even if you guard it from an external contrary, because it carries within itself the root of its own death. In just this way pearls are altered from within: they grow dark and develop a crust. Old ivory cracks, turns red through its little veins, and becomes more brittle. Birds' quills stain themselves, wear down, and breed worms, and so on. From this anyone can see that in every mixed body there is a principle of alteration within it, which seems to lie in the conflict of contraries alone and in an imperceptible motion.

units.la: Hisce accedunt agentia extrinseca, quæ per actiones in mixta exercitas iuuant in ijsdem alterationes, mouent atomos, & minima corpora, vrgent, pellunt, congregant, disgregant; v.gr. ignis operatur in lignum, & particulas, incipit in eo miscere, donec ad pugnam accitis contrarijs, tumultuarius fit motus. Aer ipse lambendo corpora ictibus crebris percellit, nam calefaciendo, exsiccando, penetrando mouet particulas, & de sua quiete suscitat. Aqua, seu agat per qualitates, aut per illapsum in poros, mea tusque insinuetur, non ne corpora sauciat? rimas inducit? abradit partes? icit? collidit? miscet?
units.tr: To these are added extrinsic agents, which, by their actions exerted upon mixed bodies, help bring about those same alterations: they move the atoms and minute bodies, press, drive, gather together and scatter them. For example, fire acts upon wood and begins to stir its particles, until, with contraries called into the fight, a tumultuous motion arises. The air itself, by lapping at bodies, strikes them with repeated blows; for by heating, drying and penetrating, it moves the particles and rouses them from their rest. Does water not wound bodies, whether it acts through its qualities or by flowing into the pores and penetrating the passages? Does it not induce cracks, rub away parts, throw, strike, or mix them?

units.la: Discitis ergo causam, quare mixta omnia corruptioni subiecta sint. Ea.n. duplex est, nempe interna, & externa. Prima consistit in partibus mixti heterogeneis, quae diuersis, contrarijsque accidentibus affectae, sensim, ac tacite, sed tamen aliquo modo agunt in se, donec altera praevalente, rixa tandem, processu temporis manifestetur. Secundo est ab extrinseco, quoties nimirum causa foris adueniens operatur in mixtum, latentesque in eo partes ad motum sollicitat magis quousque dissidium fiat, ac rei totius dissolutio. Haec doctrina veterum philosophiae concordans est; non in omnibus tamen, nam illi statuerunt atomos intrinsecè, ac formaliter calidas, frigidas, odorosas &c. nos verò insinuauimus accidentia distincta, sed ab ijs tamen naturaliter inseparabilia, vt suo loco apparebit clarius. Hisce praecognitis notetur.
units.tr: You therefore learn the cause why all mixed things are subject to corruption. For it is twofold, namely internal and external. The first consists in the heterogeneous parts of the mixed body, which, affected by diverse and contrary accidents, act upon one another gradually and silently, yet in some way, until one prevails and the strife at last becomes manifest with the passage of time. Second, it arises from without, whenever a cause coming from outside works upon the mixed body and rouses the parts lying hidden in it to motion, until a discord arises and the whole thing is dissolved. This doctrine agrees with the teaching of the ancient philosophers; yet not in all respects, for they held that atoms are intrinsically and formally hot, cold, fragrant and so on, whereas we have suggested distinct accidents which are nevertheless naturally inseparable from them, as will appear more clearly in its proper place. With these things known in advance, let this be noted.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Transmittuntur à corporibus atomi.
units.tr: That atoms are emitted from bodies.

units.la: PRobari potest conclusio ratione, quæ à tradita iam doctrina facilè nascitur. Eo quòd si corpora mixta conslantur partibus eterogeneis, & hæ per oppositas qualitates alterant se, mouent, ac denique soluunt, necessum est, corpuscula etiam tenuissima, quæ priùs cum crassioribus alligabantur, exolui, secerni, & aliò migrare. Secundò: quoties causa_ extrinseca percellit corpus, mouet in_ eo minima, siue interiùs vrgendo, siue foras educendo, & sic transpiratio atomorum ex hac etiam causa fieri videtur.
units.tr: The conclusion can be proved by reason, which follows easily from the doctrine already set out. For if mixed bodies consist of heterogeneous parts, and these alter, move and finally dissolve one another through opposed qualities, it is necessary that even the most minute corpuscles, which were previously bound to the coarser ones, be loosened, separated and carried elsewhere. Second: whenever an external cause strikes a body, it moves the smallest parts within it, either by pressing inwards or by driving them outwards, and so the transpiration of atoms seems to arise from this cause too.

units.la: Probatur 2. auctoritate. Primò quidem Aristotelis, qui passim in libris acroamaticis, & præsertim vbi tractat meteora, explicat actiones corporum ex motu locali particularum. Accedit Hyppocrates, Galenus, Auicenna_, Cardanus, Scaliger, Fernelius, Septalius, Fortunius Licetus, Aquilonius, Sennertus, aliíque Auctores, doctrina, & experientia eruditissimi, quos recenset Magnenus disput. 2. prop.3. Præcipuè verò annuunt Medici peritiores, quorum in manu Germana, seù experimentalis Philosophia optimè valet.
units.tr: It is proved, second, by authority. First, by that of Aristotle, who throughout his esoteric books, and especially where he treats of meteors, explains the actions of bodies by the local motion of particles. Add Hippocrates, Galen, Avicenna_, Cardano, Scaliger, Fernel, Septalius, Fortunio Liceti, Aquilonius, Sennert, and other authors most learned in doctrine and experience, whom Magnenus lists in his second disputation, third proposition. But above all, the more skilled physicians agree, and in their hands the German, or experimental, philosophy is most effective.

units.la: Probatur 3. experientijs, & quidem ita patentibus, vt eas vel cæci videant.
units.tr: It is proved, third, by experiences so obvious that even the blind can see them.

units.la: Imprimis enim corpora calida substantias minimas alio transmittunt ad calefaciendum, & si actio pergat, ipsa paulatim consumuntur, vt constat in carbone, qui post multam calefactionem, sub cinerea quadam lanugine tandem consumitur. Et hinc hauries rationem, cur ignis a longe stupam, chartam, aliaque comburat, si enim præcisè gignit in medio calorem vniformiter difformiter minorem, & minorem, vt docet Peripatetica, quomodo in subiecto distanti produci potest ignis per calorem remissum, si forma non inducitur, nisi per qualitatem vt acto?
units.tr: First of all, warm bodies send out very minute substances to other things in order to warm them, and if the action continues these substances are gradually used up, as is evident in charcoal, which after long heating is at last consumed, leaving a sort of ashen down. And from this you may grasp why fire burns tow, paper and other things from a distance. For if the heat produced in the medium is simply a heat that becomes uniformly or non-uniformly weaker and weaker, as the Peripatetics teach, how can fire be produced in a distant subject by a weakened heat, if the form is induced only through a quality as active?

units.la: Secundo corpora etiam frigida per effluuium agunt, quemadmodum patet in ventis borealibus, qui frigus afferunt per hoc, quòd frigidos intrudunt spiritus. Et hoc libentius debent concedere Peripatetici, qui putant aerem natura sua calidum euadere in frigidum per extraneos vapores a globo terraqueo transmissos. Hinc vinum, quod in glacie, seu niue frigescit, multoties noxium est, quia vapores intra se recipit sulphureos, nitreos, &c.
units.tr: Second, cold bodies also act through an effluvium, as is plain in north winds, which bring cold because they send forth cold spirits. The Peripatetics ought to concede this all the more readily, since they think that air, by nature warm, becomes cold through foreign vapours sent out from the terraqueous globe. Hence wine that freezes in ice or snow is often harmful, because it takes in sulphurous, nitrous and other vapours.

units.la: Tertio quæ sunt odorofa, emissionem tenuissimæ substantiæ continuo faciunt. Inde fit vt si rosam diu odores, & contredtes, odorem citius deperdat, sic enim laxantur pori, & spiritus alio migrant. Poma etiam post aliquod tempus amittunt succos, & in ijs extimum corticem vides flacefsentem, corrugatum, crispis adductum, quia nimirum substantiæ, quibus implebatur, abscesserunt: quapropter minus etiam ponderis habet, quod non accideret, si tantum qualitas deperderetur. Ex hoc discis, cur seminum vires triennio circiter lapso effætæ sint; cur ætas medicamentorum statuatur certa; cur aromata vim denique perdant, vacua, leuia, & exsucca euadant.
units.tr: Third, things that have a smell continually emit a very fine substance. Hence, if you keep a rose for a long time and handle it, it quickly loses its scent, for its pores are loosened and its spirits migrate elsewhere. Apples also lose their juices after some time, and you see their outer skin wilting, wrinkled and drawn together, because the substances with which they were filled have departed. For this reason they also weigh less, which would not happen if only a quality were lost. From this you learn why the powers of seeds are spent after about three years, why the shelf-life of medicines is fixed, and why spices at last lose their strength and become empty, weightless and dry.

units.la: Quartò animalia insensibiles halitus, in magna tamen copia eiaculantur. Ob id canis venaticus perdicem insequitur, leporem &c. & quò magis illa excurrendo incaluerint, eò certius vestigat, quia sic per conceptum calorem atomi odorosæ vaporant magis. Certè post labores, & vitæ functiones animalia deperdunt vires, non quia destruatur qualitas, verùm ex amissione substantiæ, quæ proinde sumptione cibi refici debet. Neque obstat ratio illa pinguis nimium, & rudis, quòd hi spiritus non videntur. Audi Sanctorium in statica medica, Perspiratio, qua salubriter aufert è corpore multum, idque inutile pondus, non est qua cum sudore fit, sed ille halitus insensibilis, qualis hyeme uno die naturali ad quinquaginta uncias, & ultra exhalare potest, &c. Sed in re luce ipsa clariori, diutius non moror.
units.tr: Fourth, animals give off imperceptible breaths, yet in great quantity. For this reason a hunting dog pursues a partridge, a hare and so on, and the more heated they become by running, the more surely it tracks them, because in this way the odorous atoms are vaporised more when the heat is conceived. Certainly after labours and the functions of life animals lose their strength, not because the quality is destroyed but because of the loss of substance, which must therefore be restored by taking food. Nor does that argument, too gross and crude, that these spirits are not seen, stand in the way. Hear Sanctorius in his Medical Statics: The perspiration by which the body healthfully rids itself of much useless weight is not that which occurs with sweat, but that insensible breath which, in winter, can be exhaled to fifty ounces and more in one natural day, etc. But in a matter clearer than light itself, I shall not dwell longer.

units.la: Opponis tamen. Si atomi, seu tenuissima substantiarum effluuia de corporibus emitterentur, naturalia mixta citissimè interirent quomodo substantialis hæc transpiratio fiet à lapide? à ferro? ab auro? ab adamante? 3. non est sensibilis huiusmodi emissio. 4. multi Sancti PP. ob id irascuntur Leucippo, Democrito, eiusdemque sectæ philosophis, quòd atomos adinuenerint, seu confinxerint; unde Lactantius 3. inslit: inquit Vbi sunt, aut unde ista corpuscula? cur illa nemo prater unum Leucippum somniauit? à quo Democritus eruditus hereditatem stultitiæ reliquit Epicuro? &c.
units.tr: Yet you object. If atoms, or the finest effluvia of substances, were sent out of bodies, natural mixed things would perish most quickly. How will this substantial transpiration happen from a stone? From iron? From gold? From adamant? Third, emissions of this kind are not perceptible. Fourth, many holy Fathers were angry with Leucippus, Democritus and the philosophers of their sect because they invented or fabricated atoms; whence Lactantius, in book three of his Institutes, says: Where are they, or whence are these little bodies? Why did no one dream of them except the one Leucippus? From whom the learned Democritus left the inheritance of folly to Epicurus, etc.

units.la: Respond. ad 1. naturalia mixta non tam cito dissolui, aut interire, quia minimorum transfusio non fit simul tota, sed paulatim, atque insensibiliter. Verum tamen est, quòd si ea continuetur, neque aliunde partes amissæ restaurentur, aliquando tandem perit compositum, quo modo in prunis, in floribus, & similibus fit.
units.tr: Reply to the first: natural mixed things do not dissolve or perish so quickly, because the transfusion of the smallest parts does not take place all at once, but gradually and imperceptibly. It is true, however, that if this continues, and the lost parts are not restored from elsewhere, the compound at last perishes at some point, as happens in embers and in flowers and similar things.

units.la: Resp. ad 2. non omnia mixta conflari æquè perfectè, aliqua enim per diuturniorem naturæ operam strictius coaluerunt, vnionemque inter partes habent perfectiorem, vel quia minima componentia sunt magis homogenea, unde parum, aut nihil dissident, neque se mouent: vel quia particulæ talibus constant figuris, ut singulæ se amplexentur, se infigant, se mordicus teneant. In quo casu ab interiori natura fiet rarissima transpiratio, & nisi accedat extrinsecum agens, fermè nulla. Hoc tamen non sic probat de omnibus.
units.tr: Reply to the second: not all mixed things are compounded equally perfectly. Some have cohered more tightly through a longer work of nature, and have a more perfect union among their parts, either because the component minima are more homogeneous, so that they differ little or not at all and do not move one another, or because the particles consist of such shapes that each embraces, fastens into and holds fast the others. In this case the transpiration will come from the inner nature and will be very rare, and, unless an external agent intervenes, almost none. This, however, does not prove the same of all things.

units.la: Respond. ad 3. eiaculationes atomorum aliquando sentiri per tactum, gustum, odoratum &c. Praeterea etiamsi non sentirentur ipsae, tamen à posteriori cognosci possunt, eò quia relinquuntur in mixtis vulnera, dehiscentiae, solutiones, vt supra innuimus. Quodsi neges evaporationem, quia illam non vides, ergo negandae sunt exhalationes, quae tamen apparent in meteoris; negandi puluisculi, quos tamen venti ferunt in oculos; neganda ramenta, quae tamen funis ad puteum, pes ad limina, gladius ad cotem facit. Quae omnia si negare non audeas, inquit Lucretius in I.
units.tr: Reply to the third: the emissions of atoms are sometimes perceived by touch, taste, smell and so on. Moreover, even if they were not perceived themselves, they could still be known a posteriori, because wounds, gapings and dissolutions are left in mixed things, as we have hinted above. But if you deny evaporation because you do not see it, then you must deny exhalations too, which nevertheless appear in meteors; you must deny the little dusts which the winds nevertheless carry into the eyes; you must deny the shavings which the rope makes at the well, the foot at the threshold, the sword at the whetstone. If you do not dare to deny all these things, Lucretius says in book I.

units.la: Necesse est
units.tr: It is necessary

units.la: Confiteare esse in rebus, nec posse videri.
units.tr: You must admit that they exist among things, though they cannot be seen.

units.la: Respond. ad 4. Sanctos PP. eam sibi elegisse philosophiam, quae cuiq; magis placuit, seu quam tulit suorum temporum schola. Inde nonnullis quia obtigit Aristoteles, displicuit Democritus. Alijs, quia Democritum coluerunt, Aristoteles non saput. Studia ergo diuisa sunt. Certe PP. Graeci, Nissenus, Chrysostomus, Cyrillus, Clem. Alex. & alij peripateticam doctrinam vt obscuram, metaphysicam, & à natura diuulsam damnant. Videri possunt stromata Clementis, Exameron Nisseni, & aliorum codices, vbi atomos Democriteas, non materiam primam adinuenietis. Quapropter, non quicunque opponitur Democrito, idcirco atomos negat; sed fortasse modum, quo docuerat eas concurrere ad rerum generationes, casu nimirum, rum, tumultuariò, sine duce, sine auctore, qui motibus earundem sapientissimè præsideret.
units.tr: Reply to the fourth objection. The holy Fathers chose for themselves whichever philosophy pleased each of them most, or which the school of their own time offered. So for some, because they happened upon Aristotle, Democritus displeased; for others, because they cultivated Democritus, Aristotle had no appeal. The studies were therefore divided. Certainly the Greek Fathers, Nyssen, Chrysostom, Cyril, Clement of Alexandria and others, condemn the Peripatetic doctrine as obscure, metaphysical, and divorced from nature. The Stromata of Clement, the Hexaemeron of Nyssen, and the writings of others may be consulted, where you will find the Democritean atoms, not prime matter. Wherefore, whoever opposes Democritus does not on that account deny atoms; he perhaps denies only the manner in which Democritus taught that they came together to generate things, namely by chance, at random, tumultuously, without a guide, without an author who would wisely preside over their motions.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISQUISITION II.

units.la: An, & quomodo atomi transmissa in alia corpora suscipiantur.
units.tr: Whether and how atoms that are transmitted are received into other bodies.

units.la: PRO intelligentia prælibanda hic est doctrina, quam fusiùs trademus in materia de vacuo, nimirum in omni composito insensibiles quosdam poros, meatusque interseri, per quos naturas suas obit functiones. Ita plantæ quibusdam vacuolis vbique texuntur, per quæ humorem à terra exsugunt. Lapides gerunt locula insensibilia, quæ à posito desuper oleo sensim peruaduntur. Animalia vndique scatent meatibus: in pelle, à qua exit sudor: in carne, quam penetrat sanguis: in osse, per quod stillatur medulla &c. ex hoc viuentium textura sericis comparatur tibialibus, quæ ita sunt confecta, vt facilè coeant, laxentur, vniantur, explicentur, eò quòd fila tanquam annulos habent, quæ nunc laxiuscula, nunc magis collecta pro forma pedum, surarumque sese disponunt. Ob hæc cecinit Orpheus, animal esse retis ad instar implexum ex Aristotele l.2.de gen. an. c.1. nam sicuti rete beneficio vacuorum adstringitur, & explicatur, consimili ratione motus omnis, qui fit in animali per siftolem, diastolem, transpirationem, receptionemq; huiusce vacui ope contingit.
units.tr: Before we begin, we must grasp the doctrine that we shall set out more fully in the treatment of the void: in every compound there are certain insensible pores and passages, interposed, through which the bodies perform their natural functions. Thus plants are everywhere woven with tiny vacuities, through which they draw up moisture from the earth. Stones contain insensible cavities, which oil poured on top gradually penetrates. Animals are full of passages everywhere: in the skin, from which sweat exits; in the flesh, which blood penetrates; in the bone, through which marrow is drawn off, and so on. From this, the texture of living things is like silk stockings, which are so made that they easily gather, loosen, join and unfold, because their threads are like rings, which now lie somewhat loose and now are drawn tighter, arranging themselves to the shape of the feet and calves. For this reason Orpheus sang that an animal is like a net woven together, as Aristotle reports in De generatione animalium, book 2, chapter 1. For just as a net is drawn tight and opened out by means of its empty spaces, so by a similar principle every movement that occurs in an animal, through systole, diastole, transpiration and reception, comes about by means of this void.

units.la: Oportet autem huiusmodi poros concipere tenuissimos, nam v.gr. in paruula formica si adsunt organa tam exigua, cor, hepar, venæ, ramuli, nerui &c. vt sensum effugiant, quantæ subtilitatis concipiendi sunt pori, meatusq; singulis partibus intertexti? Quod verò in animalibus vnusquisque fatetur, in cæteris quoq; compositis concedendum est. Lignum sanè habet poros, vt ostendit poculum hederaceum, quod à Plinio, alijsque obseruatum est aquam non posse capere, sed vini fidelissimum esse custodem. Quæ res oritur, vel quia particulæ, atque atomi aquæ proportionem habent figuræ cum poris ligni; aut quia minùs complexæ sunt, vnde facilè permeant: vini autem sunt magis implexæ ob substantiæ dissimilis commixtionem, ac fæcem: propterea insinuare se nequeunt. In lapidibus etiam dari hosce meatus experientia docet vt supra. Et ratio est, quam alibi attigimus, nam substantiæ componentes diuersæ sunt mole, figura, magnitudine, quare si vniantur, non adæquatè se tangunt ad omnes partes: ergo relinquunt spatium. Explicari hoc potest in aggerie granorum diuersi generis; nam si omnia in vno modo permisceantur, quia non penitus adrepunt inuicem, spatiola relinquunt, per quæ si alia minora granula inijciantur, puta milij, facilè meant. Sed fusius alibi, & interim notetur.
units.tr: We must, however, conceive such pores as very fine. For example, if in a tiny ant there are organs so small (heart, liver, veins, little branches, nerves, and so on) that they escape the senses, how fine must the pores and passages be that are interwoven through each of its parts? What everyone admits about animals must also be conceded about other compounds. Wood certainly has pores, as the ivy cup shows, which Pliny and others have observed does not take in water, but is a most faithful guardian of wine. This happens either because the particles and atoms of water have a figure proportionate to the pores of the wood, or because they are less intricately joined and so pass through easily, whereas the particles of wine are more intricately joined, owing to the mixture of a dissimilar substance and its lees, and therefore cannot insinuate themselves. That these passages exist also in stones experience teaches, as we said above. And the reason is one we touched on elsewhere: the component substances differ in mass, shape and size, so when they are united they do not touch each other fully at all points, and so leave space. This can be explained by a heap of grains of different kinds: if everything is mixed together in one way, since the grains do not fully creep into one another, they leave little spaces, through which, if other smaller grains are poured in, say millet, they pass through easily. But more fully elsewhere; and meanwhile let this be noted.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Atomi per meatus in corpora suscipiuntur.
units.tr: Atoms are received into bodies through pores.

units.la: PRobari potest innumeris experientijs ; ferri, quod ignescit per ignea corpuscula intromissa ; ligni, quod madet per aquæ minima recepta; vestiū,quæ calent per spiritus animalium inclusos, &c. Sed vnam seligamus, aut alteram,quæ videntur vulgo difficiliores .
units.tr: This can be proved by countless experiences: iron that glows through fiery corpuscles introduced into it; wood that becomes moist through the smallest particles of water received into it; garments that grow warm through enclosed animal spirits, and so on. But let us select one or two which seem more difficult to the common people.

units.la: Quando ignis calefacit aquam, spiritus ignei, qui transmittuntur, per aquæ meatus insinuant sese , donec sequente actione, ibi plures, et plures fiunt, coalescunt, reddunt〈q〉 calidam aquam. Hinc est quòd ab ea continuo expirant halitus, videlicet propter ignem tenuissimè respirante, qui trahit humorem, inquit Arift.4. Meteor. Hinc etiam quòd calida si ad solem exponatur, citiùs frigescit, quàm in loco frigido, quia nimirum calor externus adhuc magis attenuat, meatusq; aperit, vnde igniculi exeunt. Hinc similiter quòd mêbra vstulata sanantur facilius per ignem applicitum, seu adhibita re aliqua calida, vt cæpa inquit Fernelius, quia hoc modo pori membrorum non sinuntur constringi, vnde corpora ignea,quæ latebant, exhalant, sicuti è contra si obster frigus, intro magis recedunt. Hinc pariter quòd aqua ebullit, si diù maneat ad ignem ; & magis etiam, si operculo tegatur,quia nimirum spiritus ignei tunc plures ingrediuntur, & impediti ne statim exeant, particulas aquæ illabuntur, agitant, impellunt, in bullas tollunt. Quòdsi calida talis foret ob calorem tantummodo conceptum, quomodo accidens moueret substantiam, & ab imo totam commisceret? Ignis ergo latet in aqua meatuum beneficio receptus.
units.tr: When fire heats water, the fiery spirits that are transmitted insinuate themselves through the pores of the water. As the action continues, more and more of them gather there, coalesce, and make the water hot. Hence it is that vapour constantly breathes out from it, because the fire, breathing very thinly, draws up the moisture, as Aristotle says in Meteorology 4. Hence too, if warm water is exposed to the sun, it cools more quickly than in a cold place, because the external heat thins it still further and opens its pores, whence the little fires escape. Hence similarly, burnt limbs are healed more easily when fire is applied to them, or some warm thing, such as an onion, as Fernel says, because in this way the pores of the limbs are not allowed to contract; whence the fiery bodies that were lying hidden are exhaled. On the contrary, if cold is applied, they withdraw further inward. Hence likewise water boils if it stays on the fire for a long time, and even more if it is covered with a lid, because then more fiery spirits enter; hindered from leaving at once, they fall upon the particles of water, agitate and impel them, and lift them into bubbles. But if the water were hot merely from heat conceived in it, how would an accident move the substance and stir the whole thing up from the bottom? Therefore the fire lies hidden in the water, received there by means of the pores.

units.la: Sed iuuerit hic audire Scaligerum,non minus ingenuitatis, quàm acuminis virum,qui exercit.14. in Cardanum sic ait. Neq; aqua feruens est ignis, quatenus aqua est, sed quatenus ignita: est igitur habens ignem, & siccitatem,quam in sumo abeuntem comprehendimus intellectione, atque etiam sensu, vrit enim: qui enim in aqua est ignis, est contrario suo mixtus; abit igitur. Hæc nostra ratio etiam tua definitione fulta est. Ignis, inquis, est maximus calor. Argumentum procedit sic: aqua feruens vrit: omne vrens est ignis: appone tu conclusionem. Hæc ille ad Cardanum. Accedit D. Thomas, inquiens particulas igneas in terram à pluuia deferri pro mixtorum generationibus, & ideo pluuio tempore tantum frigus non sentiri. Innuit Aristoteles 4. Meteor.dum ait. Ea sunt combustibilia,qua habent meatus suscepti uos ignis. Ergo igneæ particulæ fusc ipiuntur in corpora per meatus.
units.tr: But it will be helpful to hear Scaliger here, a man of no less candour than acuteness, who in Exercise 14 against Cardan says as follows: Boiling water is not fire insofar as it is water, but insofar as it is ignited. It therefore has fire and dryness, which we grasp in the smoke that departs, both by understanding and also by sense; for it burns. For the fire that is in the water is mixed with its contrary, and so it departs. This our argument is also supported by your own definition. Fire, you say, is the greatest heat. The argument proceeds thus: boiling water burns; everything that burns is fire; now you draw the conclusion. Thus he writes against Cardan. St Thomas agrees, saying that particles of fire are carried into the earth by rain for the generation of mixed bodies, and that for this reason so little cold is felt in rainy weather. Aristotle hints at the same thing in Meteorology 4 when he says: Those things are combustible which have pores receptive of fire. Therefore the fiery particles are poured into bodies through the pores.

units.la: Probatur denique à simili, nam Aristotelei non putant absurdum, quòd in eadem subiecti parte maneant simul frigus, & calor, etiamsi hæc duo natura sua contraria sint. Quid ergo non concedant manere quoque substantias permixtas, quarum vna calorem, vna frigus habeant? Hoc sanè denegari nequit ratione contrarij, nam substantiæ non opponuntur nisi per accidentia: & per ipsos accidentia contraria manent simul. Neq; ratione corporis negandum est, quia corpuscula minima ingressum habent per vacua, & poros, qui toto seù composito, seù elemento admixti sunt.
units.tr: Finally, it is proved from a parallel case. The Aristotelians do not think it absurd that cold and heat remain together in the same part of a subject, even though these two are contrary by their nature. Why then should they not grant that mixed substances also remain, one of which has heat and another cold? This cannot be denied on the ground of contrariety, for substances are opposed only through their accidents, and the contrary accidents themselves remain together. Nor is it to be denied on the ground of body, since the smallest corpuscles have entrance through vacua and pores, which are mixed in with the whole composite or with the element.

units.la: Opponis. Quælibet aquæ pars etiam minima calida est, non ergo per suscep-tum ignem, alioquin fieret penetratio corporum. Respondeo, non fieri penetrationem ob meatus in aqua latentes. Ita etiam si sal in aquam injiciatur, nonne tota euadit falsa? & nihilominus per minima salis admixta hoc fit. Nonne aer totus euadit frigidus? peripatetici tamen dicunt, effectum oriri per ingressum exalationis. Non ne totus liquor euadit ruber, niger, flauus, prout illi commiscentur diuersi pulueres colorati? sed hoc habetur ex eorundem puluerum ingresu. Cur ergo de calida non ita dicamus?
units.tr: You object: every part of water, even the smallest, is hot; therefore it is not so through the fire received, otherwise there would be a penetration of bodies. I reply that penetration does not come about because of the pores lying hidden in the water. So too, if salt is thrown into water, does not the whole become salty? And yet this happens through the smallest particles of salt mixed in. Does not all the air become cold? Yet the Peripatetics say the effect arises from the entry of an exhalation. Does not the whole liquid become red, black or yellow, according to which coloured powders are mixed into it? But this comes from the entry of those same powders. Why then should we not say the same of heat?

units.la: DISQVISITIO TERTIA.
units.tr: DISPUTATION THREE.

units.la: An in hisce atomis alteratio consistat.
units.tr: Whether alteration consists in these atoms.

units.la: PRo intelligentia huiusce rei admodū iuuerit repetere difficultates quę opinionem de qualitatumproductione inuoluunt. Imprimis enim haud satis intelligitur quomodo qualitas producatur vniformiter difformiter, minor semper, & minor, si agens intendit assimilare sibi passum; & ad hoc requiruntur tot gradus, quot sunt in ipso. Multò minus quomodo intendatur, nam si ex vnione graduum similium, ergo videtur quòd possit augere se ipsam: si dissimilium, cur hoc fit à causa, quæ semper agit vno modo? Præterea quot ambages de actione, reactione, pugna, expulsione, &c. quæ omnia fidem faciunt Sidonio dicenti, explicat vt Plato, implicat vt Aristoteles: ob id notetur.
units.tr: To understand this matter, it will be very helpful to go back over the difficulties that the opinion about the production of qualities involves. First of all, it is not sufficiently understood how a quality is produced, whether uniformly or non-uniformly, always less and less, if the agent intends to make the patient like itself, and for this, as many degrees are required as there are in the agent itself. Much less is it understood how a quality is intensified. For if it is intensified by the union of like degrees, then it seems that it can increase itself; if by the union of unlike degrees, why does this happen from a cause that always acts in one way? Besides, how many tangles there are about action, reaction, struggle, expulsion, and so on! All of these lend support to Sidonius when he says that they explain like Plato, entangle like Aristotle. On this account, let it be noted.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Probabile videtur, quòd alteratio in motu atomorum, consistat.
units.tr: It seems probable that alteration consists in the motion of atoms.

units.la: PRobatur ex iss, quæ hucusque diximus, nam visum est, corpora mixta diuersimodè affici, variari, aliter se habere, si aut emiserint à se particulas minimas, aut easdem ab alijs receperint, ergo manet probabile in hoc tantum consistere alterationem. Antecedens luculenter probatur supra, vbi dicitur, quod ex corporum egressu flacescit pomum, arescit lignum, lassatur animal, figuram, vim, pondus amittunt corpora &c. Ex ingressu vero contrarium fit. Consequentia patet, nam si antequam concipiamus vllam fieri qualitatis productionem, habetur effectus alterationis per motum atomorum, ergo in hoc solum alteratio tota consistit.
units.tr: This is proved from what we have said so far. For it has been shown that mixed bodies are affected in different ways, vary, and are otherwise disposed, if they either emit from themselves minute particles or receive the same particles from others. Therefore it remains probable that alteration consists in this alone. The antecedent is clearly proved above, where it is said that an apple wilts, wood dries, an animal grows weary, and bodies lose their shape, power, and weight from the egress of bodies. From ingress the opposite occurs. The consequence is plain: if, before we conceive any production of a quality, there is an effect of alteration through the motion of atoms, then alteration wholly consists in this alone.

units.la: Probatur 2. auctoritate: Scaligeri, qui exerc. 12. artic. 2. contra Card. ait, quod non fit intensio qualitatum, sed accretio, sicut & quantitatis; unde infert: Non est igitur maior calor intensione eiusdem partis, sed aliarum partium accessione, alioquin si intenderetur, intenderetur & ipsa essentia. Ergo cum teneat Scaliger, hasce partes, quae faciunt calidum, esse minima ignea, intensio etiam fiet ex additione minimorum. Sequitur autem idem auctor explicare, quomodo res in intensione se habeat, sic discurrendo. Sint ferri partes nondum laborati a b. c d. in quarum singulis v. gr. totidem sint ignis partes e f. g h. malleo condensati ferri partes coeant in vnum, quod fit i. ea actio appelletur k. manifestum est eosdem gradus esse, qui prius, verum ob coniunctionem efficaciores, &c. Accedit etiam Plato in Phædone, vbi ait: quid est in corpore, quod incalescit? non dabo rudem illam respondentem, quia est calor, sed exquisitiorem, quia est ignis. Legatur Aristoteles 4. Meteororum, & patebit, quàm placeat Philosopho hæc sententia de alteratione per motus atomorum.
units.tr: Second, it is proved by authority. Scaliger, in Exercise 12, article 2, against Cardan, says: "there is no intensification of qualities, but accretion, just as with quantity; hence he infers: there is therefore no greater heat from intensification of the same part, but from the accession of other parts; otherwise, if it were intensified, the essence itself would be intensified." Therefore, since Scaliger holds that the parts which make a thing hot are minute fiery bodies, intensification too will occur by the addition of minima. The same author goes on to explain how things stand in intensification, reasoning thus: "Let there be parts of unworked iron, a, b, c, d, in each of which there are, say, as many parts of fire, e, f, g, h, condensed by the hammer. Let the parts of iron come together into one, which is i. That action is called k. It is manifest that the degrees are the same as before, but more effective because of the conjunction, etc." Plato also agrees in the Phaedo, where he says: "What is it in the body that becomes hot? I will not give that crude answer, that it is heat, but the more exact one, that it is fire." Let Aristotle, Meteorology book 4, be read, and it will be plain how much the Philosopher approves this opinion about alteration through the motions of atoms.

units.la: Probatur 3. ratione sic. Detur ignis, aut glacies, vel huiusmodi aliud agens. Constituatur in hoc gymnasio, & circa ipsum fiat vacuum ad palmi v.gr. distantiam. Deinde apponatur manus, quæ per datum quoque palmum distet. Certe probabilissimum est quòd ignis, aut quæuis alia sit causa, operabitur in manum. Cur enim suspendat actionem? fortasse ratione vacui? non videtur dicendum, nam si vacuum non impediret motus grauium, aut leuium, vt senior philosophia vult, quomodo impediet cæteras causas, ne agant? Agent igitur, v.gr. calefaciendo: sed ista calefactio non effet per qualitatem ab igne productam, ergo per corpora in manum transmissa. Probo minorem. Qualitas in communi Peripatetica non migrat se sola, neque transit de subiecto in subiectum; unde aiunt, si fieret vacuum à cælo adusque terram, cessarent influentiæ. Consequentia patet. Manus enim calefieret: non per accidens productum, ergo per corpus emissum. Quod autem in tali casu fieret, quis dicat non contingere modo, ac de facto?
units.tr: Third, it is proved by reason, as follows. Let there be fire, or ice, or some other such agent. Let it be set up in this hall, and let a vacuum be made around it at a distance of, say, a palm. Then let a hand be applied, which is likewise at the given distance of a palm. Surely it is most probable that the fire, or whatever other cause it is, will act upon the hand. For why would it suspend its action? Perhaps because of the vacuum? That does not seem to be the right answer. For if a vacuum does not impede the motion of heavy or light bodies, as the older philosophy holds, how would it impede other causes from acting? They will act, for example by heating. But that heating would not be through a quality produced by the fire; therefore it would be through bodies transmitted into the hand. I prove the minor premise. A quality, in the common Peripatetic sense, does not migrate by itself, nor pass from subject to subject; hence they say that if a vacuum were made from heaven down to earth, the influences would cease. The consequence is plain. For the hand would be heated not by an accidentally produced thing, but by an emitted body. Who would say that what would happen in such a case does not in fact also happen?

units.la: Opponis 1. si Alteratio fieret ex motu tu atomorum nulla daretur qualitas intensa: hoc dici non potest, ergo. Probatur sequela, nam plura corpuscula nequeunt simul esse in eadem parte subiecti, alioquin penetrarentur, ergo nulla fiet intensio.
units.tr: You object first: if alteration were made by the motion of atoms, no intense quality would be given. This cannot be said; therefore. The consequence is proved thus: several corpuscles cannot be at the same time in the same part of a subject, otherwise they would be penetrated; therefore no intensification will occur.

units.la: Respond. n. maiorem. Ad probationem distinguo. Plura corpuscula nequeunt esse in vna subiecti parte indiuisibili ; c. sensibili, n. ergo nulla fiet intensio, d. physica n. metaphysica transfeat. Dico igitur, quod omnis alteratio physica est sensibilis, unde fit etiam in parte quanta, & sensibili: pars vero sensibilis potest recipere in se plura, & plura corpuscula, iuxta meatus, quos habet. Quodsi concipias in vnico indiuisibili multos gradus penetrari, & ita qualitatem intendi, hoc est procedere metaphysico, & nimium subtili modo, nam vnicum indiuisibile, qua tale, non alteratur, sed quatenus vnitum alijs admittit vacuola ; meatusque, intra quos ingredi possit extraneum. Quapropter si v. gr. spongia madefiat, mador est quidem inhaesiue in tota spongia, quia reuera hoc totum est id, quod madet : sed si assumas vnumquodque indiuisibile seorsim, hoc non habet madorem inhaesiue, seu intrinsece receptum, sed tantum adhaesiue, prout nimirum intra ipsum, & alia indiuisibilia dum illabitur aqua, etiam adhaeret.
units.tr: I grant the major premise as regards a sensible part. As to the proof, I distinguish: several corpuscles cannot be in one indivisible part of the subject. I grant this for a sensible part; I deny that therefore no intensification occurs. I distinguish: let it pass in the physical sense; I deny it in the metaphysical sense. I say, therefore, that every physical alteration is sensible, whence it also happens in a quantitative and sensible part. A sensible part, however, can receive into itself several and many corpuscles, according to the pores it has. But if you conceive that many degrees penetrate a single indivisible, and thus that quality is intensified, this is to proceed in a metaphysical and overly subtle way. For a single indivisible, as such, is not altered; but insofar as it is united with others, it admits small vacuities and pores within which something extraneous can enter. Therefore, if, for example, a sponge is wetted, the moisture is indeed inherent in the whole sponge, because this whole is really what gets wet. But if you take each indivisible separately, it does not have moisture inherently, or intrinsically received, but only adherently: namely, as the water flows in, it adheres within it and to the other indivisibles.

units.la: Opponis etiam . Species consecratæ in hostia, sunt accidentia vera, & realia ; sunt qualitates fixæ , ac manentes absque vlla substantia panis , & vini : sed hæ species causant, recipiuntque in fe alterationem ; ergo alteratio non fit ex motu partium substantiarum . Explicatur magis . Hostia consecrata potest calefacere , frigefacere , humectare , siccare ; aut è contra , potest ipsa calefieri , &c. Hæc autem actio nequit ab hostia exerceri per emissionem substantiæ , quæ nulla ibi adest , ergo per qualitatis productionem . Ita quoque dum ipsa calefit , recipiet calorem ab ambiente productum ; non corpus emissum, alioquin in hostia non vnica foret Christi substantia.
units.tr: You object also: the species consecrated in the host are true and real accidents; they are fixed qualities that remain without any substance of bread and wine. But these species cause alteration and receive it in themselves; therefore alteration does not arise from the motion of the parts of substances. The point is explained further: a consecrated host can heat, chill, moisten, and dry, or conversely it can itself be heated, and so on. This action cannot be exercised by the host through the emission of a substance, since no substance is present there; therefore it is exercised through the production of a quality. Likewise, while the host itself is heated, it will receive heat produced by the surroundings, not an emitted body; otherwise the substance of Christ would not be one and the same in the host.

units.la: Refpond. in hostia consecrata reuera esse accidentia fixa , quæ à substantia distincta sunt , imò separata ; sed hæc separatio fit per miraculum, non enim naturæ vi potest accidens vllum à subiecto deiungi , vnde aqua , ferrum , &c. calescunt non per frigoris iacturam, sed per ignis admixtionem . Et quidem non capio, quomodo v gr. esse possit ignis , qui amittat calorem, & suscipiat frigus ; aqua v.gr. quæ deperdito frigore , atque humiditate fiat calida , & sicca . Quemadmodum ergo dicunt peripatetici , quantitatem esse accidens materiæ coæuum, ab ipfa vi naturæ inseparabile ; ita de omni accidente respectu fui elementi dici potest. Neque immeritò, nam corpora simplicia constituta sunt à Deo veræ, atque incorruptibiles causæ cuiusque mutationis, & ideo necessum fuit ea insignire qualitatibus, virtutibus, accidentibus, quæ nunquam separari ab isdem possent. Aristoteles certè 2. de partib. an. c.2. ait, ignem nunquam frigidum fieri. Lmò inter ipsa mixta nequeunt esse animalia sine omni calore: coruus, & æthyops absque nigredine: res nulla sine suis proprietatibus, &c. Ex his.
units.tr: I answer that in the consecrated host there are indeed fixed accidents, distinct from the substance, indeed separated from it. But this separation happens by miracle, for by the power of nature no accident can be detached from its subject. Hence water, iron, and so on become hot not by losing cold, but by the admixture of fire. Indeed, I do not grasp how, for example, there could be a fire that loses its heat and takes on cold, or water which, having lost its cold and moisture, becomes hot and dry. Just as the Peripatetics say that quantity is an accident coextensive with matter and inseparable from the very power of nature, so the same can be said of every accident with respect to its own element. Nor is this said without reason. For simple bodies were constituted by God as true and incorruptible causes of every change, and therefore it was necessary to mark them with qualities, powers, and accidents which could never be separated from them. Aristotle certainly says, in On the Parts of Animals book 2, chapter 2, that fire never becomes cold. Indeed, among mixed things there cannot be animals without any heat, nor a raven or an Ethiopian without blackness, nor anything at all without its own properties, and so on. From these considerations...

units.la: Respond. ad argumenti explicationem
units.tr: Response to the explanation of the argument

units.la: accidentia in hostia vbi reuera distincta manent à substantia, producere calorem, frigus &c. sine vlla corporis emissione: at verò hæ actiones consequuntur ad primum miraculum.
units.tr: The accidents in the host, where they really remain distinct from the substance, produce heat, cold, etc. without any emission of body; but these actions follow from the first miracle.

units.la: Dico 2. accidentia in hostia producere alia sibi similia naturaliter: sed ex hoc non sequitur non emitti atomos, quotiescunque illæ aderint. E contra si hostia madescat, frigesiat, &c. dici potest, quòd in ipsam ingrediantur atomi frigidæ, ac madidæ, vt apparebit, si panis consecrati species mergantur in aquam: tunc enim particulæ aquæ illi adhærebunt, ingressæque poros quantitatis madidam reddent. Neque dicas in hostia consecrata nullam esse substantiam: id enim verum est de illa, quæ perit, non de alia extranea, quæ potest accedere, & non subijcitur consecrationi.
