units.tr: I say, second, that the accidents in the host naturally produce other accidents similar to themselves; but it does not follow from this that atoms are not emitted whenever those accidents are present. On the contrary, if the host becomes moist, grows cold, etc., it can be said that cold and moist atoms enter into it, as will appear if the species of the consecrated bread are immersed in water: for then particles of the water will cling to them, and, entering the pores of the quantity, will make it moist. Nor should you say that in the consecrated host there is no substance: for that is true of the substance that perishes, not of another, foreign substance, which can come in and is not subject to the consecration.

units.la: DISQVISITIO QVARTA.
units.tr: Fourth Disquisition.

units.la: De alteratione per contagium, sympathiam, antipathiam, antiperistasim, & fa- scinium.
units.tr: On alteration by contagion, sympathy, antipathy, antiperistasis, and fascination.

units.la: PRO intelligentia omnium facit doctrina iam tradita iuxta principia veterum, ad quae ipsi etiam Aristotelei coguntur saepissime confugere, sive dum explicant actiones, quae antiperisticae dicuntur: seu dum exponunt meteorologicas, quae in elementis fiunt. Nos alia quaedam iuxta eandem philosophandi rationem hic breuiter deducemus. Unde magis compertum fiet quam sit recipiendus ille modus philosophandi, qui omnibus cuiuscumque scholae professoribus debet esse acceptus.
units.tr: To understand all of these matters, the doctrine already delivered according to the principles of the ancients is useful. Even the Aristotelians are very often compelled to resort to these principles, whether they explain the actions called antiperistatic or expound the meteorological phenomena that occur in the elements. Here we shall briefly deduce certain other matters by the same method of philosophizing. From this it will be more clearly known how far that method of philosophizing should be accepted, a method that ought to be acceptable to the professors of every school.

units.la: Contagium ergo est actio, vel qua duo corpora mutuo se tangunt, vel qua vnum in aliud euaporationem transmittit. In vtraque fit alteratio, nam quod tangit immediate aliud, nunc per affrictum emollit superficiem, vnde spiritus emanant foras; & sic
units.tr: Contagion, then, is an action by which either two bodies touch each other mutually, or one transmits an effluvium to another. In both cases alteration occurs. For what touches another immediately, by rubbing, now softens its surface, whence spirits emanate outward, and so

units.la: Vna contacta Liquorem ducit ab vna.
units.tr: One touched draws liquid from another.

units.la: Nunc obstando impedit egressum, & ita qui noxij sunt, manendo intus facile tabem inducunt, quae ratio pariter riter est, cur si membra diu tegantur eodem induso, marcorem⁠ sentiant. Secundo fit contagium ex corpusculis aliorsum missis, nam haec subcundo mixtorum poros, illa diuersimode afficiunt. Hinc venti propellendo spiritus noxios, propagant pestem; Hinc sepulchrorum aperitio lethalis est. Hinc paludes vicinae aerem comaculant, &c.
units.tr: Now, by obstructing, it hinders the exit, and thus those who are noxious, remaining within, easily induce corruption. This is likewise the reason why, if the limbs are long covered by the same clothing, they feel a mustiness. Secondly, contagion arises from small bodies sent elsewhere, for these, entering the pores of mixed bodies, affect them in different ways. Hence winds, by driving noxious spirits, spread the plague; hence the opening of tombs is deadly; hence neighbouring marshes foul the air, and so on.

units.la: Sympathia est actio, qua duo corpora se quodammodo assimilant, concordantque. Primo dicitur illa esse in⁠ gemmis, quarum aliae sistunt sanguinem, aliae membra corroborant, aliae neruos non sinunt contrahi, &c. quae omnia per immissionem spirituum explicari posse vi dentur. Ex hoc etiam discis cur in Selenite fit macula quaedam Lunarium aemula commutationum, illa siquidem humor est, qui iuxta varias lunae phases crescit, decrescitque, prout spiritus humidos maiori, aut minori copia transfusos recipit. Secundo sympathia est in plantis, vt inter vlmum, & vitem; oleam, & mirtum; palmam feminam, & marem, quae propesate felicius egerminant. Oritur autem effectus, vel quia singulae diuersas trahendo substatias, non furantur sibi pabulum, vel quia dum altera pascitur noxijs, relinquit meliores vicinae. Quae causa etiam est cur vegetiores floreant rosae dum prope⁠ alium implantantur, nam illud fugendo partes acidas, & infectas, quæ meliora sunt, alteri seruat. Tertio sympathia est in animalibus, aut quia constant simili forma, & membrorum textura, seu quòd ijsdem cibis nutriuntur, vnde propensiones fieri solent eædem; vel deniq; ob cognitionem indigentiæ, quam inter se habent mutuam. Quartò sympathia, est inter corpora magnetica, de qua re Kircherus in Magnetismo. Ex dictis autem possunt etiam explicari actiones per antipathiam factæ.
units.tr: Sympathy is an action by which two bodies in some way assimilate to each other and agree. First, it is said to exist in gems, of which some stop bleeding, some strengthen the limbs, and some prevent the nerves from contracting, and so on, all of which seem capable of being explained by the immission of spirits. From this you also learn why a certain spot resembling the changes of the Moon appears in selenite; for it is a humour that grows and decreases according to the various phases of the moon, as it receives humid spirits poured in in greater or lesser quantity. Secondly, sympathy exists in plants, as between elm and vine, olive and myrtle, and the female and male palm, which, planted near each other, sprout more successfully. The effect arises either because each, drawing different substances, does not steal nourishment from the other, or because, while one is fed on noxious matter, it leaves the better part to its neighbour. This is also the reason why roses flourish more vigorously when planted near another plant, for by avoiding the acid and tainted parts, which are worse, it preserves the better ones for the other. Thirdly, sympathy exists in animals, either because they share a similar form and texture of limbs, or because they are nourished by the same foods, whence the same propensities usually arise; or finally on account of the awareness of need that they have of each other. Fourthly, sympathy exists between magnetic bodies, a matter on which Kircher writes in his Magnetism. From what has been said, the actions performed through antipathy can also be explained.

units.la: Antiperistasis græcè, latinè circumobsessio contrarij, est actio illa, qua per contrarium circa positum alteratio aliqua fit. V. g. dum æstiuo tempore aqua putealis frigescit magis, hæc frigefactio dicitur nasci ob aeris calidi circumsessionem. Explicatur autem antiperistasis hoc modo. Quotiescumque corpus ambiens aliqua imbuitur qualitate, repellit à se quidquid ipsi contrarium est; unde si aer sit calidus, ab eo frigidi vapores abiguntur aliò; & è contra si frigidus, reicit aliorsum quæcumque calida sunt. Inde fit, vt vapores frigidi, qui ab aqua exhalarét, ob calorem in aere positum non ascendant; imò siqui euaporarunt, rursus in aquam redeant, quæ propterea frigidior manet. Simili modo accenditur fulgur in nube; nam spiritus igneï, qui a sole, sideribus, & globo terræ per exhalationes emittuntur, impingendo in vapores humidos, frigidosq; repelluntur: coeunt ergo in vnum, adstipantur magis, corroborantur, unde flammam accendunt. Sic etiam stomachus hyeme calet, æstate friget; nam eo tempore frigus esternum vrget intro calorem, isto vero calor extrinsecus per meatus apertos intrinsecum trahit, ac frigus relinquit. Deniq; beneficio antiperistasis innumera problemata solui possunt. Nempe cur hyeme cibi coquantur melius; & plus cibi appetamus; æstate minus? Quia calor in maiori copia facilius materiam consumit. Cur manus tument ob frigus? & membra pinguescunt? quia pori constricti non sinunt liberam euaporationem. Cur nix terram calefacit? quia contegendo meatus, impedit ne spiritus ignei egrediantur. Cur hyberno tempore tellus eruta fumat? quia in ipsa latent partes calidæ à contrario illuc pulsæ. Cur dum riget aer, sive dum grando cadit, halitus ex ore videtur? quia per frigus constipantur vaporosæ partes, unde facilius terminant visum &c.
units.tr: Antiperistasis, in Greek, or in Latin circumobsessio contrarii, is that action by which some alteration is produced in a thing through the contrary surrounding it. For example, when in summer the water of a well grows colder, this chilling is said to arise from the surrounding of hot air. Antiperistasis is explained in this way. Whenever a surrounding body is imbued with some quality, it repels from itself whatever is contrary to it. Hence, if the air is hot, cold vapours are driven away elsewhere; and conversely, if it is cold, it throws off whatever is hot. Thus it happens that cold vapours which would exhale from the water do not rise because of the heat located in the air; indeed, if any have evaporated, they return again into the water, which therefore remains colder. In a similar way lightning is kindled in a cloud. For fiery spirits, which are sent out by the sun, the stars and the globe of the earth through exhalations, striking against humid and cold vapours, are repelled; they therefore come together into one, are pressed together more tightly, are strengthened, and so kindle a flame. Thus too the stomach is warm in winter and cool in summer. For at that time the external cold presses the internal heat inward, whereas in summer the external heat draws the internal heat outward through the open passages, leaving the cold behind. Finally, by the benefit of antiperistasis countless problems can be solved: why food is cooked better in winter, and why we desire more food then, and less in summer? Because heat in greater quantity consumes matter more easily. Why do the hands swell from cold, and the limbs grow fat? Because the constricted pores do not allow free evaporation. Why does snow warm the earth? Because by covering the passages it prevents the fiery spirits from escaping. Why does earth that has been dug up steam in wintertime? Because hot parts lie hidden in it, driven there by the contrary. Why, while the air is freezing or while hail is falling, does breath appear from the mouth? Because by the cold the vaporous parts are compressed, and so more easily terminate sight, and so on.

units.la: Fascinium est actio, quæ corpora nostra malè afficiuntur. Diuiditur in duplex; naturale, atque Magicum. Istud fit à Dæmonibus iubente Mago, vel saga. Naturale autem fit vel per tractionem, vel per immissionem, & sic explicatur. Aliqua corpora vt senum, & aniculārum desiccata sunt, humidoq; benigno destituta. Quod autem est siccum, & absq; humore naturali, eum trahit aliunde, vt videtur in spongijs, quæ trahunt aquam, in pane tosto, qui vinum fugit, &c. Ex aduerso alia quædam corpora, maxime scatent humore, vt adolescentium, qui proinde carnei sunt, pingues, læti, non exsucci, & emuncti. Ex hoc fit ergo, vt si hæc duo simul sint, vnum exsugat aliud, trahendo ab ipso humorem, quo attracto contingit fascinium, ac tabes. Inde causam discis, cur infans prope senes, & maxime si ad ora vetularum accedat, ab ijsque continuo attrectetur, peßime afflatus euadat, meroremq; concipiat; Nam vetulæ siccæ, aridæ, tristes infantilem ebibunt humorem, seu etiam spiritus noxios in tenella pueri membra emittunt. Discis etiam quare pueri maciem contrahant, si versentur in officinis, vbi sal, sulphur, nitrum, & similia coquuntur, quia nimirum hæc omnia trahunt, exsiccantque humorem, quo corpora fouentur.
units.tr: Fascination is an action by which our bodies are ill affected. It is divided into two kinds, natural and magical. The magical kind is done by demons at the command of a magician or witch. The natural kind occurs either through attraction or through immission, and is explained thus. Some bodies, such as those of old men and old women, are dried up and destitute of benign moisture. What is dry, and lacks natural moisture, draws it from elsewhere, as is seen in sponges, which draw up water, in toasted bread, which shuns wine, and so on. On the other hand, certain other bodies especially abound with moisture, such as those of young people, who are accordingly fleshy, plump and cheerful, not dried out or drained. From this it happens that if these two kinds are together, one sucks out the other, drawing the moisture from it; and when that moisture has been drawn off, fascination and wasting follow. From this you learn why an infant, when it is near old people, and especially if it approaches the mouths of old women and is continually handled by them, comes out most badly affected and conceives a wasting; for dry, parched, gloomy old women drink up the infant's moisture, or they emit noxious spirits into the tender limbs of the boy. You also learn why boys grow thin if they spend time in workshops where salt, sulphur, nitre and similar things are boiled, since all these draw out and dry up the moisture by which bodies are nourished.

units.la: Ex hisce videtis quàm sit probabilis veterum philosophia, quæ actiones propemodum omnes per effluuia substantiarum exponit. Verum verè, non ausim asserere, cùm ista etiam suis non careat difficultatibus. Cæterum si ea placere debet philosophandi ratio, quæ minus affert vmbræ, minus moleßiæ, minus ambagum, hæc certè displicere non poteßt.
units.tr: From these things you see how probable is the philosophy of the ancients, which explains almost all actions through effluvia of substances. Truly, I would not dare to assert it as certain, since it too is not free from its difficulties. Still, if that method of philosophizing ought to please which brings less shadow, less trouble and less ambiguity, then surely this one cannot be displeasing.

units.la: Finis Tertij Libri.
units.tr: End of the Third Book.

units.la: LIBER QVARTVS PHYSICORVM
units.tr: LIBER QVARTVS PHYSICORVM

units.la: De motu Generationis.
units.tr: On the Motion of Generation.

units.la: OMnis alteratio fit in gratiam generationis. Non enim satis est naturali agenti praeparare subiectum alterando, & disponendo; sed praeterea mouet se se ad mixti substantialis generationem. Idcirco exigit doctrinæ ordo, vt postquam egimus de alteratione, alium aggrediamur motum, qui dicitur generationis. Quia vero generationem vnius consequitur ex communi axiomate corruptio alterius, hoc etiam libro materiam de corruptione amplectimur, totam doctrinam de ortu, & interitu, qnæ alibi traditur à Philosophis, huc opportunius, ni fallor, translaturi. Quadruplici autem disputatione rem totam expediemus. Prima erit de generatione, an & quid sit. Secunda, quomodo illa exerceatur. Tertia de corruptione, an & quid sit. Quarta, quomodo ea contingat.
units.tr: Every alteration takes place for the sake of generation. For it is not enough for a natural agent to prepare the subject by altering and disposing it; it also moves itself towards the generation of a mixed substance. Hence the order of teaching requires that, after we have treated of alteration, we take up another motion, which is called generation. Since, however, by the common axiom the generation of one thing is followed by the corruption of another, in this book we also take up the matter of corruption, and I think it will be more fitting to transfer here the whole doctrine of coming-to-be and passing-away, which the philosophers treat elsewhere. We shall settle the whole matter by a fourfold disputation. The first will be on generation: whether there is such a thing and what it is. The second: how it is carried out. The third: on corruption: whether there is such a thing and what it is. The fourth: how it comes about.

units.la: DISPVTATIO PRIMA.
units.tr: DISPUTATIO PRIMA.

units.la: De Generatione substantiali.
units.tr: On substantial generation.

units.la: DAri generationem substantialem,seu productionem substantiæ de nouo, res tam clara videtur peripateticis,vt eam nullus in quæstionem adducat. Sic, inquiunt,ignis generat ignem,terra plantas, animal animantes, &c. Fit autem generatio sic. Naturale agens altërat materiā per accidentia, quoufq; temperamentum congruum induxerit. Mox præparata materia, in illa generat substantiam de nouo, nec ante in natura visam, quæ cũ informet, actuet, vltimumq; det complementum, dicitur actus,forma, & substantia perficiens. Ita fit naturale compositum, quod ex materia,formaq; simul vnitis resultat. Sed res, quam plerique tota fide recipiunt, à nobis iuxta nostra principia in examen adducenda est. Sit ergo.
units.tr: It seems so clear to the Peripatetics that there is a substantial generation, that is, a production of a new substance, that no one calls it into question. Thus, they say, fire generates fire, earth generates plants, an animal generates animals, and so on. Generation happens in this way: the natural agent alters the matter by accidents until it has brought about a suitable temperament. Then, once the matter has been prepared, it generates in it a new substance, not previously seen in nature, which, when it informs and actuates the matter and gives it its final completion, is called the act, form, and perfecting substance. Thus arises the natural compound, which results from matter and form united together. But the thing which most people accept in full faith must, according to our own principles, be brought to examination. So let it be.

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.

units.la: An detur generatio substantialis Aristotelea.
units.tr: Whether there is an Aristotelian substantial generation.

units.la: PRO intelligentia præmoneo, me consultò in quæstione apposuisse Aristoteleam, non enim ambigendum est de generatione simpliciter, cùm satis clarè pateat,naturam vbique suos fetus edere, vbique prolificam esse, vbiq; fæcundam. Sed quæritur, an substantialis generatio fiat modo peripatetico, videlicet an generetur de nouo entitas quædam_ sustantiua, incompleta, imperfecta, quæ reuera sit substantia, sed non subsistat per se, imò indigeat substantialiter fulciri à materia, vt alibi dictum est. An potius generatio mixtorum fiat ex partibus omnino completis, in natura præexistentibus non de nouo genitis, verum de nouo tantummodo vnitis.
units.tr: BEFORE beginning, I give notice that I have deliberately put the Aristotelian view in the question. There is no doubt about generation in general, since it is clear enough that nature everywhere brings forth its offspring, everywhere is productive and everywhere fruitful. The question is whether substantial generation happens in the Peripatetic manner: namely, whether some substantial entity is newly generated which is incomplete and imperfect, which is truly a substance but does not subsist on its own, and which in fact needs to be substantially propped up by matter, as was said elsewhere. Or rather, does the generation of mixed bodies come about from parts that are entirely complete and already existing in nature, which are not newly generated but only newly united?

units.la: Secundò etiam admoneo, recolenda esse quę tradita sunt l. 1. disp. 2. quæst. 1, vbi visum est, non satis probari hanc formam de nouo substantialiter genitam. Præterea repeti debent quæ dicuntur lib. 2. disp. 1. q. 2. quo loco fuit conclusum, probabile videri, nullam generari substantiam, quæ ante in natura non exiterit. Nunc autem alia suppetunt argumenta, quæ hanc sententiam, de formæ productione mihi rē candidè cogitanti reddunt suspectam. Itaq. notetur.
units.tr: Second, I remind the reader that what was taught in book 1, disputation 2, question 1 should be recalled, where it was seen that this form, newly generated in its substance, is not sufficiently proven. Besides, what is said in book 2, disputation 1, question 2 should be repeated, where it was concluded that it seems probable that no substance is generated which did not already exist in nature. Now, other arguments are at hand which, to me thinking frankly about the production of form, make this opinion suspect. Therefore let it be noted.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Generatio substantialis non videtur fieri ex productione substan- tiæ de nouo.
units.tr: Substantial generation does not seem to come about through the production of a new substance.

units.la: PRobatur 1. à simili, quia eodem prorsus modo videtur fieri generatio substantialis, quo augmentatio: sed augmentatio non fit ex productione quantitatis nouæ, igitur nec generatio per substantiā de nouo. Maior videtur clara, enimuerò tam generatio, quàm augmentatio sunt actiones physicę, atque reales, quæ terminum habent physicum. Minor conceditur ab omnibus, augmentatio enim fit ex parte quantitatis addita parti, non de nouo genita, nam quantitas ingenerabilis est. Ergo & generatio ex vnione partium sola fiet.
units.tr: It is proved first from a parallel: substantial generation seems to happen in exactly the same way as augmentation, but augmentation does not come about through the production of new quantity; therefore neither does generation come about through a substance newly produced. The major seems clear, for generation and augmentation are both physical and real actions, which have a physical term. The minor is granted by all: augmentation takes place by quantity being added to a part, not by quantity newly generated, for quantity is ungenerable. Therefore generation too will come about by the union of parts alone.

units.la: Probatur 2. quia per Chymicam producuntur effectus naturales, vt lapides, metalla, plantæ, ac similia: sed non fiunt hæ generationes per vllam substantiæ de nouo productionem; ergo natura non gignit de nouo substantiam.
units.tr: It is proved second: natural effects such as stones, metals, plants and similar things are produced through chemistry; but these generations do not happen through the production of any new substance; therefore nature does not beget a new substance.

units.la: De maiori non est ambigendum, licet enim aliqui non concedant esse factum ope Chymicæ aurum, hoc tamen de lapidibus, alijsq; mixtis æqué perfectis, ac sunt naturales, non negant. Minor probatur, siquidem ars chymica operatur solum disponendo materias iam præexistentes, non substantialiter producendo.
units.tr: There is no doubt about the major: although some do not grant that gold has been made by the art of chemistry, they do not deny this of stones and other mixed bodies which are as perfect as natural ones. The minor is proved, since the chemical art operates only by disposing matters already existing, not by producing substances.

units.la: Consequentia bene cadit, enimuerò in Chymica principale agens ipsissima natura est, quę substantias vinculo perfecto, & naturali vnit; neq; ars agit, nisi per fomenta iuuando. Ergo natura in omni alia generatione sic operabitur, vt nullam de nouo substantiam producat.
units.tr: The consequence holds well: in chemistry the principal agent is nature itself, which unites substances by a perfect and natural bond, and art acts only by assisting with fomentations. Therefore nature will operate in every other generation in such a way that it produces no new substance.

units.la: Probatur 3. quia meteora fiunt ex vnione sola substantiæ præexistentis, commiscentur enim vapores, & exhalationes, vnde ignis, faces, grando, nix, ros, fulmen in aere cuduntur: sed hæc omnia sunt vera mixta naturalia; ergo generatio non per substantiæ productionem, sed ex mera partium collectione fit. Maior admittitur ab omnibus. Minor etiam debet concedi, meteora enim sunt partiale obiectum veræ scientiæ, nimirum physicæ. Neque opponas, illa esse composita minùs perfecta, hoc enim arguit solummodo vnionem inter partes debiliorem; sed tamen adhuc mixta naturalia sunt. Imò quæ differentia inter igné fulminarem, & hunc nostrum? Ad hæc si grando asseruetur diù, quedammodum in vallibus, ipsa tandem chrystallus est: non nisi autem quia partes comprimendo se se, vniuntur, condensantur, adstipantur magis, &c. Consequentia verò denegari non debet.
units.tr: It is proved third: meteors come about from the sole union of existing substance, for vapours and exhalations are mixed, whence fire, fiery meteors, hail, snow, dew and lightning are forged in the air. But all these are true natural mixed bodies; therefore generation comes about not through the production of substance but from the mere gathering of parts. The major is admitted by all. The minor too must be conceded, for meteors are a partial object of a true science, namely physics. Nor should you object that these are composites of lesser perfection; for this shows only that the union between their parts is weaker, yet they are still natural mixed bodies. Indeed, what difference is there between the thunderbolt's fire and this fire of ours? Further, if hail is kept for a long time, for instance in valleys, it finally becomes crystal itself; this happens only because the parts, pressed together, are united, condensed and packed more tightly, and so on. The consequence should not be denied.

units.la: Probatur 4. nam homo verè generat hominem: sed nullam de nouo producit substantiam: ergo generatio nō fit ex productione substantiæ de nouo. Maior est euidens. Minor de se patet; homo enim non generat materiam, quæ ingenerabilis est, non producit animam, quæ creatur à Deo. Quid ergo facit? vnionem inter vtramq; Imò neq; vnionem, sed ponit exigentiam tantummodo ad ipsam. Confirmatur, quia hominis corruptio fit ex sola partium separatione, igitur & generatio ex vnione sola. Confirmatur 2. nam resurrectio mortuorum vocatur à Diu. Matth. regeneratio, & nihilominus eafiet sine vlla substantiæ productione, sed per solam partium vnionem.
units.tr: It is proved fourth: a man truly begets a man, but he produces no new substance; therefore generation does not come about through the production of a new substance. The major is evident. The minor is plain in itself: a man does not generate matter, which is ungenerable, and he does not produce the soul, which is created by God. What then does he do? He brings about a union of the two. Nor indeed does he bring about a union, but only supplies the disposition for it. It is confirmed, because the corruption of a man comes about by the mere separation of parts; therefore generation too comes about by union alone. It is confirmed secondly: the resurrection of the dead is called by God the regeneration, in Matthew, and nevertheless it will be accomplished without any production of substance, but by the mere union of parts.

units.la: Probatur 5. ratione, quia mixtio naturalis definitur ab Aristotele, Mlscibilium alteratorum vnio; ergo generatio consistit in sola vnione partium, quæ mittuntur. Explico magis. Opinio communis omnium penè interpretum Aristotelis, Arabum præsertim, & Græcorum est, quòd miscibilia, hoc est elementa dum accurrunt ad generationem, ipsa non corrumpantur substantialiter, sed manent quoad formas, & solummodo alterentur quoad accidentia; unde aiunt, reuera in mixto manere ignem, aquam, terram, &c. Hoc suppositò, quod etiam suo loco probabitur, argumentor sic. In mixtione manent elementa quoad substantiam, ergo dum fit mixtio, non generatur de nouo alia forma substantialis. Probo consequentiam. Talis forma si producitur, vbinam recipitur? in materia elementorum, an in alia? non primum, alioquin duæ formæ totales in vna, eademque materia simul forent, quod repugnat. Sed neque secundum, in mixto enim non alia materia est, quàm quæ subest formis elementorum. Ergo cum in ea produci nequeat forma, nulla de nouo producetur.
units.tr: It is proved fifth by reason: natural mixture is defined by Aristotle as the union of miscible things that have been altered; therefore generation consists in the mere union of the parts that are mixed. Let me explain more. The common opinion of almost all the interpreters of Aristotle, especially the Arabs and the Greeks, is that miscible things, that is the elements, while they come together for generation, are not themselves substantially corrupted but remain as to their forms, and are altered only as to accidents; hence they say that fire, water, earth and so on really remain in the mixed body. Granting this, which will also be proved in its place, I argue thus. In mixture the elements remain as to substance; therefore while mixture takes place, no other substantial form is newly generated. I prove the consequence. If such a form is produced, where is it received? In the matter of the elements, or in another? Not the first, for otherwise two complete forms would be together in one and the same matter, which is contradictory. Nor the second, for in a mixed body there is no other matter than that which underlies the forms of the elements. Therefore, since no form can be produced in that matter, no new form will be produced.

units.la: Probatur 6. quia si produceretur noua forma substantialis, maximè id fieret, quoties corrumpitur naturale compositum, ne tunc materia prima sine forma substantiali maneret: sed corrupto naturali composito, nulla forma substantialis de nouo fit, ergo. Maior admittitur.
units.tr: It is proved sixth: if a new substantial form were produced, this would most of all happen whenever a natural compound is corrupted, lest then prime matter remain without a substantial form. But when a natural compound is corrupted, no new substantial form comes into being; therefore, and so on. The major is admitted.

units.la: Minorem sic probo. Dum ignis corrumpit lignum v. g. in elambyco, rogo quænam sit hæc substantia de nouo genita. Fortasse aqua? sed non capio quomodo contrarium generet aliud. An terra, & cinis? verùm ad terræ productionem deberet materia disponi per frigus. Quænam ergo? Rursus peto, si aqua, terra, &c. producuntur de nouo, aut sunt substantiæ simplices, aut compositæ: neutrum dici potest, ergo non producuntur. Probo minorem, quia si dicantur simplices, ergo non fit nouum compositum: si compositæ, cur ergo ignis aquam illam, seu terram nequit amplius corrumpere? Si enim pergat actio combustiua, imò si etiam crescat, nunquam cinis resoluetur, nec immutabitur; ergo non est compositus, alioquin forma componens amitteretur, separaretur, quod non fit. Concludendum est igitur, nihil de nouo substantialiter produci. Sed hoc ipsum argumentum validius alibi propositum.
units.tr: I prove the minor thus. When fire corrupts wood, for example in an alembic, I ask what this new substance generated is. Perhaps water? But I do not see how one contrary generates another. Earth and ash? But for the production of earth the matter would have to be disposed by cold. What then? Again I ask: if water, earth and so on are newly produced, they are either simple substances or compound ones. Neither can be said; therefore they are not produced. I prove the minor: if they are called simple, then no new compound comes about; if compound, why then can fire no longer corrupt that water, or earth? For if the combustive action continues, indeed even if it increases, the ash will never be dissolved nor changed; therefore it is not compound, otherwise the component form would be lost and separated, which does not happen. It must be concluded, therefore, that nothing is substantially produced anew. But this very argument has been proposed more forcefully elsewhere.

units.la: Probatur 7. quia vel hæc forma de nouo genita est substantia completa, subsistens, per se nullius indiga subiecti, vel non: si primum, ergo non est forma substantialis, quam dicunt Aristotelei: si secundum, repugnat in suo conceptu essentiali substantia, quæ indigeat substantialiter sustineri. Deinde materia prima, qua fulciri posset, metaphysica est, neque adhuc satis probatur à suis patronis, vt lib. 1. ergo, &c.
units.tr: It is proved seventh: either this newly generated form is a complete substance, subsisting on its own, needing no subject at all, or it is not. If the first, then it is not the substantial form which the Aristotelians speak of; if the second, then in its essential concept it is contradictory for a substance to need to be substantially sustained. Besides, the prime matter by which it could be supported is metaphysical, and it is not yet sufficiently proved by its own defenders, as in book 1; therefore, and so on.

units.la: Probatur denique auctoritatibus. Primò mò quidem Hippocratis, qui lib. 1. de Diæta. 5. inquit. Nihil quidem oriri, quod prius non erat, verum inuicem com mischeri. Nimirū quiquid nouì ad oculos venit, non generatur primò, & substantialiter, sed commiscetur, & crescit ex partibus, quæ aliunde in solutione alterius desumptæ sunt, nam perire, corrumpique, ac minui, idem est, ait auctor, quod secerni.. Proinde vt bene Lucret. in 1.
units.tr: It is proved finally by authorities. First, indeed, by Hippocrates, who in book 1 of On Diet, section 5, says: Nothing arises that did not previously exist, but things are mixed with one another. Clearly, whatever new thing comes into view is not generated primarily and substantially, but is mixed together and grows out of parts which were taken from elsewhere in the dissolution of something else; for to perish, to be corrupted and to be diminished are the same thing, says the author, as to be separated. Therefore, as Lucretius rightly says in book 1,

units.la: Aliud ex alio reficit natura, nec vllam
units.tr: Nature restores one thing from another, and allows no

units.la: Rem gigni patitur, nisi morte adiutam aliena.
units.tr: thing to be born unless aided by the death of something else.

units.la: Ex quo explicari poterit quomodo genera tio vnius iuxta commune axioma fit corruptio alterius, quandoquidem, si res aliqua generatur, debuerunt præfuisse materiæ simul vniendæ, ac proinde quæ supponant corruptionem alterius mixti, cuius ante fuerunt. Annuit Pythagoras apud Ouid. lib. 15. Metam. vbi ait, quòd nihil substantiæ gignit natura in mundo
units.tr: From this it can be explained how, by the common axiom, the generation of one thing is the corruption of another. For if some thing is generated, the matters to be united must have existed beforehand, and so there must have been prior substances, whose corruption accompanies the coming-to-be of the mixed body. Pythagoras agrees in Ovid, Metamorphoses book 15, where he says that nature produces no new substance in the world.

units.la: Sed variat, faciemq; nouat, nascique vocatur
units.tr: But it changes its form and makes it new, and what is called being born

units.la: Incipere esse aliud, quod non fuit. Intellige quòd præcesserint substantiæ omnes, per quarum commixtionem com. posita iam fiunt. Demum concludat S. Aug. alibi etiam allatus, qui lib. 3. de Trinit. c. 7. & 8. explicans quomodo Magi, & Dæmones in Ægypto non crearint serpentes virtute sua, sed applicando actiua passiuis, inquit. Omnium quæ ad oculos nostros trahuntur, occulta quadam sensifemina in elementis mundi latent, per quæ illa, quæ in occulto erant, in apertum progrediuntur. Et c. 9. addit quòd nec oritur, nec moritur aliquid, nec incipit esse, nec desinit (subintellige quoad substantiam) sed ex gremio naturæ tanquam ex matre grauida prodeunt. Satis ergo est naturæ, si rerum omium semina, quæ ab initio Deus per elementa dispersit, moueat, misceat, disgreget, vniat, in quo vera, & physica generatio consistit. Hinc Dæmon, cui scientia naturalis manet integra, nullo negotio naturalia composita facere potest, eo quòd substantias ad hoc requisitas nouit, colligit, applicat. Et hæc videtur sententia Sanctorum Patrum, qui Platonicæ philosophiæ studiosissimi extitere, vt ex eorum libris apparet. Sed nobis hæc annuentibus tota irascitur Schola Peripatetica, & argumentis præmunita sese opponit. Eam libenter audiamus, & siquam tulerit euidentiam, quæ substantialis formæ productionem conuincat, manum libenter, atque ingenuè, demus.
units.tr: is to begin to be something that was not before. Understand that all the substances existed beforehand, and through their combination composite things now come into being. Finally, let St. Augustine conclude this, who is also cited elsewhere. In book 3 of On the Trinity, chapters 7 and 8, explaining how the Magi and demons in Egypt did not create serpents by their own power but by applying active causes to passive matter, he says: Certain hidden seminal causes of all the things that are drawn to our eyes lie hidden in the elements of the world, and through them those things that were hidden are brought out into the open. And in chapter 9 he adds that nothing arises or dies, nothing begins to be or ceases to be (understood as to substance), but they come forth from the bosom of nature as from a pregnant mother. It is therefore enough for nature if it stirs, mixes, separates and unites the seeds of all things, which God at the beginning scattered through the elements; in this true and physical generation consists. Hence a demon, whose natural knowledge remains intact, can without any trouble make natural composites, because he knows, gathers and applies the substances required for this. This seems to be the opinion of the holy Fathers, who were most devoted to Platonic philosophy, as their books make clear. But while we agree with these things, the whole Peripatetic school grows angry and, armed with arguments, opposes us. Let us gladly hear it, and if it brings any evidence that proves the production of a substantial form, we will gladly and frankly give way.

units.la: Obiicitur 1. In omni generatione fit substantialis mutatio: sed mutatio substantialis dicit productionem substantiæ de nouo; ergo in omni generatione producitur substantia de nouo. Hæc non est materia, vtpote ingenerabilis, ergo forma substantialis. Maior admittitur. Minor probatur sic. Mutatio tria dicit: id quod mutatur:
units.tr: It is objected, first: in every generation a substantial change takes place; but a substantial change means the production of a substance anew; therefore in every generation a substance is produced anew. This is not matter, since matter is ungenerable; therefore it is a substantial form. The major is admitted. The minor is proved thus: change involves three things: that which is changed,

units.la: O terterminum à quo mutatur; & ad quem mutatur: sed terminus ad quem, prius non erat, ergo de nouo producitur: sed est substantia, ergo mutatio dicit productionem substantiæ.
units.tr: the term from which it is changed, and the term to which it is changed. But the term to which, previously did not exist; therefore it is produced anew. But it is a substance; therefore change means the production of a substance.

units.la: Respondent veteres concessa maiori negando minorem. Ad probationem distinguitur minor: terminus, ad quem fit mutatio, prius non erat quoad substantiam, n. quoad modum, c. Explicant. Generatio, quæ fit, dicitur esse motus ad aliquem terminum, videlicet ad totum compositum. Hoc autem si generatur de nouo, certè ante non erat; sed tamen erant substantiæ omnes, quarum ex vnione, atq; mixtione fieri debebat. Cum igitur fit, nulla producitur de nouo substantia, sed vnitur, & commiscetur tantum, quare terminus ad quem erat prius quoad substantiam, non quoad modum.
units.tr: The ancients answer by granting the major and denying the minor. To the proof the minor is distinguished: the term to which the change occurs previously did not exist as to substance, but yes as to mode, etc. They explain: the generation that takes place is said to be a motion toward a certain term, namely the whole composite. If this is generated anew, then certainly it did not exist before; but nevertheless all the substances existed, from whose union and mixture it had to come about. Therefore, when it comes about, no substance is produced anew, but they are only united and mixed; so the term to which existed previously as to substance, not as to mode.

units.la: Neq; dicas mutationem huiusmodi esse accidentalem, quia producitur modus, aut accidens tantùm. Contra enim est, nam foret accidentalis tantùm si terminus ad quem esset solum accidens, aut etiam substantia, sed tam exigua, vt nō sufficeret ad constituendum nouum sensibile principium agendi, quod posset habere nouam denominationem. Hoc totum explicari potest in chymica, vbi generatio dicitur fieri, quotiescumq; præviæ substantiæ in sensibili copia vnitæ, sensibile compositum, quod ante non erat, efficiunt.
units.tr: Nor should you say that this kind of change is accidental, because only a mode or an accident is produced. For the opposite is true: it would be merely accidental if the term to which were only an accident, or even a substance, but so slight that it would not suffice to constitute a new sensible principle of acting, which could have a new denomination. All this can be explained in chemistry, where generation is said to take place whenever the substances previously present, united in a sensible quantity, produce a sensible composite which did not exist before.

units.la: Obijcitur 2. pars, quæ vltimò constituit ruit naturale compositum, debet esse substantialiter incompleta; sed pars huiusmodi nequit praeexistere a materia seiuncta; ergo producitur de novo. Haec autem est forma substantialis; ergo, &c. Maior est certa, quia compositum non fit ex duplici ente in actu, alioquin vna pars non reciperetur in alia, neq; actuaret intrinsecè illam, sed tantum adhaereret, faceretque cum ea vnum ens per accidens. Minor probatur, nam pars, quae substantialiter incompleta est, subsistere nequit per se, verum in subiecto solùm, à quo sustinetur. Consequentia currit, si enim pars, quae actuat compositum, non praeexistit, ergo de novo producitur.
units.tr: It is objected, second: the part which finally constitutes the natural composite must be substantially incomplete; but a part of this kind cannot pre-exist apart from matter; therefore it is produced anew. But this is a substantial form; therefore, etc. The major is certain, because a composite does not come from two beings actually existing, otherwise one part would not be received into the other, nor would it inform it intrinsically, but would merely adhere and make with it one being by accident. The minor is proved, for a part which is substantially incomplete cannot subsist by itself, but only in a subject by which it is sustained. The consequence holds: if the part which informs the composite does not pre-exist, then it is produced anew.

units.la: Respondent Atomistae negando maiorem. Et ratio est, quia substantia incompleta in suo conceptu repugnat. Quomodo enim substantialis entitas recipiet aliunde praedicatum intrinsecum, quo substantialiter actuetur, & perficiatur, si statim ac est, essentiam habet suam, integram totamq; cui nihil addi, nihil intrinsecè detrahi potest? Ad minorem dicunt, substantiam incompletam, nec praeexistere, nec de novo produci. Et nos alibi adnotauimus, hoc materiae, siue formae, incomplementum non esse intrinsect m partibus, vt habetur 1. & 2. lib. Certè anima rationalis à corpore separata subsistit per se, neq; indiget aliquo intrinseco, & nihilominus dicitur pars hominis incompleta. Corpus etiam ab ea seiunctum per se manet, nec aliunde completur, for-ma ma enim cadauerica, quæ à peripateticis dicitur de nouo produci friget nimis in sana philosophia. Quapropter vnaquæque pars dicitur incompleta extrinsecè, atque in ordine ad totum, quatenus accepta seorsim non complet se sola totum compositum. Igitur quidquid præexistit mixto, substantia est in se completa, subsistens, ac perfecta, quæ quidem vnitur, non producitur de nouo.
units.tr: The Atomists answer by denying the major. And the reason is that an incomplete substance is contradictory in its concept. For how will a substantial entity receive from elsewhere an intrinsic predicate by which it is substantially actuated and perfected, if as soon as it is, it has its own essence, whole and complete, to which nothing can be added and from which nothing can be intrinsically taken away? As for the minor, they say that a substance which is incomplete neither pre-exists nor is produced anew. We have also noted elsewhere that this incompleteness of matter or form is not intrinsic to the parts, as is shown in books 1 and 2. Certainly the rational soul, separated from the body, subsists by itself and needs nothing intrinsic, and yet it is called an incomplete part of the man. The body, too, separated from it, remains by itself, nor is it completed from elsewhere; for the cadaverous form, which the Peripatetics say is produced anew, is too cold for sound philosophy. Therefore each part is said to be incomplete extrinsically, and in relation to the whole, inasmuch as, taken separately, it does not by itself complete the whole composite. Therefore whatever pre-exists in a mixed body is a substance complete in itself, subsisting and perfect, which indeed is united but not produced anew.

units.la: Obijcitur 3. Ignis reuera producitur in ligno: sed in ligno prius non erat; ergo producitur de nouo. Ignis autem est forma substantialis; ergo, &c. Maior admittitur, & siquis ad hæc exequi velit, non denegabit ignem de nouo productum, dummodo manu tangat prunam, aut facem. Probatur minor, quia flamma, quæ videtur, certè non latebat in ligno, in carta, in grano pulueris, &c. alioquin fuissent hæc prius combusta. Addit Lactantius: Num etiam in ferro, aut silice lateant ignis atomi? num in orbe vitreo aqua pleno, & soli exposito, cum exinde constet, ignem generari? &c. Ergo ignis producitur substantialiter de nouo.
units.tr: It is objected, third: fire is really produced in wood; but in wood it did not exist before; therefore it is produced anew. But fire is a substantial form; therefore, etc. The major is admitted, and if anyone wishes to pursue this, he will not deny that fire is newly produced, provided he touches a live coal or torch with his hand. The minor is proved, because the flame that is seen certainly was not hidden in the wood, in the paper, in the grain of powder, etc.; otherwise these things would have been burned beforehand. Lactantius adds: Are there also fire atoms hidden in iron or flint? Are there in a glass sphere full of water, when it is exposed to the sun, since it is evident that fire is generated from it? etc. Therefore fire is produced substantially anew.

units.la: Quod si concedatur, vt debet; quis imposterum formas de nouo genitas denegabit?
units.tr: But if this is granted, as it must be, who will hereafter deny that forms are newly generated?

units.la: Respondent facilè atomistæ distinguendo sic. Ignis flamma producitur de nouo, conceditur, ignis purus, & elementaris, negatur. Duplicem ergo distinguunt ignem : alter est flamma illa pinguis, humida, & crassa, quam oculis intuemur; & huiusmodi generatur de novo, non per substantiae aliquius productionem, sed tantummodo ex commixtione ignis veri cum particulis materiae, ut mox explicabimus.
units.tr: The Atomists easily answer by distinguishing thus. Fire as flame is produced anew: granted; pure and elemental fire: denied. They therefore distinguish a twofold fire: one is that fat, moist and thick flame which we see with our eyes, and this is generated anew, not by the production of any substance, but only from the mixture of true fire with particles of matter, as we shall soon explain.

units.la: Alter vero est ignis ille purus, acer, subtilis, qui egredietur ex ligno, & quem nos iniecta manu desuper flammam sentimus a longe vaporantem. Hic igitur, qui elementaris est, latet in ligno, in lapidibus, & caeteris mixtis. Neque id Aristoteleis repugnare potest, nam qui sunt meliores concedunt elementa substantialiter manere in mixto, ergo & ignem. 2. afferunt omnes, ignem concurrere ad mixtionem quando praesertim animalia gignuntur ex putri; ergo si concurrit, manet etiam, non enim potest corrumpi, ut suo loco patebit. 3. Aristoteles in 2. de gen. eap. 8. dicit. Quod solus ignis ad formam pertinere videtur. Unde tria reliqua elementa pro materia esse debent. Ergo ignis perseuerat in mixto substantialiter. 4. Diu. Thom. ut alibi vidimus tenet, particulas igneas deorsum ferri a pluuia, ob mixtorum generationes, ergo si nō corrumpitur in aqua, multo minus in mixto corrumpetur ignis, & sic manebit. 5. Plato in Phedone, ut supra etiam dictum est, non dicit corpus calescere ob calorem; sed quia in ipso ignis est. 6. Niffen. orat. 1. exam. explicat, quare in exordijs mundi tenebræ super terram incubarent. Quia, inquit, splendor ignis, qui sub materia particulis latitabat, nondum effulserat. Porro ne hoc videatur difficile, adducit in exemplum silices, in quibus non videtur ignis, licet vim lucidam, atq; illustratam naturaliter in se contineant, &c. unde si hæc foras trahatur, partibusque miscea-tur etherogeneis, apparet in flammam. Quæ opinio clarissimis nixa experimentis, fuit expresse Diu. Aug. lib. 21. de Ciu. c. 4. vbi loquēs de calce, quæ dum frigida conspergitur, inflammatur, habet. Velut ergo expiratę illa gleba, discedens ignis, qui latebat, apparet. Pater ergo igneas particulas, aut ignem elementarem inesse formaliter, & quoad substantiam in mixtis.
units.tr: The other is that pure, sharp, subtle fire, which will come out of the wood, and which we feel from a distance, when we put a hand above the flame, giving off heat. This, therefore, which is elemental, lies hidden in wood, in stones and in the other mixed bodies. Nor can this be opposed to the Aristotelians, for the better ones concede that the elements remain substantially in a mixed body, and therefore fire too. Second, all agree that fire takes part in the mixture, especially when animals are generated from putrefaction; therefore, if it takes part, it also remains, for it cannot be corrupted, as will be shown in its place. Third, Aristotle in On Generation and Corruption book 2, chapter 8, says: Fire alone seems to pertain to form. Hence the remaining three elements must be matter. Therefore fire persists substantially in the mixed body. Fourth, St. Thomas, as we have seen elsewhere, holds that fiery particles are carried downward by rain for the generation of mixed bodies; therefore, if fire is not corrupted in water, much less will it be corrupted in a mixed body, and so it will remain. Fifth, Plato in the Phaedo, as was also said above, does not say that a body grows warm because of heat, but because fire is in it. Sixth, Nyssen, in the first Homily on the Hexaemeron, explains why darkness brooded over the earth at the beginning of the world: Because, he says, the splendour of fire, which lay hidden in particles under matter, had not yet shone forth. Moreover, lest this seem difficult, he adduces as an example flints, in which fire is not seen, although they naturally contain within themselves a bright and illuminated power, etc., so that if this is drawn out and mixed with heterogeneous particles, it appears as flame. This opinion, resting on the clearest experiments, was expressly stated by St. Augustine in The City of God book 21, chapter 4, where, speaking of lime which catches fire when it is sprinkled while cold, he says: So then, as that clod is breathed upon, the fire that was hidden departs and appears. Clearly, therefore, fiery particles, or elemental fire, are present formally and as to substance in mixed bodies.

units.la: Flamma vero non præexistit in mixto, sed illa de nouo fit; non autem per substantiæ generationem, sed ex mera partiū aggregatione, quandoquidem ignis verus dum euaporat, vnit sibi particulas materiæ, illasq; permeando facit lucidas, fulgidasq; vnde oritur flamma, quæ mixtum per accidens est. Verūm res hæc non ita facilè suaderi poterit ijs, qui Aristoteleismo præoccupati iam sunt. Idcirco debet fusius exponi, & explicandus est modus, quo flamma in ligno, in lapide, in pulvere, in nitro generatur.
units.tr: Flame, however, does not pre-exist in the mixed body but is newly produced. It arises not by a generation of substance but from a mere aggregation of parts, since true fire, as it evaporates, joins itself to particles of matter and, passing through them, makes them bright and glowing; from this arises flame, which is a mixed thing by accident. But this matter will not be easily persuaded to those already preoccupied with Aristotelianism. It must therefore be explained more fully, and the manner must be set out by which flame is generated in wood, in stone, in powder, and in saltpetre.

units.la: Repetite igitur ex 1. lib. naturalia mixta componi ex duplici parte, altera quarum vtpote crassior, consistens, & materialis dici potest materia: secunda, quippequæ actiua magis, viuida, & spiritosa est, forma;non inquam Forma peripatetica incompleta, sed physica,& completissima. 2. repetite vtramq; partem nil efse aliud, quàm corpora minima, quæ inter se per humidum vnita poros habent, meatusque, vnde per eos euaporatione m substantialem à corporibus aljs recipiût. Hisce positis, flammæ generatio explicatur sic. Dum ignis externus admouetur v.g. ligno, immittit in materiam particulas igneas: hæ intrudunt se se, humidumque attenuant: fit ergo dissolutio partiû; & quæ magis viuidæ sunt, leues, igneæ, ac subtiles, in altum euolant, non solitariæ tamen, sed cum sint acres, & actiuæ, alias etiam particulas de crassiori materia decidunt, abradunt, secum ferunt. Hæ igitur particulæ sunt, quæ abrasæ per ignea corpora intus illapsa, & admixta, lucent, flammæq; speciem reddunt. Quousque igitur vaporem igneum, qui abit, fæces hę comitantur, manet flamma ; cum decidunt, ignis auolat solus, & eà destitutus opacitate non amplius videtur, licèt manu sentiatur. Explicari hoc totû potest familiari experimento eorum, qui flammas in theatris eiaculantur. Hi siquidem conterunt picem, sulphur, nitrû, factisque puluisculis totam implent volam. Deinde inter digitos candelam inserunt accensam, datoq; signo manum ia-ctant, puluisculosq; sursum abiiciunt. Hi verò tanquam nebula circa spiritus igneos (qui super candelæ flammam af-cencendunt conspersi, magnum reddunt fulgorem. Vnde quifq; deprehendit, flammam esse mixtum quoddam ex igne vero elementari, & crassis materiæ particulis factum. Ideo Ariftoteles eam sæpe in meteoris dicit ignem vocatum:exceffumq; caloris, & feruorem, non ignem verum. Eius verba 1. Meteor. c. 3. sunt id quod ex consuetudine ignem vocamus (loquitur de flamma, & carbone accenso) ignis tamen non est, cum ille fit caloris redundantia, & quasi feruor quidam.
units.tr: Recall, then, from the first book, that natural mixed bodies are composed of two parts: the one, as the grosser, solid part, may be called matter; the other, being more active, lively and spirituous, is form. I mean not the incomplete Peripatetic form but the physical and most complete form. Recall also that both parts are nothing other than very minute bodies which, united with one another by moisture, have pores and passages through which, by substantial evaporation, they receive what they need from other bodies. With these things laid down, the generation of flame is explained thus. When external fire is applied, for example, to wood, it introduces igneous particles into the matter. These insinuate themselves and thin out the moisture, so there is a dissolution of parts. Those that are more lively, light, igneous and subtle fly upward, not alone, however; since they are sharp and active, they also dislodge, scrape off and carry away other particles from the grosser matter. These particles, scraped off and carried along by the fiery bodies that have slipped in and mixed with them, shine and present the appearance of flame. So long as the fiery vapour that departs is accompanied by these dregs, the flame remains. When the dregs fall away, the fire flies off alone, and, deprived of that opacity, it is no longer seen, though it can still be felt by the hand. This whole matter can be explained by a familiar experiment of those who shoot out flames in the theatres. They grind pitch, sulphur and nitre, and when the powders are made they fill the palm of the hand. Then they insert a lighted candle between their fingers, and at a given signal they throw the hand about and fling the powders upward. These, scattered like a cloud around the fiery spirits that rise above the candle's flame, give off a great brilliance. Whence anyone may perceive that flame is a certain mixture made of true elemental fire and gross particles of matter. Therefore Aristotle often calls it in the Meteorology "what by custom we call fire", and an excess and boiling of heat, not true fire. His words in Meteor. 1, ch. 3 are: "That which we commonly call fire (he speaks of flame and of a burning coal) is not fire, since it is an overflow of heat and a kind of seething."

units.la: Exinde patet .1. cur omnis flamma in acumen desinat: quia nimirum partes à materia decisæ in processu magis attenuantur, attenuatæ magis volant, vnde in pyramidem labeunt, donec tandem ad minimas redactæ vilum etiam effugiunt. Patet 2. quare flamma non eundem femper colorem ferat, sed modò flauum, modò rubrum, modò viridem, &c. Quia videlicet partes fixæ, quæ illam reddunt, coloribus varijs imbutæ sunt. Patet 3. cur flamma denigret parietem; non ita purus ignis, qui post flammam abit: quia hæc efficitur à particulis materiæ fæculentis, quæ cum allinuntur, commaculant. Patet 4. cur si calix nuper à fornacibus eruta conspergatur aqua, flammam accendat: Quia scilicet humor aqueus obturat meatus, igneumque vetat spiritum, ne foras mittatur: hic autem collectus vim acquirit maiorem, & idcirco validius erumpés fixas etiam particulas in maiori copia decidit, ac transfert; vnde flamma videtur.
units.tr: From this it is clear, first, why every flame ends in a point: because the parts cut off from the matter become ever more attenuated as the process goes on, and, being more attenuated, fly more readily, so that they taper into a pyramid until, reduced at last to the smallest, they escape even sight. It is clear, second, why flame does not always bear the same colour but now yellow, now red, now green, and so on: because the fixed particles that render it are imbued with various colours. It is clear, third, why flame blackens a wall, whereas the pure fire that departs after the flame does not: because the flame is produced by the faecal particles of matter, which, when they settle upon a surface, stain it. It is clear, fourth, why, if a cup lately taken from the furnaces is sprinkled with water, it kindles a flame: because the watery moisture blocks the pores and forbids the fiery spirit to be sent out. This spirit, however, gathered together, acquires greater force, and so, breaking out more violently, it dislodges and carries away fixed particles in greater quantity; whence flame appears.

units.la: Patet 5. cur ex corporum collisione accendatur ignis: Quia sic aperiuntur pori, vt latens ignis egredi possit; fixæque partes diuelluntur per contusionem, & aliquæ cum igne migrando lucent. Patet 6. cur ponè phialam aquà plenam accédatur flamma: Quia certè radij solares ignei sunt, collectique magis beneficio refractionis adurunt. Ex quo etiam patet 7. cur specula vltoria, vt Archimedea ex vnica radiorum reuibratione inflammént, plumbumque vt ait Galileus colliquent, &c.
units.tr: It is clear, fifth, why fire is kindled by the collision of bodies: because thus the pores are opened so that the hidden fire can get out, and fixed parts are torn apart by the blow, and some of them, migrating with the fire, shine. It is clear, sixth, why a flame is kindled behind a flask full of water: because the solar rays are indeed fiery, and, gathered together, they burn the more by the aid of refraction. From this it is also clear, seventh, why burning mirrors, such as those of Archimedes, ignite things by the single reflection of rays, and melt lead, as Galileo says, and so on.

units.la: Flamma ergo producitur de nouo, non quòd vlla substantia formaliter generetur; sed quia substantiæ latentes cum tali dispositione miscentur. Ignis enim elementaris latet reuera in subiectis; non videtur autem, neque agit, quia particulis materiæ fixis premitur; debet enim excitari, vt operetur; commiscéri, vt luceat. Quod totum explicari potest verbis Nissení orat. 1. exam. vbi de igne ab initio creati orbis condito habet. Ignis, qui vbiq; disseminatus erat, obscurus iacebat, materiaque impotentia supprimebatur: verùm quoniam vis eius velox, atq; agilis est, simulatq; à Deo motus, principium, & incitatio adhibita est, ante illa omnia, qua grauiora sunt, exiliens, lumine cuncta statim illustrauit.
units.tr: Flame, therefore, is produced anew, not because any substance is generated formally, but because hidden substances are mixed together in such a disposition. For elemental fire truly lies hidden in the subjects; it is not seen, nor does it act, because it is pressed down by fixed particles of matter. It must be stirred up in order to operate, and mixed in order to shine. All of this can be explained by the words of Nyssen in the first Oration on the Hexaemeron, where he speaks of the fire from the beginning of the created world: "The fire, which was spread everywhere, lay obscure and was held down by matter that had no power; but since its force is swift and agile, as soon as it was moved by God, and a beginning and impulse was applied, it leapt up beyond all those things that are heavier and at once illuminated everything with light."

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.

units.la: Quid sit generatio Aristotelea.
units.tr: What Aristotelian generation is.

units.la: PRo intelligentia oportet consulere definitionem generationis traditam à Philosopho 2. de gen. cap. 4. Est, inquit, mutatio totius in totum, nullo sensibili remanente, ut subiecto eodem. Dicitur mutatio, quia dum generatur compositum, materia mutatur à priuatione formæ ad ipsam 2. totius, quia destructa prima forma, totum compositum, quod prius erat, corrumpitur, & materia suscipiente aliam formam, generatur nouum. 3. in totum, non quia singulæ partes in composito fiant, materia enim ingenerabilis est, sed quia producta forma de nouo, totum quid aliud à primo distinctum resultat. 4. nullo sensibili remanente ut subiecto eodem, quia videlicet si aliquod accidens maneat in genito, quod prius erat in corrupto, non manet veluti accidens rei corruptæ, sed ut compositi de nouo geniti. V. g. dum in sententia peripatetica ex aqua fit aer, manet certè sensibilis diaphaneitas: hæc autem non est amplius primi subiecti, nèpe aquæ, sed alterius, videlicet aeris, de quo solo prædicatur. Hæc autem definitio multas parit difficultates, breuissimè hic soluendas.
units.tr: To understand this, one should consult the definition of generation given by the Philosopher in On Generation, book 2, chapter 4: It is, he says, a change of the whole into the whole, with nothing perceptible remaining, the subject being the same. It is called change because, while the compound is generated, the matter passes from privation of form to the form itself. (2) Of the whole, because once the first form is destroyed, the whole compound that existed before is corrupted, and when the matter receives another form, something new is generated. (3) Into the whole, not because the individual parts are made within the compound (for matter is ungenerable), but because, when the form is produced anew, a whole thing distinct from the first results. (4) With nothing perceptible remaining, the subject being the same, because if some accident that was in the corrupted thing remains in the generated thing, it does not remain as an accident of the corrupted thing but of the newly generated compound. For example, when in the Peripatetic view water becomes air, the perceptible transparency certainly remains; but it no longer belongs to the first subject, namely water, but to another, namely air, of which alone it is predicated. This definition raises many difficulties, which will be resolved here as briefly as possible.

units.la: Quæres itaq; 1. an generatio in suo conceptu essentiali dicat mutationem: Aduerte prius, mutationem esse transitum subiesubiecti à priuatione ormæ ad formam. Resp. negatiuè. Ratio est, quia initio mundi potuit fieri, aut etiam facta est generatio sine transitu materiæ à priuatione ad formam; tunc enim nulla materia præcessit formam, sed cum illa fuit genita simul; ergo non transijt à priuatione ad formam, eò quòd priuatio non antecessit.
units.tr: You may ask, first: does generation, in its essential concept, imply change? Note first that change is the passage of a subject from privation to form. Answer: no. The reason is that at the beginning of the world generation could occur, and indeed did occur, without any passage of matter from privation to form; for then no matter preceded the form, but was generated together with it. Therefore it did not pass from privation to form, since privation did not precede it.

units.la: Quæres 2. an generatio, quæ modò fit, in suo conceptu essentiali dicat mutationem? Aduerte prius hic fieri suppositionem de materia prima, quæ ab vna forma se se mouetat ad aliam, &c. Resp. affirmatiuè. Ratio est, quia materia nequit suscipere formam de nouo genitam, nisi exuat se prima: sed quandiu aderat prima, fuit priuatio secundæ, igitur materia se se mouet à priuatione, dum suscipit formam secundam; & sic generatio dicit essentialiter mutationem.
units.tr: You may ask, second: does generation, as it now takes place, imply change in its essential concept? Note first that here one supposes prime matter, which moves itself from one form to another, and so on. Answer: yes. The reason is that matter cannot receive a newly generated form unless it first strips itself of the prior form; but while the prior form was present, there was privation of the second. So matter moves itself out of privation as it receives the second form, and thus generation essentially implies change.

units.la: Quæres 3. an generatio in suo conceptu essentiali dicat conuersionem? Aduerte prius conuersionem esse transitum subiecti à termino positiuo ad alium quo que positiuum, vt v. gr. cum transit manus à calore ad frigus. Resp. negatiuè. Ratio est, quia generatio non dicitur in suo formali conceptu definitionem alicuius termini positiui; sed tantummodo positionem alterius in materia, ne quidem involuendo eiusdem subiecti mutationem, vt supra. Verum tamen est, quòd generatio, prout modò exercetur, dicit conuersionem, fit .n. à termino corrupto ad genitum.
units.tr: You may ask, third: does generation in its essential concept imply conversion? Note first that conversion is the passage of a subject from one positive term to another positive term, as when the hand passes from heat to cold. Answer: no. The reason is that generation, in its formal concept, is not the positing of some positive term, but only the positing of another in matter, without even involving a change of the same subject, as above. It is true, however, that generation as it is now practised implies conversion, for it goes from the corrupted term to the generated one.

units.la: Quæres 4.quænā sit ratio formalis generationis? Aduerte priùs, nonnullos esse, qui putant, generationem formaliter consistere in productione formæ. Sed contra, quia homo verè, ac realiter generat hominem, & nihilominùs non producit animam, quæ physica forma est. Contra 2. quia potest forma generari saltem à Deo in materia, etiamsi ei non vniatur substantialiter, vt v. g. si auri formam producat Deus in ligno non vniendo illam intrinsecè, ac substantialiter: sed tunc non fieret substantiale compositum, ergo. Resp. igitur ad quæsitum compositi generationem formaliter consistere in sola productione vnionis. Ratio est,quia posita vnione, non potest non poni compositum,ergo in ea sola consistit ratio generationis compositi. Neq; dicas: forma dat rationem formalem composito. Respondetur enim quòd reuera dat, sed vt vnita, non vt producta simpliciter. Et ex his patet, vnionem esse terminum generationis quo; compositum verò terminum generationis quod.
units.tr: You may ask, fourth: what is the formal reason of generation? Note first that some hold that generation formally consists in the production of the form. But on the contrary: a man truly and really generates a man, and yet he does not produce the soul, which is the physical form. Again, against this view: a form can be produced, at least by God, in matter even if it is not substantially united with it, as if God were to produce the form of gold in wood without uniting it intrinsically and substantially; but then no substantial compound would result. Therefore... The answer to the question, then, is that the generation of a compound formally consists solely in the production of the union. The reason is that once the union is posited, the compound cannot fail to be posited; so the formal reason of generating the compound lies in the union alone. Nor should you say that the form gives the formal reason to the compound. For it is answered that it does indeed give it, but as united, not as simply produced. And from this it is clear that the union is the terminus of generation by which, while the compound is the terminus which.

units.la: Quæres 5. an generatio sit actio ab alteratione distincta? Aduerte priùs quòd alteratio est productio qualitatis dispositiuæ ad formam, seu quæ recipitur in materia, præparatq; illam, vt suscipiat formam. Resp. igitur affirmatiuè, Ratio est, quia omnin entitati diuersæ, ac distinctæ, sua correspondet actio diuersa, & distinctæ sed qualitas vtpote accidens, & forma vtpote substantia sunt diuersa, & distincta; ergo go alteratio, quæ datur ad qualitatem; & generatio, quæ fit ad substantiam, sunt duæ actiones distinctæ. 2. quia alteratio tempore antecedit generationem; ergo distinguitur ab ipsa. 3. quia posita qualibet alteratione in subiecto, etiam ultima, Deus impedire potest, ne generetur forma, ergo actio alteratiua distinguitur à generatiua, quæ proinde noua est.
units.tr: You may ask, fifth: is generation an action distinct from alteration? Note first that alteration is the production of a quality disposing towards the form, which is received in matter and prepares it to receive the form. Answer, then: yes. The reason is that to every diverse and distinct entity there corresponds a diverse and distinct action. But quality, as an accident, and form, as a substance, are diverse and distinct; therefore the alteration which is directed to the quality, and the generation which is directed to the substance, are two distinct actions. Second, because alteration precedes generation in time; therefore it is distinct from it. Third, because, whatever alteration has occurred in the subject, even the last one, God can prevent the form from being generated; therefore the altering action is distinct from the generating action, which is accordingly something new.

units.la: Quæres 6. an generatio fiat successiuè. Aduerte prius duplici modo queri posse an sit successiua. Primo extensiuè, quatenus forma producitur priùs in vna parte subiecti, deinde in alia, quemadmodum si vlnare lignum paulatim comburatur; & in hoc sensu generatio successiua est. 2. an producatur successiuè quoad intensionem, eo quia terminus, aut forma producta sit capax graduum, & graduum, qui recipiantur in eadem parte subiecti, quemadmodum plures formæ accidentales intenduntur. Et in hoc sensu Respond. quòd generatio non est successiua. Ratio est, quia non potest actio esse successiua, quando terminus producitur simul, & in instanti: sed forma, & vnio sic producuntur; ergo. Minor probatur quia forma substantialis (& hoc ipsum de vnione) non habet partes intensiuas, est enim essentia quædam simplex, & indiuisibilis, omni carens latitudine graduum; neq; v.gr. forma ignis potest esse magis, aut minùs ignis; formæ lapidis, magis, aut minùs lapis. Quodsi Aristoteles dicat, aliquam substantiæ generationem nerationem fieri successiuè, complectitur in ea & alterationem, & formæ præcedentis desitionem, quæ omnia quidem inter se comparata cum successione fiunt.
units.tr: You may ask, sixth: does generation occur successively? Note first that this can be asked in two ways. First, extensively, insofar as the form is produced first in one part of the subject and then in another, as when a piece of wood is gradually burned along its length; and in this sense generation is successive. Second, whether it is produced successively as to intensity, because the terminus or produced form is capable of degrees, and of degrees received in the same part of the subject, as several accidental forms are intensified. In this sense I answer that generation is not successive. The reason is that an action cannot be successive when its terminus is produced simultaneously and in an instant; but form and union are produced in this way; therefore. The minor is proved because a substantial form (and this holds of the union too) has no intensive parts; it is a simple and indivisible essence, lacking all breadth of degrees. Nor can the form of fire be more or less fire, or the form of stone more or less stone. But if Aristotle says that some generation of a substance occurs successively, he includes in it both the alteration and the cessation of the preceding form, all of which indeed occur successively when compared with one another.

units.la: Quæres 7. an in noui compositi generatione fiat resolutio veteris usque ad materiam primam? Quæstionem hanc reddidit celebrem sententia Thomistica, quæ docet formam sic generari de nouo, ut non solùm tota præcedens corrumpatur, verùm & accidentia omnia destruantur, maneatque sola materia prima, nuda, & expers qualitatum omnium, quæ ad primum compositum attinebant. Res paulò fusiùs discutienda est. Quare sit.
units.tr: You may ask, seventh: in the generation of a new compound, does the old compound get resolved down to prime matter? The Thomist opinion has made this question famous: it teaches that the form is generated anew in such a way that not only is the whole preceding form corrupted, but all accidents are destroyed as well, and only bare prime matter remains, devoid of all the qualities that belonged to the first compound. The matter needs to be discussed somewhat more fully. Here is why.

units.la: DISQVISITIO TERTIA.
units.tr: THIRD DISQUISITION.

units.la: An in generatione fiat resolutio vsque ad materiam primam.
units.tr: Whether in generation there is a resolution down to prime matter.

units.la: PRo intelligentia repetite vltima verba in definitione, quam supra deduximus à Philosopho, & sunt ea: Nullo sensibili remanente vt subiecto eodem. Ex quibus nõ pauci Doctores cum schola Thomistica faciunt sibi occasionem dicendi, nullum sensibile accidens manere in materia prima ex ijs, quæ præcesserunt, quando fit generatio, vnde quidquid erat in corrupto, destruitur; & quod est in genito, de nouo totum generatur. Hanc verò dicunt esse resolutionem vsq;ad materiam primam. Non placet hæc opinio, & notetur.
units.tr: To understand this, recall the final words of the definition that we derived above from the Philosopher: no sensible thing remaining as the same subject. From these words, not a few teachers of the Thomist school take occasion to say that, when generation occurs, no sensible accident from what came before remains in prime matter, so that whatever was in the corrupted thing is destroyed, and everything in the generated thing is generated anew. They call this a resolution down to prime matter. This opinion does not please me, and it should be noted.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: In generatione non fit resolutio vsque ad materiam primam.
units.tr: In generation there is no resolution down to prime matter.

units.la: PRobatur 1. auctoritate Aristotelis, qui 2. de gen. 25. ideo ait elementa symbola transmutari ad inuicem facilius quam disfymbola, quia minus operosum est vnam qualitatem destruere, quam duas; ergo in tali casu elementum de nouo genitum habet qualitatem primi. Similiter Philosophus 1. de gen. 1. 24. docet, quod cum ex aere generatur aqua, diaphaneitas eadem, seu perspicuitas, quae fuit in aere, manet in aqua; ergo non fit resolutio ad vsque materiam primam. Et cur aduersarij mentem Philosophi haurire contendunt ab obscuris eiusdem verbis, non a clarissimis?
units.tr: It is proved first by the authority of Aristotle, who in De generatione 2 (25) says that elements which agree in a quality [σύμβολα] change into one another more easily than those which do not agree [διάσυμβολα], because it is less laborious to destroy one quality than two. Therefore in such a case the newly generated element has the quality of the first. Likewise the Philosopher, De generatione 1 (24), teaches that when water is generated from air, the same transparency or clarity that was in the air remains in the water. Therefore there is no resolution down to prime matter. And why do our opponents strive to draw the mind of the Philosopher from obscure words of his rather than from his clearest ones?

units.la: Probatur 2. experientia. Constat enim quod cum fit cadauer, eadem accidentia, quae praefuerunt in corpore viuo, manent in mortuo; ergo non fit resolutio vsque ad materiam. Antecedens patet, nam si repente moriatur v.gr. canis, figura, calor, color eadem sunt, non de nouo producta. Nam quae causa est, a qua producantur? & ad quid producti debent, cum a forma cadauerica non exigantur? Sed Thomistae respondent, haec accidentia gigni de nouo, eadem tamen videri, quia sensus nostri falluntur.
units.tr: It is proved secondly by experience. For it is evident that when a corpse is formed, the same accidents that were present in the living body remain in the dead one. Therefore there is no resolution down to matter. The antecedent is plain: if, say, a dog dies suddenly, its shape, heat and colour are the same and not newly produced. For what cause is there by which they might be produced? And for what purpose ought they to be produced, since they are not required by the cadaveric form? But the Thomists reply that these accidents are generated anew, yet appear to be the same because our senses are deceived.

units.la: Contra D. Thom. 3p. qu. 75. art. 5. in corpore docet, post consecrationem in Eucharistia manere accidentia eadem, quia sensus iudicat esse eadem: sed hic etiam similiter iudicat, ergo. Denique sensus nostri circa obiectum bene applicitum non decipiuntur.
units.tr: Against St Thomas, 3 p. q. 75 a. 5 in corpore, he teaches that after consecration in the Eucharist the same accidents remain, because the sense judges them to be the same. But here too the sense judges similarly; therefore the same argument applies. Finally, our senses are not deceived about an object that is properly presented to them.

units.la: Probatur 3. ratione, quia non corrumpuntur accidentia omnia, nisi corrumpatur subiectum accidentium omnium: sed hoc non corrumpitur; ergo. Maior est certa. Minorem sic probo. In composito adest subiectum quantitatis, quod non corrumpitur; ergo. Probo minorem. Subiectum quantitatis est materia prima incorruptibilis, vt supra visum est. Ergo non corrumpitur subiectum accidentium omnium; & sic in generatione substantiali non fit resolutio adusque materiam.
units.tr: It is proved thirdly by reason: because not all accidents are corrupted unless the subject of all the accidents is corrupted; but this subject is not corrupted; therefore. The major is certain. I prove the minor thus. In the composite there is present the subject of quantity, which is not corrupted; therefore. I prove the minor: the subject of quantity is prime matter, which is incorruptible, as has been seen above. Therefore the subject of all accidents is not corrupted, and so in substantial generation there is no resolution down to matter.
