units.la: Obijcies 1. Forma est vnio accidentium in materia, ergo destructa forma, pereunt etiam accidentia omnia. Resp. negando antecedens. Nam priusquam generetur forma, quantitas habet vnionem cum materia, quae subiectum illius est; ergo pereunte forma, saltem quantitas non peribit.
units.tr: You will object first: form is the union of accidents in matter; therefore, once form is destroyed, all accidents also perish. Reply: I deny the antecedent. For before a form is generated, quantity already has union with the matter, which is its subject; therefore, when the form perishes, quantity at least will not perish.

units.la: Obijcies 2. Accidentia sunt proprietates formae substantialis; ergo hac destructa, illa etiam destrui debent, ac proinde fiet resolutio &c.
units.tr: You will object secondly: accidents are properties of the substantial form; therefore, once this is destroyed, those must also be destroyed, and consequently there will be resolution, etc.

units.la: Resp. d. accidentia omnia sunt proprietates formae, n. quantitas n. est propria materiae: Aliqua, transeat. Nam etiam quaedam accidentia debeantur, nihilominus minus, & sine illa esse possunt, quod satis probat color, & calor in cadauere manentes post formæ corruptionem.
units.tr: Reply: I distinguish. All accidents are properties of the form? No: for quantity is not a property of the form, nor is it proper to matter. Some accidents are, I grant. For even though some accidents are owed to the form, they nevertheless are fewer, and can exist without it, as the colour and heat remaining in the corpse after the corruption of the form sufficiently prove.

units.la: Obijcies 3. Accidentia existunt per existentiam formæ: igitur corrupta forma, nullum accidens manet. Resp.n. antecedens, vt patet in quantitate. 2. n. etiam consequentiam, quæ non tenet in doctrina Thomistica. Materia enim per Thomistas existit ob existentiam formæ: sed corrupta forma, non ideo corrumpitur materia; ergo sic de accidentibus.
units.tr: You will object thirdly: accidents exist through the existence of the form; therefore, once the form is corrupted, no accident remains. Reply: I deny the antecedent, as is clear in the case of quantity. Second, I deny the consequence, which does not hold in Thomistic doctrine. For according to the Thomists matter exists because of the existence of the form; but when the form is corrupted, matter is not for that reason corrupted. Therefore the same holds for accidents.

units.la: Obijcies 4. Forma, quæ producitur, est actus purus, & primus materiæ: igitur accidens nullum ex præcedentibus manet; nam alioquin hoc esset primus actus, non forma. Respond. d. forma est primus actus in ordine intentionis, c. in ordine executionis, n. secus enim deberet forma in materiam induci absq; præuijs dispositionibus, quæ tamen necessario antecedunt veluti actus alterativi 2. n. consequentiam. Imò quia forma est actus primus materiæ constituens cum illa compositum, debet in materia supponere quantitatem, semper enim inducitur in materiam quantam.
units.tr: You will object fourthly: the form which is produced is pure and first act of matter; therefore no accident from what came before remains. For otherwise this would be the first act, not the form. Reply: I distinguish. The form is the first act in the order of intention, but not in the order of execution. Otherwise the form would have to be induced into matter without preceding dispositions, which nevertheless necessarily precede it as alterative acts; I deny the consequence. Indeed, because the form is the first act of matter, constituting a compound with it, it must presuppose quantity in the matter, for it is always induced into matter that is quantified.

units.la: Hæc omnia dixerim facta communi suppositione de quantitate à materia distincta. Quòdsi quis teneat, quantitatem non esse accidens materiæ superadditum (de qua re sequenti lib. dicemus) facile defendet, resolutionem fieri ad vsq; matemateriam, quotiescumque fiet generatio, saltem formæ contrariæ. Quippe cum in subiecto generetur forma priori opposita, debent etiam illius accidentia omnia corrumpi, vtquæ contraria sunt formæ introducendæ, nec videtur aliud mansurum, nisi quantitatem. Quare si hæc à materia distincta non est, patet suturam esse resolutionem ad vsque materiam.
units.tr: I would have said all this on the common supposition that quantity is distinct from matter. But if someone holds that quantity is not an accident superadded to matter (a matter we shall discuss in the following book), he will easily defend that resolution is made down to matter whenever generation occurs, at least of the contrary form. Indeed, since a form opposite to the prior one is generated in the subject, all of its accidents must also be corrupted, insofar as they are contrary to the form to be introduced, and nothing seems likely to remain except quantity. Hence, if this is not distinct from matter, it is plain that there will be resolution down to matter.

units.la: DISPVTATIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISPUTATIO SECUNDA.

units.la: Quomodo fiat generatio substantialis.
units.tr: How substantial generation takes place.

units.la: CVm ex nihilo nihil fiat, conueniunt in hoc philosophi omnes, vt dicant, præparandam esse materiam, ex qua res genita consurgere debet, illamq; oportere ad certum, fixumque locum adduci, vbi rerum generatio exerceri possit. Dicunt ergo elementa omnia deferri ad locum generationis, vt per mutuam pugnam sese miscendo, alterando, compaginando, naturale mixtum conficiant. Non autem explicant, quomodo fiat motus hic elementorum, & qua ratione vnumquodque tendat eò, vbi cætera facilè inveniat, ijsdemq; se misceat. Aliqua nos hac de re admodum necessaria dicamus, & sit.
units.tr: Since nothing comes from nothing, all the philosophers agree on this, that the matter from which the thing generated is to arise must first be prepared, and that it must be brought to a certain and fixed place where the generation of things can be carried out. They say, then, that all the elements are carried to the place of generation, so that by mutual conflict, mixing, altering and compounding with one another they may produce a natural mixed body. They do not, however, explain how this motion of the elements comes about, or by what reasoning each one tends to that place where it readily finds the others and mixes itself with them. Let us set out some matters on this subject which are very necessary, and so let it be.

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: FIRST DISQUISITION.

units.la: Quomodo elementa moueant se ad locum generationis.
units.tr: How the elements move themselves to the place of generation.

units.la: PRO intelligentia noto, aliqua mixta fieri ex mera vnione partium elementarium, quæ immediatè se miscent; aliqua ex vi seminali. Primi generis ea sunt, lapides, mineralia, metalla: secundi, stipites, animantes &c. Hæc singula non vbique locorum, sed certis quibusdam sedibus innascuntur, vbi nimirum vel semina, vel substantiæ adsunt elementares.
units.tr: To make this clear, I note that some mixed bodies are formed from the mere union of elementary parts, which mix immediately with one another, and others from a seminal power. Of the first kind are stones, minerals and metals; of the second, plants, animals and so on. These do not arise everywhere, but in certain fixed places, namely where either seeds or elementary substances are present.

units.la: Circa prima, quæ absque semine fiunt, elementa mouent se ad locum generationis, non casu, & fortuitò, sed ex certo alicuius causæ ministerio. Hæc autem duplex est: Primò calor internus, & rei cuique innatus; vnde Arist. 4. meteor. cap. 1. habet, quòd putridis etiam in rebus bestiolæ innascuntur, propterea quod naturalis calor, idemque discretus facultatem eorum cogendorum habet, quæ excreta iam sunt. Secundò calor etiam extrinsecus, præsertim solis. Hinc naturæ prouidentia factum est, solem continua, & obliqua vertigine circa terram rotari, vt ad latera se applicando, vbique foret minister generationum. Sic etenim globum terraqueum calefacit, alterat vapores trahendo, & exhalationes; vnde cum fiant nebulæ, nix, pluuia, grando, aliaque
units.tr: As for the first things, which come into being without seed, the elements move themselves to the place of generation, not by chance and accident, but through the agency of some definite cause. This cause is twofold. First, the internal heat, innate in each thing; whence Aristotle, Meteorology 4, chapter 1, says that even in putrid things little creatures are born, because the natural heat, when it has been separated out, has the power of concocting those things which are already excreted. Second, heat also from outside, especially that of the sun. Hence, by the providence of nature, the sun was made to revolve around the earth in a continuous and oblique circuit, so that by applying itself to the sides it might be everywhere a minister of generations. For thus it warms the terraqueous globe, alters the vapours by drawing them up, and the exhalations; whence, since mists, snow, rain, hail and other

units.la: meteora, hæc omnia pro nouis generationibus materia sunt. Nam hoc modo ex aere tanquam ex mare magno defertur aqua, & ignis, quæ in terræ viscera recepta, cum eaque lentè commixta res tam varias gignunt. Iuuat etiam ad hoc subterraneus naturæ calor, qui materias continuò agitando insensibilem facit euaporationem substantiæ, illamq; intra viscera terræ vltro citroq; agit (ex qua causa terræ motus) imò etiam aere toto extramittit. Vnde Lucret. in 5.
units.tr: meteors arise, all these are matter for new generations. For in this way water and fire are carried up from the air as from a great sea, and, once received into the bowels of the earth and slowly mixed with it, they produce things so various. The subterranean heat of nature also helps toward this: by constantly agitating the materials, it makes the evaporation of the substance imperceptible, and drives it back and forth within the bowels of the earth (the cause of earthquakes), and even sends it out through the whole air. Whence Lucretius, book 5:

units.la: Quodcunque fluit de rebus, id omne aeris in magnum fertur mare.
units.tr: Whatever flows from things, all that is carried into the great sea of air.

units.la: ab eoque rursus, velut ab Oceano in terram refluit, vnde circulus fit rectilineus,per quem ait Arist. 3. & 4. meteor. fluxus, & refluxus à terra in aerem, ab eoque in istam perennatur.
units.tr: And from that sea it flows back again to the earth, as from an ocean; whence arises a straight-line circuit, through which, as Aristotle says in Meteorologica 3 and 4, there is a flow and reflow from earth into air, and from air back into earth, perpetually.

units.la: Circa secunda, quæ generantur per semen, elementa mouentur ad locum generationis vi quadam peculiari à natura feminibus insita. Nam vbi per caloris interni, externique virrutem corpora minima translata sunt,vnumquodq; semen illa trahit, quæ sibi accommoda sentit. Quod vt ritè capiamus, repetendum est à 1.lib. Deum in exordio condidisse rerum semina, ijsque virtutem indidisse, qua se mutuò fouerent,repararent, similia similibus aggregarét, adeout nullum sit quantumuis minimum, cui virtus ista ob sapientissimum Dei consilium innata non fuerit. Idcirco ea conuestiuit suis qualitatibus, vt alia forent calida, & sicca, nonnulla frigida, & humida, quædam leuitatem haberent, quædam grauitatem, hæc simili figura constarent, ista dissimili &c.vt nimirum sicca humida; grauia leuia, rotunda traherent quadrata, ab ijsque motus omnis inciperet : Audite Nifs. orat. 1. exam. Itaque cum omnia possit (subintelligo Deus) ad rerum procreationem sapienti, potentique voluntate simul omnia contulit, leuitatem, grauitatem, densitatem, raritatem, mollitudinem, duritiem: humiditatem, sicitatem, figuram &c. quæ quidem omnia sunt quædam tenues, nudaque notiones: nihil enim horum vnum per se materia est: sed cunctis inter se concurrentibus materia fit. Nimirum vnumquodque semen quatenus vnum, & exile non est materia tota, & integra mixti: sed prout beneficio sympathiæ alia trahit ad se, vnit,compaginat. Motus ergo vnius ad aliud incipit quidem à paruis, non est autem sensibilis, & quamquam nisi post multa sensibilis non fiat, ille tamen denegari non debet inquit Carus in 2. Prima mouentur .n. per se primordia rerum : (liatu Inde ea, qua primo sunt corpora conciEt quasi proxima sunt ad vires principiorum, Ictibus illarum cæcis impulsa cientur : Ipsaq; quæ porro paulo maiora lacessunt. Sic à principijs ascendit motus, & exiit paulatim nostros ad sensus.
units.tr: As to the second kind, which are generated through seed, the elements move to the place of generation by a certain peculiar power implanted in the seeds by nature. For when the smallest bodies have been carried along by the power of internal and external heat, each seed draws to itself those that it perceives to be suited to it. To grasp this properly, we must go back to the first book, where God is said to have created the seeds of things in the beginning and to have endowed them with a power by which they might cherish and restore one another, and gather like to like, so that there is no particle, however small, to which this power has not been innate by the most wise counsel of God. Therefore he clothed them with their qualities, so that some were hot and dry, some cold and moist, some had lightness and others weight, some were of a similar shape and others of a dissimilar shape, and so on; so that dry things would draw moist, heavy things light, and round things square, and from these every motion would begin. Hear Gregory of Nyssa, Oration 1 on the Hexaemeron: Since he could do all things (I understand, God) by his wise and powerful will for the production of things, he bestowed all at once: lightness, weight, density, rarity, softness, hardness, moistness, dryness, shape, and so on; all of which are certain thin and bare notions. For none of these by itself is matter; but matter comes into being when all of them concur with one another. Clearly, each seed, insofar as it is one and slender, is not the whole and complete matter of the mixed body; but by the benefit of sympathy it draws other things to itself, unites them and joins them together. The motion of one thing toward another therefore begins indeed from very small things, and is not perceptible; and although it does not become perceptible until after many steps, it ought not on that account to be denied. As Lucretius says in book 2: For the first beginnings of things are moved of themselves. Therefore those bodies which are the first to come together, being as it were nearest to the powers of the first principles, are set in motion by their blind blows; and they in turn stir up things that are a little larger. Thus motion rises from the principles and gradually comes forth to our senses.

units.la: En igitur, quomodo elementa se moueant ad locum generationis. Calor ni-mirum intrinsecus, & extrinsecus agit corpora, & circumducit ex terra inae-rem; ab aere in terram. Deinde semina ob ingenitam sibi virtutem substantias magneticè trahunt, illasque sibi vniendo in molem sensibilem augent. Vnde concipiendum est in minimis, & primis exordijs fieri, quod intuemur in magnis, certè vi magnetica sese trahentibus. Quodsi de hac virtute attractiua quæras, eam diximus à prima causa in res omnes fuisse adspersam, vnde illud vulgatum est
units.tr: Behold, then, how the elements move themselves to the place of generation. Namely, internal and external heat acts upon bodies and carries them from earth into air, and from air back into earth. Then the seeds, by the power innate in them, draw substances to themselves magnetically, and by uniting them to themselves they enlarge them into a perceptible mass. Hence we must conceive that what we see in great things happens in the smallest and first beginnings, namely that they draw one another by a magnetic power. But if you ask about this attractive power, we have said that it was sprinkled over all things from the first cause, whence the common saying is:

units.la: Ad similem Deus adducit similemque paremque
units.tr: Like is drawn to like by God, and like is matched with like

units.la: Constat hoc ab effectibus, & ratione suadetur, nam cùm natura in continua corruptione sit, eidem quoque debebatur virtus reficiendi sese, ac restaurandi, vniendo iterum quidquid soluitur, & acquirendo amissum.
units.tr: This is clear from its effects, and reason also persuades us of it: since nature is in constant corruption, it must also have been given the power to repair itself and restore itself, by joining again whatever is dissolved and recovering what has been lost.

units.la: Hæc autem vis attractiua est, non casualis, & fortuita, sed ex consilio Dei sapientissimo ad rerum vicissitudines indita. (**) ✥
units.tr: This attractive force, however, is not accidental or chance, but was implanted by the most wise counsel of God for the changes of things.

units.la: DIS-
units.tr: DIS-

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: Disquisition II.

units.la: Quomodo elementa in re genita, siue in composito maneant.
units.tr: How the elements remain in a generated thing, or in a compound.

units.la: PRO intelligentia recolite, quod initio disputationis dictum est, omnes Philosophos cum Aristot. in eam sententiam iuisse, quòd elementa simul coeant in vno loco generationis, ibique alterent se, pugnent, ac misceant, donec ex illis compositum fiat. Sed tamen inter se discrepant, inquirendo, an ea, quæ missa fuerunt, maneant actu formaliter, & quoad substantiam in mixto; an tantum virtualiter, siue quoad accidentia.
units.tr: To understand this, recall what was said at the beginning of the disputation: all philosophers, with Aristotle, held that the elements come together at one place of generation, and there act upon, fight with, and mix with one another until a compound is formed from them. They differ, however, over whether those elements that were mixed remain in the mixed body actually, formally, and in substance, or only virtually, that is, as to their accidents.

units.la: Plerisque placet hoc secundum. Aiunt enim elementorum formas, dum inter se luctam agunt, corrumpi etiam; adeout non superfit nisi materia prima, quibusdam accidentibus vestita, in qua noua forma substantialis, destructa prima elementari, generetur. Alij è contra, ijque docti viri mordicus tenent, elementa formaliter, & substantialiter in mixto perseuerare; adeout non solummodo cum fit pugna, & alteratio, sint omnia simul; sed illa etiam expleta, maneant; neque corrumpantur, sed misceantur. Vnde inquiunt in ligno, in lapide, caeterisque actu terram, ignem, aquam inesse quoad substantiam. Hæc postrema sententia videtur physica, & sana, cum qua fit.
units.tr: Most people favour the second view. They say that while the elements struggle against one another the forms of the elements are also corrupted, so that nothing remains except prime matter clothed with certain accidents, and in this matter a new substantial form is generated once the elemental form has been destroyed. Others, on the contrary, and learned men among them, hold stubbornly that the elements persist formally and substantially in the mixed body. So not only while the fight and alteration are going on are they all present together, but even when it is finished they remain; they are not corrupted but mixed. Hence they say that earth, fire and water are actually present in wood, in stone, and in other things, as to substance. This last opinion seems to be physical and sound, and it is with this that the matter agrees.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Elementa in composito manent actu formaliter, non virtualiter tantum.
units.tr: The elements remain actually and formally in the compound, not merely virtually.

units.la: PRobatur 1. auctoritate non solum modo veterum, qui ante Aristotelem floruerunt, sed etiam eorum, qui secuti sunt. Eam tenet acerrime Theophrastus auditor Aristotelis, Alex. Aphrodisieus, Philoponus, Themistius, Averroes, Avicenna, uno verbo Græci omnes, & Arabes. Accedunt Latini Albertus, Aureolus, Iandunus, Zimara, Zabarella, Fernelius, qui oppositam sententiam putat absurdam, & portentosam; aitque illius propugnatores omnem obscurare philosophiæ splendorem. Vltimò fauet D. August. tom.6. lib. vno ad Orosium contra Priscillianistas, & Origenistas cap. 8. quem egregiè philosophantem vide. Aristoteles verò hac in re sicut in alijs, quæ ardua sunt, sententiam suam aliquando facit obscuram, vnde atrox ciuile bellum inter sectarios exarsit; sed alicubi tamen apertissimè nobis fauet. Seligo eius dicta 7. metaph. cap. 17. Elementum, inquit, est in quod existens diuiditur (compositum) vt materiam; vt puta syllabæ ipsum a. & b. Ergo sicut a. & b. actu formaliter inexistunt syllabæ per ipsas conflatæ; sic &c.
units.tr: This is proved first by authority, not only of the ancients who flourished before Aristotle but also of those who followed him. Theophrastus, Aristotle's pupil, holds it most firmly, as do Alexander of Aphrodisias, Philoponus, Themistius, Averroes, Avicenna, and in a word all the Greeks and Arabs. The Latins Albertus, Aureolus, Jandunus, Zimara, Zabarella and Fernel agree, the last of whom thinks the opposing view absurd and monstrous, and says its defenders obscure the whole splendour of philosophy. Lastly, St Augustine favours it in volume 6, in the single book against Orosius, against the Priscillianists and Origenists, chapter 8, which you should see for a truly philosophical treatment. Aristotle, however, in this matter as in others that are difficult, sometimes makes his opinion obscure, whence a fierce civil war has broken out among the sects; yet in places he favours us most clearly. I select his words from Metaphysics 7, chapter 17: An element, he says, is that into which a thing that exists (a compound) is divided as its matter, as for instance the letters a and b are the elements of a syllable. Therefore, just as a and b are actually and formally present in the syllable formed from them, so likewise, etc.

units.la: Probatur 2. ratione, quia mixtio, ex Phi-
units.tr: The second is proved by reason, because mixture, according to the Philosopher,

units.la: Philosopho, est miscibilium alteratorum unio, siue vt ait lib. 2. de gen.c.10. coitio; ergo elementa vniuntur; ergo actu manent in mixto, secus enim quomodo vniri possunt? Neque dicas ly alteratorum idem sonare, ac destructorum. Contra enim est, quia haec alteratio dicit ad fumū corrumpi accidentia, non substantias; ergo elementa substantialiter manent. Probo antecedens. Nam si substantiae corrumpuntur, vel hoc faciunt inter se, vel fit ab alio: non secundum, quia in mixtione aliud non est, à quo fieri possit corruptio: non primum, alioquin debet assignari elementum quod corrumpat cæteras, ijsque vtpote validius præualeat. Hoc autem non habet superius, à quo destrui possit; ergo ipsum in mixto manet.
units.tr: is the union of things mixed and altered, or, as he says in book 2 On Generation, chapter 10, their coming together. Therefore the elements are united, and therefore they remain actually in the mixed body; for otherwise how could they be united? Do not say that the word altered means the same as destroyed. On the contrary, this alteration refers to accidents being corrupted, not substances; therefore the elements remain substantially. I prove the antecedent. For if substances are corrupted, either they do this among themselves, or it is done by something else. Not the second, because in a mixture there is nothing else from which corruption could come. Not the first, for then one element would have to be named that corrupts the others and prevails over them as the stronger. But there is nothing above these from which they could be destroyed; therefore they remain in the mixed body.

units.la: Probatur 3. & confirmatur præcedens ratio. In omni composito dicis elementū aliquod prædominari: v.g. in lapide prædominatur terra, quia videlicet materia plus retinet in se de terræ qualitatibus. Hoc dato, sic arguo. Supponamus, quòd in instanti b. fieri debeat lapis: in instanti a. præcedenti erant adhuc formæ ignis, aeris, & aquæ. Rogo cū quoto gradu qualitatis? certè cum vltimo, eoq; tenuissimo; nam in instanti b. sequenti corrumpi debet (non corrumperetur autem, nisi priùs ad vltimum gradū qualitatis formæ redactæ fuissent) ergo in instanti b. forma terræ nō corrūpetur. Probo consequētia. In instanti a. præcedenti forma ignis v.gr. conseruabatur cum vltimo gradu suæ qualitatis:
units.tr: The third proof, which confirms the preceding argument, is this. You say that in every compound some element predominates: for example, in stone earth predominates, because clearly the matter retains more of earth's qualities. Granting this, I argue thus. Let us suppose that a stone is to come to be in instant b. In the preceding instant a, the forms of fire, air and water were still present. I ask: at what degree of quality? Surely at the last degree, and the most attenuated; for in the following instant b the forms must be corrupted (they would not be corrupted unless they had first been reduced to the last degree of quality). Therefore in instant b the form of earth is not corrupted. I prove the consequence. In the preceding instant a, the form of fire, for example, was preserved at the last degree of its quality.

units.la: P at in istanti b. forma terræ multò plures habet gradus frigoris, & siccitatis(prædominaturrenim cæteris) ergo si prima cum vnico manebat, hæc multò magis conseruabitur; præsertim quia non habet aliud elementum, à quo in mixtione patiatur.
units.tr: But in instant b the form of earth has far more degrees of cold and dryness (for it predominates over the others); therefore, if the first remained with a single degree, this one will remain much more so, especially since it has no other element from which it might suffer in the mixing.

units.la: Probatur 4. nam elementa postquam conuenere ad locū generationis, & se inuicem commiscuerunt, cur substantialiter destruuntur? Duplicem causam assignare potes: vel quia per mutuam pugnā amiserunt qualitates, vnde ipsa etiam corrumpi debeant: vel quia producitur noua forma compositi, quæ priores elementorum formas non compatitur. Hæc duplex ratio est, cur dicas elementa quoad substantiam corrumpi, neque meliorem assignas. Contra tamen, &
units.tr: The fourth proof: after the elements have come together at the place of generation and have mixed with one another, why are they destroyed in substance? You can assign a twofold cause: either because through their mutual strife they lost their qualities, so that they must themselves be corrupted as well; or because a new form of the compound is produced, which does not tolerate the former forms of the elements. This twofold reasoning is why you say the elements are corrupted as to substance, and you assign no better one. On the contrary, and

units.la: Probatur 5. conclusio sic. Aut elementa dum inter se pugnant, omnino deperdunt qualitates, vel tantummodo eas debilitant, remittuntque. Si primum; ergo elementa non solùm substantialiter non manent in mixto, sed neque virtualiter, & quoad accidentia, quod est contra te. Si secundum, ergo elementa non destruuntur. Probo consequentiam: illa de facto conseruantur cum paucioribus accidentibus extra mixtum; ergo in mixto cum pluribus non corrumpentur. Antecedens patet experientia, nam aqua feruens, comburens, & ebulliens, etiamsi vt concedis totum frigus amittat, nihilominus perseuerat in esse aquæ, nec substantialiter perit; ergo multò minus peribit in mixto, vbi non ita calescit, neque frigus omnino amittit. Secundo si terra bis, ter, & septies infundatur in vas aqua feruentissima plenum, illa certè deperdit suum frigus, & siccitatem; quandiu enim ibi est, sentitur calida, & humida: sed terra quantumuis calescat, humescat &c. non corrumpitur quoad substantiam, tota enim separari potest; ergo neque inmixtione corrumpetur. Consequentia currit, quia hic, vt concedis, non tamenormiter alteratur.
units.tr: the fifth proof, the conclusion runs thus. Either the elements, while they contend with one another, lose their qualities altogether, or they only weaken and relax them. If the first, then the elements do not merely fail to remain substantially in the mixed body but not even virtually or as to accidents, which is contrary to your view. If the second, then the elements are not destroyed. I prove the consequence: they are in fact preserved outside the mixture with fewer accidents; therefore inside the mixture with more they will not be corrupted. The antecedent is plain from experience, for boiling water, scalding and bubbling, even if, as you concede, it loses all its cold, nevertheless persists in being water and does not perish in substance; therefore much less will it perish in a mixture, where it is not so heated nor does it lose all its cold. Secondly, if earth is poured two, three or seven times into a vessel full of boiling water, it certainly loses its cold and dryness; for as long as it is there it is felt as warm and moist. Yet earth, however much it is heated or moistened, etc., is not corrupted in substance, for the whole of it can be separated out; therefore neither will it be corrupted in a mixture. The consequence holds, because here, as you concede, it is not altered in the normal way.

units.la: Probatur 6. contra secundam rationē, quia si dicas elementa corrumpi, eò quod noua mixti forma succedere debet in materiam; contra est, nam ego potiùs dicam nullam de nouo succedere formam, quia elementa non corrumpuntur. 2. patet iam ex dictis, hanc formam substantialem non satis probari: & adsunt rationes, quæ oppositum conuicisse videntur. 3. dato etiam produci formam de nouo, non idcirco elementa corrumpi debent, quia hæc non constant duplici parte, materià nimirum incorruptibili, & forma, quæ possit corrumpi, vt videbimus.
units.tr: The sixth proof is against the second argument, because if you say the elements are corrupted on the ground that a new form of the mixed body must succeed into the matter, I on the contrary will say that no form succeeds anew, because the elements are not corrupted. Secondly, it is already clear from what has been said that this substantial form is not sufficiently proved, and there are arguments which seem to have refuted the opposite. Thirdly, even granting that a form is produced anew, the elements need not on that account be corrupted, because these do not consist of a twofold part, namely an incorruptible matter and a form which can be corrupted, as we shall see.

units.la: Probatur vltimo efficacissimè, quia mixtum resoluitur in elementa, ergo ista formaliter sunt in mixto. Consequentia tenet, nam vnumquodq; componitur ex iĳs, in quæ resoluitur. Antecedens iam patet ex pluribus nostræ doctrinæ, & cōuincitur experientia, si enim vt dicebamus comburatur v.gr. lignum, separantur vapores aquei auolantes per fumum, qui fenfibiliter humectant: imo fi per artem colligantur, quemadmodum in elambyco, sensibilem reddunt aquam. 2. feparatur ignis, quem iniecta manu desuper flammam, seu prunam fentis, cum eoq; multus aer exhalat. Separantur 3. cinerei pulueres, qui terra formaliter sunt, neq; differunt nisi colore, aut etiam pondere, quia per ignem ab ijs aliæ partes eterogeneæ secernuntur. Ergo hæc omnia inerant formaliter in mixto. Non enim producuntur de nouo, vt alibi diximus.
units.tr: Finally, the matter is proved most effectively, because the mixed body is resolved into the elements; therefore these are formally in the mixed body. The consequence holds, for each thing is composed of those into which it is resolved. The antecedent is now plain from many points of our doctrine, and it is confirmed by experience. For if, as we were saying, wood is burned, the watery vapours are separated and escape as smoke, which sensibly moistens; indeed, if they are collected by art, as in an alembic, they make the water perceptible. Secondly, fire is separated, which you feel when you hold your hand over the flame or the live coal, and with it a great deal of air is exhaled. Thirdly, the grey ashes are separated, which are earth formally and differ only in colour or even in weight, because through the fire other heterogeneous parts are secreted from them. Therefore all these were present formally in the mixed body. For they are not produced anew, as we have said elsewhere.

units.la: Obijcies 1. si elementa formaliter inesfent mixto, duæ formæ substantiales eandem actuarent materiam. Hoc autem fieri nequit: secus enim substantia eadem bis in recto denominaretur, v. gr. simul esset lapis ob formam lapidis; & aqua, ob formam aquæ: simul aurum, ob formam auri: & ignis ob formam ignis &c. quod cum dici non possit, concludendum est in lapide non esse nisi formam lapidis, & sic elementares corruptæ sunt.
units.tr: You will object first: if the elements were formally present in the mixed body, two substantial forms would actuate the same matter. But this cannot happen; otherwise the same substance would be denominated twice in the concrete, for example at once a stone because of the form of stone, and water because of the form of water; at once gold because of the form of gold, and fire because of the form of fire, and so on. Since this cannot be said, we must conclude that in the stone there is only the form of stone, and so the elementary forms have been corrupted.

units.la: Respond. imprimis negari posse antecedens, nam supponit argumentum generari de nouo formam substantialem, quę corruptis elementaribus in materiam succedat. Hoc verò falsum est. 2. etiam dato formam substantialem de nouo gigni. Resp. non sequi duplicem formam in materia eadem, quia elementa non habent formas, vt meliores tenent, sed ipsa tanquam corpora simplicia inseruiunt pro materia, in qua tota recipitur hæc forma (si producitur.) Neque dicas: elementa completa sunt, ergo nequeunt adesse vt materia. Vidimus enim quomodo substantiæ in composito debeant esse incompletæ, nimirum non in se actu, sed potiùs denominatiuè in ordine ad totum. 3. admissa etiam hypothesi Aristotelea de duplici forma distincta, quarum altera sit elementi, altera mixti, Respond. in materia esse posse formam v.gr. ignis vt subordinatam, & partialem; formam verò lapidis vt principalem, atque totalem. Hoc verò compositum, dici absolutè lapidem, quia denominatio sumitur à potiori, & sensibiliori. Et hoc respondere debent ij omnes, qui partiales formas defendunt.
units.tr: I reply: first, the antecedent can be denied, for the argument assumes that a substantial form is generated anew, succeeding into the matter once the elementary forms are corrupted. But this is false. Second, even granting that a substantial form is generated anew, I reply that it does not follow there are two forms in the same matter, because the elements do not have forms in the sense of holding better ones; rather they themselves, as simple bodies, serve as matter, in which the whole of this form is received (if it is produced). Nor should you say: the elements are complete, therefore they cannot be present as matter. For we have seen how the substances in a compound must be incomplete, namely not in themselves actually but rather denominatively in relation to the whole. Third, granting even the Aristotelian hypothesis of a twofold distinct form, one of the element and the other of the mixed body, I reply that in the matter there can be the form of fire, say, as subordinate and partial, but the form of stone as principal and total. This compound is absolutely called a stone, because the denomination is taken from the stronger and more sensible part. All those who defend partial forms ought to answer in this way.

units.la: Obijcies 2. omnes mixti particulæ homogeneæ sunt: sed si elementa formaliter in eo manerent, particulæ omnes non essent omogeneæ: igitur &c. maior probatur ipsa experientia, nam in lapide quæuis particula quantumlibet minima, lapis est. Minor etiam satis patet, quia si manent elementa in composito, ergo alia pars erit ignis, alia terra, &c.
units.tr: You will object (2): all mixed bodies are composed of homogeneous particles. But if the elements remained formally in the compound, the particles would not all be homogeneous. Therefore, etc. The major is proved by experience itself, for in a stone any particle however small is still stone. The minor is also quite plain, since if the elements remain in the compound, then one part will be fire, another earth, and so on.

units.la: Resp ond. d. maiorem: omnes particulæ mixti sensibiles omogeneæ sunt, c. omnes minimæ, atque vltimæ, n. Ad minorem quoque dico, partes omnes compositi sensibiles inter se omo-
units.tr: I answer: I deny the major. All sensible particles of a mixed body are homogeneous; I concede that. All the smallest and ultimate particles; I deny that. To the minor I also say that all the sensible parts of the compound are homogeneous with one another, but not the parts that are so small, insensible and ultimate.

units.la: P geneas esse; non ita minimas, insensibiles, & vltimas. Explico: in lapide v.gr. si assumatur pars a. sensibilis, haec certè similis est parti b. sensibili; & vtraque vtpote constans eodem temperamento, lapis est. Verùm si haec rursus & rursus dissoluantur quoadvsque ad sua vltima corpuscula, & minima deueniant, aliquando tandem alia erit ignis, alia terra, &c. exemplum adest in vitro, in quo si accipias vnamquamque partem sensibilem, haec sanè vitrea est: verùm si hanc ipsam iterum ad sua principia soluas, detegentur ij pulueres, ij cineres, eaeque substantiae, quae illi à peritis commixtae fuerunt, quemadmodum fatentur vitriarij Murianenses..
units.tr: I explain. In a stone, for example, if one takes a sensible part a, this is certainly similar to a sensible part b, and both, since they have the same temperament, are stone. But if these parts are dissolved again and again until they reach their ultimate and smallest corpuscles, at last one will be fire, another earth, and so on. An example is glass. If you take any sensible part of it, that part is certainly glassy. But if you dissolve that same part again into its principles, there will be revealed those powders, those ashes, and those substances which skilled workers mixed together, as the glassmakers of Murano admit.

units.la: Obijcies 3. In composito quaecumque pars copofita est, ac mixta, ergo nulla pars erit, quae sit ignis tantùm, terra tantùm, &c. ergo elementa non insunt formaliter mixto. Antecedens probatur ex Philosopho, qui docet, ex qualibet mixti particula posse quatuor elementa segregari: ergo quaelibet mixta est.
units.tr: You will object (3): In the compound, every part is compound and mixed; therefore no part will be fire only, earth only, and so on. Therefore the elements are not formally in the mixed body. The antecedent is proved from the Philosopher, who teaches that four elements can be separated from any particle of a mixed body. Therefore every particle is mixed.

units.la: Respond.d antecedens: omnis particula sensibilis est mixta, c. quaelibet prima, & insensibilis, n. Et sic ad consequens d. pars nulla sensibilis est ignis, vel terra tantùm, c. pars nulla minima, & prima, n. vt supra. Ad probationem dico ex omni parte sensibili segregari posse quatuor elementa, non ex qualibet minima, prima, & insensibili; nam si haec sit aqua tantùm, quomodo ab ea educes ignem? Deinde retorqueo argumentum: si enim ab omni mixti parte segregari elementa possunt, ergo formaliter inerant.
units.tr: I deny the antecedent: every sensible particle is mixed; I concede that; every first and insensible particle; I deny that. And so, to the consequent, I deny that no sensible part is fire or earth only; I concede that no smallest and first part is so, as above. To the proof I say that four elements can be separated from every sensible part, but not from every smallest, first and insensible particle. For if this is only water, how will you draw fire out of it? Further, I turn the argument back: if the elements can be separated from every part of a mixed body, then they are formally present in it.

units.la: Colligitur ex dictis, reddi magis probabilem Democriti sententiam, quae tenet, mixta omnia fieri ex vnica elementorum commixtione, quaecumque postea haec elementa sint, seu vocata, ignis nimirum, aer, aqua, terra; siue alia per mundi elementa dispersa, & à Deo iuxta rerum species, diuersae naturae constituta, vt nos etiam l. 1. innuimus. Quapropter effici potest argumentum sic. In mixto manent formaliter subftantię completae, quae miscentur: ergo non fit de nouo alia forma substantialis, ea praesertim incompleta, quae intrinsecè debeat actuari, & actuare, complere substantialiter, & compleri, &c. Iterum: hae substantiae completae vniuntur inter se vnione physica, & reali. Ad quid ergo excogitare materiam primam, & formam substantialiter incompletas ad hoc vt in composito vniri possint? Perpendite rem, &c. facilè suadebitur.
units.tr: From what has been said it follows that the opinion of Democritus becomes more probable, which holds that all mixed bodies arise from a single mixture of the elements, whatever these elements are afterwards, whether called fire, air, water and earth, or other elements dispersed through the world and constituted by God according to the kinds of things, of diverse nature, as we also hinted in book 1. Hence the argument can be framed thus: In a mixed body the complete substances that are mixed remain formally. Therefore no new substantial form comes into being, especially an incomplete one, which must intrinsically be actuated and actuate, complete and be completed substantially, etc. Again: these complete substances are united with one another by a physical and real union. Why then devise prime matter and substantially incomplete forms so that they can be united in the compound? Weigh the matter, etc.; it will be easily persuaded.

units.la: DISQVISITIO TERTIA.
units.tr: DISPUTATION THREE.

units.la: Quomodo vniantur partes in composito.
units.tr: How the parts are united in a composite.

units.la: PRO intelligentia suppono quod certissimum est, partes in composito formaliter vniri, nam quotiescumque in re datur effectus formalis, debet etiam concedi causa formalis. Ita v.gr. si constituitur album, id per albedinem fit, si calidum, per calorem, &c. Ergo similiter cum duo inter se actu euadunt vnita, ibi vnionem adesse opus est. Quaeritur ergo quomodo partes vniantur, an per vnionem, quae sit mera illarum iuxta positio, &c ab ijs non distincta: an vero per vnionem, quae sit aliquid a partibus actu distinctum, cuius beneficio illae inter se connectantur. Plerique Thomistae, ac nonnulli antiquiores philosophi tenent prima. Secunda sententia videtur esse probabilior, cum qua fit.
units.tr: To understand this, I take as certain that the parts in a composite are united formally. For whenever a formal effect is found in a thing, a formal cause must also be granted. Thus, for example, if something is made white, this comes about through whiteness; if something is made warm, through heat; and so on. Therefore, similarly, when two things actually become united with each other, there must be a union present there. The question, then, is how the parts are united: whether by a union that is merely the juxtaposition of those parts and not distinct from them, or rather by a union that is something actually distinct from the parts, through whose agency they are connected with one another. Most Thomists, and some older philosophers, hold the first view. The second opinion seems more probable, and I follow it.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Partes vniuntur in composito per vnionem ab ijs distinctam.
units.tr: Parts are united in a composite by a union distinct from them.

units.la: PRobatur 1. quia ea, quæ possunt existere sine aliquo, distinguuntur ab ipso: sed partes valent existere sine vnione: igitur ab ea distinctæ sunt. Ergo quoties adsunt in composito, vniuntur per vnionem à se distinctam. Maior est certa, quia signum distinctionis à separatione desumitur. Minor etiam constat in anima, & corpore, quæ ab inuicem deiunctæ manent. Neque dicas, Vnio non est præcisè materia, & forma, sed materia, & forma collectiuè, simul, iunctim, &c. vnde non est quid à partibus ita sumptis distinctum. Contra tamen, &c.
units.tr: It is proved first: things that can exist without something are distinct from it. The parts can exist without the union, so they are distinct from it. Therefore, whenever they are present in the composite, they are united by a union distinct from themselves. The major premise is certain, because the sign of distinction is taken from separation. The minor premise also holds in the case of soul and body, which remain separated from each other. Nor may you say that union is not precisely matter and form, but matter and form taken collectively, together, conjointly, and so on, so that it is not something distinct from the parts so taken. On the contrary, however, etc.

units.la: Probatur 2. conclusio, nam quoties materia, & forma sunt simul, vnitim, &c. aut ly simul est quid à partibus distinctum, aut non. Si primum, ergo cùm hoc non sit nisi vnio, habetur intentum. Si secundum, contra. Potest esse materia, potest esse forma, & non esse ly simul: ergo id est aliquid ab ijs distinctum. Neque dicas. Vnio materiæ cum forma dicit hoc tantùm, vt vna sit localiter præsens alteri: ad hoc verò non opus est admittere vnionem vt distinctam: sed satis erit concipere vtramq; partem sibi præsentem, seu non distantem. Contra tamen, &c
units.tr: The second conclusion is proved. Whenever matter and form are together, united, and so on, either the word together names something distinct from the parts, or it does not. If the first, then since this is nothing but union, the point is established. If the second, then on the contrary: matter can be, form can be, and together need not be. Therefore it is something distinct from them. Nor may you say that the union of matter with form means only this, that one is locally present to the other. For this it is not necessary to admit a union as distinct; it will be enough to conceive each part as present to the other, or not distant from it. On the contrary, however, etc.

units.la: Probatur 3. conclusio, quia possunt esse materia, & forma sibi localiter praesentes: imo penetrata cum omni dispositione ad vnionem, etiamsi tunc formaliter non sint vnitae; igitur ly vnitae aliud quid est praeter partes localiter praesentes. Probo antecedens. Penetret Deus Paulum cum Francisco: in tali casu anima vnius esset intime praesens materiae alterius, nec tamen foret actu eidem vnita (non enim forma Francisci cum Paulo constitueret hominem) ergo esse vnitam est aliud quid partibus localiter praesentibus adueniens. Hinc etiam arguitur prima ratio aduersariorum, quia esse potest forma in materia, collectiue cum materia, simul cum materia, &c. quamuis haec duo non habeant vnionem actu: ergo vnio est aliquid ab vtraque distinctum. Antecedens patet exemplo, vt supra, & similibus etiam, quia si lignum penetretur cum auro, forma vnius est simul cum alterius materia, nec tamen ipsi vnita, &c.
units.tr: The third conclusion is proved. Matter and form can be locally present to each other, indeed even penetrated with every disposition towards union, even though at that time they are not formally united. Therefore being united is something other than the parts being locally present. I prove the antecedent. Let God penetrate Paul together with Francis. In such a case the soul of the one would be intimately present to the matter of the other, and yet would not actually be united to it (for the form of Francis would not constitute a man with Paul). Therefore being united is something additional that comes to the parts when they are locally present. From this the first argument of the opponents is also answered. A form can be in matter, collectively with matter, together with matter, and so on, although these two do not have union actually. Therefore union is something distinct from both. The antecedent is clear from the example above, and from similar ones too: if wood is penetrated together with gold, the form of the one is together with the matter of the other, and yet is not united to it, etc.

units.la: Probatur vltimo ab aliquibus, nam si vnio non distingueretur a partibus, non posset assignari terminus humanae generationis. Homo enim non producit formam, non materiam: ergo si nec vnionem ab ijs distinctam, nihil producit, quod nullo modo est dicendum. Sed argumentum apud me vim non habet. Nam homo quomodo producit vnionem, si tunc fortasse nil agit, cum Deus animam infundit? imo si eo instanti potest esse iam mortuus ?. Homo ergo dici debebit: generare hominem, quia suppetit materiam, quæ ad formam habendam, & sibi vniendam apta est.
units.tr: It is proved lastly by some: if union were not distinguished from the parts, the term of human generation could not be assigned. For man produces neither the form nor the matter. Therefore if he does not produce a union distinct from them, he produces nothing, which must in no way be said. But this argument has no force with me. For how does man produce the union, if then he perhaps does nothing, since God infuses the soul? Indeed, if at that instant he may already be dead? Man must therefore be said to generate man, because there is matter suited to receive the form and to be united to it.

units.la: Obijcies: 1. Potentia, & actus debent essentialiter esse tales, quia immediate inter se vniuntur, ergo sine aliquo intermedio distincto. Respond. d. antecedens: quia immediate vniuntur potentia, seu possunt vniri, c. vniuntur actu, n. & retorqueo argumentum, materia enim, & forma etiam separatæ dici debent potentia, & actus, ergo tales non sunt, quia immediate vniantur actu, sed quia possunt vniri.
units.tr: You will object: (1) Potency and act must be essentially such, because they are united immediately with each other, therefore without any intermediate distinct from them. I answer: I distinguish the antecedent. That they are immediately united as potency, or can be united, I grant; that they are united as act, I deny. And I turn the argument back: matter and form, even when separated, ought to be called potency and act. Therefore they are not such because they are immediately united in act, but because they can be united.

units.la: Obijcies 2. Si partes vnirentur per vnionem distinctam, ergo non vnirentur immediate. Rursus. Hæc vnio certè vniretur etiam ipsa, ergo per aliam–> vnionem, & sic in infinitum. Resp. n. antecedens; vnio enim non est aliqua–> pars media inter materiam, & formam: sed ratio immediate illas vniendi. Exemplum adest in visione, quæ ab oculo quidem, & obiecto distincta est, cum tamen oculus per ipsam immediate videat obiectum. Ad secundum Respon. vnionem se ipsa immediate vniri materiæ non per aliud: nam est id, quo, seu ratio formalis, qua partes vniuntur. Quemadmodum ergo albedo non est alba per quid superadditum, eo quia sit ratio formalis constituendi album: sic vnio quia est ratio formaliter vniendi, non vnitur ipsa per aliud &c. Quæres quid sit vnio? Respond. aliqui esse modum substantialem. Arbitror ego, dici posse accidens, cum essentialiter à subiecto dependeat. Dices. Vnio est de conceptu essentiali compositi substantialis: at nullum accidens potest esse de conceptu substantiæ, ergo. Respond. accidens posse dici de conceptu substantiæ vt quo: non vt quod, quia enim substantia composita quà talis involuit vnionem partium, vt id quo, ideo vnio esse potest de conceptu substantiæ, vt quo.
units.tr: You will object (2): If the parts were united by a distinct union, then they would not be united immediately. Again: this union would itself surely be united, and so by another union, and so on to infinity. I deny the antecedent. For union is not some intermediate part between matter and form, but the reason by which they are united immediately. An example is found in vision, which is indeed distinct from the eye and from the object, and yet the eye sees the object immediately through it. To the second I answer: union is united to matter immediately, not through another, for it is that by which, that is, the formal reason by which the parts are united. Just as whiteness is not white through something superadded, because it is the formal reason for constituting the white thing, so union, because it is the formal reason of uniting, is not itself united through another, and so on. You will ask what union is. I answer: some say it is a substantial mode. I think it can be called an accident, since it depends essentially on the subject. You will say: union belongs to the essential concept of a substantial composite, but no accident can belong to the concept of a substance; therefore... I answer: an accident can be said to belong to the concept of a substance as that by which, not as that which. For since a composite substance as such involves the union of its parts as that by which, union can belong to the concept of substance as that by which.

units.la: DISQVISITIO QVARTA.
units.tr: DISQVISITIO QVARTA.

units.la: An, & quomodo in composito detur vnica vnio.
units.tr: Whether, and how, a single union is found in a composite.

units.la: PRO intelligentia notetur, hanc disquisitionem procedere suppositâ materia, & forma, tanquam duplici parte vltimò efficiente compositum. Et circa istas quæritur, vnamne habeant vnionem, an duas. Putant Arefius, Hurtado, & alij vtramque partem duplici vnione connecti: altera, quæ recipiatur in materia, & ad formam terminet: altera quæ, in forma recepta se ad materiam extendat. Secunda sententia probabilior tenet, in composito vnam dari tantummodo vnionem. Sed aut auctores variant. Alij quippe dicunt, tunc vnionem recipi tam in materia, quàm in forma, vt Complutenses; alij verò in materia solùm recipi, & ad formam terminari. Pro solutione sit.
units.tr: To understand this, it should be noted that this inquiry proceeds on the supposition of matter and form as the two parts by which the composite is ultimately efficiently constituted. And concerning these, the question is whether they have one union or two. Arefius, Hurtado, and others think that each part is joined by a twofold union: one, which is received in the matter and terminates in the form; the other, which, once received in the form, extends itself to the matter. The second opinion, which is more probable, holds that only one union is given in the composite. But the authors differ here. For some say that the union is received both in the matter and in the form, as the Complutenses do; others say that it is received only in the matter and terminates in the form. Let us proceed to the solution.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: In composito datur vnica vnio, recepta in sola materia, & ad formam terminata.
units.tr: In a composite there is a single union, received in the matter alone and terminating in the form.

units.la: PRobatur prima pars conclusionis; quia vnica sufficit vnio, ergo duæ superfluæ sunt. Probo antecedens. Vnio est essentialiter vnio duorum, ergo per vnicam & formæ vnitur materia, & materiæ forma.
units.tr: The first part of the conclusion is proved as follows. One union is sufficient, so two would be superfluous. I prove the antecedent: union is essentially the union of two things, so through one union both matter is united to form and form to matter.

units.la: Probatur 2. quia si duæ forent vniones in composito, vna posset ab alia separari. Ergo tollatur vnio, quæ se tenet ex parte formæ, ac relinquatur alia, quæ in materia est. Hoc dato, vel adhuc perseuerat compositum, vel non. Si primum, ergo vna satis est vnio. Si secundum, contra. Tunc esset forma vnita materiæ: sed compositum nil aliud est, ergo per vnicam vnionem perseueraret.
units.tr: Second, if there were two unions in a composite, one could be separated from the other. Let the union that lies on the side of the form be removed and the union in the matter be left. Granted this, either the composite still persists or it does not. If it persists, one union is enough. If it does not, then the contrary follows: the form would be united to the matter, but the composite is nothing other than that, so it would persist through a single union.

units.la: Probatur etiam secunda pars conclusionis, quia modus nequit simul esse in duplici subiecto, sed vnio est modus, ergo nequit in materia & forma recipi simul. Maior probatur, nam essentia modi est affigi subiecto, à quo educitur: sed ab vnico educitur; ergo. Et quidem si loquamur de vnione, à materia sola hæc dimanat, nam agens materiale in materiam solummodo agit.
units.tr: The second part of the conclusion is also proved. A mode cannot be in two subjects at once, and union is a mode, so it cannot be received in matter and form at the same time. The major is proved: the essence of a mode is to be attached to the subject from which it arises, but union arises from one subject only, so it is attached to one. Indeed, if we speak of union, it flows from matter alone, for a material agent acts only upon matter.

units.la: Probatur 2. à Mysterio Incarnationis, in quo vna tantùm datur vnio recepta in humanitate, atq; ad Verbum terminata. Ergo & in cæteris compositis vnio recipietur in materia, & ad formam terminabitur. Confirmatur, quia si vtraq; in parte reciperetur, ergo in homine simul adesset vnio extensa, & non extensa. Probo. Eadem tota reciperetur in materia, ergo foret extensa: eadem tota in anima spirituali, ergo non esset extensa. Quæ duo repugnant.
units.tr: Second, it is proved from the mystery of the Incarnation, in which only one union is given: it is received in the humanity and terminates in the Word. Therefore in other composites too, union will be received in the matter and terminate in the form. This is confirmed: if it were received in both parts, then in man there would be at once a union extended and a union not extended. I prove this: the same union, as a whole, would be received in the matter, so it would be extended; and the same, as a whole, in the spiritual soul, so it would not be extended. These two contradict each other.

units.la: Obijcies 1. contra primam conclusionis partem. In composito physico sunt duo vnita, ergo duæ vniones. Probatur, quia multiplicato effectu formali, & forma ipsa multiplicanda est. Respond. n. consequentiam, & dico, quòd cum vnio sit essentialiter duorum, duo vnita sunt. vnicus effectus formalis; ergo & vnica forma, nempe vnio.
units.tr: You will object, first, against the first part of the conclusion: in a physical composite there are two things united, so there are two unions. This is proved because when the formal effect is multiplied, the form itself must be multiplied. I deny the consequence, and say that since union is essentially of two, two things are united. There is a single formal effect, so there is also a single form, namely union.

units.la: Obijcies 2. contra secundam conclusionis partem. Si forma non reciperet in se vnionem, intelligi non posset vniri; ergo. Probatur antecedens, nam ideò aliquid vnitur, quia recipit in se vnionem. Respond. n. antecedens. Ad probationem, d. ideò præcisè aliquid vnitur, quia recipit vnionem, n. quia vel recipit, vel terminat, c. Satis ergo est si vnio sit biectiuè recipiatur in materia, & ad formamam terminet, sic enim cogit formam, vt in eodem subiecto sit, quemadmodum in Verbo Incarnato patet.
units.tr: You will object, second, against the second part of the conclusion: if the form did not receive union in itself, it could not be understood to be united; therefore... The antecedent is proved, for something is united precisely because it receives union in itself. I deny the antecedent. As for the proof, I grant that something is united precisely because it receives union, but I deny that it is united merely because it either receives or terminates. It is therefore enough that union be received objectively in the matter and terminate in the form; for in this way it compels the form to be in the same subject, as is evident in the Incarnate Word.

units.la: Obijcies 3. Quod transit de vno contradictorio ad aliud, recipit in se id, ratione cuius transit; sed forma talis est nam de non vnita fit vnita; ergo recipit vnionem. Respond. d. maiorem. Si transeat se solo, c. si cum alio, quod mutatur, n. Forma igitur non transit se sola de non vnita in vnitam, sed cum materia, quae satis est si mutetur ipsa, eo quòd intrinsecè recipiat vnionem. Vt patet in Verbo, quod sanè transit ad esse vnitum humanitati, etiamsi non recipiat in se vnionem, sed illam terminet solùm.
units.tr: You will object, third: whatever passes from one contradictory to the other receives in itself that by reason of which it passes; but the form is such, for it goes from not-united to united, so it receives union. I deny the major. I grant it if the thing passes by itself alone; I deny it if it passes together with another that is changed. So the form does not pass from not-united to united by itself alone, but together with the matter, and it is enough that the matter itself is changed, since it intrinsically receives union. This is evident in the Word, which indeed passes into being united to the humanity, even though it does not receive union in itself but only terminates it.

units.la: DISQVISITIO QVINTA.
units.tr: DISQVISITIO QVINTA.

units.la: An compositum distinguatur à parti- bus vnitis.
units.tr: Whether the compound is distinct from the parts united.

units.la: PRO intelligentia explicanda est breuiter doctrina Scoti, quem sequuntur sui, & aliqui etiam ex Thomistis, vt Caietanus, Ferrariensis, & alij, quorum sententiae subscribunt Conimbricenses. Ait ergo Scotus, naturale compositum esse tertiam entitatem à partibus vnitis distinctam, adeout si accipiatur materia, forma, & vnio simul, hoc totum reuera non sit compositum; sed aliud quid ab ipsis resultans. Verum tamen est quod dicitur compositum dicit aliquo modo partes, nimirum in obliquo, nam ab ijs resultare debet; sed in recto quatenus compositum, est quid tertium ab ijsdem actu, & realiter distinctum, atq; superadditum. Sed contra sit.
units.tr: To explain the doctrine clearly, I shall briefly set out the teaching of Scotus, which his followers adopt, and some of the Thomists as well, such as Cajetan, Ferrariensis and others, whose opinion the Conimbricenses subscribe to. Scotus therefore holds that a natural compound is a third entity distinct from the united parts, so that if matter, form and union are taken together, this whole is not really a compound but something else resulting from them. It is true, however, that the word "compound" refers in some way to the parts, namely in the oblique case, for it must result from them; but in the nominative, as a compound, it is a third thing, actually and really distinct from them and superadded to them. But let us consider the objection.

units.la: CONCLUSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Compositum non est quaedam tertia entitas à partibus unitis di- stincta, & superaddita.
units.tr: The compound is not some third entity, distinct from and added to the united parts.

units.la: PRobatur r. auctoritate, nam in symbolo Athanasij dicitur. Sicut anima rationalis, & caro unus est homo, ita Deus, & homo unus est Christus: at Christus non est quaedam tertia entitas Deo, & homini superaddita: ergo compositum, &c. Probo minorem, quia Christus, vt Christus in recto non aliud est, nisi Deus, & homo, seu natura humana, & Diuina simul; ergo non est quaedam tertia entitas ab ijsdem partibus vnitis distincta.
units.tr: It is proved first by authority, for the Athanasian Creed says: As the reasonable soul and flesh is one man, so God and man is one Christ. But Christ is not some third entity added to God and man. Therefore the compound, etc. I prove the minor: Christ, as Christ, in the nominative is nothing other than God and man, that is, the human and divine natures together. Therefore he is not some third entity distinct from the same united parts.

units.la: Probatur 2. ratione, quia si compositum est quaedam tertia entitas a partibus vnitis distincta, ergo non est cum illis identificata: sed partes vnitae simul erunt vnum quid, & compositum aliud quid; ea enim quae distinguuntur, sunt aliud, & aliud. Hoc posito, assumo tertiam hanc entitatem, & quaero. Vel tertia haec entitas dicit se sola totum compositum; vel non. Si secundum, ergo compositum in suo conceptu essentiali habet aliquid aliud praeter hanc entitatem; ergo sola haec entitas non saluat compositum. Si primum, contra vrgeo, &c
units.tr: It is proved second by reason. If the compound is some third entity distinct from the united parts, then it is not identical with them. But the united parts together will be one thing, and the compound another, for things that are distinguished are one thing and another. Granting this, I assume this third entity and ask: either this third entity by itself signifies the whole compound, or it does not. If the second, then the compound in its essential concept has something besides this entity, and so this entity alone does not save the compound. If the first, I press the argument against it, etc.

units.la: Probatur 3. conclusio sic. Tertia haec entitas,quia distinguitur à partibus,& est aliud ab ipsis,de absoluta saltem Dei potentia segregari poterit, nam quae actu, & realiter distinguuntur, non repugnat ab invicem separari, vt patet de anima, & corpore; de materia, & forma,&c.Separetur ergo entitas ista compositi à suis partibus; aut si non re, separetur saltem intellectu. Hoc dato, arguo sic. Vel huiusmodi entitas est in se actu composita, vel non: si secundum, ergo dici nequit compositum: si primum, ergo componitur ex partibus;ergo ab ijs distincta non est. Vrgeo rursus. Haec tertia entitas, tota quanta est, per te distinguitur à partibus: ergo totum id, quod haec entitas dicit, ipsum quoq;distinguitur à partibus:at ista entitas dicit partes, nam composita est; ergo in hac entitate sunt novae partes distinctae à primis partibus; ergo noua materia, noua forma, noua vnio, &c.
units.tr: It is proved third, in this way. This third entity, since it is distinguished from the parts and is other than them, can be separated from them at least by the absolute power of God, for things that are actually and really distinct are not incompatible with being separated from one another, as is evident in the case of soul and body, matter and form, etc. Let this entity of the compound then be separated from its parts, or if not in reality, at least in the intellect. Granting this, I argue thus. Either such an entity is in itself actually composite, or it is not. If it is not, it cannot be called a compound. If it is, then it is composed of parts, and so it is not distinct from them. I press again. This third entity, taken as a whole, is distinguished from the parts by your own account; therefore everything that this entity signifies is also distinguished from the parts. But this entity signifies parts, for it is composite. Therefore in this entity there are new parts distinct from the first parts, and so new matter, new form, new union, etc.

units.la: Objicies 1.Generatio debet habere proprium terminum: sed per generationem non producuntur partes, vt patet in homine; producitur ergo tertia quaedam entitas. Respond. d. minorem. Non producuntur partes vt vnitae, n. simpliciter, c. Terminus ergo generationis quo est vnio, vel aptitudo in materia ad vnionem; terminus vero quod, sunt partes vt vnitæ.
units.tr: You will object first: generation must have a proper term, but the parts are not produced through generation, as is evident in man. Therefore some third entity is produced. I answer: I deny the minor. The parts are not produced as united, not simply. The term of generation "by which" is therefore the union, or the aptitude of the matter for union; but the term "what" is the parts as united.

units.la: Obijcies 2. Quæuis causa debet realiter ab effectu distingui: sed partes vnitæ sunt causa composita; ergo compositum distinguitur à partibus vnitis. Resp. d. maiorem. Causa extrinseca distinguitur ab effectu, c. intrinseca, n. Partes autem vnitæ sunt causæ intrinsecæ, quæ non alio modo efficiunt compositum, nisi communicando se, atq; vniendo, adeout ipsæ vnitæ sint ipsum compositum. Et reuera quid est album, nisi albedo, & subiectum simul? quid est calidum, nisi calor, & materia simul? quid homo, nisi corpus, & anima simul?
units.tr: You will object second: any cause must be really distinct from its effect, but the united parts are the cause of the compound. Therefore the compound is distinct from the united parts. I answer: I deny the major. An extrinsic cause is distinct from its effect, but an intrinsic cause is not. The united parts are intrinsic causes, which bring about the compound in no other way than by communicating themselves and uniting, so that the united things are themselves the compound. And indeed, what is white but whiteness and a subject together? What is hot but heat and matter together? What is a man but body and soul together?

units.la: Obijcies 3. nonnulla Philosophi loca.
units.tr: You will object third: some passages of the Philosopher.

units.la: 2. Metaph. tex. 16. vbi ait, sex non esse bis tria, sed semel sex. Deinde 7. Metaph. cap. 17. vbi dicit, syllabam ba non esse b. & a, sed ba. Respond. bis tria seorsim non facere sex, quia sic accepta sunt species diuersæ numeri; vnitim verò sunt sex, quia hic numerus redditur à sex vnitatibus collectiuè acceptis. Resp. ad secundum ba non esse b. & a. seorsim; sed ita vnitim. A simili ergo composito m non. est materia seorsim, & forma, sed materia, & forma vnitim.
units.tr: In Metaphysics 2, text 16, he says that six is not twice three, but once six. Then in Metaphysics 7, chapter 17, he says that the syllable ba is not b and a, but ba. I answer: twice three taken separately does not make six, because so taken they are different species of number; but taken united they are six, because this number is made up of six unities taken collectively. To the second: ba is not b and a separately, but so united. Therefore, by a similar reasoning, the composite is not matter separately and form, but matter and form united.

units.la: DISPVTATIO TERTIA.
units.tr: DISPUTATIO TERTIA.

units.la: De corruptione substantiali.
units.tr: On substantial corruption.

units.la: AGens naturale dum generat nouum compositum, dicitur corrumpere vetus, nam quia forma de nouo genita nequit in vna, eademque materia compati aliam, necessum est praecedentem corrumpi. Ex quo emergit decantatum axioma: Generatio vnius est corruptio alterius. Quod nos quomodo intelligi debeat, iamdudum vidimus. Itaque post doctrinam de generatione, congruè sequitur disputatio de corruptione. Circa quam hic statim quaerimus, detur ne iuxta mentem Aristoteleam.
units.tr: An acting natural agent, while it generates a new compound, is said to corrupt the old one, for since the form newly brought into being cannot coexist with another form in one and the same matter, the preceding form must necessarily be corrupted. From this arises the well-known axiom: The generation of one thing is the corruption of another. How this ought to be understood, we have already seen. Therefore, after the doctrine of generation, a disputation on corruption rightly follows. Concerning this we ask at once here whether, according to the mind of Aristotle, corruption exists.

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: FIRST DISPUTATION.

units.la: An detur substantialis corruptio Aristotelea.
units.tr: Whether there is an Aristotelian substantial corruption.

units.la: PRO intelligentia. Non quaero, an fiant in natura corruptiones rerum? Quid enim saepius occurrit, quàm species miserrima, & mortis imago luctuosissima? Hæc in homines, in belluas, in metalla, in plantas falcem iacit, messemque suam cadaueribus implet. Dubium est, an talis corruptio fiat modo Aristoteleo, per hoc nimirum, quòd aliqua substantia penitus desinat esse in natura, tota pereat, & destruatur. Pro solutione adnotetur.
units.tr: For the sake of understanding: I do not ask whether corruptions of things occur in nature. For what meets us more often than that most wretched sight, the very image of death, full of sorrow? It hurls its scythe at men, at beasts, at metals, at plants, and fills its harvest with corpses. The question is whether such corruption happens in the Aristotelian manner, namely, that some substance wholly ceases to exist in nature, perishes entirely, and is destroyed. For the solution, let the following be noted.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Corruptio substantialis non videtur fieri per substantiæ destru- ctionem.
units.tr: Substantial corruption does not seem to take place through the destruction of a substance.

units.la: PRobatur 1. quia humanum compositum physicè corrumpitur: sed talis corruptio non fit per substantiæ destructionem: ergo. Maior est euidens, nam quoties moritur homo, certè corrumpitur mixtum. Minor probatur, quia nec anima destruitur, neque corpus; ergo talis corruptio non fit per substantię destructionem. Ex hoc verò licet arguere ad cæteta, vt c. p.
units.tr: I prove this first: a human compound is physically corrupted, but such a corruption does not take place through the destruction of a substance; therefore the thesis holds. The major premise is evident, for whenever a man dies, the compound is certainly corrupted. The minor is proved, because neither the soul nor the body is destroyed; therefore such a corruption does not take place through the destruction of a substance. From this one may argue to the rest, as in the preceding chapter.

units.la: Probatur 2. in plantis, quia v. g. dum in ictu oculi ramus præciditur, fit corruptio viuentis, & vt aiunt Aristotelei, cadauer: sed in ea corruptione substantia nulla perit; ergo. Maior admittitur. Minor probatur, nam substantia non perit, nisi per inductas in materiam dispositiones contrarias: hoc autem non fit, eo instanti, quo ramus cæditur; ergo. Probo minorem. Dispositiones contrariæ non inducuntur nisi per tempus, & diutinam luctam. Rursus: eo momento, quo ramus præciditur, habet colorem, figuram, humiditatem, pondus, & omnia tandem accidentia, quæ prius: ergo si non pereūt accidentia, multò minùs destrui potest substantia. Ergo corruptio viuentis non videtur fieri per substantiæ destructionē. Probatur 3. in metallis, atq; lapidibus. Nam v. g. si teratur lapis, vt Muriani faciunt vitriarij, & in puluisculos ad instar farinæ adigatur, certè corrumpitur mixtum: sed ista corruptio non dicit substantiæ destructionem; ergo. Maiorem nullus negabit. Minor probatur, quia si aliqua substantia perijt, certè fuit materialis; ergo multum materiæ sublatum est: ergo hi pulueres multum de pondere amiserunt,quod experientia non constat. Præterea, si aliqua substantia interijt; ergo alia de nouo per te succeßit. Rogo autem, quis hanc de nouo genuit? consequentia verò tenet, nam huiusmodi corruptio non videtur ab ea differre, quæ facit natura, nisi per hoc quòd natura magis adhuc dissoluit.
units.tr: I prove it second, in plants. For example, when a branch is cut off in the twinkling of an eye, a living thing is corrupted, and, as the Aristotelians say, becomes a corpse; yet no substance perishes in that corruption; therefore the thesis holds. The major is admitted. The minor is proved: a substance does not perish unless contrary dispositions are induced into the matter, but this does not happen at the instant the branch is cut; therefore it does not perish. I prove the minor: contrary dispositions are not induced except over time and through a long struggle. Again, at the moment the branch is cut off, it has the same colour, shape, moisture, weight, and in short all the accidents it had before; therefore if the accidents do not perish, much less can the substance be destroyed. Therefore the corruption of a living thing does not seem to take place through the destruction of a substance. Third, it is proved in metals and stones. For example, if a stone is ground, as the Murano glassmakers do, and reduced to dust like flour, the compound is certainly corrupted; but this corruption does not imply the destruction of a substance; therefore the thesis holds. No one will deny the major. The minor is proved: if some substance has perished, it was certainly material; therefore much matter has been taken away; therefore these powders have lost much of their weight, which experience does not confirm. Besides, if some substance has perished, then another has come into being anew in its place. But I ask, who begot this new substance? The consequence holds, for such a corruption does not seem to differ from that which nature produces, except that nature dissolves things still further.

units.la: Probatur 4. in elementis. Aqua v. gr. feruens, & ebulliens aliquando tandem absumitur, & hoc fit, aiunt Aristotelei per aquæ corruptionem: sed tunc nulla substantia deperditur: ergo. Probo minorem, aqua enim euaporans manet substantialiter aqua, etiamsi per ignem attenuata. Patet hoc circa lebetis orificium, vbi paulatim ex additione partis ad partem fiunt guttulæ quædam, & veluti sudor. Patet ex tactu, nam vapor ille non minus atq; aqua humefacit manum. Patet ex nube, in qua vapor collectus cadit in pluuiam, &c. ergo talis corruptio non fit per substantiæ destructionem.
units.tr: Fourth, it is proved in the elements. For example, water that is hot and boiling is at last entirely consumed, and this happens, as the Aristotelians say, through the corruption of the water; yet no substance is lost then; therefore the thesis holds. I prove the minor: evaporating water remains substantially water, even though it has been thinned by fire. This is plain at the mouth of a cauldron, where little droplets gradually form, part by part, like a sweat. It is plain from touch, for that vapour wets the hand no less than water does. It is plain from the cloud, in which collected vapour falls again as rain, and so on. Therefore such a corruption does not take place through the destruction of a substance.

units.la: Probatur vltimò auctoritate. Primò Hippocratis lib. 1. de Diæta. 2. Trifmegimegisti in Pimandro, aientis. Nihil moritur in mundo, sed solum transfit, & immutatur. 3. Pythagoræ apud Ouid. lib. 15. Metam.
units.tr: Finally, it is proved by authority. First, Hippocrates, book 1 of On Diet. Second, Trismegistus in the Pimander, saying: Nothing dies in the world, but it only passes over and is changed. Third, Pythagoras in Ovid, Metamorphoses book 15.

units.la: Nec perit in tanto quidquam, mihi credite, mundo, &c.
units.tr: Nothing perishes in so great a world, believe me, etc.

units.la: §. Aristotelis 8. Metaphif. tex. 16. his verbis. Materia vltima, & forma, vt dictum est, idem sunt, nimirum forma nil videtur esse aliud, quàm ipsa materia diuersimode affecta, & permixta, seu materiæ affectio. Ergo si materia non corrumpitur substantialiter, neque forma. Deinde 2. phys. tex. 12. Dicitur forma non separabilis existens, nisi secundum rationem. Denique tex. 19. Sicuti simitas, quæ à naso auferri non potest, &c. Quemadmodum ergo si à corpore tollatur figura, vt simitas, curuitas, &c. non ideo perit aliqua substantia, similiter quoties à composito dicitur auferri forma; non propterea substantia destruitur vlla; sed translocatur, & diuersimodè commiscetur. Vnde Lucretius in 2.
units.tr: §. Aristotle, Metaphysics book 8, text 16, in these words: The ultimate matter and the form, as has been said, are the same; for form seems to be nothing else than the matter itself variously disposed and mixed, or an affection of matter.
