Therefore if matter is not corrupted substantially, neither is form. Next, Physics book 2, text 12: Form is said to exist inseparably, except according to reason. Finally, text 19: Just as snubness, which cannot be removed from the nose, etc. Therefore, just as when a figure such as snubness or curvature is removed from a body, no substance perishes for that reason, so similarly, whenever form is said to be removed from a compound, no substance is destroyed at all; rather it is transposed and mixed in different ways. Hence Lucretius in book 2:

units.la: Nec sic interimit mors res, vt materiai Corpora conficiat, sed catum dissupat ollis: Inde alijs aliud iungit, & efficit, omnes Res vt conuertant formas, &c.
units.tr: Nor does death destroy things so as to annihilate the bodies of matter, but it dissolves the compound of them; then it joins one thing to another, and makes all things change their forms, etc.

units.la: Opponis. Cum fit corruptio rosæ, ligni, metalli, & similium, certè aliqua substantia cessat esse in natura.
units.tr: You object: when a rose, wood, metal, and the like are corrupted, surely some substance ceases to exist in nature.

units.la: Probatur, nam corrupta rosa, vel ea entitas manet adhuc, vel non si primum, ergo rosa non corrumpitur, sed perseuerat: si secundum, ergo rosa non amplius est: sed illa erat substantia; ergo substantia cessat esse in natura, & omnino perit. Respond. d. antecedens. Cessat esse in natura entitas mixta, c. simplex, nego. Dico igitur, quòd rosa dum corrumpitur, non perseuerat quidem, sed tamen substantiae partes, quae seorsim acceptae rosa non sunt, illae manent. Quemadmodum, ergo si resoluatur domus, tollitur sanè aliquod compositum, sed non materiae primae, lapides, caementa, trabes, &c. ita de quouis mixto dicendum, non corrumpi substantias actu, sed resolui, & haec vera mixtorum corruptio est, vt disput. sequen-ti.
units.tr: This is proved: when the rose is corrupted, either that entity still remains or it does not. If the first, then the rose is not corrupted but persists; if the second, then the rose is no longer; but it was a substance; therefore a substance ceases to exist in nature and perishes altogether. I reply: I distinguish the antecedent. That a mixed entity ceases to exist in nature I grant; that a simple one does I deny. So I say that while the rose is corrupted it indeed does not persist, but nonetheless the parts of the substance, which taken separately are not a rose, remain. Just as, if a house is dismantled, some compound is certainly destroyed, but not primary matter: the stones, rubble, beams, and so on remain; so it must be said of any mixed thing that substances are not corrupted in act but are resolved, and this is the true corruption of mixed things, as in the following disputation.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: Second Disquisition.

units.la: Quid sit substantialis corruptio Aristotelea.
units.tr: What Aristotelian substantial corruption is.

units.la: PRO intelligentia quaestionis faciunt multæ definitiones, quibus Aristotelei corruptionem describunt. Primò dicitur desitio totius permanente subiecto. 2. Desitio alicuius rei in aliam.
units.tr: Many definitions, by which the Aristotelians describe corruption, help toward understanding the question. First, it is said to be the cessation of the whole while the subject remains. Second, the cessation of one thing into another.

units.la: 3. Mutatio facta in materia à forma substantiali ad eius priuationem, &c. Quarum definitionum sensus idem est. Quòd corruptio sit quidam transitus ab esse formæ ad non esse ipsius, quæ dicitur mutatio negatiua. Porro inquiunt differre corruptionem ab anihilatione, quia in ista non manet subiectum; sed in corruptione permanet. Verùm si forma substantialis tota, quanta est, corrumpitur, quare dicunt non anihilari? video commune responsionem, cui quia melior non occurrit, quiescendum.
units.tr: Third, a change made in the matter from a substantial form to its privation, and so on. The sense of these definitions is the same: that corruption is a certain passage from the being of a form to its non-being, which is called a negative change. Moreover, they say that corruption differs from annihilation because in annihilation the subject does not remain, but in corruption it does. But if the whole substantial form is corrupted, as far as it is, why do they say it is not annihilated? I see the common answer, and since a better one does not occur to me, I shall rest content with it.

units.la: Quæres 1. an corruptio sit rebus naturalis? Aduerte priùs duplici modo posse aliquid esse naturale. Aut quia fit perfectio naturaliter debita rei, quomodo v. gr. calor est naturalis igni. Aut quia non fit quidem perfectio rei, sed tamen cum ipsa connexionem habeat naturalem, & eam sequatur. Hoc modo naturalis est homini ægritudo, quia hæc naturalem eius complexionem consequitur. Hoc posito, dico rebus naturalem esse corruptionem secundo modo, nempe minùs propriè.
units.tr: Question 2: Is corruption, like generation, intended per se by nature? Note first that something can be intended per se by nature in two ways. First, by way of an end and for its own sake, as health is intended per se by the sick man. Second, per se indeed, but not as an end; rather as a means, as walking is desired not per accidens but per se, though not as an end. The answer, then, is that corruption is intended per se by nature in the second way, not the first; namely, as a means.

units.la: Quæres 2. an corruptio, quemadmodum generatio, intendatur per se à natura? Nota priùs, duplici modo posse aliquid per se intendi à natura. Primò per modum finis, & ratione sui, quo pacto sanitas intenditur per se ab ægroto. Secundo per se quidem, non tamen vt finis, verùm vt medium: sicuti deambulatio, quæ non per accidens expetitur, sed per se, quanquam non vt finis. Resp. igitur, corruptionem intendi per se à natura secundo modo, non primo, nempè vt medium.
units.tr: You will ask, second, whether corruption, just as generation, is intended per se by nature? Note first that something can be intended per se by nature in two ways. First, as an end, and for its own sake, in the way that health is intended per se by the sick man. Second, per se indeed, but not as an end rather as a means: just as walking, which is desired not per accidens but per se, though not as an end. I answer, therefore, that corruption is intended per se by nature in the second way, not the first, namely as a means.

units.la: Quæres 3. an generatio vnius corruptio sit alterius, & quomodo? Resp. generationem, quatenus generatio est, habere terminum de nouo productum, vnde sub tali conceptu dici non potest corruptio. Quatenus autem consequitur ad ipsam prioris formæ defectus, in ordine ad hunc terminum vocari etiam potest corruptio de consequenti, non formaliter. Quapropter eadem actio sub diuerso conceptu assumpta, generatiua, & corruptiua est, nam gignendo formam de nouo, aliam expellit à materia, quæ inerat priùs, vt alibi adnotauimus.
units.tr: You will ask, third, whether the generation of one thing is the corruption of another, and how? I answer that generation, insofar as it is generation, has as its term something newly produced, whence under such a concept it cannot be called corruption. But insofar as it follows upon the very defect of the prior form, in relation to this term it can also be called corruption by consequence, not formally. Wherefore the same action, taken under a different concept, is both generative and corruptive: for by generating a new form it expels from the matter the other which was previously present in it, as we have noted elsewhere.

units.la: DISPVTATIO QVARTA.
units.tr: DISPUTATION FOUR.

units.la: Quomodo fiat substantialis corrupt o.
units.tr: How substantial corruption comes about.

units.la: NIl videtur expeditius ad rei cognitionem, quàm si consulamus originem, & causas, vnde naturale mixtum corrumpi solet. Causæ verò duæ sunt; alia intrinseca ipsi compositō: alia extrinseca. Prima consistit in complexione, atque compagine rei, quæ cum partibus constet dissimilibus, eterogeneis, & inuicem contrarijs, tandem sibi exitium parit. Nam quæ contraria sunt, mutuis plagis, & cæco quodam conflictu dum agunt, aliquando etiam rupto vinculo separantur, vnde aliijs, quæ leuiora sunt,auolantibus; & quæ grauiora subsidentibus, dissidium fit lethale, atque corruptio. Quod verò attinet ad causam curruptionis. extrinsecam, ea videtur esse multiplex. Quare claritatis gratia notetur. (†)
units.tr: Nothing seems more useful for understanding a thing than to consider its origin and causes, from which a natural mixed body is usually corrupted. There are two causes: one intrinsic to the compound itself, and one extrinsic. The first lies in the complexion and structure of the thing, which, being made up of dissimilar, heterogeneous and mutually contrary parts, eventually brings about its own ruin. For contraries, while they act upon one another with mutual blows and a kind of blind conflict, sometimes break their bond and separate. The lighter parts fly off and the heavier ones sink down, and the discord becomes lethal, and corruption follows. As for the extrinsic cause of corruption, this seems to be manifold. So that it may be clear, let it be noted. (†)

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: DISQUISITIO PRIMA.

units.la: Quænam sint causæ corruptionis.
units.tr: What are the causes of corruption.

units.la: PRO intelligentia non parum inseruiunt Aristotelis verba 1. Meteor. tex. 44. quòd sol dum per Zodiacum obliquè mouetur, quia prope fit, aut longiùs, dum vel accedit ad Cancrum, vel ad Capricornum, causa generationis, & corruptionis est. Quippe cum huc in terras modò maiores habeat irradiationes, modò minores, ideoque calorem producat diuersum, per hunc accessum, recessumque, ait Philosophus, vicissitudinem generationis, & corruptionis facit. Sicut ergo in Chymia ratio agendi tota in eo sita videtur, vt optimum adsit regimen ignis, & applicatio caloris pro materiæ indigentia, quæ alterari, disponi, & perfici debet: Ita cum sol sit ignis cælestis, natura hoc maximè prouidit, vt per accessum, & recessum diuersimodè calefaceret, materiasque mouendo ministerium ageret generationis, & corruptionis.
units.tr: For understanding this, the words of Aristotle in the first book of the Meteorologica, text 44, are of no small help: that the sun, while it moves obliquely through the Zodiac, is a cause of generation and corruption because it is near or farther away, as it approaches either the Crab or the Goat. For since it sends now greater and now lesser rays down upon this earth, and so produces a different heat, the Philosopher says that by this approach and recession it brings about the alternation of generation and corruption. Just as in chymistry the whole method of working seems to consist in having the best possible regulation of the fire, and in applying heat according to what the matter needs, which must be altered, disposed and perfected; so, since the sun is a celestial fire, nature has especially provided that by its approach and recession it should warm things in different degrees, and by moving matter should perform the service of generation and corruption.

units.la: Calor igitur est prima corruptionis causa, nam ille dum recipitur in composito, humidique particulas afficit plusquam natura vel exigat, vel ferre possit, eas cogit recedere intimè atq; à proprio centro se remouere. Oritur inde, vt in bullas minutissimas colligantur, maioremq; locum petendo, vicinas materiæ partes moueant, pellant, extrudant,vnde tandem res composita veluti sauciata corrumpitur.
units.tr: Heat, then, is the first cause of corruption. For when it is received into a compound, it affects the moist particles more than nature either requires or can bear, and forces them to withdraw inwardly and to remove themselves from their own centre. From this it comes about that they gather into very small bubbles, and, seeking a larger space, they move, push and thrust out the neighbouring parts of the matter, so that at last the compound, as if wounded, is corrupted.

units.la: Frigus etiam corruptionis minifterium exercet. Quatenus cùm omne mixtum ad fui generationem, & conferuationem exigat calorem, fi maiori frigore, quàm par est, obsideatur, particulæ ipsius contrarium effugere volentes recedunt in fe (obstat enim circumquaq: contrarium) atq; in minutiffimos circa suum centrum globulos efformantur, vt patet in ferro dum aqua temperatur, nam tunc minutiffima granula facit. Ergo frigoris vi particulæ in mixto, & præsertim humidi fe fe conglobantes deiunguntur,ijsq; ab inuicem diunctis,perit compositum.
units.tr: Cold also exercises the office of corruption. For since every mixed body requires heat for its generation and preservation, if it is beset by more cold than is fitting, its particles, wishing to escape the contrary quality, withdraw into themselves (for the contrary surrounds them on every side) and are formed into very small globules about their own centre, as is seen in iron when it is tempered in water, for then it makes very fine granules. Therefore, by the force of cold, the particles of the mixed body, and especially those of the moist, gather themselves into balls and are separated from one another, and with them thus divided the compound perishes.

units.la: Humiditas etiam affert mixtis corruptionem. Ex eo videlicet quia humor dū in partes adlabitur, fe fe illis aliquo modò commiscet, imò sæpius egregiè conglutinat. Vndè oritur, vt cum recedit, non abeat solitariè, sed cum particulis materiæ, quibus inhæserat, quousque tandem fiat diffidentia, & dissolutio, vt pabet in aqua dum alterno motu cietur; nam corpus, cui allabitur, paulatim abradit, senfimq: interimit.
units.tr: Moisture also brings corruption to mixed bodies. Namely, because the moisture, as it glides onto the parts, mingles itself with them in some way, and indeed very often glues them together firmly. Hence it happens that when it withdraws, it does not go away alone but takes with it the particles of matter to which it had adhered, until at last there comes about a disjunction and dissolution; as is seen in water when it is stirred by an alternating motion, for it gradually wears away the body onto which it flows and at length destroys it.

units.la: Siccitas denique mixtum corrumpit, quia humidum ad rei constitutionem requisitum exfugit. Quare omnia breuiter colligendo, quatuor primæ qualitates adnatæ suis corporibus, cum quibus vltrò, citrò, & circumquaque feruntur, non solum generationi, sed etiam corruptioni adseruiunt, naturæ que totius currum trahunt. Calor corrumpit, quia humidum in bullas convertit. Frigus, quia condensat in globulos. Humiditas, quia partes, quibus vnitur, foras trahit. Siccitas, quia fugit humorem.
units.tr: Finally, dryness corrupts a mixed body, because it drives out the moisture required for the constitution of the thing. Therefore, to sum up briefly: the four primary qualities, inherent in their bodies, with which they are carried hither and thither and round about, serve not only generation but also corruption, and draw along the chariot of the whole of nature. Heat corrupts, because it turns the moisture into bubbles. Cold, because it condenses it into globules. Moisture, because it draws outward the parts to which it is joined. Dryness, because it drives away the humour.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISQUISITIO SECUNDA.

units.la: Fiatne corruptio ex mera dissolu- tione partium.
units.tr: Whether corruption arises from the mere dissolution of parts.

units.la: PRO intelligentia subeat animum quod fusè diximus lib. 1. & 2. rerum naturalium principia fuisse àDeo in exordio mundi constituta omnis corruptionis expertia, ne tandem aliquando materia deficeret generationum. Hæc autem vniuntur inter se nodo physico, & reali, nempe humido, à natura ob id facto, vt leuia grauibus, materialia spiritosis, contraria contrarijs alligata teneret. Quare nuper etiam conclusimus, non fieri generationes ob aliquam de nouo substantiâ, quæ à materiæ potentia educatur; sed eò quia substantiæ diuersæ iam præiacentes, ad locum generationis adductæ, inuicem plasmentur, & compingantur. Vnde cum lex eadem sit contrariorum, non absimili ratione fieri debet corruptio, ac generatio. Ista contingit ex mera vnione partium; illam ergo exerceri per meram dissolutionem verisimillimum est. Itaq; notetur.
units.tr: To understand this, let it be borne in mind that we have spoken at length in Books 1 and 2 of Natural Things that the first principles of nature were established by God at the beginning of the world, free from all corruption, lest at some time the matter of generations should fail. These principles are bound together by a physical and real bond, namely moisture, which nature made for this very purpose, so that light things would be held with heavy, material things with spiritual, and contraries bound to contraries. Hence we have recently also concluded that generations do not come about because some new substance is drawn out of the potency of matter, but because substances already lying ready, brought to the place of generation, are moulded and joined together with one another. Since the law of contraries is the same, corruption ought to occur in a manner not unlike generation. Generation happens from the mere union of parts; it is therefore most likely that corruption is carried out by mere dissolution. Let this be noted.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Corruptio substantialis videtur fieri ex mera dissolutione partium.
units.tr: Substantial corruption seems to come about from the mere dissolution of parts.

units.la: PRobari 1. potest ex ijs, quæ deduximus hoc lib. disp. 3. disq. 1. Nam si corruptio non fit ex destitione substantiæ, quæ penitus destruatur, superest dicendum, quòd ex mera partium dissolutione fiat. Consulite ibi dicta.
units.tr: This can be proved first from what we deduced in this book, Disputation 3, Question 1. For if corruption does not come from the destruction of a substance that is wholly annihilated, it remains to be said that it comes from the mere dissolution of parts. See what was said there.

units.la: Probatur 2. experientia chymicorum, qui postquam diuersa rerum genera ministerio caloris in alterum compositum adplasmarunt, rursus idem soluendo, priores inueniunt substantias, & quidem omnes, adeout Mercurius corrupto mixto, idem pondere, mensurâ, virtute deprehendatur, &c.
units.tr: It is proved second by the experience of the chemists. After they have, by the agency of heat, moulded diverse kinds of things into another compound, they dissolve it again and find the earlier substances, indeed all of them, so that when the mixed body is corrupted, Mercury is found with the same weight, measure and virtue, etc.

units.la: Probatur 3. auctoritate Niffen. orat. 1. exam. vbi ait, oleum corrumpi, non quia substantia destruatur vlla, sed ex eò quod in minima resoluatur. Ait enim per ignem exsiccatum in minutissimas, & aspectum nostrum effugientes particulas commutari, atque ita aerem petere, indeque deffiliens in terram decidere.
units.tr: It is proved third by the authority of Nyssen, Oration 1, Examen, where he says that oil is corrupted not because any substance is destroyed, but because it is resolved into the smallest parts. For he says that when it is dried up by fire it is changed into most minute particles that escape our sight, and so seeks the air, and, falling from there, comes down to the earth.

units.la: Probatur 4. ex Diu. Bern. serm. 81. in Cant. vbi loquens de interitu plantarum, & animalium addit, quòd cum desinunt viuificare, simul viuere cessant, sed non & esse, nam soluuntur pariter, & dissoluuntur, tanquam non alligatæ tantùm, sed colligatæ. Neque .n. vnum simplex est quaq; harum; sed ex pluribus constas, & propterea non redigitur in nihilum, sed dissilit in partes, vt ad suum quodque recurrat principium: verbi causa aer ad aerem, ignis ad ignem, & reliqua in hunc modum. Inde Lucret. congruenter in i.
units.tr: It is proved fourth from Bernard, Sermon 81 on the Song of Songs, where, speaking of the death of plants and animals, he adds that when they cease to quicken, they at the same time cease to live, but not to exist, for they are dissolved and fall apart together, being not merely loosely joined but bound together. For none of these is simple in any way, but each consists of several things, and so it is not reduced to nothing but scatters into its parts, so that each returns to its own principle: for example, air to air, fire to fire, and the rest in this way. Hence Lucretius, agreeing, in Book 1.

units.la: Haud igitur redit ad nihilum res vl- la, sed omnes Dissidio redeunt in corpora materiai.
units.tr: Therefore no thing at all returns to nothing, but all return by dissolution into the bodies of matter.

units.la: Opponitur. Si corruptio fieret ex vnica partium dissolutione, posset compositum, vbi corruptum est, rursus idem compingi. Hoc autem dici nequit: ergo. Maior suadetur, quia omnes primæ substantiæ adhuc sunt in natura; quid verò prohibet, illas denuò coniungi? Minor est certa in philosophia, quia non fit vnquam regressus à priuatione ad habitum. Resp. esse moraliter impossibile, idem compositum rursus post corruptionem redire ipsum. Ratio est, nam licet partes manent omnes, non tamen in vno loco morantur; sed quæ subtiles, migrant aliò, dissipantur à ventis, disperguntur, abiguntur; quæ crassiores, confunduntur alienis, &c. Sicuti ergo centum v. gr. tali quotlibet vicibus in abacum proijciantur, impossibile moraliter est, eundem vt reddant numerum simul; ita, &c. Sin autem loloquamur physicè non video, cur fieri nequeat idem rursus compositum, si tamen partes eodem loco asseruentur, adeout nulla, seu paucæ saltem desint. Quapropter habetis experientiam de rosa ex materijs iterum suis conflata, vt supra diximus referente Gafarello. ( ✣ ) ( † )
units.tr: An objection: if corruption came from the dissolution of a single set of parts, the compound, once corrupted, could be put together again into the same thing. But this cannot be said; therefore the first claim is false. The major is urged because all the primary substances are still in nature; and what prevents them from being joined again? The minor is certain in philosophy, because there is never a return from privation to habit. Reply: it is morally impossible for the same compound to return after corruption. The reason is that, although all the parts remain, they do not stay in one place. The subtle ones migrate elsewhere, are scattered by the winds, dispersed and driven away; the cruder ones are mixed up with foreign matter, and so on. Just as, if a hundred counters, say, were thrown onto an abacus any number of times, it would be morally impossible for them to make up the same number again, so it is here. But if we speak physically, I do not see why the same compound cannot be produced again, provided the parts are preserved in the same place, so that none, or at least few, are missing. Hence you have the experience of the rose reconstituted from its materials again, as we said above, on the authority of Gaffarel.

units.la: Finis Quarti Libri.
units.tr: End of the Fourth Book.

units.la: LIBER QVINTVS PHYSICORVM
units.tr: BOOK FIVE OF PHYSICS

units.la: De motu ad Quantitatem.
units.tr: On Motion with Respect to Quantity.

units.la: STatim ac naturale compositum genitum est, certam habet mensuram suæ quantitatis, eáq; diuersimodè variat; siue quia fit maius crescendo; siue quòd per decrementum euadit minus: Quæ actiones dicuntur esse motus ad quantitatem. Exinde videtis quàm congruenter post compositi generatione, illud sub conceptu quanti consideremus.
units.tr: As soon as a natural compound has come into being, it has a fixed measure of its quantity, and it varies this in various ways: either because it becomes greater by growing, or because by decrease it becomes less. These actions are called motion with respect to quantity. From this you can see how fittingly, after the generation of the compound, we consider it under the concept of quantity.

units.la: Duplex autem quantitatis acquirendæ modus pro duplici rerum genere assignari solet. Alter dicitur continuatio: alter intus assumptio. Primus conuenit rebus, quæ carent anima; & adhuc duplex est. Nam continuatio, vel fit per additionem partis ad partem absque vnione reali, & physica, vt cùm aquæ admiscetur aqua; & hæc appellatur iuxta positio. Vel fit cum vnione physica, vt cùm lapis crescit per nouæ substantiæ additionem, & ista vocari solet aggeneratio. Secundus rerum animatarum proprius est, quando minimum aliquod viuens per vim sibi naturæ naturaliter insitam trahit pabulum, depurat, vnit, atq; in simile substantiam (vt aiunt peripatetici) conuertit. Quae actio vocatur intus assumptio, nam per illam partes modo quodam perfectiori assumuntur intus ad augmentum.
units.tr: There are two modes of acquiring quantity, assigned according to the two kinds of things. The first is called continuation, the second intus assumptio. The first belongs to things that lack a soul, and it is again twofold. For continuation either occurs by the addition of part to part without real and physical union, as when water is mixed with water, and this is called iuxta positio. Or it occurs with physical union, as when a stone grows by the addition of new substance, and this is usually called aggeneratio. The second is proper to living things, when some living minimum draws nourishment by a power naturally implanted in its nature, purifies it, unites it, and converts it into a like substance (as the Peripatetics say). This action is called intus assumptio, for by it parts are taken in from within for growth in a more perfect manner.

units.la: Quomodolibet vero fiat motus iste ad quantitatem, siue augmentatio, semper concipiendum est, non euenire quantitatem solam quantitati; sed cum illa nouam fieri substantiae additionem. Quippe siue res augeatur per accretionem accidentalem, seu per aggenerationem, aut per intus assumptionem, semper additur noua substantia primae, vtcunque postea fiat haec additio, vel (vt aiunt Aristotelei) quia producatur de novo haec substantia, quae additur; vel (vt inquiunt melius Democritei) quia vniatur solum. Ex quo colligite, motum ad quantitate non consistere formaliter in productione substantiae (dato etiam quod producatur) sed in additione, per quam solummodo res intelligitur acquirere molem, extensionem, ordinem partium, &c. Vnde patet etiam, quinam sit, & quotuplex terminus augmentationis. Ille siquidem est duplex; alter quo, nimirum vnio; alter qui, videlicet pars vt vnita, non quatenus genita.
units.tr: However this motion to quantity, or augmentation, takes place, it must always be understood that quantity does not simply come to quantity alone, but that with it a new substance is added to the substance. For whether a thing is increased by accidental accretion, or by aggeneration, or by intus assumption, a new substance is always added to the first, however this addition is later made: either (as the Aristotelians say) because the substance that is added is produced anew, or (as the Democriteans rightly say better) because it is merely united. From this gather that motion with respect to quantity does not consist formally in the production of substance (even granting that it is produced), but in the addition, through which alone a thing is understood to acquire bulk, extension, order of parts, and so on. Whence it is also clear what the term of augmentation is, and how many kinds there are. It is twofold: one is the term "by which" (quo), namely union; the other is the term "which" (qui), namely the part as united, not as generated.

units.la: Quomodo autem exercEATur in natura haec partium additio, & quaenam sint eius causae, colligi potest ex ijs; quae lib. superiori tradidimus, & magis explicabitur, cum de Anima. Quare hic manet solùm, vt de quantitatis naturà disquiramus. Porro materia hæc tam arduas habet difficultates, vt eas humana ratio expedire non posse videatur. Nam quantitas quò magis ad sensum patet, eò citiùs effugit mentis obtutum; & quamquam sit assiduè præ manibus, nunquam tamen pro dignitate tractatur. Impenetrabilis est, idcirco vel acutissimam retundit aciem, cumque gaudeat diuisibilitate, philosophos diuidit in pugnas; & extensa ipsa nos in angustias omnino cogit.
units.tr: How this addition of parts takes place in nature, and what its causes are, can be gathered from what we have set out in the previous book, and it will be explained more fully when we treat of the soul. Hence here only this remains: that we inquire into the nature of quantity. Moreover, this subject has such difficulties that human reason does not seem able to resolve them. For the more quantity lies open to the senses, the more quickly it escapes the gaze of the mind; and although it is constantly at hand, it is never treated as its dignity deserves. It is impenetrable, and so it blunts even the keenest edge of thought; and since it enjoys divisibility, it divides philosophers into battles; and being extended, it forces us altogether into narrow straits.

units.la: Res vtcumque contingat. Quantitatem aggredimur explicandam; & sanè triplici disputatione, quarum prima erit de illius naturà, quid nimirum, & quotuplex ea sit. Dicine debeat accidens à materia distinctum, per quod ipsa extendatur. Consterne partibus ante diuisionem distinctis, &c. Secunda erit de compositione quanti, seu continui, vtrum scilicet habeat partes diuisibiles in infinitum, an punctis constet indiuisibilibus. Tertia demum de raritate, densitate, ac Figura, quæ sunt passiones quantitatis. (†)
units.tr: Whatever the case, we undertake to explain quantity, and indeed in a threefold disputation. The first will concern its nature: namely what it is and how many kinds there are; whether it should be said to be an accident distinct from matter, by which matter itself is extended; whether it consists of parts distinct before division, and so on. The second will concern the composition of quantity, or of the continuum: namely whether it has parts divisible to infinity, or consists of indivisible points. The third, finally, will concern rarity, density, and figure, which are the passions of quantity. (†)

units.la: DISPVTATIO PRIMA. De Natura Quantitatis.
units.tr: FIRST DISPUTATION. On the Nature of Quantity.

units.la: VIdeamus hic statim quid sit quantitas, & in quonam consistat formalis eiusdem conceptus. Deinde quotuplex ea sit, vt ad ea, quæ maioris momenti sunt, hisce veluti gradibus deducamur. Optima ergo quantitatis definitio hauritur ex D. Tho. 5. Metaph. lect. 15. & alibi etiam, qui ait de ratione quantitatis esse ordinem partium. Quocirca quantitas poterit sic definiri. Est multitudo, & ordo partium saltem in ordine ad se. Dicitur multitudo partium, quia primarius conceptus, quem omnes efformant de re quanta, videtur consistere in colleƈtione plurium, quæ faciat longum, latum, profundum, diuisibile, &c. Dicitur saltem in ordine ad se, quia res aliqua potest esse quanta, etiamsi non habeat partes in ordine ad locum extensas, vt sunt qualitates, præsertim infusæ, quæ multos retinent gradus in parte subiecti eadem (& proinde vocantur extensæ virtute, non mole) Ita Corpus Christi sub hostia sanè quantum est, neq; tamen dicit partes quoad locum extésas, verùm penetratas, & in eadem parte simul.
units.tr: Let us consider right away what quantity is, and in what the formal concept of it consists. Then let us consider how many kinds of it there are, so that we may be led by these steps to the matters of greater importance. The best definition of quantity is drawn from St. Thomas, Metaphysics 5, lect. 15, and elsewhere also, where he says that the nature of quantity is the order of parts. Accordingly, quantity may be defined thus: it is a multitude and order of parts, at least in relation to itself. It is called a multitude of parts because the primary concept that everyone forms of a quantified thing seems to consist in the gathering together of several parts, which makes a thing long, broad, deep, divisible, and so on. It is said "at least in relation to itself" because something can be quantified even if it does not have parts extended in relation to place, as qualities do, especially infused ones, which hold many degrees within the same part of their subject (and so are called extended in virtue, not in mass). Thus the body of Christ under the host is truly quantified, yet it does not have parts extended in relation to place, but parts penetrated and together in the same place.

units.la: Primarius ergo quantitatis conceptus nō videtur consistere, quemadmodum aliqui tenent, in ratione diuisibilitatis, nam hæc potiùs quædam proprietas est, à multitudine partium, velut à substrato dimanans. Neq; in ratione mensuræ, aut extésionis que quæ alia etiam proprietas est, secundaria, & à priori collectione partium exoriens. Erit igitur iste: series, & quidam ordo partium, habens diuisibilitatem: & si partes corporeæ sint, extensionem ad locum, non semper actualem, sed saltem radicalem, aut potentiam, ut queat extendi localiter. Qui conceptus omnem quantitatem in communi acceptam decet.
units.tr: The primary concept of quantity therefore does not seem to consist, as some hold, in the notion of divisibility, for this is rather a certain property flowing from the multitude of parts as from a substrate. Nor does it consist in the notion of measure or extension, which is likewise another property, a secondary one, arising from the prior collection of parts. It will therefore be this: a series and a certain order of parts, having divisibility; and, if the parts are corporeal, extension in place, not always actual but at least radical, or potential, so that it can be extended locally. This concept fits all quantity taken in general.

units.la: Quod attinet ad secundum, quantitas diuiditur 1. in continuâ, & discretam: 2. in continuam permanentem, & successiuam. Continua est quæ partes habet continuatas, adeout prima vniatur secundæ: secunda tertiæ, &c. ut v. gr. quantitas ligni vlnaris: Discreta illa dicitur, quæ partibus constat inuicem deiunctis, & separatis, vt numerus hominum binarius. Continua verò permanens non dicit partes vnitas quomodocumque, sed præteréa manentes etiam simul. E contra successiua partes habet, quæ nunquam sunt simul, sed sibi succedunt, quemadmodum quantitas diei, orationis, &c.
units.tr: As to the second point, quantity is divided (1) into continuous and discrete, and (2) into permanent and successive continuous quantity. Continuous quantity is that which has parts joined together, so that the first is united to the second, the second to the third, and so on, as for instance the quantity of an ell-long piece of wood. Discrete quantity is that which consists of parts disjoined and separated from one another, as the number two of men. Permanent continuous quantity, however, does not merely say that the parts are united in some way, but also that they remain, even simultaneously. Successive quantity, on the contrary, has parts that are never simultaneous but succeed one another, as the quantity of a day, of a speech, and so on.

units.la: Hisce positis, oritur prima difficultas, & ea quidem ardua, vtrum scilicet quantitas, quæ de suo conceptu dicit partes in ordine saltem ad se, reuera fit aliqua entitas, & vt inquiunt, accidens à materia, rebusque corporeis distinctum, an non.v.gr. si detur lignum vlnare, quæritur, per quid habeatur hæc extensio, & mensura vlnaris, aut in quo consistat. Nimirum, esse vlnare, atque; sic extensum, dicit ne solas materiæ, seu ligni partes inuicem vnitas, & extrapositas: an præter illas, adest ibi accidens quodam superadditum, ratione cuius lignum ita extensum, & quantum fit? ideoque tale accidens appelletur quantitas?
units.tr: With these things laid down, there arises the first difficulty, and a hard one indeed: namely, whether quantity, which by its concept says parts at least in relation to themselves, is really some entity and, as they say, an accident distinct from matter and from corporeal things, or not. For example, if there is an ell-long piece of wood, the question is by what this extension and ell-measure is had, or in what it consists. Does being an ell long, and so extended, signify only the parts of the matter, or of the wood, united and placed outside one another; or, besides those, is there some accident superadded there, by reason of which the wood is so extended and quantified? And should such an accident therefore be called quantity?

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: DISPUTATION I.

units.la: Sitne quantitas accidens à materia distinctum: & an materia partes habeat à quan- titate.
units.tr: Whether quantity is an accident distinct from matter, and whether matter has its parts from quantity.

units.la: PRO intelligentia notate, quæstionem procedere circa quantitatem permanentem continuam. De successiua enim concedunt passim non distingui à partibus cum tali ordine sibi succedentibus, v.gr. quantitas horæ nil præterea dicit, nisi tot instantia temporis cum tali ordine fluentia. Quoad primam ergo docent Nominales, quantitatem non distingui à materia, & rebus corporeis, nec esse accidens additum illis, beneficio cuius materia euadat extensa, mensurabilis, quanta. Sic Aureolus, Okamus, & alij, quibus adhæret Arriaga, putans quantitatem non distingui à materia, & res alias ideo quantas euadere, quia recipiuntur in ipsa. In quo discrepat à Nominalibus, nam hi rem quamlibet ma-terialem constituunt quantam. Opposita sententia est omnium ferè scholasticorum. Habet verò pro fundamento Sacramentum Eucharistiæ, in quo destru-sta {ta} substantia panis, & vini, adhuc tota manet quantitas; ergo hæc accidens est à materia distinctum. Pro solutione poñatur.
units.tr: To understand this, note that the question concerns permanent continuous quantity. For they commonly concede that successive quantity is not distinguished from its parts, which succeed one another in such an order; for example, the quantity of an hour signifies nothing more than so many instants of time flowing in such an order. As to the first kind, therefore, the Nominalists teach that quantity is not distinct from matter and corporeal things, nor is it an accident added to them, by whose addition matter becomes extended, measurable, and quantified. So Aureolus, Ockham, and others, to whom Arriaga adheres, think that quantity is not distinct from matter, and that other things become quantified because they are received into it. In this he differs from the Nominalists, for they hold that any material thing is quantified in itself. The opposite opinion is held by almost all the scholastics. They take as their foundation the sacrament of the Eucharist, in which, the substance of bread and wine having been destroyed, the whole quantity still remains; therefore quantity is an accident distinct from matter. The answer is to be given below.

units.la: CONCLVSIO PRIMA.
units.tr: CONCLUSION ONE.

units.la: Quantitas materiæ non est accidens ab ea realiter distinctum; sed ipsa materia sua quantitas est.
units.tr: The quantity of matter is not an accident really distinct from the matter; rather, the matter itself is its quantity.

units.la: PRobatur 1. quia materia (& sic de omni re materiali) non alio modo quantitatem acquirit, nisi per additionem partis materiæ ad partem: sed hæc additio partis materiæ ad partem non ponit accidens realiter ab ipsa distinctum; ergo quantitas non est accidens realiter à materia distinctum. Maior conceditur ab omnibus, quia intelligi non potest, quomodo res aliqua materialis euadat in maiorem substantiam, acquirat molem, pondus, & corpulentiam, nisi ex additione materiæ ad materiam, substantiæ ad substantiam, partis ad partem, &c. Minor probatur, quia hæc additio partis materiæ ad partem si ponit accidens realiter à materia distinctum, vel hoc producitur de nouo, aut priùs erat productum: neutrum dici potest; ergo. Probo minorem quoad primum, quia tale accidens foret quantitas: hæc non producitur de nouo utpote ingenerabilis, ergo. Probo etiam 2 quia si pars materiæ a, iungatur parti mate-
units.tr: It is proved first: because matter (and so every material thing) acquires quantity in no other way than by the addition of part of matter to part. But this addition of part of matter to part does not posit an accident really distinct from the matter itself. Therefore quantity is not an accident really distinct from matter. The major premise is granted by all, since it cannot be understood how any material thing could become a greater substance, acquire bulk, weight and bodily size, except by the addition of matter to matter, of substance to substance, of part to part, and so on. The minor is proved thus: if this addition of part of matter to part posits an accident really distinct from the matter, then this accident is either produced anew, or was already produced before. Neither can be said; therefore the minor holds. I prove the minor as to the first alternative: such an accident would be quantity; but quantity is not produced anew, since it is ungenerable; therefore. I also prove it as to the second: if part of matter a is joined to part of matter b, nothing else seems to be produced, distinct from both, except a union; therefore not quantity. I prove the minor as to the second alternative: if quantity is not produced, then it pre-existed; therefore before a stone, for example, became a palm long, the quantity of a palm was already present. This is absurd, for otherwise the accident would exist before its subject. Therefore a quantity distinct from matter is neither produced anew nor pre-existed; therefore it is fictitious.

units.la: materiæ b. non videtur aliud produci ab vtraque distinctum, nisi vnio, ergo non quantitas. Probo minorem quoad secundum, quia si quantitas non producitur, ergo præerat; ergo antequam lapis v. gr. fieret palmaris, aderat quantitas palmi, quod repugnat, alioquin accidens foret ante subiectum. Quantitas ergo à materia distincta, nec producitur de nouo, nec priùs erat; ergo fictitia est.
units.tr: of matter b. Nothing else seems to be produced distinct from both, except a union; therefore not quantity. I prove the minor as to the second alternative: if quantity is not produced, then it pre-existed; therefore before a stone, for example, became a palm long, the quantity of a palm was already present. This is absurd, for otherwise the accident would exist before its subject. Therefore a quantity distinct from matter is neither produced anew nor pre-existed; therefore it is fictitious.

units.la: Probatur 2. Si quantitas à re materiali distincta realiter est, separetur. Hoc dato, quæro: vel tunc res ea materialis adhuc in se maneret quanta, vel non: si primum, ergo male asseritur quantitas distincta, vtpote superflua: si secundum, ergo res ea materialis, amissa quantitate, reducitur ad esse non quantum, non divisibile, non extensum. Quo posito, sic validissimè vrgeo. Ergo quantitas lata, longa, profunda recipiebatur in materia indiuisibili, & inextensa, quod repugnat, alioquin extensio centipalmaris recipi etiam posset in puncto. Itaq; dicendum est, materiam de se quantam esse, vt fieri possit subiectum huiusce tuæ quantitatis. Hoc verò si admittas, hæc tua distincta quantitas erit omnino superflua, vtpotequæ rem adinuenit iam quantam.
units.tr: It is proved second: if a quantity really distinct from a material thing exists, let it be separated. Granting this, I ask: either that material thing would then remain extended, or it would not. If the first, then it is wrongly asserted that there is a distinct quantity, since it would be superfluous. If the second, then that material thing, having lost its quantity, is reduced to a non-quantified, non-divisible, non-extended state of being. Given this, I argue most forcefully as follows: a quantity broad, long and deep would then be received in an indivisible and unextended matter, which is contradictory; otherwise an extension of a hundred palms could also be received in a point. Hence it must be said that matter is quantified of itself, so that it can become the subject of this quantity of yours. But if you grant this, your distinct quantity will be wholly superfluous, since it would find the thing already quantified.

units.la: Probatur 3. quia materia, seu res quæcumque materialis, præcisa quauis alia quantitate distincta, de se habet omnia, quæ faciunt extensum, diuisibile, quantum; ergo materia est suamet quantitas.
units.tr: It is proved third: because matter, or any material thing whatever, taken apart from any other distinct quantity, has of itself all the things that make it extended, divisible and quantified. Therefore matter is its own quantity.

units.la: Probo antecedens. Materia si tollatur siue realiter, siue per intellectum quantitas manebit adhuc materia, ergo corpus, ergo impenetrabilis cum alia, ergo faciens cum illa extensum, diuisibile, quantum; ergo materia est sua met quantitas. Confirmatur. Nam praecisa quantitate centipalmari à ligno, aut lignum quoad entitatem praecisè suam habueret partes extrapositas, aut penetratas. Primum si dicatur, ergo est quantum de se. Si secundum, adhuc manet quantum, & probo.' Partes penetratae non tollunt quantitatem, adhuc enim sunt partes in ordine ad se, sunt diuisibiles, & separabiles. Patet hoc in hostia, vbi corpus Christi quantum est, licet partes habeat penetratas. Redditur autem ratio, nam quantitas de suo conceptu dicit partes tantum in ordine ad se cum exigentia radicali eas ordinandi ad locum. Si dicas, lignum praecisa quantitate redigendum ad indiuisibile, aut hoc indiuisibile vnicum erit, aut multiplex. Non primum, alioquin centum palmi quantitatis recipiebantur in puncto. Si secundum: vniantur haec indiuisibilia per aliquam potentiam; quaero, faciunt extensum, nec ne? si affirmes, ergo de se quanta sunt; si neges, adhuc sunt quanta, nam sic vnita retinent diuisibilitatem, & exigentiam, vt ad locum extraponantur, quemadmodum in corpore Christi dictum est.
units.tr: I prove the antecedent. If matter is removed, whether really or by the intellect, quantity will still remain matter; therefore body; therefore impenetrable with another; therefore, making with it something extended, divisible and quantified. Therefore matter is its own quantity. This is confirmed: for if the quantity of a hundred palms is taken away from a piece of wood, then either the wood, in respect of its own bare entity, has parts placed outside one another, or parts interpenetrated. If the first is said, then it is quantified of itself. If the second, it still remains quantified, and I prove it. Interpenetrated parts do not remove quantity, for they are still parts in relation to one another; they are divisible and separable. This is plain in the Host, where the body of Christ is quantified although it has its parts interpenetrated. The reason is given: quantity, by its very concept, signifies parts only in relation to one another, with a radical exigency to arrange them in place. If you say that the wood, with its quantity taken away, must be reduced to indivisibles, then either this indivisible will be one, or many. Not the first, for otherwise a hundred palms of quantity would be received in a point. If the second: let these indivisibles be united by some power. I ask: do they make something extended or not? If you affirm, then they are quantified of themselves; if you deny, they are still quantified, for thus united they retain divisibility and the exigency to be placed outside one another in place, as was said of the body of Christ.

units.la: CONCLVSIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: CONCLUSION TWO.

units.la: Materia non habet extensionem, seu partes à quantitate distincta, sed à se tantùm.
units.tr: Matter does not have extension, or parts distinct from quantity, but has them only from itself.

units.la: PRobatur 1. quia in re quanta (facta hypothesi de quantitate distincta) non sola quantitas habet partes, verùm & substantia suas, nam sicuti materia est quid totum substantiale, sic etiam partes habet substantiales : At hæ partes nequeunt oriri à quantitate, quæ accidens est : ergo substantia materialis independenter à quantitate habet partes. Confirmatur quia materia non est tota sub qualibet parte quantitatis, nec enim ita se habet quemadmodum anima rationalis; ergo ita est sub quantitate, ut pars materiæ sit sub parte quantitatis; alia pars quoque sub alia quantitatis, &c. ergo præter partes quantitatis (dato etiam, quòd hæc sit distincta) dantur partes materiæ. Confirmatur 2. nam quantitas cùm sit accidens materiale, debet educi de potentia subiecti, seu materiæ : vel ergo partes omnes quantitatis educuntur ab vna, eademque indiuisibili entitate materiæ : vel vna pars quantitatis educitur ab vna materiæ; alia verò ab alia, &c. Si secundum, ergo materia antecedenter ad quantitatem habet alias, & alias partes, ac propterea extensionem entitatiuam. Si primum, ergo plures partes quantitatis in eadem indiuisibili parte materiæ sunt: ergo extensum in inextenso; quod repugnat.
units.tr: This is proved first. In a material thing, on the hypothesis that quantity is distinct from it, it is not only quantity that has parts but also substance. For just as matter is a substantial whole, so it has substantial parts. But these parts cannot arise from quantity, which is an accident. Therefore material substance has parts independently of quantity. It is confirmed that matter is not wholly under each part of quantity, for it does not stand in the same relation as the rational soul. So matter is under quantity in such a way that one part of matter is under one part of quantity, another part under another part of quantity, and so on. Therefore, apart from the parts of quantity (even granting that quantity is distinct), there are parts of matter. It is confirmed secondly: since quantity is a material accident, it must be educed from the potency of its subject, that is, of matter. Either all the parts of quantity are educed from one and the same indivisible entity of matter, or one part of quantity is educed from one part of matter and another from another part, and so on. If the second, then matter, prior to quantity, has different parts and so has entitative extension. If the first, then several parts of quantity are in one and the same indivisible part of matter, and so there is the extended in the unextended, which is contradictory.

units.la: Probatur 2. quia si diuidatur lignum centipalmare, non diuiditur sola quantitas, verùm & materia, nam in quolibet semipalmo certè substantia sua materialis est: ergo vel materia vna, & eadem replicari debet sub omni quantitatis parte, quod absurdum est: vel tot erunt partes materiæ, quot etiam quantitatis. Confirmatur, nam si Deus tollat quantitatem à substantia, videt sanè in quanam parte substantiæ fuerit ea pars quantitatis, & eandem poterit rursus collocare in priori subiecto. Similiter poterit Deus auferre quantitatem capitis, relicta quantitate pedum, in quo casu substantia capitis non erit illa, quæ pedum, ergo distincta: ergo substantia præter quantitatem suas habet partes. Confirmatur vltimò. Sit materia trium cubitorum: tollat Deus quantitatem à primo, ac tertio cubito, relicta ea, quæ secundi est: in tali casu materia primi, tertiique cubiti sanè distinguueretur à materia secundi; ergo partes materiæ sunt diuersæ, ac distinctæ à partibus quantitatis.
units.tr: It is proved secondly: if a hundred-palm piece of wood is divided, it is not only quantity that is divided but also matter, for in each half-palm there is certainly its own material substance. Therefore either one and the same matter must be repeated under every part of quantity, which is absurd, or there will be as many parts of matter as there are of quantity. It is confirmed: if God removes quantity from a substance, He surely sees in what part of the substance that part of quantity was, and He can place it again in the earlier subject. Likewise God could take away the quantity of the head while leaving the quantity of the feet; in that case the substance of the head would not be the substance of the feet, and so it is distinct. Therefore substance has its own parts besides quantity. It is confirmed finally: let there be matter three cubits long. Let God take quantity away from the first and third cubits, leaving that of the second. In such a case the matter of the first and third cubits would certainly be distinguished from the matter of the second. Therefore the parts of matter are different from, and distinct from, the parts of quantity.

units.la: Probatur 3. Nam v. gr. in hoc toto Adriatico mari vel sub omni parte quantitatis manet etiam pars aquæ: vel non. Si secundum, ergo quantitas hæret sine subiecto, unde non erit accidens à re distinctum. Si primum, tollat Deus hanc totam Adriatici maris quantitatem, quæro: tota prior aqua maneret ne adhuc, an non? secundum dici nequit, nam sublato accidente realiter distincto, non ideo perit substantia. Si primum, ergo aqua occuparet idem spatium, ac prius: ergo habet partes à quantitate distinctas. Quid respondes? fortasse aquam non habituram partes, quia sublata quantitate redigetur ad vnum indiuisibile? aude maiora, & maris fundum pede tunc sicco percalca. Dices ne melius cum Spinula, quòd ablata quantitate, manerent innumera indiuisibilia materiae, quae vt pote sperata, inuicemque deiuncta, non haberent continuationem, & ideo nec partes? Hoc sane probabilissimum est,non tamen probat materiam non habere nunc, & de facto partes à quantitate distinctas. Quia nunc de facto puncta illa sub quantitate vnita sunt, ac toti quantitati coextensa; ergo praeter quantitatem faciunt partes. Confirmatur quia illa puncta sine quantitate possent à Deo saltem vniri eodem prorsus modo,quo vniebantur sub quantitate: sed sic vnita facerent extensum, vt alibi dicemus, ergo etiam sub quantitate faciunt se solis extensum. Ergo materia non habet extensionem, & partes à quantitate.
units.tr: It is proved thirdly. For example, in the whole Adriatic Sea, either a part of the water remains under every part of quantity, or not. If the second, then quantity hangs without a subject, and so it will not be an accident really distinct from the thing. If the first, let God take away the whole quantity of the Adriatic Sea. I ask: would all the former water remain or not? The second cannot be said, for when a really distinct accident is removed, the substance does not for that reason perish. If the first, then the water would occupy the same space as before, and so it has parts distinct from quantity. What do you reply? Perhaps you will say that the water will not have parts, because once quantity is removed it is reduced to one indivisible? Dare something greater, and then tread the sea floor with a dry foot. Will you say, with Spinula, that once quantity is removed, innumerable indivisibles of matter would remain, which, being scattered and disjoined from one another, would have no continuity, and so no parts? This is certainly very probable, yet it does not prove that matter does not now, in fact, have parts distinct from quantity. For now in fact those points are united under quantity and coextended with the whole quantity. Therefore, apart from quantity, they make parts. It is confirmed: those points could be united by God, at least, without quantity in exactly the same way in which they were united under quantity. But so united they would make an extended thing, as we shall say elsewhere. Therefore even under quantity they make an extended thing by themselves. Therefore matter does not have extension and parts from quantity.

units.la: Ex his validissimè confirmatur prima nostra conclusio. Nam si materia de se habet partes independenter à quantitate distincta, ergo de se quanta est; ac proinde quantitas haec distincta per quam dicis rem fieri extensam, latam, longam, profundam, quantam, figmentum erit: Nihilominus.
units.tr: From these points our first conclusion is most strongly confirmed. For if matter has of itself parts independent of quantity, which is distinct, then it is quantified of itself; and therefore this distinct quantity, through which you say a thing becomes extended, broad, long, deep, and quantified, will be a fiction. Nevertheless...

units.la: Obijcies 1. contra primam conclusionem. Quantitas non est de conceptu materiæ, aut substantiæ: sed quod non est de conceptu alterius, realiter ab eo distinguitur; ergo quantitas est accidens à materia distinctum. Maior probatur, quia potest concipi materia sine hac, aut illa quantitate; imò sine omni, si apprehendatur vnicum indiuisibile ipsius. Minor patet inductione. Sic albedo realiter distinguitur à pariete, quia non ingreditur conceptum illius: calor distinguitur ab igne, quia hic satis concipitur, calore non concepto, &c.
units.tr: You will object first against the first conclusion: quantity is not part of the concept of matter or substance, but what is not part of the concept of another is really distinct from it. Therefore quantity is an accident distinct from matter. The major is proved because matter can be conceived without this or that quantity, indeed without any quantity, if its one indivisible is apprehended. The minor is plain by induction. Thus whiteness is really distinct from a wall, because it does not enter into the concept of the wall; heat is distinct from fire, because fire can be sufficiently conceived without heat being conceived, and so on.

units.la: Respondent aliqui negando maiorem. Ratio est, nam substantia materialis nec esse potest, neque concipi sine aliqua extensione, vt habeatur adequata distinctio à re spirituali, quæ intelligitur, manetque inextensa. Verùm concedi potest maior in nostra sententia, quam sequenti disputatione afferemus, quia materia, vt materia, in vnico indiuisibili potest esse, atque concipi; quo dato, sanè intelligitur eius tota essentia sine vlla extensione. Ad minorem nego, illud realiter ab alio distingui, quod non est præcisè de conceptu illius. Ratio est, quia hoc axioma non semper verificatur de distinctione reali; sed vt plurimum de mentali, & metaphysica per intellectum. Sic per Thomistas aliud est in homine ratio substantiæ, aliud ratio animalis, & tamen hæc duo, quæ distinguuntur in concep-tu, realiter in homine distincta nonsunt. Sic per Scotistas Misericordia in Deo non inuoluitur in conceptu iustitiæ, nec tamen hæc duo à parte rei distinguuntur. Sic per omnes ratio entis non est de conceptu v.gr. rationalis: nec proinde tamen in subiecto ens, & rationale distinctionem habent realem. A simili ergo etiamsi quantitas, & extensio non sint de conceptu substantiæ, non sequitur, eas distingui realiter, sed solùm ratione, metaphysicè, ac per conceptum. Ratio est, quia mens nostra per vim præcisiuam distinguit sæpe gradus metaphysicos, qui à parte rei distincti non sunt; & ita quantitatem abstrahit à substantia, substantiam à quantitate &c. Illud ergo axioma: Quod non est de conceptu alterius, distinguitur ab illo, probat sanè distinctionem rationis. Hoc verò aliud: Quod potest separari ab alio, distinguitur ab illo, infert distinctionem realem. Ratio est, nam separatio fit in re, ac realiter: ergo inter ea, quæ separantur, adest distinctio realis. Conceptus verò est in mente, vnde solam ponit distinctionem rationis. Ad confirmationem dico, albedinem non distingui realiter à subiecto per hoc præcisè, quia non est de concep-tu subiecti; sed quia cum sit aliud ab ipso, seiungi ab eodem potest. Vrges: concipio totam essentiam substantiæ v. gr. in vnico indiuisibili materiæ, nonconcepta quantitate: igitur hæc distinguitur à substantia. Sed resp.cum distinctione: distinguitur vt accidens, nego; vt alia substantia integratiua rei quantæ, ac extensæ, concedo: & explico. Dum concipitur vnum indiuisibile materiæ, nō concipitur sanè quantitas; vnde ista debet concedi esse aliud quid, non à substantia, sed ab eo indiuisibili substantiæ distinctum. Quid verò est hoc distinctū? non accidens, verùm alia, & alia substantia similis, atque à priori distincta,quæ si cum ea simul concipiatur, iam concipitur facere quid extensum, & quantum.
units.tr: Some reply by denying the major. The reason is that material substance can neither be nor be conceived without some extension, so that there may be an adequate distinction from a spiritual thing, which is understood and remains unextended. Yet the major can be granted in our opinion, which we will set out in the following disputation, because matter, as matter, can exist and be conceived in a single indivisible; given that, its whole essence is certainly understood without any extension. To the minor I deny that something is really distinct from another if it is not precisely part of its concept. The reason is that this axiom does not always hold for real distinction, but for the most part for mental and metaphysical distinction, made by the intellect. Thus among the Thomists, in a man the notion of substance is one thing and the notion of animal is another, and yet these two, which are distinguished in concept, are not really distinct in man. Thus among the Scotists, mercy in God is not contained in the concept of justice, and yet these two are not distinguished on the part of the thing. Thus for all, the notion of being is not part of the concept of, for example, rational, and yet in the subject being and rational do not have a real distinction. By parity, then, even if quantity and extension are not part of the concept of substance, it does not follow that they are really distinct, but only by reason, metaphysically, and through concept. The reason is that our mind, by its precisive power, often distinguishes metaphysical grades which are not distinct on the part of the thing; and so it abstracts quantity from substance, substance from quantity, and so on. Therefore that axiom: What is not part of the concept of another is distinguished from it, certainly proves a distinction of reason. But this other: What can be separated from another is distinguished from it, infers a real distinction. The reason is that separation takes place in the thing and really; therefore between those things which are separated there is a real distinction. But a concept is in the mind, whence it posits only a distinction of reason. To the confirmation I say that whiteness is not distinguished really from the subject merely because it is not part of the concept of the subject, but because, since it is other than the subject, it can be separated from it. You urge: I conceive the whole essence of a substance, for example in a single indivisible of matter, without conceiving quantity; therefore quantity is distinct from the substance. But I reply with a distinction: it is distinct as an accident, I deny; it is distinct as another integrative substance of a quantified and extended thing, I grant. And I explain. While one indivisible of matter is conceived, quantity is certainly not conceived; whence this must be conceded to be something other, not from the substance but distinct from that indivisible of the substance. What then is this distinct thing? Not an accident, but another and another similar substance, and distinct from the first; which, if it is conceived together with it, is then conceived to make something extended and quantified.

units.la: Obijcies 2. quantitas potest realiter separari à materia: ergo realiter distinguitur ab illa. Probatur antecedens in Sacramento Altaris, nam destructa materia panis, & vini, adhuc manet prior tota quantitas, quæ fuit panis, & vini. Sic in hostia perseuerat extensio, latitudo, profunditas, & longitudo; figura sphærica, circularis, &c. sed ibi substantia panis haud amplius est; ergo quantitas manet sine substantia. Separatur ergo,& sic distinguitur. Hoc vnicum est argumentum, quod scholasticos penè omnes inopposita sententia tenet. Nos conabimur solutionem, & imprimis.
units.tr: You will object (2): quantity can be really separated from matter, therefore it is really distinct from it. The antecedent is proved from the Sacrament of the Altar. When the matter of bread and wine is destroyed, the whole former quantity that belonged to the bread and wine still remains. So in the host there persist extension, breadth, depth and length, and a spherical or circular figure, and so on. But the substance of bread is no longer there. Therefore quantity remains without substance. It is therefore separated, and so distinguished. This is the one argument that almost all the Scholastics hold against the opposing view. We shall try a solution, and first...

units.la: Respondent aliqui ad argumentum,in sacramento Altaris continuum adesse miraculum, & res ibi esse obscurissimas, unde non licere ab ignotiori arguere ad ignotum. Alij dicunt non satis constare, sint ne accidentia realia, quæ apparent in hohostia; præsertim quia Tridentinum ea vocat species; quare aiunt ibi non esse albedinem actu realem, sed speciem albedinis; non reale frigus, calorem, quantitatem, sed speciem frigoris, caloris, quantitatis, &c. Propterea non posse argui quantitatem esse accidens reale à materiali substantia realiter distinctum; sed hæc omnia per Dei potentiam tale mysterium occultantis apparere. Verum talis opinio videtur nimium audere, cum SS. PP. atque omnes Theologi consentiant, in hostia manere accidentia realia, non species tantum intentionales, quæ nec viderentur, nec tangerentur (species, n. intentionalis est id, quo fit visio, tactus, &c. non quod videtur, ac tangitur) Legatur Comptonus in phys.disp. 12.sect.2. 3. & seq. Itaque concessio quod in hostia sint accidentia physica, & realia, quæ ad nostros occurrunt sensus, vt eruitur etiam ex Concil. Constantiensi anno 1414. celebrato.
units.tr: Some reply to the argument that in the Sacrament of the Altar there is a continuing miracle, and that the matters there are most obscure, so that it is not permitted to argue from the less known to the unknown. Others say it is not sufficiently established whether the accidents that appear in the host are real, especially since the Council of Trent calls them species. Hence they say that there is not actually a real whiteness there, but a species of whiteness; not a real cold, heat or quantity, but a species of cold, heat, quantity and so on. Therefore it cannot be argued that quantity is a real accident, really distinct from material substance, since all these things appear through the power of God, who hides such a mystery. But this opinion seems to dare too much, since the Holy Fathers and all theologians agree that real accidents remain in the host, not merely intentional species, which would be neither seen nor touched. (For an intentional species is that by which sight, touch and so on take place, not what is seen and touched.) Let Compton be read, Physics, disp. 12, sect. 2, 3 and following. Thus the concession that the host contains physical and real accidents, which come to our senses, is also drawn from the Council of Constance, held in 1414.

units.la: RespondeGri 2. potest cum distinctione. Manet in hostia prior tota quantitas vini, & panis, nego; alia quantitas accidentium propria, concedo; ergo quantitas realiter distinguitur à substantia, distinguo; quantitas propria substantiæ, n. quantitas accidentium, c. Explico. Id quod in hostia per Dei miraculum fuit destructum, erat certè substantia extensa, & ex parte multiplici conflata. Ratio est, quia non vnicum indiuisibile substantiæ intelligitur esse ablatum, ergo multa indi-
units.tr: I reply to the second with a distinction. That the whole former quantity of the wine and bread remains in the host: I deny. That another quantity of the accidents proper to it remains: I concede. Therefore quantity is really distinct from substance: I distinguish. Quantity proper to substance, that is, quantity of the accidents: I deny; quantity of the accidents: I concede. I explain. That which was destroyed in the host by God's miracle was certainly an extended substance, composed of many parts. The reason is that it is not one indivisible part of the substance that is understood to have been taken away, but many indivisibles...

units.la: indiuisibilia, & quidem prout erant physicè vnita, & simul connexa; in quo statu efficiebant longum, latum,profundum. Quare tali substantia destructa, sua etiam quantitas vtpote identificata destructa fuit. Ea igitur, quæ manet, alia quantitas est, nempè accidentium propria, & ipsismet accidentibus identificata; vnde sicuti accidentia realiter à materia distinguuntur, sic etiam quantitas accidentium ab ipsa. Duæ igitur sunt quantitates: altera materiæ: altera verò accidentium. In hostia destruitur prima, quæ materiæ identificata est; manet autem secunda, quæ accidentibus identificata est.
units.tr: ...indivisibles, and indeed as they were physically united and simultaneously connected. In that state they made up length, breadth and depth. Therefore, when such a substance was destroyed, its quantity too was destroyed, since it was identified with it. That which remains, then, is another quantity, namely the quantity proper to the accidents and identified with the accidents themselves. Hence, just as the accidents are really distinguished from matter, so too the quantity of the accidents is distinguished from it. There are therefore two quantities: one of matter, the other of the accidents. In the host the first, which is identified with matter, is destroyed; the second, which is identified with the accidents, remains.

units.la: Vrgetur. In hostia priusquam consecraretur, non erant duæ quantitates; altera substantiæ, altera verò accidentium. Ergo quæ manet post consecrationem, non est propria quantitas accidentium; sed substantiæ: at ista separatur, ergo quantitas materiæ à materia distincta est. Antecedens probatur, nam si duplex in hostia extitisset quantitas, ille fuissent inuicem penetratæ: sed hoc repugnat,ergo. Maior de se patet. Minor etiam constat, quantitas enim est partium extrapositio, & extensio: extraposita verò, & extensa excludunt se mutuò, vt patet in duplici saxo, in duplici ligno,&c.Confirmatur, quia hostia consecrata non penetratur cum alia hostia, ergo multò minùs penetrari poterat cum priore quantitate panis. Idcirco non aderat in pane alia quantitas, præter hanc, quæ manet post consecrationem: sed ista separatur à materia: ergo quantitas materiæ à materia distincta est.
units.tr: It is urged: in the host, before it was consecrated, there were not two quantities, one of the substance and the other of the accidents. Therefore what remains after consecration is not the proper quantity of the accidents but of the substance; but this is separated, therefore the quantity of matter is distinct from matter. The antecedent is proved: if there had been a double quantity in the host, they would have penetrated each other; but this is repugnant; therefore it is so. The major is self-evident. The minor is also clear, for quantity is the outside-placing and extension of parts; but things placed outside one another and extended exclude each other, as is evident in two stones or two pieces of wood. It is confirmed: a consecrated host is not penetrated by another host, therefore much less could it be penetrated by the former quantity of the bread. Hence there was no other quantity in the bread besides this one, which remains after consecration; but this is separated from matter; therefore the quantity of matter is distinct from matter.

units.la: Respond. negando antecedens. Et ratio manifestissima est, quia in hostia priusquam consecraretur, aderant actu hæc eadem accidentia, quæ manent post consecrationem, hæc nimirum albedo, hæc siccitas, hæc humiditas, hæc figura, longa, lata, profunda, &c. & id neque ab adversarijs negatur: sed hæc omnia sunt ipsamet quantitas accidentium, nec aliud præterea, igitur in hostia præter materiæ quantitatem, alia etiam inerat quantitas; inerant enim accidentia, quæ à sua quantitate distincta non sunt. Ad probationem dico, quantitatem utramque fuisse invicem penetratas in hostia, priusquam consecraretur. Neq; id videri potest absurdum. Quæro enim: nonne tunc penetrabantur cum substantia panis hæc albedo? hæc siccitas? hic sapor? hic odor? hæc figura tota? ergo cùm hæc omnia sint ipsa quantitas accidentium, quantitas penetrabatur cum quantitate. Probo consequentiam, quia certè accidentia hæc non erant penetrata cum substantia inextensa, indiuisibili, & non continua, secus enim extensum fuisset eductum, atq; receptum in re inextensa; diuisibile in indiuisibili, continuum in non continuo; ergo subiectum, seu materia huiusmodi accidentium erat quanta, ergo ista penetrabantur cum quantitate. Non potest autem penetrari lignum a. cum ligno b. quia substantia quanta excludit mutuò substantiam quantam; non verò accidentia quanta excluduntur à substantia quânta. Ratio autem præter dicta est; nâ rogo, quid sunt accidentia quanta, nisi accidentia vnita, & quodam ordine inter se vbicata? si ergo concedis illa priùs absolutè fuisse in substantia, cur non concedes fuisse ibi sic vnita, sic vbicata, sic extensa, & propterea sic quanta? Ergo quantitas accidentium penetrabatur cum substantia quanta.
units.tr: I reply by denying the antecedent. The reason is most manifest: in the host, before it was consecrated, these same accidents were actually present which remain after consecration, namely this whiteness, this dryness, this moistness, this figure, long, broad, deep, and so on. This is not denied even by our opponents. But all these are the quantity of the accidents themselves, and nothing else. Therefore in the host, besides the quantity of matter, another quantity was also present, for the accidents were there, and they are not distinct from their quantity. To the proof I say that both quantities were mutually penetrated in the host before it was consecrated, and this need not seem absurd. For I ask: was this whiteness, this dryness, this taste, this odour, this whole figure, not then penetrated with the substance of bread? Therefore, since all these are the quantity of the accidents, quantity was penetrated with quantity. I prove the consequence: these accidents were certainly not penetrated with an unextended, indivisible and non-continuous substance; otherwise the extended would have been drawn out and received in the unextended, the divisible in the indivisible, the continuous in the non-continuous. Therefore the subject or matter of such accidents was quantified, and so these were penetrated with quantity. But wood a cannot be penetrated with wood b, because quantified substance mutually excludes quantified substance; quantified accidents, however, are not excluded by quantified substance. The reason, besides what has been said, is this: I ask, what are quantified accidents, except accidents united and situated in a certain order among themselves? If therefore you concede that they were previously in the substance absolutely, why do you not concede that they were there so united, so situated, so extended, and therefore so quantified? Therefore the quantity of the accidents was penetrated with the quantified substance.

units.la: Ad confirmationem vltimò adductam respond. non fieri penetrationem hostiæ cum hostia, quia Deus impedit. Neque hoc videatur dici ad subterfugium difficultatis. Adduci enim potest ratio probabilis quare Deus penetrationem impediat; quia videlicet accidentia relicta_o sunt in hostia loco materiæ duplici ex causa. Primò vt occultent miraculum, quod factū est in destructione substantiæ, secus enim ad quid manerent? Secundò vt præstent id, quod faceret materia, si adesset, ideoque vice illius patiuntur, alterantur, qualitatibus afficiuntur &c. Si autem hostia consecrata penetraretur cum alia, non lateret miraculum, nam vnusquisque cognosceret euidentissimè substantiam ibi fuisse destructam. Deinde nec accidentia supplerent munus materiæ, quæ impenetrabilis cum alia est. Igitur accidentia hostiæ natura sua penetrari possunt; ex Dei voluntate non penetrantur. Primum debet concedi, quia tenent omnes, accidentia penetrari cum accidentibus, & cum substantia: ergo etiam illa penetrabilia sunt. Probatur, nam si quid hoc impedit, maximè quia sunt quanta, & extensa: sed priùs quanquam talia, penetrabantur in substantia panis quanta: ergo. Probo minorem sic. In hostia consecrata sumantur v.g. decem partes albedinis, vt sunt unitæ, continuatæ, ac extrapositæ: vel hæ omnes vt ita unitæ recipiebantur in decem partibus materiæ unitis, continuatis, & extrapositis, aut non: si primum, ergo quantum recipiebatur in quanto: si secundum, ergo accidentia continuata, & extrapolita erant in subiecto non continuato, nec extrapolito, quod repugnat, quemadmodum supra. Respond. vltimò, accidentia vnius hostiæ non penetrari cum alia, quia vt accidens penetret aliud, non illi satis est iuxtaponi localiter: sed requirit in eo produci, & per generationè intus recipi.
units.tr: To the confirmation adduced last, I reply that the host does not penetrate another host, because God prevents it. Nor should this seem to be said as an evasion of the difficulty. A probable reason can be given why God prevents the penetration: the accidents are left in the host in place of matter, for a twofold cause. First, to hide the miracle that was wrought in the destruction of the substance; otherwise to what end would they remain? Second, to do what matter would do if it were present, and therefore they suffer in its place, are altered, are affected by qualities and so on. But if the consecrated host were penetrated by another, the miracle would not be hidden, for everyone would most clearly know that the substance had been destroyed there. Nor would the accidents then supply the office of matter, which is impenetrable by another. Therefore the accidents of the host can by their nature be penetrated; by God's will they are not. The first point must be conceded, since all hold that accidents penetrate accidents and substance; therefore these too are penetrable. This is proved: if anything hinders it, it is chiefly that they are quantities and extended; but before consecration, although such, they were penetrated in the substance of bread, which was quantified. Therefore... I prove the minor thus. In the consecrated host take, for example, ten parts of whiteness, as they are united, continuous and placed outside one another. Either all these, so united, were received in ten parts of matter that were united, continuous and placed outside one another, or not. If the first, then quantity was received in quantity. If the second, then continuous and extrapositioned accidents were in a subject that was non-continuous and not extrapositioned, which is repugnant, as above. I reply finally that the accidents of one host are not penetrated by another, because for one accident to penetrate another it is not enough that it be juxtaposed locally; it requires that it be produced in it and received within by generation.

units.la: Concludo igitur, accidentia quantitatè habere suam, & iltam, quæ ab ipsismet accidentibus vnitis, & continuatis non distinguitur, penetrari cum substantiæ quantitate, quæ similiter ab ipsamet substantia distincta non est. Porro in Sacramento Euchar. non fieri penetrationem hostiæ cum hostia, sic Deo impediente, ne miraculum destructæ substantiæ detegatur. Ex quibus etiam ad argumenta, quæ contra secundam conclusionem vrgeri possunt, hauriet quisque solutionem.
units.tr: I conclude, therefore, that the accidents have their own quantity, which is not distinguished from the accidents themselves when they are united and continuous, and that this penetrates with the quantity of the substance, which likewise is not distinct from the substance itself.
