Moreover, in the Eucharist the penetration of host by host does not take place, God so preventing it, lest the miracle of the destroyed substance be detected. From these things each may also draw the solution to the arguments that can be urged against the second conclusion.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISQUISITION II.

units.la: An partes in quantitate continua, seu in continuo sint actu distincta.
units.tr: Whether the parts in continuous quantity, or in the continuum, are actually distinct.

units.la: PRo intelligentia præmoneo, quæstionem hanc traxisse originem à modo loquendi subobscuro Aristotelis, dum sæpissimè vtitur ijs terminis, actu, & potentia. Inquit enim partes in quantitate, sive in re quanta, non esse actu, sed potentia partes, nimirum quatenus diuidi possunt, ac separari. Hunc dicendi modum vsurparunt Auerroes D. Thom. & alij. Sed aperte sententiam de identitate partium continui tuentur Fonseca, Ægydius, Albertinus, Augustus de Angelis, aliique recentiores, dum tenent, in quantitate v. gr. vlnari non esse actu partem a. partem b. partem c. distinctas ab inuicem; sed hæc omnia esse vnum quid prorsus identificatum, continere autem partes in potentia, quatenus ea quantitas diuidi potest in plura. E contra volunt recentiores, in re omni quanta, etiam priùs, quàm fiat separatio, & actualis diuisio, partes adesse actu, realiterque distinctas, quarum vna non sit alia, &c.
units.tr: For the sake of understanding, I note in advance that this question arose from Aristotle's rather obscure way of speaking, since he very often uses the terms actuality and potentiality. He says that the parts in quantity, or in a quantified thing, are not actual parts but potential parts, namely insofar as they can be divided and separated. Averroes, St. Thomas and others adopted this way of speaking. But Fonseca, Aegidius, Albertinus, Augustus de Angelis and other more recent writers plainly defend the identity of the parts of the continuum, holding that in a quantity, for example a yard-long one, the parts a, b and c are not actually distinct from one another; rather they are all one thing, wholly identical, and contain parts only potentially, insofar as that quantity can be divided into many. On the contrary, more recent writers hold that in every quantified thing, even before separation and actual division takes place, parts are actually present and really distinct, so that one is not the other, etc.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Partes in quantitate continua sunt actu, & realiter ab invicem distincta.
units.tr: The parts in continuous quantity are actually and really distinct from one another.

units.la: PRobatur 1. quia partes in quantitate continua possunt actu, & realiter separari, ergo prius actu realiter distinguuntur. Probo consequentiam. Ea, quæ separantur, iunt prius aliud, & aliud; sed quæ sunt aliud, & aliud, actu realiter distinguuntur, ergo quæ separantur, actu realiter prius distinguuntur. Maior est certa, nihil enim separatur à se ipso, ac propterea quæ separantur, sunt aliud, & aliud.
units.tr: It is proved first, because the parts in continuous quantity can actually and really be separated, so they are antecedently actually and really distinguished. I prove the consequence. Things that are separated are antecedently one thing and another; but things that are one thing and another are actually and really distinguished; therefore things that are separated are actually and really distinguished beforehand. The major is certain, for nothing is separated from itself, and so things that are separated are one thing and another.

units.la: Probatur 2. quia dum v.gr. crescit arbor, & eius quantitas maior fit, vel priori quantitati accedit pars nova quantitatis, vel non: si secundum, ergo arbor non crescit contra suppositionem: Si primum, ergo pars, quæ additur, non est illa, quæ prior, ergo alia, ergo distincta. Probo consequentiam, ex eo enim quòd pars noua vnitur, non ideo tamen cum priore identificatur; alioquin & anima, quæ vnitur corpori, acquireret cum eo identificationem.
units.tr: It is proved second, because while a tree grows, for example, and its quantity becomes greater, either a new part of quantity is added to the earlier quantity, or it is not. If the latter, the tree does not grow, contrary to the supposition. If the former, the part that is added is not the one that was there before, and so it is another, and therefore distinct. I prove the consequence: for from the fact that a new part is united, it does not follow that it is identical with the earlier one; otherwise the soul, which is united to the body, would also acquire identity with it.

units.la: Probatur 3. quia si lignum v. g. vnare incipiat ab vno extremo comburi: quæro vel tunc lignum totum comburitur, vel non: si primum, ergo non incipit solum contra suppositionem. Si fecundum, ergo in ligno adest pars, quæ vritur, & pars, quæ non vritur, ergo partes actu realiter distinctæ. Probo consequentiam. Id quod exuritur, actu, & realiter non est quod non exuritur, alioquin res eadem actu combureretur, & non combureretur.
units.tr: It is proved third, because if, for example, a cubit-long piece of wood begins to be burned at one end, I ask whether then the whole piece of wood is burned or not. If the first, then it does not begin to burn only, contrary to the supposition. If the second, then in the wood there is a part that is burned and a part that is not burned, and so the parts are actually and really distinct. I prove the consequence: that which is burned away is actually and really not that which is not burned away; otherwise the same thing would actually be burned and not burned.

units.la: Probatur vltimò, facilioribus omissis, argumento insolubili, & quod sententiam oppositam, vt probè Spinula, funditus euertit. Sic: Diuidatur lignum v.g. vlnare in plures, pluresque partes (quæcumque postea hæ sint, siue aliquotæ, ac determinatæ, siue proportionales) hæ partes actu realiter priùs distinguebantur, ergo. Probo minorem. Hæ partes actu realiter priùs vniebantur; ergo actu realiter distinguebantur. Probo antecedens. Non possunt separari, nisi ab ijs tollendo vnionem, vt euidentissimè constat, ergo priùs vniebantur. Sed ea quæ actu realiter vniuntur, actu realiter distincta sunt; ergo. Probo minorem. Vnio est distinctorum vnio, nihil enim vniri ad se ipsum potest, ergo quæ vniuntur actu realiter, distinguuntur actu realiter: sed partes in quantitate continua sic vniuntur, ergo sic distinguuntur. Quoniam ergo inter eas cadit vnio actu admitti etiam debet distinctio actu, & non potentiâ.
units.tr: It is proved lastly, leaving aside the easier arguments, by an insoluble argument which, as Spinula well showed, utterly overturns the opposing opinion. It runs thus: let a cubit-long piece of wood, for example, be divided into several and more and more parts (whatever these parts afterwards are, whether aliquot and determinate or proportional); these parts were actually and really distinct beforehand. I prove the minor: these parts were actually and really united beforehand; therefore they were actually and really distinguished. I prove the antecedent: they cannot be separated unless the union is removed from them, as is most evidently clear; therefore they were united beforehand. But things that are actually and really united are actually and really distinct; therefore... I prove this minor: union is a union of distinct things, for nothing can be united to itself; therefore things that are united actually and really are distinguished actually and really. But the parts in continuous quantity are so united; therefore they are so distinguished. Since, therefore, union occurs among them, distinction must also be admitted among them actually, and not merely potentially.

units.la: Opponis. In continuo si partes admittantur distinctæ, continuum ampliùs vnum non est, sed multiplex, nam vbi est distinctio, ibi quoque multitudo. Præterea: vt vna pars distinguatur ab alia_, non debet cum illa extensionem habere communem: sed in continuo quidquid est, extensionem habet communem, ergo.
units.tr: You object: if parts are admitted to be distinct in the continuum, the continuum is no longer one but manifold, for wherever there is distinction there is also multiplicity. Moreover: for one part to be distinguished from another, it must not have a common extension with it; but in the continuum whatever there is has a common extension; therefore...

units.la: Respond. ad primum negando sequellam. Ratio est,nam omne compositum, seu essentiale sit, siue integrale, dicit ex suo conceptu plura, quæ integrant: nec proinde ipsum euadit multiplex, vt patet in homine integrato ex anima, & corpore; in albo conflato ex materia, & albedine, ac similibus. Requiritur ergo ad multitudinem separatio, non distinctio tantùm.
units.tr: I answer the first by denying the consequence. The reason is that every composite, whether essential or integral, implies in its very concept several things which make up the whole; and so it does not on that account become manifold, as is plain in a man made up of soul and body, or in a white thing compounded of matter and whiteness, and similar cases. Multiplicity therefore requires separation, not distinction alone.

units.la: Respond. ad secundum retorquendo argumentum. Quantitas .n. habet communem cum substantia extensionem, & nihilominus aduersarij eam faciunt à substantia distinctam. Dico igitur directè, sufficere ad rationem distinctionis, vt vna entitas non sit alia, quæcunq; postea copulatio extensio, & communis complexio inter eas detur. (*_*)
units.tr: I answer the second by turning the argument back. For quantity has a common extension with substance, and nevertheless our opponents make it distinct from substance. I say, therefore, directly, that it is sufficient for the notion of distinction that one entity is not another, whatever subsequent joining in extension and common complexion there may be between them. (*_*)

units.la: DISPVTATIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: SECOND DISPUTATION.

units.la: De compositione quantitatis continuæ, sive continui.
units.tr: On the composition of continuous quantity, or of the continuum.

units.la: QVantitas continua est aggregatum quodam ex multitudine partium, quæ simul physicè vnitæ integrant vnum quid totale, ac faciunt esse continuum. Non tamen satis est, si absolutè dicamus, quantitatem partibus constare: sed præterea videamus oportet, cuiusnam sint conditionis hæ quoque partes; nimirum ipsæne aliis etiam partibus componantur, an non, quousque deveniamus eò, vt dilucidè pateat, quænam sint prima elementa continui, seu principia constitutiva .. Duplex in hac re viget sententia ..
units.tr: Continuous quantity is a certain aggregate of a multitude of parts which, physically united together, make up one whole thing and cause there to be a continuum. Yet it is not enough to say simply that quantity consists of parts. We must also consider what condition these parts are in, namely whether they too are composed of further parts, or not, until we arrive at the point where it is clear what the first elements of the continuum are, or its constitutive principles. Two opinions prevail on this matter.

units.la: Prima est Aristotelis, quem philosophi penè omnes coacto agmine secuti sunt, docens continuum componi ex partibus in infinitum diuisibilibus, adeo vt facta quauis diuisione, id quod manet, diuisibile adhuc sit, nec vnquam subdividendo possit ad vltimum deduci. Secunda est Zenonis, Democriti, Anaxagoræ, Leucippi, quibus nuper aliqui recentes, ijque docti suffragium ferunt, Afferens continuit compositionem ex indiuisibilibus factam.
units.tr: The first is Aristotle's, which almost all philosophers have followed in close formation. It teaches that the continuum is composed of parts divisible to infinity, so that whatever division is made, what remains is still divisible, and it can never be reduced to ultimate parts by subdividing. The second is that of Zeno, Democritus, Anaxagoras and Leucippus, to whom some recent writers, and learned ones, lend their support, asserting that the continuum is composed of indivisibles.

units.la: Aduerto autem, peripateticos non vno modo Aristotelis opinionem tueri. Siquidem dem alij dicunt, partes in continuo non esse actu distinctas; alij vero sic, unde inter illas ponunt vniones, & has plerique dicunt esse indiuisibiles, proinde solent vocari ab ijsdem puncta continuatiua. Quidam praeterea concedunt puncta etiam terminatiua, quatenus extrema continui per superficies quoad profunditatem indiuisibiles terminantur. Nonnulli tandem omnia indiuisibilia proscribunt. Nos rem examini subijciamus.
units.tr: I note, however, that the Peripatetics do not all defend Aristotle's opinion in one way. For some say that the parts in the continuum are not actually distinct; others say they are, and so place unions between them, and most of these say the parts are indivisible, and so they are commonly called continuative points by the same people. Some besides grant terminative points too, insofar as the extremities of a continuum are terminated by surfaces indivisible in depth. Finally, some reject all indivisibles. We shall submit the matter to examination.

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: FIRST DISQUISITION.

units.la: An continui compositio fit ex partib- us in infinitum diuisibilibus.
units.tr: Whether the composition of the continuum comes from parts divisible to infinity.

units.la: PRO intelligentia edoceri debetis quod inquiunt Aristotelei, partes nimirum esse in triplici differentia. Quaedam vocantur aequales, determinatae, non communicantes: & illae sunt, quae designari possunt in mensura certa, itaut comparatae ad inuicem sint aequales, & vna de alia non participet, quemadmodum v.gr. duo palmi. Aliae dicuntur proportionales, indeterminatae, communicantes; & illae sunt, quae nunquam accipiuntur in mensura determinata, sed minores, minoresque, adeout participent de superiori, & cum eo si comparentur singillatim, semper minores sint; v.gr. duo semipalmi respectu palmi. Denique aliæ sunt partes aliquotæ, videlicet eædem ipsæ communicantes, prout non cum suo toto, quo sunt minores, & cuius aliquid semper communicant, sed quatenus inter se comparantur, v. gr. si palmus diuidatur in quatuor quadrantes, quilibet quadrans respectu palmi est pars communicans, & proportionalis; at collatus cum alio quadrante, manet aliquota, unde si quater hic replicetur, toti palmo æquiualens est.
units.tr: To understand this, you must be taught what the Aristotelians mean. There are three kinds of parts. Some are called equal, determinate and non-communicating: these are the parts that can be marked off in a fixed measure, so that when compared with one another they are equal and one does not share in the other, as for example two palms. Others are called proportional, indeterminate and communicating: these are never taken in a determinate measure but are smaller and smaller, so that they share in the larger whole and, when compared with it one by one, are always smaller, as for example two half-palms compared with a palm. Finally, there are aliquot parts, which are the very same communicating parts, not as they are compared with their whole, of which they are smaller and of which they always share something, but as they are compared with one another. For example, if a palm is divided into four quadrants, each quadrant is a communicating and proportional part in relation to the palm; but when compared with another quadrant it is an aliquot part, so that if it is repeated four times it equals the whole palm.

units.la: Hoc posito, aiunt Peripatetici, adesse partes in continuo proportionales, & communicantes, in infinitum diuisibiles, adeout facta quauis diuisione, quod manet, adhuc subdiuidi possit in alias minores, & minores. Puta si cuspis tenuissimæ acus in duo prima secetur, vnumquodq; manet diuisibile in duo secunda; omne secundum in duo tertia; quoduis tertium in duo quarta, &c. adeout si modo incipiat fieri, hæc diuisio, per totam æternitatem à parte post in minora, & minora semper segmenta continuari possit. Contra tamen, & sit. •
units.tr: With this laid down, the Peripatetics say that there are in the continuum parts that are proportional and communicating and divisible to infinity, so that, whatever division is made, what remains can still be subdivided into other parts, smaller and smaller. Suppose the point of a very fine needle is cut into two first parts; each of these remaining parts is divisible into two second parts; each second part into two third parts; each third into two fourth parts, and so on, so that if this division were once begun, it could be continued through all eternity into smaller and smaller segments. On the contrary, and let it be so.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Continuum non conflatur ex partibus in infinitum diuisibilibus.
units.tr: A continuum is not composed of parts divisible to infinity.

units.la: PRobatur I. quia si adessent in continuo partes diuisibiles in infinitum, in quantitate finita reperiretur infinitum actu: sed hoc repugnat, ergo. Probo sequelam. In continuo palmari essent partes infinitæ actu; sed tale continuum est finitum: ergo in quantitate finita reperiretur infinitum actu. Probo maiorem. In continuo palmari non essent partes infinitæ potentiâ; ergo infinitæ actu. Antecedens patet, quia nunc, & de præsenti adsunt in eo continuo entitates illæ omnes, quæ decidi possunt, ac separari; & adsunt quidem actu, realiterq; inter se distinctæ (sunt enim unitæ, alioquin separari non possent, ergo distinctæ) sed si non forent infinitæ actu, diuidi non possent in infinitum, ergo sunt infinitæ actu. Probo minorem à simili. Non possunt in quantitate separari decem palmi, nisi priùs in ea sint actu decem palmi, neq; centum, si actu centum non sint; ergo neque partes in infinitum, si partes actu non sunt infinitæ. Dicis quòd hæ partes non sunt infinitæ actu, quia nunquam omnes separabuntur, sed poterunt separari vlterius, & vlterius in infinitum. Contra. Supponamus v.g. quòd cuspis tenuissimæ acus diuidi possit in duas mi-miriades partium, sed tamen nunquam sic diuidatur ob carentiam instrumenti ad vltimam diuisionem requisiti, adhuc in ea cuspide sunt duæ miriades partium actu realiter distinctæ; igitur & in quato palmari, dato etiam quòd nunquam vltima contingat diuisio (si diuisibile in infinitum est) partes actu infinitæ concedendæ sunt. Contra 2. in quanto palmari singulæ partes (quæcumq; sint, vel communicantes, aut aliquotæ) sunt actu, realiterq; vnitæ, adeout nulla excogitari possit, quæ careat vnione, vt supra. Hoc dato, arguo sic. Tollat Deus à continuo tot, quot reperit vniones; in eo casu id quod maneret, non amplius foret diuisibile, secus non fuisset ablata omnis vnio. Quæro igitur, vel tunc manerent entia numero infinita, vel non: si primum, ergo in quanto palmari finito aderat infinitum actu: si secundum, ergo quantum palmare non poterat in infinitum diuidi. Probo consequentiam. Entitates inuicè separandæ, infinitæ non erant. Quòdsi dicas, neq; Deum posse omnem adimere vnionem à continuo. Contra. In continuo sunt partes actu distinctæ per vniones actu distinctas: quidquid verò distinctum ab alio est, separari potest ab illo, si non naturaliter, saltem diuinitus. Repetite supra dicta disp. 1. q. 2.
units.tr: I prove this first. If there were parts divisible to infinity in a continuum, an actual infinite would be found in a finite quantity. But this is impossible, so the conclusion follows. I prove the consequence: in a palm-long continuum there would be actually infinite parts, but such a continuum is finite, so an actual infinite would be found in a finite quantity. I prove the major premise: in a palm-long continuum there are not potentially infinite parts, so they are actually infinite. The antecedent is plain, because now, in the present, all those entities that can be cut off and separated are in that continuum. They are actually present and really distinct from one another (for they are united, otherwise they could not be separated, and so they are distinct). But if they were not actually infinite, they could not be divided to infinity, so they are actually infinite. I prove the minor by analogy. Ten palms cannot be separated in a quantity unless ten palms are first actually in it, nor a hundred unless a hundred are actually there. So neither can the parts be separated to infinity unless the parts are actually infinite. You say that these parts are not actually infinite, because they will never all be separated, but they could be separated further and further to infinity. On the contrary: suppose, for example, that the point of a very fine needle could be divided into two myriads of parts, but is never so divided because the instrument required for the final division is lacking. Even so, there are actually two myriads of really distinct parts in that point. Therefore, in a palm-long quantity, even granting that the final division never occurs (if the divisible is divisible to infinity), actually infinite parts must be conceded. A second objection: in a palm-long quantity each single part (whatever they are, whether communicating or aliquot) is actually and really united, so that no one can be conceived that lacks union, as was said above. Granting this, I argue thus. Let God take away from the continuum as many unions as there are. In that case, what remained would no longer be divisible, otherwise not all union would have been removed. I ask, then: would there remain entities numerically infinite, or not? If the first, then an actual infinite was present in the finite palm-long quantity. If the second, then the palm-long quantity could not be divided to infinity. I prove the consequence: entities that are to be separated from one another were not infinite. But if you say that God cannot remove every union from a continuum, I reply: in a continuum the parts are actually distinct through actually distinct unions, and whatever is distinct from another can be separated from it, if not naturally, at least by divine power. Repeat what was said above, disp. 1, q. 2.

units.la: Probatur 2. quia si quantitas foret diuisibilis in infinitum, in omni mensura, etiam palmari, etiam digitali, & minori etiam, adessent partes aptæ facere infinitam. tam extensionem, quod repugnat. Probatur antecedens. Adsit v. g. lignum palmare quoad omnem dimensionem. Incipiat hoc diuidi ratione profunditatis, certè quoad hanc, partes decisæ fient perte minores, minoresquæ; sed tamen quoad longitudinem inter se manebūt æquales. Ergo si quoad profunditatem omnes tollantur vniones (quod saltem Deo non repugnat) deinde vna pars vbicumque post aliam, fiet extensio infinita. Vel sic. Diuidat Angelus v. g. dicto modo eam quantitatem, sanè decidet partes, quæ totam globi terraquei superficiem tegant; quæ aerem totum, cælumq; coæperiant; quæ mille, si adessent, mundos conuestiant; neq; tamen adhuc vltima foret diuisio, sed quod maneret, per totam æternitatem à parte post secuturam diuidi posset. Quod ego vt credam adduci non possum.
units.tr: I prove it secondly: if quantity were divisible to infinity, then in every measure, even the palm, even the finger and smaller still, there would be parts capable of making an infinite extension, which is impossible. The antecedent is proved thus. Let there be, for example, a piece of wood a palm in every dimension. Suppose it begins to be divided in respect of depth. Certainly, in respect of depth, the parts cut off will become ever smaller, but they will remain equal to one another in length. Therefore, if all unions are removed in respect of depth (which at least is not impossible for God), then one part after another, wherever it is, will make an infinite extension. Or thus: suppose an angel divides, in the manner described, that quantity. Surely he will cut off parts that cover the whole surface of the terraqueous globe, that cover all the air and the heavens, and that would overspread a thousand worlds, if there were so many. Yet even then the final division would not have occurred, but what remained could be divided through all eternity to come. This I cannot be brought to believe.

units.la: Probatur 3. à simili. Continuum successiuum non constat partibus in infinitum diuisibilibus: ergo neq; continuum permanens. Consequentia tenet, nam si ratio continui sine huiusmodi partibus haberi potest, nullibi hæ partes admittendæ sunt. Antecedens probatur, si enim tempus habet partes communicantes, & semper diuisibiles, ergo pars ista temporis, quæ de præsenti fluit, aliis partibus constat. Hæ autem vel sunt præsentes, vel præteritæ, vel futuræ. Si secundum, ergo tempus hoc præsens, coexistit præterito, & futuro, quod absurdum est. Si primum, ergo præsens hoc tempus non est successiuum, sed permanens, habet n. partes in infinitum diuisibiles vna, & simul permanentes, cum tamen de ratione successiui sit, vna vt pars fluat immediatè post aliam, nec vnquam plures maneant simul. Deinde sequeretur, actum v. g. charitatis nunc à Petro elicitum fore meriti omnino infiniti, eò quòd meritum per omne temporis momentum, quo durat actus, augetur; sed hoc nunc haberet partes in infinitum plures, & plures, ergo actus nunc à Petro elicitus meritum haberet infinitum.
units.tr: I prove it thirdly, by analogy. Successive continuum does not consist of parts divisible to infinity; therefore neither does permanent continuum. The consequence holds, for if the notion of continuum can be had without such parts, they are to be admitted nowhere. The antecedent is proved thus. If time has parts that communicate with one another and are always divisible, then that part of time which now flows from the present consists of other parts. These are either present, past or future. If future, then this present time coexists with the past and the future, which is absurd. If present, then this present time is not successive but permanent, and it has parts divisible to infinity that are all permanent together at once. Yet it belongs to the nature of the successive that one part flows immediately after another, and never do several remain together at once. Further, it would follow that an act of charity now elicited by Peter would be of wholly infinite merit, because merit increases with every moment of time through which the act lasts. But this now present act would have parts more and more numerous to infinity, so the act now elicited by Peter would have infinite merit.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISQUISITIO SECUNDA.

units.la: An continui compositio ex indiui- sibilibus fiat.
units.tr: Whether the composition of the continuum is from indivisibles.

units.la: PRo intelligentia quàmdiligentissimè aduertite, non quærere hic nos de indiuisibilibus, quæ vocant physica, siue de atomis, quæ naturæ quidem vi præ sua exilitate diuidi vlterius non possunt, ratione tamen, & à Deo saltem diuisibiles in alia manent; sed quæstio procedere debet circa indiuisibilia mathematica, quæ nulla omnino parte constantur, adeo ut nec mente nostra, nec à Deo ipso in alia subdiuidi queant. Quare nullo modo sustineri eorum sententia potest, qui dicunt, quantitatem non ex partibus in infinitum diuisibilibus, nec ex minimis conflari mathematicis, verùm ex punctis aliis. alijs, quæ vocant physica. Non potest, inquam, hæc opinio defendi. Aut enim ista minima in se habent partes, vel non: Si secundum, ergo sunt puncta mathematica: si primum, quæro: vel hæ partes in infinitum deciduæ sunt, vel non ita: si primū, hæc est expressa Philosophi sententia: si secundum: ergo ad ea minima deueniemus, quæ nec per Dei potentiam vlterius diuidi poterunt: hæc autem sunt puncta mathematica. Propterea non habes medium inter Aristotelis, & Zenonis doctrinam, quippe alterum ex his necessario dices: Aut principia, quæ faciūt continuum, esse partes in infinitum diuisibiles: Aut puncta cuiusq; partis expertia, non composita, sed simplicissima, & mathematica. Primum superiori disquisitione reiectum est: manet ergo, vt admittatur secundum, & hoc à nobis triplici conclusione præstabitur.
units.tr: To understand this, please notice very carefully that we are not asking here about the indivisibles that they call physical, or about atoms, which by the force of nature cannot be divided further because of their extreme smallness, but which can still be divided in reason, and by God at least, into other parts. The question must instead concern mathematical indivisibles, which consist of no parts at all, so that they cannot be subdivided into others either by our mind or by God himself. Therefore the opinion of those who say that quantity is made up neither of parts divisible to infinity nor of mathematical minima, but of other points, which they call physical, can in no way be upheld. This opinion, I say, cannot be defended. For these minima either have parts in themselves or they do not. If the second, then they are mathematical points. If the first, I ask: either these parts can be divided off to infinity, or they cannot. If the first, this is the plain opinion of the Philosopher. If the second, then we shall come to those minima which cannot be divided further even by the power of God, and these are mathematical points. Hence you have no middle way between the doctrine of Aristotle and that of Zeno, since you must necessarily say one of the two: either that the principles which make up the continuum are parts divisible to infinity, or that the points of each part are free of parts, not composite, but most simple and mathematical. The first was rejected in the previous disquisition, so it remains that the second be admitted, and this we shall establish by a threefold conclusion.

units.la: Prima offendet, in continuo adesse indiuisibilia. Secunda, præter ea, nullas dari partes deciduas. Tertia demum sola indiuisibilia concludet.
units.tr: The first will show that indivisibles are present in the continuum. The second will show that, beyond these, there are no divisible parts. The third, finally, will conclude that indivisibles alone exist.

units.la: CONCLVSIO PRIMA.
units.tr: CONCLVSIO PRIMA.

units.la: Dantur in continuo indiuisibilia.
units.tr: Indivisibles are given in the continuum.

units.la: PRobatur 1. auctoritate Aristotelis, D. Thomæ, Scoti, aliorumq. Peripateticorum, quos referunt, ac sequuntur Complutenses disp. 25. q. 1. Ratio est, nā puncta, lineæ, superficies vera, & realia entia sunt, circa quæ Mathematici scientifice procedunt; alioquin tota mathesis cadit; ergo hæc omnia dantur in continuo, alioquin vbinam erunt? Sed sunt indiuisibilia, ergo.
units.tr: It is proved first by the authority of Aristotle, St Thomas, Scotus, and the other Peripatetics, whom the Complutenses cite and follow (disp. 25, q. 1). The reason is that points, lines and surfaces are true and real entities, about which mathematicians proceed scientifically; otherwise all mathematics collapses. Therefore all these things are given in the continuum; otherwise where would they be? But they are indivisibles. Therefore indivisibles are given.

units.la: Probatur 2. nam si adesset globus persectè sphæricus, aliquà potentia sic extructus; aut pyramis inuersa definens in puncto; hæc impositæ super hoc ligno tangerent secundum indiuisibila tantum, ergo in tali continuo indiuisibilia sunt. Confirmatur, quia si circulus circulum secet, vel si tangat saltem, fit mutuus contactus in puncto ex Eucl. l. 3. prop. 36.
units.tr: It is proved second. For if there were a perfectly spherical globe, formed by some power, or an inverted pyramid ending in a point, then these, placed upon this piece of wood, would touch only at indivisibles. Therefore in such a continuum there are indivisibles. It is confirmed because if one circle cuts another, or at least touches it, a mutual contact takes place at a point, from Euclid, book 3, prop. 36.

units.la: Probatur 3. quia si duo corpora tangant se mutuo, possunt assignari partes, in quibus tanguntur: sit ergo pars .a. primi corporis, & pars .b. secundi. Quæro: vel hæ sunt partes vltimæ, aut non: si primum, ergo diuidi nequeunt in alias, & sic dantur indiuisibilia: si secundum, ergo istæ non se tangunt. Probo, quia tangunt se tantummodo quæ vltimè sunt, alioquin, vt patet, fieret aliquarum penetratio. Itaque aut est dicendum, non fieri contactum, aut indiuisibilia concedenda sunt.
units.tr: It is proved third, because if two bodies touch each other, parts can be assigned at which they are touched. Let .a. be a part of the first body and .b. a part of the second. I ask: are these ultimate parts or not? If they are, then they cannot be divided into others, and so indivisibles are given. If they are not, then these parts do not touch each other. I prove this, because only what is ultimate touches; otherwise, as is plain, some penetration would occur. Therefore either it must be said that no contact takes place, or indivisibles must be granted.

units.la: Probatur 4. nam partes continui habet vniones, quarum beneficio continuantur, non enim vniuntur se ipsis per meram iuxta positionem, vt alibi dictum est: Sed hæ vniones haud quaquam diuidi possunt; ergo in continuo indiuisibilia concedenda sunt. Probatur minor, quia si vnio foret diuisibilis, ergo haberet in se partes per aliam vnionem vnitas. Aut ergo hæc noua vnio constaret partibus, aut non: si primum, abimus in infinitum: si secundum, ergo in continuo aliqua sunt, quæ diuidi nequeunt.
units.tr: It is proved fourth. The parts of a continuum have unions, by whose benefit they are continuous, for they are not united to themselves by mere juxtaposition, as was said elsewhere. But these unions cannot by any means be divided. Therefore indivisibles must be granted in the continuum. The minor premise is proved as follows: if the union were divisible, it would have in itself parts united by another union. Either this new union consists of parts or it does not. If it does, we go on to infinity; if it does not, then there are some things in the continuum which cannot be divided.

units.la: Probatur 5. nam in quantitate successiua, ex.g. in tempore debet concedi esse instantia, & indiuisibilia; ergo hæc non repugnant, cùm sint entia realia. Itaque in permanenti etiam admitti poterunt. Antecedens patet, alioquin destruimus conceptum ipsius nunc, & si pars hæc temporis de præsenti fluens non est omnino indiuisibilis, ergo habet partes vnà existentes, vnde tempus non est successiuum quoad omnes. Præterea fiunt actiones aliquæ instantaneæ, vt impressio qualitatis, productio formæ; ac similes; ergo tempus, cui correspondent, instans vnicum est.
units.tr: It is proved fifth. In successive quantity, for example in time, instants and indivisibles must be granted; therefore they are not repugnant, since they are real entities. Thus they can also be admitted in permanent quantity. The antecedent is plain: otherwise we destroy the very concept of the now. And if this part of time, flowing in the present, is not wholly indivisible, then it has parts existing together, and so time is not successive in every respect. Moreover, some actions are instantaneous, such as the impression of a quality, the production of a form, and the like. Therefore the time to which they correspond is a single instant.

units.la: CONCLVSIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: CONCLUSION II.

units.la: Praeter indiuisibilia non dantur partes diuisibiles in continuo.
units.tr: Besides indivisibles, there are no divisible parts in the continuum.

units.la: PRobatur 1. quia si præter puncta, dantur partes in continuo diuisibiles, aut hisce partibus adhærent ea puncta, vel recipiuntur in illis: neutrum dici potest, ergo præter puncta indiuisibilia non adsunt partes in continuo diuisibiles. Maior de se patet. Minore sic probo quoad primum. Non potest indiuisibile tangere partem diuisibilem; ergo nequit adhærere, siue contiguum esse parti. Antecedens probatur. Pars diuisibilis habet prius & posterius: at indiuisibile tangere nequit prius, & posterius; ergo. Probo minorem, quia si tangeret, ergo ad rem se se coextenderet diuisibilem: ergo punctum aut in se foret extensum, aut replicatum. Probatur quoad secundum, quia si punctum in parte diuisibili recipiatur, iam ponitur in subiecto habenti partes extrapositas, nimirum priores, & posteriores; ergo in duplici loco iam reperitur. Confirmatur: aut diuisibile manet intra partem diuisibilem, aut extra: si primum, ergo in loco diuisibili est, quod concipi nequit: si secundum; ergo indiuisibile potest esse totū extra id, quod tangit; ergo & extra punctum, & sic facere cum eo extensionem, quod aduersarius non concedet. Dicis, punctum non penetrati cum parte, quia non habet cum a proportionem. Contra: saltem adhęet parti, eiq; fit contiguum ; ergo coæquatur diuisibili,& sic duplici loco. Dicis iterum, quòd punctum sanè tangit parte, sed tamen indiuisibiliter. Contra: pars eo modo tangi debet, quo manet à parte rei; sed manet diuisibilis, ergo tangitur vt diuisibilis, ergo vt habens prius, & posterius: quo dato, punctum duplici iam loco respondet.
units.tr: Proof 1: if, besides points, there are divisible parts in a continuum, then those points either adhere to these parts or are received in them. Neither can be said; therefore, besides indivisible points, there are no divisible parts in the continuum. The major is self-evident. I prove the minor as follows, first for the adherence. An indivisible cannot touch a divisible part, and therefore cannot adhere to it or be contiguous with it. The antecedent is proved: a divisible part has a before and an after, but an indivisible cannot touch a before and an after; therefore. I prove the minor: if it touched, it would extend itself along with the divisible thing, and so the point would be either extended in itself or replicated. The second alternative is proved as follows: if a point is received in a divisible part, it is now placed in a subject that has parts outside one another, namely earlier and later; therefore it is now found in a double place. This is confirmed: either the divisible remains within the divisible part, or outside it. If the first, then the indivisible is in a divisible place, which cannot be conceived. If the second, then the indivisible can be wholly outside what it touches, and so outside the point too, and thus it makes an extension with it, which our opponent will not concede. You say that the point does not penetrate the part, because it has no proportion to it. Against this: at the least it adheres to the part and becomes contiguous with it; therefore it is equal to the divisible and so is in a double place. You say again that the point indeed touches the part, but indivisibly. Against this: the part must be touched in the way it actually remains in reality; but it remains divisible, therefore it is touched as divisible, therefore as having a before and an after. Given this, the point now corresponds to a double place.

units.la: Probatur 2. quia si præter indiuisibilia dantur partes in continuo, sequitur nullum corpus moueri posse : hoc nisi absurdè asseri nequit, ergo. Antequam probetur, sequela, notate Aristotelem 6. phys. cap.vltimo constanter afferere,subiectum physici motus ita debere corporeum esse, vt inextensum, & indiuisibile per se nullo modo moueri queat, contra Democritū asserentem atomos per se moueri (quamquam atomi mathematica puncta non sunt). Non tamen diffitetur Aristoteles, & cum eo peripatetici, vnum indiuisibile posse moueri per accidens, prout nimirum existit in corpore, quod per se habet motum. Hoc posito, sic probo sequelam. Non potest corpus moueri successiuè, atque continuè, nisi pari motu sua quoque indiuisibilia moueantur:sed posita doctrina Philosophi, repugnat indiuisibilia in eo moueri. ergo nec totum corpus habebit motum. Maior est euidens. Minorem probo. Indiuisibile separatum à corpore nequit moueri motu successiuo, continuo, ergo neq; vt existens in corpore. Antecedens probatur à Philosopho, vt supra. Consequentia currit, nam per hoc quòd punctum fit in corpore v. g. in acumine pyramidis, non proinde fit diuisibile, aut virtualiter extensum, vt patet: ergo nequit correspondere, nisi loco, aut spatio indiuisibili, ac proinde nunquam transibit ad partem diuisibilem (secus aut ibi replicaretur, aut esset in duplici loco) Sed per te post illud punctum, in quo iam residet cuspis v. g. inuersæ pyramidis, nō sequitur, nisi pars diuisibilis; ergo ad istā non mouebitur pyramis. Vnde satis probatum est, non secuturū corporis motum, si quantitas plani, præter puncta, etiam partes haberet.
units.tr: Proof 2: if, besides indivisibles, there are parts in a continuum, it follows that no body can be moved. This cannot be asserted except absurdly; therefore. Before proving the consequence, note that Aristotle, in the last chapter of the sixth book of the Physics, constantly maintains that the subject of physical motion must be corporeal in such a way that what is unextended and indivisible cannot in itself be moved in any way. This is against Democritus, who asserted that atoms move of themselves (although atoms are not mathematical points). Nevertheless Aristotle, and with him the Peripatetics, do not deny that a single indivisible can be moved per accidens, namely insofar as it exists in a body which has motion per se. This being granted, I prove the consequence thus. A body cannot be moved successively and continuously unless its indivisibles are moved with the same motion. But given the doctrine of the Philosopher, it is contradictory for indivisibles to be moved in it; therefore neither will the whole body have motion. The major is evident. I prove the minor: an indivisible separated from the body cannot be moved with a successive, continuous motion; therefore neither can it be so moved as existing in the body. The antecedent is proved by the Philosopher, as above. The consequence holds: because a point is in a body, for example at the tip of a pyramid, it does not thereby become divisible or virtually extended, as is plain. Therefore it can correspond only to an indivisible place or space, and so it will never pass over into a divisible part (otherwise it would be replicated there, or would be in a double place). But according to you, after that point, where the tip of, say, an inverted pyramid now rests, there follows only a divisible part. Therefore the pyramid will not move onto it. Hence it is sufficiently proved that there would be no motion of the body if the quantity of a plane had parts besides points.

units.la: Probatur 3. quia si præter puncta dantur quoq; partes in infinitum diuisibiles, ergo in omni quantitate adest numerus punctorum continuantium actu infinitus. Probo consequentiam. Si esset finitus tantùm, ergo post multam, & multam diuisionem finiretur. Hoc dato, quæro: vel tunc manerent partes actu diuisibiles, aut non: primum dici nequit, non enim fieri potest diuisio vbi non adest continuum, non adesset verò, postquam puncta continuatiua sublata forent. Si secundum, ergo quantitas in infinitum decidua non esset. Confirmatur, quia eatenus per aduersarios non adsunt in continuo partes infinitæ actu, quia hæ non sunt partes inuicem distinctæ, ac determinatæ, sed communicantes, atque complexæ, itaut per diuisionem tantummodo possint fieri partes, quia sic manebunt vnaqueque distincto, ac determinato modo: sed puncta continuatiua non communicant, neq; inter se mutuo participant; sunt enim determinata, & distincta, ergo si vniunt partes in infinitum deciduas, ipsa faciunt numerum actu infinitum.
units.tr: Proof 3: if, besides points, there are also parts infinitely divisible, then in every quantity there is an actually infinite number of continuative points. I prove the consequence. If there were only a finite number, then after much and much division it would come to an end. Granting this, I ask: would the parts then remain actually divisible or not? The first cannot be said, for division cannot take place where there is no continuum, and there would be no continuum once the continuative points were removed. If the second, then the quantity would not be infinitely divisible. This is confirmed: so far, according to our opponents, there are no actually infinite parts in a continuum, because these are not parts distinct and determined from one another, but communicating and interwoven, so that they can become parts only by division, since in that way each will remain in a distinct and determined manner. But continuative points do not communicate, nor do they mutually share with one another; for they are determined and distinct. Therefore, if they unite parts infinitely decreasing, they themselves make up an actually infinite number.

units.la: Probatur 4. argumento celebri de globo sphaerico in plano. Detur per aliquam potentiam perfectè sphaericus, & rotetur motu continuo per superficiem plani. Globus hic tanget semper in puncto: sed totam tanget dicti plani superficiem, ergo tota constat ex punctis. Vnde concludendum euidenter erit, praeter puncta, non dari partes in plano. Maior est citra dubium, neq; negatur ab aduersarijs. Minor etiam satis patet, nam quis vnquam dicat, globum successiuè per totam plani superficiem non posse rotari? Consequentia probè cadit; enim vero si per totam, nulla omissa parte, succedit, per totam quoque sola puncta designat. Neque respondeas cum Hurtado, fieri contactum globi, sed in parte indeterminata, quae minor semper, & minor à Deo saltem assignari potest; Contra enim instatur. Globus habet certum, ac determinatissimum tactum, ergo tangit aliquid certum, & determinatum: nonnisi punctum; ergo. Neque dicas iterum, quod aiunt Complutenses discalceati, Corpus illud sphaericum in plano moueri, sed per saltus, adeout de vno puncto continuatiuo ad ad aliud, relinquendo partem intermediam, saltet. Nimis enim acuti est ingenij sphæra, si cognoscat hîc, & ibi esse partem à se transiliendam. Transiliunt potiùs difficultatem qui per saltus ita respondent. Si enim inter duo plana trudatur globus, & sic vltrò citroq; moueatur, an tunc etiam saltabit? Si hoc erit, premant globum ipsi, qui tam graui doctrina ponderant.
units.tr: Proof 4, by the well-known argument of the spherical globe on a plane. Suppose that a globe is made perfectly spherical by some power, and is rolled by continuous motion over the surface of a plane. This globe will always touch at a point, but it touches the whole surface of the said plane; therefore the whole consists of points. From this it will be evidently concluded that, besides points, there are no parts in a plane. The major is beyond doubt, and it is not denied by our opponents. The minor also is quite plain, for who would ever say that the globe cannot be rolled successively over the whole surface of the plane? The consequence certainly holds: for if it passes over the whole, no part omitted, it also marks out the whole by points alone. Nor reply with Hurtado that the contact of the globe occurs at an indeterminate part, which God can always assign as smaller and smaller. For against this it is urged: the globe has a certain and most determinate contact; therefore it touches something certain and determinate, and that is nothing but a point; therefore. Nor say again, as the Discalced Complutensians say, that the spherical body moves on the plane not continuously but by leaps, so that it jumps from one continuative point to another, leaving the intermediate part behind. For the sphere would need to be of too subtle a wit if it knew here and there that there is a part to be leapt over. They leap over the difficulty who answer by leaps. For if the globe is pressed between two planes and so moved back and forth, will it then also leap? If it will, let those who weigh things with such a grave doctrine press the globe upon it.

units.la: CONCLVSIO TERTIA.
units.tr: THIRD CONCLUSION.

units.la: Continuum solis indiuisibilibus constat.
units.tr: The continuum is composed of indivisibles.

units.la: PRobatur satis per ea, quæ hucusque dicta sunt. Enimuero si dantur in continuo indiuisibilia, & præter hæc, nullæ partes in infinitum deciduæ, sequitur euidenter, continuum solis coalescere punctis indiuisibilibus. Confirmatur, quia vt probatum est, partes in continuo sunt omnes actu distinctæ, igitur per vniones distinctas continuaræ. Modò fac, vt hæ vniones aliquâ potentia tollantur (si enim distinctæ sunt, bene possunt omnes auferri) sed tunc manebunt indiuisibilia tantùm; ergo, Confirmatur secundò, quia si Deus à re materiali separet quantitatem (supponitur enim hæc esse distincta, vnde separari etiam potest) res illa materialis non erit amplius extensa, non quanta, non extrapolita, ergo in eo statu redigitur ad entitates omnino indiuisibiles, vt clarè patet consideranti. Sed tam bene à quantitate auferri possunt vniones omnes, quàm ipsa quantitas a re materiali; ergo vtrobiq; sola indiuisibilia concedenda sunt. Probo minorem, quia ratio separandi quantitatem à re materiali est distinctio inter vtramque. Cùm ergo & vniones in quantitate distinctæ sint, separari omnes possunt. Quo dato, partes entitatiuę quantitatis manent omnino indiuisibiles. Itaq;
units.tr: This is sufficiently proved by what has been said so far. For if there are indivisibles in the continuum, and beyond these no parts divisible to infinity, it follows clearly that the continuum coalesces out of indivisible points. It is confirmed because, as has been proved, all the parts in a continuum are actually distinct, and so they are held together by distinct unions. Now suppose that these unions are removed by some power (if they are distinct, they can all well be taken away). Then only indivisibles will remain. It is confirmed secondly: if God separates quantity from a material thing (for this is assumed to be distinct, and so can also be separated), that material thing will no longer be extended, nor quantified, nor spread out. So in that state it is reduced to entities wholly indivisible, as is clear to anyone who considers it. But all the unions can be removed from quantity just as well as quantity itself can be removed from a material thing. Therefore in both cases only indivisibles must be granted. I prove the minor: the reason for separating quantity from a material thing is the distinction between the two. Since the unions are also distinct within quantity, they can all be separated. Once this is granted, the entitative parts of quantity remain wholly indivisible. Therefore,

units.la: Probatur etiam auctoritate. Imprimis Veterum, qui duce Zenone hanc de continui compositione doctrinam secuti sùt. Hoc edocit Pythagoras, Democritus, Leucippus, Plato, & alij non pauci. 2. Christifidelium, ita enim voluit Io: Maior, Ariminensis, Patritius Capreolus, Aureolus Pereria, Basso, qui hanc veritatem libro toto de motu probat, aliq. plures. 3. Recentiorum, sic enim philosophantur Arriaga, Tellez, Cornelius de S. Patritio, Spinula, quos iam innumeri aperto Marte sequuntur.
units.tr: It is also proved by authority. First, the authority of the ancients, who followed this doctrine of the composition of the continuum under the leadership of Zeno: Pythagoras, Democritus, Leucippus, Plato and not a few others teach it. Second, of Christian writers (for so John Major, Ariminensis, Patricius Capreolus, Aureolus, Pereira and Basso wished, the last of whom proves this truth throughout a whole book on motion, and several others). Third, of recent writers: for so Arriaga, Tellez, Cornelius de S. Patricio and Spinula philosophize, whom now innumerable others follow with open war.

units.la: Verùm Zenoniste philosophi adhuc inter se diuiduntur. Quippe alij admittunt in continuo indiuisibilia numero infinita, vt Mathematici quidam. Alij pùcta, quæ vocant inflata, eò quia licèt in se maneant indiuisibilia, tamen diuisibilem retineant vbicationem, qua diuisibiliter sint in spatio, modò maiori, modò minori, quemadmodum Angelus, qui sanè indiuisibilis est, loco tamen diuisibili coexistere potest.
units.tr: But the Zenonist philosophers are still divided among themselves. Some admit that there are infinitely many indivisibles in the continuum, as certain mathematicians do. Others admit points which they call "inflated", because although they remain indivisible in themselves, they nevertheless retain a divisible location, by which they are divisibly in space, now in a larger space, now in a smaller one, just as an angel, which is indeed indivisible, can nonetheless coexist with a divisible place.

units.la: Sed neutra sententia probè collimat in punctum. Non prima, ideo enim infinita concedit puncta, quia pauca nullam facerent extensionem. Contra tamen, & rogo: cur v. gr. centum puncta non darent extensum? Respondent, quia inuicem penetrarentur. Si hoc verum est, igitur & infinita penetrabuntur. Probo sic. Centesimum v. g. punctum etiamsi octo, & nonaginta intermedia sint, penetratur cum primo; ergo penetrabit, quamuis & alia innumera interponantur.
units.tr: But neither opinion aims well at the point. Not the first, for it concedes infinitely many points on the ground that a few would make no extension. Yet I ask: why would, say, a hundred points not make an extended thing? They answer that they would penetrate one another. If this is true, then infinitely many will also penetrate. I prove it thus: the hundredth point, even though ninety-eight intermediate points lie between it and the first, is penetrated with the first; therefore it will penetrate, though countless others be interposed.

units.la: Secunda quoque opinio de punctis inflatis omnino difflanda est, quippe ventosa magis, quàm solida. Quomodo enim indiuisibile per modum extensum ac diuisibilem vbicari potest? alioquin deber concedi, extensum aliquid in inextenso esse receptum. Deinde modus, quem habet Angelus occupandi locum diuisibilem, & extensum, conuenit illi ratione spiritualitatis, & replicationis eidem naturaliter debitæ: sed punctum est materiale, neque vi suæ naturæ potest vnquam replicari, ergo ad locum diuisibilem coextendi nequit.
units.tr: The second opinion, about inflated points, must also be utterly dispelled, being more windy than solid. For how can an indivisible be located in the manner of an extended and divisible thing? Otherwise it must be conceded that something extended is received in what is unextended. Next, the mode which an angel has of occupying a divisible and extended place belongs to it by reason of its spirituality and of the replication naturally due to it. But a point is material, and by virtue of its nature can never be replicated; therefore it cannot be co-extended with a divisible place.

units.la: Dicendum igitur est, continuum solis punctis mathematicis, & quidem finitis componi.
units.tr: Therefore it must be said that the continuum is composed of mathematical points, and indeed of finitely many.

units.la: Lacunæ in fine.
units.tr: Lacunae at the end.

units.la: Resoluuntur obiectiones.
units.tr: The objections are resolved.

units.la: EA est veritatis, aut saltem probabilitatis in tota Philosophia conditio, vt quò magis detegit se, atque ostendit, eò etiam facilius in tela occurrat argumentorum. Quod enim extat, obuium, & ad manum est, facilè prehendi, atq; concuti potest. Vnde non mirum si doctrina de solis punctis in continuo, quæ tam plana, suasibilis, & rationi conformis videtur, hoc sibi præiudicium creat, quòd ex vmbra dum prodit, vndique ictibus pateat. Innumeri sunt, qui proripiunt arma, & mathematica puncta cæsim, punctimq; profligare contendunt. Quid nos? an labimur animo qui ratione fulcimur? ipsa nos teget quantitas; & cum nequeat penetrari, procul etiam abiget ictus. Primò autem argumeta ex physicis; mox verò ex mathematicis excipienda sunt.
units.tr: Such is the condition of truth, or at least of probability, throughout the whole of philosophy: the more it reveals and displays itself, the more easily it falls under the darts of arguments. For what lies open and at hand is easily seized and can be shaken. Hence it is no wonder that the doctrine of points alone in the continuum, which seems so plain, persuasive and in conformity with reason, brings this prejudice upon itself: as soon as it comes out of the shadow, it lies exposed to blows from every side. Innumerable men rush forward with weapons and strive to cut down and rout the mathematical points piecemeal. What shall we do? Do we slip in spirit, we who are supported by reason? Quantity itself will cover us, and since it cannot be penetrated, it will also drive the blows far away. First, however, the arguments from physics must be taken up; afterwards those from mathematics.

units.la: Obijcies 1. ex physicis. Vnum indiuisibile additum alteri non facit extensionem, ergo ex solis indiuisibilibus constare non potest continuum. Probatur antecedens Indiuisibile additum alteri penetratur cum illo, ergo non facit extensionem. Antecedens patet. Indiuisibile tangit aliud secundum se totum, si enim tangeret quoad partem solummodo, iam diuisibile foret; sed quod aliud tangit secundum se totum penetratur cum illo; ergo. Probatur minor. Quod tangit aliud secundum se totum, nihil habet extra illud, ergo penetratur.
units.tr: You will object first, from physics: one indivisible added to another does not make an extension; therefore the continuum cannot consist of indivisibles alone. The antecedent is proved: an indivisible added to another is penetrated with it; therefore it does not make an extension. The antecedent is plain: an indivisible touches another according to its whole self. For if it touched only in part, it would already be divisible. But what touches another according to its whole self is penetrated with it. Therefore... The minor is proved: what touches another according to its whole self has nothing outside it; therefore it is penetrated.

units.la: Respond. imprimis retorquendo argumentum. Qui enim sic arguit, vel admittit cum Philosopho puncta terminativa, & continuatiua, aut partes dumtaxat. Si primum, arguo sic. Indiuisibile tangit partem secundum se totum; ergo penetratur cum illa, & in duplici loco iam est. Similiter in contactu corporum: superficies tangit aliā quoad se totam, ergo penetratur cū illa. Ita in globo: punctum globi tangit aliud in plano secundū se totū, ergo penetratur cū illo: sed hæc aduersarius nō concedit, ergo male arguit, indiuisibile penetrari cū alio, eò quòd tangit illud quoad se totū. 2. si partes tantùmodo admittit, cōtra sic retorqueo. Pars tangit aliā secundū aliquid sui, ergo penetratur cum illa secundū aliquid sui. Probo consequentiam. Indiuisibile ideo totum penetratur cum alio, quia tāgit illud quoad se totū: sed etiam pars tangit aliam quoad aliquid sui, ergo cum ea penetratur quoad aliquid sui. Ratio est, nam pars tam bene tangit secundum aliquid, sicut indiuisibile secundum totum.
units.tr: I reply, first, by retorting the argument. For whoever argues thus either admits, with the Philosopher, terminative and continuative points, or admits only parts. If the first, I argue thus: an indivisible touches a part according to its whole self; therefore it is penetrated with it and is already in a double place. Similarly in the contact of bodies: a surface touches another surface according to its whole self; therefore it is penetrated with it. So too in a globe: a point of a globe touches another point on a plane according to its whole self; therefore it is penetrated with it. But the opponent does not concede this; therefore he argues badly that an indivisible is penetrated with another because it touches it according to its whole self. If he admits only parts, I retort thus: a part touches another according to some portion of itself; therefore it is penetrated with it according to some portion of itself. I prove the consequence. An indivisible is penetrated with another for this reason, that it touches it according to its whole self. But a part also touches another according to some portion of itself; therefore it is penetrated with it according to that portion. The reason is that a part touches in some respect just as well as an indivisible touches according to its whole.

units.la: Resp. autem directè negando vtrumque antecedens. Non enim sequitur, punctum penetrari cum alio, quia tangit illud secundum se totum, adhuc enim indiuisibile .a. v. gr. totum iacet extra .b. vnde non penetratur. Et ratio facilis est; quia licèt punctum quoad se totum tangat aliud, non tamen reperitur in vna, eademque vbicatione cum illo, sed omnino diuersa. Ex.g. designemus in extrinseco spatio decem puncta vnum immediatè post aliud: collocetur in spatio .a. primum indiuisibile; in .b. secundum, in c. tertium, & sic vsque ad vltimum. Certè hoc dato, satis facilè concipitur, vnum indiuisibile manere omnino extra illud, quod immediatè post sequitur: & adhuc tangere secundum se totum; ad hoc enim requiritur solum, vt primum immediatè sit post secundum, siue illi contiguum. Et probo, si enim eisdem in spatijs, a. b. c. d. &c. immediatè sibi succedentibus collocentur decem Angeli, primus tanget secundum, & sanè quoad se totum; secundus tertium, &c. Nam vbi non sunt partes, aliqua duo tanguntur quoad tota, dummodo simpliciter se tangant. Quemadmodum vero in dato casu Angelus non penetraretur cum alio (maneret enim vnusquisque in diuersa vbicatione) ita de punctis dicendum, quæ licèt materialia, in ratione tamen se tangendi explicari commodè possunt ex dicto exemplo.
units.tr: But I reply by directly denying both antecedents. For it does not follow that a point is penetrated with another because it touches it according to its whole self. The indivisible, say a, as a whole still lies outside b, and so it is not penetrated. The reason is easy: although a point touches another according to its whole self, it is nevertheless not found in one and the same location with it, but in a wholly different one. For example, let us mark ten points in extrinsic space, one immediately after another. Let the first indivisible be placed at a, the second at b, the third at c, and so on to the last. Certainly, with this granted, it is quite easy to conceive that one indivisible remains entirely outside that which immediately follows it, and yet touches it according to its whole self. For it is required only that the first be immediately after the second, or contiguous to it. And I prove it: if ten angels were placed in the same successive spaces a, b, c, d, etc., the first would touch the second, and indeed according to its whole self; the second would touch the third, and so on. For where there are no parts, any two things touch as wholes, provided they simply touch each other. Just as in the given case an angel would not be penetrated with another (for each would remain in a different location), so it must be said of points. Although they are material, in the account of touching they can be conveniently explained by the example just given.

units.la: Vrges. Indiuisibile si tangit aliud secundum se totum, eo ipso nihil habet extra illud, secus enim non tangeret secundum se totum; ergo est intra, & sic penetratur. Consequentia patet, nam si Deus vellet, duo puncta, quæ iam se tangunt, inuicem penetrari, vel eorum contactus fieret maior, vel non: si secundum, ergo prius iam penetrabantur; si primum, ergo tunc non se tangebant secundum totum, sed quoad partem solummodo. Probatur, quia data penetratione se tangerent magis, ac proinde non tangebant se prius omnino.
units.tr: You press: if an indivisible touches another according to its whole self, then by that very fact it has nothing outside it; otherwise it would not touch according to its whole self. Therefore it is within, and so it is penetrated. The consequence is plain: for if God willed that two points which already touch should penetrate each other, either their contact would become greater or it would not. If it would not, then they were already penetrating before. If it would, then they were not touching according to their whole selves before, but only in part. This is proved because, with penetration granted, they would touch more closely, and consequently they did not touch wholly before.

units.la: Resp. negando antecedens, & pariter consequentiam. Ratio manifesta est, quia punctum alteri contiguum, & ideo tangens illud secundum se totum, adhuc totum iacet extra, non intra. Et probo ut supra, nam v.g. superficies digiti .a. tägit quoad se totam superficiem digiti .b. contigui,& nihilominus ambę manent extra: indiuisibile sphaerici tangit quoad se totum indiuisibile plani, vt concedit Philosophus, cum tamen alterum in suo sphaerico maneat: alterum quoque in suo plano. Itā etiam in circulo ducuntur lineae à circumpherentia in centrum: sed hoc manet extra lineas: ergo indiuisibile per hoc quòd alteri addatur non ideo intra constitutum est. Minor patet, nam si centrum, quòd omnes terminat lineas, fieret intra, iam effet in singulis, & ideo replicatum. Ratio autem deducta est supra, quia contactus non fit per modum informationis; duo enim puncta quoad se tota se tangentia, semper distinctas retinent vbicationes, di uersisque spatij loculis correspor dey, vnde non sequitur penetrat o.
units.tr: Reply: I deny the antecedent and likewise the consequence. The reason is plain: a point contiguous to another, and so touching it with its whole self, still lies wholly outside it, not inside. I prove this as above. For example, the surface of finger A touches the whole surface of the adjoining finger B, and yet both remain outside each other. An indivisible of the sphere touches with its whole self an indivisible of the plane, as the Philosopher concedes, yet each remains in its own place: the one in its sphere, the other in its plane. So too in a circle lines are drawn from the circumference to the centre, yet the centre remains outside the lines. Therefore an indivisible, by being added to another, is not thereby placed inside it. The minor is clear: if the centre, which terminates all the lines, were inside them, it would be in each of them and so would be replicated. The reason was deduced above: contact does not occur by way of informing, for two points touching with their whole selves always keep distinct locations and correspond to different places of space. Hence it does not follow that they penetrate.

units.la: Quare ad probationem argumenti, resp. quòd si Deus penetrare vellet punctum cum puncto, ea poneret intra, nimirum in eadem vbicatione,adeout vni spatij loco ambo corresponderent. In quo casu punctum .a. nõ tangeret magis .b.sed vbicatio vnius intima euaderet alteri. Adest exemplum de Angelis, immediatè vno post alium collocatis, vt supra, nam fi primus existat in loco .a. fecundum in .b. ille tangit istum quoad fe totum, non tamen penetratur: fiet verò penetratio, fi vterque aut in solo .a. siue in .b. solo constituatur. Ex quibus tandem hauritis quomodo ex punctis haberi posit extensio.
units.tr: So to the proof of the argument, I reply that if God wished to penetrate point with point, he would place them inside one another, namely in the same location, so that both would correspond to one place of space. In that case point A would not touch B more closely, but the location of the one would become intimate to the other. There is an example in the angels, placed immediately one after another, as above. For if the first exists in place A and the second in place B, the first touches the second with its whole self, yet is not penetrated. Penetration would occur only if both were established in A alone or in B alone. From these things you may finally grasp how extension can be had from points.

units.la: Obiicies 2. Si continuum componitur solis punctis, necessario sequitur, omnem motum localem æquè fieri velocem:sed hoc experientijs contradicit,ergo. Sequela probatur, nam fi aquila v. g. incipiat moueri cum testudine super aliquod planum, in quo decem puncta signata sint, dum aquila primum transit punctum,etiam testudo illud ipsum transire debet. Ratio est, nam fi tunc mouetur, vnum indiuisibile saltem dimetitur. Similiter dum aquila præteruolat fecundum, testudo pariter it præter illud; ergo tandem aliquando aquila cum testudine pari velocitate spatium tranfibunt.
units.tr: You will object (2): if the continuum is composed of points alone, it necessarily follows that every local motion is equally fast; but this contradicts experience; therefore the premise is false. The consequence is proved thus: if an eagle begins to move together with a tortoise over some plane on which ten points are marked, then when the eagle first crosses a point, the tortoise must also cross that same point, for if it moves at all, it measures at least one indivisible. Likewise, while the eagle flies past the second point, the tortoise also passes beyond it. Therefore at last the eagle and the tortoise will traverse the space with equal speed.

units.la: Refpond. imprimis retorquendo argumentum in eos, qui admittunt partes in continuo cum punctis, hac ratione.
units.tr: I reply first by turning the argument back on those who admit parts in the continuum along with points, in this way.

units.la: Dum aquila in instanti .a. incipit moueri, primam solummodo transit partem in spatio, ergo & punctum continuatiuum, alioquin pars ea non foret diuisibilis, vt concedunt: sed etiam testudo facit hoc ipsum ; ergo vtrinque par motus. Probo minorem, quia testudo, vtcunq; paululu in instanti .a. moueatur, si reuera mouetur, primam in spatio transit partem cum suo puncto. Similiter in instanti .b. aquila transit secundam spatij partem cum secundo puncto ; sed etiam testudo totum hoc facit; ergo par motus contingit.Neq; dicas, Aquilam in instanti .a. maiore trasite partem,ideoq; ferri velociorem.Contra .n. insto : Ergo pertransfit multa puncta simul. Hoc vero si concedas, & ego dicam, velocius moueri aquilam super quantitate solis punctis conflata, quia plura puncta,quàm testudo, pertransfit simul. Contra 2. sic. Excogito in re mobili vnum ex punctis, quæ aduersarij cocedunt; mox insto. Punctum hoc nequit deferri ad partem spatij diuisibilem, vt supra diximus in pyramide ; igitur mobile nequit moueri: sed mouetur; ergo in continuo post puncta non inuenit partes.
units.tr: While the eagle begins to move at instant A, it crosses only the first part of the space; therefore also the continuative point, otherwise that part would not be divisible, as they concede. But the tortoise does the very same thing; therefore on both sides there is equal motion. I prove the minor: however slightly the tortoise is moved at instant A, if it really moves, it crosses the first part of the space with its point. Likewise at instant B the eagle crosses the second part of the space with the second point, and the tortoise does all of this too; therefore equal motion occurs. Nor should you say that the eagle at instant A crosses a greater part and is therefore carried more swiftly. For against this I insist: then it passes over many points at once. But if you grant this, I too will say that the eagle moves more swiftly over a space compounded of points, because it passes over more points at once than the tortoise does. Against the second point, I argue thus: I take one of the points in a moving body, which your opponents concede. Then I insist: this point cannot be carried to a divisible part of space, as we said above in the case of the pyramid. Therefore the mobile cannot move. But it does move; therefore, in the continuum, after the points they find no parts.

units.la: Respondetur directè, motum testudinis fieri segniùs ; aquilæ autem velocius, quia hæc pauciores nectit morulas in spatio : illa verò plures habet quietes. Ita senserunt Empedocles, Democritus, & Epicurus, quorum sententiæ ingeniosi, doctique neoterici assenassentiuntur. Et ratio est, quia vt fequenti libro videbimus, nequit alio modo tarditas, & velocitas modus ex-poni.
units.tr: The direct answer is that the motion of the tortoise is slower, while that of the eagle is faster, because the eagle makes fewer pauses in space, whereas the tortoise has more rests. So Empedocles, Democritus and Epicurus thought, and the clever and learned moderns assent to their opinions. The reason is that, as we shall see in the following book, slowness and speed cannot otherwise be explained.

units.la: Obijcies 3. Sint duo puncta .a. & c. quæ tangant aliud intermedium b. ilta non facerent extensionem, ergo nulla facient. Probatur minor, nam sicut ea, quæ sunt eadem vni tertio, sunt eadem quoque inter fe; ita quæ sunt proxima vni tertio, sunt proxima inter fe: at punctum .a. & c. proxima sunt vni tertio b. igitur & inter fe, ac proinde sunt omnino in .b. non faciunt ergo extensum.
units.tr: Objection 3: let there be two points A and C which touch another, intermediate point B. They would not make an extension; therefore nothing will make one. The minor is proved thus: just as things that are the same as a third thing are the same as each other, so things that are near a third thing are near each other. But points A and C are near the third point B; therefore they are near each other too, and consequently they are wholly in B. Therefore they do not make an extended thing.

units.la: Respondetur cum distinctione: quæ sunt proxima vni tertio sunt proxima inter fe, illo modo, quo approximantur tertio, concedo; alio modo, negatur. Itaque cum .a. & c. sint proxima .b. per contactum, non per idem vbi, sequitur etiam, quòd sint proxima inter fe non per vnum, idemque, sed per vbi diuersum; quod cum ita fe habeat, vt primum fit extra fecundum, & hoc extra tertium, facit etiam vt .a. c. b. maneant extra fe ipsa, & sic reddant extensionem.
units.tr: I reply with a distinction. Things near a third are near each other in the way in which they approach the third, I grant; in another way, I deny. Thus, since A and C are near B through contact, though not through the same where, it follows also that they are near each other not through one and the same thing, but through a different where. Since this is so, and the first is outside the second and the second outside the third, it also makes A and C remain outside each other, and so renders an extension.

units.la: Axioma Qua sunt eadem vni tertio, &c. intelligitur de identitate adæqua-ta.
units.tr: The axiom "things that are the same as a third," etc., is to be understood of adequate identity.

units.la: Obijcies 4. ex Mathematica. Euclides lî. 1. propof. 10. demonstrat omnem lineam diuidi posse in duplicem æqualem partem: sed fi ea solis con-staret staret indiuisibilibus, id non contingeret, ergo indiuisibilia non faciunt quantitatem. En tibi Euclidis verba. Sit data recta linea terminata .a. b. Constituatur in ea triangulum æquilaterum a. b. c. & secetur angulus a. c. b. bisariam per lineam. c. d. Dico lineam rectam a. b. in puncto d. æqualiter secari. Adest exemplum in subiecta figura.
units.tr: Objection 4, from mathematics. Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 10, demonstrates that every line can be divided into two equal parts. But if a line consisted only of indivisibles, this would not happen; therefore indivisibles do not make quantity. Behold Euclid's words: "Let a given straight line AB be terminated at A and B. On it construct an equilateral triangle ABC, and let the angle ACB be bisected by the line CD. I say that the straight line AB is cut equally at the point D." There is an example in the figure below.

units.la: Minor argumenti probatur sic. Demus, lineam .a. b. constare v. gr. vndecim punctis: ad hoc vt æquè diuidatur, oportet quinque puncta cum dimidio relinqui ex vna parte; quinque alia cum pari dimidio relinqui ex altera: sed hoc repugnat, quia linea cadens c. d. nequit punctum secare in duo dimidia, cum sit incapax diuisionis, ergo recta .a. b. non potest diuidi bifariam. Similiter si data linea constet paribus punctis v. gr. decem, diuidi ex æquo non potest, quia sic perpendicularis c. d. inter duo caderet puncta. sed punctum alteri vnitum nil intermedium admittit, secus iam non esset vnitum, neq; tangeret secundum se totum; ergo admissis punctis in linea, hæc ex æquo non secabitur contra Euclidem.
units.tr: The minor of the argument is proved thus. Suppose the line AB consists, say, of eleven points. For it to be divided equally, five points with a half must remain on one side, and five others with a like half on the other. But this is impossible, because the falling line CD cannot cut a point into two halves, since a point is incapable of division. Therefore the straight line AB cannot be bisected. Similarly, if the given line consists of an even number of points, say ten, it cannot be divided equally, since the perpendicular CD would then fall between two points. But a point united to another point admits nothing intermediate; otherwise it would no longer be united, nor would it touch with its whole self. Therefore, if points are admitted in the line, it will not be cut equally, contrary to Euclid.

units.la: Respond. retorquendo argumentum. Primò quia si aduersarij loquuntur de triangulo rigorosè mathematico, & de linea exquisitissimè recta, perinde ac fieri possint hæc omnia instrumento aliquo physico, igitur debent etiam concedere sphæricum in toto rigore perfectum, pyramidem in puncto mathematicè definentem, &c. Sed hoc dato, rotaretur globus, & moueretur inuersa pyramis per totam lineam a. b semper in ea defignando puncta, ergo. Retorqueo 2. quia dato etiam, quòd basis a. b. fiat ex partibus in infinitum deciduis, non potest à cadente c. d. secari, ergo. Probo antecedens. Linea c. d. quæ ratione longitudinis per te habet partes, ratione tamen latitudinis in rigore indiuisibilis est, secus foret non linea, sed superficies; ergo nequit secare basim a. b. Probo. Si secaret, vel vtrinque in secta basi tangeret puncta vel partes: non primum, alioquin fuissent prius tria puncta simul continuata, nempe alterum hinc, alterum inde, atq; tertiū in sectione ablatum: Neque secundum, alioquin linea secans tangendo partem ratione longitudinis diuisibilem, tangeret prius, & posterius foret in duplici loco, replicaretur, & alia sequerentur absurda, vt c p.
units.tr: Reply: I retort the argument. First, if the opponents speak of a triangle rigorously mathematical and of a line most exquisitely straight, as though all these things could be produced by some physical instrument, then they must also concede a sphere perfect in full rigour and a pyramid mathematically ending in a point, and so on. But granting this, a globe would be rolled and an inverted pyramid would be moved along the whole line AB, always marking points on it. Therefore... I retort secondly: even granting that the base AB is made of parts infinitely divisible, it cannot be cut by the falling line CD. I prove the antecedent. The line CD has parts in respect of its length, but in respect of its breadth it is indivisible in rigour; otherwise it would be not a line but a surface. Therefore it cannot cut the base AB. I prove this: if it did cut it, it would touch on either side of the cut base either points or parts. Not points, for then three points would previously have been continuous at once, namely one on this side, one on that, and a third removed in the section. Nor parts, for then the cutting line, touching a part divisible in respect of length, would touch first, and the later part would be in a double place, would be replicated, and other absurdities would follow, as in c. p.

units.la: Respond. directè, omnem lineam diuidi posse in duas partes æquales, adeo ut æqualitas hæc sit ad sensum, & hoc tantum intendit Euclides. Linea ergo aut paribus constet punctis, aut imparibus, æquè bifariam diuidetur quoad sensum, quippe cùm vna medietas non excedat aliam, nisi vnico puncto, quod insensibile prorsus est: sequitur vtramque partem fore sensibiliter æqualem.
