Confirmatur, quia cum lineæ, figuræque omnes fiant per instrumenta rudia, impolita, imperfecta, non possunt in rigore toto mathematico esse perfectæ, sed tantummodo apparenter: vnde satis etiam est, si sectio, atq; diuisio fiat in partes ad sensum æquas. Hinc peroptimè Aristoteles 3. Metaph. c. 2. Nec enim sensibiles lineæ tales sunt, quales geometria dicit: nihil enim sensibilium ita rectum, atq; rotundum. Tangit enim circulus regulam, non secundum punctum, sed sicut Protagoras dicebat redarguens Geometras, &c. Præterea 2. Metaph. c. vltimo dixerat: Certitudinem verò sermonis Mathematicam non oportet in cunctis quærere, sed in his, quæ non habent materiam: quare non est naturalis modus, tota .n. natura forte habet materiam. Sensus est, operationes mathematicas non fieri omnino exactè in subiecta materia pingui, & rudi; sed per intellectum, qui abstrahendo à re materiali, capit lineas, puncta, figuras optimè ductas, & elaboratas. Quare sufficiet si ad sensum in triangulo materiali secetur linea ex æquo. Nec dicas. In quantitate sunt actu mathematica puncta, ergo mathematicè diuidi possunt. Negatur enim consequentia, nam ad hoc præstandum opus esset lineis à materia diuulsis figurisq; mathematicè perfectis, quæ tamen nullo modo vbi adest materia semper crassa, & rudis, haberi queunt, quemadmodum supra Philosophus. Quapropter diuidit sanè mathematicus lineam ex æquo, sed quia eam supponit, seu concipit constare punctis infinitis. Quo dato, mentaliter quidem linea secabitur in partes æquales, nam vbicumque contingat sectio, semper hinc inde relinquet segmen infinitum, & sic alteri par. Verum in subiecta materia puncta finita sunt; vnde si adsint imparia, diuidi nequibunt ex æquo. Præterea.
units.tr: I answer directly that every line can be divided into two equal parts, so that the equality holds to sense, and this is all Euclid intends. A line made up of either an even or an odd number of points will therefore be bisected equally as far as sense is concerned, since one half exceeds the other only by a single point, which is wholly insensible. It follows that each part is sensibly equal. This is confirmed by the fact that all lines and figures are produced by rough, unpolished and imperfect instruments, so they cannot be perfect in full mathematical rigour, but only in appearance. Hence it is enough if the section and division are made into parts that are equal to sense. Aristotle says this very well in Metaphysics 3, chapter 2: "For sensible lines are not such as geometry describes, since nothing sensible is so straight or so round. For the circle touches the ruler not at a point, but," as Protagoras used to say when refuting the geometers, etc. Moreover, at the end of Metaphysics 2 he had said: "Mathematical certainty of discourse is not to be sought in all things, but in those which have no matter; wherefore it is not the natural way, for all nature perhaps has matter." The sense is that mathematical operations are not carried out with complete exactness in gross and rough material; they are performed by the intellect, which, abstracting from material things, grasps lines, points and figures drawn and worked out perfectly. So it is sufficient if, in a material triangle, a line is cut equally to sense. Nor should you say: "In a quantity there are actually mathematical points, therefore they can be divided mathematically." The consequence is denied, for to achieve this we would need lines separated from matter and figures mathematically perfect, which in no way can be had where matter is always thick and rough, as the Philosopher showed above. Therefore the mathematician does indeed divide a line equally, but only because he supposes, or conceives, that it consists of infinitely many points. Given this, the line will be cut mentally into equal parts, for wherever the section falls, it always leaves an infinite segment on each side, and so one equal to the other. But in material substance the points are finite; hence, if they are odd in number, they cannot be divided equally. Furthermore.

units.la: Obijcies 2.
units.tr: Objection 2.

units.la: Si quantitas constaret solis punctis, dari posset aliqua perfecta pyramis, in qua linea basis foret minor aliqua superiori linea intra laterales contenta: sed hoc repugnat; ergo. Probatur sequela, nam si appositâ figura supponatur habere lineam basis a.10. punctorum, vnamquamque autem ex lateralibus conflatam ex 20. ducatur linea b. supra basim, hæc habebit 19. puncta: similiter super istam ducatur linea c.; pariter hæc habebit 18. puncta; & ita decrescendo vsque ad angulum o. ergo tam linea b. quàm c. sunt longiores basi. Hoc autem repugnat, quia si omnis linea inter latera ducta fit minor, & maior descendendo à vertice pyrapyramidis (nam quo magis descenditur, latera distant magis) ergo basis, quæ vltima est, debet esse cæteris longior, quod non contingit in dato casu. Adest exemplum in hac pyramide. [Triangle diagram with apex O, horizontal lines labelled C and B, base labelled A]
units.tr: If quantity consisted only of points, some perfect pyramid could exist in which the base line was shorter than some upper line contained between the sides. But this is impossible; therefore. The consequence is proved thus: if, with the figure placed here, the base line a. is supposed to have 10 points, and a line b. is drawn above the base, from the 20 points that make up each of the sides, this line will have 19 points; similarly above it a line c. is drawn, which will likewise have 18 points; and so, decreasing, down to the angle o. Therefore both the line b. and the line c. are longer than the base. But this is impossible, because if every line drawn between the sides becomes shorter and longer as one descends from the apex of the pyramid (for the further one descends, the more the sides are apart), then the base, which is the last, must be longer than the rest, which does not happen in the given case. An example is found in this pyramid. [Triangle diagram with apex O, horizontal lines labelled C and B, base labelled A]

units.la: Refpond. negando suppositum. Ratio est, quia non potest construi pyramis exactè, ac mathematicè perfecta, in qua linea basis minor fit lateralibus. Probatur, nam laterales in rigore mathematico debent sic protendi, vt quanto magis defcendunt à cuspide, tanto magis recedant à se: at descensus à cuspide fit per omne punctum, ergo per omne punctum recedere debent à se. Ponamus igitur quòd latera descendant per assignata viginti puncta; ergo illa in extremis distabunt ab invicem 20. punctis; vnde linea basis a. erit 20. punctorum; superior b. 19. c. 18. &c. Patet autem, quòd latera quò magis à vertice cadunt, eò magis etiam recedunt invicem, alioquin non effent lineæ per omne punctum inclinatæ, sed per aliqua spatia perpendiculares rectæ, quod in pyramide fieri nequit, si hæc ad scrupulum extruatur mathematicum.
units.tr: I answer by denying the supposition. The reason is that a pyramid perfect in exact mathematical accuracy cannot be constructed in which the base line is shorter than the sides. This is proved thus: in mathematical rigour the sides must extend so that the further they descend from the apex, the further they move apart from each other. But the descent from the apex goes through every point; therefore they must move apart from each other through every point. Let us suppose, then, that the sides descend through twenty assigned points; then at their extremities they will be 20 points apart from one another; hence the base line a. will be 20 points long, the upper b. 19, c. 18, and so on. It is clear that the more the sides fall from the apex, the more they also recede from each other; otherwise the lines would not be inclined through every point, but would be straight lines perpendicular through certain spaces, which cannot happen in a pyramid if it is built to a mathematical scruple.

units.la: Obijcies 3. Si foret vera Zenonis opinio, sequeretur, quòd extructo circulo maiori, & minori concentrico, tot puncta essent in minori, quot in maiori: sed hoc repugnat: ergo. Sequela probatur, nam ex quolibet puncto circuli exterioris, puta ex a. b. c. d. &c. duci possunt lineæ ad centrum. e: sed hæ transibunt per circulum interiorem, qui minor est; ergo tot puncta designabunt in minori, quot in maiori. Minor etiam de se patet, quia si circulus concentricus minor est, quomodo tot punctis conflabitur, quot maior externus? Exemplum adest in hac figura.
units.tr: Objection 3. If Zeno's opinion were true, it would follow that, when a larger circle and a smaller concentric circle are constructed, there would be as many points in the smaller as in the larger. But this is impossible; therefore. The consequence is proved thus: from any point of the outer circle, say a. b. c. d. etc., lines can be drawn to the centre e. But these will pass through the inner circle, which is smaller; therefore they will mark as many points in the smaller as in the larger. The minor premise is evident in itself, for if a concentric circle is smaller, how can it be formed of as many points as the larger outer one? An example is found in this figure.

units.la: Respond. negando sequelam. Ad probationem dico, ex quolibet puncto circuli exterioris non posse duci lineam ad centrum. Ratio est, quia lineæ ductæ à punctis circuli maioris occupabunt prius totum interiorem circulum, quàm totum
units.tr: I answer by denying the consequence. To the proof I say that from every point of the outer circle a line cannot be drawn to the centre. The reason is that the lines drawn from the points of the larger circle will occupy the whole inner circle before they occupy the whole

units.la: A. B. C. D. E. (labels of the figure) tum exteriorem. Et probatur, nam quo magis descendunt lineæ ab externo circulo, magis accedunt inter se, vnde maiora semper designabunt, seu relinquent spatia in primo circulo, & minora in secundo. Quare ad hoc tandem erit deueniendum, vt occupparo circulo toto concentrico, adhuc maneant spatia in externo ad linearum ductiones, vt patet in hac figura.
units.tr: A. B. C. D. E. (labels of the figure) then the outer one. And this is proved thus: the further the lines descend from the outer circle, the closer they come to one another; hence they will always mark, or leave, larger spaces in the first circle and smaller in the second. Therefore it must finally be granted that, once the whole concentric circle is occupied, there still remain spaces in the outer circle for the drawing of lines, as is seen in this figure.

units.la: Hoc autem dato, non possunt â quouis puncto loculorum a.b. c. d. cæterisque in peripheria manentibus duci lineæ ad centrum, eò quòd aliquando tandem non aderunt in circulo minori spatia vlla, per quæ transeant sine penetratione, vt patet in superiori parte lineis occupata. Vnde patet non verificari axioma, quòd ab omni puncto ad omne duci possit linea (nisi mentaliter, & in abstracto) constat igitur, pauciora esse puncta in minori circulo, quàm in maiori: ab isto enim aliæ possent deduci lineæ, quæ non transirent per illum.
units.tr: Given this, lines cannot be drawn to the centre from every point of the loci a. b. c. d., and the others that remain on the periphery, because at some point there will be no spaces left in the smaller circle through which they can pass without penetrating one another, as is seen in the upper part, which is occupied by lines. Hence it is evident that the axiom "a line can be drawn from every point to every point" is not true (except mentally and in the abstract). It is clear, therefore, that there are fewer points in the smaller circle than in the larger, for from the former other lines could be drawn which would not pass through the latter.

units.la: Objicies 4.demonstrat Euclides in omni ni quadrato lineam diametralem esse longiorem quauis laterali: sed posita sententia Zenonis hoc verum non esset, ergo. Maior patet in subiecto quadrato a.b.c.d. in quo si adhibito circino mensures lateralem a.c. breuior erit diametrali c.b. Minor probatur, nam data Zenonis doctrina, tot effent puncta in latere a. c. quot in diametro c: b. Si enim ducantur lineae à laterali a. c. ad lateralem b. d., singulae transibunt per diametralem, ergo tot in ista, quot in illis designabunt puncta. Quare si lineae per omnia successiua puncta ductae totum occupent latus, à quo fluunt; hae pariter totam diametrum occupabunt. Vnde puncta vtrobique parria sunt. Adest exemplum in figura.
units.tr: Objection 4. Euclid demonstrates that in every square the diagonal line is longer than any side. But if Zeno's view were held, this would not be true; therefore. The major premise is evident in the square a. b. c. d. given here, in which, if the side a. c. is measured with a compass, it will be shorter than the diagonal c. b. The minor premise is proved thus: on Zeno's doctrine, there would be as many points on the side a. c. as on the diagonal c. b. For if lines are drawn from the side a. c. to the side b. d., each will pass through the diagonal, so they will mark as many points in it as in those. Hence, if the lines drawn through all the successive points cover the whole side from which they flow, these likewise will cover the whole diagonal. Therefore the points on each are equal in number. An example is found in the figure.

units.la: Respond. imprimis retorquendo argumentum. Licet enim lateralis, atque diametralis constarent ex partibus, idem sequeretur absurdum; tot enim essent partes, & inter se omnino aequales in laterali, quot in diametrali. Probatur, quia omnis linea dum à latere fluit, designat in eo tantam partem, quantam in diametro
units.tr: I answer first by turning the argument back. For even if the side and the diagonal consisted of parts, the same absurdity would follow; for there would be as many parts in the side, and those entirely equal among themselves, as in the diagonal. This is proved because every line, while it flows from the side, marks on it as great a part as on the diagonal

units.la: {y} ... tro, supra quam transit: ergo tandem partes non solùm tot, sed æquales etiam in vtroque designabuntur. Hoc autem dici nequit, secus diameter non effet longior laterali.
units.tr: {y} ... over which it passes: therefore in the end not only as many, but also equal, parts will be marked on each. But this cannot be said, otherwise the diagonal would not be longer than the side.

units.la: Dicis quòd linea dum transit supra diametrum, designat in ipsa maiorem partem, & hoc ratione inclinationis, quam diameter habet; nam ista quò magis in clinatur, eò semper maiorem sui partem exhibet accipiendam, vt patet in linea, vel superficie o. n. quæ maius designat spatium in diametro, quàm in laterali sic vti patebit si mensures circino; vnde patet diametralem semper fore maiorem.
units.tr: You say that a line, while it passes across the diagonal, marks out a larger part of it, and this by reason of the inclination the diagonal has. For the more it is inclined, the more of its own length it always shows to be taken, as is plain in the line or surface o. n., which marks a larger space on the diagonal than on the side, as will be plain if you measure with a compass. Whence it is plain that the diagonal will always be larger.

units.la: Admitto responsionem ab aduersarijs datam: sed hæc ipsa fauet etiam nobis. Nam sicuti linea manendo inuariata, maiorem semper, maioremque partem occupat in diametro, prout magis, & magis hæc fuerit inclinata: similiter si diameter constet punctis, linea super ipsam ducta non vnicum, sed plura puncta occupabit ratione inclinationis. Neque dicas, lineam vtpotequæ indiuisibilis est, non posse occupare nisi punctum. Resp. n. hoc esse verum, quoties transit super aliam perpendiculariter rectam, non inclinatè rectam. Sicuti dicis tu, quòd partem designat partem, si diameter sit perpendicularis: maiorem verò, si procedat inclinatè. Ratio autem est, quia puncta diametri non sunt deorsum tantummodo (alioquin linea non effet inclinata) sed etiam recedunt ad costam. Ex quo fit, vt punctum non fit perpendiculariter sub alio, sed occupet locum immediatè sequentem extra perpendiculum,non enim puncta ordinantur quemadmodum in serie: a. 6.
units.tr: I admit the answer given by the opponents, but this very answer favours us too. For just as a line, remaining unchanged, always occupies a larger and larger part of the diagonal, the more and more this is inclined, so if the diagonal consists of points, a line drawn across it will occupy not one point but several, by reason of the inclination. Nor should you say that a line, being indivisible, cannot occupy anything but a point. I reply that this is true whenever it crosses another straight line perpendicularly, not when it crosses an inclined one. As you yourself say, it marks a part for a part if the diagonal is perpendicular, but a larger part if it proceeds at an incline. The reason is that the points of the diagonal lie not only downward (otherwise the line would not be inclined) but also recede toward the side. From this it follows that a point is not perpendicularly below another, but occupies a place immediately following, outside the perpendicular, for points are not ordered as in a series: a. 6.

units.la: {fig}
units.tr: {fig}

units.la: Sed vt in linea d. e. Si ergo ducatur linea ex costa, illa transeundo super diametrum vel occupabit quidem omnia puncta, quæ deorsum perpendiculariter sunt, sed non omnia etiam, quæ ad costam lateris recedunt (ex quo intelligis, diametrum habere plura puncta, quàm latus) vel occupabit omnia prorsus, quia linea discedens à latere, dum est in diametro tangit non vnicum punctum; & id ratione inclinationis. Verùm quidquid afferatur, hoc difficillimum est. Vnde
units.tr: But as in line d. e. If then a line is drawn from the side, crossing over the diagonal, it will either occupy indeed all the points which lie perpendicularly below, but not all those also which recede toward the side of the edge (from which you understand that the diagonal has more points than the side), or it will occupy absolutely all, because the line departing from the side, while it is on the diagonal, touches not a single point, and this by reason of inclination. But whatever is alleged, this is most difficult. Hence

units.la: Responderi tandem ad hæc omnia, & similia possunt, dicendo non valere a principijs mathematicis contra Zenonistas argumentari. Et ratio est, quia mathematica non loquitur de quantitate, prout in concreto, & à parte rei iacet, sed tantum de illa vt abstracta. Nimirum de puncto, quod mentaliter accipitur instar indiuisibilis, etiamsi reuera tale non possit à nobis in materia separari: de linea mentaliter sumpta sine latitudine, ac profunditate, quamquam in subiecto non possit illa sic distingui, &c. Hinc est quòd Plato 7. de Repub. dixerat, mathematicos circa quantitatem quodammodo somniari. Quippe illam sibi mente concipiunt à quauis materialitate auulsam. Et inde fit, quòd lineas diuidunt in partes æquales; non enim attendunt ad hoc, vtrum punctis constent paribus, an imparibus; verùm suppositò in illis numero punctorum infinito, qui proinde non habet vllum extremum vicinius, aut remotius alio, semper eas in æqualia segmenta diuidunt. Sic supponit, duci posse à nobis circulum rigorosè perfectum, &c. Quia mentalis operatio eum ita ducit. In re autem nequeunt hæc prorsus mathematicè fieri, quia materia neq; in lineas, neque in puncta, neque in superficies rigorosè diuidi potest. Ideo male arguitur ex abstracto ad concretum. Deinde si etiam admissa contraria opinione de partibus, aliqua tamen absurda in mathematica ex illa sequuntur; cur doctrinam nostram de punctis ob id ipsum refellunt? Absurda verò sunt, quia si linea basis confletur ex partibus, non modò bifariam secari nequit, sed nullo modo, vt supra. Ita etiam à quolibet puncto ad quodlibet non poterit duci linea in centrum, vt dictum est. Similiter nulla erit linea, quæ ad centrum terminari valeat: nam vel hoc faceret secundùm partem sui diuisibilem, aut indiuisibilem: si primum, ergo prius,& posterius in vnico puncto: si secundum, tollatur hæc pars vltima indiuisibilis: tunc sic. Linea hæc potest rursus terminare ad centrum; ergo finitur in puncto, & sic successiuè faciendo, aut cognoscemus, lineam solis constare indiuisibilibus, aut, si partibus, non posse duci ad centrum. Quæ omnia contra mathematicos etiam sunt.
units.tr: Finally, a reply to all these and similar points can be given, by saying that it is not valid to argue against the Zenonists from mathematical principles. The reason is that mathematics does not speak of quantity as it is in the concrete, and lying in the thing itself, but only of it as abstracted: namely of a point, which is taken mentally as an indivisible, even though in reality such a thing cannot be separated by us in matter; of a line mentally conceived without breadth or depth, although in the subject it cannot be so distinguished, etc. Hence it is that Plato in the seventh book of the Republic said that mathematicians somehow dream about quantity. For they conceive it in their minds, stripped of all materiality. And from this it comes that they divide lines into equal parts; for they do not attend to whether the lines consist of an even or an odd number of points, but, supposing in them an infinite number of points, which therefore has no extreme nearer or more remote than another, they always divide them into equal segments. So they suppose that a perfectly exact circle can be drawn by us, etc., because the mental operation draws it so. In reality, however, these things cannot be done mathematically at all, because matter can be divided rigorously neither into lines, nor into points, nor into surfaces. Therefore it is wrongly argued from the abstract to the concrete. Next, even if the contrary opinion about parts be admitted, some absurdities in mathematics still follow from it; why, then, do they refute our doctrine of points on that ground? The absurdities are these: if a base line is made up of parts, it cannot only not be bisected, but cannot be divided in any way, as above. Thus also a line cannot be drawn from any point to any point toward the centre, as has been said. Similarly there will be no line that can be terminated at the centre: for this would happen either according to its divisible part or its indivisible one. If the first, then there is a prior and a posterior in one point; if the second, let this last indivisible part be removed, and then: this line can again terminate at the centre; therefore it ends in a point. So proceeding successively, we shall either know that a line consists of indivisibles, or, if of parts, that it cannot be drawn to the centre. All of which is also against the mathematicians.

units.la: DISPVTATIO TERTIA.
units.tr: DISPUTATIO TERTIA.

units.la: De passionibus quantitatis raritate, densitate, ac figura.
units.tr: On the passions of quantity: rarity, density, and figure.

units.la: HÆ tres maximè passiones quantitatem afficere solent, ea siquidem rarescit, addensatur, figuramque vel retinet suam, vel subindè permutat. Inde non incongruum doctrinæ ordini, accommodum verò eruditioni arbitror nostræ, si postquam egimus de natura, & quantitatis compositione, de modo etiam quo eius rarefactio, addensatio,& figura contingit, nonnulla breuiori stylo deducamus.
units.tr: These three passions are chiefly wont to affect quantity: for it is rarefied, condensed, and either retains its figure or changes it from time to time. Hence I judge it not out of keeping with the order of our teaching, and suited to the learning of our readers, that after we have treated of the nature and composition of quantity, and also of the manner in which its rarefaction, condensation and figure come about, we should set out a few points in a rather briefer style.

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: DISQUISITIO PRIMA.

units.la: Quomodo raritas, & densitas in quan- titate fiant.
units.tr: How rarity and density come about in quantity.

units.la: PRO intelligentia præmitto definitionem rari, & densi à peripateticis traditam. Rarum definiri solet id, quod parum obtinens materia, multum occupat loci. Densum, quod multum obtinens materia, parum occupat loci. Ex quo raritatis, ac densitatis definitionem in abstracto haurire potestis.
units.tr: To prepare the understanding, I first set out the definitions of the rare and the dense handed down by the Peripatetics. The rare is usually defined as that which, having little matter, occupies much place. The dense is that which, having much matter, occupies little place. From this you can draw the definition of rarity and density in the abstract.

units.la: Hinc verò statim oritur difficultas, qua videlicet ratione res cum fit rara, sine partium disiunctione, aut replicatione se ad maiorem extendat locum: Quæ autem densa, breuiori spatio sese accommodet, sine aliquarum penetratione v.g. hoc sudariolum, quod præ manibus habeo, si explicetur æquè super cathedræ podio, tegET quatuor spatij palmos: at si nisu aliquo distrahatur hinc inde, occupabit facilè quintum. E contra si complicetur, si prematur, si manuü volis intercipiatur, ne quidem vnius digituli spatium replebit. Qui ergo fit illa distractio ad nouum loci palmum; & quomodo ista collectio ad tantulum spatij.
units.tr: Here, however, a difficulty arises at once: by what means does a thing, when it becomes rare, extend itself to a greater place without the separation or duplication of its parts; and how does a dense thing fit itself into a smaller space without some parts penetrating others? For example, this little handkerchief which I have in my hands, if spread out evenly over the cushion of a chair, covers four palms of space; but if it is pulled apart by some effort on this side and that, it easily occupies a fifth. On the contrary, if it is folded, pressed, or gripped in the fist, it does not fill even the space of a single finger. How, then, does that stretching to a new palm of place come about, and how does that gathering into so small a space?

units.la: Scotus cum suis in 4. sentent. q.4. dist. 12. putat in rarefactione acquiri nouam quantitatem, præcedenti superadditam, in eadem prorsus materia, & in densatione aliquam eius partem deperdi. Pōponacius, & Auersa censent in rarefactione, atque condensatione totam destrui priorem quantitatem, aliamque de nouo produci, maiorem fi fiat raritas; minorem fi fiat densitas.
units.tr: Scotus and his followers, on the Fourth Book of the Sentences, distinction 12, question 4, think that in rarefaction a new quantity is acquired, superadded to the previous one in the very same matter, and that in condensation some part of it is lost. Pomponazzi and Averroes hold that in rarefaction and condensation the whole prior quantity is destroyed and another is produced anew: a greater one if rarity results, a lesser one if density results.

units.la: Sed contra, quia in sententia Scoti fequeretur vel duplicem quantitatem penetrari; vel quantitate esse abfq; materia, vel quantitatem de subiecto migrare in subiectum. Probatur, nam fi dum corpus rarescit, acquiriuur noua quantitas, hæc fubiecaturne in priori materia? fi concedas, ergo duæ quantitates penetratæ.Si non:ergo cum non adueniat recens materia, noua quantitas manet fine subiecto. Si tandem quantitas recedat quousque faciat locum aduenienti; ergo accidens migrat de subiecto in subiectum. Sententia quoque Auersæ opponitur experientiæ, qua videmus in hostia v. gr. consecrata fieri rarum fine iactura primæ quantitatis &c.
units.tr: But against this: on the opinion of Scotus it would follow either that a double quantity is penetrated, or that quantity exists without matter, or that quantity migrates from subject to subject. This is proved thus. If, while the body rarefies, a new quantity is acquired, does this inhere in the prior matter? If you concede it does, then two quantities are penetrated. If not, then since no fresh matter comes in, the new quantity remains without a subject. If finally the quantity recedes until it makes room for the incoming matter, then the accident migrates from subject to subject. Averroes' opinion is also opposed to experience, by which we see, for instance, that in the consecrated host it becomes rare without loss of the first quantity, and so on.

units.la: Sanctus Thomas, cui præter suos, adhærent Complutenfes, docet rarefactionem, & densitatem fieri ex productione, ac variatione modi cuiufdam, seu qualitatis distinctæ, vi cuius magis, aut minùs extendatur quantitas ad locum, adeo tamen vt ipsa entitas quantitatis, & materiæ inuariata semper maneat.
units.tr: St Thomas, who is supported not only by his own followers but also by the Complutensians, teaches that rarefaction and density come about from the production and variation of a certain mode, or distinct quality, by virtue of which quantity is extended to a place more or less; yet in such a way that the very entity of quantity and of matter always remains unchanged.

units.la: Sed contra,quia dum corpus fit rarum, & occupat ratione talis modi superadditi locum duplo maiorem, aut vna medietas dicti corporis occupat locum totum, qui prius à tota quantitate implebatur; & sic
units.tr: But against this: when a body becomes rare and, by reason of such an added mode, occupies a place twice as large, either one half of that body occupies the whole place which was previously filled by the whole quantity, and so

units.la: vna medietas manet in duplici loco: Aut ea non implet nisi locum sibi æqualem: & sic intelligi non potest, quomodo tegat spatium duplò maius, nisi noua interueniat quantitas, vel partes interiecto vacuo deiungantur, elongentur, separentur, quæ à Thomistis non conceduntur. Similiter dum res addensatur, vel partes aliquæ recedunt intra; vel manent suo modo, vt priùs vnitę: Si primum, ergo quantitas penetratur: si secundum, ergo corpus densum non fit, vt c. p.
units.tr: one half remains in a double place; or it fills only a place equal to itself, and then it cannot be understood how it covers a space twice as large, unless a new quantity intervenes, or the parts are separated and lengthened and drawn apart with an empty space between them, which the Thomists do not grant. Similarly, when a thing is condensed, either some parts recede inward, or they remain in their former manner, united as before. If the first, then quantity is penetrated; if the second, then a dense body does not come about, as is clear.

units.la: Proinde fuit sententia Okami, cui subscribunt ingeniosi recentes, & maximè Zenonistæ, raritatem fieri per intromissionem corpusculorum; densitatem verò per eorumdem expulsionem. Quatenus nimirum corpus habet sanè quantitatem solis punctis contextam; sed puncta hæc non omnia, & singula continuata sunt: aliqua enim deiuncta manent, seu terminant extremitates materiæ, quæ ab alijs immediatè sequentibus deiunguntur. Hinc fiunt vacua quædam paruula, minima, & insensibilia, quæ per ingressum alterius corporis (maximè autem aeris tenuissimi, & summè mobilis, qui ne adsit vacuum semper ingreditur poros) modò magis, modò minùs diduci possunt, sicuti per egressum constringi. Et sic facilè capitur, qua ratione raritas, & densitas contingat. Videte hanc sententiam ingeniosè à Spinula nostro explicatam.
units.tr: Therefore the opinion of Occam came next, to which recent ingenious writers subscribe, and above all the Zenonists: that rarity comes about through the entry of corpuscles, and density through their expulsion. This is because a body indeed has quantity woven only of points, but these points are not all and each continuous; for some remain disjoined, or terminate the extremities of matter, and are separated from the others immediately following. Hence certain small, minute and insensible voids arise, which through the entry of another body (especially of the most subtle and most mobile air, which always enters the pores lest a void remain) can be spread apart now more, now less, just as they are constricted by its exit. And so it is easily grasped by what reason rarity and density occur. See this opinion ingeniously explained by our Spinula.

units.la: Sed tamen non adhuc omnino placet. Nam cùm dicit hæc opinio, quòd meatus &
units.tr: But nevertheless it still does not wholly please. For when this opinion says that the passages

units.la: & pori, qui vbique interseruntur, ne inanes, & inexpleti maneant, semper alijs corpusculis, & praesertim aeris opplentur, dicit sanè quod aliquando contingit; sed vt plurimum non videtur hoc posse fieri.
units.tr: and pores, which are interspersed everywhere lest they remain empty and unfilled, are always filled by other corpuscles, and especially by air, it surely says something that sometimes happens; but for the most part it does not seem that this can take place.

units.la: Quomodo enim corpora ex natura sua rara in suo naturali statu consortium extranei necessario admittent? Aer ipse, qui saepe rarescit, vndenam petet corpuscula in tanta copia, vt ijsdem vacua repleat sua? Deinde corpuscula haec, quae ad poros implendos alùnde accurrunt, non ne ibi relinquent vacuum, vnde migrant? Praeterea si dicitur ignis disgregare per calorem etherogenea, qua ratione cum rarescit, corpora in se patitur extranea? Demum aliqua sunt, quae rarescunt, quāuis eò subire non valeant minima, siue atomi ad vacuitates implendas, puta cùm in vase ferreo, vel aeneo hermeticè, atque apprimè clauso aqua, seu liquor huiusmodi per subiectum ignem, causamue persimilem rarefit; nam etsi tunc spiritus ignei per minimos illabantur meatus, non tamen videntur ingredi ad tantam copiam, quae insignem causent rarefactionem. Exinde stabilienda est.
units.tr: For how will bodies which are rare by their very nature admit a foreign companion of necessity in their natural state? The air itself, which often rarefies, from where will it seek corpuscles in such abundance as to fill its voids with them? Next, do not these corpuscles, which hasten from elsewhere to fill the pores, leave a void where they came from? Moreover, if it is said that fire separates heterogeneous things by its heat, by what reasoning, when it rarefies, does it suffer foreign bodies to enter into itself? Finally, there are some things which rarefy although no minute particles or atoms can enter to fill their voids: for instance, when water or a liquid of this kind is rarefied in a hermetically and very tightly closed vessel of iron or bronze, by a fire placed beneath it or some very similar cause. For although the fiery spirits then slip in through the smallest passages, yet they do not seem to enter in such quantity as to cause a notable rarefaction. Hence the matter must be settled otherwise.

units.la: CONCLVSIO PRIMA.
units.tr: CONCLUSIO PRIMA.

units.la: Dantur in corporibus vacua minima, quæ nullo corpore alio repleta sunt.
units.tr: There are in bodies minimal voids, which are filled by no other body.

units.la: PRobatur 1. in animalibus, quæ insensibilem faciunt substantiæ transpirationem, vt alibi satis effusè probatum est: sed non posset fieri huiusmodi transpiratio, si vacua minima ijs non inessent; ergo. Probatur minor, quia v. gr. dum sudor exit per meatus, porosque sub cute latentes, aut eos inuenit omnino repletos corpore, aut non. Si primum, concipis iam non posse fieri sudoris egressum, eò quòd corpus corpori obstat; vel si fit, cogeris admittere penetrationem. Si secundum, concedis iam vacua, nam quid est, poros non esse omnino plenos, nisi hoc quòd in ijs vacuola sunt? Hinc optimè dixit Orpheus apud Aristotelem 2. de gen. anim. cap. 1. Vt retis implexu animalia constituit. Nam sicuti retia filis intexuntur per vacua intercepta connexis, ita corpus animalium. Accedunt plantæ, quæ humorem à radicibus trahunt, eumque toto corpore in truncū, & ramos, in sirpos, folia, fructusq; distribuunt, adeo sanè, vt non adsit fibra, porus, venula, per quam insensibilis non meet vapor nutritiuus. At nisi adessent minimæ quedā vacuitates, quomodo corpora hæc subirent? sibi aditu facerent? alia de loco truderet? Confirmatur, quia ignis particulæ recipiuntur in aere; aeris minima sub aquas labuntur; aquarum guttulę sese terram insinuant. Corpora demum odorosa, calida, frigida, noxia, &c. in continuo motu sunt, abeunt, redeunt, feruntur sursum, deorsum, circum. Quod, inquit Lucret. in 1.
units.tr: It is proved first from animals, which make an insensible transpiration of their substance, as I have shown at length elsewhere. Yet such a transpiration could not occur if minimal voids were not present in them. Proof of the minor: when, for example, sweat comes out through the pores and passages lying beneath the skin, either it finds these wholly filled with body or it does not. If the first, you must suppose that the sweat cannot get out, since body hinders body; or, if it does get out, you are forced to admit penetration. If the second, you already concede voids, for what does it mean that the pores are not wholly full, except that there are little vacuities in them? Hence Orpheus, cited by Aristotle, De generatione animalium 2, ch. 1, rightly said that he constituted animals as the interlacing of a net: for just as nets are woven from threads joined with empty spaces between them, so is the body of animals. Plants also draw moisture from their roots and distribute it through the whole body, into trunk and branches, stalks, leaves and fruits, so that there is no fibre, pore or little vein through which the nourishing vapour does not pass unseen. But if there were not some minimal vacuities, how could these bodies enter, make a way for themselves, or push one another out of place? It is confirmed also because particles of fire are received into air, minute parts of air sink under water, and drops of water insinuate themselves into the earth. Finally, odorous, warm, cold, harmful bodies and the like are in constant motion: they go out, come back, and are carried up, down and around. Which, says Lucretius, book 1:

units.la: Nisi inania sint, qua possent corpora quaque
units.tr: Unless there were empty spaces, through which bodies could pass in every direction,

units.la: Transfire, haud illa fieri ratione videres.
units.tr: You would see that things could not be done in that way.

units.la: Probatur 2. quia si non adessent in natura hæc vacua, nullus fieri posset motus localis. Consequens absurdum est; ergo. Probatur antecedens à Lucretio 1 1. adducendo exemplum de piscibus, dum innatant vndis. Nam quoties mouetur piscis, certè hic pellit vndam, & ista quidem cedit aliò: aut igitur cedit in vacuum, aut non: Si primum, hoc est, quod volo: si secundum, inuenit resistens, & sic non mouetur vnda. Dicis moueri piscé, nullo etiā dato vacuo, nam quidquid antrorsum pellitur, hoc non abit ad occupandum inane interspersum, sed confluit à tergo, vt repleat locum à pisce relictum. Contra tamen, quia reuera cum piscis mouetur, circumquaque per orbem pellit aquas, vt in crispis circulariter ductis apparet, neq; vndæ motæ antrorsum illæ sunt, quæ statim à tergo refluant. Vel igitur quæ pelluntur antrorsum, cedunt in alias, & hoc non, quia penetrarent; Vel abeunt in vacua, & sic, &c. Contra 2. nam si manus injiciatur in aquam, & maneat immota, certè occupat locum priùs ab aqua occupatum. Quò igitur abiere partes depulsæ? nil profecto superest, nisi multitudo vacuorum. Neque respondeas, tunc aquam circumcirca turgere, seu magis ad littus refundi. Contra enim est, quia si turget aqua, ergo de suo loco aliquantrudit aeris partem supra se accumbentem, de qua redibit argumentum. Vel enim hæc cedit in aliam, aut post se inuenit vacuum: si neutrum dicas, ergo aer nequit moueri, & sic nec aqua fuit mota, nec piscis, &c.
units.tr: It is proved second, because if these voids did not exist in nature, no local motion could occur. The consequence is absurd; therefore so is the antecedent. The antecedent is proved by Lucretius, book 1, using the example of fish as they swim in the waves. For whenever a fish moves, it certainly pushes the water, and the water indeed yields and gives way somewhere else. Either, then, it gives way into a void, or it does not. If the first, that is what I want. If the second, the water meets resistance, and so the water is not moved. You say the fish moves even with no void given, for whatever is pushed forward does not go off to fill the empty space scattered through the water, but flows in from behind to fill the place the fish has left. Against this: in fact, when the fish moves, it pushes the water all round in a circle, as appears in circular ripples on the surface, and the waves are not only those moved forward; those which flow back immediately behind it are moved too. Either, then, what is pushed forward gives way into other parts, and this does not happen because they would have to penetrate; or it passes into voids, and so on. Second against this: if a hand is put into water and kept still, it certainly occupies a place previously occupied by water. Where, then, have the parts that were pushed away gone? Surely nothing remains except a multitude of voids. Nor should you reply that the water then swells all around, or is poured back more towards the shore. On the contrary, if the water swells, then it certainly thrusts part of the air lying above it out of its place, and the same argument returns. For either this air gives way into another place, or it finds a void behind it. If you say neither, then air cannot be moved, and so neither water nor fish was moved, and so on.

units.la: Aut igitur motu priuandum est corpora quaque.
units.tr: Either, therefore, all bodies must be deprived of motion,

units.la: Aut esse admixtum dicendum rebus inane.
units.tr: Or it must be said that void is mixed in with things.

units.la: Vnde initium primium capiat res quaque mouendi.
units.tr: So that every thing may take its first beginning of moving.

units.la: Inde Xutus quidam, vt refert Aristot. 4. phys.c.9. arguebat inferens, quòd nisi tale vacuum daretur, in quouis motu orbis vniuersus fluctuare deberet. Quando enim quid mouetur, partesq; abigit proximas, quònam istæ recipiunt se? an in loca prorsus occupata? si hoc verum est; corpora ergo, quæ occupant, alió cedant necessum est. Sed offendent in alia; & sic illa etiam recedent, vnde processus hic adusque superficiem orbis vltimam fiet. Ergo dato quocumque motu, vel vniuersus fluctuat orbis, vel interiecta corporibus vacua concedenda sunt. Hæc sanè concedit Aristoteles in aqua, & præcipuè marina. Quærens enim sect.22.problem. T 2 15.
units.tr: Hence a certain Xutus, as Aristotle reports (Phys. 4, ch. 9), argued by inference that unless such a void were granted, the whole universe would have to ebb and flow in every motion. For when something is moved and drives away the neighbouring parts, where do those parts withdraw? Into places wholly occupied? If that is true, then the bodies that occupy those places must necessarily give way to others; but they will strike against others, and so these too will recede, and this process will go on right up to the outermost surface of the universe. Therefore, given any motion whatever, either the whole universe ebbs and flows, or empty spaces must be granted between the bodies. Aristotle certainly concedes this in the case of water, and especially sea water. For inquiring (Problems, sect. 22, problem 15) why the sea is clearer and more transparent than water fit for drinking, he answers himself that this happens because the salt, being larger, leaves empty interstices, etc. Then in Meteorology 4, ch. 8, he says that some bodies do not melt, nor expand any further, because they have passages into which something can penetrate.

units.la: 15. cur mare fit perfpectius, & dilucidius, quàm aqua potu idonea, respondet sibi, hoc fieri, eò quod falsa amplioribus interstitijs inanit, &c. Deinde 4. meteor. c.8. ait aliqua corpora non liquescere, nec magis ampliari, quia gerunt meatus, intra quos penetrare nequeunt corpulentis aquæ gutta, &c.
units.tr: 15. Why the sea is clearer and more transparent than water fit for drinking: he answers himself that this happens because salt water is emptied through wider interstices, etc. Then at Meteorology 4, chapter 8, he says that some bodies neither melt nor expand more, because they have passages through which the coarse drops of water cannot penetrate, etc.

units.la: Probatur vltimò ratione à priori ex ipfa corporum constitutione. Siquidem atomi primigeniæ, quæ pro rerum compaginationibus à Deo factæ sunt, cùm diuersa, multiplicique constent figura, eò ipso quòd in mixto vniuntur, non accòmode prorsus adhærent, adrepunt, sed iuxta ponunt; sed suismet angulis, mucronibus, extantijsq; impeditæ vacuitates inter se relinquunt, insensibiles quidem, sed aliquas tamen. Pulchrum ad rei explicationem affert exemplum Gaffendus epist. 4. de apparente magnitudine solis. Concipe grana diuersorum generum effusa in modium. Profecto ibi nullum granum est, quod à proximis non attingatur; sed tamen quædam adhuc interstitia manent; vnde si modium aliqualiter succutias, equidem subsidit, non granis in grana cedentibus, verùm quia singula cuspides æquè magis adaptant cuspidibus, latera lateribus, &c. & sic quò maior succutiendo habebitur granorum accommodatio, eò minor ab ijsdem locus occupabitur. Plura, & quidem non inuenusta in rei huiusce confirmationem addere possem; at iam scitis quæ nos premant angustiæ. Pro cunctis erit venustissimum opus manuscriptum, ab Illustriss. & Reu. Io: Delphino Aquileiae Patriarcha nuper confectum, in quo Democriti Philosophiam de vacuo rebus adspersso ad poeticae lyrae metrum, vir ipse chordatissimus, omniq; scientiarum numero absolutissimus cecinit.
units.tr: It is proved last by an argument a priori from the very constitution of bodies. For the primordial atoms, which were made by God for the composition of things, though they consist of diverse and manifold shapes, when they are united in a mixed body, do not adhere perfectly closely or creep into one another, but lie side by side; and, hindered by their own corners, points and projections, they leave empty spaces between them, insensible indeed, but still some. To explain the matter Gassendi offers a fine example in his fourth letter on the apparent size of the sun. Imagine grains of different kinds poured into a measure. Certainly there is no grain there which is not touched by its neighbours; yet some interstices still remain; hence if you shake the measure a little, it sinks down, not because the grains yield to one another, but because each point fits more closely against points and each side against sides, and so the more the grains are packed by shaking, the less space they occupy. I could add more, and indeed not inelegant, things to confirm this matter; but you already know what straits press upon us. For all of these there will be a most charming work in manuscript, recently composed by the Most Illustrious and Reverend Giovanni Delfino, Patriarch of Aquileia, in which that most harmonious man, perfect in the whole number of the sciences, sang the philosophy of Democritus concerning the void, sprinkled with flowers, to the metre of the poetic lyre.

units.la: CONCLVSIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: SECOND CONCLUSION.

units.la: Raritas non fit solum ex corporum egressu verum & per maiorem vacui apertionem. Densitas etiam ex corporum ingressu, & ob vacui exclusionem.
units.tr: Rarity arises not only from the going out of bodies but also from a greater opening of vacuum. Density arises too from the entry of bodies and from the exclusion of vacuum.

units.la: PRobatur experientijs, quae satis ostendunt, quantitatem rarescere, quoties à re quanta extramittuntur corpuscula, ut v. gr. si à panno ex repetita virgarum verberatione puluisculi excutiantur, & minima quaedam lanugo pilorum de textura meatulis efferatur, in quo casu pannum euadit molle, rarum, ad plicas aptū, &c. Tunc autem fit maior partium vnius ab alia deductio, & proinde vacuolorum intercapedo. Patet hoc magis in cera, pice, resina, & similibus, quae si ad ignem purgentur, extramittendo faeces, & quidquid extranei commixtum erat, rationes manent, locumque implent maiorem. At quomodo substantia, quae per alterius egressum certe minor est, ad noui spatij occupationem explicat se, nisi quia pars à parte abscedit magis, & crebra vacua fiunt? Hinc est quòd corpora quò magis euadunt rara, eò etiam fragiliora sunt, nimirum præ deiunctione partium. Hinc pariter quòd magis diaphana manent, scilicet ob maius vacuum, facilè admittens lucem. Hinc similiter quòd minùs impediunt sonum, videlicet præ interruptione meatuum, &c. Quapropter fiet etiam raritas, quamquam nulla corpuscula foras mittantur, modò tamen contingat hæc partium vnius ab alia deductio.
units.tr: This is proved by experiments, which sufficiently show that quantity becomes rarer whenever small particles are sent out from a quantified body. For example, if dust is shaken out of cloth by repeated beating with rods, and some minute fluff is drawn out of the texture of its pores, the cloth becomes soft, rare, apt for folds, and so on. Then one part is drawn further away from another, and so there is an interval of small vacua. This is more evident in wax, pitch, resin and similar things: when they are purified by fire, sending out dregs and whatever foreign matter was mixed in, the remaining parts stay and fill a greater space. But how does a substance, which is certainly smaller because something has gone out of it, extend itself to occupy a new space, unless because part recedes from part more, and many vacua arise? Hence bodies, the rarer they become, the more fragile they are, namely because their parts are pulled apart. Likewise they remain more transparent, namely because of the greater vacuum, which readily admits light. Likewise they impede sound less, namely because of the interruption of their passages, and so on. Therefore rarity will also arise, although no corpuscles are sent out, provided only that this drawing apart of one part from another takes place.

units.la: Probatur 2. circa densitatem. Quamuis enim possit corpus addensari ob ingressum, & commixtionem alterius, quemadmodum cinis in patera, qui ex aqua infusa constipatur magis, & ad minus contrahitur spatium. Nihilominus addensatio ex mera maioris vacui exclusione vtplurimum haberi solet; si nimirum comprimantur partes, adeout quæ longiùs distabant, propriùs accedant. Recolitæ quod supra deduximus à Gassendo in exemplo de modio granis referto. Sed res hæc facilis est, fæque ipsa suadet satis.
units.tr: It is proved in a second way concerning density. For although a body can be condensed by the entry and mixing of another, as ash in a dish is packed more tightly when water is poured into it and contracts into less space, nevertheless condensation is commonly held to arise from the mere exclusion of a greater vacuum, namely when the parts are pressed together so that those which were further apart come closer. Recall what we deduced above from Gassendi, in the example of a bushel filled with grain. But this matter is easy, and the thing itself sufficiently persuades.

units.la: Placet hic apponere theorema non inuenustum. Quantitas quælibet sine rarefactione, sine inflatione, sine aliculus partis acquisitione maiorem, & minorem locum occupare naturaliter potest. Hæc propositio probatur euidenter ex principijs geometricis, nam inter figuras isoperimetras, aut æqualis ambitus, quæ plures continet angulos, capaciorem habet aream, locumque occupat maiorem. Hinc circulus inter figuras isoperimetras capacissimus est. Consulite Clavium in sphæram Ioan. de Sacro B. cap. 1.
units.tr: It pleases me to set down here a not unpleasing theorem. Any quantity, without rarefaction, without inflation, without the acquisition of any part, can naturally occupy a greater or a smaller place. This proposition is clearly proved from geometrical principles: among figures of equal perimeter, the one that contains more angles has a larger area and occupies a greater place. Hence the circle is the most capacious of figures of equal perimeter. Consult Clavius on the Sphere of John of Sacrobosco, chapter 1.

units.la: Eadem igitur quantitas absque rarefactione potest maiorem, & maiorem occupare locum, si nimirum varias, variasq; subeat figuras, vt ex 35. primi Euclidis confirmari potest in parallelogrammatibus.
units.tr: The same quantity, therefore, without rarefaction, can occupy a greater and greater place, if it undergoes various and varied figures, as can be confirmed from the thirty-fifth proposition of the first book of Euclid, in parallelograms.

units.la: Hinc ingeniosa nequitia quispiam vicino suo imposuit, cui erat ager quadratus, qualis e. f. Ipse vero habebat qualis b. d. persuasus n. antiquæ simplicitatis vir, vt commutaret agrum, ratus æqualis esse areæ, quod æqualis esset peripheriæ, inuenit experimento minùs fæcundum b. d. quàm esset primus e. f. Discite hinc, posse duas vrbes, quæ parem habeant ambitu, esse magnitudine inæquales, vnde solent falli qui magnitudinem loci ab externo ambitu dimetiuntur. Demum aduertite, hoc debere intelligi de quantitate secundum lineas, quæ inuariata maius, minusquè spatiū tenere potest; non de quantitate, quoad omnem dimensionem, quæ si maiore occupat locū, rarescat etiam opus est.
units.tr: Hence a clever rogue once tricked his neighbour, who had a square field such as e.f. The rogue himself had one such as b.d. He persuaded the man, who was of old-fashioned simplicity, to exchange fields, thinking them equal in area because they were equal in perimeter. He found by experiment that b.d. was less fertile than the first, e.f. Learn from this that two cities which have an equal circuit can be unequal in size, which is why those who measure the size of a place by its outer circuit are often deceived. Finally, notice that this must be understood of quantity according to lines, which, unchanged, can hold a greater or smaller space; not of quantity in every dimension, which, if it occupies a greater place, must also be rarefied.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISQUISITION II.

units.la: Vndenam figura in quantitate contingat.
units.tr: Whence figure arises in quantity.

units.la: PRO intelligentia notetur, ad tria rerum genera praesentem attinere disquisitionem, videlicet ad ea, quae sensu pollent, quae solum vegetant, quae animà prorsus destituta sunt. Singula enim sua gaudent figura, eamq; naturali quodam instinctu amant. Sic araneam v.gr. videmus nasci corpore breuiusculam, sed abdomine plenam, ore valde patulo, renui collo, rotundo capite, cruribus praelongis, articulatim distinctis. Ita etiam inter plantas cornum intuemur hinc inde flexam, nodis contortam, ramis incondite refertam, sed è contra pinus recta ex pede consurgit, aequa, procera,& quadam veluti manu dolata. Sic lapilli, & gemmae suis quaeque gaudent figuris, vt vnio rotundà, coralium ramosa, crystalus cubicà, &c. Vndenam igitur haec in animalibus, plantis, inanimisq; figurarum varietas? Res quidem obscura est; verùm praestat aliquid attentare. Videtur itaque triplici ex capite oriri, vt res omnis naturae ingenio sua figura donetur. Primò ex intentione agentis ad finem. Secundò ex necessitate materiae. Tertiò ex loci dispositione, in quo res quaeque formatur.
units.tr: To begin with, let it be noted that the present inquiry concerns three kinds of things: those that have sense, those that only grow and live, and those that are wholly without soul. Each has its own figure, and each loves its figure by a certain natural instinct. Thus we see, for example, that the spider is born small in body but full in the abdomen, with a very wide mouth, a slender neck, a round head, and very long legs, jointed one by one. Likewise among plants we see the horn-tree bent this way and that, knotted with joints, and crowded with branches in no order; but on the other hand the pine rises straight from its root, even and tall, as if shaped by some hand. So too pebbles and gems each have their own figures: the pearl is round, coral branched, the crystal cubic, and so on. Whence, then, comes this variety of figures in animals, plants, and inanimate things? The matter is indeed obscure, yet it is worth making an attempt. It seems, therefore, that the figure of every natural thing, given by the skill of nature, arises from three sources. First, from the intention of the agent toward its end. Second, from the necessity of matter. Third, from the arrangement of the place in which each thing is formed.

units.la: Et quidem ex intentione agentis ad finem habetur figura in animalibus, nam opus naturæ cum sit opus intelligentiæ, ipsumque esse rei ad operandum ordinetur, ideo Sapientissimus rerum Opifex, vim & facultatem dedit seminibus, qua sese in hanc, & in aliam figuram efformient, prout singulæ iuuant magis ad obeundas animalium functiones. Hæc autem virtus illa est, quæ dicitur à Philosophis organica, & formatrix, de qua egregiè Galenus l. de visu partium, & per eam ita expeditur membrorum fabrica, vt vitalium actionum sit ministra industris ad finem intentum deducens. Ita homo v. gr. pedes habet oblongos, quia cum rectus debeat incedere, basis requiritur non nimis angusta ne cadat. Equus, & bos quia multiplici gradiuntur, eos habent minus producios. Auiculæ, quæ duobus consistunt, latos quidem habent, sed non plenos, ne grauarent volantes. Ita quoque dentes facti sunt alij à natura expansi ad hoc vt cibum auferant; alij acutiores, vt scindant; lingua mobilis, humida, spongiosa, vt veluti manus fragmina prehendat, sub maxillas deferat, si nimis arescant, infundat humorem, &c. Eodem prorsus modo in homine, aliisque animalibus causam facile inuenies, cur tale membrumeiusmodi habuerit figuram, obseruabisq; cōmodiorem seligi non potuisse ad proprias obeundum operationes. Vt in araneis capacem altiuum, quia ibi congeri debet materia pro telarum contextu.
units.tr: And indeed, the figure in animals arises from the intention of the agent toward its end. For since the work of nature is the work of intelligence, and the very being of a thing is ordered to its operation, the most wise Maker of things has given the seeds a power and faculty by which they shape themselves into this figure or that, as each best serves the performance of the animal's functions. This power is what the philosophers call organic and formative, of which Galen speaks admirably in his book On the Use of the Parts; through it the structure of the limbs is so fashioned that, being the servant of the vital actions, it leads them by suitable means to the end intended. Thus man, for example, has long feet, because since he ought to walk upright, a base is needed that is not too narrow, lest he fall. Horses and oxen, because they walk on many feet, have them less long. Small birds, which stand on two feet, have broad feet but not full ones, lest they weigh down their flight. So too teeth are made, some by nature spread out for the purpose of tearing off food, others sharper for cutting; the tongue is mobile, moist, and spongy, so that, like a hand, it may gather up the fragments, carry them under the jaws, and, if they dry out too much, pour on moisture, and so on. In exactly the same way, in man and other animals you will easily find the reason why a given member has such a figure, and you will observe that a more suitable one could not have been chosen for performing its proper operations. So in spiders the belly is wide, because there matter must be gathered for the weaving of webs.

units.la: T
units.tr: T

units.la: in apibus aculeum, quia figendus est ad succum è floribus hauriendum; in formicis patulum os,& dentulis preacutum, quia granula decidunt, surripiunt, alioq; adsportant, &c.
units.tr: In bees the sting, because it must be thrust in to draw up the juice from flowers; in ants the open mouth, with very sharp little teeth, because they cut off the grains, snatch them away, carry them elsewhere, and so on.

units.la: Secundò nascitur figura ex necessitate materiæ, quod tam in animalibus, quàm in vegetantibus fit. Hoc autem sic expli-co. Materia seminalis, quam natura pro singulis rerum generibus initio constituit, vim retinet in se plasticam, siue vt supra diximus, formatricem. Et hæc illa est, quæ similia congregando simlibus,trahit hinc inde partes,apponit, vnit, quousque paruulum semen ex aliorum additione corporum augeatur, & in debitam concrescat molem. Quare virtus hæc plastica, & seminalis ita est concipienda,vt adinstar magnetis circum emittat suos radios, qui profecto non omnes vno modo censendi sunt validi, sed prout membri,aut prope, aut procul efformandi conditio poscit. Inde partes, quæ trahuntur, in eam subibunt configurationē, qua illas radij plasticæ virtutis configurabunt. Nisi mauis dicere figuram ex materiæ necessitate contingere: sic, quia in femine puta nucis, piri, coronei, &c. sic iam graphicè ducta totius arboris fabrica, sed per stamina sic leuia tenuia, subtilia, vt quidem ibi lateat radix, truncus, ramus, frons, fructus, ea tamen sensu attingi non possint ob paruitatem, cui veritati egregiè videtur annuere D. Aug. l.6. de Gen.ad litt. c. 23. inquiens. In ipso grano iam sui-
units.tr: Second, figure arises from the necessity of matter, which happens in animals as well as in plants. I explain this as follows. The seminal matter, which nature at the beginning established for each kind of thing, retains within itself a plastic, or, as we said above, a formative power. This is the power that, gathering like things to like, draws parts from here and there, applies them, joins them together, until the tiny seed is enlarged by the addition of other bodies and grows into its proper bulk. Therefore this plastic and seminal power is to be conceived as sending out its rays on every side, like a magnet; these rays are certainly not all to be judged equally strong, but are such as the condition of the member being formed, whether near or far, requires. Thus the parts that are drawn in take up that configuration into which the rays of the plastic power shape them. Unless you would rather say that figure arises from the necessity of matter: for example, in the seed of a nut, a pear, or a quince, the whole structure of the tree is already, as it were, drawn in outline, though through fibres so fine, slender, and subtle that the root, trunk, branch, leaf, and fruit lie hidden there and cannot be perceived by the senses because of their smallness. To this truth St. Augustine seems admirably to assent, in On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 6, chapter 23, saying: "In the grain itself all those things were already present invisibly together, which in the course of time rise up as a tree.

units.la: Some lines at the foot of the page are cut off or illegible. inuisibiliter erant omnia simul, quæ per tempora in arborem surgunt. Quamobrē sicut magni artificis est, ait Seneca epist. clausisse totum in exiguo, ita Deus opificij sui miracula in eo videtur ostendisse, vt in parvo seminę rerum ingentium structuras elegantissimo nexu delineauerit. Hoc autem posito, facillime quis causam dabit, cur hæc planta, frons ista, hic fructus, hoc animal vnam potius, quàm aliam petat figuram. Eò videlicet quia prima eius textura hoc prorsus modo præerat in semine, cumque fiat augmentum ex sola partium iuxta priorem formam appositione, haud mirum, si ex hoc semine talis compositi figura, ex alio diuersa corsurgat. Inde possunt cuique fieri suasibilia, quæ refert Plutar. 8. simpos. culmum ordeaceum excreuisse in homine, qui vrinæ difficultatem diu passus erat. Similiter id, quod perhibent de spica pharis è naso fœminæ prognata. Pariter quod inquit Cabeus 1. meteor. r. 53. se vidisse oleum à nuce muscata expressum, quod in ampulla hermeticè clausa positū, ingenio, & vi sua efformauerat se in arborem, in qua ramuli, folia, fructusq; viruerant. Hac etiam ratione quod scribit Gassendus 1.4. de plantis c. 4. extitisse pastorem Taraconensem, è cuius pectore succreuit prunulus, cùm ipse delapsus in prunum non eruisset quidquid spinarum inhæserat cuti. Enim vero, si vno in seminulo tota latet rei adaugendæ, atq; ad nostrum sensum educendæ structura mi-
units.tr: Wherefore, as it is the mark of a great craftsman to have enclosed the whole in a small space," says Seneca in his Epistles, "so God seems to have shown the wonders of his workmanship in this, that in a small seed he has traced the structures of great things with most elegant connection." Having granted this, anyone may very easily give the reason why this plant, this leaf, this fruit, or this animal takes one figure rather than another. Namely, because its first texture was just this very one in the seed, and since growth takes place only by the addition of parts in accordance with the earlier form, it is no wonder if from this seed a figure of such a composition arises, and from another a different one. Hence there can be made for anyone the plausible stories that Plutarch relates in the eighth book of the Symposiacs: that a barley stalk grew in a man who had long suffered difficulty in passing urine. Similarly, what they report of an ear of spelt sprung from a woman's nose. Likewise what Cabeus says in the first book of his Meteorology, chapter 53, that he saw oil pressed from nutmeg, which, placed in a flask sealed by the hermetic method, had by its own power and vigour shaped itself into a tree, in which twigs, leaves, and fruits had grown green. By the same reasoning is what Gassendi writes in the fourth book of his work on plants, chapter 4: that there was a shepherd of Tarragona, from whose breast a little plum tree grew up, after he had fallen onto a plum tree and had not pulled out whatever thorns had stuck in his skin. Indeed, if in one tiny seed the whole structure of a thing to be enlarged and brought out to our senses lies hidden,

units.la: Vnde tam. rum non est, si hæc omnia enascantur, vbi exordia iam sua tenent. Vellem adesset opus eruditissimum P. Athanasij Kircheri, quod audio nuper editum hoc titulo inscriptum (Mundus Subterraneus) in quo recepi mira esse, quæ refert de seminalibus corpusculis, intra quæ dicit à se visas rerum augendarum icunculas, & imagunculas plusquam phrygio textu depictas. Vnde fatetur, se adhibito microscopio intuitum esse in animalium seminibus quasi animalcula ipsa iam egregiè configurata. Quæ si vera sunt, habetis iam causam varietarum in compositis configurationum, ex materiæ seminalis necessitate ortarum. Quidquid tamen sit hæc de re, illud est citra dubitationem, quòd in rerum productionibus, incrementisque nulla de nouo substantia producitur, sed à virtute plastica, in seminibus, radicibusue abdita substantiales particulæ circumquaque trahuntur, apponuntur, complasmantur; & inde oriuntur configurationes, vt supra. Vnde inquit August. l. 5. de gen. c. 23. quòd copiâ terra, humorique magnitudo illa congesta est.
units.tr: it is no wonder that all these things sprout forth when they already hold their beginnings. I would wish that the most learned work of Father Athanasius Kircher were at hand, which I hear was lately published under this title, Mundus Subterraneus, in which I have read the marvels he relates about the seminal corpuscles, within which he says he has seen little images and little pictures of things to be enlarged, depicted in more than Phrygian embroidery. Whence he confesses that, using the microscope, he has looked into the seeds of animals and seen as it were little animals already admirably configured. If these things are true, you already have the cause of the variety of compound configurations, arising from the necessity of the seminal matter. Whatever the truth of this matter, this is beyond doubt: that in the production and growth of things no new substance is produced; rather, by the plastic power, substantial particles hidden in seeds or roots are drawn from every side, applied, and joined together, and from this arise the configurations, as above. Whence Augustine says, in book 5 of On Genesis, chapter 23, that "that great mass was gathered from the abundance of earth and moisture."

units.la: Demum figura rerum exoriri videtur à loci dispositione, in quo fiunt. Exemplum adest luculentum ex modulis quibusdam ligneis, vbi recondi solent pira, poma, fructusque alij, qui diuersas hominum, equorum, ac similium configurationes referre videntur. Fructus enim paruus formâ ligneâ, siue modulo inclusus, multo illo, quo potest, incremento in circumferentiam crescit, cumq. per tempus vnamquamq: interioris modulivacuitatem repleat, assumit ipse figuram, quam intra se modulus habet. Consimili etiam ratione res naturales diuersimodè figurantur iuxta loci capacitatem. Vnde in metallis marchesitæ, in lapidibus gemmæ, sal in succis, nix in concretionibus, prout in fodinis, mineris, locisque vbi se premunt, se terúnt, se patiuntur, ad hunc, illumue modum configurantur. Ex quibus hic obiter discite, figuram siuè à natura, siue per artem rebus inductam, nil esse aliud omnino, quàm tales, ac tot materiæ partes, hoc, illoq; modo vbicatas.
units.tr: Finally, the figure of things seems to arise from the arrangement of the place in which they are made. A clear example is found in certain wooden moulds, in which pears, apples, and other fruits are commonly kept, and which seem to take the shapes of men, horses, and similar things. For a small fruit, enclosed in a wooden form or mould, grows outward into its circumference with as much growth as it can, and as time goes on it fills the emptiness of the mould within, and so takes on the very figure which the mould has inside itself. In a similar way natural things are variously shaped according to the capacity of the place. Hence in metals marcasite, in stones gems, salt in juices, snow in concretions, are configured in this or that way, according as they are pressed together, rubbed, and suffer in the mines, the ore-beds, and the places where they are confined. From these examples learn here in passing that figure, whether given to things by nature or by art, is nothing else at all than such and so many parts of matter, placed in this or that manner.

units.la: Finis Quinti Libri.
units.tr: End of the Fifth Book.

units.la: LIBER SEXTVS PHYSICORVM
units.tr: Book Six of the Physics

units.la: De motu ad Locum.
units.tr: On Motion to a Place.

units.la: REbus iam quantis, & in debita magnitudinis mole constitutis natura indidit facultatem se se mouendi ad locum, quæ facultas in mobili ante cæteras nobilissima est. Siue quia motus localis aduenit subiectis in esse iam suo constitutis, ideoq; perfectis; vel quia per hunc res omnis eo deferri potest, vbi melius tueatur se, aliamq; sibi consimilem ad suæ speciei propagationem gignat. Quæ duæ causæ præcipuæ sunt, cur natura motum localem amet. Nos proinde cum naturalia composita sub ratione mensuræ, quantitatisq; contemplati iam simus, non nisi aptè ad motum localem, qui præcipua est eorundem qualitas, gradum facimus, in eo paulisper mansuri.
units.tr: Things already of definite size, and fixed in their due mass of magnitude, nature has endowed with the faculty of moving themselves to a place. Among mobile things this faculty is the most noble. It is so either because local motion comes to subjects already established in their being and therefore perfected, or because by it every thing can be carried to where it may better preserve itself and beget another like itself to propagate its species. These are the two chief reasons why nature loves local motion. Therefore, having now considered natural composites under the aspect of measure and quantity, we take our step rightly to local motion, which is their chief quality, and we shall remain in it for a little while.

units.la: Sed imprimis aduerto, motum abire in duplicem. Alius enim est, qui dicitur Continuus; & alius, qui Discretus. Per illum res mouetur ab extremo ad extremum, itaut successiuè coexistat spatio intermedio, priusquè transeat vicinio-rem, deinde partem longius distantem: sic se mouet res quæcumq; materialis; v. g. lapis quando cadit, seu proijcitur. Per discretum è contra, mouetur aliquid sic, vt priorem totum locum relinquat simul, & alium quoq; locum simul totum acquirat. Hoc modo se se mouent spiritualia, vt Angelus v.g. qui totum gymnasiū potest simul destituere, totumq; cubiculum immediatè sequens occupare simul.
units.tr: But first I note that motion is of two kinds. One is called continuous, the other discrete. By the former, a thing is moved from extreme to extreme, so that it successively coexists with the intervening space, passing first to the nearer part and then to the part more distant. In this way any material thing moves, for example a stone when it falls or is thrown. By the discrete kind, on the other hand, something is moved in such a way that it leaves its whole former place at once, and at the same moment acquires another place entire. In this way spiritual beings move, for example an Angel, who can at once abandon a whole gymnasium and immediately occupy, all at once, the bedchamber next to it.

units.la: Secundo aduerto, posse rem in loco dupliceter constitui; Videlicet per motum localem; & per meram præsentiæ collationem. Priori modo res constituitur in loco naturaliter, eo quòd natura non alia ratione ad noua loca res defert, nisi per motum. Posteriori modo acquiritur locus miraculose, quando nimirum à Deo producitur noua præsentia localis, quæ recepta in corpore, statim absq; motu de termino ad terminum, illud constituit in loco. Sic v.g. Corpus Christi ponitur sub hostia, non quia producatur de novo, aut per motum è cælo descendat, sed quia confertur illi noua præsentia, virtute cuius intelligitur esse hic, aut alibi, &c..
units.tr: Secondly I note that a thing can be constituted in a place in two ways: namely by local motion, and by the mere conferral of presence. In the first way a thing is placed in a place naturally, since nature brings things to new places by no other means than motion. In the second way a place is acquired miraculously, when God produces a new local presence, which, once received by the body, establishes it in a place immediately, without motion from term to term. Thus, for example, the body of Christ is placed under the host, not because it is produced anew, or descends from heaven by motion, but because a new presence is conferred upon it, by virtue of which it is understood to be here, or elsewhere, and so on.

units.la: Res ergo præsens non attinet ad motum Discretum, sed continuum, qui corporearum rerum proprius est. Neq; ad modum locandi miraculose per collationem præsentiæ, sed per motum physicum, & realem, qui naturalis dicitur. Agemus enim de motu locali prout fit à natura, & de loco etiam prout acquiritur naturaliter. pis cadit; casus iste non est simul totus in toto spatio, sed prius in una parte, deinde in alia, itaut cum fit in secunda, cessat in prima. Haec autem successio partium sive motus non uno modo a philosophis explicatur. Chrysost. Magnenus l. de atomis disp. 3. prop. 43. dicit esse quandam entitatem simul in natura manentem, nec nisi quoad spatia extrinseca successivam. Alij putant, esse accidens ab vbicationibus distinctum, illisque superadditum, &c. Nos doctrinam seligimus communem, &c. solidam.
units.tr: A present thing therefore pertains not to discrete motion but to continuous motion, which is proper to corporeal things. Nor does it pertain to the miraculous mode of placing by the conferral of presence, but to physical and real motion, which is called natural. For we shall treat of local motion as it is effected by nature, and of place as it is acquired naturally. [...] a stone falls; this fall is not all at once in the whole space, but first in one part, then in another, so that when it is in the second, it has ceased to be in the first. This succession of parts, or motion, is not explained in one way by the philosophers. Chrysost. Magnenus (De atomis, disp. 3, prop. 43) says it is a certain entity remaining in nature at once, and successive only with respect to extrinsic spaces. Others think it is an accident distinct from the ubications and added to them, and so on. We choose the common doctrine, which is sound.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Motus non aliud est, nisi multitudo vbicationum successiuarum, seu quae in re mota sibi vna post aliam succedunt.
units.tr: Motion is nothing other than a multitude of successive ubications, that is, those which in the moved thing succeed one another, one after another.

units.la: PRobatur quia non alio modo potest concipi res esse in motu, nisi per hoc, quod vbicationem, in qua reperitur, iam deserat, aliam immediate post acquirat, deinde aliam successiue, quousque ad vltimam venerit. Sed in hoc nihil praeterea est, quam tales inuicem successiuae vbicationes; ergo. Probo minorem, quia si aliud quid est, maxime actio productiua vbicationum: sed haec admitti non debet; ergo solae ipsae vbicationes. Probo minorem, quia vbicatio cum sit modus, non producitur per actionem distinctam, sed immediate ipsa de rebus dimanat, sicuti curuitas, circulatio ; rectitudo , &c. Igitur motus non aliud est, quàm hæ vbicationes per successionem productæ.
units.tr: It is proved thus: a thing cannot be conceived as being in motion except by this, that it abandons the place (ubication) in which it is found, then immediately acquires another, and then successively another, until it comes to the last. But in this there is nothing besides such successive ubications one after another; therefore (motion is nothing besides them). I prove the minor: for if something else were involved, it would above all be a productive action of the ubications; but this ought not to be admitted; therefore only the ubications themselves. I prove the minor: since ubication, being a mode, is not produced by a distinct action, but flows immediately from the things themselves, just as curvature, circularity, rectitude, etc. Therefore motion is nothing other than these ubications produced in succession.

units.la: Opponis. Debet fieri motus, vt acquirantur vbicationes, ergo motus aliud quid est præter ipsas. E contra. Potest haberi hæc, & illa vbicatio sine motu ; ergo motus in vbicationibus non consistit. Primum patet, quia vt res vbicetur in r. f. t. debet ad eas ferri per motum ; ergo motus ante vbicationes iam adest. Probatur & secundum, quia dum res iam reperitur in r. aut in f. habet sanè aliquam vbicationem : sed tunc potest ibi quiescere, igitur hæc, aut illa vbicatio sine motu erit.
units.tr: You object: motion must occur in order that the ubications be acquired; therefore motion is something other than them. On the contrary: this ubication and that one can be had without motion; therefore motion does not consist in the ubications. The first is clear, because for a thing to be ubicated in r, f, t it must be carried to them by motion; therefore motion already exists before the ubications. The second is also proved, because while the thing is already found in r or in f, it certainly has some ubication; but then it can rest there, therefore this or that ubication will be without motion.

units.la: Resp. ad primum distinguendo antecedens. Vt acquirantur vbicationes, debet fieri motus per alias vbicationes, concedo; sine aliis prioribus, nego. Itaque vt mobile constituatur in r. f. t. debet sanè moueri ex a. b. c. &c. sed tamen ille motus prior non aliud erit, quàm ipsæmet vbicationes a. b. c. cum cæteris inuicè successiuis. Non ergo adest motus ab aliqua vbicationum collectione distinctus. Resp. ad secundum, posse quidem haberi hanc, illamue vbicationem sine motu, puta si mobile quiescat in r. aut in f. vel in t. disiunctiuè tamen, & per modum terminij non collectiuè, ac per immediatam successionem: quomodo enim concipies rem deserere vbicatione m r, & se immediatè recipere in f. deinde in t. sine motu ?
