units.tr: I reply to the first by distinguishing the antecedent. For the ubications to be acquired, motion must occur through other ubications: I grant it; without other prior ones: I deny it. Thus, for the mobile to be constituted in r, f, t, it must indeed be moved from a, b, c, etc.; but that prior motion will be nothing other than the ubications a, b, c themselves together with the rest, successive one to another. So there is no motion distinct from some collection of ubications. I reply to the second that indeed this or that ubication can be had without motion, for instance if the mobile rests in r, or in f, or in t, but disjunctively, and by way of terminus, not collectively, and by immediate succession: for how would you conceive a thing deserting the ubication r, and immediately receiving itself in f, then in t, without motion?

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: SECOND DISQUISITION.

units.la: An motus naturalis in fine sit velocior.
units.tr: Whether natural motion is swifter at its end.

units.la: PRO intelligentia notandum est, procedere quæstionem de motu grauium decidentium. De leuibus enim, aut de ijs, quæ comparatiuè dicuntur leuia, & ascendunt, erit à nobis dicendum alibi. Hac in re autem P. Rodericus Arriaga disp. 4. de gener. sec. 5. subsec. 3. negat motum naturalem esse in fine velociorem, & dicit, quodcumq; mobile siue graue sit & deorsum; aut leue sit, & sursum feratur, semper vna ratione moueri. Conuincunt experientiæ ipsæ in contrarium, vnde sit.
units.tr: To understand this, it should be noted that the question concerns the motion of heavy bodies falling. Light bodies, or those called light in comparison, which rise, will be discussed by us elsewhere. On this point, however, P. Rodericus Arriaga (disp. 4, de generatione, sec. 5, subsec. 3) denies that natural motion is swifter at its end, and says that whatever mobile body, whether heavy and carried downward or light and carried upward, always moves by one and the same rule. Experience itself refutes this, as follows.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Motus naturalis descendentium in fine velocior est.
units.tr: The natural motion of things descending is swifter at the end.

units.la: PRobatur 1. in aqua de tegulis domorum cadentE; nam à principio descendit continua, in progressu autem in varias guttas diuellitur, non aliam certè ob causam, nisi quia pars aquæ longius à tecto delapsa incitatur maiori velocitate, ac proinde à superiori discontinuata citius in terram cadit.
units.tr: It is proved first from water falling from the tiles of houses. At first it descends in a continuous stream, but in its progress it breaks apart into separate drops. This happens for no other reason than that the part of the water which has fallen farther from the roof is driven with greater velocity, and so, being separated from the water above, it reaches the ground more quickly.

units.la: Probatur 2. ex maiori sonitu, ac strepitu, quem res motæ faciunt, si ex loco editiori mouentur. Quare si v. g. ex altitudine 20. pedum globus ligneus demittatur in peluim, & postea hic ipse descendat ex 30 longè maior fiet sonitus in vltimo casu, quàm in primo: ergo quia maior impetus conceptus est: sed hic non habetur, nisi per motum velociorem, vt de se patet, ergo.
units.tr: It is proved second from the greater sound and noise that moving things make when they move from a higher place. So if, for example, a wooden ball is dropped from a height of 20 feet into a pool of mud, and afterwards the same ball falls from 30 feet, the sound in the last case will be much louder than in the first. This is because a greater impetus has been acquired. But this is not possible unless the motion is swifter, as is plain of itself. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Probatur 3. nam quò altior est lapsus, idem corpus grauiorem causat ictum, quod videtur ab aquila naturaliter aduerti, dum arreptam vnguibus testudinem ex alto demittit, quemadmodum Æschilus poeta nimirum tragicè sensit. Nequit autem res imprimere magis, vrgere, intus ire nisi per motum, qui maior sit. Nā si crescit effectus, causam quoque crescere necessum est.
units.tr: It is proved third: the longer the fall, the heavier the blow the same body delivers. This seems to be something that the eagle naturally notices, when it drops a tortoise seized in its talons from a great height, as the tragic poet Aeschylus surely understood. Now a thing cannot strike harder, press more forcefully, or penetrate more deeply except through a motion that is greater. For if the effect increases, the cause must necessarily increase as well.

units.la: Probatur 4. euidenti, eaq; facillima experientia, nam si demittas globum ex altitudine vlnarum 20. enumera pulsu quantum temporis in eo motu insumatur, & sint v. gr. 4. pulsationes. Mox eumdem globum demitte, sed ex altitudine duplò maiori, deprehendes in toto eo casu non insumi 8. pulsationes, verùm circiter 6. cum globus terminat 40. spatij vlnas; ergo motus globi velocior in fine, quàm in principio est; alioquin si æquè semper succederet, non dimetiretur in duplici pulsatione spatium æquè magnū, ac illud, quod in quadruplici transit.
units.tr: It is proved fourth, by an evident and very easy experiment. If you drop a ball from a height of 20 ells, count with your pulse how much time is spent in that motion, say it is 4 beats. Then drop the same ball again from a height twice as great, and you will find that the whole fall does not take 8 beats, but about 6, when the ball reaches the end of 40 ells of space. Therefore the motion of the ball is swifter at the end than at the beginning. For otherwise, if it always proceeded at the same rate, it would not cover in two beats a space equal to that which it crosses in four.

units.la: Quæres causam huiusce incrementi velocitatis? Resp. eam sanè perdifficilem esse ad inueniendam, quapropter à philosophis diuersa etiam assignari solet. Keplerus, & Gassendus autumant, grauia trahi à terræ globo, simili prorsus modo, quo ferrum à magnete. Quæ opinio non ita facilè, vt videtur aliquibus, irridenda est. Legatur Gassendus in Epist. 1. de motu impresso à motore translato c. 12. Non tamen omnino placet, quia præter cætera sequeretur, corpora, quæ viciniora terræ sunt, quamuis ab editiori non caderent, fore trahenda velociùs; quòd repugnat experientiis, vt supra.
units.tr: You will ask the cause of this increase in speed. I reply that it is indeed very hard to discover, and for this reason philosophers commonly assign various causes. Kepler and Gassendi hold that heavy bodies are drawn by the globe of the earth in exactly the same way that iron is drawn by a magnet. This opinion is not to be dismissed as lightly as it seems to some. Let Gassendi be read in his first Epistle on motion impressed by a mover, chapter 12. Yet it does not altogether please me, because among other things it would follow that bodies nearer to the earth would be drawn more quickly, even if they did not fall from a higher place. This contradicts experience, as shown above.

units.la: Secunda sententia communis tenet, hanc motus accelerationem oriri ex medio. Sed hoc etiam non vno modo explicatur. Seligo probabiliorem, & eum redarguo. Sebastianus Basso art. 4. de motu, supposito id à natura inditum esse rebus, vt mutuam abhorreant à se deiunctionem; ideoque foras pellant quidquid societatem frangit, quemadmodum patet in mari, fluminibus, &c. vnde nec aeri denegandum est: Inquit, posse duas afferri causas cur grauia decidentia motum accelerent. Prima est quia dum graue cadit, aer confluens à tergo ad vacuum replendum premit magis. Alia quia subiectus aer vtpote successiue motus, in processu resistit minùs, & minùs.
units.tr: The second opinion, which is the common one, holds that this acceleration of motion arises from the medium. But this too is not explained in only one way. I select the more probable version and refute it. Sebastian Basso (art. 4, on motion) supposes that nature has implanted in things a mutual aversion to being separated, and that therefore they drive out whatever breaks their union, as is seen in the sea, in rivers, and so on. For this reason air must not be denied the same. He says that two causes can be given why falling heavy bodies accelerate their motion. The first is that as the heavy body falls, the air flowing in from behind to fill the void presses harder. The second is that the air below, since it is moved successively, resists less and less as the motion proceeds.

units.la: Verùm hæc opinio, quæ totam causam accelerationis refundit in medium, probabilis mihi non est. Primò quia si per aerem fieret compressio à tergo decidentis, cur etiam à tergo ascendentis non contingeret, motumque sursum non iuauaret? nam ad vtrumque confluit aer, seq; ponè mobile claudit. Secundò quæ magna compressio hæc est, si prope cadentem lapidem non extinguitur candelæ flamma, & ne vix mouetur? Quæ rursus compressio, si ab aere titionum cadêtium fumus deorsum non traditur? Tertio neq; aer infernè scissus potest causare accelerationem. Primo quia mobile decidens non scindit solummodo, sed etiâ aerem condensat. Patet hoc in sputo, quod prope terram in frustra scinditur, ob aerem densum, ac resilientem. Et multò magis patet, si tabula expansa in latitudinem deiiciatur, quippe licèt aerem sub se positum addenset, velocius tamen in fine cadit. Præterea si aeris discissio est causa tota maioris motus: ergo si post lapidem cadat immediatè alius, hic posterior citiùs cadet, primiqué tergus percutiendo vrgebit, quod tamen non constat. Denique si adesset vacuum, an non putas in eo lapidem casurum perniciùs?
units.tr: But this opinion, which attributes the whole cause of acceleration to the medium, does not seem probable to me. First, if compression of the air came from behind the falling body, why would it not also occur behind a rising body, and aid its upward motion? For air flows in to both, and closes the mobile in from behind. Second, what great compression is this, if the flame of a candle near the falling stone is not extinguished and hardly even moves? And again, what compression is it, if the smoke from falling embers is not carried downward? Third, the air split apart below cannot cause acceleration either. For first, the falling mobile does not only split the air but also condenses it. This is evident in spittle, which near the ground breaks into fragments because of the dense and resisting air. It is even more evident if an expanded board is thrown down flat, for although it condenses the air beneath it, nevertheless it falls faster at the end. Besides, if the splitting of the air is the whole cause of the greater motion, then if another body falls immediately after a stone, this second body will fall more quickly and, by striking the back of the first, will press it onward. Yet this is not established. Finally, if a void were present, do you not think the stone would fall there more swiftly?

units.la: Proinde cum huiusce celeritatis causa (tota saltem) non sit ab extrinseco, in ipso mobili adinuenienda est, dicendumque per motum; (siue conditio siue causa sit) produci aliquid rebus intrinsecum. Inde fit etiam vt cum saltare velimus, quodam naturæ instinctu retrocedamus: Dum ictum incutere, manum emouemus: dum saxum funda proijcere, illam crebro circumducamus, &c. In his enim omnibus producitur in mobili qualitas quædam, siue impetus; & sic mirum non est, fi motus augeatur in fine, quia tunc plures adsunt causæ impellentes, noui scicet impetus acquisiti. Sed quia medium prout rarius, aut densius est, aliquo modo etiam confert ad motum, vt experimur in aqua, concludendum videtur, causam accelerationis in motu esse prosectò impetum ab ipso mobili productum in se: Causam verò accelerationis, quæ hic signatim fit, partim esse impetum, sed partim quoque medium.
units.tr: Therefore, since the cause of this speed is not extrinsic (at least not wholly), it must be sought in the mobile itself. It must be said that through motion (whether it is a condition or a cause) something intrinsic is produced in things. Hence it also happens that when we wish to jump, by a certain instinct of nature we step back; when we wish to strike a blow, we draw back the hand; when we wish to throw a stone from a sling, we swing it around again and again, and so on. For in all these cases some quality, or impetus, is produced in the mobile. So it is no wonder if the motion increases at the end, since then more impelling causes are present, namely the newly acquired impetus. But since the medium, according as it is rarer or denser, also contributes somewhat to motion, as we experience in water, it seems we must conclude that the cause of the acceleration in motion is certainly the impetus produced by the mobile in itself. But the cause of the acceleration that occurs here in particular is partly the impetus and partly also the medium.

units.la: DISQVISITIO TERTIA.
units.tr: DISQVISITIO TERTIA.

units.la: Quid sit velocitas, atque tar- ditas motus.
units.tr: What velocity and slowness of motion are.

units.la: PRO intelligentia hic statim appono motus tardi, & velocis definitionem. Velox dicitur, qui paruo tempore conficit magnum spatium. Tardus qui magno tempore paruum conficit spatium. Et vniuersaliter motus ille dicitur esse alio velocior, qui per tempus æquale spatium maius dimetitur. V. gr. per integrum horæ quadrantem volat musca, & accipiter in eadem linea: musca vix decimam transit milliarij partem, quando accipiter milliaria præteruolat plus quàm centum, ideo posterior motus velocior est. Difficultas autem sese obijcit maxima in explicando quid sit, seu in quo formaliter consistat velocitas hæc, siue tarditas, adeout nullibi magis ingenii hæhæreat, quàm in motu veloci; nec sæpius cadat, quàm in tardo.
units.tr: To understand this at once, I first set down a definition of slow and fast motion. A motion is called fast which covers a large space in a short time, and slow which covers a small space in a long time. Generally, that motion is said to be faster than another which traverses a greater space in an equal time. For example, a fly and a hawk fly along the same line for a full quarter of an hour: the fly scarcely passes a tenth part of a mile, whereas the hawk flies past more than a hundred miles; therefore the latter motion is faster. The greatest difficulty, however, presents itself in explaining what this velocity, or slowness, is, or in what it formally consists; so that nowhere does the intellect stick more than over fast motion, and nowhere does it fall into error more often than over slow motion.

units.la: Prima sententia docet,motus velocitatem non distingui ab essentia talis motus, qui se ipso citius decurrit multum spatij. Sic pariter motus tarditatem non distingui ab essentia talis motus, qui de se tardiùs parum spatij ex natura sua dimetitur.
units.tr: The first opinion teaches that the velocity of a motion is not distinct from the essence of such a motion as, by its very nature, runs through much space more quickly. Likewise, the slowness of a motion is not distinct from the essence of such a motion as, by its own nature, traverses a little space more slowly.

units.la: Sed contra quia motus nequit essentialiter esse velocior, nisi partes in eo priores fluant citiùs ante posteriores, & minùs citò fluant in motu tardo: sed hoc admitti non potest,ergo motus nec essentialiter velox, nec essentialiter tardus est. Maior consideranti est euidens. Minorem probo, quia si partes, quæ sunt priores,fluunt citiùs in motu veloci, & minùs citò in motu tardo, sequitur quòd in motu tardo partes non tam citò fluentes parùm demorentur, & per consequens ille motus non sit successiuus, aut quòd mobile quiescat. Rogo enim: quid est, partes in motu priores non ita citò labi; hoc profecto est aliqua negatio motus, aut quod idem est, interpositio quietis, vnde motus interrumpitur, nec successiuus est.
units.tr: But against this: a motion cannot be essentially faster unless the earlier parts of it flow by more quickly than the later ones, and in a slow motion they flow less quickly; but this cannot be admitted; therefore motion is neither essentially fast nor essentially slow. The major is evident to anyone who considers it. I prove the minor: if the earlier parts flow more quickly in a fast motion and less quickly in a slow motion, it follows that in a slow motion the parts that do not flow so quickly linger a little, and consequently that motion is not successive, or that the moving body is at rest. For I ask: what is it for the earlier parts of a motion not to slip by so quickly? This is surely some negation of motion, or, what is the same, an interposition of rest, whereby the motion is interrupted and is not successive.

units.la: Secunda opinio docet, motus velocitatem constituere in qualitate; seu modo superaddito essentiæ motus,ratione cuius paucæ partes in motu veloci correspondeant magno spatio. Et sic tarditatem constituere in alio modo,virtute cuius multæ partes in motu tardo correspondeant breui spatio ⁞ Simili modo quo, aiunt, rarefactio modus quidam est, per quem paucæ partes in quantitate coextenduntur ad multum spatij; & è contra densitas.
units.tr: The second opinion teaches that the velocity of a motion consists in a quality, or a mode added to the essence of the motion, by virtue of which few parts in a fast motion correspond to a great space. And likewise that slowness consists in another mode, by virtue of which many parts in a slow motion correspond to a small space. They say this is in the manner in which rarefaction is a certain mode by which few parts are extended in quantity over a large space, and, conversely, density.

units.la: Sed contra, quia si paucæ partes in motu veloci correspondent magno spatio, sequitur quòd pars vna, eademq; motus reperiatur simul in multiplici parte spatij: hoc asseri nequit; ergo. Probatur sequela, non enim intelligi potest, quòd pars .a. motus velocis correspondeat spatijs b. c. nisi illa ipsa reperiatur in duplici loco, siue spatio c. b. Sed hoc dicere absurdum est. Probo, quia si motus manet simul in b. atq. c. iam in omni parte spatij non est successiuus. Deinde quia si motus .a. manet in b. c. simul, ergo si velocior fit manebit in b. c. d. e. cæterisque spatij partibus: ergo motus v. gr. velox vt centum, simul correspondebit centum partibus loci, & sic res mota constituetur simul in ijs omnibus. Fac modò, vt res mota decem partes habeat longitudinis; ergo iste occupabunt centum in spatio simul: sed longitudo vt 10. nequit comensurari longitudini, vt 100. igitur dicendum est, quòd pars vna motus nequeat pluribus correspondere in spatio. Similiter si tarditas consistit in eo, vt plures motus partes paucioribus correspondeant spatijs, ergo aliquæ partes in motu sibi coexistunt, ac proinde motus tardus non est successiuus.
units.tr: But against this: if few parts in a fast motion correspond to a great space, it follows that one part of the motion, and the same one, is found simultaneously in many parts of space; this cannot be asserted; therefore. The consequence is proved: for it cannot be understood that part a of the motion corresponds to the spaces b and c unless that same part is found in two places, or spaces, c and b. But to say this is absurd. I prove it: if the motion remains simultaneously in b and c, then in every part of space it is no longer successive. Next, if motion a remains in b and c at the same time, then if it becomes faster it will remain in b, c, d, e, and the other parts of space; therefore a fast motion, for example one of a hundred, would correspond simultaneously to a hundred parts of place, and thus the moved thing would be constituted simultaneously in all of them. Suppose now that the moved thing has ten parts of length; then these would occupy a hundred in space at once; but a length of ten cannot be measured by a length of a hundred. Therefore it must be said that one part of motion cannot correspond to several in space. Similarly, if slowness consists in this, that many parts of motion correspond to fewer parts of space, then some parts coexist with one another in motion, and consequently a slow motion is not successive.

units.la: X
CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Velocitas motus in minori moru- larum copia ; tarditas in ma- iori consistit.
units.tr: The speed of a motion consists in a smaller number of little delays; its slowness consists in a larger number.

units.la: PRobatur , & explicatur conclusio facillimè à P. Nostro Spinula 3. phys. disp. 15. sect. 3. hoc feré modo . Partes motus,quæ sunt vbicationes,quoad suam essentiam acceptæ, non solùm habent in differentiam, vt producantur hoc , aut illo tempore; sed etiam vt magis, & minùs durent, eo quòd enim potest mobile magis, minúsue quiescere in illis,ideo potest quælibet pars magis durare, aut minùs . Igitur secundum quòd magis , aut minùs durabunt partes, velocior etiam , seu tardior erit motus . Proinde motus ille dicetur esse tardus, cuius partes, aut obicationes non pereunt, statim ac producte sunt,sed per aliquas durant moras , aut quod idem est , in quibus mobile plures nectit moras, & quietes . Et hæ quidem paruulæ moræ consistunt in eo, vt per plura, seu pauciora instantia partes durét in esse, quemadmodum è contra negatio morularum dicit partes durare tantùm per vnicum instans . Interrumpetur ergo motus tardus, eiusque partes,iuxta quod magis, minusue durabunt, concipi debebunt non] vt entia successiua ; sed permanentia .
units.tr: Proved and explained very easily by our Father Spinula, Phys. disp. 3, disp. 15, sect. 3, in roughly this way. The parts of motion, which are the locations, taken in their essence, differ not only in that they are produced at this or that time, but also in that they last longer or shorter. For since the moving body can rest in those locations for more or less time, any part can last for more or less time. Therefore, according as the parts last longer or shorter, the motion will also be faster or slower. Accordingly, that motion will be called slow whose parts or locations do not perish as soon as they are produced, but last through some delays, or, what is the same, in which the moving body interposes many delays and rests. These small delays consist in the parts persisting through more or fewer instants, just as, on the contrary, the denial of such delays means that the parts last only through a single instant. Therefore a slow motion is interrupted, and its parts, according as they last longer or shorter, must be conceived not as successive entities but as permanent ones.

units.la: Volet igitur aquila , & per idem spatiū testudo se moueat. Motus aquilæ fiet velocior, quia hæc suis in vbicationibus per minores durabit morulas: testudo vero per frequentiores. Vnde non sequetur vnquam, poni aquilam in duplici loco; sed illud tempus, quod testudo insumit in vno spatii puncto, ab aquila insumi deuolando per decem, per quindecim, &c. Eatenus ergo motus, qui tardior fit, paucas habet partes in multo tempore quia mobile in paucis loci partibus conficiendis multum tempus insumit, eò nimirum quia frequenter quiescit. E contra motus velox in paruo tempore multus est, quia mobile dum plures conficit vbicationes, parum, aut nihil in ijsdem quiescit. Partes igitur motus non durant instantaneæ, nisi motus fiat summè velox, & consequenter citiùs, vel tardiùs fluere possunt, quatenus potest mobile magis, vel minùs quiescere in illis.
units.tr: Let the eagle and the tortoise then move over the same space. The motion of the eagle will be faster, because it lasts through fewer delays in its locations; the tortoise's lasts through more frequent ones. Hence it does not follow that the eagle is ever placed in two places at once; rather, the time that the tortoise spends at one point of the space, the eagle spends in flying across ten, fifteen, and so on. So far, then, the motion that is slower has few parts in a long time, because the moving body spends much time in completing few parts of the place, namely because it rests often. On the contrary, a fast motion is great in a short time, because the moving body, while it completes many locations, rests little or not at all in them. Therefore the parts of a motion do not last instantaneously unless the motion is extremely fast; and consequently they can flow more quickly or more slowly, to the extent that the moving body can rest in them more or less.

units.la: Probat igitur semet ipsam conclusio ex mira facilitate, qua rem difficillimam explicat, redditq; conceptui nostro accommodam. Quapropter etiamsi contra fieri possint obiectiones aliquæ acutiores, in ea tamen quiescendum puto, donec melius quid occurrat. Sed videamus argumenta, quæ magis vrgere solent.
units.tr: The conclusion therefore proves itself by the remarkable ease with which it explains a very difficult matter and makes it fit our understanding. Accordingly, even if some rather sharp objections can be raised against it, I think we may rest in it until something better occurs. But let us look at the arguments that are usually pressed more strongly.

units.la: Obiicies 1. pila bombardæ tanta vi ex plosa, vt ne quidem oculis præ raptu speciem videatur, potest adhuc de absoluta saltem potentia velociùs moueri; ergo nunc pila dum explodi tur, in aere moratur, & quiescit. Hoc autem non videtur credendum.
units.tr: You will object first: a cannonball, discharged with such force that it cannot even be seen by the eye because of its speed, can still, at least by absolute power, be moved more quickly; therefore the ball, while it is being fired, lingers and rests in the air. But this does not seem to be credible.

units.la: Respond. morulas bene posse interponi à globo, quia causa mouens limitatæ virtutis est, unde non potest in mobili tãtam producere vim, atque impetum, quo instantaneas, omnesq; moras tollat. Hoc autem & aduersarij tenere debent. Nam peto, quid est partes motus fluere citius, aut lentius? certè magis, aut minus durare. Quid est vbicationes durare magis, minusue? certè mobilem magis, aut minus quiescere in illis. Quid est, pilam de absoluta potentia posse citiùs transfire ? certè modò plus quiescere, plus morari, & c.
units.tr: I reply that the globe can indeed be delayed by interposed pauses, because the moving cause has limited power, so it cannot impart to the moving body a force and impetus great enough to remove all instantaneous pauses and delays. Indeed, the opponents too must hold this. For I ask: what is it for the parts of a motion to flow more quickly or more slowly? Surely, to last longer or shorter. What is it for locations to last longer or shorter? Surely, for the moving body to rest in them more or less. What is it to say that the ball could, by absolute power, pass over more quickly? Surely, only that it would rest more, linger more, and so on.

units.la: Obijcies 2. si dantur hæ morulæ, omnis motus interrumpitur: sed hoc repugnat experientiis, ergo. Maior est certa, non enim potest quiescere mobile, quin motus interrumpatur, ac cesset. Minor constat in ijs, quæ continuò mouentur, puta in aquila, in saxo cadente, cæterisq; non enim hæc videntur vnquam cessare à motu, dum actu feruntur.
units.tr: You will object second: if such delays exist, every motion is interrupted; but this contradicts experience; therefore. The major is certain: the moving body cannot rest without the motion being interrupted and ceasing. The minor is evident in things that are moving continuously, such as the eagle, a stone falling, and others; for these do not seem ever to cease from motion while they are actually being carried.

units.la: Respond. distinguendo maiorem. Omnis motus interrumpitur insensibiliter in se, concedo si non fit maximus; interrumpitur ad sensum, nego. Ad minorem dico experientiam fieri à sensibus, unde cum hæ morulæ minutæ, atque insensibiles nequeant sensibiliter percipi, constat experientia motum non interrumpi. Ratio autem plus cognoscit, reiq. naturam vestigando, illa detegit, quæ sensus nequit. Secus enim si ratio semper, & vbi que accommodari sensui deberet, neque astra diceres moueri, neq: radium in horologio rotari, &c.
units.tr: I reply by distinguishing the major. Every motion is interrupted insensibly in itself: I grant this, if it is not the greatest; it is interrupted to the senses: I deny this. As to the minor, I say that experience is made by the senses; therefore, since these small and insensible delays cannot be perceived by the senses, experience shows that motion is not interrupted. But reason knows more, and by investigating the nature of the thing it uncovers what the senses cannot. For otherwise, if reason ought always and everywhere to be adapted to the senses, you would not say that the stars move, or that the hand of a clock turns, and so on.

units.la: Obijcies 3. celebre argumentum. Sit rota, quæ pernici motu circumagatur: certè superior radij pars maiorem habet motum, quàm inferior propè axem. Hæc igitur plures nectit moras, & illa pauciores; Quo dato sequitur necessario dicti radij fractio. Probatur, quia pars vltima vicina centro vel semper mouetur cum superiori, vel non: si primum, ergo æquè velociter agitur, quod falsum est: si secundum, ergo inferior quiescit, dum superior motum habet, & sic vna discontinuatur ab alia.
units.tr: You will object third, a famous argument. Let there be a wheel that is turned with a swift motion: surely the upper part of the spoke has a greater motion than the lower part near the axle. This part therefore has more delays, and that part fewer; given this, the breaking of the said spoke necessarily follows. It is proved thus: the last part, near the centre, either is always moved together with the upper part, or it is not. If the first, then it is driven equally fast, which is false; if the second, then the lower part rests while the upper part has motion, and so one is separated from the other.

units.la: Respond. imprimis retorquendo argumentum, quia sequitur idem absurdum, & in contraria sententia. Probo sic. In quocunque consistat velocitas: atq: tarditas motus, certè pars radij superior maiorem habet motum ipsâ inferiori: sed quoties duo simul continuata mouentur, alterum velocius, alterum segnius, necesse omnino est, ea deiungi ab inuicem, & frangi, ergo. Maior est etiam aduersariorum, & hoc docet experientia. Minor patet, quia si duo continuata moueantur, alterum citius, alterum tardius, ergo primum ante ibit; secundum relinquetur post: fiet itaque disruptio.
units.tr: I reply first by turning the argument back, because the same absurdity follows on the opposing view too. I prove it thus. In whatever the speed and slowness of a motion consist, surely the upper part of the spoke has a greater motion than the lower part itself. But whenever two continuous things are moved together, one faster and the other slower, it is absolutely necessary that they be pulled apart from one another and broken. Therefore. The major is also held by the opponents, and experience teaches it. The minor is clear: if two continuous things are moved, one more quickly and the other more slowly, then the first will go ahead, and the second will be left behind; so a rupture will occur.

units.la: Respond. directè radium in rota constare partibus, vna sub alia immediatè positis, & continuatis, quæ propterea singulæ sicuti procedendo à circumferentia
units.tr: I reply directly that the spoke in the wheel consists of parts placed immediately one beneath another and continuous, which, as one proceeds from the circumference towards the centre, each is successively farther from that one; so each does not keep the same motion, but always a smaller and smaller one, and is thus interrupted by its own delays, though insensible.

units.la: V in centrum, successiuè ab illa magis distant, sic vnaquæque non eundem retinet motum, sed minorem semper, & minorem ; adeoue suis morulis interruptum licèt insensibilibus . Pars ergo secunda immediatè sub prima deficit per insensibilis moræ interpositionem . Pars tertia deficit quoque à secunda per vnam moram, & à prima per duplicem . Quarta pariter deficit à tertia per vnam, à secunda per duas, à prima per tres, & ita successiuè, donec illa, quæ centro proxima est, plures, & plures habere quietes intelligatur . Quamuis autem appareat oculis continuò, & sine mora vlla circumagi, tamen decipitur sensus, qui minimas quietulas, omnino insensibiles percipere nequit . Simili prorsus modo quo in testudine, quæ pigerrimè suas relinquit vbicationes, quietem nullam discernit .
units.tr: The second part, immediately beneath the first, lags behind through the interposition of an insensible delay. The third part lags behind the second by one delay, and behind the first by two. The fourth likewise lags behind the third by one, the second by two, the first by three, and so on successively, until the part nearest the centre is understood to have more and more rests. Although it appears to the eyes to turn continuously and without any delay, nevertheless the senses are deceived, since they cannot perceive the smallest, wholly insensible little rests. In exactly the same way as in the tortoise, which leaves its locations very slowly, the senses discern no rest at all.

units.la: Non sequitur ergo fractio, siue deiunctio superioris partis ab inferiori quiescente, quia morulæ istæ, quietesq. minimæ sunt, insensibilesque; fractio verò non nisi per sensibilem, ac diuturnam alterius partis quietem fit. Secundo quia pars inferior in linea radiali semper correspondet superiori, vnde non diuelletur ab ea, quemadmodum patet in hac figura . Nam si moueatur .a. superior in b. superiorem, a. quoque inferior erit in b. inferiori; & si .a. superior pergat in c. inferior etiam ibit in c. quæ puncta sibi correspondentia sunt. Fieret sanè fractio, si procedente a. superiori ad c: a. inferior maneret in b. inferiori; sed hoc non contingit. [Circle diagram with radii A, B, C, D, E, G; not transcribed as text]
units.tr: Therefore no fracture, or separation of the upper part from the lower one that is at rest, follows, because these delays and minimal rests are small and insensible; a fracture, however, occurs only through a sensible and lasting rest of one part. Second, because the lower part on the radial line always corresponds to the upper part, it will not be torn away from it, as is clear in this figure. For if the upper point a moves to the upper point b, then the lower point a will also be at the lower point b; and if the upper a proceeds to c, the lower one will also go to c, these points being mutually corresponding. A fracture would indeed occur if, while the upper a proceeds to c, the lower a remained at the lower b; but this does not happen.

units.la: Ratio autem est, quia pars in radio quò inferior manet, eò minus etiam conficere spatium debet, ergo per minorem motum semper correspondebit superiori, & sic ab ea non diuelletur, etiamsi quiescat, nam quietes hæ minimæ, atque insensibiles motui semper sensibili adspergentur. Imò si linea radialis per vnicum in peripheria punctum dimoueretur, subsequentes, & maximè vltima propè centrum ita quiescèrent, vt nullum prorsus haberent motum. Probo, quia si moueatur pars a vnico puncto, quæro: sequens pars mouetur æquè, an minùs? certè minùs, quia minus dimetitur spatium; ergo absolutè quiescit, cum fieri nequeat motus, nisi saltem per vnum punctum. Denique si mota superiori parte, inferiores non habeant morulas aliquot, pars in radio superior deberet vnico instanti moueri ad maximum spatium, quod tamen est contra experientiam. Probo sequela sic. Moueatur hoc instanti temporis linea s. in apposita figura. Per te hoc ipso tempore mouetur & pars .a. efficiendo v. gr. spatium vt vnum: mouetur .b. sed quia superior,facit spatium vt 2.mouetur c. sed quoniā ad hūc superior , faciet spatium vt 3. & sic per successionem.Ergo si linea radialis cōstet v.g.mille partibus , vt postrema pars .a. moueatur vt.1. superior debebit moue ri vt 1000. quod tamen salsū est,potest 'n. illa moueri ad minimum; quinimo si per vnicum instans moueatur, necessariò motus debet esse minimus.
units.tr: The reason is this: the part of the radius where the lower end remains is the less it has to traverse, so it always keeps pace with the upper part by a smaller motion, and so it will not be torn away from it, even if it seems to be at rest. For these very small rests, which are insensible in comparison with the motion that is always perceptible, are everywhere mingled in. Indeed, if the radial line were moved through a single point on the circumference, the following parts, and especially the last one near the centre, would remain so still that they would have no motion at all. I prove it: if a part is moved from a single point, I ask whether the following part is moved equally or less. Surely less, because it traverses less space. Therefore it is absolutely at rest, since motion cannot occur except at least through one point. Finally, if, when the upper part has been moved, the lower parts did not have some delays, the upper part in the radius would have to be moved through the greatest space in a single instant, which is nevertheless contrary to experience. I prove the consequence thus. Let the line s be moved in this instant of time, as in the figure set alongside. In this same time the part a also moves, covering, say, a space of one; the part b moves, and because it is higher, it covers a space of two; the part c moves, and since the part above it again... it will cover a space of three; and so on by succession. Therefore, if the radial line consists, say, of a thousand parts, so that the last part a is moved by one unit, the upper part must be moved by a thousand, which is nevertheless absurd. That part can be moved at least, indeed, if it is moved through a single instant, the motion must necessarily be the least.

units.la: DISQVISITIO QVARTA.
units.tr: FOURTH DISQUISITION

units.la: Quanam velocitate mobilia ina- qualia mouentur:
units.tr: With what velocity unequal moving bodies move

units.la: PRO intelligentia notare priùs, mobilia quædam esse graviora, & alia minas grauia. Rursus nonnulla graviora sunt in specie,nōnulla in indiuiduo. Grauius in specie illud est, quod in mole pari, & æqua naturaliter ipsi conueniente maioris est pōderis: ita plumbum grauius est cera in specie nam globus plumbeus excedit pondere cereum sibi magnitudine parem. Grauius in indiuiduo est quod absolutè maius habet pondus, aut fit postea eiusdem, aut speciei diuersæ respeƈtu illius, quo dicitur grauius : ita globus cereus mille vnciarum grauior in indiuiduo est globo plumbeo vnius vnciæ. Rursus notatæ, mobilia esse posse diuersa in figuris, vt si alterum sit sphæricum, & alterum planum: hoc triangulare, illud quadrangulum, &c. quæ omnia diligenter aduertenda sunt. Hoc posito.
units.tr: To understand this, first note that some moving bodies are heavier and others less heavy. Again, some are heavier in species, others in the individual. That is heavier in species which, in an equal and similar mass naturally belonging to it, has greater weight: thus lead is heavier than wax in species, for a leaden globe outweighs a waxen globe equal to it in size. That is heavier in the individual which absolutely has greater weight, whether it is of the same species or of a different species, relative to that which is called heavier: thus a waxen globe of a thousand ounces is heavier in the individual than a leaden globe of one ounce. Again, it is noted that moving bodies can differ in figure, as when one is spherical and the other flat, this triangular, that quadrangular, and so on; all of which must be carefully observed. With this laid down:

units.la: Fuit communis philosophorum opinio, quòd mobilia inter se inæqualia mouerétur etiam impari velocitate, adeout, quæ absolute grauiora sunt, siue in specie, siue in indiuiduo, motum haberent præ aliis maiorem. Imo aliqui peripatetici cum Aristotele 3. de cœlo cap. 2. dixerunt, sic se habere velocitatem, sicuti grauitas ad grauitatem. V. g. si mobile.a. fit vnius vnciæ, mobile b. decem, hoc decuplò citiùs moueri.
units.tr: It was the common opinion of the philosophers that moving bodies that are unequal to one another move at unequal speeds, so that those which are absolutely heavier, whether in kind or as individuals, have a greater motion than the others. Indeed, some Peripatetics, following Aristotle, De caelo book 3, chapter 2, said that speed stands in the same relation as weight to weight. For example, if moving body a weighs one ounce and body b ten, then b moves ten times more quickly.

units.la: Sed iampridem recentiores eam sententiam omnino falsam detexere, factis .n. experimentis, cognouerunt mobilia omnia pari velocitate ferri, præsertim si eiusdem speciei sint. Quàuis pleriq; id absolutè de quocúq; mobili asserant, quanticumq; postea sit ponderis, & cuiuscunq; figuræ.
units.tr: But recent writers long ago showed this opinion to be entirely false: by actual experiments they found that all moving bodies fall at the same speed, especially if they are of the same kind. Yet most of them assert this absolutely of every moving body, whatever its weight afterwards and whatever its shape.

units.la: Hanc tamen doctrinam, quæ plurimis & facillimis experimentis videbatur certa, nouissimè labefactat Ricciolus in Almagesto l. 9. f. 4. c. 16. vbi non paucas refert experientias exactissimè à se in contrariū factas è Turri Asinelorū Bononiēsi. expertus igitur est, quòd duo globi argilacei mole, ac figura pares, alter quorum erat 10. vnciarū, alter 20. eodē temporis momento ex altitudine pedū 280. demissi non percussere pauimētū simul, eodemq; tēpore; sed qui leuior erat, apparuit distās à terra pedes 15. eo instanti, quo grauior iā percusserat inq; sexcēta frusta dissiluerat. Quod experimentū duodecies repetitū, semper successum habuit eundē. Quapropter nonnulli, qui aderant philosophiæ professores, & cum Galileo, Cabeo, a'ijsq; in contrarium opinabantur, illico sententiam deposuerunt. demissis etiam globis magnitudine imparibus, modò eiusdem, & modò specie diuersæ, vt duplici argilaceo, duplici plumbeo; siue altero ex argila, & altero ex plumbo, factisq; varijs inter se collationibus, deprehensa fuit semper inæqualitas in motu inter grauiorem, & leuiorem. Vide Ricciolum citato loco.
units.tr: However, this doctrine, which seemed certain from very many and very easy experiments, has most recently been shaken by Riccioli in his Almagestum, book 9, page 4, chapter 16, where he reports not a few experiments made by himself, most exactly, to the contrary, from the Tower of the Asses at Bologna. He tested, therefore, that two clay globes, equal in size and shape, one of which weighed 10 ounces and the other 20, released from a height of 280 feet at the same instant, did not strike the pavement together and at the same time; rather, the lighter one was seen to be 15 feet above the ground at the moment when the heavier had already struck and had shattered into six hundred pieces. When this experiment was repeated twelve times, it always had the same result. Therefore some professors of philosophy who were present, and who had held the contrary opinion with Galileo, Cabeo and others, at once abandoned their view. When globes of unequal size were released, sometimes of the same material and sometimes of different kinds, such as two clay globes, two leaden globes, or one of clay and one of lead, and various comparisons were made between them, an inequality in motion was always found between the heavier and the lighter. See Riccioli in the passage cited.

units.la: Quid concludendum? si Riccioli experientiæ habitæ sunt exactè, quemadmodum ipse fatetur, & perito, ingenuoque viro credendum est, dici debet, mobilia inæqualia impari etiam velocitate moueri. Sed aliunde per domestica experimenta constat contrarium. Demissō enim ex pinnaculo huiusce templi duplici saxo, altero 3, altero viginti vnciarum, simul ambo in terram impacti sunt. Demissa rursus triplici sphæra plumbea, prima 1.libræ, secunda 2. tertia 3. vno, eodemque momento percussere terram,&c. Itaq; res valdè manet dubia, nisi dicamus, inæqualia mobilia ferri quidem velocitate inæquali, sed hanc non apparere ad sensum, nisi ex motu insigni, per eximiā altitudinem facto, ad quod turris Bononiæ quameditissima potuit esse magis idonea. Sed tamen aliquid statuendum est.
units.tr: What is to be concluded? If Riccioli's experiments were made exactly, as he himself confesses, and a skilled and honest man must be believed, it must be said that unequal bodies move at unequal speeds. But on the other hand, domestic experiments show the contrary. For when a double stone, one of three ounces and the other of twenty, was dropped from the pinnacle of this very church, both struck the ground together. Again, when a triple leaden sphere, the first of one pound, the second of two and the third of three, was dropped, they struck the earth at one and the same moment, and so on. So the matter remains very doubtful, unless we say that unequal bodies indeed move at unequal speeds, but that this difference does not appear to the senses except in a notable motion through a very great height, for which the tower at Bologna, which is quite high, could be more suitable. Still, something must be settled. ## FIRST CONCLUSION. Bodies that are equal in kind and as individuals, but unequal in shape, move at unequal speeds.

units.la: CONCLVSIO PRIMA.
units.tr: FIRST CONCLUSION

units.la: Mobilia æquè grauia in specie, atq; individuo, figurā tamen inæqualia, inæquali mouentur velocitate.
units.tr: Moving bodies that are equal in weight, both in species and in the individual, but unequal in figure, move with unequal velocity.

units.la: PRobatur 1. experientia, nam demissa lignea tabula extensa, & in duplicem superficiem complanata cum globo item ligneo eiusdem speciei, & ponderis, hic tetigit pavimentum, quando illa turbinatim adhuc per aerem ferebatur. Probatur etiam ratione, quia si mobile habeat angulum contactus acutiorem, facilius etiā scindit medium, sicuti è contra si obtusum habeat, difficiliùs. Itaque citiùs descendet figura sphærica, quàm complanata, cum hæc addenser medium, & illa disgreget, siue scindat. Ex quo statui potest axioma. Ea, quæ cæteris paribus, acutiori constant figura, facilius medium scindunt, citiúsq; descendunt.
units.tr: It is proved, first, by experience: for when a flat wooden board, spread out and flattened into a double surface, was dropped together with a wooden globe of the same species and weight, the globe touched the floor while the board was still being carried through the air in a whirling motion. It is also proved by reason: if a moving body has a sharper angle of contact, it cuts through the medium more easily; conversely, if it has a blunter one, it does so with more difficulty. Therefore a spherical figure will descend more quickly than a flattened one, since the latter condenses the medium while the former parts and cuts through it. From this an axiom can be stated: Those things which, other things being equal, have a sharper figure, cut through the medium more easily and descend more quickly.

units.la: V
units.tr: V

units.la: CONCLVSIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: SECOND CONCLUSION.

units.la: Vorofimilius est mobilia inaequatia, maxime speciei diuersa, ina- quali velocitate moueri.
units.tr: It is more probable that unequal moving bodies, especially those of different species, move with unequal speed.

units.la: PRobatur 1. experientijs omnibus à Ricciolo exactissimè factis, non .n. suspicari quis potest, in ijs ab ingenuo viro extitisse fraudem, vel errorem irrepsisse à docto, & experto. Quare si apud nos per domesticas experimenta contrarium obtingit (nam pondera inaequalia maximè speciei eiusdem pari motu descendunt) suspicor hanc velocitatem apparere sensibiliter æqualem, sed si motus è maiori, & maiori altitudine procederet, fore vt inæqualitas in motu detegeretur. Secundo accedit ratio, nam inter duo pondera, maximè speciei eiusdem, quod grauius est, maiorem facit impetum subiectique medij partes abigit facilius, & licet figuram habeat crassiorem, tamen suomet pondere citius vincit medium. Neque dicas, mobile maius non posse moueri velocius, quia licet v. gr. sit vnciarum 20. vncia tamen a. non auget pondus vnciæ b. neque ista grauitatem vnciæ c. quapropter ita mouebuntur 20. simul vnitæ in magno mobili ac si forent inuicem deiunctæ. Dico enim quòd etsi pars a. non grauitet in b. neque ista in c.&c. (non enim simile agit in simile) hoc tamen totum, nempe mobile 20. vnciarum validiùs agit in medium, eumque fortiùs depellit; vnde velociùs mouetur.
units.tr: It is proved first by all the experiments most exactly made by Riccioli. For one cannot suspect that an honest man committed fraud in them, or that error crept into them from a learned and experienced man. Therefore, if among us the contrary turns out in domestic experiments (for unequal weights of the same species fall with equal motion), I suspect that this speed appears sensibly equal, but that if the motion proceeded from greater and greater heights, the inequality in the motion would be detected. Secondly, reason agrees. Between two weights of the same species, the heavier produces the greater impetus and drives the parts of the surrounding medium aside more easily; and although it has a thicker shape, it overcomes the medium more quickly by its own weight. Nor should you say that a larger mobile cannot move faster, because although, for example, it weighs 20 ounces, the ounce a does not add weight to the ounce b, nor does that add weight to ounce c; so the 20 ounces united in a large body would move as if they were separated from one another. For I say that although part a does not weigh upon b, nor b upon c, and so on (for like does not act on like in that way), yet this whole, namely the mobile of 20 ounces, acts more strongly on the medium and drives it back more forcibly; hence it moves more quickly.

units.la: CONCLVSIO TERTIA. Mobilia inaequalia non mouentur natu- raliter velocius pro mensura gravitatis.
units.tr: CONCLUSION THREE. Unequal mobiles are not naturally moved faster in proportion to the measure of their weight.

units.la: PRobatum est experientijs, quae oftenderunt, nunquam in motu seruari hanc proportionem, vt si mobile alterum sit 100. vnciarum, alterum verò vnius, illud centuplò citiùs descenderit. Secundò accedit ratio, nam si globus a. quia 100. vnciarum imprimeret vim vt 100. globus verò b. quia vnius vnciae, impetum haberet vt vnum, ergo ambo demittantur è fenestra in hoc instanti: eo tempore, quo globus minor efficiet primum spatij palmum, globus maior centesimum dimetietur, quod certè numquam visum est. Vnde constat, ipsum quoque Aristotelem, in cubiculo sibi fecisse aliquando philosophiam, non eam semper à natura excepisse fidelem.
units.tr: It has been proved by experiments, which showed that this proportion is never preserved in motion, so that if one body weighs 100 ounces and the other only one ounce, the heavier would fall a hundred times faster. Secondly, reason agrees. For if globe a, because it weighs 100 ounces, impressed a force of 100, and globe b, because it weighs one ounce, had an impetus of one, then if both were let fall from a window at the same instant, in the time in which the smaller globe covered the first palm of space, the larger would cover the hundredth, which has certainly never been seen. Hence it is clear that Aristotle himself, in his study, sometimes made philosophy for himself, and did not always take it faithfully from nature.

units.la: DISPVTATIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISPUTATIO SECUNDA.

units.la: De motu violento, seu proiectorum.
units.tr: On violent motion, or of projectiles.

units.la: AMotu naturali migramus ad violentum, nempe illum, qui mobilia defert extra locum sibi debitum, & naturalem. Sicut autem à principio intrinseco nascitur motus, qui naturalis est, sic ex aduerso motus violentus oritur ab extrinseco, qualis v. gr. est motus in lapide sursum, qui à potentia extrinseca, puta bracchio enascens quandiu perdurauerit, lapidem alio agit.
units.tr: From natural motion we pass on to violent motion, namely that which carries movable things out of the place due and natural to them. Just as natural motion arises from an intrinsic principle, so violent motion arises from the opposite side, from an extrinsic principle. For example, the motion of a stone upward comes from an extrinsic power, such as an arm, which, as long as it lasts, drives the stone elsewhere.

units.la: Exinde vero statim colligite, quaenam sit motus proiectorum causa. Fuit sententia, quae tribui solet Philosopho, motus violenti causam esse aerem, siue medium illud, per quod mobile agitur. Sed hoc redarguitur falsitatis, nam si proiecta mouerentur à medio, quomodo lapis contra ventum, quomodo naues contra fluuium remis impellerentur? quomodo pilae tormentariae tantum à solo aere haberent impetum, quo moenia quaterent? quomodo violentus motus in aere tandem finiretur, si medium semper adest impellens? &c.
units.tr: From this, you should at once infer what the cause of the motion of projectiles is. There was an opinion commonly attributed to the Philosopher that the cause of violent motion is the air, or that medium through which the movable thing is carried. But this is refuted as false. For if projectiles were moved by the medium, how would a stone be thrown against the wind, or ships be driven against the river by oars? How would cannonballs have so much impetus from the air alone that they could shatter walls? How would violent motion in the air ever come to an end, if the medium is always present to drive it? And so on.

units.la: Est igitur doctrina recentioribus acceptissima, causam violenti motus quandam esse potentiam ab extrinseco proiectore impressam, & hanc vocant impulsum, impetum, virtutem, qualitatemue motiuam, &c. à qua tanquam à causa immediata motus efficitur proiectorum. Duplex ergo huiusce motus causa est: alia mediata, & extrinseca, videlicet proiector; alia immediata, & intrinseca, nempe virtus impressa.
units.tr: The doctrine most widely accepted by modern writers is therefore that the cause of violent motion is a certain power impressed by the extrinsic projector. They call this an impulse, an impetus, a virtue, or a motive quality, and so on, and from it, as from an immediate cause, the motion of projectiles is produced. The cause of this motion is therefore twofold: one mediate and extrinsic, namely the projector; the other immediate and intrinsic, namely the impressed virtue.

units.la: Porro virtus haec, sive impetus de se omnino indifferens est ad omnem terminum, ideoque a proiectore ad hunc potius locum, quam ad alium determinatur. Sic impetus, qui sagittae imprimitur, ex varia, & sola collimatione arcus ad hunc aliumue scopum defert sagittam. Secundo impulsus hic licet sit qualitas composita ex gradibus, & suscipiens magis, minusque, tamen producitur simul totus, & in instanti. Ratio est, quia secus non fieret unquam intensus. Nam si produceretur successive, unus videlicet gradus post alium, primus non expectaret secundum; ille quidem primus de se formaliter sui subiecti motivus est, ergo illico moveret, ergo subiectum non expectaret productionem secundi, & sic virtus haec impressa non suscipieret magis.
units.tr: Moreover, this virtue, or impetus, is in itself wholly indifferent to every terminus, and so it is directed by the projector to this place rather than to another. Thus the impetus imparted to an arrow carries the arrow to this or that target, depending on the varied and sole aim of the bow. Second, although this impulse is a quality composed of degrees, and admits of more and less, it is nevertheless produced all at once and in an instant. The reason is that otherwise it would never become intense. For if it were produced successively, one degree after another, the first would not wait for the second; the first, indeed, is of itself formally a motive force for its subject, so it would at once move, and so the subject would not await the production of the second, and in this way the impressed virtue would never gain in strength.

units.la: Fit autem virtus haec impressa maior, & deinde paulatim languet, ac diminuitur. Primum ostendit motus proiectorum, qui validior est in medio, quam in principio, ut experientia docet, nam v.g. pila tormentaria maiorem facit impulsum quando corpus in aliqua distantia illi obijcitur, quam si prope tormentum sit. Secundum quoque ostendit experientia, pila enim tandem aliquando a sua
units.tr: This impressed virtue becomes greater and then gradually weakens and diminishes. The first point is shown by the motion of projectiles, which is more powerful in the middle of its course than at the beginning, as experience teaches: for example, a cannonball produces a greater impulse when the body is set against it at some distance than when it is near the cannon. The second point is also shown by experience, for a ball, after some time,

units.la: à sua directione mota segniùs cadit, vimque totam deperdit.
units.tr: once it has been moved from its direction, falls more slowly and loses all its force.

units.la: Et huius rei duplex ratio assignatur. Prima hæc, quòd vel impetus initio impressus alium sibi similem, & hic alium succesiuè producit; vel mobile prout maiori, aut minori vi motum fuit, correspondentem in se impetum gignit, unde velocius mouetur in medio, eo quòd præter primum, tunc alium de nouo impulsum habet. Verùm quia imprimitur semper hæc qualitas cum repugnantia mobilis, aut in mobili eam non exigente, hinc oritur vt paulatim debilitetur, donec omnino destruatur. Quod magis etiam ex dicendis patebit.
units.tr: And two reasons are assigned for this. The first is this: either the impetus originally impressed produces another like itself, and this one in turn produces another in succession; or the movable thing, according as it has been moved with greater or lesser force, generates in itself a corresponding impetus, whence it moves more swiftly through the medium, because, besides the first, it then has another impulse freshly acquired. But since this quality is always imprinted with resistance from the movable thing, or in a movable thing that does not require it, it follows that it is gradually weakened until it is wholly destroyed. This will become clearer from what is to be said below.

units.la: Est autem hic dignum adnotatione quod asserit Galileus, impetum, siue conceptum, siue impressum non retardare motum rei naturalem. Proinde si detur bombarda, quæ ad horizontis libellam, æquè collocata globum explodat in vnius milliarij distantiam, tanto tempore detinebitur globus vi proiectionis in aere, ne decidat in planum horizontis, quanto ex ore bombardæ naturà (uà perpendiculariter caderet. Quæ res nisi adsit experimentum, non ita facilè inueniet fidem.
units.tr: Here it is worth noting what Galileo asserts: that impetus, whether conceived or impressed, does not retard the natural motion of a thing. Accordingly, if there were a cannon placed level with the horizon, which fires a ball to a distance of one mile, the ball would be held up in the air by the force of its projection for as long a time as it would take to fall perpendicularly by nature from the mouth of the cannon, so that it does not drop onto the plane of the horizon. This would not easily win belief unless there were experiment to confirm it.

units.la: Videtur enim conceptu difficile, quòd impetus à bombarda impressus non suffineat pilam in aere diutius, quàm si ea naturaliter, & absque impetu anterorsum accepto ex ore tormenti caderet. Alioquin non adesset bombarda, quæ globum tuum longiùs emitteret, quàm alia, quo- [?] tiescumque plures inter se inæquales æquè horizontaliter collocarentur; Patet, quia si vno temporis momento cadant globi à singularum ore, omnes percutiunt simul terram; ergo etiam pari vi explosi eam percutient simul; & sic non erit quæ longiùs eiaculetur. Sed tamen vbi experientia cõuincit, ratio cedat.
units.tr: For it seems hard to conceive that the impetus imparted by the cannon does not sustain the ball in the air any longer than if it fell naturally from the mouth of the gun without any forward impetus. Otherwise there would be no reason why one cannon should throw its ball farther than another, however many unequal cannons were placed level with one another. This is clear: if the balls fall from the mouths of each at the same instant, they all strike the ground together; therefore, when fired with equal force, they will also strike together, and so none will be thrown farther. But where experience convinces, reason must yield.

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: FIRST DISQUISITION.

units.la: Quam lineam proiecta describant.
units.tr: Which line projected bodies describe.

units.la: PRO intelligentia notare, posse gratia non vno proijci modo. Proijciuntur perpendiculariter sursum, vel deorsum; horizontaliter; & demum obliquè inter lineam horizontalem, & perpendicularem, ex quibus concipitur fieri angulus rectus. Quæ mouentur ex perpendiculo sursum, vel deorsum, lineam semper designant rectam. Difficultas igitur est de linea, quæ per alios motus describitur. Qua in re diligentius exploranda nihil aptius video, quàm si vtamur experimento, quod nobis proponit P. Cabeus l.3.q.9. in meteoris.
units.tr: To understand this, note first that bodies can be thrown in more than one way. They are thrown perpendicularly upward or downward, horizontally, and finally obliquely, between the horizontal and the perpendicular, from which an right angle is understood to be formed. Bodies moved upward or downward along a plumb line always describe a straight line. The difficulty, then, concerns the line described by the other motions. In examining this more carefully, I see nothing more suitable than the experiment that Father Cabeus proposes to us in book 3, question 9, On Meteors.

units.la: Sumatur, inquit, bombarda, siue sclopus a. & vt habeatur præcisa directio axis tubi, supra ipsum notetur punctum e. Similiter correspondenter ad e. sumatur punctum b, in altero extremo. Tum iniecto conuenienti puluere, atq; globo in tormentū, dirigatur ad scopum exactè destinatum natum collimando visuali radio per extrema puncta e.b. Hoc facto, habeantur folia chartæ super ligneis cancellis adinstar fenestræ oppansa, vt possint erigi directa contra sclopum. Figatur ergo primus cancellus in distantia decempedali à puncto e. postea collimando per e. b. noteturin eodem folio punctum f. adeo vt e. b. f. d. sint omnino in eodem radio visuali; & sic alia folia in eadem successiuè distantia erigantur.
units.tr: He says: take a cannon or musket, a. And so that the exact direction of the axis of the barrel is known, mark a point e on top of it. Similarly, mark a point b at the other end, corresponding to e. Then, with a suitable charge of powder and the ball placed in the barrel, aim it at the intended target by sighting along the extreme points e and b. Having done this, set up sheets of paper on wooden frames, like windows, so that they can be stood upright facing the gun. Fix the first frame at a distance of ten feet from the point e. Then, sighting along e and b, mark on that sheet a point f, so that e, b, f, d all lie exactly on the same line of sight. In this way, set up other sheets successively at the same distances.

units.la: Rebus ita dispositis applicetur ignis nitrio pulueri, deuolabit globus ab e.perforabitque chartas per certa spatia collocatas. Nota igitur in singulis, qua distantia ex notato axis puncto globus chartam perforet; quia enim folia æquè inter se distant, habebis præcisè viam, quam signat globus de ore sclopi ad vltimum signum latus.
units.tr: With things arranged thus, apply fire to the nitre powder. The ball will fly from e and pierce the papers placed at the given intervals. Note, then, for each sheet, how far from the marked point on the axis the ball has pierced it. For since the sheets are equally spaced, you will have exactly the path that the ball traces from the mouth of the gun to the last marked sheet.

units.la: Facto exactissimè semel, & iterum experimento, deprehensum fuit, quòd omnis charta prout magis erat distans à puncto e. perforata est semper in maiori, & maiori distantia ex notato puncto per visum. Globus ergo in nulla itineris parte ad lineam axis rectam processit, sed à sclopo deiunctus, illicò iuxta impetum suæ grauitatis declinare cæpit.
units.tr: When the experiment was done with the greatest care, once and again, it was found that each sheet, the farther it was from the point e, was always pierced at a greater and greater distance from the point marked by sight. The ball therefore did not advance along the straight line of the axis at any part of its course; separated from the gun, it at once began to swerve, following the impulse of its weight.

units.la: Ex hoc experimento elicitur primò, lineam, quæ describitur à proiecto, non esse rectam inclinatam à directione, quam à proijciente accepit. Probatur, quia in experimento globus non designat lineam rectam inclinatam à directione tubi, quæ faciat angulum cum axe. Ratio est, nam si linea ita foret inclinata, distantiæ foraminum, quæ fiunt in chartis, distarent à punctis in axe dispositis duplò semper magis: hoc non contingit; ergo. Maior probatur. Nam data linea directionis tubi a.b. si globus procederet per lineam rectam e.g. distantia d.h. in secunda charta, esset duplò maior, quàm distantia f.c. in primo folio. Et sic deinceps proportionaliter; vt enim e.d. ad f.d. ita d.h. ad f.c. sed e.d. est dupla ipsius e.f. ergo d.h. est dupla ipsius f.c. Suppono enim chartas ita esse collocatas, vt radius directionis incidat in illas perpendiculariter, & consequenter sint parallelæ: Igitur globus non incedit per lineam rectam inclinatam, quod erat demonstrandum. Multò minus describit lineam circularem, secus distantiæ foraminum, quæ fiunt in notatis punctis, deberent crescere per incrementa iuxta tabulas tangentium, & secantium. Superest ergo.
units.tr: From this experiment we deduce, first, that the line described by a projectile is not a straight line inclined from the direction it received from the thrower. This is proved because in the experiment the ball does not trace a straight line inclined from the direction of the barrel, making an angle with the axis. The reason is this: if the line were so inclined, the distances of the holes made in the papers from the points marked on the axis would always be double the previous ones. This does not happen; therefore. The major premise is proved as follows. Given the line of direction of the barrel, a–b, if the ball proceeded along a straight line e–g, the distance d–h in the second sheet would be twice the distance f–c in the first sheet. And so on proportionally: for as e–d is to f–d, so d–h is to f–c; but e–d is double e–f, therefore d–h is double f–c. I assume that the sheets are so placed that the line of direction falls on them perpendicularly, and consequently they are parallel. Therefore the ball does not move along an inclined straight line, which was to be demonstrated. Much less does it describe a circular line, since the distances of the holes made at the marked points would then have to increase according to the tables of tangents and secants. What remains, therefore, is...

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Proiecta omnia describunt lineam parabolicam.
units.tr: All projectiles describe a parabolic line.

units.la: PRobatur ex facto experimento, in quo distantiæ foraminum neque lineam inclinatè rectam, neque circularem efficere posse videntur, ergo manet quòd parabolicam designent, in quam sententiam Cabeus etiam propendet. Sed pro intelligentia explicandum est, quid sit linea parabolica; deinde quomodo à mobili describi possit.
units.tr: It is proved from the experiment described, in which the distances of the holes seem able to produce neither an inclined straight line nor a circular one; therefore it remains that they trace a parabolic line, to which opinion Cabeus also inclines. But for understanding, it must be explained what a parabolic line is, and then how it can be described by a moving body.

units.la: Quocirca notate definitionem coni ex l. II. Elem. Eucl. desin. 16. Conus est quando rectanguli trianguli manente uno latere, circumductum triangulum in ipsum rursus revoluitur, unde moueri caperat circumassumpta figura, &c. Concipite igitur conum ita obliquè versus basim resecari, vt sectio parallela fiat lateri oppositò, integroque relicto. Quoniam area segmenti nuncupatur parabola, eiusdem ambitus linea est, quam vocant parabolicam.
units.tr: Hence note the definition of a cone from Book II of Euclid's Elements, definition 16: "A cone is when, with one side of a right-angled triangle remaining fixed, the triangle is turned around and carried back again into itself, whence the figure taken around begins to move, etc." Conceive, therefore, a cone cut obliquely towards its base, so that the section becomes parallel to the opposite side, the whole being left intact. Since the area of the segment is called a parabola, the line of its boundary is what they call the parabolic line.

units.la: Sed rem aliquali exemplo magis etiam illustro. Vidistisne vnquam fontanas aquas è tubulo cum impetu erumpentes? hæ non è recto perpendiculariter, sed cum aliqua semper inclinatione cadunt. Quæ inclinatio maior, minorue; acutior, vel obtusior fiet, prout multùm, seu parum tubus ipse inclinabitur. Ea igitur linea, quæ successiuè aliquantulum cutua per aquam fluentem describitur, Parabolica est, describiturque à proiectis.
units.tr: But I illustrate the matter even more with an example. Have you ever seen fountain water bursting out with force from a small tube? These do not fall perpendicularly but always with some inclination. This inclination will be greater or less, more acute or more obtuse, according as the tube itself is inclined more or less. That line, therefore, which is successively described, somewhat curved, by the flowing water, is parabolic, and it is described by projectiles.

units.la: Ratio autem huiusce motus non difficilis est, vnde probatur etiam conclusio 2. quia proiectum habet grauitatem innatam, simulque impetum incussum. Grauitas innata, quæ sanè otiosa non manet, causat motum deorsum; sed hic non fit statim perpendiculariter, adest enim & impetus incussus, qui vrget mobile antrorsum, nec sinit, citò vt cadat. Ex hac igitur duplici causa, mouente deorsum, & vrgente antrorsum, nascitur, vt etiam linea fit simul deorsum, & antrorsum descripta. Sed (notate) non ita deorsum, vt recta inclinata fiat, quemadmodum supra in figura ostenditur. Et ratio est, quia impulsus antrorsum non sinit eam labi ad rectitudinem rigorosè inclinatam; sed aliquantulum successiuè sustinet. Ex quo concipis describi lineam, quæ inter horizontalem, & rectè inclinatam fit.
units.tr: The reason for this motion is not difficult, and by it conclusion 2 is also proved: a projectile has innate heaviness and at the same time impressed impetus. The innate heaviness, which certainly does not remain idle, causes motion downward; but this does not happen at once perpendicularly, for the impressed impetus is also present, which urges the moving body forward and does not let it fall quickly. From this twofold cause, moving downward and urging forward, it comes about that the line is described both downward and forward at once. But (note) not so downward that a rigidly inclined straight line results, as is shown above in the figure. The reason is that the forward impulse does not allow it to slide down to a straight inclined line, but sustains it somewhat successively. From this you can conceive that the line described lies between the horizontal and the straight inclined line.

units.la: Hæc autem Parabolica est.
units.tr: This line, moreover, is the parabolic.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.

units.la: De motu impressso à motore translato.
units.tr: On motion impressed by a moved mover.

units.la: PRO intelligentia eorum, quæ hoc loco disquirimus, aduertite, posse mobilia ita proijci, vt proiector ipse tunc transferatur per motum alterius corporis, in quo sit, v.gr. si quis deuehatur navi, aut equo, tunc temporis eijcere potest v.gr. pilam, emittere sagittam, &c. quæ proinde mobilia dicerentur habere motū impressum à motore translato. Quærimus ergo, quomodo fieret, seu per quamnam lineam huiusmodi motus.
units.tr: To understand what we are investigating here, note that movable things can be thrown in such a way that the thrower himself is at the same time carried along by the motion of another body in which he is. For example, if someone is being conveyed on a ship or a horse, he can at that time throw, say, a ball, or shoot an arrow, and so on. Such movables would therefore be said to have motion impressed on them by a moved mover. We inquire, then, how this would come about, or along what line such motion occurs.

units.la: Galileus dial. 2. de mundi systemate, Cabeus l. 1. meteor. & Gassendus epist. speciali ad hoc explicandum non pauca referunt experimenta. Primò siquis de summo nauis malo, dum cursu fertur incitatissimo, demittat saxum, etiamsi ventus in contrariam partem nonnihil spiraret, in eadem semper à malo distantia, secundum lineam parallelam apparebit, adeoque ad ipsius mali pedem cadat. 2. siquis in navi stans recta sursum eijciat pilam, rursus eam in manus recipiet, sive nauis maneat immota, seu velocissimo cursu feratur. 3. siquis moto curru etiam perniciissimè, globum explodat sursum, dummodo sclopus adamusim rectus perpendiculariter constituatur, ille super explodentem redibit. Ex aduerso autem si ad arborem, aut simile quidpiam collimet, met, semper à scopo aberrabit. Hinc si à lapidis eiecti sursum casu timueris, non eodem tenore debes incedere, ac quando eiecisti; sed vel concitatius, vt ponè, vel segnius, vt ante cadat; alioquin si te moueas æquè ac priùs, quemadmodum illi semper subiectus fies, ita ictum non eua des. Hæc,& huiusmodi experimenta ferunt egregij viri, quibus videtur omnino adhibenda esse fides. Inde natum est paradoxicum illud theorema: Si corpus, cui insistimus, transferatur, motus omnes nostros, rerumque à nobis mobilia perinde fieri, atque apparere, ac si illud quiesceret. Deinde aliud quoque mirabile deductum est: Mobile ad parem altitudinem assurgere, seu moueatur, seu quiescat motor, à quo emittitur pari vi.
units.tr: Galileo (Dialogue 2, on the system of the world), Cabeus (Meteorology, book 1), and Gassendi, in a special letter on explaining this, report not a few experiments. First, if someone lets a stone fall from the top of a ship's mast while the ship is moving at full speed, then even if the wind blows somewhat in the opposite direction, the stone will always appear at the same distance from the mast, along a parallel line, and so falls at the foot of the mast. 2. If someone standing in a ship throws a ball straight up, he will catch it again in his hands, whether the ship stays still or is carried along at very great speed. 3. If someone, while a carriage is moving very swiftly, fires a ball upward, provided the gun is set exactly upright and perpendicular, the ball will fall back onto the one who fired it. On the other hand, if he aims at a tree or something similar, he will always miss the mark. Hence, if you fear the fall of a stone thrown upward, you must not walk at the same pace as when you threw it, but either faster, so that it falls behind you, or slower, so that it falls ahead; otherwise, if you move just as before, you will always be under it, and so you will not avoid the blow. These and similar experiments are reported by distinguished men, to whom full credence seems due. From this arose the paradoxical theorem: If the body on which we stand is transported, all our motions, and those of the movables relative to us, happen and appear just as if it were at rest. Then another remarkable consequence was drawn: A movable rises to the same height, whether the mover from which it is emitted with equal force is moving or at rest.

units.la: Ratio autem est, quia omne quod mouetur, eundem imprimit motum rei, quâ in se habet. Quare cum quis naui currente sursum eijcit pilam, debes in ea duplicem concipere vim, alteram ipsius propriam, alteram nauis, quæ transfert. Porro hæ vires coeunt in vnam, vnde mobile non tam duplici, quàm vna vi agitur, & per eam ad vnicum terminum, scilicer obliquum contendit. Manus ergo imprimit motum sursum; at verò quia & ipsa tunc temporis fertur à naui antrorsum, pariter motum indit antrorsum. Inde oritur pilam non tendere sursum recta, vt si à manu tantùm proiceretur; neque directè antrorsum, vt si veheretur à sola naui; sed fertur motu mixto, & obliquo, describitque per aerem quasi arcum, seu potius lineam parabolicam. Hinc est cur lapis neque minus altum tendat, quàm si à sola iaceretur manu; neque minus antrorsum, quàm si navi tantum proucheretur. Nam linea parabolica est quidem prolixior, quàm simpliciter sursum, & deorsum perpendicularis; verùm ad hoc supplet incussio à navi; & prolixior etiam, quàm simplex progressio; verùm ad hoc supplet impressio à manu. Hæc explicatio duo continet. Primum, quòd proiectum à motore translato moueatur parabolicè. Secundum, quòd motus antrorsum, & sursum non impediant se; unde mobile habere debeat eundem progressum ante, ac si ante solummodo perget; ret; eundemque motum sursum, ac si dumtaxat moueretur sursum.
units.tr: The reason is that whatever is moving imparts to the thing it carries within itself the same motion. Therefore, when someone throws a ball upward while the ship is running, you must conceive in it a double force: one its own, the other that of the ship, which carries it. Moreover, these forces unite into one, so that the movable is driven not by a double force but by a single one, and by it strives toward a single terminus, namely an oblique one. The hand therefore imparts motion upward; but because the hand itself is at that time carried forward by the ship, it likewise imparts motion forward. Hence it comes about that the ball does not travel straight upward, as it would if thrown only by the hand, nor directly forward, as it would if carried only by the ship; but it moves with a mixed and oblique motion, and describes through the air something like an arc, or rather a parabolic line. Hence the stone travels neither less high than if it were thrown by the hand alone, nor less far forward than if it were carried only by the ship. For a parabolic line is indeed longer than a simple perpendicular rising and falling; but the impulse from the ship makes up for this. And it is longer also than a simple forward progress; but the impression from the hand makes up for this. This explanation contains two points. First, that what is thrown by a moving mover is moved parabolically. Second, that the forward and upward motions do not impede each other; so that the movable must have the same progress forward as if it moved only forward, and the same upward motion as if it were moved only upward.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Motus incussus à motore translato parabolicè fit. An æquè fiat ac si motor non transferretur, experientia consulenda sunt.
units.tr: Motion impressed by a moving thrower is made parabolically. Whether it is made in the same way as if the thrower were not moving, experience must be consulted.

units.la: PRima pars conclusionis patet in iam allata explicatione, quæ desumpta est à Gassendo. Nam si proiector ipse mouetur, eundem sanè motum indit rei omni,quam in se habet. Propterea si dum vehitur naui, teneat pilam super manu expansa, hæc eundem concipit motum, quo ipse agitur.
