Fac ergo, ut eidem pilæ incutiatur vis à proiectore sursum, illa iam duos habet impetus, videlicet à naui antrorsum, & à proiectore sursum. Ex quo fit,ne possis concipere, illud mobile ferri simpliciter ad horizontem, neq; simpliciter ad perpendiculum,sed mixtim quodammodo, seu motu, qui sursum simul, & prorsum tendit. Hoc autem est moueri parabolicè, vt supra vidimus; ergo, &c. Quòdsi hunc motum parabolicè designatum non videant ij, qui suspiciùt è naui; ratio est, nam globus antrorsum actus, dum consequitur nautas, iminere semper debet eorum vertici, vnde illis vbique ad perpendiculum apparebit. Cæterùm siquis in ripa extra nauim stet, procul dubio motum videbit parabolicum.
units.tr: The first part of the conclusion is clear from the explanation already given, which is taken from Gassendi. For if the thrower himself is moving, he certainly imparts that same motion to everything he holds. So if, while travelling on a ship, he holds a ball on his outstretched hand, the ball takes on the same motion by which he is carried. Now let an upward force be imparted to the same ball by the thrower. It then has two impulses, one forward from the ship and one upward from the thrower. Hence you cannot conceive that this moving body is carried simply to the horizon, nor simply straight up and down, but in a mixed way, with a motion that tends at once upward and forward. This, however, is to move parabolically, as we saw above; therefore, etc. But if those who look up from the ship do not see this motion as parabolic, the reason is that the ball, driven forward, must always hover over the heads of the sailors as it keeps pace with them, so that to them it will appear to fall perpendicularly everywhere. If, however, someone stands on the bank outside the ship, he will without doubt see a parabolic motion.

units.la: X
units.tr: X

units.la: Secundam conclusionis partem dixi notanter statuendam esse per experientias. Nam si relinquatur soli rationi, res ardua videtur concipere, quòd validissimus impetus à motore incussus nihil penitus disturbet motum horizontaliter faciendum, itaut mobile ipso eodem tempore, quo conficeret lineam simpliciter horizontalem, signet parabolicam decuplò, imò centuplò maiorem, & rursus cadat in manum proiectoris. Difficulter, inquam, id concipit mens. Nam sicuti bombarda ex libella in horizonte constituta quò validius globum explodit, eò magis impedit motum grauitatis deorsum, sustinendo globum in aere diutius, ita videtur, quòd impetus à motore sursum incussus, motum antrorsum aliqualiter præpediat, ne tam citò fiat. Sed clarius in appositta figura.
units.tr: I said that the second part of the conclusion must be established carefully by experiments. For if it is left to reason alone, it seems hard to conceive that a very strong impetus impressed by the thrower disturbs in no way the horizontal motion to be made, so that the missile, in the same time in which it would traverse a line that is simply horizontal, describes a parabola ten times, indeed a hundred times, larger, and falls back into the thrower's hand. I say the mind conceives this with difficulty. For just as a cannon set level on a spirit-level, the more violently it fires its ball, the more it impedes the downward motion of gravity by holding the ball longer in the air, so it seems that an impetus impressed upward by the thrower somewhat hinders the forward motion, so that it does not occur so quickly. But it is clearer in the attached figure.

units.la: Sit linea horizontalis a. b. à duobus æquitantibus pernicissimè conficienda. Vterque dum reperitur in loco a. proijciat globum ad perpendiculum c. Sed primus v. gr. centuplò vehementiùs incutiat motum, quàm secundus. Pilæ non procedent rectà perpendiculariter, sed cum eijciantur à motoribus translatis, efficient lineas parabolicas a.d.b. a.e.b.Hoc dato, non videtur fore, vt mobilia conficiendo suam parabolam, possint eodem tempore totam decurrere lineam a.b. horizontaliter designatam, itaut quando equitantes reperientur in b. tunc simul excepturi sint manu suas pilas. Probatur. Supponamus v. gr. quòd per vnum horæ quadrantem decurrenda sit ab equitantibus a.b.Motus ergo vtrique pilæ in equitatione incussus efficietur à pilis antrorsum per eundem horæ quadrantem: sed hoc videtur non posse fieri; ergo. Probo minorem. Detur quòd pila, quæ minorem describit parabolam, dum cadit in b. totum horæ quadrantem simul cum equitantibus insumat; eo temporis momento non cadet in b. secunda pila, quæ maiorem designat parabolam; ergo non cadet in manum proiectoris. Probo minorem, quia linea parabolæ à posteriori globo descripta est v. gr. centuplò maior, ergo requirit plus temporis, vt cadat in b. & sic equitans, cùm illa ceciderit, non reperietur in b. sed processerit ad i. ad l. ad m. &c.
units.tr: Let AB be a horizontal line to be traversed very swiftly by two horsemen. Each, when found at point A, throws a ball perpendicularly to C. But the first throws his ball, let us say, a hundred times more vehemently than the second. The balls will not proceed straight up and down; since they are thrown by the moving riders, they will make parabolic lines A.D.B. and A.E.B. Given this, it does not seem that the missiles, in tracing their parabolas, can run through the whole horizontal line AB in the same time, so that when the riders are found at B they will at that moment catch their balls in hand. This is proved as follows. Suppose, for example, that the horsemen must traverse AB in one quarter of an hour. The motion impressed on each ball by the riding will then be carried forward by the balls through the same quarter of an hour; but this seems impossible; therefore. I prove the minor. Suppose that the ball which describes the smaller parabola, while falling at B, uses up the whole quarter of an hour together with the riders. At that moment the second ball, which describes the larger parabola, will not have fallen at B; therefore it will not fall into the thrower's hand. I prove the minor: the line of the parabola described by the second ball is, let us say, a hundred times greater, so it requires more time to fall at B; and so, when the first ball has fallen, the rider will not be found at B but will have advanced to I, L, M, and so on.

units.la: Deinde sic. Quotiescumque duo, quæ simul incipiant motum, pari velocitate mouentur, si alterum plus habeat spatij; emetiendum non deuenient simul eodem tempore ad eundem terminum: sed globus eiectus, qui cum equitante simul incipit motum, habet parem cum ipso velocitatem, & plus etiam spatij metiendum; ergo non deueniet simul cum ipso ad eundem terminum. Et sic equitans erit in b. quando globus per lineam suam parabolicam eo non pertigerit. Maior est certa. Minor etiam constat, parabola enim valdè prolixior est, quàm horizontalis. Præterea globus, qui facit parabolam in ordine ad motum antrorsum non mouetur velociùs equitante ipso, alioquin priùs illo deueniret in b. Rursus, quæ causa motum pilæ antrorsum auget? an fortasse impetus illi sursum incussus? Verùm hic potiùs motum antrorsum disturbat. Ergo citiùs deveniet equitans ad lineæ terminum b. quàm pila; vnde motus à proiectore translato non erit æquè talis, ac si fieret à non translato. Si tamen experientiæ contrarium ostendant, non repugno.
units.tr: Again, thus. Whenever two bodies that begin to move together move with equal velocity, if one has more space to traverse, they will not arrive at the same end at the same time. But the thrown ball, which begins its motion together with the rider, has the same velocity as he does, and also has more space to traverse; therefore it will not arrive at the same end together with him. And so the rider will be at B when the ball has not yet reached it along its parabolic line. The major is certain. The minor is also evident, for a parabola is much longer than a horizontal line. Moreover, the ball which makes the parabola is not moved forward more swiftly than the rider himself; otherwise it would reach B before him. Again, what cause increases the forward motion of the ball? Perhaps the impetus impressed upward? But here it rather disturbs the forward motion. Therefore the rider will reach the end of the line, B, more quickly than the ball. Whence the motion from a thrower who is in motion will not be altogether such as it would be from one who is not. If, however, experience shows the contrary, I do not object.

units.la: Porro ex tradita doctrina non illepida solutio aliquorum problematum exhauritur. Primò enim:cur ij,qui stant in naui, seu curru agitato, cadunt quoties repentè sistitur nauis, aut currus? Quia nihil mirum quidquid est in naui mota concipit motum ad eandem nauis partem:dum verò hæc subitò sistitur, pedes etiam, qui naui adhærent, sistuntur; sed caput,ac reliquum corpus, quod versus eandem partem concitabatur, non ita citò sistit se: pergit ergo immotis pedibus, & ita cadit, vel minatur casum: Secundò, cur dum rota sistitur, quidquid prius adhæserat, procul à se iacit? Quia voluente se rota, cætera illi adhærentia motum recipiunt eundem, quare si rota iniecta manu detineatur, non ita detinentur quæ adhærent, ac proinde ab ipsa diuellantur opus est. Tertiò: cur malleus manubrio inseritur, etiamsi ad terram vertatur: deberet enim deorsum cadere malleus, cum tamen ascendat, magisq; inseratur. Quia manubrium incitatè fertur ad eam partem, ad quam fit percussio; malleus autem non tam citò ad eandem propellitur, quia vtpotè grauior, magis resistit; dum ergo manubrium validè motum inuenit molleum non tam facilè cedentem, inserit illi sese. Quæ causa etiam est, cur perficum pompum, nucleumque simul findat cultellus, quamquam in aere pendeat.
units.tr: Further, from the doctrine delivered, a not unpleasant solution of several problems can be drawn. First: why do those who stand in a ship or a moving carriage fall whenever the ship or carriage is suddenly brought to a halt? Because everything in a moving ship naturally takes on motion toward the same part of the ship; but when the ship is suddenly stopped, the feet, which adhere to the ship, are stopped too, while the head and the rest of the body, which were being carried toward the same part, do not stop so quickly. The body therefore continues with its feet unmoved, and so falls, or threatens to fall. Second: why, when a wheel is stopped, does whatever had been sticking to it fly off? Because while the wheel turns, the other things adhering to it receive the same motion; hence if the wheel is held with the hand, the things adhering to it are not held in the same way, and so they must be torn away from it. Third: why is a hammer driven onto its handle even when the head is turned toward the ground? For the hammer ought to fall downward, yet it rises and is driven on more firmly. Because the handle is carried swiftly toward the part to which the blow is struck; but the hammer head is not propelled toward the same part so quickly, since, being heavier, it resists more. Therefore, when the handle finds the hammer, which does not yield easily, already moving with force, it inserts itself into it. This is also the reason why a knife splits a peach together with its stone, even though the peach hangs in the air.

units.la: Quartò: cur quò leuior est res, eò minùs mouetur si magnus impetus incutiatur? Quia vis impressa minùs durat in re leui, quàm in graui: deinde quia rei leui magis resistit medium. Quintò: cur baculi extrema permutantur in aere, quando in eius proiectione anteponitur quod leuius est? Quia grauius ob materiæ densitatem recipit magis vim incussam, ideoq; citiùs fertur. Sed alia plura, & curiosa videbimus alibi.
units.tr: Fourth: why is it that the lighter a thing is, the less it moves if a great impetus is impressed on it? Because the impressed force lasts less in a light body than in a heavy one, and also because the medium resists a light body more. Fifth: why do the ends of a stick exchange places in the air when, in throwing it, the lighter end is put in front? Because the heavier end, on account of the density of its matter, receives the impressed force more, and is therefore carried more quickly. But we shall see many other curious matters elsewhere.

units.la: DISQVISITIO TERTIA. De motu resultantia, seu resilientia.
units.tr: DISQUISITIO TERTIA. On motion of rebounding, or resilience.

units.la: PRO intelligentia notate, corpora quæ violento motu contra naturam suam ferri solent, aliquando tandem redire, siue quia in aliud resistens impacta nequeant progredi vlterius, & sic repelluntur; vel quia impetu, qui fuerat impressus, deficiente, rursus coguntur deorsum labi. Ex hoc duo puncta sese nobis offerunt examinanda. Primum, quomodo fiat ea mobilis repulsio, aut resilientia, quotiescunque allisum alteri ad oppositam redit partem. Secundum, quomodo motus, qui fit directus, continuetur motui reflexo, an videlicet quies aliqua inter vtrumque siue, vt aiunt, in puncto reflexionis detur. Quod spectat ad primum sit. (*,*) (†)
units.tr: To make this clear, note first that bodies which are commonly driven with violent motion against their nature do at last return, either because, striking against something that resists, they cannot advance further and so are thrown back, or because, the impetus that had been impressed upon them failing, they are compelled to slide downward again. From this two points present themselves for examination. The first is how that mobile repulsion, or resilience, comes about whenever a body that has struck another returns to the opposite side. The second is how the motion that begins as a direct motion is continued into the reflected motion, that is, whether some rest exists between the two, or, as they say, at the point of reflection. Let us take the first point first. (*,*) (†)

units.la: CONCLVSIO PRIMA.
units.tr: FIRST CONCLUSION.

units.la: Motus resilientia fit ex partium com- pressione subitaque restitutione- in pristinum.
units.tr: Resilience of motion arises from compression of the parts and their sudden restoration to their former state.

units.la: PRobatur quoad primum. Satis enim constat experientia, quod quæ alliduntur ad corpus aliquod, comprimunt sese. Ita globus plumbeus in parietem excussus apparet statim complanatus. Cera etiam in obstaculum impacta fit compressior ad eandem partem. Lusoria pila carbone tincta, & pauimento incussa orbiculatam in eo figuram relinquit; ergo signum est fuisse complanatam, secus allinifset punctum non orbem. Ratio autem huiusce rei est, quia cum virtus motiua quando fit allisio, adhuc sit valida, & mouere vlterius possit, necesse omnino est, per eam vrgeri mobile. Quoties vero aliquid ex altera parte vrgetur, & ex altera impeditur ne transeat, necessario sequitur compressio. Inde
units.tr: PIt is proved first. For experience makes it sufficiently clear that bodies which are struck against some object compress themselves. Thus a leaden ball thrown against a wall at once appears flattened. Wax too, when driven against an obstacle, becomes more compressed on the same side. A playing ball smeared with charcoal and struck against the pavement leaves a round figure there; this is a sign that it was flattened, for otherwise it would have marked a point, not a circle. The reason for this is that when impact occurs, the motive force is still strong and can move the body further, so the moving body must necessarily be pressed by it. Whenever something is pressed on one side and hindered on the other from passing through, compression necessarily follows. Hence

units.la: Probatur quoad secundum, quia dum res illisa, & incussa corpori comprimitur, tunc habet partes in statu violento. Coguntur ergo ad pristinum redire, figuramque sibi suam restituere; dumque mira celeritate hoc præstant, resilientiam efficiunt. Hinc est quòd reticulare instrumentum, fidibus neruosis contextum, vulgò dictum rachetta sic vehementer pilam impellit, nempe quia dum hæc impingitur, illud retrò cedit; sed pari velocitate sese rursus restituit. Hinc figura sphærica maximè apta est resilientiæ, quia cum tangat planum in minore sui parte, citiùs resurgit. Hinc plumbum, lana, pluma, & similia non resiliunt, quia cum partes habuerint pressas, non tamen easdem recolligunt, neque in pristinam figuram restituunt. Hinc magna pila, qua bracchialibus ligneis ludunt, per inflationem aptior est ad resilientiam, quia tunc vix impacta, illico se revocat à statu violento.
units.tr: It is proved second, because while the body struck and dashed against is compressed, its parts are then in a violent state. They are therefore forced to return to their former state and restore their own shape; and in doing this with remarkable speed they produce resilience. Hence it is that the racket, the netted instrument woven of gut strings, commonly called the racchetta, drives the ball so vehemently: while the ball is struck, the racket gives way backwards, but with equal speed it restores itself again. Hence a spherical figure is most apt for resilience, because, touching the plane with its smaller part, it springs back more quickly. Hence lead, wool, feathers, and similar things do not rebound, because once their parts have been pressed they do not gather themselves together again, nor restore themselves to their former shape. Hence a large ball, with which they play using wooden arms, is better suited to resilience by being inflated, because it immediately recalls itself from its violent state once struck.

units.la: Pro secundo quæstionis puncto aduertite, motum directum, & reflexum posse utrumque naturalem esse; vt est restrictio cordis, & dilatatio. Secundo esse posse utrumque violentum, vt est proiectio pilæ ad parietem, eiusque repercussio. Tertio esse posse directum naturalem, & reflexum violentum; vt est descensio lapidis, eiusdemque resilitio.
units.tr: As to the second point of the question, note that a direct motion and a reflected motion may each be natural, as is the contraction and dilation of the heart. Second, each may be violent, as is the throwing of a ball against a wall and its rebound. Third, a direct motion may be natural and a reflected motion violent, as is the falling of a stone and its bouncing back.

units.la: Quartò esse posse directum violentum, & reflexum naturalem: vt est eiectio pilæ sursum, & illius reditio deorsum. Quoad omnia notetur. (†)
units.tr: Fourth, a direct motion may be violent and a reflected motion natural, as is the throwing of a ball upward and its return downward. Let all of these be noted.

units.la: CONCLVSIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: SECOND CONCLUSION.

units.la: Inter motum localem, directum, & refle- xum, quicumque ille fit, aliquam interponi quietem verosi- milius est.
units.tr: Between local motion, whether direct or reflexive, whatever it may be, some rest is more likely to be interposed.

units.la: PRobabant nonnulli philosophi ratione, quam deducunt ex Aristotele 8. phys. t.65. quia si utrumq; inter motum, directum, & reflexum,non interponitur quies, debet pro eodem instanti ultima pars motus directi simul esse cum prima parte reflexi: hoc fieri nullo modo potest; ergo. Minor patet, quia secus pro uno, eodemque instanti mobile ferretur ante, ac retro, ut c. p. sequelam probant, quia si nulla quies inter directum, reflexumq; motum est, ergo cum extrema parte directi penetratur pars reflexi; aut si non penetratur, ergo inter utramque aliqua intermissio contingit. Sed haec probatio non videtur satis efficax. Dici enim potest, nullam dari quietem inter utrumq; motum, ex eo quia ultima pars directi cessat in uno instanti temporis; & prima reflexi oritur immediatè in sequenti. Sicut ergo inter instans a. & b. temporis non datur medium, ita neque inter motum directum, qui cessat in a. & reflexum incipientem ex b. datur quies.
units.tr: Some philosophers used to prove this by reasoning drawn from Aristotle, Physics 8, text 65: if no rest is interposed between direct and reflexive motion, then at the same instant the last part of the direct motion must coincide with the first part of the reflexive motion, and this cannot happen in any way; therefore (there is a rest). The minor premise is plain, because otherwise the mobile would be carried forward and backward at one and the same instant. They prove the consequence thus: if there is no rest between the direct and the reflexive motion, then the extreme part of the direct motion penetrates the part of the reflexive motion; or, if it does not penetrate it, then some interval occurs between the two. But this proof does not seem very effective. For it can be said that no rest is given between the two motions because the last part of the direct motion ceases in one instant of time, and the first part of the reflexive motion arises immediately in the following instant. Just as no middle lies between instants a and b of time, so there is no rest between the direct motion, which ceases at a, and the reflexive motion beginning at b.

units.la: Probatur itaque melius conclusio per ea, quae diximus de morularum interpositione. sitione, quia mobile dum à motu directo in vltima spatij vbicatione constitutum est, non relinquit ipsum tota ea velocitate, quæ possibilis est, adeout redire citius nullo modo possit; ergo in ea vltima vbicatione qu es aliqua, insensibilis, & minima inseritur. Antecedens probatur, quia mobile quò grauius est, citius etiam descendit ab vbicatione, per motu directu vltimò possessa; sed assignato quocumq; mobili, poterit dari aliud grauius, quod proinde semper citius vbicationem relinquet; igitur primum non ita citò ab ea descendit; ergo ibi aliquantisper moratur. Quid enim est non remoueri tam citò, nisi aliqualiter morari? Sed consutare quæ alibi diximus.
units.tr: The conclusion is better proved by what we have said about the interposition of short delays. For the mobile, when it has come to rest at the final position reached by the direct motion, does not leave that position with all the velocity that is possible, so that it cannot return any sooner; therefore in that final position some insensible and minimal rest is introduced. The antecedent is proved because the heavier a mobile is, the sooner it descends from the position it holds at the end of its direct motion; but for any mobile assigned, another heavier one can be given, which will always leave the position sooner; therefore the first does not leave it so quickly, and therefore it lingers there for a little while. For what is it not to be removed so quickly, except to linger in some way? But consult what we have said elsewhere.

units.la: Opponis. Pila resiliens à terra si quiesceret in puncto reflexionis, amitteret impetum, ergo non resiliret. Deinde si datur quies ista, sequitur, quòd sursum eiectus lapis valeat in puncto reflexionis totum sustinere montem. Probatur, quia si caderet mons, posset incurrere in lapidem eo instanti, quo quiesceret, ergo tunc sustineretur à lapide; secus enim lapis non haberet quietem.
units.tr: You object: a ball rebounding from the ground, if it rested at the point of reflection, would lose its impetus, and so would not rebound. Further, if such a rest is given, it follows that a stone thrown upward could at the point of reflection hold up an entire mountain. This is proved: if the mountain were to fall, it could run into the stone at the instant when the stone was at rest; therefore the stone would then be sustaining it; otherwise the stone would not have rest.

units.la: Respond. ad primum negando antecedens. Non enim amittitur impetus ob insensibiles moras, vnde quamuis ille semper vigeat, quia tamen finitus, ac limitatus est, ideo nequit deferre mobile omni prorsus velocitate possibili: habet ergo quietulas. Ad secundum Respond. quòd mons cadendo non à lapide sustineretur, sed à semet per minimas quietes, morulasque suo pariter motui adspersas. Deinde respondeo. Si eo instanti, quo mons impingit, ipse non quiescens lapidem minuenitet quiescentem, disturbaret eundem à quiete. Sed inde nil contra nos, tunc enim adesset causa destructiua morae alioquin futurae. Tertiò dico. Ille lapis detrudi posset citius à Deo, siue ab Angelo, quàm ab hoc monte, igitur vrgente monte, non ita citò descendit, ergo insensibiliter in puncto reflexionis moratur.
units.tr: I reply to the first by denying the antecedent. For impetus is not lost through insensible delays; hence, although it always persists, because it is finite and limited it cannot carry the mobile with every possible velocity, and so there are small rests. To the second I reply that the mountain, in falling, would not be sustained by the stone but by itself, through minimal rests and delays scattered equally throughout its motion. Next I reply: if at the instant the mountain strikes, it, not itself resting, were to push back the resting stone, it would disturb the stone from its rest. But nothing against us follows from this, for then there would be a destructive cause of the delay that would otherwise occur later. Thirdly I say: that stone could be pushed more quickly by God or by an Angel than by this mountain; therefore, under the pressure of the mountain, it does not descend so quickly; therefore it lingers insensibly at the point of reflection.

units.la: Porro inter motus locales certè admirabilis est Mechanicus in vecte, troclea, caeterisque machinis, & instrumentis, unde ingeniosissima Philosophiae pars facta est speculationibus Aristotelis, Archimedis, aliorumque veterum, quas deinde illustrarunt acutissimi recentiores. Itaq; de hoc etiam erudilionis gratia esset agendum; sed quidquid pulchri, & curiosi habet haec scientia, maximè in problematum solutionibus videri potest in Physica Vniuersali, quam habetis editam à P. Stephano Cosmo doctissimo Praeceptore meo. Eum itaque praestat consulere, quàm hoc loco referibere, quae iam sunt ad manum.
units.tr: Among local motions, the mechanics of the lever, the pulley and the other machines and instruments is certainly admirable; from it a most ingenious part of philosophy has been made by the speculations of Aristotle, Archimedes and other ancients, which more acute recent writers have since illustrated. So this too ought to be treated for the sake of learning; but whatever is beautiful and curious in this science can be seen above all in the solutions of problems in the Universal Physics, which you have in print from Fr. Stephen Cosmus, my most learned teacher. It is better, therefore, to consult that work than to repeat here what is already at hand.

units.la: x
units.tr: x

units.la: DISPVTATIO TERTIA. De Loco.
units.tr: DISPUTATIO TERTIA. On Place.

units.la: MOtus, qui habet pro termino locū, in quo mobilia constituit, nobis quoque de loco affert disputationem. In hac igitur studium collocemus nostrum, & ita quidem, vt ad ea, quæ physicæ clau fulam decent, in hac extrema temporis angustia demus locum. Sed locus omnino duplex est: alter extrinsecus; intrinsecus alter. De primo hic statim quærimus; de secundo post.
units.tr: Motion, which takes as its term the place in which it sets moving things, presents us also with a disputation concerning place. Let us therefore direct our study to this, and do so in such a way that, in this extreme shortness of time, we give room to those matters which befit the closing part of physics. But place is altogether twofold: one is extrinsic, the other intrinsic. Of the first we inquire here immediately; of the second, afterwards.

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.

units.la: Quid sit locus extrinsecus.
units.tr: What an external place is.

units.la: PRO intelligentia statim adduco sententiam Philosophi, qui lib. 4. phys. cap. 4. & 5. sic definit locum. Est vltima superficies corporis ambientis immobilis. V. g. vltima superficies aeris, quæ tangit, ambitque turrim, ei se adæquatè, ac secundum figuram accommodando, vocatur ab Aristotele physicus, realisq; locus. Dicitur autem immobilis, non quia nullo modo moueri possit, sed quia per se non ordinatur, vt secum deferat locatum.
units.tr: To begin with, for the sake of understanding, I adduce at once the opinion of the Philosopher, who in Book 4 of the Physics, chapters 4 and 5, defines place thus: It is the innermost surface of the surrounding body, which is immovable. For example, the innermost surface of the air, which touches and surrounds the tower, fitting itself to it exactly and conforming to its shape, is called by Aristotle physical and real place. It is said to be immovable not because it can in no way be moved, but because it is not by its own nature ordered to carry along what is placed in it.

units.la: Sed hęc doctrina suas patitur difficultates. Primò enim ille tantummodo in omnium opinione censetur, locus ad quem per se datur motus localis : non fit autem localis motus ad talem superficiem, sed vt corpus hic, ibi, alibi constituatur. Deinde turris flante vento non dicitur mutare locum; neq; scopulus alia succedente, vel decrescente aqua, secus mutaretur locus à corpore immoto: & nihilominus mutatur superficies corporis ambientis immobilis, nempe medii, quod ex natura sua non defert locatum.
units.tr: But this doctrine has its difficulties. For first, that surface is considered by everyone's opinion to be only that to which local motion is directly directed; yet local motion is not made toward such a surface, but so that the body is set down here, there, or elsewhere. Next, when a tower is struck by the wind we do not say that it changes its place; nor does a reef change its place when another wave comes in or the water recedes, although the body is immovable; and yet the surface of the surrounding body that is immovable, namely of the medium, which by its nature does not carry along what is placed in it, is changed.

units.la: Est igitur definitioni Aristotelæ aliud quid apponendum, nempe talis, ac tanta distantia rei locatæ à certis, fixisque partibus medij, in quo locus est. V. g. si moremur in terra. Locus definiri potest sic. Superficies corporis ambientis connotando talem distantiam rei locatæ à certis, atq; signatis partibus terræ fixis.
units.tr: Something else, then, must be added to Aristotle's definition, namely such a distance, and so great, of the placed thing from certain fixed parts of the medium in which the place is. For example, if we remain on the earth, place may be defined thus: The surface of the surrounding body, connoting such a distance of the placed thing from certain and marked fixed parts of the earth.

units.la: Dico terræ, non vniuersi, nam huiusmodi partes non assumuntur, nisi centrū, & polis: sed moueri quis potest per Æquatorem, aut parallelum, seruando semper eandem à centro, & polis distantiam; ergo mouebitur localiter, & non mutabit locum, quod absurdum est. Debet igitur hæc distantia sumi à partibus terræ certis, ac signatè notatis, in ordine ad quas vel accedendo, vel recedendo fiat loci mutatio. Hinc si nauis certa quadam à ripis distantia constituatur in anchoris, quantumlibet ventus, & aqua nouas illi asserant superficies, non ideo mutat locum, quia nec ad ripam accedit magis, neq; recedit.
units.tr: I say of the earth, not of the universe, for parts of that kind are assumed only in the case of the centre and the poles; but someone may be moved along the equator or a parallel, always keeping the same distance from the centre and the poles; therefore he will be moved locally and will not change his place, which is absurd. This distance must therefore be taken from certain parts of the earth, distinctly and clearly marked, with reference to which the change of place occurs by approaching or receding. Hence if a ship is held at a certain distance from the banks by its anchors, however much the wind and water bring it new surfaces, it does not for that reason change its place, because it neither comes nearer to the bank nor moves away from it.

units.la: Sequitur ex dictis, cœlum Empyreum, quà qua parte Paradisus vocatur, non esse in loco reali extrinseco. Et ratio est, quia non ambitur à superficie corporis circumaccumbentis, nullum enim tale ibi reperitur. Quo modo etiam Philosophus, 4. phys. t. 46. docuit, octauam sphæram supra quam aliud corpus non agnouit, proprie non esse in loco extrinseco.
units.tr: It follows from what has been said that the Empyrean heaven, which is called Paradise in the part where it is, is not in a real external place. The reason is that it is not surrounded by the surface of a body lying around it, for no such body is found there. In the same way the Philosopher also taught, Physics 4, text 46, that the eighth sphere, beyond which he recognised no other body, is not properly in an external place.

units.la: Postremò variæ solent assignari proprietates loci. Primò enim locus potest seiungi à locato. 2. est æqualis locato, scilicet quoad superficiem, ratione cuius illi extrinsecè commensuratur. 3. est immobilis, continet conseruatq; locatum, &c. Similiter in corporibus locatis diuersas positionum differentias notant, eæque dicuntur omnino sex, nempe sursum, deorsum, ante, retro, dextrorsum, sinistrorsum, &c.
units.tr: Finally, various properties of place are usually assigned. First, place can be separated from what is placed in it. Second, it is equal to what is placed in it, namely as to its surface, by reason of which it is extrinsically measured against it. Third, it is immovable, and contains and preserves what is placed in it, etc. Similarly, in bodies that are placed they note various differences of position, and these are said to be altogether six, namely upward, downward, before, behind, to the right, to the left, etc.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISQUISITION II.

units.la: An idem corpus esse possit simul in pluribus locis.
units.tr: Whether the same body can be in several places at once.

units.la: PRO intelligentia notetur, modum in loco existendi (prout attinet ad rem nostram) esse duplicem. Primus dicitur circumscriptiuus, quando scilicet corpus ita coexistit alicui spatio, vt illi commensuretur, habeatque partem extra partem, singulas diuersis loci vbicationibus correspondentes. Quo pacto v. g. existo ego in cathedra, quia pars quælibet mea extraponitur alteri, nempe manus extra locum brachij, humerus extra locum pectoris, &c. Secundus existendi modus appellatur definitiuus, & conuenit substantiæ spirituali, est verò talis, vt per eum constituatur quidem res in loco finito, sed tamen intra illum indiuisibiliter maneat, nimirum tota in toto loco, atque tota in quauis parte loci. Sic existeret Angelus in hoc gymnasio; existit anima rationalis in corpore humano; existit Christus in hostia, videlicet non habens partem extra partem, sed omnes vnà penetratas, adeout sub omni hostiæ particula sit miraculosè corpus totum simul. Quapropter hæ duæ præsentiæ locales conueniunt in eo, quòd sunt finitæ, ac limitatæ: differunt verò penes modum locandi. Hoc posito.
units.tr: To understand the question, it should be noted that the mode of being in a place (as far as it bears on our matter) is twofold. The first is called circumscriptive, when a body so coexists with some space that it is measured by that space and has part outside part, each part corresponding to a different position in the place. For example, I am in a chair in this way, because each part of me lies outside another: my hand outside the place of my arm, my shoulder outside the place of my chest, and so on. The second mode of existing is called definitive. It belongs to spiritual substance, and it is such that a thing is indeed constituted in a finite place, yet remains within it indivisibly, namely whole in the whole place and whole in any part of the place. In this way an angel would exist in this school-hall; the rational soul exists in the human body; Christ exists in the host, not having part outside part, but all his parts penetrating one another, so that by a miracle the whole body is at once under every particle of the host. Hence these two local presences agree in this, that they are finite and limited, but they differ in their mode of locating. This being laid down,

units.la: Supponunt omnes, nullam creaturam esse posse naturaliter in duplici loco adæquato, nam quia finita, & limitata est, nō nisi vno loco limitato, ac finito circumscribi potest. Secundò tenent non implicare, quòd corpus idem simul sit in multiplici loco etiam distanti. Docet enim fides, Christi corpus non solùm esse in cælo, verùm & in omni hostia, quæ immolatur. Difficultas igitur eò tendit, an corpus idem simul esse possit in pluribus locis extensiuè, atq; circumscriptiuè. Puta: Franciscus quemadmodum hic adest circumscriptiuè, longus, profundus, atus, itane sic extensus potest de absoluta potentia simul esse Muriani? Aliqui negant. Affirmant alij, cū quibus notetur.
units.tr: All hold that no creature can naturally be in two adequate places at once, for since it is finite and limited, it can be circumscribed by only one limited and finite place. Secondly, they hold that it implies no contradiction for the same body to be at once in many places, even distant ones, for faith teaches that the body of Christ is not only in heaven but also in every host that is offered. The difficulty therefore comes down to this: whether the same body can at once be in several places both extensively and circumscriptively. For instance: Francis, who is here present circumscriptively, long, deep and high, can he by absolute power be at once extended in this way also at Murano? Some deny it. Others affirm it, and with them this is to be noted.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSIO.

units.la: Non implicat corpus idem simul esse circumscriptiue in pluribus locis.
units.tr: It does not imply a contradiction that the same body should be circumscriptively in several places at once.

units.la: PRobatur .1. quia Christus circumscriptiuè manet in cælo, & simul definitiuè sub hostijs, ergo vtrobiq; manere poterit circumscriptiuè. Probo consequentiam. Præsentia circumscriptiua, quam Christus habet in cælo, non impedit quò minus alibi constituatur; ergo quemadmodum ponitur alibi definitiuè, sic etiam extensiuè constitui poterit. Res videtur citrà dubium, &
units.tr: It is proved first, because Christ remains circumscriptively in heaven and at the same time definitively under the sacramental species; therefore he will be able to remain circumscriptively in both places. I prove the consequence. The circumscriptive presence which Christ has in heaven does not prevent him from being situated elsewhere; therefore, just as he is placed elsewhere definitively, so also he can be situated extensively. The matter seems beyond doubt, and

units.la: Probatur 2. sic: Adest iam Christus in hostia sacramentaliter, definitiuè, ac penetratus quoad partes. Quæro: si Christus in altari existens vellet extendere se, porrigere caput extra pectus, extra humeros bracchia, pedes extra crura, &c. posset, necne? Certè nil video, cur nequeat, sigue impediatur. Tunc verò adesset in cælo, & in altari extensiuè. Dicis adesse impotentiâ, quia præsentia circumscriptiua ita limitat corpus ad vnum locum essentialiter, vt extra illum constitui non possit. Contra, &
units.tr: It is proved secondly, thus. Christ is already present in the host sacramentally, definitively, and penetrating it as to its parts. I ask: if Christ, existing in the altar, wished to extend himself, to stretch his head beyond his breast, his arms beyond his shoulders, his feet beyond his legs, and so on, could he or could he not? I certainly see nothing to prevent it or hinder it. Then he would be in heaven and on the altar extensively. You say he is not present because of an inability, since circumscriptive presence limits the body essentially to one place, so that it cannot be constituted outside that place. On the contrary, and

units.la: Probatur 3. quia vel præsentia circumscriptiua limitat corpus ad vnum essentialiter locum, adeout non possit vllo modo esse alibi, aut non possit esse alibi circumscriptiuè. Non primum, alioquin Corpus Christi non esset in cælo, & in hostia. Neq; secundum; quæro enim cur nequit corpus etiam alibi existere_ circumscriptiue? da rationem formalé, & præcisam. Dicis: quia præsentia illa prima de se ordinata essentialiter est ad constituendum in vno tantùm loco. Contra: Sed exinde non sequitur negatio alterius præsentiæ circumscriptiuæ. Probo quia licèt corpus locetur alibi circumscriptiuè, non locatur ex vi prioris præsentiæ, sed per aliam; ergo prima illa_ præsentia semper essentialiter habet constituere corpus in vno tantùm loco; ergò non destruitur eius essentia, si alia similis eidem corpori adueniat.
units.tr: It is proved thirdly. Either circumscriptive presence limits the body essentially to one place, so that it cannot be anywhere else in any way, or it cannot be elsewhere circumscriptively. Not the first, for otherwise the body of Christ would not be in heaven and in the host. Nor the second. For I ask why the body cannot also exist elsewhere circumscriptively. Give the formal and precise reason. You say: because that first presence is by its nature essentially ordered to constitute the body in only one place. On the contrary: but it does not follow from this that the other circumscriptive presence is denied. I prove it, because although the body is placed elsewhere circumscriptively, it is not placed by the force of the first presence, but by another. Therefore that first presence always essentially has to constitute the body in only one place. Therefore its essence is not destroyed if another presence like it comes to the same body.

units.la: Probatur 4. nam si præsentia circumscriptiua impedit aliam circumscriptiuam; ergo impedit etiam definitiuam: hoc dici non debet; ergo. Minorem tu quoque admittis, nam Christus circumscriptiuè in cælo existens, manet in altari definitiuè. Probo sequelam sic. Ideo præcisè circumscriptiua præsentia impedit aliam quoque circumscriptiuam, quia_ de se limitatiua est corporis ad vnum tantummodo locum, ergo excludit quidquid constitueret alibi corpus: at præsentia_ definitiua constituit corpus alibi; ergo excludit præsentiam definitiuam; quod absurdissimum est.
units.tr: It is proved fourthly. For if circumscriptive presence prevents another circumscriptive presence, then it also prevents definitive presence. This should not be said. Therefore the premise is false. You too admit the minor, for Christ, existing circumscriptively in heaven, remains definitively in the altar. I prove the consequence thus. Circumscriptive presence prevents another circumscriptive presence precisely because it is by its nature what limits the body to only one place. Therefore it excludes whatever would constitute the body elsewhere. But definitive presence constitutes the body elsewhere. Therefore it excludes definitive presence. This is most absurd.

units.la: Probari vltimò potest per dignissimas fide historias de Christo, qui visibiliter apparuit Saulo eunti Damascum, Beatissimæ Virgini animam efflanti, D. Petro se scRoma surripienti. 2. de S. Antonio Patauino, qui vno tempore Vlysipone,ac Pata-
units.tr: It can be proved lastly by the most worthy histories about Christ that are sure by faith: how he appeared visibly to Saul as he was going to Damascus; how he appeared to the Most Blessed Virgin as she breathed her last; and how he appeared to St Peter, who was fleeing from Rome. Secondly, there is St Anthony of Padua, who at one time showed himself preaching from the pulpit both at Lisbon and at Padua.

units.la: Patauij de pulpito concionantem se ostedit. Postremò de alijs innumeris,ad quæ deneganda non ratio, sed sola opinionis præoccupatio suadere potest.
units.tr: Lastly, there are countless other cases, which to deny cannot be urged by reason, but only by a prejudice of opinion.

units.la: Obijcies .r. si corpus idem simul esset in pluribus locis, foret diuisum à se ipso, atq; adeo non maneret amplius idem. Probatur sequela, nam loca sunt ab inuicem diuisa ;ergo & corpus vtrobiq; constitutum diuideretur à semet.
units.tr: You will object first: if the same body were at the same time in several places, it would be divided from itself and so would no longer remain the same. The consequence is proved, for places are divided from one another; therefore the body, constituted in each place, would be divided from itself.

units.la: Respond. retorquendo argumentum, quia Corpus Christi non diuiditur à se, licèt in cælo, & sub hostia sit. Resp. 2. negando sequelam. Ratio est, nam diuisio non dicit solùm duplicem localem præsentiam, sed principaliùs duplicem entitatem. Corpus autem bilocatum esset vnica entitas, vnde à semet non diuideretur. Sicut ergo duo corpora in vno loco posita manerent adhuc inter se diuisa; ita è contra vnum corpus in duobus locis à semet ipso non diuideretur.
units.tr: I answer by turning the argument back, because the body of Christ is not divided from itself, although it is in heaven and under the host. I answer secondly by denying the consequence. The reason is that division signifies not merely a double local presence but, more principally, a double entity. But a body bilocated would be a single entity, so it would not be divided from itself. Just as two bodies placed in one place would still remain divided from each other, so, on the contrary, one body in two places would not be divided from itself.

units.la: Obijcies 2. Non potest vna, eademque res distare à se: at si corpus in duplici loco foret, iam distaret à se : igitur &c. Probatur minor, quia v. g. Venetiæ distant Roma; ergo quidquid Venetijs est, distat quoq; Roma : sed Petrus foret Venetiis, ergo distaret à se posito Romæ.
units.tr: You will object secondly: one and the same thing cannot be distant from itself. But if the body were in a double place, it would already be distant from itself. Therefore, etc. The minor is proved, for example, because Rome is distant from Venice. Therefore whatever is at Venice is also distant from Rome. But Peter would be at Venice; therefore he would be distant from himself, being placed at Rome.

units.la: Respond. retorquendo argumentum in corpore Christi, vt supra 2. nego minorem primi. Ratio est, quia distantia cadit solùm inter duo : corpus verò bilocatum esset vnicum, ergo non distaret à se. 3. ad probationem distinguo consequens. Quidquid est Venetiis distat Roma, si hoc ipsum non sit etiam Romæ, cœcedo; si è contra, nego. Corpus autem esset simul vtrobique, vnde non distaret à se. Quid ergo esset distans? præsentia Venetia à Romana, quia illa non esset Romæ; neq; ista Venetiis.
units.tr: I answer by turning the argument back on the body of Christ, as above in the second answer, and I deny the minor of the first. The reason is that distance falls only between two things, but a bilocated body would be a single thing, and therefore would not be distant from itself. Third, as to the proof I distinguish the consequent. Whatever is at Venice is distant from Rome, if that very thing is not also at Rome, I grant; if on the contrary it is, I deny. But the body would be at both places at once, so it would not be distant from itself. What then would be distant? The presence at Venice from the presence at Rome, because the former would not be at Rome, nor the latter at Venice.

units.la: Obiicitur 3. Si corpus existeret circumscriptiuè in duplici loco, in neutro existeret circumscriptiuè. Probatur, nam præsentia circumscriptiua ita limitat corpus ad locum, vt extra illum esse nequeat: secus non est amplius circumscriptiua: sed iam corpus foret extra primum locum, ergo, &c.
units.tr: You will object thirdly: if a body existed circumscriptively in a double place, it would exist circumscriptively in neither. This is proved, for circumscriptive presence so limits the body to a place that it cannot be outside it. Otherwise it is no longer circumscriptive. But now the body would be outside the first place. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Resp. negando sequelam. Ad probationem distinguo. Præsentia circumscriptiua limitat corpus ad vnum tantummodo locum naturaliter, concedo: essentialiter, nego. Si enim corpori eidem noua contingat præsentia (quæcunque sit) alibi etiam constituetur. Simili modo quo albedo v. g. constituit solummodo album naturaliter, non verò essentialiter, si .n. Deus relinquat in subiecto & nigredine, res eadem foret alba, & nigra simul. Foret inquam alba tantùm, ratione albedinis, & nigra tantùm, respectu nigredinis. Ita ergo idem corpus foret Romæ tantùm per vbi Romanum: & Venetiis tantùm per vbi Venetum. Distinguo 2. præsentia circumscriptiua limitat corpus ad vnū tantummodo locum respectu sui, concedo: respectu locati, nego. Nimirum præsentia sentia circumscriptiua, hæc vna numerò, certè de se habet hoc, vt non possit constituere corpus nisi vno in loco, est enim forma tali spatio, & non alteri essentialiter affixa. Verùm adhuc finit corpus locatum esse indifferens, vt constituatur etiam alibi, si noua præsentia eidem accideritio.
units.tr: I answer by denying the consequence. As to the proof, I distinguish. Circumscriptive presence limits the body to only one place naturally, I grant; essentially, I deny. For if a new presence (of whatever kind) comes to that same body, it will be constituted elsewhere as well. In the same way, whiteness, for example, constitutes the thing white only naturally, not essentially. For if God were to leave blackness in the same subject, the thing would be white and black at once. It would be white only by reason of the whiteness, and black only with respect to the blackness. So the same body would be at Rome only through a Roman where, and at Venice only through a Venetian where. I distinguish a second time: circumscriptive presence limits the body to only one place with respect to itself, I grant; with respect to the located body, I deny. Namely, circumscriptive presence, this one numerically, certainly has this by its nature: that it can constitute a body only in one place, for it is a form suited to such a space and not essentially fixed to another. But the located body still remains indifferent, so that it can be constituted elsewhere as well, if a new presence should happen to befall it.

units.la: Obijcies 4. Si corpus in duplici loco poneretur, locus foret maior locato. Rursus, locatum esset extra locum; quæ omnia repugnant. Probatur, quia corpus maneret semper vnum, & loca duo; igitur locus maior locato. Præterea, corpus Romæ positum existeret Venetiis; ergo maneret extra locum.
units.tr: You will object fourthly: if a body were placed in a double place, the place would be greater than the located body. Again, the located body would be outside its place. All these things are contradictory. It is proved, because the body would always remain one and the places two. Therefore the place is greater than the located body. Moreover, the body placed at Rome would exist at Venice; therefore it would remain outside its place.

units.la: Respond. retorquendo argumentum in Corpore Christi. 2. nego vtramq; sequelam. Ratio est quia etiamsi locus reuera sit duplex, tamen corpus æquiualet ipsi vi replicationis,& duplicis præsentiæ, ob quam redditur virtualiter duplex, & ideo nequit locus dici maior locato. Insuper neq; corpus Romæ positum extra suum locum est, quia & Venetiis reperiatur; nam virtute duplicis præsentiæ, constituitur æquè bene intra duplice locum.
units.tr: I answer by turning the argument back on the body of Christ. I deny both consequences. The reason is that even if the place is really double, nevertheless the body is equal to it by virtue of replication and of the double presence, by which it is rendered virtually double. Therefore the place cannot be called greater than the located body. Moreover, the body placed at Rome is not outside its place, although it is also found at Venice, for by virtue of the double presence it is constituted equally well within the double place.

units.la: Obijcies vltimò. Causa formalis constitutiua corporis in loco circumscriptiuè, vna tantum est, ergo per ipsam nequit existere corpus in duplici loco. Antecedens probatur, nam corpus manet in loco circumscriptiuè per quantitatem, quæ semper vnica est. Consequentia currit, non enim ab vna causa formali potest haberi duplex formalis effectus, vt patet.
units.tr: You will object lastly. The formal constitutive cause of a body in a place circumscriptively is only one. Therefore through it alone the body cannot exist in a double place. The antecedent is proved, for the body remains in a place circumscriptively through quantity, which is always single. The consequence holds, for a double formal effect cannot be had from one formal cause, as is plain.

units.la: Respond. distinguendo antecedens: Causa formalis constitutiua in loco est vna, si loquamur de remota, concedo; si de proxima, nego. Ad probationem quoq. distinguo: Corpus manet circumscriptiuè in loco per quantitatem, vt per causam remotè constitutiuam, concedo; proximè constitutiuam, nego. Aduerte igitur, quantitatem non esse id, quo formaliter proximè constituatur corpus in loco: sed vbi locale, aut præsentia talis est; vnde prout ista fuerit circumscriptiua, seu definitiua, corpus etiam circumscriptiuè, aut definitiuè locabitur. Et sic etiã iuxta quòd præsentia multiplicatur, corpus quoque in multiplici loco statuitur. Quantitas ergo est causa remota radicalis, & materialis, quare aliqua res circumscriptiuè sit in loco, nam & ipsa per aliud superadditum locari debet. Satis est igitur, si causa formalis proxima sit duplex, vt effectus etiam duplex fiat. Respond.
units.tr: I answer by distinguishing the antecedent. The formal constitutive cause in a place is one, if we speak of the remote cause, I grant; if of the proximate cause, I deny. As to the proof also I distinguish. The body remains circumscriptively in a place through quantity, as through a remote constitutive cause, I grant; as through a proximate constitutive cause, I deny. Note therefore that quantity is not that by which the body is formally and proximately constituted in a place. Rather, what is local is the presence, or such a presence. So, as that presence is circumscriptive or definitive, the body too will be placed circumscriptively or definitively. And thus, in proportion as the presence is multiplied, the body is also established in multiple places. Quantity, then, is the radical and material remote cause why some thing is in a place circumscriptively, for quantity itself must also be placed by something else superadded. It is enough, therefore, if the proximate formal cause is double, so that the effect too becomes double. I answer.

units.la: 2. Quantitatem esse vnam in se quoad entitatem; sed eo ipso quòd afficitur alia præsentia, fit virtualiter duplex, vnde circumscriptiuè in duplici loco esse, atque constituere potest. (†) ✠
units.tr: Secondly, quantity is one in itself as to its entity. But by the very fact that it is affected by another presence, it becomes virtually double. Hence it can be in a double place circumscriptively and constitute it. (†) ✠

units.la: DISQVISITIO TERTIA.
units.tr: DISQUISITIO TERTIA.

units.la: An corpus in duplici loco posi- tum debeat se vtrobique habere vno modo.
units.tr: Whether a body placed in two places ought to be affected in the same way in both.

units.la: PRO intelligentia sciendum est, prædicata, quæ conueniunt corpori (vt ad præsentem rem attinet) esse in duplici genere. Alia siquidem sunt localia, seu à loco dependentia, quæ proinde ab eo transferri nullo modo possunt. Alia omnino absoluta, & à loco independentia, quæ propterea se habent indifferenter, vt sint hic, ibi, alibi; &c. Prima, seu primi generis prædicata sunt v. g. vbicatio Veneta, sessio Romana, deambulatio Patauina, &c. hæc enim accidentia ita suis locis affixa sunt, vt nullatenus possint alibi esse. Quocirca repugnat omnino vbicationem Venetam, qua ego sum constitutus Venetijs, replicari Romæ, statim ac enim foret ibi, non amplius Veneta esset, sed Romana. Ita sessio, qua quis Patauii sedet, essentialiter affigitur Patauio, neq. illa eadem reproduci Parisijs potest; secus eo ipso amitteret essentiam suam, quæ consistit in hoc, vt situet corpus Patauii, & non alibi, alioquin non foret amplius eadem sessio Patauina, sed alia Parisiensis. Prædicata secundi generis absoluta sunt, neq; dependent à loco, vt esse calidum, esse frigidum; vigilare, dormire, viuere, mori, &c. Hæc si-quiquidem nullam gerunt connexionem, cū loco, vtpotequæ mutatis etiam locis eadem prorsus manent. Hoc posito.
units.tr: To understand this, it must be known that the predicates which belong to a body (as far as the present question goes) fall into two kinds. Some are local, or dependent on place, and for that reason cannot be transferred from it in any way. Others are wholly absolute and independent of place, and so they stand in the same relation whether the body is here, there, or elsewhere. Predicates of the first kind are, for example, being situated at Venice, sitting at Rome, walking at Padua, and so on. These accidents are so attached to their places that they can in no way be elsewhere. Hence it is quite impossible for my being-at-Venice, by which I am located in Venice, to be reproduced at Rome: as soon as it was there, it would no longer be a Venetian location but a Roman one. Likewise, the sitting by which someone sits at Padua is essentially fixed to Padua, and that same sitting cannot be reproduced at Paris. Otherwise it would lose its essence, which consists in this, that it places the body at Padua and not elsewhere; for then it would no longer be the same Paduan sitting, but another, a Parisian one. Absolute predicates of the second kind do not depend on place, such as being warm, being cold, keeping watch, sleeping, living, dying, and so on. These have no connection with place, since they remain exactly the same even when the place is changed. This being laid down:

units.la: Quæstio est, an illa prædicata, siue accidentia, quæ afficiunt corpus in vno loco existens, debeant similiter afficere idipsum alibi positum. V. g. si Petrus calesiat Venetijs, debetne pati eundem calorem & Romæ, dato quòd illic etiam reperiatur? Vel si Romæ sederet, cogeretur ne sedere quoque Venetijs? Et ita si vno in loco moreretur, possetne viuere in alio simul, an mori vtrobiq; deberet?
units.tr: The question is whether those predicates or accidents which affect a body existing in one place ought likewise to affect the same body when it is placed elsewhere. For example: if Peter is warmed at Venice, ought he to suffer the same heat at Rome as well, granting that he is also there? Or if he were sitting at Rome, would he be compelled to sit at Venice too? And so, if he were to die in one place, could he live in another at the same time, or ought he to die in both?

units.la: CONCLVSIO PRIMA.
units.tr: FIRST CONCLUSION.

units.la: Replicato corpore, nequeunt replicari accidentia, quæ à loco essentialiter pendent.
units.tr: When the body is replicated, the accidents that depend essentially on place cannot be replicated.

units.la: PRobatur,quia si prædicata, quæ à loco essentialiter pendent, replicarentur, eo ipso amitterent essentiam suam, ergo manendo eadem replicari non possunt. Probo antecedens: Accipio enim hoc vbi Venetum, seu hanc præsentiam, qua Petrus formaliter constituitur Venetijs, & arguo. Si hoc vbi poneretur etiā Parisiis, vel maneret vbi Venetum, vel non: si secundum, ergo vbi Venetum quà tale necessariò, & essentialiter soli affigitur loco Veneto: si primum, ergo aliquod vbi, quod esset Parisiis, constitueret corpus etiam Venetiis. Probatur quia iam esset vbi Venetum. Repugnat autem quod vbi affixum loco Parisiensi, atq; adeo constitutiuum rei Parisiis,valeat eadem & Venetiis reddere præsentem. Igitur accidens à loco essentialiter dependés replicari non potest; nam sic essentiam suam eo ipso deperderet.
units.tr: This is proved, because if predicates which depend essentially on place were replicated, they would by that very fact lose their essence; therefore, remaining the same, they cannot be replicated. I prove the antecedent. Take this Venetian where, that is, this presence by which Peter is formally constituted at Venice, and argue thus. If this where were also placed at Paris, either it would remain a Venetian where, or it would not. If the second, then the Venetian where, as such, is necessarily and essentially bound to the Venetian place alone. If the first, then some where which was at Paris would constitute the body at Venice as well. This is proved, because it would already be a Venetian where. But it is contradictory that a where fixed to the Parisian place, and therefore constitutive of a thing at Paris, should also be able to make the same thing present at Venice. Therefore an accident which depends essentially on place cannot be replicated, for in that case it would by that very fact lose its essence.

units.la: Opponis. Replicato corpore, omnia etiam in eo contenta replicantur, ergo & vbi. Nego consequentiam. Ratio est iam dicta, quia v. gr. vbi Venetum est forma essentialiter de se talis, nimirum constitutiua Venetiis: Verùm si & hoc ipsum esset indifferens, vt per aliud vbi poneretur Romæ, Parisijs, &c. iam non esset forma essentialiter, ac de se in loco tali constituens. Quemadmodum si albedo sese haberet indifferenter ad posse constitui albam per aliam, ea iam non esset forma de se talis, & essentialiter constituens album.
units.tr: You object: when the body is replicated, all the things contained in it are replicated too; therefore so is the where. I deny the consequence. The reason is the one already given: the Venetian where is a form which is by its very nature essentially such, namely constitutive of Venice. But if this very thing were indifferent, so that it could be placed at Rome, at Paris, and so on by another where, then it would no longer be a form essentially and in itself constituting a thing in such a place. Just as, if whiteness were indifferently capable of making something white by another whiteness, it would no longer be a form that is white in itself and essentially makes a thing white.

units.la: CONCLVSIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: SECOND CONCLUSION.

units.la: Replicato corpore, accidentia quæ non dependent à loco, exigunt replicari, & ideo replicantur.
units.tr: When the body is replicated, accidents which do not depend on place require to be replicated, and so they are replicated.

units.la: PRobatur prima pars conclusionis a naturali congruentia, sita in eo,quòd res omnis poscit secum habere accidentia, & affectiones, quæ iam suæ factæ sunt. Etenim uero si naturalem cum ijs vnionem habet, congruum est etiam, vt vbicumque reperitur, ea deposcat. Multò magis vero de accidentibus hoc dicendum, ex eo enim quod à subiecto dependent (quocirca solent etiam vocari entis entia) exigunt omnino illud sequi vbicunq; replicetur.
units.tr: The first part of the conclusion is proved from natural fitness, which lies in this: every thing desires to have with it the accidents and affections which have already been made its own. For if it has a natural union with them, it is also fitting that, wherever it is found, it should demand them. Much more must this be said of accidents, for since they depend on their subject (for which reason they are also commonly called the beings of a being), they demand altogether that they follow it wherever it is replicated.

units.la: Probatur secunda pars, quia si accidentibus inest exigentia, vt corpus iā replicatum sequantur, dicendum prorsus est, Deum, qui ex lege ordinaria exigétjis rerum accommodat se, ipsa quoq. accidentia replicare. Confirmatur ex Trid. sess. 13. c. 3. vbi Theologi docent in Euchar. poni ex concomitantia Diuinitatem, & animam Christi, licèt corpus tantum, & sanguis ibi ex verborum vi cõstituatur. Quia .n.anima exigit esse cum suo corpore, hoc posito, illa quoq. venit. Confirmatur 2. ex D. Thoma 3. p. q.8. art. 4. vbi ait. Quodsi hostia consecrata tempore passionis Christi asseruata fuisset, debere examinatum esse, mortuum esse, &c. conuenire corpori tam extra hostiam, quàm in hostia.
units.tr: The second part is proved as follows. If accidents have in them a demand that they follow the body already replicated, then it must be said that God, who by the ordinary law accommodates himself to the demands of things, also replicates the accidents themselves. This is confirmed from the Council of Trent, session 13, chapter 3, where the theologians teach that in the Eucharist the Divinity and the soul of Christ are placed there by concomitance, although only the body and blood are constituted there by the power of the words. For because the soul demands to be with its body, when that is placed there, the soul comes too. It is confirmed secondly from Thomas Aquinas, Summa 3, q. 8, art. 4, where he says: If the consecrated host had been kept from the time of Christ's passion, it would have to be said that what belongs to the body, to have been dead and so on, belongs to the body both outside the host and in the host.

units.la: Opponis. Dū Petrus v. g. calefit Venetijs ad ignem, non adest causa, quæ calorem eundem producat Romæ, vbi replicatur; ergo replicato corpore, non ideo & accidentia replicatur. Probatur antecedes, quia si calor idē produceretur & Romæ, certè ab igne Veneto produceretur: sed hoc dici nequit, secus admitti deberet actio causę in distans, ergo.
units.tr: You object: when Peter, for example, is warmed at Venice by the fire, there is no cause present which produces the same heat at Rome, where he is replicated. Therefore, when the body is replicated, the accidents are not thereby replicated too. The antecedent is proved as follows: if the same heat were produced at Rome too, it would certainly be produced by the Venetian fire; but this cannot be said, since otherwise the action of a cause at a distance would have to be admitted. Therefore...

units.la: Resp. negando antecedens. Ad probationem dico, non fore, vt ignis Venetus gigneret calorem & Romæ, alioquin nō effugeretur actio in distans. Verùm in eo casu ipse idem calor à Deo per nouū vbi foret, Romæ constituendus. Neq: hoc videatur gratis dictum. Posito enim priori miraculo, & data exigentia vnionis, quam habent accidentia cum suo subiecto, Deus iam ex lege consueta ponit in eo quidquid ipsum consequitur.
units.tr: I reply by denying the antecedent. As for the proof, I say that it is not the case that the Venetian fire would generate heat at Rome as well, since otherwise action at a distance would not be avoided. Rather, in that case the very same heat would be set up at Rome by God through a new where. Nor should this be thought to be said without warrant. For, given the earlier miracle, and given the demand for union which accidents have with their subject, God, by the customary law, places in the body whatever follows upon it.

units.la: CONCLVSIO TERTIA. Replicato corpore, accidentia quæ non pendent à loco possunt Diuinitus non replicari.
units.tr: THIRD CONCLUSION. When the body is replicated, accidents that do not depend on place may by God's power not be replicated.

units.la: <bl>P</bl>Robatur, nam ideo replicantur, quemadmodum supra, eò quòd illa exigūt vnionem cum suo corpore: sed potest facere Deus contra rerum exigentias: ergo diuinitus possunt non replicari. Quapropter idem corpus non repugnat esse Venetiis calidum, & simul Patauij frigidum; in hac schola viuum, & in Templo Salutis eodem tempore mortuum; hic amare, alibi exercere odium, &c. Confirmatur, quia forma caloris in materiam inducatur, potest facere Deus, ne forma frigoris abeat, in quo casu idem subiectum esset simul frigidum, calidumque. Igitur multò magis poterit vnum, idemq. corpus calidum Venetiis, non calescere, imò esse actu frigidum Romæ. Probo, nam vt fiat calidum Romæ, debet in eo loco replicari à Deo calor: sed hæc replicatio potest multò magis omittit à Deo, vt potequæ ab ipso tantū immediatè pédet; ergo.
units.tr: This is proved. Accidents are replicated, as shown above, because they require union with their body. But God can act against the exigencies of things; therefore by divine power they can fail to be replicated. For this reason the same body is not repugnant to be warm at Venice and at the same time cold at Padua; living in this school and at the Temple of Salvation at the same time dead; here loving and elsewhere exercising hatred, and so on. It is confirmed: God can bring it about that the form of cold does not depart when the form of heat is induced into the matter, in which case the same subject would be at once cold and warm. Therefore much more can one and the same body be warm at Venice, not be heated there, and indeed be actually cold at Rome. I prove it: for the body to become warm at Rome, heat must be replicated by God in that place. But this replication can much more easily be withheld by God, since it depends on him alone, immediately. Therefore it follows.

units.la: Opponis. Quæ sunt contradictoria non possunt verificari de vno, eodemq. Sed calidum, & non calidum talia sunt: ergo de vno, eodemque corpore verificari non possunt. Igitur si Petrus calefiat Venetiis, necessariò etiam calescet Romæ.
units.tr: You object: contradictories cannot be verified of one and the same thing. Warm and not warm are such contradictories; therefore they cannot be verified of one and the same body. So if Peter is warmed at Venice, he will necessarily also be warm at Rome.

units.la: Respond. concesso toto, negando vltimam consequentiam. Et dico, ex conclusione iam posita non sequi, corpus fore calidum, & non calidum, quia ly non negat simpliciter, & pro quolibet loco: si autem corpus fiat saltem Venetiis calidum, satis est ne de ipso negetur calor. Quare cum dicitur: effet calidum, verum est: cum additur: non effet calidu, falsum est, nam certè aliquo in loco haberet calorem. Quodsi arguas ita: Venetiis foret calidum, & Romæ non calidum: Hæc non sunt amplius contradictoria, nam respectu ad vbi Venetum, Romanumque redditur corpus virtualiter duplex, vnde potest in vno habere calorem: in alio non, si à Deo calor idem non replicetur. Hinc etiam est, quòd hic potest amare, alibi non amare, imò & odisse. Nam si amet, à Deo autem non replicetur amor, amat Venetijs, non amat Romæ: si Romæ oderit, neque odium replicetur, odit Romæ, non odit Venetiis. Quæ absurditas in hoc, si corpus virtualiter multiplex est? Neque dicas, prædicata hæc non dependere à loco, vnde conuenire corpori absolute, ac simpliciter. Quauis enim essentia liter non pendeant à loco, naturaliter tamen pendent à præsentijs, & vbicationibus, virtute quarum debent replicari. Quoniam igitur hæ vbiciones possunt à Deo non multiplicari, sequitur, posse accidentia non replicari.
units.tr: I reply: I grant the whole major and deny the last consequence. I say that from the conclusion just laid down it does not follow that the body will be both warm and not warm, because the word not does not deny simply and for every place. If, however, the body becomes warm at least at Venice, it is enough that heat is not denied of it. Therefore when it is said that it would be warm, this is true; when it is added that it would not be warm, this is false, for certainly in some place it would have heat. But if you argue thus: it would be warm at Venice and not warm at Rome, these are no longer contradictories. With respect to the where of Venice and of Rome, the body is rendered virtually double, so that it can have heat in one place and not in the other, if God does not replicate the same heat. Hence also it is that here it can love and elsewhere not love, and indeed even hate. For if it loves, but love is not replicated by God, it loves at Venice and does not love at Rome; if it hates at Rome, and the hatred is not replicated, it hates at Rome and does not hate at Venice. What absurdity is there in this, if the body is virtually multiple? Nor should you say that these predicates do not depend on place and so belong to the body absolutely and simply. Although they do not depend on place essentially, they do naturally depend on presences and whereabouts, by virtue of which they ought to be replicated. Since these whereabouts can be not multiplied by God, it follows that accidents can be not replicated.

units.la: Opponis iterum. In eodem corpore nequit simul esse vita, & mors: ergo si Petrus in Ecclesia est mortuus, nequit simul viuere in schola. Probatur antecedens, quia vita est anima vnita corpori, mors priuatio animæ in corpore, sed implicat, formam, & priuationem simul esse, igitur quoties aderit priuatio, tunc temporis non erit anima in corpore. Si ergo Petrus in vno loco moriatur, in alio quoque necessariò morietur.
units.tr: You object again: in the same body life and death cannot be present at once. Therefore if Peter is dead in the Church, he cannot at the same time be living in the school. The antecedent is proved: life is the soul united to the body, and death is the privation of the soul in the body; but it is impossible for a form and its privation to be present together. Therefore whenever the privation is present, at that time there will be no soul in the body. If, then, Peter dies in one place, he will necessarily die in another also.

units.la: Respond. distinguendo antecedens. Nequit simul esse mors, & vita simpliciter abstrahendo à loco, verum est; pro locorum, siue præsentiarum diuersitate, nego. Ad confirmationem distinguo minorem. Implicat in vno subiecto formam,& priuationem simul esse quoad vnum locum,siue præsentiam, concedo; quoad multiplicem, nego. Itaq. dico, repugnare, quòd Petrus v. g. tantùm existens Venetijs habeat animæ priuationem, & simul animam; si enim hæc deperdidit vbicationem Venetam in corpore, quomodo simul retinet eandem? At vero si Petrus adsit etiam Romæ, profecto ponitur ibi per vbicationes omnino distinctas, anima enim habet sum vbi, & corpus quoque aliud ubi , distincta omnino à Venetis. Ergo si anima deperdat ubi , quo Venetijs constituitur in corpore, Deus facere potest, ne tollatur aliud ubi, quo ponitur in eodem corpore constituto Romæ, ac proinde Venetiis maneret corpus Petri, sed absq. anima; ergo inortuum; & Romæ corpus eiusdem, sed cum anima, ergo viuum. Ratio autem est, quia per hoc quod accidens aliquod ponatur, siue tollatur à corpore, non ideo replicatur quemadmodum corpus. Confirmatur, quia potest si velit Deus replicare Patauij corpus tantummodo Petri, omissa illius anima Venetijs. Tunc verò Petrus foret cadauer Patauij, non hic Venetijs. Collige hinc posse creaturam eandem esse beatam simul, & damnatam; trui cælesti gloria, & pœnis inferni excruciari. Si enim anima in cælo existens replicetur quoq; in inferno, poterit Deus in eo loco non replicare lumen beatificum, quo illustratur in cælo; & in isto non ponere cruciatus, quibus angitur in inferno.
units.tr: I reply by distinguishing the antecedent. That death and life cannot be present together, simply abstracting from place, is true; with respect to diversity of places or presences, I deny it. To the confirmation I distinguish the minor. That in one subject a form and a privation cannot both be present with respect to one place or presence, I concede; with respect to many, I deny. Therefore I say it is repugnant that Peter, for example, existing only at Venice, should have the privation of the soul and at the same time the soul. For if he has lost the Venetian where in the body, how does he retain the same at the same time? But if Peter is also present at Rome, then he is certainly posited there by wholly distinct whereabouts: the soul has its own where, and the body has another where, wholly distinct from the Venetian one. Therefore if the soul loses the where by which it is established in the body at Venice, God can bring it about that the other where, by which it is placed in the same body established at Rome, is not removed. Consequently at Venice the body of Peter would remain, but without a soul, and therefore dead; and at Rome the same body would remain, but with its soul, and therefore living. The reason is that the fact that some accident is posited in or removed from a body does not mean that it is replicated in the way the body is. It is confirmed: if God wills, he can replicate the body of Peter alone at Padua, with his soul omitted at Venice. Then indeed Peter would be a corpse at Padua, though not here at Venice. From this, gather that the same creature can be at once blessed and damned, enjoying heavenly glory and tormented by the pains of hell. For if the soul, existing in heaven, is also replicated in hell, God can in that place fail to replicate the beatifying light by which it is illumined in heaven, and in the other place fail to impose the torments by which it is racked in hell.

units.la: DISQVISITIO QVARTA.
units.tr: Disquisitio Quarta.

units.la: An praeter locum extrinsecum detur in corpore locato etiam intrinsecus.
units.tr: Whether, besides the external place, there is also an internal place in a located body.

units.la: PRO intelligentia debetis aduertere, pro loco intrinseco intelligi à philosophis eam vbicationem, de qua sæpe in superioribus loquebamur: seu formam de nouo in rebus enascentem, vi cuius illæ actu formaliter constituuntur in loco. Quæritur ergo, an reuera cum res aliqua vbicatur, præter ipsam rem, & locum, aliquid præterea sit, ab iis distinctum, quo tamquam forma res actu locetur. An esse in loco nil dicat aliud, nisi rem ipsam, & locum. Recentiores tenent primum, quamuis meo iudicio, & secundum habeat multum probabilitatis.
units.tr: To understand the matter, you must notice that by "internal place" the philosophers mean that ubication of which we often spoke in the earlier sections: namely, the form newly arising in things, by virtue of which they are actually and formally located in a place. The question therefore is whether, when some thing is located, there is really something over and above the thing itself and the place, distinct from both, by which the thing is actually located as by a form; or whether being in a place signifies nothing other than the thing itself and the place. The more recent writers hold the former, although in my judgment the latter also has considerable probability.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Præter locum extrinsecum in re locata videtur concedendus etiam intrinsecus.
units.tr: Besides extrinsic place, an intrinsic place also seems to be conceded in the thing placed.

units.la: PRobatur 1. Potest existere locus; potest existere quoq; res, & nihilominus posRunt hæc duo non esse coniunctim, seu simul: ergo ly coniunctim, ly simul dicit aliquid supra locum, & rem: Nonnisi vbicationem: ergo. Antecedens patet, nam reuera existimus iam nos: exiftit locus Romanus, neque tamen fumus cum loco Romano simul. Consequentia probatur, quoties enim aliquid potest acquiri de novo, aut amitti, ac separari, hoc ipsum est aliqua entitas omnino distincta: sed ly simul, sive unitim acquiri potest de novo, & à re separari; ergo. Maior est certa. Minor etiam patet, si enim quis nostrum ab scedat à schola, manet adhuc iste locus; manet etiam corpus, nec manent simul: ergo ly simul separatur. Iterum: potest redire corpus, & in loco eodem constitui, ergo potest rursus acquiri ly simul, quod proinde aliqua tertia entitas est.
units.tr: It is proved first. A place can exist, and a thing can exist, and yet these two cannot be together, or at the same time. Therefore the word "together" and the words "at the same time" signify something above the place and the thing, namely the whereness. The antecedent is plain, for we already exist in fact: the Roman place exists, and yet we are not at the same time with the Roman place. The consequence is proved: whenever something can be acquired anew, or lost and separated, that very thing is a wholly distinct entity. But "at the same time", or "being united", can be acquired anew and separated from the thing; therefore it is a distinct entity. The major is certain.
