The minor is also plain: if one of us leaves school, the place remains, and the body remains, yet they do not remain together; therefore "together" is separated. Again, the body can return and be established in the same place; therefore "together" can be acquired again, and so it is a third entity.

units.la: Dicis. Rem esse hic nil dicit praeterea, nisi rem non distare: seu dicit rem huic spatio applicitam; ergo rem esse in loco non est nisi entitas rei, & locus. Frustra igitur conceditur vbi distinctum. Contra tamen, quia ly non distare profecto non est locus tantum, neq: corpus tantum: ergo aliquid aliud, nimirum simul, praesens, &c. igitur ly praesens, ly simul est aliud quid, ratione cuius formaliter non distat res à loco. Similiter: esse rem applicatam loco, si dicit rem solummodo, & locum, ergo nos iam existimus Romae, Parisiis, Neapoli, &c. Probo, quia iam sunt haec duo, Roma, & nos: ergo si esse Romae applicitum nil praeterea dicit, iam fumus appliciti Romae, &c.
units.tr: You say: "To be here" says nothing beyond the thing not being distant, or it says the thing is applied to this space. Therefore being in a place is nothing but the entity of the thing and the place, and the distinct "where" is conceded in vain. On the contrary, "not being distant" is certainly not place alone, nor body alone; therefore it is something else, namely "together", "present", and so on. So the word "present" and the word "together" are something else, by reason of which the thing does not formally differ from the place. Similarly: if being applied to a place says only the thing and the place, then we now exist at Rome, Paris, Naples, and so on. I prove it: these two, Rome and we, are now there. Therefore, if being applied at Rome says nothing further, we are now applied at Rome.

units.la: Probatur 2. à simili. Animam esse vnitam corpori, non dicit solummodo corpus, & animam, sed aliud quid etiam, ab vtroque distinctum, scilicet vnionem, vt alibi vidimus: ergo & rem esse vbicatam non dicit rem tantummodo, & locum, sed præterea vbicationem. Paritas currit, nam sicuti dum anima est vnita corpori, non intelligitur solum corpus, & anima, sed etiam vnio; similiter non bene res apprehenditur vbicata, nisi admittatur vbi, per quod locetur. Vel si hoc negas, vnionem quoq: inter corpus, & animam denegare potes, dicendo animam vniri corpori, non esse quid aliud, nisi entitatem vtriusq;sed hoc videtur absurdum, alioquin viueret homo, postquā à corpore anima seiuncta foret;ergo, &c.
units.tr: It is proved secondly from likeness. The soul's being united to the body says not only the body and the soul, but something else too, distinct from both, namely the union, as we saw elsewhere. Therefore being whereified also says not only the thing and the place, but besides them the whereness. The parity holds: just as, while the soul is united to the body, we understand not only the body and the soul but also the union, so a thing is not rightly grasped as placed unless a "where" is admitted by which it is placed. Or if you deny this, you may also deny the union between body and soul, saying that the soul's being united to the body is nothing but the entity of each. But this seems absurd; otherwise a man would still live after the soul had been separated from the body. Therefore, and so on.

units.la: Opponis. Vbicatio producitur à re iam in loco existente, igitur per illam res non ponitur in loco. Probatur consequentia, nam res intelligitur esse in loco antequam producat vbicationem: quomodo.n. Petrus causat vbicationem sui v.g. in hac schola, si actu ipse non fit prius in eadem schola? Confirmatur, nam actio sequitur ad esse; igitur qui agit, prius est: sed Petrus agit producendo hic vbi suum: ergo prius intelligitur esse in hoc loco, quàm ab ipso fluat vbicatio.
units.tr: You object: whereness is produced by a thing that already exists in place; therefore the thing is not placed in place through it. The consequence is proved: a thing is understood to be in place before it produces its whereness. For how does Peter cause his whereness, say, in this school, unless he is actually in the same school first? It is confirmed: action follows being; therefore the agent is prior. But Peter acts by producing his own "here"; therefore he is understood to be in this place before the whereness flows from him.

units.la: Respondetur, negando antecedens; & pariter consequentiam. Ad probationem dico, rem esse in loco prius, quàm vbicatio, prioritate naturæ, non temporis. Nam res quidem est illa entitas, à qua dependet vbi, & in qua velut in subiecto recipitur: Verùm hæc entitas non est prius tempore in loco ante ipsum vbi, quinimo per illud formaliter vbicatur. Eo igitur momento, quo res constituitur in esse, indiuisibiliter fluit ab ipsa vbicatio quædam intrinseca, virtute cuius formaliter in loco est. Itaque res non manet prius in loco, vt deinde producat suum vbi, sed eo ipso quòd est, fluit ab ipsa vbi, per quod vbicatur. Simili modo quo corpus eo ipso quòd mouet se, recipit motum, vi cuius mouetur; non recipit motum ante, secus moueretur ante motum.
units.tr: I answer by denying the antecedent, and likewise the consequence. To the proof I say that the thing is in place before the whereness, by priority of nature, not of time. For the thing is indeed that entity on which the where depends and in which it is received as in a subject. But this entity is not prior in time in place before the where itself; rather, it is formally placed through it. So at the moment the thing is brought into being, a certain intrinsic whereness flows from it indivisibly, by virtue of which it is formally in place. Thus the thing does not remain in place first and then produce its where. Rather, by the very fact that it is, it flows from the where by which it is placed. In the same way a body, by the very fact that it moves itself, receives the motion by which it is moved. It does not receive motion before, or else it would be moved before it moved.

units.la: Quæres, an vbicato corpore, omnia quæcumque sunt in illo, vbicentur per vnicum vbi? an singulis entitatibus diuersæ correspondent vbicationes? Respond. verisimilius esse hoc secundum. Ratio est, quia si materiæ, formæ, accidentibus, vnicum, & commune vbi, assignetur, quoties aliquid ex his tollitur, periret vbicatio tota, per quam & cætera sunt in loco: sed hoc non sequitur, ergo singula posita in corpore habent suum vbi distinctum. Sequela probatur, nam sublata forma, perit vbi proprium illius: hoc vero est etiam vbi materiæ, atque accidentium; ergo tollitur vbi, per quod singula existunt. Quomodo autem illa tunc erunt in loco? Minor etiam probatur, nam destructo calore in corpore, non ideo tollitur vbicatio accidentium omnium, vel formæ; aut materiæ. Similiter ademptâ forma, durat etiam vbicata materia; ergo hæc singula suum habent vbi distindistinctum, quo vbicantur. Insto: calor, quem de nouo mea manus acquirit, non supponit vbi praeuium, quo collocetur, sed eum ipsemet sibi produicit. Postremò vnicum vbi nequit inferuire animae simul, & corpori, alioquin foret spirituale, ac materiale simul, vt c. p.
units.tr: You may ask whether, when a body is placed, all the things in it are placed through one single where, or whether each entity has its own distinct whereness. I answer that the second is more probable. The reason is this: if one common where were assigned to matter, form and accidents, then whenever any of these was removed, the whole whereness would perish, by which the others too are in place. But this does not follow. Therefore each thing posited in the body has its own distinct where. The sequel is proved: when the form is taken away, its proper where perishes; but this is also the where of the matter and the accidents. Therefore the where through which each of them exists is removed. But how will they then be in place? The minor is also proved: when heat is destroyed in a body, the whereness of all the accidents, or of the form, or of the matter, is not thereby removed. Similarly, when the form is taken away, the placed matter also endures. Therefore each of these has its own distinct where by which it is placed. I press the point: the heat which my hand acquires anew does not presuppose a prior where in which it is placed; rather it produces that where for itself. Lastly, a single where cannot serve the soul and the body at once, otherwise it would be spiritual and material at once, and so on.

units.la: Quaeres adhuc possitne res aliqua omni vbicatione spoliari, adeout existat, sed nullibi sit? Respond. verosimilius esse, quòd non possit. Ratio est, quia nil creatum existere potest, cui saltem Deus non sit praesentissimus; ergo semper existet alicubi. Antecedens nititur in fide Catholica. Probo consequentiam. Si v. g. producatur Angelus, hic certè non erit praesens Deo vt existenti vbique, secus creatura foret immensa, ergo fiet praesens Deo, vt habenti vnam potiùs virtualem praesentiam, & non aliam. Et sic Angelus correspondebit vni potiùs virtuali vbicationi Dei, quàm alteri; ergo haberet aliquid, ratione cuius huic, & non illi coexisteret: nonnisi locum intrinsecum, ergo, &c. Vrgeo etiam. Angelus Deo praesens certè de se indifferens est ad coexistendum ipsi tam in .a. quàm in b. &c. debet igitur dari forma, per quam potiùs constituatur praesens in .a. quam in b. Haec non erit nisi vbi seu locus intrinsecus; ergo. Postremò quidquid est (in spatijs etiam imaginarijs) aut magis, aut minùs à mundo nostro distans est: non nisi per locum, vel magis, vel minùs remotum; ergo. Hinc S.S. P.P. Nazianz. & Aug. aiebant. Quae nullibi sunt, non sunt. Neque dicas: Vbi, siue locum esse quid re vbicata posterius; omne autem prius manere posse absque suo posteriori, & sic rem aliquam esse possibilem sine vbi, seu quae nullibi sit. Contra enim est quia minor propositio non est absolute vera, nam aliquod prius dependet aliquando à posteriori ob necessariam inter vtrumque connexionem. Ita quantitas pendet à figura; durans à duratione; agens ab actione; potentia demum à possibilibus. Vnde non mirum, si res etiam vbicata pendeat à suomet vbi, sine quo existere nunquam possit.
units.tr: You may ask further whether a thing can be stripped of all whereness, so as to exist and yet be nowhere. I answer that more probably it cannot. The reason is that nothing created can exist to which God, at the very least, is not most present; therefore it will always exist somewhere. The antecedent rests on the Catholic faith. I prove the consequence. If, say, an angel is produced, he will certainly not be present to God as existing everywhere, for otherwise the creature would be immense. Therefore he will become present to God as having one virtual presence rather than another. So the angel will correspond to one virtual whereness of God rather than to another, and therefore he would have something by which he coexists with this and not with that. This can only be an intrinsic place; therefore, and so on. I press it also: the angel, being present to God, is certainly indifferent in himself to coexisting with him in a as well as in b, and so on. There must therefore be some form by which he is constituted present in a rather than in b. This will be nothing but whereness or intrinsic place; therefore, and so on. Lastly, whatever exists (even in imaginary spaces) is either more or less distant from our world, and this only through a place more or less remote. Hence the holy Fathers, Nazianzen and Augustine, said: "Things that are nowhere are not." Nor may you say that "where", or place, is something posterior to the thing placed, and that every prior can remain without its posterior, so that a thing could be possible without a where, that is, a thing that is nowhere. For against this, the minor proposition is not absolutely true: a prior sometimes depends on a posterior because of the necessary connection between the two. So quantity depends on figure, duration on enduring, agent on action, and power, finally, on possibles. Whence it is no wonder that even a placed thing depends on its own where, without which it can never exist.

units.la: DISPVTATIO QVINTA.
units.tr: DISPUTATIO QUINTA.

units.la: De Vacuo.
units.tr: On the Void.

units.la: QVia contrariorum vna est disciplina: ideo à loco procedimus: ad Vacuū, nempe ad id, quod physico, realiq. loco se se opponit. Et definitur spatium, aut superficies omni prorsus corpore intra se carens. Quapropter si adesset ambiens aliquod, puta vas, intra quod nec aer, nec aliud quid simile foret, ibi reuera daretur vacuum. Oportet igitur quaeramus, an in natura sit, vel dari possit haec superficies ambientis, intra quam nil penitus reperiatur, quod vacuitatis atque inanis repletiuum sit.
units.tr: Since the study of contraries is one discipline, we proceed from place to the void, namely to that which stands opposed to physical and real place. It is defined as a space, or surface, wholly lacking any body within itself. Accordingly, if there were some surrounding thing, say a vessel, within which there was neither air nor anything else of the kind, a void would truly exist there. We must therefore inquire whether this surface of a surrounding thing, within which nothing at all is found that could fill up the emptiness and void, exists in nature or can exist.

units.la: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.
units.tr: DISQVISITIO PRIMA.

units.la: An detur, vel dari possit vacuum.
units.tr: Whether a vacuum is, or can be, found.

units.la: PRO intelligentia suppono, quæstionem hanc non fieri de vacuis minimis, quæ cuique corporum intexta sunt, quemadmodum supra cum Democrito, Leucippo, aliisque conclusimus. Verùm de vacuo quodam insigni, & Magno, puta si tolleretur quantitas aeris advsque… milliare protensa, & alius acr, vel corpus huiusmodi non accurreret ad replendum.
units.tr: To make the question clear, I assume at the outset that it does not concern the minute vacua which are interwoven with every body, as we concluded above with Democritus, Leucippus and others. Rather, it concerns a certain large and considerable vacuum, for instance if the quantity of air stretching a mile or more were removed, and no other air or body of this kind rushed in to fill it.

units.la: CONCLVSIO PRIMA.
units.tr: FIRST CONCLUSION.

units.la: Natura viribus totis abhorret à vacuo. Inde probabilius est, de facto non dari.
units.tr: Nature abhors a vacuum with all its strength. Hence it is more probable that there is in fact none.

units.la: PRobatur quoad primum experientiis. Constat enim, grauia contra naturalem ponderis vim ascendere, vt vacuum impediant. Sic dum tubus altera extremitate aquis immergitur, si ex altera trahatur aer, aqua ipsa vt repleat inane… ascendit. Pro qua re ingeniosissimè philosophatur Mechanica, fontanas aquas ad ascensus, & lusus non illepidos erudiendo. Hinc verò exhauritè probabilem causam, quare in montium culminibus aquæ scaturiant perennes. Videlicet saxa, quæ compaginant montes, non omnia eiusdem figuræ sunt: quare simul aggesta vacuitates aliquas inter se faciūt: sed eò fortasse non patet aditus aeri: proinde aquæ ad montium radices vtplurimum enascentes, attolluntur naturæ ingenio ad inane replendum, & sic de sumitate scaturiunt. Videmus etiam ascendere, atque descendere aquam in ampulla vitrea, vbi aer inclusus modò calescit, modò frigefit: nam si rarus est, occupatque locum, aqua cedit; si densus, & vacuum facit, illa sursum redit. Similiter in cucurbitis medicis, dum humeris applicantur, quò magis addensatur aer ob deperditum calorem, caro trahitur intus, atque tumescit, nempe vt vacuo succurrat, &c.
units.tr: That the first part is true is proved by experience. For it is evident that heavy bodies rise against their natural force of weight, so as to prevent a vacuum. Thus, when a tube is dipped at one end in water and air is drawn out of the other end, the water rises to fill the empty space …. Mechanics explains this most ingeniously, teaching the rising of fountain water and its not unpleasant sports. From this it also gives a thoroughly probable cause why perennial waters gush out on the mountain peaks. Namely, the rocks that make up mountains are not all of the same shape, so when they are heaped together they leave some gaps between them, but perhaps there is no open passage for the air. Therefore the waters that generally arise at the foot of mountains are lifted up by nature's ingenuity to fill the void, and so they spring out from the summit. We also see water rise and fall in a glass flask, where the enclosed air is sometimes warmed and sometimes cooled. If the air is rarefied and takes up the space, the water gives way; if it is dense and leaves a vacuum, the water rises again. Similarly, in medical cupping vessels applied to the shoulders, as the air becomes denser from the loss of heat, the flesh is drawn inward and swells, namely to relieve the vacuum, and so on.

units.la: Probatur etiam secunda pars conclusionis. Constat enim res quantumlibet solidas, naturæ solius ingenio diuelli, & frangi, quoties ad impediendum inane, corpus aliud submitti nequit. Præterea si duo sint, ex quorum separatione adsit periculum vacui, natura impedit, ne vlla vi, seu ardue saltem deiungantur. Experientia primi fiet, si vas argillaceum, seu vitreum admoueas ori, & liquorem fugendo, nihil aeris per orificium ingredi sinas: tunc enim dissilit vas, frangiturque, ne maneat vacuum. Experientia secundi erit, si v. gr. pileum æquè pansis alis terræ applicitum coneris totū attollere vno impetu: nam tunc senties illum adhærere magis, & reluctari. Hoc autem oritur ex eo, quia si totus attollatur simul, non potest uno momento circumfluere aer ad occupandum spatium, quod prius implebatur a pileo. Ex his ergo, & similibus valde probabile videtur, naturam non habere actu insigne vacuum.
units.tr: The second part of the conclusion is also proved. For it is plain that things, however solid, are torn apart and broken by nature's power alone whenever another body cannot be brought in to prevent a vacuum. Moreover, if there are two bodies whose separation would create a danger of a vacuum, nature prevents them from being parted by any force, or at least only with great difficulty. The first point can be tested if you press a clay or glass vessel to your mouth and, while drawing off the liquid, allow no air to enter through the opening: the vessel then bursts and shatters, lest a vacuum remain. The second point can be tested if, for instance, you try to lift a felt hat with its brim spread out, pressed flat against the ground, all at once in a single effort: you will then feel it clinging more and resisting. This happens because, if the whole hat is lifted at the same moment, air cannot flow in quickly enough to occupy the space that the hat had filled. From these and similar examples it seems highly probable that nature does not actually contain a notable vacuum.

units.la: CONCLVSIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: SECOND CONCLUSION.

units.la: Non difficile videtur dari posse vacuum in natura.
units.tr: It does not seem difficult that a vacuum can exist in nature.

units.la: PRobatur, quia potest contingere, ut adsit vacuum vbi natura neque habeat corpus, quod submittatur ad impediendum; neque vim, quæ circumferentiam valide resistentem frangat. Puta si mons aliquis cauernosus, & ad cameras naturaliter factus, haberet saxa obnixè congesta, & apprimè fulta, non tam citò euerti, atque intimè subrui possent. Quid autem si ad oppletendum vacuum nulla tunc subesset aqua trahibilis? aut quid, si aqua eò vsque non posset niti? obseruat enim Galil. dial. 1. in noua scientia de motu, aquam vltra bracchia octodecim eleuari non posse (quæcunque postea huius rei causa sit) in quo casu natura vel inuita vacuum admittere cogeretur, &c.
units.tr: It is proved thus: it can happen that there is a vacuum where nature has neither a body that could be let down to fill it, nor a force that could break a surrounding that resists strongly. Suppose some cavernous mountain, naturally formed into chambers, had rocks heaped tightly together and very firmly propped. They could not be so quickly overturned or undermined from within. But what if, to fill the vacuum, there were then no water that could be drawn up? Or what if the water could not strive so far? For Galileo observes, in the first Dialogue of his New Science of Motion, that water cannot be raised beyond eighteen cubits (whatever the later cause of this may be). In that case nature would be forced to admit a vacuum, even against her will, and so on.

units.la: Quinimo contendunt aliqui hoc iam de facto contingere in nobili experimento Mercurij tubo vitreo incluso, quo P. Valerianus Magnus, Capucinus, Anno 1647. vacuum ostendisse Poloniæ Regibus. bus profitetur, & hac de re peculiarem quoque libellum edidit. Experimentum sæpius deinde repetitum, quod & ego hic Venetijs in Templo D. Georgij à P. Terra Rubra factum vidi, fuit huiusmodi. Acceptus est vitreus tubus 5. aut 6. palmorum ex altera parte clausus: fuit impletus Mercurio advsq; orificium, & hoc etiam applicito digito clausum, adeout nec ingredi, nec aliquid egredi posset. Mox tubus qua parte foramen habebat, in catinum, vbi aderat aqua, immersus est. Post immersionem visus fuit Mercurius, qui tubum totum occupabat, descendere ad spatium circiter dimidium, & linquere superius. Hoc facto, arguebatur sic. In parte superiori nullum corpus esse poterat, nam prius aderat ibi solus Mercurius, & nihil ingredi potuit vice illius ad occupandum; ergo in ea datur vacuum. Adfuit in confirmationem secunda experientia, nam rubus Mercurio semiplenus cum primum aquæ in catino asseruatæ impositus fuit, aqua valido impetu ad implendum spatium illico ascendit. Ergo ibi nullum erat corpus, alioquin cur ascenderet aqua?
units.tr: Moreover, some contend that this already happens in fact, in the noted experiment with mercury in a glass tube. By this experiment Father Valerianus Magnus, a Capuchin, professed in the year 1647 to have shown a vacuum to the Kings of Poland, and he also published a special little book on the matter. The experiment, often repeated afterwards, which I too saw performed here in Venice in the Church of St George by Father Terra Rubra, was of this kind. A glass tube five or six palms long, closed at one end, was filled with mercury up to the opening, and the opening too was closed by applying a finger, so that nothing could enter or leave. Then the tube, at the open end, was immersed in a basin where there was water. After immersion, the mercury, which had filled the whole tube, was seen to sink to about half the space and leave the upper part empty. This done, the argument ran thus: no body could be in the upper part, for previously only mercury was there, and nothing could enter in its place to occupy it; therefore a vacuum is present there. A second experiment was added in confirmation. For when the tube, half full of mercury, was placed in the water kept in the basin, the water at once rose with strong force to fill the space. Therefore there was no body there; otherwise, why would the water rise?

units.la: Placuit quidem experimentum, & magnam penes me semper vim habuit, iamque suasisset opinionem de vacuo, si adhuc scrupulus non hæreret. Vidi enim in superiori tubi parte adesse lumen, nam apparebat superficies interior, & siquid aliud, puta leuis acus, aut paleæ aristæ ibi extitisset, visa quidem esset. Quærebam igitur: Aut lux accidens est, vel corpus: hoc secundum excluderet vacuum: si dicas primum, quomodo accidens in vacuo manet sine subiecto, cui haereat? Respondum fuit, lumen transmitti ex lateribus tubi, non ex medio interiori. Sed gratis hoc dicebatur, apparebat enim pars intima, & concava superficies, imo liquid intro fuisset, procul dubio sui speciem reddidisset. Lux ergo aderat, ergo & aliquod corpus. Verum cur aqua tanto impetu ascendit, si vacuum ibi non erat? An dici potest, ibi fuisse minimas particulas a Mercurio relictas, aquam vero illuc ascendisse, quia natura levior est? Saltem dicamus ubique adesse umbras..
units.tr: The experiment pleased me, and it has always carried great weight with me, and it would already have persuaded me of the opinion about a vacuum, had a doubt not still clung to me. For I saw that light was present in the upper part of the tube, since the inner surface was visible; and if anything else, say a light needle or a chaff-awn, had been there, it would surely have been seen. I therefore asked: is light an accident or a body? The second would exclude a vacuum; if you say the first, how does an accident remain in a vacuum without a subject to cling to? It was answered that light is transmitted through the sides of the tube, not through the inner middle. But this was said without warrant, for the inner part, the concave surface, was visible; indeed, had anything been inside, it would doubtless have reflected its image. Light therefore was there, and therefore some body too. But why did the water rise with such force, if there was no body there? Can it be said that minute particles were left behind by the mercury, and that the water rose there because it is lighter by nature? At the least, let us say that shadows are present everywhere.

units.la: DISQVISITIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: DISQUISITIO SECUNDA.

units.la: An dato vacuo fieret in eo motus localis, & quomodo.
units.tr: Whether, given a vacuum, local motion would occur in it, and how.

units.la: PRO intelligentia distinguo motum in progressivum, & naturalem deorsum, circa quos praecipue versatur quaestio. Rursus aduerto, medium per quod mobile agitur, aliquam in motu causare diuersitatem, vt initio huiusce libri dictum est. Semper enim aliquo modo resistit iuxta crassitiei proportionem; unde mobile citius per aerem, tardius per aquam descendit. Non ideo tamen tota successio motus habetur ex medio: sed praesertim ex alia duplici causa; nimirum ex virtute limilimitata mobilis, ratione cuius non potest vno momento per totum spatium deduci. Secundò ex terminorum distantia in eodem spatio: & ex eo fit, ne mobile simul esse possit vbique, nempe in termino à quo, & ad quem simul. Postremò hæreat memoriæ quod nuper innuimus, naturam vt impediat vacuum, impedire quoque corporis deiunctionem ab alio quantum potest, quemadmodum in superiori exemplo. Inde sequitur.
units.tr: To understand this, I distinguish motion into progressive and natural downward motion, and it is chiefly about these that the question turns. Again, I note that the medium through which a moving body is driven causes some difference in the motion, as was said at the beginning of this book. For it always offers some resistance in proportion to its density; hence a body falls more quickly through air and more slowly through water. Yet the whole succession of the motion does not come from the medium; it comes chiefly from another twofold cause: namely, first, from the limited power of the moving body, by reason of which it cannot be carried through the whole space in a single moment; and secondly, from the distance between the termini in the same space, and from this it follows that the moving body cannot be everywhere at once, namely in the terminus from which and in the terminus to which it moves at the same time. Lastly, let it stick in the memory that we lately observed that nature, in order to prevent a vacuum, also prevents the separation of one body from another as far as it can, as in the example above. From this it follows:

units.la: CONCLVSIO PRIMA.
units.tr: CONCLUSION ONE.

units.la: Dato vacuo, animal existens in superficie terra, non sine difficultate motum haberet progressiuum.
units.tr: Given a vacuum, an animal standing on the surface of the earth would have progressive motion not without difficulty.

units.la: PRobatur conclusio, quia natura quantum potest impedit vacuum, & vbi adest illius periculum, reluctatur, ne corpora separentur: sed in motu progressiuo pedes animalium à terra separantur: ergo non sine difficultate fieret in vacuo motus animalium progressiuus. Maior patet experientijs vt supra, quibus addo hanc familiarem. Si vitreum vas ad motum fit ori, & liquor ita exhauriatur, vt aer subingredi nequeat, sentis labia ita infigi orificio, vt nonnisi adhibita vi remoueri possint, &c. Minor de se constat, si enim fit gressus, attolluntur itidem pedes à terra, in quo certè nonnihil difficultatis animal experiretur. Reuera tamen procederet, si tantam habe-ret ret vim, quæ sufficeret ad se terræ globo discontinuandum; secus hæreret semper immotum.
units.tr: The conclusion is proved as follows: nature prevents a vacuum as far as it can, and where there is danger of one, it resists, so that bodies are not separated; but in progressive motion the feet of animals are separated from the earth; therefore progressive motion of animals in a vacuum would not occur without difficulty. The major premise is evident from the experiences cited above, to which I add this familiar one: if a glass vessel is applied to the mouth, and the liquid is drawn out so that air cannot get in underneath, you feel your lips so fixed to the opening that they can be removed only with force applied, and so on. The minor premise is self-evident: if a step is taken, the feet are likewise lifted from the earth, in which the animal would certainly experience some difficulty. In truth, however, it would proceed, if it had such power as would suffice to detach itself from the globe of the earth; otherwise it would always stay motionless.

units.la: CONCLVSIO SECVNDA.
units.tr: CONCLUSION TWO.

units.la: Dato vacuo, fieret in eo motus deorsum successiuè, non in instanti.
units.tr: Given a vacuum, motion downward in it would occur successively, not in an instant.

units.la: PRobatur, quia si fieret motus in instanti, mobile simul esset in spatio toto, nempe in termino à quo, in medio, & in termino ad quem: sed hoc repugnat; ergo. Probo sequelam. Et claritatis gratia supponamus fieri vacuum à lunari globo ad superficiem terræ. Hoc dato, cadat lapis à Luna; quæro vel hoc mobile primo temporis momento erit in primo spatij palmo a deinde in b mox in c &c. vel in omnibus constitueretur simul in instanti: Si primum, ergo motus fiet successiuè, vt patet: si secundum, ergo lapis erit simul in termino à quo, in medio, & in termino ad quem; & sic non mouebitur. Probo, nam ad motum requiritur essentialiter, vt relinquatur terminus à quo, cum terminus occupatur ad quem. Deinde: si mobile simul esset vbique in spatio, ergo saxum v. gr. palmare foret millepalmare, imò infinities maius. Probo, quia saxum palmare in vnico instanti, & simul coexisteret toti spatio inter lunare cælum, ac terram; ergo tam foret extensum, ac totum hoc spa-
units.tr: The proof: if motion occurred in an instant, the moving body would be at once in the whole space, namely in the terminus from which, in the middle, and in the terminus to which; but this is contradictory; therefore. I prove the consequence. For the sake of clarity let us suppose a vacuum to be made from the lunar globe to the surface of the earth. Given this, let a stone fall from the Moon. I ask: either this moving body will in the first moment of time be at the first palm of space, then at the second, soon at the third, and so on; or it would be placed in all of them at once in an instant. If the first, then the motion occurs successively, as is clear; if the second, then the stone would be at once in the terminus from which, in the middle, and in the terminus to which; and thus it would not move. I prove this: for motion essentially requires that the terminus from which be left as the terminus to which is occupied. Further: if the moving body were at once everywhere in the space, then a stone, say a palm long, would be a thousand palms long, indeed infinitely greater. I prove this: because a stone a palm long, in a single instant, would coexist with the whole space between the lunar heaven and the earth; therefore it would be extended as far as the whole of this space.

units.la: spatium. Et alia sequerentur absurda quae consideranti patebunt.
units.tr: And other absurdities would follow, which will become evident to one who considers them.

units.la: Opponis. In vacuo nullum adesset medium resistens; ergo motus fieret in instanti. Venit sero argumentum; vidimus enim successionem motus non enasci a medio, sed a virtute limitata mobilis, & a distantia extremorum in spatio. Recolite dicta.
units.tr: You object: in a vacuum there would be no resisting medium; therefore motion would occur in an instant. The argument comes too late; for we have seen that the succession of motion arises not from the medium but from the limited power of the moving body and from the distance of the extremes in space. Recall what has been said.

units.la: Finis Sexti Libri.
units.tr: End of the Sixth Book.

units.la: LIBER SEPTIMVS, ET OCTAVVS PHYSICORVM
units.tr: BOOK SEVEN AND EIGHT OF THE PHYSICS

units.la: De Primo Motore.
units.tr: On the First Mover.

units.la: Motus, qui totius naturæ veluti anima est, ad Primum graditur Motorem Physica nostra, vtque sui cursus optatissimam habeat metam, in eius tandem sinu quieturam se pollicetur. Finis ergo rei præsentis est Primum indagare Motorem, cuius existentiam hucusque vt certam supposituimus. Ad hoc autem vtimur Septimo, & Octauo Libro simul, quia vtriusque idem argumentum est: in priori enim præparat Philosophus mentem auditoris ad graviorem doctrinam sequentis, vt in hoc tandem existentia Primæ Causæ facilius convincatur. Philosophi argumenta nos etiam adducemus. Deinde alia quædam à metaphysicis, & naturæ totius effectibus petita. Hisce demum nixi atheistarum obiectiones, & Politicorum diluemus.
units.tr: Motion, which is as it were the soul of all nature, moves on toward the First Mover, and our Physics promises that, so as to reach its most desired goal of its course, it will at last rest in his bosom. The aim of the present matter, therefore, is to investigate the First Mover, whose existence we have so far assumed as certain. For this purpose we use the Seventh and Eighth Books together, since both have the same subject: for in the former the Philosopher prepares the mind of the hearer for the weightier doctrine that follows, so that in the latter the existence of the First Cause may more easily be established. We shall also adduce the arguments of the Philosopher. Then certain others, drawn from metaphysics and from the effects of all nature. Relying finally on these, we shall refute the objections of the atheists and of the politicians.

units.la: DISPVTATIO VNICA.
units.tr: DISPUTATIO UNICA.

units.la: De Motoris Primi existentia.
units.tr: On the existence of the First Mover.

units.la: NON defuere qui Deum vel esse dubitarunt, vel impijssimè negarunt, quemadmodum Protagoras, Theodorus, & alij, vt refert Cic. 1. de natur. Deor. & Plut. 1. de placit Phil. vnde Atheistarum, nempe sine Deo, infamem retulere appellationem. Hisce accedunt plurimi hæretici nostri temporis, & maximè illi, qui animam rationalem vnà cum homine interire putant. Contra hos, qui humanam, diuinamq; fidem planè contemnunt, euidentissimè insurgit naturalis philosophia, quæ per motum à posteriori, Motoris Primi existentiam vestigat. sit ergo. (✠)
units.tr: There have not been lacking those who either doubted that God exists or most impiously denied it, as Protagoras, Theodorus and others did, as Cicero reports (De natura deorum, book 1) and Plutarch (De placitis philosophorum, book 1). Hence they earned the infamous name of Atheists, that is, men without God. To these are added many heretics of our own time, and especially those who think that the rational soul perishes together with the man. Against these, who utterly despise both human and divine faith, natural philosophy rises up most evidently, which by motion, argued a posteriori, investigates the existence of the First Mover. Let it be so. (✠)

units.la: DISQVISITIO VNICA.
units.tr: THE SINGLE DISQUISITION.

units.la: Vtrum sit euidens Motoris Primi existentia.
units.tr: Whether the existence of the First Mover is evident.

units.la: PRo intelligentia vos hic monitos volo, me non quaerere, an existentia Primae Causae probabiliter ostendi possit; sed quaero, an euidenter, itaut nullus de ipsa relinquatur locus dubitandi, nullusq; animi scrupulus teneat nos anxios. Aliqui enim ex Catholicis arbitrati sunt, non posse demonstrari euidenter esse Deum, sed ratione tantum probabili. Quam sententiam D. Thomas vocat manifeste salsam, & erroneam; Banez temerariam, non tutam in fide Molina; damnatam erroris, ac temerariam Suarez, &c.
units.tr: For the sake of clarity, I want you to be warned here that I am not asking whether the existence of the First Cause can be shown to be probable. I am asking whether it can be shown to be evident, so that no room for doubt remains about it and no scruple of mind keeps us anxious. Some Catholics have judged that it cannot be demonstrated evidently that God exists, but only by probable reasoning. D. Thomas calls this opinion plainly false and erroneous; Báñez calls it rash and not safe in faith; Molina likewise; Suárez condemns it as erroneous and rash, etc.

units.la: CONCLVSIO.
units.tr: CONCLUSION.

units.la: Existentia Primi Motoris euidenter demonstratur.
units.tr: The existence of the First Mover is demonstrated evidently.

units.la: PRobatur argumento, quo vtitur Aristoteles initio septimi lib. Euidens est, omne quod mouetur, ab alio moueri; ergo super omnia, quae mouentur, est id, quod mouet: sed quod mouet super omnia, euidenter constat esse Primum Motorem; ergo euidenter ostenditur Motoris Primi existentia. Maior non intelligitur de motu alterationis, alioquin nimis crasse aberrasset Philosophus, patet enim quod agentia possunt mouere se alterando, siue vt aiunt æquiuocè: sic animal producit in se motum, generat qualitates, &c. Graue trudit se deorsum, leue mouet sursum, &c. Elementa in se proprietates generant suas, calorem, frigus, &c. Explicatur ergo propositio illa de motu generationis, in quo sensu certissima, & euidentissima est. Quidquid enim producitur, debet à causa distincta produci, eò quod nulla res primò se producere potest, alioquin si foret causa sui, iam pro aliquo priori existeret, antequam generaretur. Vnde patet verissimum axioma, quòd nimirum Quidquid mouetur, seu producitur, ab alio mouetur.
units.tr: This is proved by the argument that Aristotle uses at the beginning of book seven. It is evident that everything that is moved is moved by another. Therefore, above all the things that are moved, there is that which moves them. But what moves above all things is evidently the First Mover. Therefore the existence of the First Mover is evidently shown. The major premise is not to be understood of motion of alteration, for otherwise the Philosopher would have gone badly wrong. It is plain that agents can move themselves by altering, or as they say equivocally: an animal produces motion in itself, generates qualities, and so on. A heavy body pushes itself downward, a light body moves upward, and so on. The elements generate their own properties in themselves, heat, cold, and so on. That proposition, then, is to be explained of motion of generation, and in that sense it is most certain and most evident. For whatever is produced must be produced by a distinct cause, since no thing can produce itself first. Otherwise, if it were the cause of itself, it would already exist before it was generated. Hence the most true axiom is plain, namely that whatever is moved, or produced, is moved by another.

units.la: Sed hoc aliud non habet causam supra se, à qua moueatur (& hæc fuit minor propositio) Probo item ex Aristotele, quia si data quacumque causa mouente, seu generante, assignari deberet alia superior, fieret processus in infinitum in dependentia, & subordinatione causarum: sed hoc repugnat; ergo euidens est, data quacumque causa mouente, non debere assignari superiorem, & superiorem. Maior patet. Minor probatur, quia dato processu in infinitum in causis, quæ inuicem subordinantur, numquam produceretur effectus; numquam fuisset conditus mundus; numquam fieret v.gr. hic homo. Probo sequelam: vt produceretur hic homo, deberet influxus causæ vltimæ deriuari priùs à superiori; & huius etiam influxus ab alia; & istius quoque
units.tr: But this thing has no cause above itself by which it is moved (and this was the minor premise). I prove it likewise from Aristotle: if, given any moving or generating cause, another superior cause had to be assigned, and another above that, there would be a process to infinity in the dependence and subordination of causes. But this is impossible. Therefore it is evident that, given any moving cause whatever, one must not assign a superior and a superior again. The major premise is plain. The minor is proved as follows: if there were a process to infinity among causes that are subordinated to one another, the effect would never be produced; the world would never have been founded; this man, for example, would never come into being. I prove the consequence: for this man to be produced, the influence of the last cause would have to be derived first from a superior cause; and the influence of that cause from another; and that of yet another

units.la: ab alia superiori, & superiori: atque adeo non moueretur causa vltima, nisi mota prius infinita serie causarum antecedentium: ergo vt generetur hic homo, debet expectare infinitos alios, qui subinde vnus pœst alium generentur: sed infinita hæc series nequit vnquam transire tota, ergo hic homo nunquam generabitur, quia pendet ab ea tota. Explicatur exemplo. Disponantur v.gr.ex hac schola infiniti lapides versus Orientem tum tali ordine, vt primus incipiendo ab hoc loco non possit moueri nisi à secundo, neque secundus nisi à tertio, & sic deinde cum dependentia in infinitum. Quæro: lapides isti haberent primum versus Orientem, qui motum inciperet, eumque traderet cæteris, an non? si concedis, ergo non datur processus in infinitum, sed sistitur in lapide, qui non motus ab alio, cæteros mouet: si negas, igitur lapis in hac schola non mouebitur, quia numquam præcedentes mouebuntur omnes. Ergo à simili, si non sistamus in aliqua causa prima, vltra quam nulla sit alia, numquam generabitur hic homo: sed actu generatur: ergo euidens est dari Causam Primam, quæ non mota, seu non producta ipsa moueat.
units.tr: from another superior, and a superior again. And so the last cause would not be moved unless the infinite series of antecedent causes had first been moved. Therefore, for this man to be generated, he must wait for infinitely many others, each of which would be generated one after another. But this infinite series can never pass through in its entirety. Therefore this man will never be generated, because he depends on the whole of it. This is explained by an example. Let us suppose, for instance, that from this school an infinite number of stones are set out towards the East, in such an order that the first, starting from this place, cannot be moved except by the second, nor the second except by the third, and so on in dependence to infinity. I ask: would those stones have a first one towards the East, which would begin the motion and hand it on to the rest, or not? If you grant it, then there is no process to infinity, but it stops at a stone which, not moved by another, moves the rest. If you deny it, then the stone in this school will not be moved, because all the preceding stones will never be moved. Therefore, by parity, if we do not stop at some first cause, beyond which there is no other, this man will never be generated. But he is actually generated. Therefore it is evident that there is a First Cause, which, not moved or produced, moves itself.

units.la: Probatur 2. argumento metaphysico sic. Vel datur optimum in natura rerum, vel non: si concedis, hoc certè non pendet à superiori, secus non esset optimum: ergo iam datur Causa Prima. Si negas, quæro: vel optimum est saltem possibile, aut non: si affirmas, ergo iam est. Probo consequentia. Si non esset deberet posse generari: non à se, quia nihil producit se ipsum, vt diximus; itaq. ab alio: sed hoc dici nequit, secus non illud esset optimū, sed hoc aliud; ergo, velis nolis, datur iam actu quod Optimum est. Confirmatur. Nam certè in hac præsenti rerum serie aliquid esse debet cætera omnia in persectione antecedens. Aut igitur supra hoc est possibile aliud quid perfectius, aut nō: qui dicit secundum, iam concedit Primā Causam: Si est possibile, igitur adest qui potest illud producere, secus quomodo foret possibile? sed qui potest sic producere, ille de facto est, ac perfectissimus; ergo datur actu Perfectissimus. Et hæc omnia euidenti rationi patent.
units.tr: It is proved by a second, metaphysical argument, as follows. Either there is a best thing in the nature of things, or there is not. If you grant it, this certainly does not depend on a superior, otherwise it would not be the best. Therefore a First Cause already exists. If you deny it, I ask: is the best at least possible, or not? If you affirm it, then it already exists. I prove the consequence. If it did not exist, it would have to be able to be generated: not by itself, because nothing produces itself, as we have said; therefore by another. But this cannot be said, for otherwise that would be the best, not this other thing. Therefore, whether you like it or not, that which is best already exists in act. This is confirmed. For certainly, in this present series of things, there must be something that surpasses all others in perfection. Either, then, something more perfect than this is possible, or it is not. Whoever says the second already concedes the First Cause. If it is possible, then there is someone who can produce it; otherwise how would it be possible? But whoever can so produce it, he in fact exists, and is most perfect. Therefore a Most Perfect exists in act. And all these things are plain from evident reason.

units.la: Probatur 3. ab effectibus, quia Mundus nos fuit à se ipso, ergo dependenter ab alia causa, quæ per consequens Prima est. Probatur antecedens, nam vt constat experientia, Mundus componitur ex contrarijs: hæc vero si naturæ suæ relinquatur, sese abhorrent, effugiunt, debellant: quomodo ergo pacifice suomet ingenio conuenere? complexa sunt? in mixtorū generatione conspirarunt? Debuerunt ergo à superiori Causa benevola, & potenti ordinari; & ideo antiquitas mundum fecit Amoris filium. Præterea: Vel hæc materia, quæ sponte sua confecit corpora, est prædita intellectu, & perfectissimā habet cognitionem, aut non. Primum dici nequit, non enim hæc materia, siue sint elementa, siue aliud quidpiam vti potest ratione, ac discursu ad finem? Si secundum, quomodo hæc materia cum non cognoscat, non reflectat, non ratiocinetur, potuit vnquam ex se tam prodigiosa conficere? Quomodo paruula radix procreat arborem, pingit flosculos, distinguit folia, generat fructus, puta malum puniicum, vbi granula vides inuicem seposita, loculis distincta, membranulis tecta, ne se premant, affligant, corrumpant? Quomodo semper insensata stirps tam erudite facit, nunquam vt erret in elegantia, in textura, in virtute, sed quouis tempore sibi constans, eadem vno modo elaborat? Dic mihi: si hæc facit materia ex naturali necessitate absque vllo intellectu, non ne multo magis faciet, qui mentem habet, vsuque rationis fruitur? equidem sic. At hominis industria, quæ tam prouida, sagax, intelligens est, nunquam se potuit acuere, vt vni arbusculo vitam, vni flosculo fragrantiam, vni fructui saporem, vni api, vni muscæ, vni acato miram corporis organizationem ingenerarèt. Cur ergo rudi materiæ sine ratione, atq. consilio agenti das, quod animali sagacissimo post multam, diuturnamq. mentis reflexione concedetur nunquam?
units.tr: It is proved a third time from effects, because the world did not exist from itself; therefore it depends on another cause, which consequently is First. The antecedent is proved as follows. As experience shows, the world is composed of contraries. These, if left to their own nature, abhor one another, flee from one another, and wage war. How then did they come together peacefully by their own disposition? Were they bound together? Did they conspire in the generation of mixed bodies? They must therefore have been ordered by a benevolent and powerful superior Cause. And for this reason antiquity made the world the son of Love. Moreover: either this matter, which of its own accord made up bodies, is endowed with intellect and has the most perfect knowledge, or it is not. The first cannot be said. For can this matter, whether it be the elements or something else, use reason and discourse toward an end? If the second, how, since it does not know, does not reflect, does not reason, could it ever of itself produce such prodigious things? How does a tiny root produce a tree, paint its little flowers, distinguish its leaves, generate its fruits, such as the pomegranate, where you see the grains set apart from one another, distinguished by their compartments, covered by thin membranes, so that they do not press on, injure, or corrupt one another? How does a senseless stock always make things so skilfully, never erring in elegance, in texture, in virtue, but at every time consistent with itself, always working out the same thing in the same way? Tell me: if matter does this by natural necessity, without any intellect, will not one who has a mind and enjoys the use of reason do much more? Surely so. Yet human industry, which is so provident, shrewd, and intelligent, has never been able to sharpen itself so as to give one little shrub its life, one little flower its fragrance, one fruit its flavour, one bee, one fly, one gnat its marvellous bodily organisation. Why then do you give to crude matter, acting without reason and counsel, what will never be granted to the most sagacious animal after long and lasting reflection of mind?

units.la: Addo. Putasne fieri vnquam posse, vt causæ naturales (nisi regantur à Suprema intelligente) vniant se in vnius equi, leonis, tauriue imagine pingenda, quemadmodum cernis ab arte fingi? Putas fore, vt materia (quotquot influxus à cælo, totoq; totóq; mundo recipiat) si relinquatur vi suæ naturali, factura sit vnquam simulacrum aliquod ex marmore, vt sculptoria venustissimè facit? Quinimo adhuc miraris, dum audis impactam à Protogene spongiam reliquisse ad os æqui spumam, cui effingendę pictor frustra insudauerat. Miraris adhuc in Regis Pirri annulo Musas cum Apolline casu quodam, & natura ludente fuisse incisas, &c. Verum quid hæc? opera sanè rudia, impolita, vitiosa, tota in exteriori figura posita. Iam verò expendas rogo intimam, extimamq; vnius hominis fabricam, quæ Galeno stuporem, estasimque tulit. Quàm bene substrata ossa, vt fulciatur animal? quàm bene per iuncturas commissa, vt complicetur? quàm bene tecta carne, vt impingens non offendatur? Excogita caput, pectus, aluum, in ijsq; organa, vt sanguis meet, ascendat spiritus, refundentur humores. Quot vasa? quot venæ? quot fibræ? quot alia miris modis implexa, quæ tamen anatomes dictim distinguit, ac stupet? An dices hanc fabricam ex materiæ necessitate, casuq: à natura factam? sed à qua natura? nimirum ab ea, quam concedis nunquam effecisse de ligno statuam, de pigmentis imagine, de fidibus citharam. Sed quomodo casus, & necessitas ad ea laboriosissima, & miranda tulit naturam; non sic ad hæc facillima, & vulgaria erudiuit?
units.tr: I add this. Do you think it could ever happen that natural causes, unless they are governed by a supreme intelligence, would come together to paint the image of a horse, a lion, or a bull, as you see art shaping them? Do you think that matter, however many influences it receives from heaven and from the whole world, if it were left to its natural force, would ever produce some statue of marble, as the sculptor's art does most beautifully? Indeed you still marvel when you hear that a sponge thrown by Protogenes left behind, on the picture, the foam of a horse's mouth, which the painter had vainly laboured to depict. You still marvel that in the ring of King Pyrrhus the Muses with Apollo were engraved by a certain chance, with nature at play, and so on. But what are these? Surely rough, unpolished, faulty works, all of whose beauty lies in outward figure. Now, I ask you to consider carefully the inner and outer structure of a single man, which left Galen in amazement and ecstasy. How well are the bones placed beneath, so that the animal is supported! How well are they joined by articulations, so that it can bend! How well covered with flesh, so that a striking thing is not hurt! Think of the head, the chest, the belly, and in them the organs, so that the blood may flow, the breath rise, the humours be poured back. How many vessels? How many veins? How many fibres? How many other things intertwined in wonderful ways, which yet anatomy distinguishes point by point, and marvels at! Will you say that this structure was made by nature from the necessity of matter and by chance? But by what nature? Surely by that nature which you concede has never made a statue out of wood, a picture out of paints, or a lyre out of strings. But how is it that chance and necessity have not taught nature to do these very easy and common things, when they have brought it to those most laborious and wonderful ones?

units.la: Addo etiam Si homo (& sic de omni animalculo) ex materia suomet ingenio accurente factus est: vel in utero feminæ ut modo experimur, se natum sensit, vel extra. Rursus, aut infans oriebatur, aut iam adultus. Quid rogo? An in aluo feminæ? igitur natura ut procrearet hominem, vsa fuit homine? sed ille prior quomodo factus? Deinde, si extra vterum fecit, cur & modo non facit? Secundo, si Natura primum hominem genuit puellu (debet enim assignari primus, quia nec datur processus in infinitum, ut vidimus; nec mundus fuit ab æterno, ut videbimus) vndenam lac propinauit infanti? an capræ, sicuti de Ioue sunt fabulati, applicarunt mammas? Quòdsi homo sine lactis indigentia nascebatur adultus, non video, cur & modo non nascatur. Ergo dicendum est, primum hominem extra vterum fuisse conceptum: non ex necessario materiæ impetu, sed per actionem Superioris causæ, quæ sapientissima sit, ac potentissima.
units.tr: I add also: if man (and the same holds for every living creature) was made from matter by its own accurate ingenuity, then either he was formed in the mother's womb, where he felt himself born, as we experience now, or outside it. Again, either the infant came into being, or he came into being already grown. What then, I ask? Was he formed in the belly of a woman? If so, did nature use a man in order to produce a man? But how was that first man made? Next, if nature made him outside the womb, why does it not do so now? Secondly, if Nature first begot a boy (for a first must be assigned, since there is no infinite regress, as we have seen, and the world was not from eternity, as we shall see), from where did it give milk to the infant? Did goats apply their udders, as the fables tell of Jove? But if man was born grown, without need of milk, I do not see why he is not born so now. Therefore we must say that the first man was conceived outside the womb: not by the blind force of matter, but by the action of a superior cause, which is most wise and most powerful.

units.la: Probatur vltimò conclusio. Mundus non fuit ab æterno; ergo in tempore cæpit: sed hoc dato, concedenda est Causa Prima, quæ illum ex nihilo fecerit; ergo euidens est dari Causam Primam. Antecedens patet, quia nullus hominum est, neq. fuit, qui de rebus ante Adam gestis meminerit; nullæ historiæ loquuntur; nulla vestigia durant; nullus rumor viget, quod tamen fieret. Nam quæ procella, quod fulmen, quæ temporum, & iniuriarum eluuies omnia penitus obliterauit? Ergo cum supra dies Antiqui Adam non conconstet fuisse mundum, est omnino dicendum quòd in tempore cæperit. Consequentia hæc tota humana fide nixa est. Nam viri quarumcumq; nationum sapientissimi, Ægyptij, Chaldæi, Græci, Latini, omnes, qui fabulas, poemata, historiasq; scripsere, de mundo incæpto meminerunt. Quemadmodum ergo non inficiaris viguisse Romæ sub Regibus; deinde se ad legem Reip. conformasse; postremo Imperatoribus paruisse, quia hoc tradiderunt historiæ; non secus mundi exordium, & principia tenere debes, quia id frequentes, ac dignissimæ fide historiæ contestantur. Hoc autem admisso, concedenda est Prima quædam Causa, quæ illum condiderit. Probatur sic. Quia nulla res potest se ipsam primo producere, vt euidenter de se patet. Secundo, quia si Mundus fuit à se, cur tantùm ab hinc sex mille annis circiter extitit? cur non priùs? aut enim fuit liberè, vel necessariò. Non liberè, quia non potuit se determinare ad esse ndum priusquam esset: si necessariò, debuit semper fuisse, quia semper fuit ea necessitas. Ergo si reuera mundus habuit initium, à Superiori aliqua Causa liberè se determinante factus est. Cumq; sit vbiq. partium venustissimus, & omni perfectione donatus, Causa item Persectissima, & Potentissima ex hac mira Cæli, siderum, elementorum, ac generationum in se concinna, & nunquam fracta lege redeuntium, arguenda infallibiliter est. Hinc Apostolus ad Rom. 1. Innisibilia Dei per ea, quae facta sunt intellecta, conspiciuntur. Et Sap. 13. A magnitudine speciei, & creatura poterat cognoscibiliter Creator omnium videri, & quidem est ne vllus hominum, qui si pulcherrima m horologij fabricam videat, si citharam, si organum, si aliquam huiusmodi rem, suspicetur esse factam a se, ingenio suo, & absq; artificis opera? Quid ergo, inquit Augusti. 15. de Trinit. si hanc Mundi architecturam contempletur? annon haec loquitur Creatorem suum? Sed videamus quae obijciant vel Politici, vel Atheistae.
units.tr: Finally, the conclusion is proved. The world did not exist from eternity; therefore it began in time. But granting this, we must concede a First Cause which made it out of nothing; therefore it is evident that a First Cause exists. The antecedent is plain, because no man is or was who remembers the things done before Adam; no histories speak of them; no traces remain; no rumour survives of them, though there would have been one if there had been any. For what storm, what lightning, what flood of time and injury has entirely obliterated all of them? Therefore, since it is not known that the world existed before the days of Adam of old, it must be wholly said that it began in time. This whole inference rests on human faith. For the wisest men of every nation, Egyptians, Chaldeans, Greeks, Latins, all who wrote fables, poems and histories, have recorded that the world had a beginning. Just as you do not deny that Rome flourished under kings, then conformed itself to the law of the commonwealth, and at last obeyed emperors, because the histories hand this down, so you ought to hold to the origin and beginnings of the world, since many and most trustworthy histories attest it. Having admitted this, we must grant a certain First Cause which founded it. It is proved thus. No thing can produce itself first, as is evident of itself. Secondly, if the world was from itself, why has it existed only some six thousand years or so? Why not earlier? For it either existed freely or necessarily. Not freely, because it could not determine itself to exist before it existed; if necessarily, it must always have existed, since that necessity always existed. Therefore, if in truth the world had a beginning, it was made by some superior cause determining itself freely. And since it is everywhere most beautiful in its parts and endowed with every perfection, the cause also must be inferred infallibly as most perfect and most powerful, from this wonderful harmony of heaven, stars, elements and generations, which returns in order and never breaks its law. Hence the Apostle in Romans 1: The invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made. And Wisdom 13: From the greatness and beauty of creatures the Creator of all can be seen by analogy. And is there any man who, if he sees the most beautiful workmanship of a clock, or a lyre, or an organ, or some such thing, would suppose it was made by itself, by its own cunning, without the work of an craftsman? What then, says Augustine in De Trinitate 15, if he contemplates this architecture of the world? Does it not speak of its Creator? But let us see what the politicians or the atheists object.

units.la: Resoluuntur Obiectiones.
units.tr: The Objections Are Resolved.

units.la: OBijcitur 1. Cur si Deus est, atque omnia aequitate summa, sapientia, consilioq: ad hominis beatitudinem agit, cur tot bella, tot caedes, tot vndiq. malorum temporum calamitates? cur planetarum eclypses, & maligni astrorum aspectus in haec inferiora pessime influunt? Cur terrae motus: aquarum eluu es, regionum, vrbiumq. ruinae, quas diet deploramus? Itaque, aut nullus est, qui rerum praesideat moderationi, at illae sese valde impotentem, ignarumq. ostendit.
units.tr: It is objected first: If God exists, and orders all things with the highest equity, wisdom and counsel for the happiness of man, why are there so many wars, so many slaughters, so many calamities of evil times on every side? Why do eclipses of the planets, and the malign aspects of the stars, work so badly upon these lower things? Why earthquakes, floods of waters, the ruins of regions and cities, which we daily deplore? Therefore either there is no one who presides over the governance of things, or else that nature shows itself to be very weak and ignorant.

units.la: Argumento impudenti non impudentia, & iurgio, sed ratione respondendum est. Priùs autem occurrit apponendum quod fingit Claudianus. Iupiter senulum viderat Archimedem, qui sibi adinstar Dei mundum ex vitro condiderat: nec ita potuit cohiberi, vt se in risum non soleret.
units.tr: To an impudent argument one must reply not with impudence and abuse, but with reason. First, however, it occurs to add what Claudian invents: Jupiter had seen old Archimedes, who had constructed for himself a world of glass, like God; and he could not restrain himself from laughing.

units.la: Risit & ad Superos talia dicta, dedit.
units.tr: He laughed, and gave such words to the gods above.

units.la: Haccine Mortalis progressa potentia cura, &c.
units.tr: Has the power of mortal skill progressed so far?

units.la: Verum quanto magis atheista risu excipiendus est, dum sibi nouum naturae ordine condit, praesentemque audet arguere, vt vitijs obnoxium, & erroribus? Itaque directe Resp. collig. potius hinc Dei existentiam. Quippe si, vt inquis, male regitur haec naturae vniuersitas, ergo melius gubernari potest. Quaero iam, a quo? non a semet, quia de facto sic regeretur: Itaq; ab alio. Ergo datur qui possit melius, atq. sapientius moderari. Vides ne, te sic admisisse Primam Causam? Resp. 2. cum Lactant. lib. 2. de ira Dei prouidentia hominibus contingere, quia ex beneficijs redditi iam funtoscitantes, & Diuinae bonitatis penè obliti: At verò si quā necessitas grauis presserit, tum demum recordantur; si belli terror infremuerit, si alimenta frugibus longa siccitas denegauerit, si sæua tempestas, si grando ingruerit, ad Deum confugitur, Dei petitur auxilium, Deus vt succurrat, oratur.
units.tr: But how much more is the atheist to be met with laughter, when he devises for himself a new order of nature and dares to accuse the present one of being subject to vices and errors! So I answer directly that from this one may rather infer the existence of God. For if, as you say, this universe of nature is badly governed, then it can be governed better. I ask now: by whom? Not by itself, since then it would already be governed in that way; therefore by another. Therefore there is one who can govern better and more wisely. Do you not see that in saying this you have admitted a First Cause? Second answer, with Lactantius (On the Anger of God, bk. 2): men come to recognise providence only when they are worn out by benefits and have nearly forgotten the divine goodness. But if some grave necessity has pressed upon them, then at last they remember. If the terror of war has roared, if a long drought has denied food to the crops, if a savage storm or hail has rushed upon them, they flee to God, seek God's help, and pray that God may come to their aid.

units.la: Obijcitur 2. ex impiorum felicitate, atque iustorum depressionibus, quae res etiam poetae nobili circa Dei existentiam iniecit dubitationem.
units.tr: The second objection is drawn from the good fortune of the wicked and the depression of the righteous, a matter which also cast doubt upon the existence of God in a noble poet.

units.la: Sape, mihi dubiam traxit sententiam mentem,
units.tr: Often a doubtful opinion has drawn my mind this way and that,

units.la: Curarent superi terras, an nullus inesset
units.tr: whether the gods above take care of the lands, or whether there is none at all.

units.la: Quod argumentum indicatur quoque ab Origene, Sinesio 1. Offic. cap. 3. & Diu. Ambrosio his verbis: Occurrimus opinioni eorum, qui videntes quosdam diuites, latos, honoratos, potentes, cum plerique iustorum egeant, &c. putant Deum nil curare de nobis.
units.tr: This argument is also raised by Origen, by Synesius (On Providence, bk. 1, ch. 3), and by St Ambrose in these words: We meet the opinion of those who, seeing some men rich, prosperous, honoured and powerful, while most of the righteous are in want, and so on, think that God cares nothing for us.

units.la: Resp. facilè, non semper ab improbis effugi poenam, quam luerè debent; unde Claudianus etiam de se.
units.tr: I answer easily: the wicked do not always escape the punishment they owe. Hence Claudian also says of himself:

units.la: Abstulit hunc tandem Rufini poena tumultum,
units.tr: At last the punishment of Rufinus put an end to that tumult,

units.la: Absoluitq; Deos, &c.
units.tr: and absolved the gods, and so on.

units.la: & sic passim occurrit iis, qui pessimè agunt, ex quo potiùs Dei vindicis iustitia nobis elucet. Resp. 2. si horum aliqui temporaneas euitant vltiones, non sic æternas eludunt, quæ apud inferos intermittente nunquam supplicio animas impiorum excruciant. E contra siquis bononum egeat, laboret, deprimatur, hoc dicendum est oriri à summa Dei prouidentia, quæ homini tot incommodis exercito æternam parat beatitatem. Resp. 3. ex iam facto argumento argui potiùs Dei existentiam. Probatur, nam si dicis, immeritò, & contra iustitiâ eos fortunari, qui pessimè viuunt; ergo debes concedere, hanc esse debere naturæ legem, vt impij castigentur; probis autem bene sit. Cum itaque apud nos hoc semper non fiat, ergo alius rerum status concedendus est, in quo de reprobis iustæ pœnæ sumâtur; probis verò condigna præmia dentur. Quis autem hæc faciet, nisi Iustissimus Iudex, qui pro meritis hominum, castigationes, aut remunerationes decernat? Hic verò Deus optimus est:
units.tr: And so, everywhere, he meets those who act most wickedly, whereby rather the justice of God the avenger shines forth to us. Second answer: if some of these escape temporal punishments, they do not thereby escape eternal ones, which in the nether world torment the souls of the wicked with a punishment that is never interrupted. On the other hand, if someone good is in want, labours or is oppressed, this must be said to arise from the supreme providence of God, which prepares eternal blessedness for a man exercised by so many troubles. Third answer: from the very argument just made, the existence of God is rather proved. For if you say that those who live most wickedly are made prosperous undeservedly and contrary to justice, then you must concede that the law of nature ought to be this: that the wicked be punished, and the good be well off. Since this does not always happen among us, another state of things must be granted, in which the reprobate receive just punishment and the righteous receive their due rewards. Who, however, will do this, except the most just Judge, who decrees chastisements or rewards according to men's deserts? And this God is supremely good.

units.la: Obiicitur 3. Si Deus esset, qui rerum gubernationi se immisceret, eò ipso quòd nostra hæc munia obiret, hominumq; actionibus ingereret se, non esset Deus, nimis enim vilia, & sordida perageret. Vnde apud Herodotum loquitur Epicurus: Existimare non oportet, aut motum cæli, aut æstiuam, hibernamq; solis conuersionem, &c. ideo fieri, quòd sit Perfectus aliquis, qui sic disponat, dispofueritq. ac simul beatitudinem, immortalitatemq; possideat, non enim cum felici congruunt negotia, solicitudines, &c. Et Plinius, lib.2. cap. 7. Non esse credendum, inquit, existere Deum, qui polluatur tam tristi negotio.
units.tr: The third objection: if there were a God who mixed himself into the governance of things, then by the very fact that he undertook these our duties and interfered in human actions, he would not be God, for he would be performing tasks too base and sordid. Hence Epicurus speaks in Herodotus: One must not suppose that the motion of the heavens, or the summer and winter turnings of the sun, and so on, happen because there is some Perfect being who so arranges them, and who at the same time possesses blessedness and immortality; for business and cares do not agree with a happy being, and so on. And Pliny, book 2, chapter 7: one should not believe, he says, that God exists, who would be defiled by so grim a business.

units.la: Resp. cum Ausonio. Id, quod beatum est, æternumq; morte carens, nec sibi parere negotium, nec alteri. Videlicet quemadmodum solis radius cum in hæc inferiora per vaporum sordes, per luti fæces illabitur, non ideo tamen contrahit maculas, aut vitium; sic multò minus polluitur Deus tristi vt aiunt negotio. Deinde quodnam hoc est in naturæ actionibus, quòd habeat speciem tristis, vel tristitiam creet? an soli præstare vim ad motum? an elementis virtutem, vt agant? an plantis energiam, vt viuant? an animalibus facultatem, vt sentiant? &c. Quinimo hæc summa nobilitas, & summæ inditium potentiæ tentiæ semper extitit. Multò minùs tristabitur Deus, eò quòd inferioribus vtatur causis, & cum ipsis agere velit. Non enim esse potest, quemadmodum terreni Principes, qui sæpe dolent, cum vident se aliorum ope indigere. Hi siquidem reuera indiget ex impotentia; Deus verò ex amore, ac sola munificentia nos ad commertium admisit.
units.tr: Reply to Ausonius: "That which is blessed and eternal, free from death, neither makes trouble for itself nor for another." Just as a ray of the sun, when it slides down into these lower things through the filth of vapours and the dregs of mud, does not on that account contract any stain or defect, so God is far less polluted by what they call a sad business. Next, what is there in the actions of nature that has the appearance of sadness or produces sadness? Does the sun lend force to motion? Do the elements have power to act? Do plants have energy to live? Do animals have the faculty to feel? And so on. Indeed, this is the highest nobility and has always been a sign of supreme power. God will be far less saddened because he makes use of secondary causes and wishes to act through them. It is not as with earthly princes, who often grieve when they see that they need the help of others. For they truly need others out of weakness, whereas God has admitted us to fellowship out of love and sheer bounty alone.

units.la: Obijciuntur alia, & alia maximè contra Dei prouidentiam. Sed non licet omnia transferre. Ne vos tamen Politicorum dolis relinquam expositos, arbitror me factur um operæ prætium, si ad respodendum non inualidà ratione præmuniá. Itaq; remaduertite quæ citra dubium prorsus est; nimirum non esse vias Dei quemadmodum hominis, nam ille fines constituit sibi, longe dissitos ab humano captu, quos proinde nec possumus, nec debemus curiosè nimium scrutari. Quis enim audeat velle Dei mentem comprehendere, vel quis fuit illi à secretis? Inde siquid obtingat quod nobis naturæ ordini parum concinere videatur, hoc tamen non debet censeri positum extra finem Diuini Consilij; neq; casu factum; sed ita vel permittente, vel iubente Deo, cui omnia futura patentissima sunt. Propterea si bella, si morbi, si hæresum pestes, malorumque semina erumpunt, non idcirco de prouidentia Diuina illico dubitandum est. Cur enim arguis medium, si nescis finem? Annon Deus maxima bona tulit ex ijs, quæ videbantur ad hominum, orbisq;
units.tr: Other objections, and many of them, are brought especially against God's providence. But it is not possible to take all of them up here. Still, so that I do not leave you exposed to the tricks of the politicians, I think I shall be doing a worthwhile task if I equip you with a reason strong enough to answer them. So note what is beyond all doubt: the ways of God are not like the ways of man. Man sets himself ends far removed from human understanding, and these we can neither nor should scrutinise too curiously. For who would dare to wish to comprehend the mind of God, or who was his counsellor? Hence, if anything happens that seems to us poorly in harmony with the order of nature, this should not be judged to lie outside the end of the divine counsel, nor to have happened by chance. Rather it happens either by God's permission or by his command, to whom all future things are most fully open. Therefore, if wars, diseases, the plagues of heresies and the seeds of evils break out, one should not on that account at once doubt divine providence. For why do you find fault with the means, if you do not know the end? Did not God bring the greatest goods out of those things which seemed made for the ruin of men and of the whole world?

units.la: . orbisq; totius perniciem facta? cur ergo hunc euentum, illudne damnas? Non illepidum erit ad hoc, quod ferunt de Diogene. Steterat ille iuxta scopi signum, in quod eiaculator sagittas collimabat. Rogatus, cur hoc fecisset, respondit, ne iaculis offendar. Anne tu Diogenem coarguisses vt notae stoliditatis virum anne voce illum absterruisses, vt eo se loco subduceret? Verum quod temere censuisses factum, non sine consilio Diogenes praestitit. Quippe cum semper a scopo longe aberraret iaculator, nequibat Diogeni tutior esse locus, quam id scopo. Itaq. licebit rogare atheistam, sciatne ipse, quem sibi finem constituerit Deus? hoc sane ignorat, aeternumq; ignorabit. Cur ergo media, quae ad illius consecutionem ducunt, adeo temere, ac impudenter coarguat, ipsiusq; Dei Prouidentiam neget?
units.tr: Why then do you condemn this event or that one? What they tell about Diogenes is not without its charm here. He had stood beside the mark at which an archer was aiming his arrows. Asked why he did this, he replied: lest I be struck by the arrows. Would you have rebuked Diogenes as a man of plain stupidity, or frightened him with a shout so that he would withdraw to another spot? Yet Diogenes did, not without good reason, what you had rashly judged to be done. For since the archer always missed the target by a wide margin, no place could be safer for Diogenes than the target itself. So one may ask the atheist whether he himself knows what end God has set for himself. Surely he does not know this, and never will. Why then does he so rashly and shamelessly condemn the means that lead to its attainment, and deny God's providence itself?

units.la: Deum nos reuera summe bonum, summe prouidentem pijssimo animi cultu suspicimus, eiq. maximas, & ex corde gratias peraginus, qui tenuissimos nostri studij labores ad sui vsq; cognitionem deduxit, vt in eo, qui Primus est Motor, ad caelestem quoq. Philosophiam promoueamur.
units.tr: We indeed acknowledge God as supremely good and supremely provident, with the most pious devotion of mind, and we give him the greatest and heartfelt thanks, for he has led the slight labours of our study to the knowledge of himself, so that in him who is the First Mover we may be advanced also to celestial philosophy.

units.la: Hic igitur ad gloriam Dei, Beata M. V. Curiaque Caelestis. Physica nostra sit finis.
units.tr: Hence let our physics be to the glory of God, of the Blessed Mary the Virgin, and of the heavenly court.

units.la: SECVNDA PARS PHILOSOPHIÆ NATVRALIS.
units.tr: SECOND PART OF NATURAL PHILOSOPHY.

units.la: De Mundo, Cœlo, Elementis, Meteorisque. In breuem assertionum epitomen digesta.
units.tr: On the World, the Heavens, the Elements, and Meteors. Digested into a brief epitome of assertions.

units.la: XPletis octo Physicorum libris, occurrit statim Philosophia de Mundo, qui vnicus est, non anima, vel motu præditus, nec mole infinitus, vt nouissimè Argolus opinabatur. Constat enim figurà limitatà, quam esse orbicularem æquiùs arbitramur. Eius autem creatio non fuit ab æterno, etiamsi penes entia, quæ carent successione, sic esse potuerit; sed in tempore, quod ipsum tunc etiam cæpit. Et quidem tempus duplex est; extrinsecum, & intrinsecum: illud à motu cælestium corporum non distinguitur: istud, quod vocant durationem, videtur esse modus, à re, ac tempore distinctus. Licèt verò quidquid per creationem Deus eduxit, naturà finitum sit; nihilominus infinitum actu, siue vt aiunt cathegorematicum, facere potest.
units.tr: Having finished the eight books of the Physics, philosophy at once turns to the world, which is one, not animated or endowed with motion, and not infinite in mass, as the recent Argolus supposed. For it has a limited figure, which we judge more fairly to be spherical. Its creation was not from eternity, although with respect to beings that lack succession it could have been so; it was in time, and time itself began then. Time is twofold, extrinsic and intrinsic. The former is not distinguished from the motion of the heavenly bodies. The latter, which they call duration, seems to be a mode distinct from both the thing and time. Although whatever God brought forth by creation is finite in nature, nevertheless he can make it infinite in act, or, as they say, categorematically.

units.la: 2 Verùm inter Mundi partes eminentior locus cessit Cœlo; quod vnicum est, natura fluidum, non multiplici, & solida orbium fabrica digestum. Quinimò nullo motu, siue circulari, siue trepidatinis, aut consimili agitur Cælum. Hoc autem quia ex aquâ Spiritus Domini attenuatâ conflatur, immeritò quis crediderit, esse quintam substantiam ab elementari prorsus diuersam. Et ex eo desumi etiam potest ratio generationum, & corruptionú, quas dietim contingere in cælo Astronomi obseruant, quemadmodum & Veteres, maximè Tycho, in cathedra Cassiopeæ, in genu Sagittarij, & pectore Cicni detexerunt. Quare materia Cæli (etiam factâ hypothesi de Materiâ, & Formâ) nullatenus differt à sublunari.
units.tr: 2. Among the parts of the world, however, the heaven holds the more eminent place. It is one, fluid in nature, not manifold, and arranged in a solid fabric of spheres. Indeed, the heaven is moved by no motion, whether circular, trembling, or similar. Since it is compounded of water thinned by the Spirit of the Lord, one may rightly doubt that it is a fifth substance wholly different from the elementary. From this too can be drawn the explanation of the generations and corruptions which astronomers observe to occur daily in the heaven, as the ancients also detected, especially Tycho, in the chair of Cassiopeia, the knee of Sagittarius, and the breast of the Swan. Hence the matter of the heaven (even granting the hypothesis about matter and form) in no way differs from the sublunary.

units.la: 3. Cœlum sequuntur Astra, quæ si PP. auctoritati, sensibusque fidamus, ignea naturæ censenda sunt. Hæc ad bonum Vniuersi dum excubant, motu indigent circulari, quem enasci ab eorum naturâ, non tradi ab Intelligentijs, verisimile apparet.
