Vnicus est ab Oriente in Occasum, quia tamen sit per helices, aut more spirarum, ex eo videtur confundi cum alio motu contranitentiæ ab Occidente in ortum: licèt hic secundus mente sola fingatur. Quoad Planetas concordat magis apparentijs eorundem systema Tychonicum, vt circa terram Luna, & Sol; circa Solem Planetæ maiores; circa Iouem, Saturnumque minores à Galilæo, cæterisque detecti ferantur. Nitent sidera luce ingenita; eam Planetæ mutuantur à Sole, non tanquam accidens ab eo producstum, sed vt corpus tenuissimè diffusum, per quod hæc etiam interiora illuminantur. Sed præterea influunt cælestia corpora qualitatibus, vt aiunt, occultis; non tamen in actiones humanas, quæ à siderum configurationibus nullâ prædictione hauriri possunt.
units.tr: 3. The stars follow the heaven, and if we trust the authority of the Fathers and the senses, they are to be counted of fiery nature. While they keep watch for the good of the universe, they need circular motion, which appears likely to arise from their nature rather than to be imparted by the Intelligences. Their motion is single, from east to west; yet because it proceeds by helices, or in the manner of spirals, it seems thereby to be confused with another motion, a counter-striving from west to east, although this second motion is feigned by the mind alone. As for the planets, the Tychonic system agrees better with their appearances: the Moon and Sun revolve about the earth, the greater planets about the Sun, and the lesser ones, Jupiter's and Saturn's, are said to have been discovered by Galileo and others. The stars shine with innate light; the planets borrow theirs from the Sun, not as an accident produced by it, but as a most finely diffused body through which these inner bodies are also illuminated. Moreover, the heavenly bodies exert influence through qualities, as they say, occult; yet not on human actions, which cannot be drawn from any prediction based on the configurations of the stars.

units.la: 4 A Cælo descendentibus occurrunt statim elementa, ignis, aer, aqua, terra, sic dicta, quia corpora simplicia sunt; nec enim ex materia, & forma constantur. Vnde sequitur, ea non esse per vim naturæ corruptioni subiecta. Singulis autem suæ qualitates inhærent, quæ physicæ, realesque sunt, ab ijs revera distinctæ, sed naturaliter inseparabiles. Non tamen hæ qualitates naturam constituunt elementarem: sed ab ea iam constitutâ veluti proprietates dimanant; sic eQUIdem, vt vna saltem qualitas in omni elemento summè intensa sit; altera remissa, cuius tamen defectum nulla ratio probat resarciri à contraria. Præter hæc, habent elementa insitam sibi virtutem, qua moventur ad locum, & ea sola grauitas est. Non enim datur leuitas positiua; sed minor ad summum grauedo, per quam constituitur elementum in centro; in quo sic positum, actu non grauitat.
units.tr: 4. Descending from the heaven, we at once meet the elements: fire, air, water, and earth, so called because they are simple bodies, for they are not made up of matter and form. Hence it follows that they are not subject to corruption by the force of nature. Each has its own qualities inhering in it, which are physical and real, truly distinct from the elements but naturally inseparable from them. Yet these qualities do not constitute the elementary nature; rather, they flow from it as properties once it is already constituted. Thus, in every element one quality is highly intense and the other remitted, yet no reason proves that its lack is made good by the contrary. Besides these, the elements have an inborn power by which they are moved to their place, and this power is gravity alone. For there is no positive levity; there is only a lesser heaviness, at its greatest, by which the element is set in the centre. Placed there, it does not actually weigh.

units.la: 5 Prima inter elementa, quoad nos, terra est. Figitur hæc in centro Mundi, hæretq; immota, quidquid audeant Copernicani, solis motum deferentes in terram. Sic autem figitur, vt ne quidem trepidinem sentiat. Cuius rei causa est gragravitas ponderum circa hærentium. Ex quo etiam oritur figura terræ sphærica, quæ tamen, & cum aqua cauitates implente adhuc rudis est, quemadmodum cortex in pomo arancio scrupulosior. Inde Geometrici occasionem arripiunt asserendi, & explicandi nonnulla, quæ prosus curiosa sunt: v.gr. posse constitui pontem circa terræ globum, qui nullo nitatur fundamento, sed in aere suspensus inconcusse maneat. Posse turrim erigi eximie inclinatam, de cuius lapsu timendum non sit. Posse aliquem sentire maius pondus movendo terram dimidiam, quàm si totam moveret &c.
units.tr: 5. The first of the elements, as far as we are concerned, is earth. It is fixed in the centre of the world and remains immovable, whatever the Copernicans dare in transferring the motion of the sun to the earth. It is fixed in such a way that it does not even feel a tremor. The cause of this is the gravity of the weights that hang about it. From this also arises the spherical figure of the earth, which, however, even with water filling its hollows, is still rough, as the peel of an orange is more uneven. Hence geometers seize the opportunity to assert and explain some things that are quite curious: for example, that a bridge can be built around the globe of the earth which rests on no foundation but remains unshaken, suspended in the air; that a tower can be erected at a remarkable slant without fear of its falling; that someone can feel a greater weight by moving half the earth than if he were to move the whole, and so on.

units.la: 6 Secundum elementum est aqua, superficiei terræ accumbens, cum eaque unum globum constituens, vt conuincitur ex vmbra conica in Lunam. Sed non ideo terræ habitabilis altitudinem superat, quicumq; tumor in medio Mari fiat. Imò nec inter maria vnum alio eminentius est. Quare fluxum, refluxumq; Maris non rite aliqui explicant ab inæquali tumore aquarum. Enimvero præcipuam huius phænomeni causam reijciunt sapientes in Lunam: Sicuti eiusdem falsedo in impurâ cum terrestri materia commixtionem. A qua cùm aquæ marinæ per terræ meatus illabendo purgentur, in flumina, lacusque prædulces abeunt. A Mari enim hæc omnia scaturire, indubitatum videtur. Porro mirabiles omnino sunt rerum in aqua natantium effectus, qui per hydrologiæ scientiam erudite ab aqua exhauriuntur.
units.tr: 6. The second element is water, lying upon the surface of the earth and with it forming one globe, as is proved from the conical shadow cast on the Moon. Yet it does not therefore rise above the height of the habitable earth, whatever swelling occurs in the middle of the sea. Indeed, nor is one part of the seas higher than another. Hence some do not rightly explain the flow and ebb of the sea from unequal swelling of the waters. The wise reject the principal cause of this phenomenon as lying in the Moon, and likewise its falsity lies in the mixing with impure earthly matter. Since sea water is purified by sinking through the passages of the earth, it passes into rivers and very sweet lakes. For it seems beyond doubt that all of these spring from the sea. Moreover, the effects of things floating in water are altogether marvellous, and these are learnedly drawn out of water by the science of hydrology.

units.la: 7 Sequitur tertio loco aer, qui tres in regiones distribui solet. Omnes autem finitæ sunt. Nam suprema cæteris maior ex halitibus, qui reddunt lucem crepusculinam, probatur esse milliarium 43 circiter, si rite probant Geometrici. Quoad aeris naturam, nullus ei color ingenitus est, sed quicumque obtigerit ex incidentia lucis, eum reddit peregrinum, & varium. Illi tamen suæ inexistunt qualitates primæ, quarum altera frigus, altera siccitas, vt conuincitur experientia, quæ omni combinationi ex arbitrio factæ Aristoteleorum, anteire debet.
units.tr: 7. Third in order comes air, which is usually distributed into three regions. All of them, however, are finite. For the highest, the largest of the exhalations that give the twilight its light, is proved to be about 43 miles high, if the geometers prove it rightly. As to the nature of air, it has no innate colour; whatever colour it takes from the incidence of light, it renders foreign and varied. Yet its primary qualities inhere in it, of which one is cold and the other dryness, as experience proves; and this must precede every combination of qualities made at will by the Aristotelians.

units.la: 8 Quartum elementum est ignis, bifariam diuisus, in vulgarem scilicet, ac ele-mentarem. Primus gignitur, alituraq; in materia crassa, vt sulphuris, ligni, & similium, qui etiam latet in visceribus terræ vt probant Vulcani, & aquæ thermarum calidæ. Secundus ille dicitur, qui de re omni combusta in halitum euaporat; solutus enim ex materia crassa, præ ingenita leuitate, sursum conatur, aereq; toto dispersus, ad miras effectuum vices minister acerrimus deuolat. Quapropter nulla super aerem ignis vulgati sphæra est; neque faciunt sapienter qui pro illa tuenda in Lunę concauo stant. Non enim ad sublimia se tollit nisi pura exhalatio, quæ rursus in terram pro mixtorum generatione opportune defertur. Hinc est quòd silice icto, rudente auulso, palpebrā confricta, sæpè flammulæ accenduntur; ignis enim semina vbique sunt.
units.tr: 8. The fourth element is fire, divided into two kinds: the common and the elementary. The first is generated and fed in gross matter, such as sulphur, wood, and the like; it also lies hidden in the bowels of the earth, as the volcanoes and the hot waters of the springs prove. The second is that which evaporates into vapour from any burnt thing; for, released from gross matter, it strives upward by its innate lightness, and spreading through the whole air it flies down as a most keen servant to wondrous changes of effects. Therefore there is no sphere of common fire above the air, and those who stand in the concavity of the Moon to defend such a sphere do not act wisely. For only a pure exhalation rises to the heights, and this is again conveyed down to earth, as fitting, for the generation of mixed bodies. Hence it is that when flint is struck, a rope is torn off, or the eyelid is rubbed, little flames are often kindled; for the seeds of fire are everywhere.

units.la: 9 Porro inter elementa quot effectus? quàm noui? quàm prodigijs pleni quotidie fiunt? Hæc videlicet meteora, quorum apta materia ex duplici fonte venit, nimirum exhalatione, ac vapore: Forma ex earundem commixtione, in qua nihil de nouo substantiale gignitur, sed miscetur tantùm. Causa extrinseca duplex: efficiens, quæ materiam parat, vnitque ut planetæ, astra, subterraneus ignis &c* Finalis,nempe commodum inferni orbis, generatio viuentium,expurgatio elementorum, &c huiusmodi. Hæ siquidem causæ dum influendo conueniunt, miris effectibus naturam implent, humanæque curiositati, ac saniori meteoristarum Philosophiæ theatrum parant.
units.tr: 9. Moreover, among the elements, how many effects are produced, how new, how full of prodigies, every day! These are the meteors, whose matter, suitable for them, comes from a twofold source, namely exhalation and vapour. Their form arises from the mixture of these, in which nothing substantial is newly generated, but only mixed. The extrinsic cause is twofold. The efficient cause prepares and joins the matter, as do the planets, the stars, subterranean fire, and so on. The final cause is the benefit of the lower world: the generation of living things, the purging of the elements, and things of this kind. For these causes, when they concur by their influence, fill nature with marvellous effects and prepare a theatre for human curiosity and for the sounder philosophy of the meteorologists.

units.la: TERTIA PARS PHILOSOPHIÆ NATURALIS
units.tr: THIRD PART OF NATURAL PHILOSOPHY

units.la: De Corpore Animato.
units.tr: On the Animate Body.

units.la: INter omnia corpora illud præstat nobilitate, quod anima præditum est. Verumtamen animatorum genus in triplex abit, iuxta diuisionem Animæ, in vegetatiuam, sensitiuam, & rationalem, quæ definiuntur actus primus corporis physici organici. Fit autem corpus organicum per formas, quæ dicuntur partiales. Vt verò de singularum natura dicamus, Anima vegetatiua nil esse aliud apparet, quàm humor quidam lectissimus intra plantarum fibras à natura diffusus. Duplici gau- det potentia, nutriendi, & generandi. Nutritio fit per adhæsionem substantiæ, ope caloris in planta distributæ. Genera- tio ex vi seminis, cui tota plantæ fabrica subtili textura ducta inesse videtur. Anima sensitiua est spiritus quidam igneus, & virtute acerrimus, qui per organa corporis ad vitæ functiones celerrimè abit. Hæc etiam exequitur duo, nutritionem, & generationem. Illa effici solet per cibum vi caloris concoctū. Hæc vel fit ex putri, vel per vim seminis. Et quia semen materiali anima est animatum, hæc in eo latens veluti architecta, corporis fabricam elaborat. Cui rei dum materia sufficitur à parentibus, utrumque ad generationem actiue concurrere dicendus est.
units.tr: Among all bodies, the one endowed with a soul is the most noble. Yet the kind of animate things divides into three, according to the division of the soul into vegetative, sensitive, and rational, which are defined as the first actuality of a physical organic body. An organic body, however, is made by forms that are called partial. To say something about the nature of each: the vegetative soul appears to be nothing other than a certain most choice moisture diffused by nature through the fibres of plants. It has a twofold power, of nourishing and of generating. Nutrition takes place by the adhesion of substance, by means of heat distributed through the plant. Generation comes from the power of the seed, in which the whole structure of the plant seems to be present, drawn out in a fine texture. The sensitive soul is a certain fiery spirit, very keen in its power, which moves very swiftly through the organs of the body to carry out the functions of life. It too performs two things, nutrition and generation. The former is usually effected through food digested by the power of heat. The latter comes either from putrefaction or by the power of the seed. And because the seed is animated by a material soul, this soul, lying hidden in it like an architect, works out the structure of the body. Since the matter for this is supplied by the parents, both are to be said to concur actively in generation.

units.la: 2 At omnium potissima est anima Rationalis, nimirum substantia simplex, & spiritualis, à Deo creata, indiuisibilis natura, & immortalis, quæ per sui replicationem tota in toto, ac tota in omni parte totius manet. Habet præcæteris modum agendi nobiliorem, ex intellectu, voluntate, Memoria, quæ tamen non sunt potentiæ realiter distinctæ ab eadem. Hęc enim à se immediatè suos actus educit, ad quos vt facilius concurrat, nullum requirit habitum: sed species obiectorum tantummodo, quæ cum fuerint plures, aut clatiores, omnem causant facilitatem. Anima verò ita corpus actuat, vt in eo sanguis etiam animetur: imo & capilli, vnguesque animam gerant: An rationalem, probabiliùs negatur. Hinc si rationi tantùm nitamur, non apparet, in homine vnicam esse animam, si vegetatiua in solo humore, sensitiua in spiritu igneo consistit, quemadmodum nobis visum est. Quinimo si vera est sententia Philosophi, tres animæ debent in homine admitti. Hærendo tamen extrinsecæ Doctorum auctoritati, vna tantum concedenda.
units.tr: 2 But the most powerful of all is the rational soul, namely a simple and spiritual substance, created by God, indivisible in nature and immortal, which by its own replication remains whole in the whole and whole in every part of the whole. Beyond all others it has a nobler mode of acting, through intellect, will, and memory; yet these are not powers really distinct from it. For it draws its own acts directly from itself, and in order to concur with them more easily it requires no habit, but only the species of objects, which, when they are more numerous or clearer, cause every facility. The soul, however, so actuates the body that even the blood within it is animated; indeed the hair and nails too have a soul. Whether they have a rational soul is more probably denied. Hence, if we rely on reason alone, it does not appear that there is a single soul in man, if the vegetative soul consists in moisture alone and the sensitive in fiery spirit, as we have shown. Moreover, if the opinion of the Philosopher is true, three souls must be admitted in man. Yet, adhering to the external authority of the Doctors, only one is to be conceded.

units.la: 3 Sed anima pro statu vitæ præsentis indiget organo, tam externo, quàm interno ad agendum. Illud ex quinque sensuum fabrica exurgit, nimirum visus, auditus, gustus, odoratus, tactus. Quoad primum, sensus visorij organum est oculus, constructus neruo, tunica, & humore. Humor triplex: aqueus, crystallinus, vitreus. In hisce visio non fit, sed in retina, quæ ad oculi fundum retinet species. Quapropter crystallinus ad hoc facit solum, vt species frangendo restituat, seu transmutet, inferiorem in locum supremæ, & è contra: secus omne obiectū appareret inuersum. Et hinc sequitur visionem fieri post radiorum, siuè specieū decussationem. Visus obiectum est color, qui à luce diuersimodè in subiecto & reflexa, & refracta nullatenus distingui videtur.
units.tr: 3 But the soul, in the present state of life, needs an organ to act, both external and internal. The external organ arises from the structure of the five senses, namely sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. As to the first, the organ of the sense of sight is the eye, constructed of a nerve, coats, and humours. There are three humours: aqueous, crystalline, and vitreous. In these vision does not take place, but in the retina, which holds the species at the back of the eye. Hence the crystalline humour serves only this purpose, that by refracting the species it restores them, or changes them, from the lower place to the upper, and conversely; otherwise every object would appear inverted. And hence it follows that vision occurs after the crossing of the rays, or species. The object of sight is colour, which, depending on the light, is in no way seen to be distinguished in its subject whether reflected or refracted.

units.la: 4 Auditus parum cedit nobilitate. Huius organum duplex: auricula exterior, in meandros varie complexos ad capiendū, & retinendum aerem sapienter duƈta. Mox interior, cuius maxime partes quatuor, scilicet meatus auditorius, tympanum, labyrinthus, & cochlea. In his tamen non fit auditio, sed in neruo, qui sub tympano, vbi aer ingenitus est, per totam cochleam procurrit. Eius obiectum dicitur qualitas à collisione genita solidorum. Probabilius autumant qui volunt esse aerem vibratiunculis agitatum ad vsq:organum exundantem. De olfactu, gustu, ac tactu cuique patet.
units.tr: 4 Hearing yields little in nobility. Its organ is twofold: the outer ear, skilfully shaped into variously winding passages for taking in and holding the air; and next the inner ear, whose principal parts are four, namely the auditory passage, the tympanum, the labyrinth, and the cochlea. Yet hearing does not take place in these, but in the nerve, which runs under the tympanum, where the innate air is, through the whole cochlea. Its object is said to be the quality of solid bodies produced by collision. Those who hold that the air, agitated by tiny vibrations, overflows to the organ, assert this more probably. Concerning smell, taste, and touch, it is clear to everyone.

units.la: 5 Post sensationem externo sensu elicitam, indiget anima sensu etiam interno, qui species, vt aiunt, sensatas recipiat. Hic autem vnicus est, nimirum phantasia, cuius organum insidet cerebro, & quidem iuxta Galenum, in cella postre ma, vbi nerui ex omni sensu deducti colliguntur. Obiectum duplex: remotum, vt odor, color, &c. proximum, quod idem est, ac prius obiectum, sed quatenus cognitum à sensibus, aut sensatum. His ergo pro huius vitæ statu indiget Anima, vt operetur. In alio, qui separationis est, non segnitie, otioq; torpebit, sed ijsdem speciebus, & habitibus, quos vel sibi acquisitos, vel infusos recepit, similes actiones præstabit. Quinimo & circa obie-cta superna, quorum imagines ad implendam animæ beatitatem Deus optimus æternum dabit cognoscendo, & amando sese exercebit.
units.tr: 5 After sensation has been elicited by the external sense, the soul also needs an internal sense, which receives, as they say, the sensed species. This is single, namely the phantasy, whose organ sits in the brain, and indeed, according to Galen, in the back ventricle, where the nerves drawn from every sense are gathered together. Its object is twofold: remote, such as odour, colour, and the like; and proximate, which is the same as the former object, but insofar as it is known by the senses, or sensed. The soul therefore needs these for its operations in the state of this life. In the other life, which is one of separation, it will not grow torpid through sluggishness or idleness, but will perform similar acts by the same species and habits which it has received, either acquired for itself or infused. Moreover, it will exercise itself in knowing and loving the higher objects, whose images God, the best, will give eternally to fill the soul's blessedness.

units.la: QVARTA PARS PHILOSOPHIÆ NATVRALIS.
units.tr: FOURTH PART OF NATURAL PHILOSOPHY.

units.la: De Scientia Metaphysica.
units.tr: On Metaphysical Science.

units.la: {Ø}Ostremus in Philosophia locus datur Metaphisicæ, nimirum sublimi scientiæ, per quam res omnes prout conueniunt sub vno conceptu entis, contemplari solemus. Hinc patet, quodnam sit Metaphisicæ obiectum: videlicet ens prout ens; & hoc est, quod à puro nihilo distinguitur, vnde per omnia rerum genera etiam effertur. Itaque circa ens multa possunt quæri: De illius existentia, & possibilitate: De præcisione, ac prædicatione: De vnitate, de relatione, atq; huiusmodi.
units.tr: The last place in philosophy belongs to Metaphysics, namely that sublime science through which we are accustomed to contemplate all things insofar as they agree under the single concept of being. From this it is clear what the object of Metaphysics is: being as being. This is what is distinguished from pure nothing, and it is therefore extended through all the genera of things. Many questions can thus be asked about being: about its existence and possibility; about precision and predication; about unity, relation, and the like.

units.la: 1 Quoad primum: existentia entis non distinguitur actu realiter ab eiusdem essentia: vnde res antequam sit actu, nihil in se ipsa, & ab intrinseco est; sed meram dicit possibilitatem, quæ possibilitas à virtute causæ potentis reŭ producere, nullam habet distinctionem.
units.tr: 1. As to the first: the existence of a being is not really distinguished, in act, from its essence. Hence a thing, before it actually exists, is nothing in itself and intrinsically; it signifies only possibility. This possibility, which depends on the power of a cause able to produce things, admits of no distinction.

units.la: 2 Quoad secundum: inter ens, & inseriora datur præcisio, sed non mutua. Ens.n. in suo communi conceptu obiectiuè præcindit ab inferioribus; non ita hæc ab ente ipso. Eius autem prædicatio non analogicè, sed vniuocè tantùm fit.
units.tr: 2. As to the second: there is precision between being and the inferior things, but not a mutual one. For being, in its common concept, objectively prescinds from the inferiors; they do not prescind from being in the same way. Moreover, its predication is made not analogically but univocally only.

units.la: 3 Quoad ertium: vnitas entis non confistit formaliter in negatione, sed in entitate rei hac tali, quæ dici etiam solet ecceitas, & indiuiduatio: per quam res omnis ab alia distinguitur, cum tamen hæc ipsa ex natura rei, à re, seu essentia non distinguatur.
units.tr: 3. As to the third: the unity of being consists formally not in negation but in the entity of this particular thing, which is also commonly called haecceity and individuation, and through which every thing is distinguished from another. Yet this itself is not distinguished from the thing or its essence by the nature of the thing.

units.la: 4 Postremo diuidi potest ens in absolutum, & relatiuum: in substantiam, & accidens: in reale, atq; rationis. Absolutum est id, cuius esse non est se habere ad aliud: e contra relatiuum: & hoc refertur à se ipso transcendaliter; vel ab intellectu prædicamen taliter: unde relatio prædicamentalis non est quid in re à fundamento distinctum. Ens verò substantiale dicitur quod per se subsistit: Accidentale, quod alteri adiacet. Reale tandem illud, quod in se veritatem physicam: Rationis, quòd esse tantùm obiectiuè in intellectu habet. Hoc autem cum sit ens fictum, nequit fieri per cognitionem veram. Hinc neque Angeli, neque Deus illud facere possunt, &c.
units.tr: 4. Finally, being can be divided into absolute and relative; into substance and accident; into real and of reason. The absolute is that whose being is not a relation to another; the relative is the opposite. The relative is referred to from itself transcendentally, or by the intellect predicamentally; hence predicamental relation is not something in the thing distinct from its foundation. Substantial being is said to be what subsists through itself; accidental being, what inheres in another. Real being is that which has physical truth in itself; being of reason is that which has being only objectively in the intellect. But since this is fictitious being, it cannot be produced by true knowledge. Hence neither angels nor God can make it, etc.

units.la: FINIS
units.tr: END
